ADDENDUM

Pages 847-847

The following was omitted among the preparations of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>. g. Carbonas Ferri præcipitatus, E. Precipitated carbonate of iron. Prepared by decomposing a solution of sulphate of iron by a solution of carbonate of soda; washing and drying the precipitate. Similar in its virtues to 961. Dose five to 30 grains. The space allotted to this article was so small, and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> for preparing it so short, that it is, of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>, much less full and complete than it might otherwise have been. As it was impossible, under such circumstances, to produce any thing like an original and complete treatise, the compiler has endeavoured to render as useful as possible the selection that he found it necessary to make, and to supply the unavoidable deficiencies by a reference to the most respectable works on the subject.

ANIMAL MAGNETISM

Pages 418-421

Animal Magnetism, a sympathy supposed by some persons to exist between the magnet and the human body: by means of which the former, it was thought, possessed the property of curing many diseases. The notion of animal magnetism appears to have originated in 1774, with a German philosopher named Father Hehl, who greatly recommended the use of the magnet in medicine. M. Mesmer, a physician of the same country, by adopting the principles of Hehl, became the direct founder of the system; but afterwards deviating from the tenets of his instructor, he lost his patronage, as well as that of Dr Ingenhousz, which he had formerly enjoyed. Mesmer had already distinguished himself by "A dissertation on the influence of the Stars upon the human body," which he publicly defended in a thesis before the university of Vienna; but he

CUPRUM

Pages 845-845

E. L. D. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">Copper</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, p. 674. SUBACETAS CUPRI. SUBACETIS CUPRI, E. ÆRUGO. Subacetate of copper. Verdigris. See Chemistry, No 1995. Employed chiefly as an escharotic, to destroy callos edges <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fungous <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, or as a stimulant to foul ulcers. Officinal Preparations. a. ÆRUGO PRÆPARATA, L. D. Prepared verdigris. Prepared like other substances not soluble in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. b. OXYMEL ÆRUGINIS, L. Oxymel of verdigris. Prepared by dissolving one ounce of prepared verdigris in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> ounces of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, straining through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> with 14 ounces of clarified <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a> to a proper consistence. Sometimes used as a detergent gargle to venereal ulcerations of the mouth and tonsils, but with much precaution. More generally employed, mixed with some stimulant ointment, as an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> stimulant and escharotic. c. UNGUENTUM SUBACETITIS CUPRI, E. Ointment of subacetite of copper. Prepared by mixing 15 parts of resinous ointment, and one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of subacetite of copper. d. LIQUOR CUPRI AMONNIATI, D. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AQUA">AQUA</a> CUPRI AMONNIATI, L. AQUA SAPPHARINA. Water of ammoniated copper. Sapphire water. Prepared by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, by mixing four grains of prepared verdigris, and two scruples of sal ammoniac, with eight ounces of fresh made lime water, digesting for 24 hours, and pouring off the clear liquor. Used as a stimulant and detergent <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOTION">lotion</a>.

DRARGYRUS MURIATUS

Pages 840-841

L. Muriate of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>. Corrosive muriated mercury. Corrosive sublimated muriate. See <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, No 1736. Prepared by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> two pounds of purified quicksilver in two pounds and a half of sulphuric acid, in a glass vessel, over a sand bath, to dryness, triturating the dried <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> when <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> with four pounds of dried muriate of soda, then subliming in a glass <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CUCURBIT">cucurbit</a> with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> gradually increased, and separating the sublimed <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> from the scoriae. Used as a sialagogue; dose one-eighth to one-fourth of a grain; as an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> stimulus <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> escharotic to venereal ulcers, chancre, and herpetic eruptions, in the proportion of about a grain or more to the ounce of liquid. d. Submuriatas hydrargyri, E. Hydrargyrum muriatum mite sublimatum, D. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALOMEL">Calomel</a>, L. Submuriate of mercury. Sublimed mild muriate of mercury. Calomel. See Chemistry, No 1742, where the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> is much the same as that of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>. Given in most <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> where mercury is indicated. Dose, as a diaphoretic or alterative, about a grain; as a cathartic or anthelmintic, three to 10 grains; as a sialagogue, one or two grains twice a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. e. Submuriatas hydrargyri precipitatus, E. Precipitated hydrargyrum muriatum mite precipitatum, D. Hydrargyrum muriatus mite, L. Precipitated submuriate of mercury. Precipitated mild muriate of mercury. Procured by adding to a solution of half a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> of purified quicksilver in the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of diluted nitrous acid, a solution of four pounds and a half of muriate of soda in eight pounds of boiling <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; washing and drying the precipitate. Much the same in its effects and doses as the foregoing. f. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CALX">Calx</a> hydrargyri <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBA">alba</a>, L. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">White</a> calx of mercury. White precipitate. Prepared by dissolving first half a pound of sal ammoniac, and then half a pound of muriated mercury, in distilled water, adding to the mixed solution half a pound of water of prepared kali, filtering and washing and drying the precipitate. See Duncan's Dispensatory. g. Unguentum calcis hydrargyri albae, L. Ointment of white calx of mercury. Ointment of white calx of mercury. Prepared by mixing a dram of the foregoing with an ounce and a half of ointment of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HOG">hog</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-LARD">lard</a>. Used to destroy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VERMIN">vermin</a>, and in some cutaneous eruptions. h. Oxidum hydrargyri cinereum, E. Pulcinereus vis hydrargyri cinereus, D. Cinereous oxide of mercury. Prepared by dissolving four parts of purified quicksilver in five parts of diluted nitrous acid; then gradually adding 15 parts of distilled water, and pouring in a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of water of carbonate of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMMONIA">ammonia</a> to precipitate the whole of the oxide, which is to be washed and dried. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">Part</a> IV.

LET US NOW SUPPOSE ANY NUMBER OF GEOMETRICAL

Pages 80-80

t us now suppose any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of geometrical means to be interposed between each two adjoining terms of the preceding geometrical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a>, and the same number of arithmetical means between every two adjoining terms of the arithmetical series; then, as the results <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> still be a geometrical and an arithmetical series, the interpolated terms of the latter will be the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOGARITHMS">logarithms</a> of the corresponding terms of the former, and the two new series will have the very same properties as the original series. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> we suppose the number of interpolated means to be very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, it will follow that among the terms of the resulting geometrical series, some one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other will be found nearly equal to any proposed number whatever. Therefore, although the preceding <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> exhibits the logarithms of 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, &c., but does not contain the logarithms of the intermediate numbers, 3, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10, &c. yet it is easy to conceive that a table might be formed by interpolation which should contain, among the terms of the geometrical series, all numbers whatever to a certain <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, (or at least others very nearly equal to them) together with their logarithms. If such a table were constructed, or at least if such terms of the geometrical progression were found together with their logarithms, as were either accurately equal to, or coincided nearly, with all num-

LILLO

Pages 34-34

GEORGE, an excellent dramatic writer, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in 1693. He was a jeweller by profession, and followed his business for many years in that neighbourhood with the fairest reputation. He was at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> strongly attached to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">muses</a>, yet seemed to have laid it <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> as a maxim, that the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> paid to them ought always to tend to the promotion of virtue, morality, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. In pursuance of this aim, Lilly was happy in the choice of his subjects, and showed <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> power of affecting the heart, by working up the passions to such a height as to render the distresses of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> equally interesting to the audiences as that of kings and heroes, and the ruin brought on private families by an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a> of avarice, lust, &c. as the havoc made in states and empires by ambition, cruelty, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> tyranny. His "George Barnwell," "Fatal Curiosity," and "Arden of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEVERSHAM">Feversham</a>," are all planned on common and well known stories; yet they have perhaps more frequently drawn tears from an audience than the more pompous tragedies of Alexander the Great, All for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">Love</a>, &c. In the prologue to "Elmeric," which was not acted till after the author's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, it is said, that when he wrote that play, he "was depressed by want," and afflicted by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>; but in the former particular there appears to be evidently a mistake, as he died possessed of an estate of 60l. a-year, besides other effects to a considerable value. His death happened in 1739, in the 47th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. His works have been collected, and published, with an account of his life, in 2 vols 12mo.

LILLY

Pages 34-35

JOHN, a dramatic poet, was born in the Wealds of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, about the year 1553, and educated in Magdalen <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, where he took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of bachelor of arts in 1573, and that of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> in 1575. From Oxford he removed to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>; but how <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> there is uncertain. On his arrival in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, he became acquainted with some of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>'s courtiers, by whom he was caressed, and admired as a poet and a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>; and her majesty, on particular festivals, honoured his dramatic pieces with her presence. His plays are <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>. His first publication, however, printed in 1580, was a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROMANCE">romance</a> called Euphues, which was universally read and admired. This romance, which Blount, the editor of six of his plays, says introduced a new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, especially among the ladies, is, according to Berkenhout, in fact a most contemptible piece of affectation and nonsense: nevertheless it seems very certain, that it was in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> estimation by the women of fashion of those times, who, we are told by Whalley, the editor of Ben Johnson's works, had all the phrases by heart: and those who did not speak Euphues were as little regarded at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they could not speak French. "He was (says Oldys) a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a>, good <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>, ready <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of application, and uncommon eloquence; but he ran into a vast excess of allusion." When <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> where he died is not known. Anthony Wood says he was living in 1597, when his last <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a> was published. After attending the court of Queen Elizabeth 13 years, notwithstanding his reputation as an author, he was under the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of petitioning the queen for some small stipend to support him in his old <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. His two letters or petitions to her majesty on this subject are preserved in manuscript.

LILY

Pages 35-35

William, a noted English astrologer, born in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEICESTERSHIRE">Leicestershire</a> in 1602; where his father not being able to give him more learning than <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a>, he resolved to seek his fortune in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. He arrived in 1629, and lived four years as a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> to a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANTUA">mantua</a>-maker in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of St Clements Danes; but then moved a step higher to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of Mr Wright, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the Salters <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> in the Strand, who not being able to write, Lilly among other offices kept his books. In 1627, when his master died, he paid his addresses to the widow, whom he married with a fortune of 1000l. Being now his own master, he followed the puritanical preachers; and, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> his mind to judicial astrology, became pupil to one Evans, a profligate Welsh parson, in that pretended art. Getting a MS. of the Ars Notitia of Corn. Agrippa, with alterations, he drank in the doctrine of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGIC">magic</a> circle, and the invocation of spirits, with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> eagerness. He was the author of the Merlinus Anglicus junior; The Supernatural Sight; and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">White</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a>'s Prophecy. In him we have an instance of the general <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> that prevailed in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the civil <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. and his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>: for the king consulted this astrologer to know in what <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> he should conceal himself, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he could escape from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAMPTON">Hampton</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>; and General Fairfax, on the other side, sent for him to his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, to ask him if he could tell by his art, whether God was with them and their cause? Lilly, who made his fortune by favourable predictions to both parties, assured the general that God would be with him and his army. In 1648, he published his Treatise of the Three Suns seen the preceding winter; and also an astrological judgment upon a conjunction of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>. This year the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of state gave him in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> 50l. and a pension of 100l. per annum, which he received for two years, and then resigned on some disgust. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1660, he was taken into custody by order of the parliament, by whom he was examined concerning the person who cut off the head of King Charles I. The same year he sued out his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> under the great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> of England. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a> raging in London, he removed with his family to his estate at Hersham; and in October 1666 was examined before a committee of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of commons concerning the fire of London, which happened in September that year. After his retirement to Hersham, he applied himself to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of physic, and, by means of his friend Mr Ashmole, obtained from Archbishop Sheldon a license for the practice of it. A little before his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> he adopted for his son, by the name of Merlin junior, one Henry Coley, a taylor by trade; and at the same time gave him the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALMANACK">almanack</a>, after it had been printed for 36 years. He died in 1681 of a dead palsy. Mr Ashmole set a monument over his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Walton upon <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>. His "Observations on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a> and Death of Charles, late king of England," if we overlook the astrological nonsense, may be read with as much satisfaction as more celebrated histories; Lilly being not only very well informed, but strictly impartial. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, with the Lives of Lilly and Ashmole, written by themselves, were published in one vol. 8vo, in 1774, by Mr Burman. LILY. See LILIUM, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Lily of the Valley. See Convallaria, Botany Index. LILYBÆUM, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, situated on the most westerly promontory of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Sicily, and said to have been founded by the Carthaginians on their expulsion from Motya by Dionysius, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRACUSE">Syracuse</a>. It is remarkable for three sieges it sustained; one against Dionysius the tyrant, another against Pyrrhus, king of Epirus, and the third against the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. The two first failed in their attempts, but the Romans with great difficulty made themselves masters of it. No remains of this once stately city are now to be seen, except some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AQUEDUCTS">aqueducts</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>; though it was standing in Strabo's time. LILYÉ, WILLIAM, the grammarian, was born in the year 1466 at Oldham in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAMPSHIRE">Hampshire</a>; and in 1486 was admitted a semi-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMONER">commoner</a> of Magdalen <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. Having taken the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of bachelor of arts, he left the university, and travelled to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>. Returning from thence, he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> five years in the island of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RHODES">Rhodes</a>, where he studied the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, several learned men having retired thither after the taking of Constantinople. From Rhodes he travelled to Rome; where he improved himself in the Greek and Latin languages, under Sulpitius and P. Sabinus. He then returned to London, where for some time he taught a private <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>-school, being the first person who taught Greek in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>. In 1510, when Dr Colet founded St Paul's school, Lilyé was appointed the first master; at which time, it seems, he was married and had many children. In this employment he had laboured 12 years, when, being seized by the plague, which then raged in London, he died in February 1523, and was buried in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> yard of St Paul's. He had the character of an excellent grammarian, and a successful teacher of the learned languages. His <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> work is Brevissima institutio seu ratio grammaticae cognoscendi; Lond. 1513. Reprinted times without <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called Lilyé's grammar. The English <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> were written by Dr Colet, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> of St Paul's; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> to the first edition, by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Wolsey. The English <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNTAX">syntax</a> was written by Lilyé; also the rules for the genders of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-NOUNS">nouns</a>, beginning with propria qua maribus: and those for the preterperfect tenses and supines, beginning with As in presenti. The Latin syntax was chiefly the work of Erasmus. See <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARD">Ward</a>'s preface to his edition of Lilyé's grammar, 1732.

LIMA

Pages 35-37

the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>, contains 229 squares of buildings, which comprise 8222 doors of dwelling houses and shops, and these are branched out into 355 streets. In order to maintain peace and tranquility among Lima among the inhabitants, and for the accommodation of the <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol18.html#article-POLICE">police</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> is divided into four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>, containing 35 districts, over each of which there presides an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALCAID">alcaid</a>, who is always elected from among the people of the most distinguished <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a>, according to estimate made at different periods, is as follows: | Year | Population | |------|------------| | 1600 | 14,262 | | 1614 | 25,435 | | 1700 | 37,259 | | 1746 | 60,000 | | 1755 | 54,000 | | 1781 | 60,000 | | 1790 | 52,627 | By this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> it appears, that from 1746 to 1755, the population suffered a diminution of 6000, which was owing to an earthquake that happened at the former <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>—a calamity with which that city is often visited. Were it not for this circumstance, Lima would be a perfect paradise, as the adjacent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> abounds with corn, wine, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>. Such abundance of wealth do the inhabitants enjoy, that when the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Palata was sent from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> as viceroy to Peru, they paved the streets through which he was to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> with ingots of silver. Libertinism and debauchery are the distinguishing characteristics of the people of Lima, for which even the nuns are as notorious as the rest of the females, seldom being free from venereal complaints. In the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1543, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. established an audience at Lima, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which the inhabitants were freed from the painful <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of seeking a redress of their grievances at so <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> a distance as <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PANAMA">Panama</a>. Among the excellent institutions by which the Peruvian <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> is distinguished, we may rank the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> councils, which shew the constant zeal of the sovereigns of Spain for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> and preservation of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>. The prelates, by their pastoral vigilance, spare neither pains nor labour to promote their views, to accomplish their sacred and interesting purposes. By a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> of the Spanish emperor, which reached Lima in 1553, a university was begun in a central spot of the capital, called the university of St Mark, which is now in a most flourishing condition. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DON">Don</a> Francisco <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOLEDO">Toledo</a> assigned 20,312 piastras as a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FUND">fund</a> for the maintenance of the professors, arising from the tributes paid by the Indians. Two lectures are given daily on <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>, one on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, three on <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, three on <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, three on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, two on canons, and two on medicine. In the year 1790 an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a> was erected for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the anatomical students. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> orphans was founded by Mateo Pastor de Valesco, not at the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which often gives to charitable endowments an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> of suspicion, but when he was in the full possession of perfect <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>. In 1597 a pious <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> founded a charitable <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> for the support of such helpless children as were laid <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in the streets by their unfeeling parents. This <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> was destroyed by the earthquake of 1687, which laid in ruins the greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the city. It was afterwards rebuilt, and is at present in a flourishing condition. In 1559 an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> was erected for the relief of the unfortunate sick, who might otherwise have perished for want of medical aid, and obtained the name of the Fellowship of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARITY">Charity</a> and Compassion. A general hospital for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> was begun about 1758, but not completed till 1770, which in 1790 afforded a comfortable <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a> to 29 poor people. The asylum for penitent females was founded in 1669. It has been said that there is not a city in the world in which so many alms are distributed as in Lima. In the centre of the great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> there is a fountain of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRONZE">bronze</a>, the ornaments of which are conformable to the rules of the Composite order. It has an elevation of 15½ yards to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HELMET">helmet</a> of Fame, from which deducting 1½ yards for the height of that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, the remainder gives the part to which the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> rises in order to diffuse itself. This production of art, combining magnificence in every part of it with fine architectural <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, is surrounded by 24 pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>, and 16 <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> chains, a narrow space being left for access to the inhabitants. Coffee-houses were not known in Lima till the year 1771, when one was opened in the street of Santo Domingo, and another the year following. A third was established in 1775, a fourth in 1782, and a fifth in 1788, in each of which there is a billiard table for the amusement of the inhabitants. We are sorry to say that the barbarous practice of cock-fighting obtains in Lima, for which purpose a building was erected in the year 1762. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENNIS">tennis</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> is open to the public, and affords the spectator an agreeable hour of relaxation from more serious pursuits. Lima is situated in W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 76. 44. S. Lat. 12. 1. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIMASSOL">Limassol</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Limissos, a town of Cyprus, in the south of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. Of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> city nothing but ruins now remain; though it was a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, even under the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the dukes. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Richard, the conqueror of the last of these vassals of the empire, razed it in 1191, and it was never afterwards rebuilt. This city originally was the same as Amathus, or Amathonte; so famous, as Pausanias tells us, for its temple erected in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Venus and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADONIS">Adonis</a>. Amathus was the residence of the first <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> kings of the island; and, amongst others of Onelistas, who was subjected afterwards by the arms of Artabanes, the Persian general. This city, erected into an archbishopric in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, has produced a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of personages celebrated for their knowledge and the sanctity of their lives. In the neighbourhood there are several <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, which the Turks have been forced to abandon. The following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, in the tenth book of Ovid's Metamorphoses, prove that they were known in the time of that poet: Capta viri forma, non jam Cytherea curat Littora, non alto repetit Paphon aquore cinctam, Piscosamque Gnidon, gravidamque Amathunta metallis. The place where the new Limassol now stands, formerly had the name of Nemosia, from the multitude of woods by which it was surrounded. Richard, king of England, having destroyed Amathonte, Guy de Lusignan, in the 12th century, laid the foundation of that new city which the Greeks called Neopoleos. The family of Lusignan, who <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to embellish and fortify it, built there palaces, and Greek and Latin churches; and made it the seat of a bishop. When Limassol the island was taken by the Turks in 1570, the Ottoman <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> entered this city on the 2d of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, and ravaged it without mercy. It was then destroyed by the flames; and at present it is only a wretched place, in which one can scarcely distinguish any remains of its ancient edifices. It is governed by a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMISSARY">commissary</a> and a cadi: the latter judges <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> only provisionally, before they are carried to the superior tribunal of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NICOSIA">Nicosia</a>. The harbour is very commodious: and being sheltered from impetuous winds, it affords a safe and calm asylum to vessels when overtaken by a storm. The carob tree is here more abundant than anywhere else; and it is from the port of Limassol that the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of its fruit is exported. The inhabitants export also <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, procured from a lake near <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SALINES">Salines</a>. Cotton, wheat, barley, and mulberry trees, are both plentiful and well cultivated in this part of the island: the ground also produces all kinds of garden stuffs. The best Cyprus wine is made from the vines that grow on the hills of Limassol. All the wines of the country are collected in this city to be transported to Larnac, where there are the largest cellars, and which on that account becomes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> centre of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>.

LIMAX

Pages 37-37

the Slug, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Naked Snail; a genus of animals belonging to the class vermes. See <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELMINTHOLOGY">Helminthology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

LIMB

Pages 37-38

in general, denotes the border <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> edge of a thing; thus we say, the limb of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRANT">quadrant</a>, of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, of a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>, &c. Limb, in Anatomy, an appellation given to the extremities of the body, as to the arms and legs. Limb, Limbus, in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Rome, is used in two different senses. 1. The limb of the patriarchs is said to be the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the patriarchs waited the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDEMPTION">redemption</a> of mankind: in this place they suppose our Saviour's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> to his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a>. 2. The limb of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a> dying without <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>, is a place supposed to be distinct both from heaven and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELL">hell</a>; since, say they, children dying innocent of any actual sin, do not deserve hell; and, by reason of their original sin, cannot be admitted into heaven. Limbat, the name of a periodical <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Cyprus, and of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> in moderating the heats of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, which would otherwise be intolerable. According to the abbé Mariti, it begins to blow at eight in the morning the first <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>; increases as the sun advances till noon; then gradually weakens, and at three falls entirely. On the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> day it arises at the same <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>; but it does not attain its greatest strength till about one in the afternoon, and ceases at four precisely. On the third day it begins as before; but it falls an hour later. On the five succeeding days, it follows the same progression as on the third; but it is remarked, that a little before it ceases, it becomes extremely violent. At the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of five days it commences a new <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> like the former. By narrowly observing the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> on that side from which it is about to blow, a little before it arises, one may determine what <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of strength it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have during the day. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the horizon is clear, and entirely free from <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>, the wind will be weak, and even almost insensible; but if it is dark and cloudy, the wind will be strong and violent. This limbat wind, notwithstanding its utility in moderating the excessive <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, often becomes the cause of fevers, especially to Europeans, from their being less habituated to the climate, and more apt than the natives to suffer themselves to be surprised by the cool <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> when in a state of perspiration. This wind, the falling of which happens an hour sooner or later, is succeeded by a calm, accompanied by a certain moisture that renders the air somewhat heavy. This moisture disappears in the evening, being dissipated by a wind which arises every day at that period. This wind is considered as a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> breeze by the inhabitants of the southern and eastern parts of the island; but it is called a sea breeze by those in the northern and western, who indeed receive it immediately from the sea. In <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> it blows till four o'clock in the morning, and when it ceases, it leaves a profound calm, which continues till the hour when the limbat commences. In autumn and winter it never falls till daybreak, when it is succeeded by other winds, which proceed from the irregularity of the season. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> it does not continue longer than midnight; and is then succeeded by that happy calm, during which those refreshing dews are formed that moisten the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> at sunrise. The limbat winds, which arise in the beginning of summer, cease about the middle of September; and this is the period when the most insupportable heats commence, because their violence is not moderated by the smallest breeze. They are, however, luckily not of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>; and about the latter end of October they decrease sensibly, as the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> begins to be loaded with watery clouds. Limborch, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a>, a learned writer among the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REMONSTRANTS">remonstrants</a>, born at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> in 1633. After having made great proficiency in his studies, he was, in 1655, admitted to preach in public, which he did first at Haerlem. His sermons had in them no affected eloquence; but were <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a>, methodical, and edifying. He was chosen minister of Goudja; from whence he was called to Amsterdam, where he had the professorship of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, in which he acquitted himself with great reputation till his death, which happened in 1712. He had an admirable genius, and a tenacious <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>. He had many friends of distinction in foreign parts as well as in his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Some of his letters to Mr Locke are printed with those of that celebrated author. He had all the qualifications suitable to the character of a sincere divine, lived an example of every virtue, and preserved the vigour of his body and mind to a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. He wrote many works, which are esteemed; the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of which are, 1. Amica collatio de veritate religiosis Christiana cum credito Judaeo, in 12mo. 2. A Complete Body of Divinity, according to the opinions and doctrines of the Remonstrants. 3. A <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">Inquisition</a>; which has been translated into English by Dr Samuel Chandler. Limborch also published the works of the famous Episcopius, who was his great-uncle by the mother's side. Limburgh <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">Duchy</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the Austrian <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, bounded by the duchy of Juliers on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> and east, by Luxemburgh on the south, and by the bishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIEGE">Liege</a> on the west. It is about 30 miles in length, and 25 in breadth; and consists of good arable and pasture land, with plenty of wood, and some <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>. Limburgh, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the duchy of Limburgh, Limburgh burgh, in the Austrian Netherlands, is seated on a steep rock near the river Vesse. This town is small, but pleasantly seated on a hill, with shady woods; and consists chiefly of one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> street, not very well built. It is strong by situation, and almost inaccessible; however, it was taken by the French in 1675, and by the confederates under the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARLBOROUGH">Marlborough</a> in 1703, for the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, to whom it remains by the treaties of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RASTADT">Rastadt</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BADEN">Baden</a>, after having been dismantled. It is famous for its cheese, which is exceeding good. E. Long. 6. 8. N. Lat. 50. 40.

LIMERICK

Pages 38-39
or Lough-Meath, a market town, a borough, and a bishop's see, now the metropolis of the province of Munster. It is situated on the river Shannon, 94 miles from Dublin; and was the strongest fortress in the kingdom. Its ancient name was Lounaneah; and during the first ages it was much frequented by foreign merchants, and after the arrival of the Danes was a place of considerable commerce until the 12th century. It was plundered by Mahon, brother of Brien Boromh, after the battle of Sulchoid, in 970; and Brien, in a future period, exacted from the Danes of this city 365 tons of wine as a tribute, which shows the extensive traffic carried on by those people in that article. About the middle of the 6th century, St Muachin erected a church and founded a bishopric here; which, however, was destroyed by the Danes on their taking possession of this port in 853, and remained in ruins until their conversion to the Christian faith in the 10th century; at which period the church of St Munchin was rebuilt, and the bishopric established. Donald O'Brien, about the time of the arrival of the Limerick English, founded and endowed the cathedral; and Domnat O'Brien, bishop of Limerick, in the 13th century, contributed much to the opulence of the see. About the close of the 12th century, the bishopric of Inniscathay was united to that of Limerick. It was besieged by King William III. in the year 1690, and though there was no army to assist it, the king was obliged to raise the siege. In the year 1691, it was again besieged by the English and Dutch on the 21st of September; and it was obliged to surrender on the 13th of October following, not without the loss of abundance of men; however, the garrison had very honourable and advantageous conditions, and the Roman Catholics by these articles were to be tolerated in the free exercise of their religion. Within a century this place was reckoned the second city in Ireland: at present it has lost its rank; not because it thrives less, but because Cork thrives more. It is composed of the Irish and English town; the latter stands on the King's island, formed by the river Shannon. The town is three miles in circumference, having weekly markets on Wednesday and Saturday, and fairs on Easter Tuesday, 1st July, 4th August, and 12th December. There is a privilege annexed to the fair held on 4th August, that, during 15 days, no person can be arrested in the city or liberties, on any process issuing out of the tholsel court of Limerick. Ardclert and Achadoch, in the county of Kerry, are united to the bishopric of Limerick. This city formerly returned two members to parliament; and now sends one to the British parliament. It gives title of viscount to the family of Hamilton. It is governed by a mayor, sheriffs, recorder, aldermen, and burgesses; there is also a barrack and a military governor and town major: it had some time the privilege of coinage; and different parliaments have been held there. The town was formerly entirely walled in; and in 1760, there were 17 of the city gates standing; but to the great improvement of the place they are now all demolished, except the water-gate of King John's castle. The linen, woollen, and paper manufactures, are carried on here to great extent, and the export of provisions is very considerable. Here are many charitable hospitals, and handsome public buildings, besides the cathedral and other churches. A charter was granted to this city by King John, and confirmed in succeeding reigns. Dr Campbell observes, that as you approach Limerick, the grounds grow rich and exquisitely beautiful; the only disagreeable matter is, that the situation renders the air moist, and consequently rather unwholesome to strangers. About six miles from this is the famous Castleconnell spa. Limerick is 50 miles from Cork, 50 from Galway, and 73 from Waterford. It appears that Limerick obtained the privilege of having mayors 10 years before that right was allowed to the citizens of London. It was before governed by provosts, of which the first was John Spallard in 1195 and 1197; during the provostship of Henry Troy a charter was granted, 9 Richard I. whereby the citizens were allowed to choose mayors and bailiffs, Adam Servant, in 1198, being the first mayor. It continued to be governed by mayors and bailiffs, until the office of bailiff was changed into that of sheriff in 1609. LIMBERICK is also the name of a fair-town in the county of Wexford and province of Leinster; the fairs are four in the year.

LIMIT

Pages 39-39

in a restrained <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, is used by mathematicians for a determined <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> to which a variable one continually approaches; in which sense, the circle may be said to be the limit of its circumscribed and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> polygons. In <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALGEBRA">Algebra</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> limit is applied to two quantities, one of which is greater and the other less than another quantity; and in this sense it is used in speaking of the limits of equations, whereby their solution is much facilitated.

LIMITED PROBLEM

Pages 39-39

denotes a problem that has but one solution, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> some determinate <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of solutions; as to describe a circle through three given <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> that do not <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> line, which is limited to one solution only; to divide a parallelogram into two equal parts by a line <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to one side, which admits of two solutions, according as the line is parallel to the length or breadth of the parallelogram; or to divide a triangle in any ratio by a line parallel to one side, which is limited to three solutions, as the line may be parallel to any of the three sides.

LIMME

Pages 39-39

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, in England, near Hithe, and four miles from Romney, was formerly a port, till choked up by the sands; and though it is thereby become a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> town, yet it has the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">horn</a> and mace and other tokens left of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>, and used to be the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> warden of the cinque ports was sworn at his entrance upon his office. The Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, called Stane-street, ended here; and from the brow of its hill may be seen the ruinous Roman walls almost at the bottom of the marshes. Here formerly was a castle, now converted into a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARM">farm</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. When <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> by whom this edifice was erected is not known. It has, however, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> marks of antiquity; as has also the adjoining <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, on which are several old tombstones with crosses on them.

LIMOGES

Pages 39-39

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town of France, in the late <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Guienne, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the department of Upper <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIENNE">Vienne</a>, with a bishop's see. It is a trading <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and its horses are in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> esteem. It is seated on the river Vienne, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 20. N. Lat. 45° 50'.

LIMOSIN

Pages 39-39

a late <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of France, now the department of Upper <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIENNE">Vienne</a>, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by La Marche, on the east by Auvergne, on the south by Quercy, and on the west by Perigord and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGOUMOIS">Angoumois</a>. One <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> is very <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, but the other more temperate. It is covered with forests of chestnut trees; and contains <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, tin, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>; but the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> trade consists in cattle and horses.

LIMPURG

Pages 39-39

a town of Germany, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELECTORATE">electorate</a> of Triers <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Trevcs, and in Wetteravia, formerly free and imperial, but now subject to the electorate of Trevcs. It is seated on the river Lhon. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8° 13'. N. Lat. 50° 18'.

LINACRE

Pages 39-40

Thomas, physician, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a> about the year 1460, and there educated under the learned William Selling: thence he removed to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, and in 1484 was chosen fellow of All-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">Soul</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>. Tilly, alias Selling, his former instructor, being at this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> appointed <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Henry VII. to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Rome, Mr Linacre accompanied him to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, where he attained the highest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of perfection in the Greek and Latin languages. At Rome, he applied himself particularly to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> and Galen, in the original. On his return to Oxford, he was incorporated <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of physic, and chosen public professor in that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a>. But he had not been <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> in England, before he was commanded to court by King Henry VII. to attend the young <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTHUR">Arthur</a> as his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> and physician. He was afterwards appointed physician to the king, and after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, to his successor Henry VIII. Dr Linacre founded two medical lectures at Oxford, and one at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>; but that which most effectually immortalized his name among the faculty, is his being the first founder of the college of physicians in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. He beheld with vexation the wretched state of physic in those times; and, Linacre by an application to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Wolsey, obtained a patent in 1518, by which the physicians of London were incorporated. The intention of this corporation was to prevent illiterate and ignorant mediciners from practising the art of healing. Dr Linacre was the first <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>, and held the office as long as he lived. Their meetings were in his own <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIGHT">Knight</a>-rider street, which house he bequeathed to the college. But our doctor, when he was about the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 50, took it into his head to study <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>; entered into orders; and was collated, in 1509, to the rectory of Mersham. In the same year he was installed prebendary of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">Wells</a>, in 1518 prebendary of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, and in the following year was admitted precentor of that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>. This, we are told, he resigned for other preferments. He died of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> in the bladder in October 1524, aged 64; and was buried in St Paul's. Thirty-three years after his death, Doctor John <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIUS">Caius</a> caused a monument to be erected to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>, with a Latin inscription, which contains the outlines of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and character. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> sagacity, a skilful physician, a profound grammarian, and one of the best Greek and Latin scholars of his time. Erasmus in his epistles speaks highly of the Doctor's translations from Galen, preferring them even to the original Greek. His works are, 1. De emendata structura Latinae sermonis, libri <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a>; London, printed by Pynson, 1524, 8vo, and by Stephens, 1527, 1532. 2. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDIMENTS">Rudiments</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the princess <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, printed by Pynson. Buchanan translated it into Latin; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, 1536. He likewise translated into very elegant Latin several of Galen's works, which were printed chiefly abroad at different times. Also Procli Diadachi sphera, translated from the Greek; Venet. 1499, 1500. LINARIA. See Fringilla, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

LINCOLN

Pages 40-42

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of England, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of the same name, is distant 132 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It stands on the side of a hill; at the bottom of which runs the river Witham in three small channels, over which are several bridges. The old Lindum of the Britons, which stood on the top of the hill, as appears from the vestiges of a rampart, and deep ditches still remaining, was taken and demolished by the Saxons; who built a town upon the south side of the hill <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the river side, which was several times taken by the Danes, and as often retaken by the Saxons. In Edward the Confessor's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, it appears, from Doomsday book, to have been a very considerable <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; and in the time of the Normans, Malmesbury says, it was one of the most populous cities in England. William I. built a castle upon the summit of the hill above the town. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a>, though the bishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELY">Ely</a> was taken out of it by Henry II. and those of Peterborough and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> by Henry VIII. is still vastly <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, containing the counties of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEICESTER">Leicester</a>, Huntingdon, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEDFORD">Bedford</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUCKS">Bucks</a>, making 1255 parishes. Though the other churches are <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINSTER">minster</a> is a most magnificent piece of Gothic <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>. Here is a prodigious large <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELL">bell</a>, called Tom of Lincoln, which is near five ton in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, and 23 feet in compass. The hill on which the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> stands is so <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and the church itself so lofty, that it may be seen 50 miles to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> and 30 to the south. Besides other tombs, it contains one of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, in which are the entrails of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> Eleanor, wife to Edward I. It is said there were anciently 52 churches, which are now reduced to 14. Such is the magnificence and elevation of the cathedral, that the monks thought the sight of it must be very mortifying to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a>; whence it came to be said of one who was displeased, that he looked like the devil over Lincoln. The declivity on which the city is built being steep, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> betwixt the upper and lower town is very troublesome, and coaches and horses are obliged to make a compass. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Edward III. made this city a staple for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, &c. It was once burnt; once besieged by King Stephen, who was here defeated and taken prisoner; and once taken by Henry III. from his rebellious barons. It abounded heretofore with monasteries and other <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> houses. There is a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> pool here, formed by the river on the west side of it, called Swan Pool, because of the multitude of swans on it. The Roman north gate still remains entire, by the name of Newport Gate. It is one of the noblest of this sort in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. It is a vast <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEMICIRCLE">semicircle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> of very large dimensions laid without <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>, connected only by their uniform shape. This magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> is 16 feet in diameter, the stones are four feet thick at the bottom. It seems to have a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> in the middle, not a keystone; and on both sides, towards the upper part, are laid <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> stones of great dimensions, some 10 or 12 feet <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>. This arch arises from an impost of large <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOULDINGS">mouldings</a>, which are not perceivable now; there are also <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> fragments of the old Roman wall. Over against the castle is an intrenchment <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> up by King Stephen; and here are carved the arms of John of Gaunt <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANCASTER">Lancaster</a>, who lived here like a king, and had a mint. The city has a communication with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a>, by a canal called the Foss-dyke. In the centre of the old ruined castle there is a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> structure for holding the assizes. Its walls are almost entire, and very substantial: the keep or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> tower is situated on a high and very steep mount, which yet continues in its original state; but the remains of the tower on it are only five or six yards high. The outer walls of the castle are of very considerable height, which appear still higher than they really are from their lofty situation and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOAT">moat</a> below them. The great gateway is still entire. This city is a county of itself, and has a viscountial jurisdiction, for 20 miles round, which is a privilege that no other city in England can equal. It now consists principally of one street above two miles long, well paved, besides several <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> streets well peopled. Here are some very handsome modern buildings, but more antique ones; upon the whole, it has an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> greatness, arising in a great <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of monastic remains, most of which are now converted into stables, out-houses, &c. Upon the hill, in the castle, are the ruins of the bishop's <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, and other ruins of ancient <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> and magnificence. The city is supplied with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> by several conduits, among which is a modern one, somewhat in the pyramidal style, enriched with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>. It is governed by a mayor, twelve aldermen, two sheriffs, a recorder, four chamberlains, a swordbearer, four coroners, and above forty <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> men. Here are four <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, where 120 <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> children are taught by the. the widows of clergymen. The neighbouring course is noted for its frequent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-races. On the down of Lincoln, towards <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOSTON">Boston</a>, that rare fowl the bustard is sometimes seen, as well as on <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALISBURY">Salisbury</a> plain. Lincoln-Heath extends above 50 miles, viz. from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLEAFORD">Sleaford</a> and Aneaster south to the Humber north, though it is but three or four miles over where broadest. Five miles from Boston, on this extensive heath, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> le Despenser built a tower for the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of strangers. It is a lofty <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> with a staircase, terminating in a flat <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a>; and round the base is a square <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>-yard. Great part of this extensive heath has been enclosed. We read that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a> king of Scots met King John here, on the 22d of November, in the third year of his reign, and performed homage to him on a hill without the city, for his English territories, in presence of the archbishops of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAGUSA">Ragusa</a>, 13 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, and a vast number of temporal lords and knights. King Henry VII. kept his court here at Easter in 1486. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of Lincoln in 1811 was 8861. The Jews were once its <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> inhabitants, till they were forced to remove, after having impiously crucified the child of one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANTHAM">Grantham</a>, and thrown it into a well, to this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> called Grantham's Well. Lincoln has given the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> to the family of Clinton ever since the reign of Queen <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>. W. Long. 35. N. Lat. 53° 16'. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> county of England, 77 miles in length and 48 in breadth, is bounded on the east by the German ocean, on the west by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NOTTINGHAMSHIRE">Nottinghamshire</a>, on the north by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, on the south by Rutlandshire, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHAMPTONSHIRE">Northamptonshire</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGESHIRE">Cambridgeshire</a>. It contains 631 parishes, and 31 market <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, and returns 12 members to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. The principal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are the Humber, the Trent, the Witham, the Nene, the Welland, the Ankham, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUN">Dun</a>. It is divided into three parts, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LINDSEY">Lindsey</a>, Kesteven, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>; the air of which last is unwholesome and foggy, on account of the fens and large marshes. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> of the north and west parts is very fertile, and abounds in corn and pastures. The east and south parts are not so proper for corn; but then they supply them with fish and fowl, in great plenty, particularly ducks and geese. Lincoln is the principal town. By inland <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, this county has communication with the rivers <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERSEY">Mersey</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEE">Dee</a>, Ribble, Ouse, Darwent, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, Avon, &c.; which navigation, including its windings, extends above 500 miles through different counties. This county, in 1811, contained 46,368 houses; and the total number of inhabitants amounted to 237,891. Lindefarn, or Landisfarn. See Holy-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">Island</a>. Lindsey, Sir David, a celebrated Scots poet, was descended of an ancient family, and born in the reign of King James IV. at his father's seat, called the Mount, near Cupar, in Fife-shire. He was educated at the university of St Andrew's; and, after making the tour of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, returned to Scotland in the year 1514. Soon after his arrival, he was appointed <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>-of-the-bedchamber to the king, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> to the young <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, afterwards James V. From the verses prefixed to his dream, we learn that he enjoyed several other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> employments at court: but, in 1533, he was deprived of all his places, except that of Lyon king at arms, which he held to the time of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. His disgrace was most probably owing to his invectives against the clergy, which are frequent in all his writings. After the decease of King James V. Sir David became a favourite of the earl of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARRAN">Arran</a>, regent of Scotland; but the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAISLEY">Paisley</a> did not suffer him to continue long in favour with the earl. He then retired to his paternal estate, and spent the remainder of his days in rural tranquillity. He died in the year 1553. His poetical talents, considering the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> in which he wrote, were not contemptible; but he treats the Romish clergy with great severity, and writes with some humour: but whatever merit might be formerly attributed to him, he takes such licentious liberties with words, stretching or carving them for measure or <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RHYME">rhyme</a>, that the Scots have a proverb, when they hear an unusual <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, that, There is nae sic a word in a' Davie Lindsay. Mackenzie tells us, that his comedies were so facetious, that they afforded abundance of mirth. Some fragments of these comedies are still preserved in manuscript. He is said to have also written several tragedies, and to have first introduced dramatic <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> into Scotland.
