One of his comedies was played in 1515. Mackenzie says, he understood nothing of the rules of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>. He was <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with John Heywood, the first English dramatic poet. His poems are printed in one small volume; and fragments of his plays, in manuscript, are in Mr William Carmichael's collection. Lindsey, the third and largest <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the county of Lincolnshire in England. On the east and north it is washed by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, into which it runs out with a large <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a>; on the west it has Yorkshire and Nottinghamshire, from which it is parted by the rivers Trent and Dun; on the south it has Kesteven, from which it is separated by the river Witham and the Foss-dyke, which is <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> miles long, and was cut by Henry I. between the Witham and the Trent, for the convenience of carriage in those parts. It had its name from Lincoln, the capital of the county, which stands in it, and by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> called Lindum, by the Britons Lindcolne, by the Saxons Lindo-colype, probably from its situation on a hill, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> or woods that were anciently thereabouts; but the Normans called it Nichol. It gives title of earl and marquis to the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCASTER">Ancaster</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINDUS">Lindus</a>, in Ancient <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RHODES">Rhodes</a>, situated on a hill on the west side of the island. It was built by Tlepolemus the son of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, according to Diodorus Siculus; by one of the Heliades, grandsons of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">Sun</a>, named Lindus, according to Strabo. It was the native place of Cleobulus, one of the wise men. Here we see the famous temple of the Lindian <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>, which was built by the daughters of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DANAUS">Danaus</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CADMUS">Cadmus</a> enriched this temple with many splendid offerings. The citizens dedicated and hung up here the seventh of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PINDAR">Pindar</a>'s Olympic odes, written in letters of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>. The ruins of that superb edifice are still to be seen on the top of a high hill which overlooks the sea. Some remains of the walls, consisting of stones of an enormous size, still show it to have been built in the Egyptian style. The pillars and other ornaments have been carried off. On the most elevated peak of the rock are the ruins of a castle, which may have served as a fortress to the city. Its circumference is very extensive, and is filled with rubbish. Lindo, the modern city, stands at the foot of the hill. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of considerable wideness and depth serves as a harbour to the city. Ships find good anchorage there in 20 fathoms water. They are safely sheltered from the south-west winds, which constantly prevail through the severest season of the year. In the beginning of winter, they cast <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a> off a small village named Massary. Before the building of Rhodes, Lindus was the harbour which received the fleets of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRE">Tyre</a>. It was enriched by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>. Mr Savary observes, that a judicious <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, by taking advantage of its harbour and happy situation, might yet restore it to a flourishing state.

LINE

Pages 42-43

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> extended in length only, without any breadth <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> thickness. It is formed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUX">flux</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of a point. See <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUXIONS">Fluxions</a>, and Geometry. **Line**, in the art of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, is understood of the disposition of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> ranged in order of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, with the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> extended as far as may be, that it may not be flanked. **Line of Battle**, is also understood of the disposition of a fleet in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of engagement; on which occasion the vessels are usually drawn up as much as possible in a straight line, as well to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> and keep the advantage of the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> as to run the same board. See Naval <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TACTICS">Tactics</a>. **<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">Horizontal</a> Line**, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, a line drawn <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the horizon of any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. **Equinoctial Line**, in Geography, is a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> circle on the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-EARTH_S">earth's</a> surface, exactly at the distance of 90° from each of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>, and of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> bisecting the earth in that part. From this imaginary line, the degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> and latitude are counted.—In astronomy, the equinoctial line is that circle which the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> seems to describe round the earth on the days of the equinox in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> and September. See Astronomy and Geography. **Meridian Line**, is an imaginary circle drawn through the two poles of the earth and any part of its surface. See Geography <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. **Ship of the Line**, a vessel <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> enough to be drawn up in the line, and to have a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in a seafight. **Line**, in Genealogy, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> or succession of relations in various degrees, all descending from the same <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> father. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">Descent</a>. **Line**, also denotes a French <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> containing the 12th part of an inch, or the 144th part of a foot. Geometricians conceive the line subdivided into six <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a>. The French line answers to the English barleycorn. **<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">Fishing</a> Line**. See Fishing Line. **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">Lines</a>**, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, the figures used in armories to divide the shield into different parts, and to compose different figures. These lines, according to their different forms and names, give denomination to the pieces or figures which they form, except the straight or plain lines. See Heraldry. **Linea <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBA">alba</a>**, in Anatomy, the concourse of the tendons of the oblique and transverse muscles of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a>; dividing the abdomen in two, in the middle. It is called linea, line, as being straight; and alba, from its <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, which is <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>.—The linea alba receives a twig of a nerve from the intercostals in each of its digitation or indentings, which are visible to the eye, in lean persons especially. **Lineament**, among painters, is used for the outlines of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a>. **Linear numbers**, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">Mathematics</a>, such as have relation to length only; such is a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> which represents one side of a plain <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the plain figure be a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, the linear figure is called a root. **Linear Problem**; that which may be solved geometrically by the intersection of two <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> lines. This is called a simple problem, and is capable but of one solution. **Linens**, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, a well known kind of cloth, chiefly made of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>.—Linens was not worn by the Jews, Greeks, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, as any part of their ordinary dress. Under-tunics of a finer texture supplied the place of shirts: Hence the occasion for frequent <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATHING">bathing</a>. Alexander Severus was the first <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> who wore a shirt: but the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of so necessary a garment did not become common till <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> after him. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> manufacture was probably introduced into <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> with the first settlement of the Romans. The flax was certainly first planted by that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> in the British <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>. The plant itself indeed appears to have been originally a native of the east. The woollen-drapery would naturally be <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> in its origin to the linen; and the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FIBROUS">fibrous</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> from which the threads of the latter are produced, seem to have been first noticed and worked by the inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>. In Egypt, indeed, the linen manufacture appears to have been very early: for even in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> it had risen to a considerable height. From the Egyptians the knowledge of it proceeded probably to the Greeks, and from them to the Romans. Even at this day the flax is imported among us from the eastern nations; the western kind being merely a degenerate <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of it. In order to succeed in the linen manufacture, one set of people should be confined to the ploughing and preparing the soil, sowing and covering the seed, to the weeding, pulling, rippling, and taking care of the new seed, and watering and dressing the flax till it is lodged at home: others should be concerned in the drying, breaking, scutching, and heckling the flax, to fit it for the spinners; and others in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a> and reeling it, to fit it for the weaver: others should be concerned in taking due care of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEAVING">weaving</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLEACHING">bleaching</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a>, and finishing the cloth for the market. It is reasonable to believe, that if these several branches of the manufacture were carried on by distinct dealers in Scotland and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, where our home-made linens are manufactured, the several parts would be better executed, and the whole would be afforded cheaper, and with greater profit. **Staining of Linen**. Linen receives a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> colour with much more difficulty than woollen or cotton. The black struck on linen with common vitriol and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALLS">galls</a>, or logwood, is very perishable, and soon washes out.—Instead of the vitriol, a solution of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> in sour strong beer is to be made use of. This is well known to all the calico-printers; and by the use of this, which they call their iron-liquor, and madder root, are the blacks and purples made which we see on the common printed linens. The method of making this iron liquor is as follows: A quantity of iron is put into the sour strong beer; and, to promote the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of the metal, the whole is occasionally well stirred, the liquor occasionally drawn off, and the rest <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> from the iron, after which the liquor is poured on again. A length of time is required to make the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPREGNATION">impregnation</a> perfect; the solution being reckoned unfit for use till it has stood at least a twelves <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a>. This solution stains the linen of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, and different shades of buff-colour; and is the only known substance by which these colours can be fixed in linen. The cloth stained deep with the iron-liquor, and afterwards boiled with madder, without any other addition, becomes of the dark colour which we see on printed linens and cottons; which, if not a perfect black, has a very near resemblance to it. Others are stained paler with the same liquor diluted with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and come out purple. Linens may also be stained of a durable purple by means of solution of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AQUA">aqua</a> regia. The solution for this purpose should be as fully saturated as possible; it should be diluted with three times its quantity of water; and if the colour is required deep, the piece, when dry, must be repeatedly moistened with it. The colour does not take place till a considerable time, sometimes several days, after the liquor has been applied: to hasten its appearance, the subject should be exposed to the sun and free <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, and occasionally removed to a moist place, or moistened with water.—When solution of gold in aqua regia is soaked up in linen cloths, the metal may be recovered by drying and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> them. Linens flowered with <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GOLD_LEAF">Gold-<a c</a>lass="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>. Dr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> mentions a manufacture established in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> for embellishing linen with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> and ornaments of gold-leaf. The linen, he says, looks whiter than most of the printed linens; the gold is extremely beautiful, and bears washing well. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> informs us, that he had seen a piece which he was credibly informed had been washed three or four times, with only the same precautions which are used for the finer printed linens; and on which the gold <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> entire, and of great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. Concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> used in this manufacture, he gives us no particulars. Fossil Linen, is a kind of amianthus, which consists of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a>, parallel, soft fibres, and which has been celebrated for the use to which it has been applied, of being woven, and forming an incumbrable cloth. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">Paper</a> also, and wicks for lamps, have been made of it. See Amianthus, Asbestos, and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a> Index.

LING

Pages 43-49

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of fish belonging to the genus Gadus, which see in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINGEN">Lingen</a>, a strong town of Germany, in the circle of Westphalia, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of the same name. It belongs to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>; and is situated on the river Embs, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7° 30' N. Lat. 52° 32'. Liniment, in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of a consistence somewhat thinner than an unguent, and thicker than an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a> Index. Linlithgow, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town of West <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOTHIAN">Lothian</a> in Scotland. It is supposed to be the Lindum of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>; and to take its name from its situation on a lake, which the word Lin <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Lyn signifies.—It is distant 16 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, and is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> borough and seat of a presbytery. Here is carried on a considerable trade in dressing of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, which is sent abroad to be manufactured; and many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> are employed in dressing of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>; also in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>-combing, the wool for which is brought from the borders. Its port, was formerly Blackness; but since the decline of that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BORROWSTOUNNESS">Borrowstounness</a>, about two miles distant from Linlithgow. The town consists of one open street, from whence lanes are detached on both sides; the houses are built of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, tolerably neat and commodious; and the place is adorned with some stately public edifices. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, built, as Sibbald supposed, on the seat of a Roman station, forms a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> with towers at the corners, and stands on a gentle eminence, with the beautiful loch behind it to the west. It was one of the noblest of the royal residences; and was greatly ornamented by James V. and VI. Within the palace is a handsome square; one side of which is more <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> than the others, having been built by James VI. and kept in good repair till 1746, when it was accidentally damaged by the king's forces making fires on the hearths, by which means the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOISTS">joists</a> were burnt. A stone ornamented fountain in the middle of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> was destroyed at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. The other sides of the square are more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>. In one is a room ninety-five feet long, thirty feet six inches wide, and thirty-three <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. At one end is a gallery with three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>, perhaps for music. Narrow galleries run quite round the old <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, to preserve <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with the rooms; in one of which the unfortunate <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> Stuart first <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. On the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side of the high street, on an eminence east of the palace, stands St Michael's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; a handsome structure, where James V. intended to have erected a throne and twelve stalls for the sovereign and knights of the order of St Andrew. In the market-place is another fountain, and surmounted like the former with an imperial <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. In one of the streets is shown the gallery where the regent Murray was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a>. Here was a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Carmelites, founded by the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> people in 1292, destroyed by the Reformers 1559. The family of Livingston, who took the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> from this place, were <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> keepers of the palace, as also bailiffs of the king's bailiary, and constables of Blackness castle; but by their concern in the rebellion of 1715 all these honours with their estate were forfeited to the crown. Sir James Livingston, son of the first earl by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> with a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Callendar, was created earl of Callendar by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. 1641, which title sunk into the other. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">Population</a>, in 1811, 4022. Linlithgowshire, or West Lothian, nearly approaches in form to a parallelogram, about 20 miles long from east to west, and from 10 to 13 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, from north to south. It is bounded by the river Forth on the north; by the river Almond on the southeast; by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LANARKSHIRE">Lanarkshire</a> on the south-west, and by the river Avon on the west. It is allowed to be one of the richest counties in Scotland, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> in general being a rich loam, in a high state of cultivation and improvement. Its surface is diversified by gentle swells and fertile plains; and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of elegant seats almost everywhere to be met with, gives it both a rich and delightful appearance. The whole is a composition of all that is <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> and beautiful; towns, villages, seats, and ancient towers, decorate each <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of that fine expanse of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, the firth of Forth. The lofty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> Linnæus, Sir Charles, a celebrated botanist and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> historian, was born on May 24, 1707, in a village called Roeshult in Smaland, where his father, Nicholas Linnæus, was then <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a>, but afterwards preferred to the curacy of Stenbrohult. We are told, that on the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARM">farm</a> where Linnæus was born, there yet stands a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> lime tree, from which his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> took the surnames of Tiliander, Lindelius, and Linnæus; and that this origin of surnames, taken from natural objects, is not uncommon in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>. This eminent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, whose talents enabled him to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REFORM">reform</a> the whole science of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY">natural <a clas</a>s="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, accumulated, very early in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, some of the highest honours that await the most successful proficients in medical science; since we find that he was made professor of physic and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, in the university of Upsal, at the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 34; and six years afterwards, physician to Adolphus king of Sweden; who in the year 1753 honoured him still farther, by creating him <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> of the order of the Polar <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAR">Star</a>. His honours did not terminate here: for Linnæus, in 1757 he was ennobled; and in 1776 the king of Sweden accepted the resignation of his office, and rewarded his declining years by doubling his pension, and by a liberal donation of landed <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> settled on him and his family. It seems probable, that Linnæus's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> was caught from the example of his father; who, as he has himself informed us, cultivated, as his first amusement, a garden plentifully stored with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. Young Linnæus soon became acquainted with these, as well as with the indigenous ones of his neighbourhood. Yet, from the straitness of his father's income, our young naturalist was on the point of being destined to a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> employment; fortunately, however, this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> was overruled. In 1717 he was sent to school at Wexsio; where, as his opportunities were enlarged, his progress in all his favourite pursuits was proportionally extended. At this early <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> he paid <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to other branches of natural history, particularly to the knowledge of insects. The first part of his academical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> Linnæus received under Professor Stobæus, at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUND">Lund</a>, in Scania, who favoured his inclinations to the study of natural history. After a residence of about a year, he removed in 1728 to Upsal. Here he soon contracted a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> friendship with Artedi, a native of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Angermania, who had already been four years a student in that university, and, like himself, had a strong bent to the study of natural history in general, but particularly to ichthyology. Soon after his residence at Upsal, our author was also happy enough to obtain the favour of several gentlemen of established character in literature. He was in a particular manner encouraged in the pursuit of his studies by the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> of Dr Olaus Celsius, at that time professor of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, and the restorer of natural history in Sweden; who, being struck with the diligence of Linnæus in describing the plants of the Upsal garden, and his extensive knowledge of their names, not only patronized him in a general way, but admitted him to his house, his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, and his library. Under such encouragement it is not strange that our author made a rapid progress, both in his studies and the esteem of the professors: in fact, we have a very striking <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of his merit and attainments; since we find, that, after only two years residence, he was thought sufficiently qualified to give lectures occasionally from the hotanic <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, in the room of Professor Rudbeck. In the year 1731, the Royal Academy of Sciences at Upsal having for some time meditated the design of improving the natural history of Sweden, at the instance particularly of Professors Celsius and Rudbeck, deputed Linnæus to make the tour of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAPLAND">Lapland</a>, with the sole view of exploring the natural history of that arctic region; to which undertaking, his reputation, already high as a naturalist, and the strength of his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, equally recommended him. He left Upsal the 13th of May, and took his route to Govalia or Gevels, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> town of Gestricia, 45 miles distant from Upsal. Hence he travelled through Helsingland into Medalpadia, where he made an excursion, and ascended a remarkable mountain before he reached Hudwickswald, the chief town of Helsingland. From hence he went through Angermanland to Hernosand, Linnaeus, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port on the Bothnian <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a>, 70 miles distant from Hudwickswald. When he had proceeded thus far, he found it proper to retard his journey, as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> was not sufficiently advanced; and took this opportunity of visiting those remarkable caverns on the summit of Mount Skula, though at the hazard of his life. When Linnaeus arrived at Uma, in West Bothnia, about 90 miles from Hernoosand, he quitted the public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, and took his course through the woods westward, in order first to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRAVERSE">traverse</a> the most southern parts of Lapland. Being now come to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> that was more particularly the object of his inquiries, equally a stranger to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> and to the manners of the people, and without any associate, he committed himself to the hospitality of the inhabitants, and never failed to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> it fully. He speaks in several places, with peculiar satisfaction, of the innocence and simplicity of their lives, and their freedom from diseases. In this excursion he reached the mountains towards <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>; and after encountering great hardships, returned into West Bothnia, quite exhausted with fatigue. Our traveller next visited Pitha and Lula, upon the gulf of Bothnia; from which latter place he took again a western route, by proceeding up the river of that name, and visited the ruins of the temple of Jockmook in Lula Lapland or Lap Mark: thence he traversed what is called the Lapland <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESERT">Desert</a>, destitute of all villages, cultivation, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>, or any conveniences; inhabited only by a few straggling people, originally descended from the Finlanders, and who settled in this country in remote ages, being entirely a distinct people from the Laplanders. In this district he ascended a noted mountain called Wallervar; in speaking of which he has given us a pleasant relation of his finding a singular and beautiful new plant (<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANDROMEDA">Andromeda</a> tetragon) when travelling within the arctic circle with the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> in his view at midnight, in search of a Lapland hut. From hence he crossed the Lapland <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a> into Finnmark, and traversed the shores of the North sea as far as Sallero. These journeys from Lula and Pitha on the Bothnian gulf, to the north shore, were made on foot; and our traveller was attended by two Laplanders, one his interpreter, and the other his guide. He tells us that the vigour and strength of these two men, both old, and sufficiently loaded with his baggage, excited his admiration: since they appeared quite unhurt by their labour, while he himself, although young and robust, was frequently quite exhausted. In this journey he was wont to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> under the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> with which they forded the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> against <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, and the gnats, which in the Lapland <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> are not less teasing than in the torrid zones. In descending one of these rivers, he narrowly escaped perishing by the upsetting of the boat, and lost many of the natural productions which he had collected. Linnaeus thus spent the greater part of the summer in examining this arctic region, and those mountains on which, four years afterwards, the French philosophers secured immortal fame to Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton. At length, after having suffered incredible fatigues and hardships, in climbing precipices, passing rivers in miserable boats, suffering repeated vicissitudes of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, and not unfrequently <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a> and thirst, he returned to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TORNEA">Tornea</a> in September. He did not take the same route from Tornea as when he came into Lapland, having determined to visit and examine the country on the eastern side of the Bothnian gulf: his first stage, therefore was to Ula in East Bothnia; from thence to Old and New Carlebay, 84 miles south from Ula. He <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> his route through Wasa, Christianstad, and Bjorneburgh, to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABO">Abo</a>, a small university in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINLAND">Finland</a>. Winter was now setting in apace; he therefore crossed the gulf by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALAND">Aland</a>, and arrived at Upsal in November, after having performed, and that mostly on foot, a journey of ten degrees of latitude in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, exclusively of those deviations which such a design rendered necessary. In 1733 he visited and examined the several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> in Sweden; and made himself so well acquainted with <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERALOGY">mineralogy</a> and the docimastic art, that we find he was sufficiently qualified to give lectures on these subjects upon his return to the university. The outlines of his system on mineralogy appeared in the early editions of the Systema Naturae; but he did not exemplify the whole until the year 1768. In the year 1734 Linnaeus was sent by Baron Ruterholm, governor of Dalecarlia, with several other naturalists in that province, to investigate the natural productions of that part of the Swedish dominions; and it was in this journey that our author first laid the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of an excellent <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>, which was afterwards executed, in a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> at least, by himself, with the assistance of many of his pupils, and the result published under the title of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAN">Pan</a> Succicus, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> volume of the Amaranites Academicae. After the completion of this expedition, it appears that Linnaeus resided for a time at Falun, the principal town in Dalecarlia; where he tells us that he taught mineralogy and the docimastic art, and practised physic; and where he was very hospitably treated by Dr More, the physician of the place. It also appears, that he contracted at this time an intimacy with one of that <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>'s daughters, whom he married about five years afterwards upon his settling as a physician at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STOCKHOLM">Stockholm</a>.—In this journey he extended his travels quite across the Dalecarlian Alps into Norway; but we have no particular account of his discoveries in that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. In 1735 Linnaeus travelled over many other parts of Sweden, some parts of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a> and Germany, and fixed in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, where he chiefly resided until his return to Stockholm, about the year 1739. In 1735, the year in which he took the degree of M.D., he published the first sketch of his Systema Naturae, in a very compendious way, and in the form of tables only, in 12 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAGES">pages</a> in folio. By this it appears that he had at a very early period of his life (certainly before he was 24 years old), laid the basis of that great structure which he afterwards raised, not only to the increase of his own fame, but to that of natural science. In 1736, Linnaeus came into England, and visited Dr Dillenius, the learned professor at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, whom he justly considered as one of the first botanists in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. He mentions with particular respect the civilities he received from him, and the privileges he gave him of inspecting his own and the Sherardian collections of plants. It is needless to say, that he visited Dr Martyn, Mr Rand, and Mr Miller, and Linnaeus, that he was in a more singular manner indebted to the friendship of Dr Isaac Lawson. He also contracted an intimate friendship with Mr <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Collinson, which was reciprocally increased by a multitude of good offices, and continued to the last without any diminution. Dr Boerhaave had furnished him with letters to our great naturalist Sir Hans Sloane; but, it is with regret that we must observe, they did not procure him the reception which the warmth of his recommendation seemed to claim. One of the most agreeable circumstances that happened to Linnaeus during his residence in Holland, arose from the patronage of Mr Clifford, in whose house he lived a considerable part of his time, being now as it were the child of fortune:—Ex vivi patria triginta <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a> nummis aureis dices—are his own words. With Mr Clifford, however, he enjoyed pleasures and privileges scarcely at that time to be met with elsewhere in the world; that of a garden excellently stored with the finest exotics, and a library furnished with almost every botanic author of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a>. How happy he found himself in this situation, those only who have felt the same kind of ardour can conceive. Whilst in Holland, our author was recommended by Boerhaave to fill the place, then vacant, of physician to the Dutch settlement at Surinam; but he declined it on account of his having been educated in so opposite a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>. Besides being favoured with the particular patronage and friendship of Boerhaave and Mr Clifford, as is above mentioned, our author had also the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> of being <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with, and of reckoning among the number of his friends, many other learned persons who have since proved ornaments to their profession, and whose merit has most deservedly raised them to fame and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>. Among these we may properly mention Dr John Burman, professor of botany at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>, whose name and family are well known in the republic of letters, and to whom our author dedicated his Bibliotheca Botanica, having been greatly assisted in compiling that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> by the free access he had to that gentleman's excellent library; John Frederick Gronovius of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, editor of Clayton's Flora Virginica, and who very early adopted Linnaeus's system; Baron Van Swieten, physician to the empress <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>; Isaac Lawson, before mentioned, afterwards one of the physicians to the British <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, who died much regretted at Oosterhout in the year 1747, and from whom Linnaeus received singular and very important civilities; Kramer, since well known for an excellent treatise on the docimastic art; Van Royen, botanic professor at Leyden; Lieberkun of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a>, famous for his skill in microscopical instruments and experiments. To these may be added also the names of Albinius and Gaubius, and of others, were it requisite to show that our author's talents had very early rendered him conspicuous, and gained him the regard of all those who cultivated and patronized any branch of medical science; and to which, doubtless, the singular notice with which Boerhaave honoured him did not a little contribute. Early in the year 1738, after Linnaeus had left Mr Clifford, and, as it should seem, when he resided with Van Royen, he had a long and dangerous fit of sickness; and upon his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> went to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, where he was properly entertained by the Jussieus, at that time the first botanists in France. The opportunity this gave him of inspecting the Herbaria of Royen and Tournefort, and those of the above-named gentlemen, afforded him great satisfaction. He had intended to have gone from thence into Germany, to visit Ludwig and the celebrated Haller, with whom he was in close correspondence; but he was not able to complete this part of his intended route, and was obliged to return without this gratification. Our author did not fail to avail himself of every advantage that access to the several museums of this country afforded him, in every branch of natural history; and the number and importance of his publications, during his absence from his native country, sufficiently demonstrate that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FUND">fund</a> of knowledge which he must have imbibed before, and no less testify his extraordinary application. These were Systema Naturae, Fundamenta Botanica, Bibliotheca Botanica, and Genera Plantarum; the last of which is justly considered as the most valuable of all the works of this celebrated author. What immense application had been bestowed upon it, the reader may easily conceive, on being informed, that before the publication of the first edition the author had examined the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of 8000 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>. The last book of Linnaeus's composition, published during his stay in Holland, was the Classes Plantarum, which is a copious illustration of the second part of the Fundamenta. About the latter end of the year 1738, or the beginning of the next, our author settled as a physician at Stockholm; where he seems to have met with considerable opposition, and was oppressed with many difficulties; but all of these at length he overcame, and got into extensive practice; and soon after his settlement married the lady before spoken of. By the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> Tessin, who was afterwards his great <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a>, and even procured medals to be struck in honour of him, he obtained the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of physician to the fleet, and a stipend from the citizens for giving lectures in botany. And what at this time especially was highly favourable to the advancement of his character and fame, by giving him an opportunity of displaying his abilities, was the establishment of the Royal Academy of Sciences at Stockholm; of which Linnaeus was constituted the first <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>, and to which establishment the king granted several privileges, particularly that of free postage to all papers directed to the secretary. By the rules of the academy, the president held his place but three months. At the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, Linnaeus made his Oratio de memorabilibus in Insectis, Oct. 3, 1739; in which he endeavours to excite an attention and inquiry into the knowledge of insects, by displaying the many singular phenomena that occur in contemplating the nature of those animals, and by pointing out, in a variety of instances, their usefulness to mankind in particular, and to the economy of nature in general. During all this time, however, Linnaeus appears to have had his eye upon the botanic and medical chair at Upsal, at this time occupied by Rudbeck, who was far advanced in life. We learn indeed that he was so intent on pursuing and perfecting his great designs in the advancement of his favourite study of nature, that he had determined, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he failed in procuring the Linnaeus, the professorship at Upsal, to accept the offer that had been made to him by Haller of filling the botanic chair at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOTTINGEN">Gottingen</a>. However, in course of time, he obtained his wish. In the year 1741, upon the resignation of Roberg, he was constituted <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> professor of physic, and physician to the king, with Rosen, who had been appointed in the preceding year on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Rudbeck. These two colleagues agreed to divide the medical departments between them; and their choice was confirmed by the university. Rosen took anatomy, physiology, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATHOLOGY">pathology</a>, and the therapeutic part; Linnaeus, natural history, botany, materia medica, the dietetic part, and the diagnosis morborum. During the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> of his removal from Stockholm to Upsal in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this appointment, our professor was deputed by the states of the kingdom to make a tour to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OELAND">Oeland</a> and Gotland in the Baltic, attended by six of the pupils, commissioned to make such inquiries as might tend to improve <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a> and arts in the kingdom, to which the Swedish <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> had for some time paid a particular attention. The result of this journey was very successful, and proved fully satisfactory to the states, and was afterwards communicated to the public. On his return he entered upon the professorship, and pronounced before the university his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORATION">oration</a> de Peregrinationum intra Patriam necessitate, October 17, 1741; in which he forcibly displays the usefulness of such excursions, by pointing out to the students that vast field of objects which their country held out to their cultivation, whether in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a>, physics, mineralogy, botany, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">zoology</a>, or economics, and by showing the benefit that must accrue to themselves and their country as rewards to their diligence. That animated spirit which runs through the whole of this composition, renders it one of the most pleasing and instructive of all our author's productions. Linnaeus was now fixed in the situation that was the best adapted to his character, his taste, and abilities; and which seems to have been the object of his ambition and centre of his hopes. Soon after his establishment, he laboured to get the academical garden, which had been founded in 1657, put on a better footing, and very soon effected it; procuring also a house to be built for the residence of the professor. The whole had been in ruins ever since the fire in 1702; and at the time Linnaeus was appointed professor of botany, the garden did not contain above fifty plants that were exotic. His correspondence with the first botanists in Europe soon supplied him with great variety. He received <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> plants from Jussieu of Paris, and from Van Royen of Leyden; European plants from Haller and Ludvig; American plants from the late Mr Collinson, Mr Catesby, and others; and variety of annuals from Dillenius: in short, how much the garden owed to his diligence and care in a few years, may be seen by the catalogue published under the title of Hortus Upsaliensis, exhibens Plantas exoticas horto Upsalien- sis Academiae à seculo (Linnaeo) illatas <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">ab</a> anno 1742, in annum 1748, additis differentiis synonymis, habitatio- nibus, hospitiis, variarumque descriptionibus, in gratiam studiosae juventutis; Holm. 1748, 8vo. pp. 306. tab. 3. By this catalogue it appears, that the professor had introduced 1100 species, exclusively of all the Swedish plants and of varieties: which latter, in ordinary gardens, amount not unfrequently to one-third of the whole number. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> contains a curious history of the climate at Upsal, and the progress of the seasons throughout the whole year. From the time that Linnaeus and Rosen were appointed professors at Upsal, it should seem that the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> of that university, as a school of physic, had been increasing: numbers of students resorted thither from Germany, attracted by the character of these two able men; and in Sweden itself many young men were invited to the study of physic by the excellent manner in which it was taught, who otherwise would have engaged in different pursuits. Whilst Linnaeus was meditating one of his capital performances, which had long been expected and greatly wished for, he was interrupted by a tedious and painful fit of the gout, which left him in a very weak and dispirited state; and, according to the intelligence that his friends gave of him, nothing was thought to have contributed more to the restoration of his spirits than the seasonable acquisition, at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNCTURE">juncture</a>, of a collection of rare and undescribed plants. The fame which our author had now acquired by his Systema Naturae, of which a sixth edition, much enlarged, had been published at Stockholm in 1748 in 8vo. pp. 232, with eight tables explanatory of the classes and orders (and which was also republished by Gronovius at Leyden), had brought, as it were, a conflux of every thing rare and valuable in every branch of nature, from all parts of the globe, into Sweden. The king and queen of Sweden had their separate collections of rarities: the former at Ulriksdahl; the latter, very rich in exotic insects and shells, procured at a great expense, at the palace of Drottningholm; both of which our author was employed in arranging and describing. Besides these, the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a> of the Royal Academy of Upsal had been augmented by a considerable donation from the king, whilst hereditary <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, in 1746; by another from Count Gyllenborg the year before; by a third from M. Grill, an opulent citizen of Stockholm. From this time we see the professor in a more elevated rank and situation in life. His reputation had already procured him honours from almost all the royal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> in Europe; and his own sovereign, truly sensible of his merit, and greatly esteeming his character and abilities, favoured him with a mark of his distinction and regard, by creating him a knight of the Polar Star. It was no longer laudatur et alget. His emoluments kept pace with his fame and honours: his practice in his profession became lucrative; and we find him soon after possessed of his country house and gardens at Hammarby, about five miles from Upsal. He had moreover received one of the most flattering testimonies of the extent and magnitude of his fame that perhaps was ever shown to any literary character, the state of the nation which conferred it, with all its circumstances, duly considered. This was an invitation to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MADRID">Madrid</a> from the king of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, there to preside as a naturalist, with the offer of an annual pension for life of 2000 pistoles, letters of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, and the perfect free <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of his own <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>: But, after the most perfect acknowledgments of the singular honour done him, he returned for answer, Linnaeus. 'that if he had any merits, they were due to his own country.' In the year 1755, the Royal Academy of Sciences at Stockholm honoured our professor with one of the first premiums, agreeably to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> of Count Sparree, who had decreed two <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> medals, of ten ducats value each, to be annually given by the academy to the authors of such papers, in the preceding year's Stockholm Acts, as should be adjudged most useful in promoting agriculture particularly, and all branches of rural economy. This medal bore on one side the arms of the count, with this motto, *Superstes in scientiis amor Frederici Sparree.* Linnaeus obtained it in consequence of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> *De Plantis quae Alpium Saecriarum indigenae, magno rei oeconomice et medicinae emolumento fieri possint:* and the ultimate intention was to recommend these plants as adapted to culture in Lapland. This paper was inserted in the Stockholm Acts for 1754, vol. xv. Linnaeus also obtained the *premium centum aureorum,* proposed by the Imperial Academy of Sciences at Petersburgh, for the best paper written to establish or disprove, by new arguments, the doctrine of the sexes of plants. It was, if possible, an additional <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> to Linnaeus to have merited this premium from the Petersburgh academy; inasmuch as a professor of that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, a few years before, had with more than <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> zeal, although with a futility like that of the other antagonists of our author, endeavoured to overturn the whole Linnaean system of botany, by attempting to show that the doctrine of the sexes of plants had no foundation in nature, and was unsupported by facts and experiments. It appears that Linnaeus, upon the whole, enjoyed a good constitution; but that he was sometimes severely afflicted with a *hemiergia,* and was not exempted from the gout. About the close of 1776, he was seized with an apoplexy, which left him paralytic; and at the beginning of the year 1777, he suffered another stroke, which very much impaired his mental powers. But the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> supposed to have been the more immediate cause of his death, was an ulceration of the urinary bladder; of which, after a tedious indisposition, he died, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 11, 1778, in the 71st year of his age. His principal other works, beside those already mentioned, are, *The Iter Oelandicum et Gotlandicum, Iter Scanicum, Flora Suecica, Fauna Suecica, Materia Medica, Philosophia Botanica, Genera Morborum,* different papers in the *Acta Upsaliensia,* and the *Amoenitates Academicae.* The last of this great man's treatises was the *Mantissa Altera,* published in 1771; but before his death he had finished the greatest part of the *Mantissa Tertia,* afterwards completed and published by his son. To the lovers of science it will not appear strange, nor will it be unpleasant to hear, that uncommon respect was shown to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of this great man. We are told, "that on his death a general <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOURNING">mourning</a> took place at Upsal, and that his funeral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a> was attended by the whole university, as well professors as students, and the pall supported by sixteen doctors of physic, all of whom had been his pupils." The king of Sweden, after the death of Linnaeus, ordered a medal to be struck, of which one side exhibits Linnaeus's bust and name, and the other Cybele, in a dejected attitude, holding in her left <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEY">key</a>, and surrounded with animals and growing plants; with this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEGEND">legend</a>, *Linnaeus. Deam luctus angit amissi;* and beneath, *<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">Post</a> Obitum Upsalise, die x. Jan. m.DCC.LXXVIII. Regie jubente.* The same generous monarch not only honoured the Royal Academy of Sciences with his presence when Linnaeus's commemoration was held at Stockholm, but, as a still higher tribute, in his speech from the throne to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of the states, he lamented Sweden's loss by his death. Nor was Linnaeus honoured only in his own country. The late worthy professor of botany at Edinburgh, Dr Hope, not only pronounced an eulogium in honour of him before his students at the opening of his lectures in the spring 1778, but also laid the foundation stone of a monument (which he afterwards erected) to his memory, in the botanic garden there; which, while it perpetuates the name and merits of Linnaeus, will do honour to the founder, and, it may be hoped, prove the means of raising an emulation favourable to that science which this illustrious Swede so highly dignified and improved. As to the private and personal character of this illustrious <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>: His stature was <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a> and puny; his head large, and its hinder part very high; his look was ardent, piercing, and apt to daunt the beholder; his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a> not sensible to music: his temper quick, but easily appeased. Nature had, in an eminent manner, been liberal in the endowments of his mind. He seems to have been possessed of a lively imagination, corrected however by a strong judgment, and guided by the laws of system. Add to these, the most retentive memory, an unremitting industry, and the greatest perseverance in all his pursuits; as is evident from that continued vigour with which he prosecuted the design, that he appears to have formed so early in life, of totally reforming and fabricating anew the whole science of natural history; and this fabric he raised, and gave to it a degree of perfection unknown before; and had moreover the uncommon felicity of living to see his own structure rise above all others, notwithstanding every discouragement its author at first laboured under, and the opposition it afterwards met with. Neither has any writer more cautiously avoided that common <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> his own fame on the ruin of another man's. He everywhere acknowledged the several merits of each author's system; and no man appears to have been more sensible of the partial defects of his own. These anomalies which had principally been the objects of criticism, he well knew every <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> arrangement must abound with; and having laid it <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> as a firm maxim, that every system must finally rest on its intrinsic merit, he willingly commits his own to the judgment of posterity. Perhaps there is no circumstance of Linnaeus's life which shows him in a more dignified light than his conduct towards his opponents. Disavowing controversy, and justly considering it as an unimportant and fruitless sacrifice of time, he never replied to any, numerous as they were at one season. To all who see the aid this extraordinary man has brought to natural science, his talents must appear in a very illustrious point of view; but more especially to those who, from similarity of tastes, are qualified to see more distinctly the vast extent of his original design, the greatness of his labour, and the elaborate execution he has given to the whole. He had a happy command Linnaeus mand of the Latin tongue, which is alone the language of science; and no man ever applied it more successfully to his purposes, or gave to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> such copiousness, united with that precision and conciseness which so eminently characterize his writings. The ardour of Linnaeus's inclinations to the study of nature, from his earliest years, and that uncommon application which he bestowed upon it, gave him a most comprehensive view both of its pleasures and usefulness, at the same time that it opened to him a wide field, hitherto but little cultivated, especially in his own country. Hence he was early led to regret, that the study of natural history, as a public institution, had not made its way into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>; in many of which, logical disputations and metaphysical theories had too long prevailed, to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCLUSION">exclusion</a> of more useful science. Availing himself therefore of the advantages which he derived from a large share of eloquence, and an animated style, he never failed to display, in a lively and convincing manner, the relation this study hath to the public good; to incite the great to countenance and protect it; to encourage and allure youth into its pursuits, by opening its manifold sources of pleasure to their view, and showing them how greatly this agreeable employment would add, in a variety of instances, both to their comfort and emolument. His extensive view of natural history, as connected with almost all the arts of life, did not allow him to confine these motives and incitements to those only who were designed for the practice of physic. He also laboured to inspire the great and opulent with a taste for this study; and wished particularly that such as were devoted to an ecclesiastic life should share a portion of natural science; not only as a means of sweetening their rural situation, confined, as many are, perpetually to a country residence, but as what would almost inevitably <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, in a variety of instances, to discoveries which only such situations could give rise to, and which the learned in great cities could have no opportunities to make. Not to add, that the mutual communication and enlargement of this kind of knowledge among people of equal rank in a country situation, must prove one of the strongest bonds of union and friendship, and contribute, in a much higher degree than the usual perishing amusements of the age, to the pleasures and advantage of society. Linnaeus lived to enjoy the fruit of his own labour in an uncommon degree. Natural history raised itself in Sweden, under his culture, to a state of perfection unknown elsewhere; and was from thence disseminated through all Europe. His pupils dispersed themselves all over the globe; and, with their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>'s fame, extended both science and their own. More than this, he lived to see the sovereigns of Europe establish several public institutions in favour of this study; and even professorships established in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> universities for the same purpose, which do honour to their founders and patrons, and which have excited a curiosity for the science, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of its worth, that cannot fail to further its progress, and in time raise it to that rank which it is entitled to hold among the pursuits of mankind. LINNET. See Fringilla, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> Index.

LINING

Pages 39-39

the art of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> colours, in contradistinction to painting which is done in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>-colours. Limning is much the more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> kind of painting. Till a Flemish painter, one John van Eyck, better known by the name of John of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUGES">Bruges</a>, found out the art of painting in oil, the painters all painted in water and in fresco, both on their walls, on wooden boards, and elsewhere. When they made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of boards, they usually glued a fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> cloth over them, to prevent their opening; then laid on a ground of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>; lastly, they mixed up their colours with water and size, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> with water and yolks of eggs, well beaten with the branches of a fig tree, the juice whereof thus mixed with the eggs; and with this mixture they painted their pieces. In limning, all colours are proper enough, except the white made of lime, which is only used in fresco. The azure and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ULTRAMARINE">ultramarine</a> must always be mixed with size or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUM">gum</a>; but there are always applied two layers of hot size before the size colours are laid on: the colours are all ground in water, each by itself; and, as they are required in working, are diluted with size water. When the piece is finished, they go over it with the white of an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a> well beaten; and then with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VARNISH">varnish</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> required. To limn, or draw a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> in colours: Having all the materials in readiness, lay the prepared <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> on the card even and thin, free from hairs and spots, over the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> is to be. The ground being laid, and the party placed in a due position, begin the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, which is to be done at three sittings. At the first you are only to dead-colour the face, which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> require about two hours. At the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> sitting, go over the work more curiously, adding its particular graces or deformities. At the third sitting, finish the whole; carefully remarking whatever may conduce to render the piece perfect, as the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> of the eyes, moles, scars, gestures, and the like.

LINSEED

Pages 49-49

the seed of the plant linum.—Linseed steeped and bruised in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> gives it very soon a thick mucilaginous <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and communicates much of its emollient virtue to it. See LINUM. LINT. See <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">Flax</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">Linen</a>; and Linum, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Lint, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, is the scrapings of fine linen, used by surgeons in dressing wounds. It is made into various forms, which acquire different names according to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of the figures.—Lint made up in an oval <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> orbicular form is called a pledgit; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> in a cylindrical form, or in shape of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a>, or olive-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, it is called a dassit. These different forms of lint are required for many purposes; as, 1. To stop blood in fresh wounds, by filling them up with dry lint before the application of a bandage: though, if scraped lint be not at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, a piece of fine linen may be torn into small rags, and applied in the same manner. In very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> hemorrhages the lint or rags should be first dipped in some styptic liquor, as <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALCOHOL">alcohol</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of turpentine; or sprinkled with some styptic powder. 2. To agglutinate or heal wounds; to which end lint is very serviceable, if spread with some <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGESTIVE">digestive</a> ointment, balsam, or vulnerary liquor. 3. In drying up wounds and ulcers, and forwarding the formation of a cicatrix. 4. In keeping the lips of wounds at a proper distance, that they may not hastily unite before the bottom is well digested and healed. 5. They are highly necessary to preserve wounds from the injuries of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>.—Surgeons of former ages formed compresses of sponge, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, feathers, or cotton; linen being scarce: but lint is far preferable to all these, and is at present universally used.

LINTERNUM

Pages 49-49
or LITERUM, in Ancient Geography, a city of Campania, situated at the mouth of the Clanius, which is also called Liturnus, between Cumae and Vulturnum. It received a Roman colony at the same time with Puteoli and Vulturnum; was improved and enlarged by Augustus; afterwards forfeited its right of colonyship, and became a prefecture. Hither Scipio Africanus the Elder retired from the mean envy of his ungrateful countrymen; and here he died, and was buried: though this last is uncertain, he having a monument both here and at Rome. No vestige of the place now remains.

LINTSTOCK

Pages 49-49

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> affairs, a wooden <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAFF">staff</a> about three feet <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, having a sharp point in one end and a sort of fork <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> crotch on the other; the latter of which serves to contain a lighted <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MATCH">match</a>, and by the former the lintstock is occasionally stuck in the ground, or in the deck of a ship during an engagement. It is very frequently used in small vessels, where there is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> one fixed between every two guns, by which the match is always kept dry, and ready for firing.

LINTZ

Pages 49-50

a town of Germany, in the circle of the Lower <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELECTORATE">electorate</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOGNE">Cologne</a>, subject to that that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a>. It is seated on the river Rhine, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7. N. Lat. 50. 31.

LINUM

Pages 50-50
Flax; a genus of plants belonging to the pentandria class; and in the natural method ranking under the 14th order, Gruinales. See Botany Index.

LINUS

Pages 50-50

in classical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a native of Colehis, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORPHEUS">Orpheus</a>, and one of the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> poets and musicians of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>. It is impossible, at this distance of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, to discover whether Linus was the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Orpheus, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Orpheus of Linus. The majority, however, seem to decide this question in favour of Linus. According to Archbishop Usher, he flourished about 1286 B.C. and he is mentioned by Eusebius among the poets who wrote before the time of Moses. Diodorus Siculus tells us, from Dionysius of Mitylene the historian, who was contemporary with Cicero, that Linus was the first among the Greeks who invented verses and music, as <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CADMUS">Cadmus</a> first taught them the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of letters. The same writer likewise attributes to him an account of the exploits of the first <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>, and a treatise upon Greek <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a>, written in Pelasgian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, which were also those used by Orpheus, and by Pronapides the preceptor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>. Diodorus says that he added the string lichanos to the Mercurial lyre; and ascribes to him the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RHYME">rhyme</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MELODY">melody</a>; which Suidas, who regards him as the most ancient of lyric poets, confirms. Mr Marpurg tells us, that Linus invented cat-gut strings for the use of the lyre, which, before his time, was only strung with thongs of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, or with different threads of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a> strung together. He is said by many writers to have had several disciples of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> renown; among whom were <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, Thamyris, and, according to some, Orpheus.—Hercules, says Diodorus, in learning from Linus to play upon the lyre, being extremely dull and obstinate, provoked his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> to strike him; which so enraged the young <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a>, that instantly seizing the lyre of the musician, he <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> out his brains with his own <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>.

LIONCELLES

Pages 50-50

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used for several lions borne in the same coat of arms.

LIOTARD

Pages 50-50
