called the Turk, an eminent painter, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a> in 1702, and by his father was designed for a merchant; but, by the persuasion of his friends, who observed the genius of the young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, he was permitted to give himself up to the art of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>. He went to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1725, and in 1738 accompanied the marquis de Puisieux to Rome, who was going <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>. At Rome he was taken notice of by the earls of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SANDWICH">Sandwich</a> and Besborough, then <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Duncaon, who engaged Liotard to go with them on a voyage to Constantinople. There he became acquainted with the late Lord Edgcumbe, and Sir Everard Fawkener, our ambassador, who persuaded him to come to England, where he staid two years. In his journey to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a> he had adopted the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, and wore it here with a very <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARD">beard</a>. It contributed much to the portraits of himself, and some thought to draw customers; but he was really a painter of uncommon merit. After his return to the continent, he married a young wife, and sacrificed his beard to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYMEN">Hymen</a>. He came again to England in 1772, and brought a collection of pictures of different masters, which he sold by auction, and some pieces of glass Liotard painted by himself, with surprising effect of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>, but a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> curiosity, as it was necessary to darken the room before they could be seen to advantage; he affixed, too, as usual, extravagant prices to them. He staid here about two years, as in his former journey. He has engraved some Turkish portraits, one of the empress <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> and the eldest archduchess in Turkish habits, and the heads of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> and empress. He painted admirably well in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINIATURE">miniature</a>; and finally in enamel, though he seldom practised it. But he is best known by his works in crayons. His likenesses were as exact as possible, and too like to please those who sat to him; thus he had <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> business the first year, and very little the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>. Devoid of imagination, and one would think, of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>, he could render nothing but what he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> before his eyes. Freckles, marks of the smallpox, every thing found its <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; not so much from fidelity, as because he could not conceive the absence of any thing that appeared to him. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">Truth</a> prevailed in all his works, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> in very few <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> none. Nor was there any ease in his outline; but the stiffness of a bust in all his portraits. Walpole.

LIPARA

Pages 50-50

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> called Eolii, situated between <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, with a cognominal town, so powerful as to have a fleet, and the other islands in subjection to it. According to Diodorus Siculus, it was famous for excellent harbours and medicinal waters. He informs us also, that it suddenly emerged from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> about the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HANNIBAL">Hannibal</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. The name is Punic, according to Bochart: and given it, because, being a volcano, it shone in the night. It is now called Lipari, and gives name to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> others in its neighbourhood; viz. Stromboli, Pare, Rotto, Panaria, Saline, Voleano, Feneusa, Alicor, and Ustiea. These are called, in general, the <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIPARI_ISLANDS">Lipari Islands</a>. Some of these are <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> volcanoes at present, though Lipari is not. It is about 15 miles in circumference; and abounds in corn, figs and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>, bitumen, sulphur, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, and mineral waters.

LIPARI

Pages 50-53

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and very strong town, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the same name in the Mediterranean, with a bishop's see. It was ruined by Barbarossa in 1544, who carried away all the inhabitants into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>, and demolished the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; but it was rebuilt by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 15. 30. N. Lat. 38. 35. Lipari, properly, is the general name of a cluster of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>. These, according to M. Houel, are principally ten in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, the rest being only uninhabitable rocks of narrow <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>. The largest and the most populous of them, that above mentioned, communicates its name to the rest. Volcano is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> but habitable island, lying south from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> island of Lipari. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SALINES">Salines</a>, which lies west-<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west from the same island; Felicudi, nearly in the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, but 20 miles farther distant; and Alicudi, 10 miles south-west of Felicudi; are inhabited. Panarea is east of Lipari, the famous Stromboli north-east, and both of them are inhabited. The rest are in a desert state; such as Baziluzzo, which was formerly inhabited; Aitalo, which might be inhabited; and L'Exambianca, on which some remains of ancient dwellings are still to be found. L'Escanera is nothing but a bare rock. The Fermicoli, a word signifying ants, are a chain of small <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cliffs which run to the north-east of Lipari, till within a little way of Exambianca and Escanera, rising more <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> less above the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, according as the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> is more or less agitated. Ancient authors are not agreed with respect to the number of the <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIPARI_ISLANDS">Lipari islands</a>. Few of those by whom they are mentioned appear to have seen them; and in places such as these, where subterraneous fires burst open the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and raise the ocean from its <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>, terrible changes must sometimes take place. Volcanello and Volcano were once separated by a strait, so as to form two islands. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAVA">lava</a> and ashes have filled up the intervening strait; and they are now united into one island, and have by this change become much more habitable. The castle of Lipari stands upon a rock on the east <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of the island. The way to it from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> leads up a gentle declivity. There are several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> to it. This castle makes a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the city; and on the summit of the rock is the citadel, in which the governor and the garrison reside. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> stands in the same situation. Here the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, in conformity to their usual practice, had built the temple of a tutelary god. This citadel commands the whole city; and it is accessible only at one place. Were an hostile force to make a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> on the island, the inhabitants might retreat hither, and be secure against all but the attacks of famine. The ancient inhabitants had also fortified this place. Considerable portions of the ancient walls are still standing in different places, particularly towards the south: Their structure is Grecian, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> are exceedingly large, and very well cut. The layers are three feet <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, which shows them to have been raised in some very remote <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>. These remains are surrounded with <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> buildings. The remains of walls which are still to be seen here, have belonged not only to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, but to all the different sorts of buildings which the ancients used to erect. The vaults, which are in a better state of preservation than any of the other parts of these monuments, are now converted to the purpose of a prison. In the city of Lipari there are <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a> of monks of two different orders; but there are no convents for women, that is to say, no cloisters in which women are confined; those, however, whose heads and hearts move them to embrace a state of pious celibacy, are at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to engage in a monastic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, with the concurrence of their confessors. They put on the sacred <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOW">vow</a> perpetual virginity, but continue to live with their father and mother, and mix in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> like other women. The vow and the habit even enlarge their liberty. This <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, no doubt, M. Houel observes, appear very strange to a French woman; but this was the way in which the virgins of the primitive <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> lived. The idea of shutting them up together did not occur till the fifth century. The life of these <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> ladies is less gloomy than that which those under the same vows <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> in other countries. They wear clothes of particular colours, according as they belong to this or that order. Their dress gives them a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to frequent the churches at any hours; and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> of censure, which takes particular <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> in directing her attacks against pious ladies, goes so far as to assert that some young women assume the habit with no other views but that they may enjoy greater freedom. In this island oxen of a remarkably beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> are employed in ploughing the ground. The ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a> is still in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> here. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a> practised here is very expeditious. One <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> traces a furrow, and another follows to sow in it grain and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>. The ploughman, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> the next furrow, covers up that in which the seed has been sown: and thus the field is both ploughed and sown at once. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a> seems to be here uncommonly vigorous and fertile. Vegetation is here more luxuriant, and animals gayer and more healthful, than almost anywhere else. Near the city of Lipari, the traveller enters deep narrow roads, of a very singular appearance. The whole island is nothing but an assemblage of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, all of them consisting of ashes or lava discharged from the depths of the volcano by which it was at first produced. The particles of this puzzolana, or ashes, are not very hard; the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> water has accordingly cut out trenches among the mountains; and these trenches being perhaps less uneven than the rest of the surface, have of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> been used as roads by the inhabitants, and have been rendered much deeper by being worn for so many ages by the feet of men and other animals. These roads are more than five or six fathoms deep, and not more than <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> or eight feet wide. They are very crooked, and have echoes in several places. You would think that you were walking through narrow streets without doors or windows. Their depth and windings shelter the traveller from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> while he is passing through them; and he finds them deliciously cool. The first volcanic eruption in the Lipari islands mentioned in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, is that of which Callias takes notice in his history of the wars in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>. Callias was <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with Agathocles. That eruption <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> without <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> for several days and nights; and threw out <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> stones, which fell at more than a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a>'s distance. The sea boiled all around the island. The works of Callias are lost, and we know not whether he descended to a detail of particulars concerning the ravages produced by this eruption. Under the consulship of Emilius Lepidus and L. Aurelius Orestes, 126 years before the Christian era, these islands were affected with a dreadful earthquake. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> of Aetna was the first cause of that. Around Lipari and the adjacent islands, the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> was all on fire. Vegetation was withered; animals died; and fusible bodies, such as wax and resin, became liquid. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the inhabitants of Lipari, from whom our author received these facts, and the writers who have handed <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> an account of them, have not exaggerated the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, we must believe that the sea then boiled around the island; the earth became so hot as to burn the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CABLES">cables</a> by which vessels were fixed to the shore, and consumed the planks, the oars, and even the small boats. Pliny, the naturalist *, speaks of another similar * Lib. iii. event which happened 30 or 40 years afterwards, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 106. the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> of the allied states of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> against Rome. One of the Æolian islands, says he, was all on fire as well as the sea; and that prodigy continued to appear, till the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> appeased, by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTATION">deputation</a>, the wrath of the gods. From the time of that war, which happened 86 years before the birth of our Saviour, till the year 1444 of our era, we have no account of any eruption of these volcanoes: and from that period again, till the year 1444, we hear of no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPLOSION">explosion</a> from them, that is, for the space of 1300 years. But at that time both Sicily and the Æolian isles were agitated by dreadful shocks of earthquakes: the volcano of those isles poured forth streams of lava with an awful violence, and emitted a volume of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> which rose to an amazing height. After that it discharged enormous stones which fell at the distance of more than six miles. A century later, in the year 1550, the fury of this volcano was again renewed. The ashes and stones discharged from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRATER">crater</a> filled up the strait between Volcano and Volcanello. About two centuries after that, in the year 1739, there was a sixth eruption. The burstings of the volcanic fire were attended with a noise so dreadful, that it was heard as far as Melazzo in Sicily. Father Leandro Alberti says, that on one of those dreadful occasions, the women of Lipari, after imploring in vain all the saints, vowed to drink no more wine if the volcano should spare them. Their giving up this small gratification was doubtless of great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>; yet the eruptions still continue, and have even become more frequent since that time. Only 36 years intervened between this eruption and that which happened in the year 1775. The whole island was then shaken; subterraneous <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> was heard; and considerable streams of flame, with smoke, stones, and vitreous lava, issued from the crater. Lipari was covered over with ashes; and part of these was conveyed by the winds all the way into Sicily. Five years after, however, in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of April 1780, there issued a new explosion from Volcano; the smoke was thick, the shocks constant, and the subterraneous noise very frequent. So great was the consternation among the inhabitants of Lipari on this occasion, that the commander Deodati Dolomieu, who visited these islands not long after that event, informs us, that the inhabitants in general, but especially the women, devoted themselves as slaves to the service of the blessed virgin; and wore on their arms, as tokens of their servitude, small <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> chains, which they still continue to wear. This <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of piety, however, was not so efficacious as the deputation of the senate had been. For after that deputation, more than 200 years passed before the Æolian isles were afflicted by any other eruption, at least by any considerable one: Whereas, in three years after the ladies devoted themselves in so submissive a manner to the service of the virgin, the isles of Lipari were agitated anew by that fatal earthquake which ravaged <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a> and part of Sicily, on the 5th of February 1783. The dry <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a> of St Calogero, in the island of Lipari, are stoves, where sulphureous exhalations, known to be of a salutary nature, ascend out of the earth by holes or spiracles. A range of apartments are built around the place where the exhalations arise. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> is communicated through those apartments, in such a way, that when entering at one end, you advance towards the other, the heat still increases upon you till you <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> the middle apartment, and again diminishes in the same manner as you proceed from the middle to the other end of the range of chambers. In consequence of this disposition of these apartments, the sick person can make choice of that temperature which best suits the nature of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>. There are a few miserable huts and a small chapel for the accommodation of the people who repair to these baths. The people of the place are ready to attend them. Physicians likewise follow their patients thither, when the disease is of such a nature as to render their attendance requisite, and the patient rich enough to afford them handsome fees: but there is no physician settled in the place. Besides these dry baths, there are baths of hot water, distinguished by the name of St Calogero's Baths. There are around them buildings sufficient to lodge a considerable number of sick people with their necessary attendants. At present, however, these buildings are but in a bad condition. The baths consist of two halls; one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, the other round. The former is antique; it has been built by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; it is arched with a cupola, and 12 feet in diameter; it has been repaired: The other is likewise arched with a cupola both within and without. The water comes very hot into the first. It gushes up from among pieces of lava, which compose a part of the mountain at the foot of which these baths are built. Those stones remain in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> state. All that has been done is the raising of a square <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> enclosing them. Within that building the sick persons either sit down on the stones, or immerse themselves in the intervening cavities which are filled with water. They continue there for a certain time, and approach nearer to, or remain at a farther distance from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, according as their physician directs. The place serves also as a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STOVE">stove</a>. The hot vapours arising from the water communicate to the surrounding <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of heat. It is indeed not inferior to that of the hot baths of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TERMINI">Termini</a>, which owe their heat to a similar cause. In these baths, therefore, a person can have the benefit either of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATHING">bathing</a> in the hot water, or of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> himself to the vapour, the heat of which is more moderate. The bath before mentioned, under the appellation of dry bath, is also a stove; but the hot vapour with which it is filled issues directly from the volcano. The place of the bath is, however, at such a distance from the volcanic <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FOCUS">focus</a>, that the heat is not at all intolerable. The mountain at the foot of which these baths are situated is round, and terminates at the summit in a rock of petrified ashes, which are very hard and of a very fine grain. This petrifaction consists of pretty regular <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STRATA">strata</a>, and appears to have been greatly <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> in its origin to the adjacent rocks; which consist likewise of ashes, but ashes that have been deposited at a much later period. From this rock there proceeds likewise a stream of hot water, by which some <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a> in the neighbourhood are moved. It cannot but appear surprising that nature has placed nearly on the summit of a volcanic mountain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> springs which supply so considerable a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of water. To account for such a phenomenon would be well worthy of some ingenious naturalist. Nor are these hot springs all; proceeding around the same hill, at about a mile's distance, we find a spring of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> water rising from the summit of the same rock, which on the north-west produces three hot springs. The cold water is very pleasant to drink, and much used both by men and cattle. Among these mountains there are many enormous loose masses of lava, the appearance of which, M. Houel informs us, naturally leads the observer to take notice, that the lava of the volcano of Lipari is of a much greater diversity of colours, and those richer and more lively, than the lava of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VESUVIUS">Vesuvius</a> and Ætna. The lava of Lipari is in some places, for several miles, of a beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. It contains likewise in great abundance small black crystallized scoriae, as well as the small <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> grains which are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> found in lava. Among the eminences which overlook the city of Lipari, there are some rocks of a species which is very rare in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. These are large masses of vitrified <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, which rise six or eight feet above the surface of the ground, and appear to extend to a great depth under it. They exist, through that range of mountains, in enormous masses, mixed with lavas of every different colour, and always standing detached and insulated. Were they cut and followed under ground, they would probably be found to exist in immense quarries in the bowels of the earth. The glass of which they consist might be employed with great advantage in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>. It is ready made, and might be easily purified. It is green, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a>, and transparent. The cultivation of the ground is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> employment of the inhabitants of Lipari. The possession of a few acres of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> here gives a man great importance. Parents, when they <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> their children, rather give them <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> than any part of their lands. More than two-thirds of the island are planted with vines: three-fourths of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a> which these produce are dried, and sent mostly to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> under the name of passola. There are different sorts of passola: one of these, called the black passolina, is prepared from a particular kind of grape, of which the berries are uncommonly small; and sold to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARSEILLES">Marseilles</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRIESTE">Trieste</a>. The vines are in small arbours, which rise only to the height of two feet and a half above the ground. Under these arbours there grow beans, gourds, and other <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEGUMINOUS">leguminous</a> vegetables. In so hot a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> of the vines does not injure but protect the vegetables growing under it: they would otherwise be withered by the heat of the sun. The method of preparing passola and passolina is curious enough: They first make a lixivium of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> ashes; after <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> this, they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> it through a cloth or a sieve; they then put it again on the fire; and when it is observed to boil hard, suddenly immerse the grapes, but instantly bring them out again, and expose them to the sun to dry on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> frames of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANE">cane</a>. When sufficiently dry, the raisins are put into casks and barrels to be sold and exported. The number of casks of different sorts of raisins annually exported from Lipari is estimated at 10,000. This island likewise produces figs. There is some white malmsey and a little red wine exported from it. About 60 or 80 years since, sulphur was one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> with which the inhabitants of this island supplied foreign <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>. But that trade has been given up, from an idea which the Liparese entertain, that sulphur infects the air so as to injure the fertility of the vines. The same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> prevails in Sicily, but it seems to be ill founded. There are courts of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> in Lipari of the same powers and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> with those in the cities of Sicily. Causes of more than ordinary importance are carried to Palermo. The island is entirely free from every kind of imposition. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> receives nothing from it; because <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> Roger anciently bestowed on its bishop all his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of royalty over Lipari. The bishop there received annually from the inhabitants a tenth part of the products of their lands. They afterwards, to prevent fraud, estimated the value of that tithe for one year; and on the condition of their paying in future a sum of money equal to what that year's tithe was valued at, he not only gave up his right to the tithe, but also ceded to them a considerable extent of land which belonged to him. In the archiepiscopal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, and in the palace of the Baron de Monizzio, there are some noble pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> by Sicilian painters:—A St <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>, a St Rosalia, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> disputing with the Jewish doctors, the adulterous woman, the incredulity of St Thomas.

LIPI

Pages 53-54

LORENZO, a painter of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and portraits, was born in 1606, and learned the principles of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> from Matteo Roselli. He had an exquisite genius for music and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, as well as for painting, and in the latter his proficiency was so <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, that some of his compositions in the historical style were taken for those of Roselli. However, growing at last dissatisfied with the manner of that <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, he chose the manner of Santi di Titi, who was excellent both in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>, and appeared to have more of simple <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> in his compositions than any other <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. At <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a> Lippi painted many <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> designs for the chapels and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>, by which he enlarged his reputation; and at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Innspruck, he painted a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of portraits of the first <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>. LIS bility, which were deservedly admired. Yet, although he was fond of imitating simple nature without any embellishments from invention, his works are held in the highest esteem for the graceful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRS">airs</a> of the heads, for the correctness of his outline, and for the elegant disposition of the figures. He died in 1664.

LIPIUS

Pages 54-54

Justus, a learned critic, was born at Isch, a small village near <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUSSELS">Brussels</a>, in 1547. After having distinguished himself in polite literature, he became secretary to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> de Granvellan at Rome, where the best <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a> were open to him; and he spent much labour in collating the MSS. of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> authors. He lived 13 years at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>; during which he composed and published what he esteems his best works; but settled at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUVAIN">Louvain</a>, where he taught polite literature with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation. He was remarkable for steadfastness in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, fluctuating often between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> and Papists; but he became finally a bigotted catholic. He died at Louvain in 1606; and his works are collected in six volumes folio.

LIPOTHYMIUM

Pages 53-53

Fainting, may arise from several causes; as too violent <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>, suppression of the menses <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other accustomed evacuations, &c. See MEDICINE <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

LIPPA

Pages 53-53

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, with a castle. It was taken by the Turks in 1552; by the Imperialists in 1688; and by the Turks again in 1691; who abandoned it in 1695, after having demolished the fortifications. It is seated on a mountain, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 21° 55', N. Lat. 36° 5'.

LIPPE

Pages 53-53

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of the same name in Germany, and the circle of Westphalia. It is seated on a river of the same name, and was formerly the residence of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> branch of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Lippe. It is now in the possession of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, and carries on a good trade in preparing <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> vessels on the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, with which it has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> by the river Lippe. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> round it is unwholesome and marshy. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8° 12'. N. Lat. 51° 43'.

LIQUEFACTION

Pages 54-54

an operation by which a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> body is reduced into a liquid by the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>. See Fluidity, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

LIQUID

Pages 54-54

among grammarians, is a name applied to certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSONANTS">consonants</a> opposed to mutes. Thus l, m, n, and r, are liquids.

LIQUIDAMBAR

Pages 54-54

Sweet-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUM">gum</a>-tree, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the monœcia class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking with those of which the order is doubtful. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

LIQUOR

Pages 54-54

a name for any fluid substance of the aqueous <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> spirituous kind. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEVERAGE">beverage</a> amongst the Jews, as well as the Greeks and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, in their early state, was <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, and the juices of various <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> infused therein. For a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, under the commonwealth of Rome, wine was so scarce, that in their sacrifices to the gods the libations were made with milk only. Wine did not become <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> there till A. U. C. 600, when vines began to be planted. Liquor of Flints. See <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, No 1450. Smoking Liquor of Libavius. See Chemistry, No 1809. Mineral Anodyne Liquor of Hoffman. This is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of highly rectified spirit of wine, vitriolic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETHER">ether</a>, and a little of the dulcified <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of vitriol. See Chemistry, No 849. LIQUORICE. See Glycyrrhiza, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

LIRIODENDRON

Pages 54-54

the Tulip tree, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the polyandra class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 52d order, Coadunate. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

LIS

Pages 54-54
or Lis, John Vander, painter of history, landscapes, and conversations, was born at Oldenburgh in 1570, but went to Haerlem to place himself as a disciple under Henry Goltzius; and as he was endowed with great natural talents, he soon distinguished himself in that school, and imitated the manner of his master with great success. He adhered to the same style till he went to Italy; where, having visited Venice and Rome, he studied the works of Titian, Tintoretto, Paolo Veronese, and Domenico Fetti, so effectually, that he improved his taste and judgment, and altered his manner entirely. He soon received marks of public approbation; and his compositions became universally admired for their good expression, for their lively and natural colouring, and the sweetness and delicacy of his pencil: although it must be acknowledged, that he could never totally divest himself of the ideas and taste peculiar to the Flemings. His subjects usually were histories taken from the sacred writings, or the representations of rural sports, marriages, balls, and villagers dancing, dressed in Venetian habits; all which subjects he painted in a small as well as a large size, with a number of figures, well designed, and touched with a great deal of delicacy. He was likewise accounted to paint naked figures admirably, with natural and elegant attitudes, and a very agreeable turn of the limbs. A capital picture of this master is, Adam and Eve lamenting the death of Abel; which is extremely admired, not only for the expression, but also for the beauty of the landscape; and in the church of St Nicholas at Venice is another of his paintings, representing St Jerome in the desert, with a pen in his hand, and his head turned to look at an angel, who is supposed to be sounding the last trumpet. The colouring of this picture is rather too red; but it is designed in a fine style, and charmingly penciled. The paintings of this master are very rarely to be purchased. He died in 1629. Lis, John Vander, of Breda, historical painter, was born at Breda about the year 1601, and became a disciple of Cornelius Polemburg, whose manner he imitated, with extraordinary exactness, in the tint of his colouring, his neatness of penciling, and the choice of his subjects. There are some paintings of this master's hand, which, though they appear to have somewhat less freedom and lightness of touch, are nearly equal to those of Polemburg, and are frequently taken to be his. At Rotterdam, in the possession of Mr Bischof, there is a delicate painting representing Diana in the bath, attended by her nymphs; and his most capital performance, in England, is said to be in the possession of the viscount Middleton. The portrait of Vander Lis, painted by himself, is in the possession of Horace Walpole, Esq., which is described by that ingenious gentleman as being worked up equal to the smoothness of enamel.

LISBON

Pages 54-55

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, situated in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESTREMADURA">Estremadura</a>, on the banks of the river <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TAGUS">Tagus</a>, in W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9° 25'. N. Lat. 38° 42'. It was anciently called Olisipo, Olissippo, and Ulissippo. It first became considerable in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Emanuel; from that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> it has been the capital of the kingdom, the residence of its monarchs, the seat of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> tribunals and offices of the metropolitans, a noble university, and the receptacle of the richest merchandise of the East and West Indies. Its <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> is excellent; being refreshed by the delightful <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> breezes, and those of the Tagus. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> extends for about two miles along the Tagus; but its breadth is inconsiderable. Like old Rome, it stands on <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> hills; but the streets in general are narrow and dirty, and some of them are very steep; neither are they lighted at night. The churches, in general, are very fine; but the magnificence of the chapel <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> is amazing. Here is one of the finest harbours in the world; and there were a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> not only of fine churches and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a> here, but also of other public buildings, and particularly of royal palaces, and others belonging to the grandees; but the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of them, and of the city, were destroyed by a most dreadful earthquake, on Nov. 1, 1755, from which it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> require a long time to recover. The inhabitants, before the earthquake, did not at most exceed 150,000. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of it is lodged in a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, consisting of a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>, six counsellors, and other inferior officers. The harbour has <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> enough for the largest ships, and room enough for 10,000 sail without being crowded. For its security, there is a fort at the mouth of the river, on each side, and a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> that runs across it, and is very dangerous to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> without pilots. Higher up, at a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the river is considerably contracted, there is a fort called Torre de Belem, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the Tower of Belem, under whose guns all ships must pass in their way to the city; and on the other side are several more forts. Before the earthquake, most of the private houses were old and unsightly, with lattice windows; and the number of convents and colleges amounted to 50, namely, 32 for monks, and 18 for nuns. The king's <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> stands on the river, and is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and commodious. Of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>, that called the Great is obliged to receive all persons, of what <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> soever, without exception. At the village of Belem, near Lisbon, is a noble <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> for decayed gentlemen who have served the king, and have not wherewithal to maintain themselves. That called the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">House</a> of Mercy is also a noble <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>. In the centre of the city, upon one of the highest hills, is the castle, which commands the whole, being large and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, and having always a garrison of four regiments of foot. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> is a vast edifice of the Gothic kind, but heavy and clumsy: it contains, however, great <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>. The whole city is under the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> jurisdiction of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a>, who was appointed in the year 1717. Here is also an archbishop, who has, or at least had, before the erection of the patriarchate, a revenue of 40,000 crusadoes, or 600l. The university, which was removed for some time to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COIMBRA">Coimbra</a>, but afterwards restored to its ancient seat, makes a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, though much inferior to that of Coimbra. In <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1807 the Portuguese <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> retired from Lisbon to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRAZIL">Brazil</a>, and the city was occupied by the French, who retained possession of it till August 1808, when it was given up under the convention of Cintra.

LISBURN

Pages 55-55

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Antrim and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Ulster, 73 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>. It was burnt <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> about 50 years ago; but is now rebuilt in a neat and handsome manner, and has a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> manufactory. It is seated on the river Laggan, in W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6° 20' N. Lat. 54° 31'. It gives <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> to the family of Vaughan, and formerly returned two members to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>.

LISIEUX

Pages 55-55

a considerable town of France, in Upper Normandy, with a bishop's see. The churches and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> houses, and the bishop's <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, are all very handsome structures. It is a trading <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; and is seated at the confluence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Arbeck and Cassi, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0° 20' N. Lat. 49° 11'.

LISLE

Pages 55-57
Joseph Nicholas de, an eminent astronomer and geographer, was born at Paris in the year 1688. His father having taught him the principles of grammar, he afterwards attended lectures in the Mazarine college, where he delivered his rhetorical exercises in 1706. A total eclipse of the sun having taken place on the 12th of March that year, his taste for mathematics was thus discovered, and he was accordingly placed under a proper tutor, who taught him the elements of geometry, fortification and mechanics; but his favourite study was the science of astronomy. In 1707 he was offered the place of an engineer at Martinico, which made him acquainted with the art of drawing, an acquisition which proved highly useful to him in his geographical labours, and also in the study of astronomy. His father having got a copy of An Account of a Voyage to the South sea from his son's master, young de Lisle was excited by the perusal of it to the study of href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural history, and he began to make collections of insects, and sketch their varieties; but being afterwards persuaded that so extensive a study, requiring such immense collections to be made as he found in Aldrovandus, was wholly incompatible with that unremitting attention which his favourite science required, he relinquished it accordingly. The attention he paid to astronomical researches was so great, that he was considered as meriting the correspondence of some of the ablest astronomers of Europe at the early age of 21. In 1709 he made a wooden quadrant, which he divided with the utmost accuracy, and which answered the intended purpose in his early observations. He likewise constructed a table for M. Cassini, of the right ascensions and declinations, adapted to all the degrees of latitude and longitude of the planets, and the obliquity of the ecliptic; this table was made use of by M. Cassini in foretelling the occultations of the stars by the moon. De Lisle being informed by Cassini in 1710 of his method of representing an eclipse of the sun, by the projection of a terrestrial parallel on a plane; he instantly conceived the idea of applying it to every part of the earth, by means of a globe mounted and prepared for that purpose. Such astronomers as he made acquainted with his project, conceived it to be impracticable; but when the machine was completed, they bestowed the highest encomiums on the noble invention. The first memorable observation made by de Lisle was Lisle, that of the moon, on the 23rd of January 1712, after which his labours experienced some interruption from bodily indisposition. About this time the situation of his father's numerous family rendered it necessary that he should provide for himself, so that he was obliged to make his astronomical knowledge subservient to the absurdities of astrology, receiving pecuniary presents from the regent for his services. He received also in 1715 the grant of a pension of 600 livres, on which occasion he calculated tables of the moon according to the Newtonian theory, prior to Halley's communications to him, which were printed in 1719. De Lisle was chosen a member of the Academy of Sciences in 1714, on which account his exertions were redoubled. In 1720 he delivered a proposal to the academy for ascertaining in France the figure of the earth, a design which was carried into execution some years afterwards. In 1723 he delivered to the same academy a memoir on the transits of Mercury, wherein a method of calculating them was proposed by him, the way in which they were to be observed, and the inferences to be deduced from these observations. He proposed the use of the quadrant in observing the transits of Venus and Mercury, which has been found superior to any other instrument for that important purpose, and is sanctioned since his day by the practice of the ablest astronomers. Our distinguished philosopher came over to England in the year 1724, where he became acquainted with Newton and Halley, and had the honour of obtaining their approbation. Newton made him a present of his own portrait, and Halley gave him a copy of the tables which he had published in 1719. He was also created a member of the Royal Society, and he enjoyed similar honours from every literary society in Europe before his death. In 1721 he received an invitation from Peter the Great to go to Petersburgh, to fill the chair of astronomer in the Imperial Academy of Sciences. On the death of that emperor, his successor Catharine renewed the invitation, offering him a considerable pension, of which he accepted, and, in 1726, set out for Petersburgh, accompanied by his brother Lewis and M. Vignon, who were to act as his assistants. He reached Petersburgh in the month of October, and was established in the observatory erected by Peter the Great, which he occupied for 21 years. It was in every respect commodious, but extremely deficient in astronomical apparatus, which his own ingenuity and indefatigable application in a great measure supplied. A transit of Mercury over the sun's disc was expected in the year 1740, which would not be visible in Europe, and therefore de Lisle undertook a journey to the distant regions of Asia; but after travelling through the inhospitable wilds of Siberia, the cloudiness of the atmosphere prevented him from observing the transit,—a mortification which he endeavoured to support by his geographical and physical remarks, and in drawing up a description of the country. He constructed an interesting map of Russia, assisted by his brother Lewis, who was appointed to make observations in the most distant parts of that immense empire. He was occasionally employed for the long period of forty years, in making meteorological observations, which he executed with an accuracy almost incredible. After a number of discouragements and difficulties, and the irregular payment of his pension, had been long experienced by de Lisle at Petersburgh, he returned disgusted to his native place, and was chosen professor of mathematics at the college-royal, where he did the most essential service to the sciences, by the important instructions which he gave to his numerous pupils, many of whom became afterwards the most distinguished characters, such as M. M. de la Lande and Messier. When the transit of Mercury over the sun was eagerly expected in 1753 by the greatest astronomers, de Lisle published an interesting map of the world, representing the effect of Mercury's parallaxes in different countries, that such places might be known as were proper for making those observations on the transit as might determine the distance of the sun. As the apparent orbit of the planet traversed nearly the centre of the sun, de Lisle made use of this circumstance to determine the diameter of that luminary. The last work of our author which was inserted in the volumes of the French academy, was a memoir on the comet which appeared in the year 1758, discovered by a peasant in the vicinity of Dresden. It may perhaps be asserted with justice, that the most important service which this great man rendered to astronomers was, his correction of the double error of Halley respecting the transit of Venus, looked for in the year 1761, as by this means he prevented many learned men from undertaking long voyages in order to observe it. About the year 1754, de Lisle was appointed by the king of France, astronomical geographer to the marine, in which capacity he was to collect plans and journals of naval captains, to arrange them methodically, and to make extracts from them of whatever might be beneficial to the service. About the year 1758 he withdrew into quiet retirement at the abbey of St Genevieve, where much of his time was spent in devotional exercises, and in acts of charity and beneficence. Still, however, he continued to prosecute those studies which had been so dear to him during the earlier part of his life; but in 1768 he was seized with a scorbutic complaint, of which he was cured by his medical friends; but in the month of September the same year he was seized with a species of apoplexy, which carried him off on the 11th day of that month, in the 81st year of his age. His extraordinary merit as a man of science may in some measure be gathered from this concise account of his life; and as a citizen of the world his piety was unaffected, his morals pure, his integrity undeviating, his spirit generous and disinterested, and his whole manners highly amiable. The only publication of our author's, besides those already mentioned, consisted of "Memoirs illustrative of the History of Astronomy," in two volumes 4to. Lisle, Sir John, a brave loyalist in the time of the civil wars, was the son of a bookseller in London, and received his education in the Netherlands. He signalized himself upon many occasions in the civil war, particularly in the last battle of Newbury; where, in the dusk of the evening, he led his men to the charge in his shirt, that his person might be more conspicuous. The king, who was an eye-witness of his bravery, knighted him on the field of battle. In 1648, he rose for his majesty in Essex; and was one of the royalists who who so obstinately defended Colchester, and who died for the defence of it. This brave man having tenderly embraced the corpse of Sir Charles Lucas, his departed friend, immediately presented himself to the soldiers who stood ready for his execution. Thinking that they stood at too great a distance, he desired them to come nearer: one of them said, "I warrant you Sir, we shall hit you." He replied with a smile, "Friends, I have been nearer you when you have missed me." He was executed August 28, 1648.

LISMORE

Pages 57-57

a borough town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATERFORD">Waterford</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a>, 100 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>; N. Lat. 52° 5'. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7° 30'. It was anciently called Lissmore <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Lismore, i.e., the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> enclosure, or habitation; it is now a bishopric, united to Waterford, and formerly had an university. St Carthagh or Moehuda, in the beginning of the seventh century, founded an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> and school in this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, which in a short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> was much resorted to, not only by the natives, but also by the Britons and Saxons, during the middle ages. According to an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writer of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of St Carthagh, Lismore was in general inhabited by monks, half of it being an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a> into which no woman dared enter; consisting entirely of cells and monasteries, the ruins of which, with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> churches, are yet visible. A castle was built here by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> John. The site of Lismore was in early ages denominated magh skia, or the "chosen shield," being the situation of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUN">dun</a> or fort of the ancient chieftains of the Deeces, one of whom granted it to St Carthagh on his expulsion from the abbey of Ratheney in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WESTMEATH">Westmeath</a>. On becoming an university, Math Sgiath obtained the name of Dunsginne, or the "fort of the Saxons," from the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of Saxons who resorted thereto; but soon after, it was called Lis-s-more or Less-more, and now Lismore; the bishopric of which was united to that of Waterford in 1363, being 730 years after its foundation. The public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> to Cork was formerly through this place, and at that time it had a better <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> of business. St Carthagh, who retired to this place with some of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> in 636, to avoid the fury of the then Irish monarch, tied his disciples to a most strict rule of life; they never were allowed the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, fish, or fowl; only the vegetables that the ground produced at the expense of their own labour. Father Daniel, in his Histoire Monastique, mentions one on the same foundation in France. The castle here, which, as we have formerly mentioned, was built by King John, was erected in 1195 on the ruins of the abbey of St Carthagh: it belonged to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, and gave birth to the great <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> Robert Boyle. In 1189 it was demolished by the Irish, who took it by surprise. Being afterwards re-edified, it was for many years an episcopal residence, till Myler Magrath, archbishop of Cashel, and bishop of this see, granted the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANOR">manor</a> of Lismore to that noted scholar and soldier Sir Walter Raleigh, in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, at the yearly rent of £3l. 6s. 8d.; but that estate was lopped off with his head in the reign of King James I. After which it fell into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of Sir Richard Boyle, who purchased all Sir Walter's lands; he beautified the whole, and added many buildings to it, most of which were burned <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in the Irish rebellion; at the breaking out of which, it was closely besieged by 5000 Irish commanded by Sir Richard Beling, and was well defended by the young <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Broghill, third son of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Cork, who obliged them to raise the siege. The castle is boldly seated on the verge of a rocky hill, rising almost perpendicular to a considerable height over the river Blackwater. The entrance is by an ancient and venerable avenue of trees. Over the gate are the venerable arms of the first earl of Cork. Opposite to the entrance is a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> portico of Bath <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, of the Doric order, designed by Inigo Jones. Most of the buildings have remained in ruins since the era of the rebellion; but the several offices that make up two sides of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> are kept in repair. At each <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> is a tower, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> remains of its former magnificence. In October 1785, the late duke of Rutland, then lord-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> of Ireland, whilst on a tour in Munster, held a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> in, and issued proclamations from this castle. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> is still pretty well kept in repair. Here is a fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> over the river Blackwater, erected at a very great expense by the duke of Devonshire: this bridge is remarkable for the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAN">span</a> of it being 102 feet. Below the town is a rich fishery for salmon, which is the greatest branch of trade here. Though this place is at present much reduced, yet Cambrensis informs us, that, not many years after the conquest, this was a very rich <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and held out some time against the English, who took it at last by storm, and gained rich plunder here, enough to load 16 sail of ships.

LISSA

Pages 57-57

a village of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SILESIA">Silesia</a>, 16 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRESLAU">Breslau</a>, remarkable for a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> fought between the Prussians and the Austrians on the 15th of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1757, when the latter were entirely defeated.

LISSUS

Pages 57-57

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, the last town of Illyricum, towards <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>, situated on the Drilo. It had a capacious port, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of Dionysius the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">Tyrant</a>, who led the colony thither, enlarged and walled it round, (Diodorus Siculus). Now called Alessio, in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBANIA">Albania</a>, on the Drino, near the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 20° N. Lat. 42'.

LIST

Pages 57-58

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, the border of cloth <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> stuff; serving serving not only to show their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, but to preserve them from being torn in the operations of fulling, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DYEING">dyeing</a>, &c.—List is used on various occasions; but chiefly by gardeners for securing their wall trees. List, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, a little <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> moulding, otherwise called a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FILLET">fillet</a>, listel, &c. See Architecture. List, is also used, to signify the enclosed field or ground wherein the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> knights held their justs and combats. It was so called, as being hemmed round with pales, barriers, or stakes, as with a list. Some of these were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a>, one for each cavalier which kept them apart, so that they could not come nearer each other than a spear's length. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">Just</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOURNAMENT">Tournament</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUEL">Duel</a>, &c. Civil List, in the British polity. The expenses defrayed by the civil list are those that in any shape relate to civil <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>; as, the expenses of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>; all salaries to officers of state, to the judges, and every one of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s servants, the appointments to foreign ambassadors; the maintenance of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> family; the king's private expenses, or privy-purse; and other very numerous outgoings, as secret-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, pensions, and other bounties: which sometimes have so far exceeded the revenues appointed for that purpose, that application has been made to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> to discharge the debts contracted on the civil list; as particularly in 1724, when one million was granted for that purpose by the statute 11 Geo. I. c. 17, and, in 1769, when half a million was appropriated to the like uses by the statute 9 Geo. III. c. 34. The civil list is indeed properly the whole of the king's revenue in his own distinct capacity; the rest being rather the revenue of the public, or its creditors, though collected and distributed again in the name and by the officers of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>: it now standing in the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, as the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> income did formerly; and as that has gradually diminished, the parliamentary appointments have increased. The whole revenue of Queen <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> did not amount to more than 600,000l. a-year: that of King <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. was 800,000l., and the revenue voted for King Charles II. was 1,200,000l. though complaints were made (in the first years at least) that it did not amount to so much. But it must be observed, that under these sums were included all manner of public expenses; among which <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Clarendon, in his speech to the parliament, computed that the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> forces amounted annually to 800,000l. which was ten times more than before the former troubles. The same revenue, subject to the same charges, was settled on King James II.; but by the increase of trade, and more frugal management, it amounted on an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> to 1,500,000l. per annum, (besides other additional customs granted by parliament, which produced an annual revenue of 400,000l.), out of which his fleet and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> were maintained at the yearly expense of 1,100,000l. After the Revolution, when the parliament took into its own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> the annual support of the forces both <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a>, a civil list revenue was settled on the new king and queen, amounting, with the hereditary duties to 700,000l. per annum; and the same was <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to Queen <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> and King George I. That of King George II. was nominally augmented to 800,000l. *, and in fact was considerably more: but that of his present majesty is expressly limited to that sum; though 100,000l. hath been since added. And upon the whole, it is doubtless much better for the crown, and also for the people, to have the revenue settled upon the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> footing rather than the ancient. For the crown, because it is more certain, and collected with greater ease; for the people, because they are now delivered from the feudal hardships, and other odious branches of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a>. And though complaints have sometimes been made of the increase of the civil list, yet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we consider the sums that have been formerly granted, the limited <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> under which it is now established, the revenues and prerogatives given up in lieu of it by the crown, the numerous branches of the present royal family, and (above all) the diminution of the value of money compared with what it was worth in the last century, we must acknowledge these complaints to be void of any rational foundation; and that it is impossible to support that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, which a king of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> should maintain, with an income in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> less than what is now established by parliament. See Revenue. To List or Enlist <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">Soldiers</a>, to retain and enroll men as soldiers, either as volunteers, or by a kind of compulsion. Persons listed must be carried within four days, but not sooner than 24 hours after, before the next <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of peace of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, riding, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, or place, or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> of any city or town corporate (not being an officer in the army); and if before such justice or magistrate they dissent from such enlisting, and return the enlisting money, and also 20 shillings in lieu of all charges expended on them, they are to be discharged. But persons refusing or neglecting to return and pay such money within 24 hours, shall be deemed as duly listed as if they had assented thereto before the proper magistrate; and they shall, in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, be obliged to take the oath, or, upon refusal, they shall be confined by the officer who listed them till they do take it.

LISTER

Pages 58-58

Dr Martin, an eminent English physician and naturalist, was born in 1638, and educated at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>. He afterwards travelled into France; and at his return practised physic at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, and afterwards at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. In 1683, he was created <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of physic, and became fellow of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a> of Physicians in London. In 1698, he attended the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Portland in his embassy from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> William III. to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of France; of which journey he published an account at his return, and was afterwards physician to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>. He also published, 1. Historia animalium, Angliae, quarto. 2. Conchyliorum synopsis, folio. 3. Cochlearium et limachum exercitatio anatomica, 4 vols. 8vo. 4. Many pieces in the Philosophical Transactions; and other works.

LISTOWEL

Pages 58-59
