a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>, also a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> and fair town, of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KERRY">Kerry</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a>, 131 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> Lis Tuathal, i.e. "the fort of Tuathal," who was exiled in the first century, but returned; and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> forms a brilliant era in Irish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. Near this are the ruins of a castle, pleasantly situated on the river Feale: it was taken in November 1600, by Sir <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Wilmot, being then held out for <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Kerry against <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>. Five miles beyond Listowel are the ruins of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> are three in the year. LITANA Silva, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a wood of of the Boii, in Gallia Togata, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Cispadana, where the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, under L. Posthumius <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBINUS">Albinus</a> (whose head the Boii cut off, and carried in triumph into their most sacred temple), had a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> defeat; of twenty- five thousand, scarcely ten escaping (Livy). Hol- stenius conjectures, that this happened above the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> of the Scultenna, in a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Appen- <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a>, between Cersinianum and Mutina. Now Selva di Lugio.

LITANY

Pages 59-59

a solemn form of supplication to God, in which the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> utters some things fit to be prayed for, and the people join in their intercession, saying we beseech thee to hear us, good <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>, &c. The word comes from the Greek ἀνακρίνω “supplication;” of ἀνακρίνω, ‘I beseech.’ At first the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of litanies was not fixed to any stat- ed <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, but were only employed as exigencies re- quired. They were observed, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the Ni- nevites, with ardent supplications and fastings, to avert the threatening judgments of fire, earthquakes, inun- dations, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> hostile invasions. About the year 400, li- tanies began to be used in processions, the people walking barefoot, and repeating them with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> de- votion; and it is pretended, that by this means several countries were delivered from great calamities. The days on which these were used were called rogation days: these were appointed by the canons of different councils, till it was decreed by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOLEDO">Toledo</a>, that they should be used every <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> throughout the year; and thus by degrees they came to be used <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEEK">week</a>- ly on Wednesdays and Fridays, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STATIONARY">stationary</a> days for fasting. To these days the rubric of our <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> has added Sundays, as being the greatest days for assembling at divine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. Before the last review of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>, the litany was a distinct service by itself, and used some time after the morning prayer was over; at present it is made one office with the morning service, being ordered to be read after the third collect for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>, instead of the intercessional prayers in the daily service.

LITCHFIELD

Pages 59-60

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STAFFORDSHIRE">Staffordshire</a>, in Eng- <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, 117 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It stands low, about three miles from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a>: and its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> name is said to have been Licidfield, signifying, “a field of carcasses,” from a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> having, as it is pretended, suffered martyrdom here in the per- secution under Diocletian. In the Saxons <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, it was a bishoprick for a short space; and is now, toge- ther with <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COVENTRY">Coventry</a>, a bishoprick. It is divided into two parts by a rivulet and a kind of shallow lake, over which are two causeways with sluices. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> straggling <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; but has some very handsome houses, and well paved clean streets. That <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> on the south side of the rivulet is called the city, and the other the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>. The city is much the largest, and contains seve- ral public structures. It was incorporated by Edw. VI. with the name of bailiffs and burgesses; and is both a town and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, governed by 2 bailiffs chosen yearly out of 24 burgesses, a recorder, a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a>, and other officers. The city has power of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> within their jurisdiction, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of record, and a pie- powder court. Here is a goal both for debtors and felons, a free school, and a pretty <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> well endowed <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>, for a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> and 12 brethren. The county of the city is 10 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 12 miles in compass, which the Litchfield sheriff rides yearly on the 8th of September, and then feasts the corporation and neighbouring gentry. The close is so called from its being enclosed with a wall and a deep dry ditch on all sides except towards the city, where it is defended by a great lake or marsh formed by its brook. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, which stands in the close, was originally built by Oswiu <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Nor- thumbeland about 300. It was rebuilt and enlarged by Offa king of Mercia in 766. In 1148 it was rebuilt, and greatly enlarged in 1296. In the civil wars its spire was destroyed, and it converted to a stable. In 1776 a beautiful painted window, by the benefaction of Dr Adenbrook, was set up at the western end of the cathedral. In the civil wars it was several times taken and retaken, and thereby suffered much; but was so repaired after the Restoration, at the expense of 20,000l. that it was one the fairest and noblest structures of the kind in England. It is walled in like a castle, and stands so <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> as to be seen 10 miles round. It is 450 feet long, of which the choir is 110, and the breadth in the broadest place 80. Its portico is hard- ly to be paralleled in England. There were, till lately, 26 <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> of the prophets, apostles, kings of Judah, and some kings of this land, in a row above it, as big as the life; and on the top, at each corner of the por- tico, is a stately pipe, besides a fine high steeple on the middle of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. The choir is paved in great part with alabaster and cannel coal, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> marble. In 1789 it underwent a general repair, when the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASSIVE">massive</a> groined <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> betwixt the west end of the church and the transept, which had forced the side wall out of its perpendicular, was removed. The prebendaries stalls, which are thought to be the best in England, were most of them re-erect- ed at the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> gentlemen, whose names and arms are painted at the top of the stalls. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> door is extremely rich in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>, but much injured by time. The body which is supported by pillars formed of numbers of slender columns, has lately had its decayed leaden <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> replaced by a neat slated covering. The choir merits <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> on ac- <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> of the elegant sculpture about the windows, and the embattled gallery that runs beneath them; to which the altarpiece of Grecian <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> but ill corresponds; behind which is <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>’s chapel, divided from it by a most elegant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> skreen of beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>- manship. Here stood St Chad’s shrine, which cost 2000l. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> is an octagon room. In the same close are the palaces of the bishop and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">dean</a>, and the prebendaries houses in a court on the hill. Here are three other churches; one of which, St Mi- chael’s, has a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCHYARD">churchyard</a> of 6 or 7 acres. There was a castle here, long since destroyed: and ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMPS">camps</a> have been discovered in its environs. In the neigh- bourhood are frequent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> races. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> here are on Tuesday and Friday, and six <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> in the year. By inland <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, this place has <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERSEY">Mersey</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEE">Dee</a>, Ribble, Ouse, Trent, Darwent, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a>, Humber, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, Avon, &c.; which navigation, including its windings, extends above 500 miles in the counties of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>, Notting- <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAM">ham</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANCASTER">Lancaster</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WESTMORELAND">Westmoreland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">War</a>- wick, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEICESTER">Leicester</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORCESTER">Worcester</a>, &c. Litchfield Litchfield sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> in 1811 was 5,022. Literature, any thing belonging to Literature. Literary <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">Property</a>, or Copy <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">Right</a>. See Copy Right. Literati (letrodos, "lettered"), an epithet given to such persons among the Chinese as are able to read and write their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. The literati alone are capable of being made mandarins. Literati, is also the name of a particular <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> either in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, or politics, consisting principally of the learned men of that country; among whom it is called jukiao, i.e., "learned." It had its rise in the year of Christ 1400, when the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, to awaken the native affection of the people for knowledge, which had been quite banished by the preceding civil wars among them, and to stir up emulation among the mandarins, chose out 42 of the ablest among the doctors, to whom he gave a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> to compose a body of doctrine agreeable to that of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, which was then become the rule or standard of the learned. The delegates applied themselves to the business with very great attention: but some fancied them rather to have wrested the doctrine of the ancients, to make it consist with theirs, than to have built up theirs on the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of the ancients. They speak of the Deity, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it were no more than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> power or virtue that produces, disposes, and preserves, the several parts of the universe. It is, say they, a pure, perfect principle, without beginning or end; it is the source of all things, the essence of every being, and that which determines it to be what it is. They make God the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> of the world; they say, he is diffused through all <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, and produces all the changes that happen there. In short, it is not easy to determine, whether they resolve God into nature, or lift up nature into God; for they ascribe to it many of those things which we <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> to God. This doctrine, in lieu of the idolatry that prevailed before, introduced a refined kind of atheism. The work, being composed by so many persons of learning and parts, and approved by the emperor himself, was received with infinite applause by all the people. Many were pleased with it, because it seemed to subvert all religion; others approved it, because the little religion that it left them could not give them much trouble. And thus was formed the sect of the Literati: which consists of the maintainers and adherents to this doctrine. The court, the mandarins, and the persons of fortune and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, &c., are generally retainers to it; but a great part of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people still hold to their worship of idols. The literati freely tolerate the Mahometans, because they adore, with them, the King of heaven, and Author of nature; but they bear a perfect aversion to all sorts of idolaters among them: and it was once resolved to extirpate them. But the disorder this would have occasioned in the empire prevented it; they now content themselves with condemning them, in general, as heresies: which they do solemnly every year at Pekin.

LITERATURE

Pages 60-61

e denotes learning <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> skill in letters. Litternum. See Litternum. Lithanthrax, or Pit-Coal, is a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>, laminated, bituminous substance; not very easily inflammable, but, when once inflamed, burns longer and more intensely than any other substance. See <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LITHARGE">Litharge</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, usually in form of soft flakes, of a yellowish reddish <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> calcined lead be urged with a hasty fire, it melts into the appearance of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and on cooling concretes into litharge. Greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the litharge met with in the shops is produced in the purification of silver from lead, and the refining of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver by means of this metal: according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of fire and other circumstances, it proves of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> or deep colour: the first has been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called litharge of silver, the other litharge of gold. See Lead, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> Index. Lithgow, William, a Scotsman, whose sufferings by imprisonment and torture at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALAGA">Malaga</a>, and whose travels, on foot, over <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, seem to raise him almost to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARTYR">martyr</a> and a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a>, published an account of his peregrinations and adventures. Though the author deals much in the marvellous, the horrid account of the strange cruelties of which he tells us, he was the subject, have however, an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. Soon after his arrival in England from Malaga, he was carried to Theobald's on a feather-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>, that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> James might be an eyewitness of his martyred anatomy, by which he means his wretched body, mangled and reduced to a skeleton. The whole <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> crowded to see him; and his majesty ordered him to be taken care of, and he was twice sent to Bath at his expense. By the king's command he applied to Condamor, the Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a>, for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> and other things of value which the governor of Malaga had taken from him, and for 100l. for his support. He was promised a full reparation for the damage he had sustained: but the perfidious minister never performed his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a>. When he was upon the point of leaving England, Lithgow upbraided him with the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> of his word in the presence-chamber, before several gentlemen of the court. This occasioned their fighting upon the spot; and the ambassador, as the traveller oddly expresses it, had his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISTULA">fistula</a> (with which disorder he was afflicted) contrabanded with his fist. The unfortunate Lithgow, who was generally condemned for his spirited behaviour, was sent to the Marshalsea, where he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> a prisoner <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> months. At the conclusion of the octavo edition of his Travels he informs us, that, in his three voyages, "his painful feet have traced over (besides <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> of seas and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>) 36,000 and odd miles, which draweth near to twice the circumference of the whole <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>." Here the marvellous seems to rise to the incredible; and to set him, in point of veracity, below Corvat, whom it is nevertheless certain that he far outwalked. His <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> is whimsical and curious. This, together with the narrative of his sufferings, is reprinted in Morgan's Phoenix <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITANNICUS">Britannicus</a>. Lithiasis, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">Stone</a>. See Medicine Index. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-LITHOMANTIA">Lithomantia</a>, in antiquity, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVINATION">divination</a> performed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. Sometimes the stone called siderites was used: this they washed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> in the night by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>; the person that consulted Lithuania consulted it was to be purified from all manner of pollution, and to have his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> covered: this done, he repeated divine prayers, and placed certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> in an appointed order; and then the stone moved of itself, and in a soft gentle murmur or (as some say) in a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> like that of a child, returned an answer. By a stone of this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, Helenus is reported to have foretold the destruction of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>. **LITHONTRIPTICS** (from λίθος, "a stone," and ἐκβάλλειν, "to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a>") an epithet for medicines that are supposed to break the stone in the bladder. Though the different stones that are <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> bladder require different solvents when out of the body; and though art hath not yet afforded a medicine which, when injected into the bladder, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, without injury thereto, dissolve the stone therein lodged; it cannot thence be concluded, that there are no lithontriptic medicines. It may be here observed, that one solvent affects one subject, but hath no effect on another; so a solvent may yet be met with that will destroy the stone, and not hurt the human body. The water into which the boiled <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a> dissolves will liquefy <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYRRH">myrrh</a>, but may be put into the human eye without causing any uneasiness. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOAP">Soap</a> ley taken at first in small doses in broth that is freed from all its fat, succeeds in most <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> which require an alkaline solvent. The patient may begin with 20 drops, and gradually increase the dose as he is able; and by repeating it three times a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> for six, eight, or twelve months, the wished-for effects often follow.

LITHOPIYTA

the name of Linnaeus's third order of vermes. See <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELMINTHOLOGY">Helminthology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

LITHOSPERMUM

Gromwell**, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 41st order, Asperiflorae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

LITHOSTROTON

Pages 61-61

among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, was a pavement of mosaic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, consisting of small pieces of cut marble of different kinds and colours, first used in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Sylla, who made one at Praeneste in the temple of Fortune, and afterwards in private houses; and were brought to such perfection, that they exhibited most lively representations of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> with all the accuracy of the finest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>.

LITHOTOMY

Pages 61-61

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, the operation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. See Surgery <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

LITHUANIA

Pages 61-61

an extensive <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>. By the natives it is called Letuva, and has <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> Poland and Russia on the west; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Muscovy on the east; <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIVONIA">Livonia</a>, the Baltic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and part of Muscovy, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> Russia, Volhynia, and Podolia, on the south; and the Ukraine on the south-east. Its length is said to be about 360, and its breadth 340 miles; but it is much indented both ways. Lithuania was anciently overrun with wood; and there are still many forests in it, which yield a great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, wax, pitch, tar, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>; and abound with wild boars, buffaloes, elks, wild horses, wild asses, urii, and woodcocks. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> are also numerous, and well stored with fish; but the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, by reason of these forests and lakes, is said to be thick and foggy. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> produces a great deal of buck wheat and other corn; the pastures are luxuriant, and the flocks and herds numerous: so that, notwithstanding <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a> is much neglected, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> are exceeding cheap, and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> so scarce, that 10 per cent. is the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> have <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> estates, and live in great pomp and splendour, generally retaining some <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a> of those that are <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of domestics. The established <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPERY">Popery</a>; but Lutherans, Calvinists, Jews, Turks, Greeks, and Socinians, are very numerous. Lithuania was governed by its own dukes till it was united to Poland, towards the end of the 14th century, when the great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> Jagello married Hedwig, the dowager of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Poland and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>. It had even dukes after that, but they were subordinate to the king; and at this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, though one diet serves for both countries, yet each has its peculiar laws, customs, dialect, and privileges. In a diet held at Lubin in 1569, it was enacted, that both countries, for the future, should form but one state under the same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>. As to their courts of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, the tenth part of what is adjudged in all real actions goes always to the judge's box, and is immediately paid in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>; and in personal actions he claims half the damages given. A nobleman is only fined for <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, as in Poland. The dialect is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of the Slavonic; and they speak here, as in Poland, a barbarous kind of Latin. Lithuania was divided into <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> palatinates. In 1772 the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">Poles</a> were compelled to cede a part of this province to Russia; and at the partition in 1793, this power acquired nearly the whole. In 1815 the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Poland was revived, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> being united to that of Russia, but the part of Lithuania formerly disjoined from this kingdom still continues annexed to Russia.

LITMUS

Pages 61-62
or LACMUS**, in the arts, is a blue pigment, formed from archil. It is brought from Holland at a cheap rate; but may be prepared by adding quicklime and putrified urine, or spirit of urine distilled from lime, to the archil previously bruised by grinding. The mixture having cooled, and the fluid suffered to evaporate, becomes a mass of the consistence of a paste, which is laid on boards to dry in square lumps. It is only used in miniature paintings, and cannot be well depended on, because the least approach of acid changes it instantly from blue to red. The best litmus is very apt to change and fly. **LITTER (lecteria)**, a kind of vehicle borne upon shafts; anciently esteemed the most easy and genteel way of carriage. Du Cange derives the word from the barbarous Latin lecteria, "straw or bedding for beasts." Others will rather have it come from lectus, "bed." Pliny calls the litter the traveller's chamber; it was much in use among the Romans, among whom it was borne by slaves kept for that purpose; as it still continues to be in the east, where it is called a palanquin.—The Roman lectica, made to be borne by four men, was called tetraphorum; that borne by six, hexaphorum; and that borne by eight, octaphorum. The invention of litters, according to Cicero, was owing to the kings of Bithynia; in the time of Tiberius they were become very frequent at Rome, as appears from Seneca; and even slaves themselves were borne in them, though never by more than two persons, whereas men of quality had six or eight. **LITTER** also denotes a parcel of dry old straw put on the floor of a horse's stall for him to lie down and rest upon. When a horse comes tired into a stable, fresh Litter has the virtue of making him stale immediately. This is known to be of very great advantage to a horse in a tired state; and when the litter is old and dirty, it never has any such effect upon him. If the owners knew how refreshing it is for a horse to discharge his urine on his return from labour, they would be more careful of giving them all means and occasions of it than they are. This staling after fatigue prevents those obstructions in the neck of the bladder or urinary passages which horses are too subject to.

LITTLETON

Pages 62-62

Sir Thomas, judge of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMMON_PLEAS"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> pleas, was the eldest son of Thomas Westcote, Esq. of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Devon, by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, sole heiress of Thomas Littleton of Frankley in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORCESTERSHIRE">Worcestershire</a>, at whose request he took the name and arms of that family. He was educated at one of our <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, probably at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>. Thence he removed to the Inner-Temple, where he became one of the readers; and was afterwards, by Henry VI. made <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> judge of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, or marshalsea of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>. In 1455, the thirty-third of that reign, he was appointed king's serjeant, and rode the northern circuit as judge of assize. In 1462, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> of Edward IV., he obtained a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>; and, in 1466, was appointed one of the judges of the common pleas, and rode the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHAMPTONSHIRE">Northamptonshire</a> circuit. In the year 1474 he was, with many of the first <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, created <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> of the Bath. He died in 1481; and was buried in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORCESTER">Worcester</a>, where a marble <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a>, with his statue upon it, was erected to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>. As to his character as a lawyer, it is sufficient to inform the reader, that he was the author of the Treatise upon tenures, on which Sir Edward <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COKE">Coke</a> wrote a comment, well known by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Coke upon Littleton. Littleton, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a>, descended from an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHROPSHIRE">Shropshire</a>, was born in 1627, educated at Westminster school, and went to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> a student of Christ-church, whence he was ejected by the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> visitors in 1648. Soon after, he became usher of Westminster school, and in 1648 was made second <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of Westminster school. After the Restoration he taught a school at Chelsea in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MIDDLESEX">Middlesex</a>, of which church he was admitted rector in the year 1664. In 1670 he accumulated the degrees in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, being then chaplain in ordinary to his majesty. In 1674, he became prebendary of Westminster, of which church he was afterwards sub-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">dean</a>. Beside the well-known Latin and English <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>, he published several other works. He died in 1694, and was interred at Chelsea. He was an universal scholar; and extremely charitable, humane, and easy of access.

LITURGY

Pages 62-62

denotes all the ceremonies in general belonging to divine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. The word comes from the Greek λιτουργίας, "service, public ministry;" formed of λύτος, "public," and ἔργον, "<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>." In a more restrained signification, liturgy is used among the Romanists to signify the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a>; and among us the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>. All who have written on liturgies agree, that in the primitive days divine service was exceedingly simple, only clogged with a very few ceremonies, and consisting of but a small <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of prayers; but, by degrees, they increased the number of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> ceremonies, and added new prayers, to make the office look more awful and venerable to the people. At length things were carried to such a pitch, that a regulation became necessary; and it was found proper to put the service, and the manner of performing it, into <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>; and this was what they called a liturgy. Liturgies have been different at different times, and in different countries. We have the liturgy of St Chrysostom, that of St <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>, of St James, the liturgy of St <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>, the Armenian liturgy, the liturgy of the Maronites, of the Copts, the Roman liturgy, the Gallican liturgy, the English liturgy, the Ambrosian liturgy, the Spanish and African liturgies, &c. In the more early ages of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, every bishop had a power to form a liturgy for his own <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a>; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he kept to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> and doctrine, all circumstances were left to his own <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>. Afterwards the practice was for the whole <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> to follow the metropolitan church, which also became the general rule of the church; and this Lindwood acknowledges to be the common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> of the church; intimating, that the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of several services in the same province, which was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> in England, was not to be warranted but by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>. The liturgy of the church of England was composed in the year 1547, and established in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> year of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Edward IV. stat. 2. and 3. Ed. VI. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 1. In the fifth year of this king it was reviewed; because some things were contained in that liturgy which showed a compliance with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> of those times, and some exceptions were taken against it by some learned men at home, and by Calvin abroad. Some alterations were made in it, which consisted in adding the general confession and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTION">absolution</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> to begin with the ten commandments. The use of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> unction was left out, and also prayers for souls departed, and what tended to a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> of Christ's real presence in the eucharist. This liturgy, so reformed, was established by the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of 5 and 6 Ed. VI. cap. 1. However, it was abolished by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, who enacted that the service should stand as it was most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> used in the last year of the reign of King Henry VIII. The liturgy of 5 and 6 Ed. VI. was re-established with some few alterations and additions, by 1 Eliz. cap. 2. Some further alterations were introduced, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the review of the common-prayer book, by order of King James, in the first year of his reign; particularly in the office of private <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>, in several rubrics and other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a>, with the addition of five <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> six new prayers and thanksgivings, and all that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the catechism which contains the doctrine of the sacraments. The book of common-prayer, so altered, remained in force from the first year of King James to the fourteenth of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. But the last review of the liturgy was in the year 1661, and the last act of uniformity enjoining the observance of it is 13 and 14 Car. II. cap. 4. See COMMON-PRAYER. Many applications have been since made for a review, but hitherto without success.

LITUUS

Pages 62-64

among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, was the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAFF">staff</a> made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of by the augers in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-QUARTERING">quartering</a> the heavens. It bore a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> resemblance to the crozier of a bishop, but was shorter. It was crooked at one end, and thickest in the curved <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, according to A. Gellius. We frequently meet with a representation of it upon medals, amongst other pontifical instruments. It was called *Lituus Quirinalis*, from Quirinus, a name of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a>, who was skilled in all the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> of augury. *Lituus* was also an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of music in use in the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. It was straight, excepting that it had a little <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> at the upper end like a lituus <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> sacred staff of the augurs; and from the similitude it derived its name. *<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIVADIA">Livadia</a>*, anciently *Achaia* and *<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELLAS">Hellas</a>*, or *<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> properly so called*; a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Epirus and Thessaly, from which it is separated by Mount Oeta, now Banina, and by the Euripus, now the strait of Negropot; on the east, by the Archipelago; on the south, by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of Engia or Egina, the isthmus of Corinth, and the gulf of Leptanto; and on the west, by the Ionian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> and part of Epirus. Its <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> is about 130 miles from north-west to south-east; but its greatest breadth is not above 36 miles. It is in general a mountainous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; but neither unpleasant nor unfruitful. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> are, Mount Oeta in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOEOTIA">Boeotia</a>, where is the famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> of Thermopylae, not above 25 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARNASSUS">Parnassus</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELICON">Helicon</a>, and Cytheron in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHOCIS">Phocis</a>, which were sacred to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">muses</a>, and consequently much celebrated by the poets. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> of most <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a> are, the Sionapre, anciently the Achelous, the Cephissus, the Ismenus, and the Asopus. This province is at present divided into Livadia proper, Stramulippa, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>. The principal places are, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEPANTO">Lepanto</a>, anciently <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAUPACTUS">Naupactus</a>; Livadia, anciently Libadria or Lebadia; the celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Athens, now Setines; Thebes, now Stibes; Lepsina, anciently <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELEUSIS">Eleusis</a>; Castris, formerly <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DELPHI">Delphi</a>; and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEGARA">Megara</a>. *Livadia*, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town of Turkey in Europe, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a province of the same name in Greece. It is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and populous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, seated on the gulf of Lepanto, about 25 miles from the city of that name. It has now a considerable trade in woollen stuffs and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>. Anciently it was celebrated for the oracle of Trophonius, which was in a cavern in a hill above the town. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 23° 29'. N. Lat. 38° 40'. *<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVER">Liver</a>*, see Anatomy, No. 95.—<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>, and others of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, fix the principle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> in the liver; whence the Latin proverb, *Cogit amare jecur*: and in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> Horace frequently uses the word, as when he says, *Si torrefic jecur quærus Idonæum*. The Greeks, from its concave <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, called it *πάγκης*, "vaulted, suspended;" the Latins call it *jecur*, q. d. *juxta cor*, as being "near the heart." The French call it *foye*, from *foyer*, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FOCUS">focus</a>, or "fireplace;" agreeable to the doctrine of the ancients, who believed the blood to be boiled and prepared in it.—<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERASISTRATUS">Erasistratus</a>, at first, called it *<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARENCHYMA">parenchyma</a>*, i.e. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EFFUSION">effusion</a>, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of blood; and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HIPPOCRATES">Hippocrates</a>, by way of eminence, frequently calls it the *hypochondrium*. *Liver of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTIMONY">Antimony</a>*. See <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. *Liver of Arsenic*, is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> arsenic with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POTASH">potash</a>. See Arsenic, Chemistry Index. *Liver of Sulphur*. See Potash, Sulphuret of, Chemistry Index. *Liverwort*. See Marchantia and Lichen, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index. *<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-LIVERPOOL">Liverpool</a>*, a large, flourishing, and populous town of England, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANCASTER">Lancaster</a>, situated at the influx of the river <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERSEY">Mersey</a> into the sea, in North Lat. 53° 24', and West Long. 2° 50'. This town was of little importance till the end of the 17th century, but from that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> it has increased with extraordinary rapidity. In 1699 the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> was about 5000, and in 1710, when the first wet <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOCK">dock</a> was constructed, there were about 84 ships belonging to the port, averaging 70 tons and 11 men each. In 1720 an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> was procured for opening an inland <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MANCHESTER">Manchester</a>, and for improving the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with the Cheshire <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, both of which have been of immense advantage to Liverpool. In 1764 the population was 26,000, in 1790 it was 56,000, in 1801 it was 77,600, and in 1811 it was 94,376, exclusive of 7000 sailors. In 1793 she possessed 92,008 tons of shipping. In the year ending 5th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1818, the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of ships that entered the port amounted to 6779, the tonnage to 754,690. The dock duties, which in 1724 amounted to £10,113. 6d., were £6,915l. 8s. 8d. in 1815, when the official value of the imports was £8,000,000 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>, and of the exports £12,000,000. In 1818 the dock duties amounted to £98,538l. 8s. 3d. It is by far the greatest sea-port in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, except <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It has been estimated that one twelfth of the shipping of Great Britain is furnished by Liverpool; that it has one fourth of her foreign trade, and one sixth of her general <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>; and that its exports and imports amount to not less than one half of those of London. The Liverpool <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> have engaged eagerly in the trade to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> since it was thrown open. One vessel was sent out in 1815; next year there were eight vessels in the trade; in 1817 they were increased to 17, with a tonnage of 7538; and from the commencement to September 1818, no fewer than 80 vessels have been employed in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> trade. The exports in this trade are chiefly broad cloths and woollens, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRMINGHAM">Birmingham</a> hardware and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHEFFIELD">Sheffield</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTLERY">cutlery</a>, Manchester and Glasgow piece goods, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NOTTINGHAM">Nottingham</a> hosiery, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STAFFORDSHIRE">Staffordshire</a> earthen <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARE">ware</a>, Irish linens, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, salt, glass, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-HATS">hats</a>, malt liquors, and dollars. The imports are cotton, rice, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIGO">indigo</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALTPETRE">saltpetre</a>, ginger, pimento, and other spices, turmeric, safflower, and other dyes. The docks of Liverpool are upon a very extensive <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>. When the new one begun in 1816 is finished, the total space occupied by the whole <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> exceed 60 acres. They communicate with one another by tunnels, by which means the water of one is made to wash out the others, and carry off the mud. Along the docks are extensive warehouses, into which goods are removed from the ships with great ease. There are few manufactories in Liverpool. The most considerable are those for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> connected with the shipping, such as cordage. There is also an extensive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POTTERY">pottery</a>, some salt-works, glass-houses, and upwards of 50 breweries, from some of which large quantities of malt liquor are sent abroad. Many of the buildings are elegant; but the old streets are narrow; which defect will soon be removed, as the corporation Liverpool corporation have lately obtained an act of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> for the improvement of the town, which they have already begun to put in force with great spirit, having taken <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the principal streets in the centre of the town, and rebuilt them in a spacious and most magnificent manner; so that in a few years it will be one of the handsomest <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> in England. This town contains sixteen churches, namely, St <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>'s, St Nicholas's, St George's, St Thomas's, St Paul's, St Ann's, St John's, Trinity, St James's, St Catherine's, St <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>'s, St Stephen's, St Matthew's, St Mark's, Christ <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a>, and All Saints. There are also meetings for <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDEPENDENTS">independents</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANABAPTISTS">anabaptists</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUAKERS">quakers</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METHODISTS">methodists</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESBYTERIANS">presbyterians</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> is a noble structure, built of white <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> in the form of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, and round it are piazzas where the merchants assemble to transact business. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> is twice the extent of that of London. Above it are the mayor's offices, the sessions-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>-chamber, and two elegant <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a>-rooms. The expense of erecting this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> amounted to nearly £100,000. In its centre is a superb <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROUP">group</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRONZE">bronze</a> statuary, representing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Nelson. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CUSTOM_HOUSE"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> is situated at the head of the old dock, and is a handsome and convenient structure. Here are many charitable foundations, among which is an excellent <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> school well endowed, and many of the youth taught in it have exhibitions in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>. The infirmary is a large edifice of brick and stone, situated on a hill in a very pleasant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRY">airy</a> situation, at one end of the town. Above 1500 patients are admitted annually. In the town is a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>-school, supported by voluntary subscriptions and contributions, for 50 boys and 12 girls, who are not only clothed and educated, but also provided with food and lodging: likewise several almshouses for the widows of seamen; and an excellent <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>-house, superior to any in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, where upwards of 800 men, women, and children, are supported, many of whom are employed in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a> cotton and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>. The new prison is a noble edifice, and upon a very extensive scale. It is built entirely on the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of the great and benevolent Mr Howard, for solitary confinement; and is perhaps the most convenient, airy, magnificent building of the kind of Europe. Liverpool received its <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> John; but it was a borough by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESCRIPTION">prescription</a> long before his reign. It is under the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of a recorder, mayor, and an unlimited number of aldermen, two bailiffs, and a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> council of forty of the principal inhabitants, with a town-clerk and other proper officers. The town has a weekly market on Saturday, and is distant from London 224 miles. The income of the corporation is not less than £60,000 a-year. It sends two members to parliament, who are chosen like the magistrates, by the votes of all the free burgesses not receiving alms. The number who polled at the general <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> in 1818 was 2905. By means of inland navigation, Liverpool has communication with the rivers <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEE">Dee</a>, Ribble, Ouse, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a>, Darwent, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a>, Humber, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, Avon, &c.; which navigation, including its windings, extends above 500 miles, in the counties of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>, Nottingham, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WESTMORELAND">Westmoreland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STAFFORD">Stafford</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARWICK">Warwick</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEICESTER">Leicester</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORCESTER">Worcester</a>, &c. The Mersey, upon which the town is situated, abounds with salmon, cod, flounders, turbot, plaice, and smelts; and at full sea it is above two miles over. Fresh water is brought into the town by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a>, from some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> four miles off, pursuant to an act of parliament in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>. The dispensary of this town does <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and has been of the most singular advantage to the afflicted, since 172,273 diseased persons were cured between the years 1778 and 1794, being on an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> about 10,000 persons every year. The Union News Room was instituted on the 1st of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1801; the Lyceum much about the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, the erection of which cost the sum of £11,000l. and the Commercial News Room in 1803. The Liverpool <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> for the promotion of science, literature, and the arts, was founded in 1817. The institution for restoring drowned persons is worthy of notice, as more than 400 people have become objects of it since it was founded, and more than one half of that number have been restored. The Athenaeum, which comprises a news room and library, was projected in 1798, and finished before the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the year. There are four weekly papers published at Liverpool.

LIVERY

Pages 64-64

in matters of dress and equipage, a certain <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> and form of dress, by which noblemen and gentlemen choose to distinguish their servants. Liveries are usually taken from fancy, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in families by succession. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> cavaliers, at their tournaments, distinguished themselves by wearing the liveries of their mistresses: thus people of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> make their domestics wear their livery. Father Menestrier, in his Treatise of Carousals, has given a very ample account of the mixtures of colours in liveries. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DION">Dion</a> tells us, that Oenomas was the first who invented green and blue colours, for the troops which, in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CIRCUS">circus</a>, were to represent <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> fights. The Romish <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> has also her several colours and liveries; <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, for confessors and virgins, and in times of rejoicing; <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, for the dead; <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, for the apostles and martyrs; blue or violet, for penitents; and green, in times of hope. Formerly, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> men gave liveries to several, who were not of their family or servants, to engage them in their quarrels for that year; but this was prohibited by the statutes 1 Rich. II. 1 Hen. IV. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 27. 2 and 7 Hen. IV. 8 Hen. VI. cap. 4. 8 Ed. IV. cap. 2; and no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, of whatever condition, was allowed to give any livery, but to his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> officers, and counsel learned in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>. However, most of the above statutes are repealed by 3 Car. I. cap. 4. LIVERY of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEISIN">Seisin</a>, in Law, signifies delivering the possession of lands, &c. to him who has a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to them. LIVERYMEN of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, are a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of men chosen from among the freemen of each <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>. Out of this body the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a>-conceil, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>, and other superior officers for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, are elected; and they alone have the privilege of giving their votes for members of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, from which the rest of the citizens are excluded.

LIVIUS

Pages 64-67

Titus, the best of the Roman historians, as he is called by Mr Bayle, was born at Patavium <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a>. Few particulars of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> have been handed Livius handed <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to us. Coming to Rome, he acquired the notice and favour of Augustus, and there he <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> resided. Some have supposed, (for there is not any <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of it), that he was known to Augustus before, by certain Philosophical Dialogues which he had dedicated to him. Seneca says nothing of the dedication; but mentions the dialogues, which he calls historical and philosophical; and also some books, written purposely on the subject of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. Be this as it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, it is probable that he began his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> as soon as he was settled at Rome; and he seems to have devoted himself so entirely to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> he had undertaken, as to be perfectly regardless of his own advancement. The tumults and distractions of Rome frequently obliged him to retire to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>; not only that he might be less interrupted in the pursuit of his destined task, but also enjoy that retirement and tranquillity which he could not have at Rome, and which yet he seems to have much sought after: for he was greatly dissatisfied with the manners of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and tells us, that "he should reap this reward of his labour, in composing the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMAN_HISTORY">Roman history</a>, that it would take his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> from the present numerous evils, at least while he was employed upon the first and earliest ages." He used to read parts of this history, while he was composing it, to Mecenas and Augustus; and the latter conceived so <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of him, that he pitched upon him to superintend the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of his grandson Claudius, who was afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>. After the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Augustus, Livy returned to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his birth, where he was received with all imaginable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> and respect; and there he died, in the fourth year of the reign of Tiberius, aged above seventy. Some say, he died on the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> with Ovid: it is certain that he died the same year. Scarce any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> was ever more honoured, alive as well as dead, than this historian. Pliny the younger relates, that a native <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> travelled from <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GADES">Gades</a>, in the extremest parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, to see Livy: and, though Rome abounded with more stupendous and curious <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPECTACLES">spectacles</a> than any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> in the world, yet he immediately returned: as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a>, after having seen Livy, nothing farther could be worthy of his notice. A monument was erected to this historian in the temple of Juno, where was afterwards founded the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> of St Justin. There, in 1413, was discovered the following epitaph upon Livy: *Ossa Titii Livii Patavinii, omnium mortalium judicio digni, cujus prope invicto ca- lamo invicti populi Romani res gestae conscriberentur*; that is, "the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> of Titus Livius of Patavium, a man worthy to be approved by all mankind, by whose almost invincible <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEN">pen</a> the acts and exploits of the invincible <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> were written." These bones are said to be preserved with high reverence to this day, and are shown by the Paduans as the most precious remains. In 1451, Alphonsus, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Arragon, sent his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a>, Anthony Panormita, to desire of the citizens of Padua the bone of that arm with which this their famous countryman had written his history; and, obtaining it, caused it to be conveyed to Naples with the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> as a most invaluable relic. He is said to have recovered from an ill state of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> by the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> he found in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> this history: and therefore, out of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a>, put upon doing extraordinary honours to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of the writer. Panormita also who was a native of Palermo in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, and one of the ablest men of the 15th century, sold an estate to purchase this historian. The history of Livy, like other great works of antiquity, is transmitted down to us exceedingly mutilated and imperfect. Its books were originally a hundred and forty-two, of which are extant only thirty-five. The epistles of it, from which we learn their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, all remain, except those of the 136th and 137th books. Livy's books have been divided into decades, which some will have to have been done by Livy himself, because there is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> to every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECADE">decade</a>; while others suppose it to be a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> contrivance, since nothing about it can be gathered from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. The first decade, beginning with the foundation of Rome, is extant, and treats of the affairs of 460 years. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> decade is lost; the years of which are seventy-five. The third decade is extant, and contains the second Punic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, including eighteen years. It is reckoned the most excellent <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the history, as giving an account of a very long and sharp war, in which the Romans gained so many advantages, that no arms could afterwards withstand them. The fourth decade contains the Macedonian war against <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a>, and the Asiatic war against Antiochus, which take up the space of about 23 years. The five first books of the fifth decade were found at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORMS">Worms</a>, by Simon Gryneus, in 1431, but are very defective; and the remainder of Livy's history, which reaches to the death of Drusus in Germany in 746, together with the second decade, are supplied by Freinsheimius. Never man perhaps was furnished with greater advantages for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> a history than Livy. Besides his own great genius, which was in every respect admirably formed for the purpose, he was trained as it were in a city, at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the empress of the world, and in the politest reign that ever was; having scarcely had any other school than the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Augustus. He had access to the very best materials, such as the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of Sylla, Caesar, Labienus, Pollio, Augustus, and others, written by themselves. "What writers of memorials (says <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Bolingbroke), what compilers of the Materia Historica, were these! What genius was necessary to finish up the pictures that such masters had sketched! Rome afforded men that were equal to the task. Let the remains, the precious remains, of Sallust, of Livy, and of Tacitus, witness this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>.—What a school of public and private virtue had been opened to us at the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a> of learning, if the latter historians of the Roman commonwealth, and the first of the succeeding <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>, had come down to us entire! The few that are come down, though broken and imperfect, compose the best body of history that we have; nay, the only body of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> history that deserves to be an object of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>. It fails us indeed most at that remarkable and fatal <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, where our reasonable curiosity is raised the highest. Livy employed forty-five books to bring his history down to the end of the sixth century, and the breaking out of the third Punic war: but he employed ninety-five to bring it down from thence to the death of Drusus; that is, through the course of 120 or 130 years. Appian, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DION">Dion</a> Cassius, and others, nay, even Plutarch included, make us but <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> amends for what is lost of Livy." Speaking then of Tully's orations and letters, as the best best adventitious helps to supply this loss, he says, that the age in which Livy flourished, abounded with such materials as these: they were fresh, they were au- thentic; it was easy to procure them; it was safe to employ them. How he did employ them in executing the second part of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, we may judge from his execution of the first; and, I own, I should be glad to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>, if it were possible, what we have of this history for what we have not.
