Would you not be glad my Lord, to see, in one stupendous draught, the whole progress of that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to servitude; the whole <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of causes and effects, apparent and real, public and private?" &c. The encomiums bestowed upon Livy, by both an- cients and moderns, are great and numerous. He not only entertains like <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>; he also instructs and interests in the deepest manner. But his great probity, candour, and impartiality, are what have distinguished Livy above all historians; for neither complaisance to the times, nor his particular connexions with the emperor, could restrain him from speaking well of Pomp- eys; so well, as to make Augustus call him a Pom- peian. This we learn from Cremutius Cordus, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TA">Ta</a>- citus; who relates also, much to the emperor's ho- nour, that this gave no interruption to their friend- ship. But whatever eulogies Livy may have received as an historian, he has not escaped censure as a writer. In the age wherein he lived, Asinius Pollio <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> him with <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATAVINITY">Patavinity</a>; which Patavinity has been vari- ously explained by various writers, but is generally sup- posed to relate to his style. The most <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> is, that this noble Roman, accustomed to the delicacy of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> spoken in the court of Augustus, could not bear with certain <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> idioms, which Livy, as a Paduan, used in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> places of his history. Pignorius is of another opinion, and believes that this Patavinity regarded the orthography of certain words, wherein Livy used one <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> for another, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, writing sibe and quase for sibi and quasi; which he attempts to prove by several ancient inscrip- tions. The expressions, however, or the orthography of words, are not loaded with obscurity, and the per- fect classic is as familiarly acquainted with those sup- posed provincialisms as with the purest Latinity.—Livy has been censured too, and perhaps with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, for be- ing too credulous, and burdening his history with vul- gar notions and superstitious tales. He may disgust when he mentions that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a> and blood were rained from heaven, or that an ox spoke or a woman changed her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a>; yet he candidly confesses that he recorded only what made an indelible <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> upon the minds of a credulous age. Is it worth while to mention here the capricious and tyrannic humour of the emperor Caligula, who accused Livy of being a negligent and wordy writer, and resol- ved therefore to remove his works and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> out of all <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a> where he knew they were curiously preserved? Or the same humour in Domitian, another prodigy of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, who put to death Metius Pomposianus, because he made a collection of some orations of kings and gen- erals out of Livy's history? Pope Gregory the Great, also, would not suffer Livy in any Christian library, be- cause of the Pagan <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> wherewith he abounded: but the same reason held good against all ancient au- thors; and indeed Gregory's zeal was far from being levelled at Livy in particular, the pontiff having de- clared war against all <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> learning. Though we know nothing of Livy's family, yet we learn from Quintilian, that he had a son, to whom he addressed some excellent precepts in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>. An an- cient inscription speaks also of one of his daughters, named Livia Quarta: the same, perhaps, that espoused the orator Lucius Magius, whom Senecca mentions; and observes, that the applauses he usually received from the public in his harangues, were not so much on his own account, as for the sake of his father-in- <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>. Our author's history has been often published with and without the supplement of Freinsheimius. The best editions are, that of Gronovius, cum notis vario- rum et suis, Lugd. Bat. 1679, 3 vols. 8vo; and that of Le Clerc at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>, 1729, 10 vols. 12mo; and that of Crevier, at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, 1735, 6 vols. 4to. These have the supplements.—Learning perhaps never sustained a greater loss, in any single author, than by the destruc- tion of the latter and more interesting part of Livy. Several eminent moderns have indulged the pleasing ex- pectation that the entire work of this noble historian might yet be recovered. It has been said to exist in an Arabic version: and even a complete copy of the origi- nal is supposed to have been extant as late as the year 1631, and to have perished at that time in the plunder of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MAGDEBURG">Magdeburg</a>. The munificent <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of learning Leo X. exerted the most generous zeal to rescue from oblivion the valuable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>, which one of his most bigotted predecessors, above mentioned, had expelled from every Christian library. Bayle has preserved, un- der the article Leo, two curious original letters of that pontiff, concerning his hopes of recovering Livy; which afford most <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> proofs of his liberality in the cause of letters.—A lately discovered fragment of Li- vy's history was published in 1773 by Dr Bruns. <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-LIVIUS_ANDRONICUS">Livius Andronicus</a>, a comic poet who flourished at Rome about 240 years before the Christian era. He was the first who turned the personal satires and fescen- <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> verses, so long the admiration of the Romans, in- to the form of a proper <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIALOGUE">dialogue</a> and regular play. Though the character of a player, so valued and ap- plauded in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, was reckoned vile and despicable among the Romans, Andronicus acted a part in his dramatical compositions, and engaged the attention of his audience, by repeating what he had laboured after the manner of the Greeks. Andronicus was the freeman of M. Livius Salinator, whose children he educated. His <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> was grown obsolete in the age of Cicero, whose nicety and judgment would not even recommend the reading of it. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIVONIA">Livonia</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the Russian empire, with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a>. It is bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Esthonia, on the west by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGA">Riga</a>, on the south by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURLAND">Courland</a>, and on the east, partly by Ples- cow, and partly by Novogorod. It is about 200 miles from north to south, and 150 from east to west. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> is so fertile in corn, that it is called the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANARY">granary</a> of the north; and would produce a great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> more, if it was not so full of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>. The fish that abound here are salmons, carps, pikes, flat fish, and many others. In the forests there are wolves, bears, elks, rein-deer, stags, and hares. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> animals are very numerous; but the sheep bear very bad <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>. Here are a great number number of forests, which consist of birch trees, pines, and oaks; and all the houses of the inhabitants are built with wood. The merchandises which they send abroad are <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, wax, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> skins, and potatoes. The Swedes were formerly possessed of this province, but were obliged to abandon it to the Russians after the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Pultowa; and it was ceded to them by the peace of the north, concluded in 1722, which was confirmed by another <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> in 1742. It formerly included Estonia, with the two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> called Oesel and Dagho. Riga is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>.

LIVONICA-TERRA

Pages 67-67

a kind of fine <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALE">bale</a> used in the shops of Germany and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. It is found in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIVONIA">Livonia</a>, from whence it takes its name. It is in the form of little cakes.

LIVRE

Pages 67-67

a French <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> of account, containing 20 sols. See Money-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">Table</a>.

LIXIVIOUS

Pages 67-67

an appellation given to salts obtained from burnt vegetables by pouring <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> on their ashes.

LIXIVIUM

Pages 67-67

in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, &c., a ley obtained by pouring some liquor upon the ashes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; which is more <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> less powerful, as it has imbibed the fixed salts contained in the ashes.

LIXNAW

Pages 67-67

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BARONY">barony</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KERRY">Kerry</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, which gives <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of baron to the earls of Kerry; the village here of this name being their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> seat, where the castle was erected. This seat stands agreeably on the river Brick, which is here cut into several pleasant navigable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a>, that adorn its plantations and gardens. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9° 15'. N. Lat. 52° 15'. LIZARD. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LACERTA">Lacerta</a>, Reptology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Lizard, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">cape</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> promontory of Cornwall, situated, according to the most <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> computation, in W. Long. 5° 47'. N. Lat. 49° 50'. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LLANDAFF">LLANDAFF</a>. See Landaff.

LLOYD

Pages 67-67

WILLIAM, a most learned English writer and bishop, was born in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERKSHIRE">Berkshire</a> in England in 1627. He was educated under his father, rector of Sonning, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a> of Tyle-hurst in Berkshire; then went to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, and took orders. In 1660 he was made prebendary of Rippon; and in 1666 chaplain to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>. In 1667 he took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>; in 1672 he was installed <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANGOR">Bangor</a>; and in 1680 was consecrated bishop of St Asaph. He was one of the six <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> who, with Archbishop Sancroft, were committed prisoners to the tower of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, for subscribing a petition to the king against distributing and publishing his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a>. Soon after the Revolution he was made almoner to King William and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>: in 1692 he was translated to the bishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LITCHFIELD">Litchfield</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COVENTRY">Coventry</a>; and in 1699, to the see of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORCESTER">Worcester</a>, where he sat till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which happened in 1717, the 91st year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Dr Burnet gives him an exalted character, and his works are highly esteemed. LOACH. See Cobitis, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

LOAD

Pages 67-67
or LODE, in Mining, a word used especial- ly in the tin-mines, for any regular vein or course, whether metallic or not; but most commonly load means a metallic vein. When the substances forming these loads are reducible to metal, the loads are by the English miners said to be alive; otherwise they are termed dead loads. In Cornwall and Devonshire the loads chiefly hold their course from eastward to westward, though in other parts of England they frequently run from north to south. See Veins, Geology Index. Load also used for nine dishes of ore, each dish being about half a hundred weight. LOADSTONE. See Magnet.

LOAMS

Pages 67-67

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, are defined to be earths composed of dissimilar particles, stiff, dense, hard, and rough to the touch; not easily broke while moist, readily diffusible in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and composed of sand and a tough viscid clay. Of these loams some are whitish, and others <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>.

LOANDA

Pages 67-67

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGOLA">Angola</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. It is an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> about 15 miles in length, and three in breadth; remarkable chiefly for the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Angola situated upon it, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 12° 25'. S. Lat. 8° 45'. This town was built by the Portuguese in 1578, under the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the first Portuguese governor in these parts. It is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, populous, and pleasantly seated on the declivity of a hill near the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, and facing the south-west. The island is supplied with fresh <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a> dug in it; and which are not sunk below the depth of three feet when they are filled with excellent water. It is remarkable, however, that the water of these wells continues good only during the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> tide; for, as that sinks, the water becomes more and more brackish, till at last it is quite <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, almost as much as the sea itself. On the coast of this island are fished the zimbis, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> shells used in several parts of Africa instead of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>; and with these shells, instead of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, is carried on a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the traffic of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>.

LOANGO

Pages 67-68

a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, extending itself about 180 geographical miles in length from south to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>; that is, from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> St Catherine under the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of south latitude, to a small river called Lorando Louisia, on the 5th degree of the same. From west to east it extends from Cape Negro on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> towards the Buchumalcan <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, so called on account of the vast <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> droves of elephants, about 300 miles. It is divided into four <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> provinces, viz. those of Lovangiri, Loango-mongo, Chilongo, and Piri. The inhabitants are very <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, well shaped, and of a mild temper. The men wear <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> petticoats, from the waist downwards, and have a piece of cloth round their waist. The women's petticoats are made of straw. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> abounds with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a>, oxen, cows, sheep, goats, elephants, tigers, leopards, civet-cats, and other animals; so that there are great quantities of elephants <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, and fine furs, to be traded for. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, where the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> resides, called Louango, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a>, Boartic, is situated in South Lat. 4½ degrees, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> and a half from... Losango from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-coast, and is shaded and adorned with bananas, and other trees. The king, who resides in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> in the middle of it, has about 1500 concubines. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> any of them is surprised in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADULTERY">adultery</a>, she and her paramour are instantly conveyed to the top of a very <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> hill, whence they are hurled <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> headlong from the steepest <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. Every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> marries as many wives here as he pleases, who are obliged to get their husbands a livelihood, as is the practice all along the African coast inhabited by blacks. The women, therefore, cultivate the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, sow and reap, while the lazy husbands loiter away their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in idleness. The king's revenue consists in elephants' teeth, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, and a kind of petticoats made of palm-tree leaves, and called lavogus: he has whole store-houses full of these lavogus; but his greatest <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> consist in slaves of both sexes.

LOBBY

Pages 68-68

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, is a small <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> waiting-room: it is also an entrance into a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> apartment, where there is a considerable space between that and a portico or vestibule, and the length or dimensions <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not allow it to be considered as a vestibule or an anteroom. See Antichamber.

LOBELIA

Pages 68-68
Cardinal-flower; a genus of plants belonging to the syngenesia class; and in the natural method ranking under the 29th order, Campanaceae. See Botany Index.

LOBETUM

Pages 68-68

anciently a town of the Hither <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>: said to have been built by the Libyan <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, (Pliny). Now <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBARAZIN">Albarazin</a>, a town of Arragon on the confines of New Castile, on the river Guadalavir. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. N. Lat. 40° 40'.

LOBO

Pages 68-68

Jerome**, a Jesuit missionary, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a> in the year 1593. He became a member of the Jesuit <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> at 16 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and in 1622 went out as a missionary to the East Indies. He sailed to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOZAMBIQUE">Mozambique</a>, after making some stay at Goa; and afterwards penetrated into <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABYSSINIA">Abyssinia</a>, where his zeal and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> brought on him the hatred of the monks, from which he incurred much danger and suffering. As he returned to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a> he was shipwrecked on the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATAL">Natal</a>, where <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> months were spent in constructing shallops to bring them away. One of them founded, but that in which Father Lobo sailed arrived safe at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGOLA">Angola</a>. After a variety of adventures he arrived at Lisbon; and he employed himself in the cause of the Ethiopian mission both at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MADRID">Madrid</a> and Rome. He took a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> voyage to the Indies, where he was made rector of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> at Goa. He returned to Lisbon in 1658, and was chosen rector of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COIMBRA">Coimbra</a>, where he died in 1678, at the age of 84. Lobo wrote an historical account of Abyssinia in the Portuguese <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, which contains information both curious and valuable. It was translated into French by the abbé le <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a> in 4to, in 1728; and the earliest production of Dr Samuel Johnson was an abridged version of this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>.

LOCAL

Pages 68-68

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, something fixed to the freehold, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> tied to a certain <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; thus, real actions are local, since they must be brought in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> where they <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a>; and local customs are those peculiar to certain countries and places. **Local Medicines**, those destined to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> upon particular parts; as fomentations, epithems, vesicatories, &c.

LOCARNO

Pages 68-68

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a bailiwick of the same name, seated at the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> end of the lake Maggiore, near the river Magia. It carries on a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> trade; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> abounds in pastures, wine, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>. It contains 1500 inhabitants. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8. 41'. N. Lat. 46. 6.

LOCH-LOMOND

Pages 188-188

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> lake of Dunbarton <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Lennox-shire in Scotland, of which Mr Pennant gives the following <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>. "Loch-Lomond, the last, the most beautiful of the Caledonian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>. The first view of it from Tarbet presents an extensive serpentine winding amidst lofty hills; on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, barren, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, and rocky, which darken with their <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> that contracted <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. On the west side, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> are clothed near the bottoms with woods of oak quite to the water edge; their summits lofty, naked, and craggy. On the east side, the mountains are equally <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; but the tops form a more even ridge <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the lake, except where Benlomond, like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAUL">Saul</a> amidst his companions, overtops the rest. The upper parts were black and barren; the lower had <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> marks of fertility, or at least of industry, for the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> corn was finely contrasted with the verdure of the groves intermixed with it. "This eastern boundary is part of the Grampian hills, which extend from hence through the counties of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERTH">Perth</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGUS">Angus</a>, Mearns and Aberdeen. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> runs sometimes through woods; at others is exposed and naked; in some, so steep as to require the support of a wall; the whole the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of the soldiery: blessed <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> of instruments of destruction for those that give safety to the traveller, and polish to the once Loch-inaccessible native! Two great headlands covered with trees separate the first <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> from one totally different; the last is called the Point of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIRKIN">Firkin</a>. On passing this <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">cape</a> an expanse of water bursts at once on your eye, varied with all the softer beauties of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. Immediately beneath is a flat covered with wood and corn: beyond, the headlands stretch far into the water, and consist of gentle risings; many have their surfaces covered with wood, others adorned with trees loosely scattered either over a fine verdure or the purple bloom of the heath. Numbers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> are dispersed over the lake, of the same elevated form as the little capes, and wooded in the same manner; others <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> peep above the surface, and are tufted with trees; and numbers are so disposed as to form magnificent vistas between. "Opposite Luss, at a small distance from shore, is a mountainous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> almost covered with wood; it is near half a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and has a most fine effect. I could not <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of islands, but was told there are 28; the largest two miles long, and stocked with deer. "The length of this charming lake is 24 miles; its greatest breadth 8; its greatest depth, which is between the point of Firkin and Benlomond, is 120 fathoms. Besides the fish <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to the lochs are gunniads, called here poans. "The surface of Loch-Lomond has for several years past been observed gradually to increase, and invade the adjacent shore: and there is reason to suppose that churches, houses, and other buildings, have been lost in the water. Near Luss is a large heap of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> at a distance from the shore, known by the name of the old <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; and about a mile to the south of that, in the middle of a large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, between Camstraddan and the isle Inch-tavanack, is another heap, said to have been the ruins of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. To confirm this, it is evident by a passage in Camden's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATLAS">Atlas</a> Britannica, that an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, existing in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, is now lost; for he speaks of the isle of Camstraddan, placed between the lands of the same name and Inch-tavanack, in which, adds he, was an house and orchard. Besides this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>, large trees with their branches still adhering are frequently found in the mud near the shore, overwhelmed in former times by the increase of water. This is supposed to be occasioned by the vast quantities of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> and gravel that are continually brought <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by the mountain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, and by the falls of the banks of the Leven; the first filling the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> of the lake, the last impeding its discharge through the bed of the river."

LOCHABER

Pages 68-68

a district of the shire of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERNESS">Inverness</a> in Scotland. It is bounded by Moydart on the west, Glengarry on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, Badenoch on the east, and Iorn on the south. It derives its name from the lake <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> loch Aber; and extends about 20 miles from east to west, and 30 from north to south. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is barren, bleak, mountainous, and rugged. Near the mouth of the river Aber, in the centre between the West and North Highlands, stands Fort William, with the town of Maryburgh, built upon a navigable arm of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, not far from the foot of Ben <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEVIS">Nevis</a>. The town, designed as a saltery for the garrison, was erected into a borough; and the fort itself was designed as a check upon some of the clans, who had been guilty of depredations and other irregularities. Lochaber is inhabited mostly by the Macdonalds, Camerons, and Mackintoshes. The castle of Macdonald of Glengary, in this district, was burnt to the ground in the year 1715, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of his declaring for the Pretender. The elegant <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> and gardens belonging to Cameron of Lochiel underwent the same fate, for the same reason, in the year 1746.

LOCHIA

Pages 68-68

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MIDWIFERY">Midwifery</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUX">flux</a> from the uterus consequent to delivery. See Midwifery.

LOCK

Pages 72-72
or Weir, in inland navigations, the general name for all those works of wood or stone made to confine and raise the water of a river: the banks also which are made to divert the course of a river, are called by these names in some places. But the term lock is more particularly appropriated to express a kind of canal enclosed between two gates; the upper called by workmen the sluice gate, and the lower called the flood gate. These serve in artificial navigations to confine the water, and render the passage of boats easy in passing up and down the stream. See CANAL.

LOCKE

Pages 72-72

JOHN, an eminent English <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> and writer in the latter end of the 17th century, was son of Mr John Locke of Pensford in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOMERSETSHIRE">Somersetshire</a>, and born at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WRINGTON">Wrington</a>, near <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a>, in 1632. He was sent to Christ-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>; but was highly dissatisfied with the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> course of studies then pursued in the university, where nothing was taught but the Aristotelian <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>; and had a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> aversion to the disputes of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> then in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. The first books which gave him a relish for philosophy were the writings of Des Cartes: for though he did not always approve of his notions, yet he thought he wrote with great perspicuity. He applied himself with vigour to his studies, particularly to physic, in which he gained a considerable knowledge, though he never practised it. In 1664, he went to Germany as secretary to Sir William Swan, envoy from the English <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a> and some other German princes. In less than a year, he returned to England; where, among other studies, he applied himself to that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> philosophy, as appears from a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a> of the changes of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, which he kept at Oxford from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 24, 1666, to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 28, 1667. There he became acquainted with the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> Ashly, afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHAFTESBURY">Shaftesbury</a>, who introduced him into the conversation of some of the most eminent persons of that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. In 1670, he began to form the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">Human</a> Understanding; but his employments and avocations prevented him from finishing it then. About this time he became a member of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>. In 1672, his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a>, now earl of Shaftesbury, and lord <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of England, appointed him secretary of the presentations, which <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> he held till the earl resigned the great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>. In 1673, he was made secretary to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> of trade, worth £500 a-year; but that commission was dissolved in 1674. The earl of Shaftesbury being restored to favour, and made <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> in 1679, sent for Mr Locke to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; but that nobleman did not continue <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>, being sent prisoner to the Tower; and after his discharge retired to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> in 1682. Mr Locke followed his patron thither. He had not been absent from England a year, when he was accused at court of having written certain tracts against the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, which were afterward discovered to be written by another person; and in November 1684, Locke he was deprived of his place of student in Christchurch. In 1685, the English envoy at the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAGUE">Hague</a> demanded him and 83 other persons to be delivered up by the states general: upon which he lay concealed till the year following; and during this time formed a weekly <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> with Mr Limboreh, Mr Le Clerc, and other learned men at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>. In 1689 he returned to England in the fleet which conveyed the princess of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>; and endeavoured to procure his restoration to his place of student of Christ-church, that it might appear from thence that he had been unjustly deprived of it: but when he found the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> would admit him only as a supernumerary student, he desisted from his claim. Being esteemed a sufferer for revolution principles, he might easily have obtained a more profitable post; but he contented himself with that of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMISSIONER">commissioner</a> of appeals, worth £500 a-year, which was procured for him by the lord Mordaunt; and about the same time he was offered an appointment in a diplomatic character, but the infirm state of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> prevented him from accepting it. He went afterwards to reside with Sir Francis <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASHAM">Masham</a> and his lady, at Oates in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>, about 25 miles from London, where he spent most of his time during the rest of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. In this agreeable situation he enjoyed that health and vigour which enabled him to exert his talents in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> on <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> subjects. Hence he appears in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the revolution in one piece; and considering the great national concern at that time, the ill state of the silver <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, and proposing remedies for it, in others. Hence he was made a commissioner of trade and plantations in 1695, which engaged him in the immediate business of the state; and with regard to the church, he published a treatise the same year, to promote the scheme which <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> William had much at heart, of a comprehension with the dissenters. This, however, drew him into one controversy; which was scarcely ended, when he entered into another in defence of his essay, which he held till 1668; soon after which the asthma, his constitutional disorder, increasing with his years, began to subdue him; and he became so infirm, that in 1700 he resigned his seat at the board of trade, because he could no longer bear the air of London sufficient for a regular attendance upon it. After this resignation he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> altogether at Oates; in which retirement he employed the remaining last years of his life entirely in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the Holy Scriptures. He died in 1704, aged 73. His writings <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> immortalize his name. The earl of Shaftesbury, author of the Characteristics, though in one place he speaks of Mr Locke's philosophy with severity; yet observes, concerning his Essay on the Human Understanding, in general, "that it may qualify men as well for business and the world, as for the sciences and the university." His Discourses on Government, Letters on Toleration, and Commentaries on some of St Paul's Epistles, are also held in much esteem. LOCKED JAW. See MEDICINE <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

LOCKMAN

Pages 72-72

an officer in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">Man</a>, who executes the orders of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, much like our undersheriff.

LOCLE

Pages 72-75

a town in a district of the same name <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, adjacent to Neuchatel and Vallen- gin, and united with another named La Ghoux de Fond. But these districts occupy some valleys formed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JURA">Jura</a>; the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of which not many years ago was one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> forest, though now converted into fine pasture ground filled with flour- ishing villages. The inhabitants are remarkable for their industry, and excel in many <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> arts, par- ticularly in watch and clock making; 40,000 watches, it is said, are made in a year. The most singular ob- ject at this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, is three subterranean <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>, erected on the river Bied, vertically above one another, and 100 feet below the surface of the ground.

LOCRI

Pages 75-75

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of Achaia in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>; twofold, and divided by Mount <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARNASSUS">Parnassus</a>. The Hither was oc- cupied by the Locri Ozolae, called also Zephyrii, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Western, contained between Aetolia and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHOCIS">Phocis</a>. The Farther Locris lay beyond Parnassus, running out to- wards Thermopylae, and reaching to the Euripus of Euboea; occupied by the Locri Opuntii, and Epicnem- idi, who were called the Eastern Locri.

LOCULAMENTA

Pages 75-75

and Loculi, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, cells <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pockets: The internal divisions of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPSULE">capsule</a>, or other dry seed-vessel, enclosing the seeds. LOCUST. See Gryllus, Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Locust-Eaters. See Acridophagi. American Locust, or Frog-hopper. See Cicada, Entomology Index. Locust-Tree. See Hymenaea and Gleditsia, Bo- tany Index.

LOCUS GEOMETRICUS

Pages 75-75

denotes a line by which a local <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDETERMINATE">indeterminate</a> problem is solved. A locus is a line, any point of which may equally solve an indeterminate problem. Thus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> line suffice for the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of the equation, it is called locus <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> rectum; if a circle, locus ad circulum; if a pa- rabola, locus ad parabolam; if an ellipse, locus ad elip- sin: and so of the rest of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONIC_SECTIONS">conic sections</a>.

LOCUTIUS

Pages 75-75

in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">Mythology</a>, the god of speech a- mong the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, called by Livy Anis Locutius. LUCOTORIUM. A <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> apartment in monas- teries, where the monks and other <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> met after dinner to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a> together.

LODGMENT

Pages 75-75

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> affairs, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> made by the besiegers in some <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of a fortification (after the besieged have been driven out), to maintain it, and be covered from the enemy's fire.

LOG

Pages 75-79

in the Jewish antiquities, a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> which held a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a cab, and consequently five-sixths of a pint. There is mention of a log, 2 Kings vi. 25. under the name of a fourth <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of a cab. But in Levi- ticus the word log is often met with, and signifies the measure of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> which lepers were to offer at the temple after they were cured of their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>. Dr Ar- buthnot says, that the log was a measure of liquids, the seventy-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> part of the bath <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ephah, and twelfth part of the hin, according to all the accents of the Jewish writers. Log, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, signifying a small piece of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> a, (fig. 3.) of a triangular, sectoral, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUADRANTAL">quadrantal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, on board a ship, generally about a quarter of an inch thick, and five or six inches from the angular point to the circumference. It is balanced by a thin plate of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, nailed to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>, or circular side, so as to swim perpendicularly in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. Log-Line, a little <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a>, or line, about a hundred and fifty fathoms <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, fastened to the log by means of two legs a b (fig. 4.), one of which passes through a hole at the corner, and is knotted on the opposite side, while the other leg is attached to the arch by a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIN">pin</a> fixed into another hole, so as to draw out occasionally. By these legs the log is hung in equilibrio; and the line thus annexed to it is wound round a reel (fig. 2.), fixed for that purpose in the gallery of the ship. This line, from the distance of about ten, twelve, or fifteen fathoms off the log, has certain knots or divisions, which ought to be at least fifty feet from each other; though it was the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> practice at sea not to have them above forty-two feet asunder. The length of each knot ought to be the same part of a sea <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> as half a minute is of an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>; and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a>- mitting the measurement of Mr Norwood, who makes a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> on a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> circle of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> to contain 367,200 English feet, or about 69½ English statute miles, and therefore ⅝ th part of it, or a nautical mile, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be 6120 feet; ⅝ th of 6120, or 51 feet, should be the length of each knot. But because it is safer to have the reckoning rather before the ship than after it, therefore fifty feet may be taken as the pro- per length of each knot. The knots are sometimes made to consist only of forty-two feet each, even in the present practice; and this method of dividing the log- line was founded on the supposition that 60 miles, each of 5000 English feet, made a degree; for ⅝ of 5000 is 41⅔, or, in round numbers, 42 feet. Mari- ners rather than quit the old way, though known to be erroneous, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> glasses for half minute ones, that run but 24 or 25 seconds. They have also used a line of 45 feet or 30 seconds, or a glass of 28 seconds to 42 feet. When this is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, the distance between the knots should be corrected by the following pro- portion: as 30 is to 50; so is the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of seconds of the glass to the distance between the knots upon the line. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> or moisture of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> has of- ten a considerable effect upon the glass, so as to make it run slower or faster; it should, therefore, be fre- quently tried by the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENDULUM">pendulum</a> in the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>- ner. On a round nail hang a string that has a musket- <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> fixed to one end, carefully measuring between the centre of the ball and the string's loop over the peg 39½ inches, being the length of a second pendulum; then swing it, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> one for every <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> it passes under the peg, beginning at the second time it passes, and the number of swings made during the time the glass is running out shows the seconds it contains. The line also is liable to relax and shrink, and should there- fore be occasionally measured. The use of the log and line is to keep account and make an estimate of the ship's way or distance run; which is done by observing the length of line unwound in half a minute's time, told by a half-minute glass; for so many knots as run out in that time, so many miles the ship sails in an hour. Thus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> there be four knots veered out in half a minute, the ship is computed to run four miles an hour. The author of this device for measuring the ship's way is not known; and no mention of it occurs till the year 1671, in an East <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> voyage published by Purchas; but from that time its name occurs in other voyages among his collections; and henceforward it was taken notice of both by our own authors and by foreigners; as by Gunter in 1623; Snellius in 1624; and almost by all the succeeding writers on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>. To Heave the Log, as they call it, they throw it into the water on the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEE">lee</a>-side, letting it run till it comes without the eddy of the ship's wake; then one holding a half-minute glass, turns it up <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> as the first knot, or the mark from which the knots begin to be reckoned, turns off the reel (fig. 2.) or passes over the stern. As soon as the glass is out, the reel is stopped, and the knots run off are told, and their parts estimated. It is usual to heave the log once every hour in ships of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> and East Indiamen, and in all other vessels once in two hours, allowance being made for the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> having increased or abated in the intervals. The log is a very precarious way of computing, and must always be corrected by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, there being much uncertainty from the motions of the ship, the winds of variable force, the friction of the reel and lightness of the log in the course of the current. Yet this is a much more exact way of computing than any other in use; much preferable certainly to that of the Spaniards and Portuguese, who guessed at the ship's way by the running of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FROTH">froth</a> or water by the ship's side; or to that of the Dutch, who used to heave a chip overboard, and to number the paces they walk on the deck while the chip swims between any two marks or bulk heads on the side. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOUND">Compound</a> Log. The above-mentioned errors, and particularly the log's being subject to drive with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the water at its surface, whereas the experiment requires it to be fixed in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where it is when the mark commencing the knots goes off the reel, have been considered, and many methods proposed to remove or to lessen them. M. Bouguer proposed the following method. Take for the log a conical piece of wood, which fix to the log-line passed through or along its axis, at about 40°, 50°, or 60°, or more feet, from one end; and to this end fix the diver, which is a body formed of two equal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> pieces of tin, or of thin <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> plate, fixed at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> to one another along their diagonals; and its size so fitted to that of the cone, that the whole may float. A cone of three inches diameter in the base, and of six inches in the slant height, is proposed by M. Bouguer to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> a diver made of plates about 9½ inches square; the intersection of the diagonals is joined to the log-line, and the loop and peg fixed as in the common log. However, it has been found, that no kind of wood used in British dockyards, when formed into a cone of the above dimensions, will float a diver made of stout tin-plates, one side of the square being 9½ inches. Such a diver weighing 1½ lb. avoirdupois, required to float it a cone of five inches diameter and twelve inches on the slant side, so as the point of the cone, which was made of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> fir, should just appear above the water. Now, supposing one side of such a square tin diver to be about ten inches, and made of plates only two-thirds of the thickness of the former, such a diver would weigh, with its solder, about 20 ounces, and can be floated by a light fir cone of four inches diameter in the base, and ten inches in the slant height or length; and such a compound log might perhaps be found on <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> to be affected by about as much again as that proposed by M. Bouguer; and consequently the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the numbers given by the common log and compound log, must be augmented by two-thirds of itself for the necessary correction as below. When the compound log of Bouguer, above described, is hove overboard, the diver will sink too deep to be much affected by the current or motion of water at the surface, and the log will thereby keep more steadily in the place where it first fell; and consequently the knots run off the reel will show more accurately the ship's rate of sailing. As the common log is affected by the whole motion of the current, so this compound log will feel only a part thereof, viz. such a part nearly as the resistance of the cone is to the resistance of the diver; then the resistances of the above cone and diver are about as 1 to 5; and consequently this log will drive but one-fifth part of what the common log would do; and so the ship's true run will be affected by one-fifth only of the motion of the waters. To obtain the true rate of sailing, it will be proper to heave alternately, hour and hour, the common log, and this compound log; then the difference of their knots run off, augmented by its one-fourth part, is the correction; which applied to the knots of the common log, will give the ship's true rate of sailing at the middle time between the hours when these logs were hove. The correction is additive when the compound log's run is the greatest, otherwise it is subtractive. To find the course made good: increase the observed <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> between the log <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> by one-fourth part; and this gives the correction to be applied to the apparent course, or the opposite of that shown by the common log; the correction is to be applied to the right of the apparent course, when the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> of the common log is to the left of the compound log. Or, thus: the lengths run off both logs, together with their bearings, being known; in a card or compass apply the knots run off, taken from a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> of equal parts along their respective bearings from the centre; join the ends; and in this line produced, on the side next the compound log's length, take one-fourth of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a>; then a line drawn from the end, thus produced, to the centre of the card, will show the true course and distance made good. When a current, such as a tide, runs to any depth, the velocity of that current may be much better ascertained by the compound log than by the common one, provided the diver does not descend lower than the run of the current; for as those ships which are deepest immersed, drive fastest with the tide; so the diver, by being acted on below, as well as the log on the surface, their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> motion will give the total effect of the current's motion better than what could be derived from the motion at the surface only. Also, by such a compound log, the depth to which any current runs may be easily tried. Other Logs. We have an account in the voyage to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> LOG North Pole, p. 97, of two other logs, which were tried by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Phipps; one invented by Mr Russel, the other by Foxon; both constructed upon this principle, that a spiral, in proceeding its own length in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of its axis through a resisting medium, makes one revolution round the axis; if therefore the revolutions of the spiral arc registered, the number of times it has gone its own length through the water will be known. In both these the motion of the spiral in the water is communicated to the clockwork within board, by means of a small line fastened at one end to the spiral, which tows it after the ship, and at the other to a spindle, which sets the clockwork in motion. That invented by Mr Russel has a half spiral of two threads, made of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, and a small <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIAL">dial</a> of clockwork, to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a> the number of turns of the spiral. The other log has a whole spiral of wood with one thread, and a larger piece of clockwork with three dials, two of them to mark the distance, and the other divided into knots and fathoms, to show the rate by the half-minute glass, for the convenience of comparing it with the log. This kind of log will have the advantage of every other in smooth water and moderate weather; and it will be useful in finding the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TRIM">trim</a> of a ship when alone, in surveying a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> in a single ship, or in measuring distances in a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> between headlands and shoals; but it is subject to other inconveniences, which will not render it a proper substitute for the common log. Perpetual Log, a machine so called by its inventor, Mr Gottlieb of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, is intended for keeping a constant and regular account of the rate of a ship's velocity in the interval of heaving the log. Fig. 1. is a representation of the whole machine; the lower part of which, EFG, is fixed to the side of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEEL">keel</a>; H representing only the boundary line of the ship's figure. EF are the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECTION">section</a> of a wooden <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> case, left open at the ends KL, to admit the passage of the water during the motion of the ship. At M is a copper grating, placed to obstruct the entrance of any dirt, &c., into the machine. I is a section of a water wheel, made from 6 to 12 inches in diameter, as may be necessary, with floatboards upon its circumference, like a common water wheel, that turn by the resistance of the water passing through the channel LK. It turns upon a shouldered axis, represented by the vertical section at K. When the ship is in motion, the resistance of the water through the channel LK turns round the wheel I. This wheel, by means of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PINION">pinion</a>, is connected with and turns the rod contained in the long copper tube N. This rod, by a pinion fixed at its upper extremity, is connected with and turns upon the whole system of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a> contained in the dial of the case ABCD. This dial, by means of the copper tube N, may be fixed to any convenient place aboard the ship. In the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of the dial are several useful circular graduations, as follow: The reference by the dotted line A has a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> which is moved by the wheels within, which <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> out the motion of the ship in fathoms of 6 feet each. The circle at B has a hand showing the knots, at the rate of 48 feet for each knot; and is to be observed with the half-minute glass at any time. The circle at C has a short and a long hand; the former of which points out the mile in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> measure, and the latter or longer the number of knots contained in each mile, viz. 128, which is in the same proportion to a mile as 60 minutes to the hour in the reckoning. At e, a small portion of a circle is seen through the front plate called the register; which shows, in the course of 24 hours (if the ship is upon one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TACK">tack</a>) the distance in miles that she has run; and in the 24 hours the mariner need take but one observation, as this register serves as an useful check upon the fathoms, knots, and miles, shown upon the two other circles. f Is a plate showing 100 degrees or 6000 miles, and also acts as another register or check; and is useful in case of any mistake being made in observing the distant run by the other circles. The reckoning by these circles, without fear of mistake, may therefore be <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to nearly 12,000 miles. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> from this machine may easily be made to the captain's bedside, where by touching a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> only, a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELL">bell</a> in the head ABCD will <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> as many times in a half minute as the ship sails miles in an hour. Log-Board, a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, divided into several columns, containing the hours of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> and night, the direction of the winds, the course of the ship, and all the material occurrences that happen during the 24 hours, or from noon to noon; together with the latitude by observation. From this table the officers of the ship are furnished with materials to compile their journals. Log-Book, a book into which the contents of the log-board is daily copied at noon, together with every circumstance deserving notice that may happen to the ship, either at sea or in a harbour. See Navigation.
