But his best works are portraits; and of these he produced a considerable number, which are esteemed. They are mostly after Vandyck.—He also engraved historical subjects, from Poussin, Raphael, Annibal Carracci, Guido, and other masters. LOMENTACEÆ, in Botany, (from lomentum, a colour used by painters), the name of the 33d order in Linnaeus's Fragments of a Natural Method, consisting of the following genera, many of which furnish beautiful tinctures that are used in dyeing, viz. adenanthera, baubinia, cesalpina, cassia, ceratonia, cercis, gleditsia, guilandina, haematoxylon, hymenaea, mimosa, parisonia, poinciana, polygana. See BOTANY.

LOMONOZOF

Pages 188-222

a celebrated Russian poet, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> refiner of his native tongue, was the son of a dealer in fish at Kolmogori: he was born in 1711, and was fortunately taught to read; a rare circumstance at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> for a person of his station in Russia. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> genius for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> was first kindled by the perusal of the Song of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>, done into <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> by Polotski, whose rude compositions, perhaps scarcely superior to our version of the psalms by Sternhold and Hopkins, inspired him with such an irresistible <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">muses</a>, that he fled from his father, who was desirous of compelling him to marry, and took refuge in the Kaikonospaski <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOSCOW">Moscow</a>; there he had Lomonozof had an opportunity of indulging his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for letters and of studying the Greek and Latin languages. In this seminary he made so considerable progress in polite literature, as to be noticed and employed by the Imperial Academy of Sciences. In 1736 he was sent at the expense of that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, to the university of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARBURG">Marburg</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HESSE">Hesse</a> Cassel, where he became a scholar of the celebrated Christian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WOLF">Wolf</a>, under whom he studied universal <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. He <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> at Marburg four years, during which time he applied himself with indefatigable diligence to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>, which he afterwards pursued with still greater success, under the famous Henckel at Freyberg in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>. In 1741 he returned into Russia; was chosen in 1742 adjunct to the Imperial Academy; and in the ensuing year member of that society and professor of chemistry. In 1760 he was appointed inspector of the seminary then annexed to the academy; in 1764 he was gratified by the late empress with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of counsellor of state, and died April 4th that year, in the 54th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Lomonozof excelled in various kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>: but his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> merit, by which he bears the first <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> among the Russian writers, is derived from his poetical compositions, the finest of which are his odes. The first was written in 1739, while he studied in Germany, upon the taking of Kotschin, a fortress in Crim <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>, by Marshal Munich. The odes of Lomonozof are greatly admired for originality of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>, sublimity of sentiment, and energy of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>; and compensate for the turgid style which, in some instances, has been imputed to them, by that spirit and fire which are the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> characteristics in this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of composition. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PINDAR">Pindar</a> was his great <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a>; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we may give <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> to a person well versed in the Russian tongue, he has succeeded in this daring attempt to imitate the Theban bard, without incurring the censure of Horace. In this, as well as several other species of composition, he enriched his native language with various kinds of metre, and seems to have merited the appellation bestowed upon him of the Father of Russian Poetry. A <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a> recapitulation of the principal works of Lomonozof, which were printed in three volumes oe-Lomonozof, tavo, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> serve to show the versatility of his genius, and his extensive knowledge in various branches of literature. The first volume, besides a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">Preface</a> on the advantages derived to the Russian tongue from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> writings, contains ten sacred and nineteen <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a> odes, and several occasional pieces of poetry. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> comprises An <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> in Prose on the Rules for Russian Poetry; Translation of a German Ode; Idylls; Tamira and Selim, a tragedy; Demophoon, a tragedy; Poetical Epistle on the Utility of Glass; two cantos of an epic poem, entitled, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> the Great; A Congratulatory Copy of Verses; An Ode; Translation of Baptist Rousseau's Ode Sur le Bonheur; Heads of a Course of Lectures on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY">Natural Philosophy</a>; certain <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> translated in verse and prose, according to the original, from Cicero, Erasmus, Lucian, Ælian, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMMIANUS_MARCELLINUS">Ammianus Marcellinus</a>, Quintus Curtius, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, Martial, Ovid, Horace, and Seneca, which Russian translations were brought as examples in his Lectures upon Rhetoric; lastly, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">Description</a> of the Comet which appeared in 1744. The third volume consists chiefly of Speeches and Treatises read before the Academy; Panegyric on the Empress <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>; on Peter the Great; Treatise on the Advantages of Chemistry; on the Phenomena of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">Air</a> occasioned by the Electrical Fire, with a Latin translation of the same; on the Origin of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">Light</a> as a new <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">Theory</a> of Colours; Methods to determine with precision the course of a Vessel; on the origin of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-METALS">Metals</a> by the means of Earthquakes; Latin Dissertation on Solidity and Fluidity; on the Transit of Venus in 1761, with a German translation. Besides these various subjects, Lomonozof made no inconsiderable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, having published two small works relative to that of his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The first, styled Annals of the Russian Sovereigns, is a short <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">chronology</a> of the Russian monarchs; and the second is, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> History of Russia, from the Origin of that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">Nation</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">Death</a> of the Great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> Yaroslaf I. in 1054; a performance of great merit, as it illustrates the most difficult and obscure <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> in the annals of this country. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. London, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MIDDLESEX">Middlesex</a> in England, the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> of Great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, and one of the most wealthy and populous cities in the world, is situated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, in 51° 31' <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude, 400 miles south of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, and 270 south-east of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>; 180 miles west of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>, 210 north-west of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, 500 south-west of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPENHAGEN">Copenhagen</a>, 600 north-west of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a>, 700 south-west of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STOCKHOLM">Stockholm</a>, 800 north-east of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MADRID">Madrid</a>, 820 north-west of Rome, 850 north-east of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a>, 1360 north-west of Constantinople, and 1414 south-west of Moscow. This city was by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> first called Londinium <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Landinum, as we find it in Tacitus, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, Antoninus, and Ammianus. That name was afterwards changed into Augusta. How <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> this name prevailed, is not certainly known; but after the establishment of the Saxons we find it called Caer Lundain, Lundoun Byrig, Lunden Ceaster, Lunden-ye, Lundenne, Lunden-beth or Lundenburg; since the Conquest the records call it Londinia, Lundonia, Londine, Londres; and, for several ages past, it has been called London, a manifest corruption from Tacitus's Londinium. The most probable derivation of these names appears to be, either from the British words thong, "a ship," and din, "a town," i.e. a town or harbour for ships; or from Llin, "a lake," i.e. Llin din, "the town upon the lake," the Surry side being supposed, upon very probable grounds, to have been anciently a great expanse of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. Londinium, however, was not the primitive name of this famous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, which existed before the invasion of the Romans; being, at the time of Caesar's arrival in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the Trinobantes or Trinouantes. The name of this nation, as appears from Baxter's British Glossary*, was derived from the three following British words, tri, nou, hant, which signify the "inhabitants of the new city." This name, it is supposed, supposed, might have been given them by their neighbours, on account of their having newly come from the continent into Britain, and having there founded a city called *tri-noue*, or the "new city;" the most ancient name of the renowned metropolis of Britain. The Trinobantes had come so lately from <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELGIUM">Belgium</a>, that they seem scarcely to have been firmly established in Britain at the time of the first Roman invasion: For their new city, which soon after became so famous, was then so inconsiderable, that it is not mentioned by Caesar; though he must have been within sight of the place where it was situated. His silence about this place, indeed, is brought as a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> that he did not <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> the Thames; while Norden by the *firmissima civitas* of the Trinobantes understands the city in question, the Trinobantes themselves having been among the first of the British states who submitted to that conqueror. By Ptolemy, and some other ancient writers of good authority, indeed, Londinium is placed in Cantium, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, on the south side of the Thames; and it is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of some moderns, that the Romans probably had a station there, to secure their conquests on that side of the river, before they reduced the Trinobantes. The place fixed upon for this station is St George's Field, a large plot of ground situated between Lambeth and Southwark, where many Roman coins, bricks, and chequered pavements, have been found. Three Roman ways from Kent, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SURREY">Surrey</a>, and Middlesex, intersected each other in this place; this therefore is supposed to be the original Londinium, which it is thought became neglected after the Romans reduced the Trinobantes, and settled on the other side of the Thames; and the name was transferred to the new city. The Romans possessed themselves of London, on their second invasion in the reign of Claudius, about 105 years after their first under Caesar. They had begun with Camelodunum, the present <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALDON">Maldon</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>; and having taken it, planted there a colony consisting of veterans of the 14th legion. London and Verulam were next taken possession of about one and the same time. Camelodunum was made a *colonia* or place governed entirely by Roman laws and customs; Verulam (on the site of which St Alban's now stands), a *municipium*, in which the natives were honoured with the privileges of Roman citizens, and enjoyed their own laws and constitutions; and Londinium only a *praefectura*, the inhabitants, a mixture of Romans and Britons, being suffered to enjoy no more than the name of citizens of Rome, being governed by praefects sent annually from thence, without having either their own laws or magistrates. "It was even then of such concourse (says Mr Pennant), and such vast trade, that the wise conquerors did not think fit to trust the inhabitants with the same privileges as other places of which they had less reason to be jealous." But others observe, that this is a mistake; and that the Romans, in order to secure their conquest, and to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> the affections of those Britons who had already submitted to their authority, made London equally a municipium or free city with Verulamium, as may be seen by referring to Aulus Gellius, lib. xvi. c. 13, and to Spanhem. orbis Roman. tom. ii. p. 37, 38. It is difficult to say what were the particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> exported from and imported into the port of London at this period. The imports and exports of History, the island in general we know: Strabo says, "Britain produceth corn, cattle, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>; besides which, skins, slaves, and dogs, naturally excellent hunters, are exported from that island." It is probable that the two first and three last articles were exported from London; and perhaps, too, the *gagates* or jet-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> mentioned by Solinus as one of the productions of Britain, together with horses, were exported from thence. The imports were at first <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, earthen <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARE">ware</a>, and works in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, polished bits of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> emulating <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> collars, toys of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBER">amber</a>, glasses, and other articles of the same material. In the reign of Nero, as Tacitus informs us, London was become a city highly famous for the great influx of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>, her extensive commerce, and plenty of all things. No fewer than <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> of the fourteen itinera of Antoninus begin or end at London; which tends to corroborate the many proofs which might be adduced, that this city was the capital of Britain in the Roman times. At first London had no walls or other fortifications when first to defend it, and was therefore exposed to the attacks surrounded of every enemy; and thus it suffered severely about the year 64, being burnt by the Britons under <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOADICEA">Boadicea</a>, and all the inhabitants massacred. But it was soon restored by the Romans; and increased so much, that in the reign of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Severus it is called by Herodian a *great and wealthy city*. It continued, however, in a defencless state for more than a century after this last period; when at last a wall of hewn stone and British bricks was erected around it. London at this time extended in length from Ludgate-hill to a spot a little beyond the Tower. The breadth was not half equal to the length, and at each end grew considerably narrower. Maitland ascribes the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of the walls to Theodosius governor of Britain in 369. Dr Woodward, with more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, supposes them to have been founded under the auspices of Constantine the Great; and this seems to be confirmed by the numbers of coins of that emperor's mother Helena, which have been discovered under them, placed there by him in compliment to her. The same emperor made it a bishop's see; for it appears that the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> of London and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, and another English bishop, were at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARLES">Arles</a> in the year 314; he also settled a mint in it, as is plain from some of his coins. The ancient course of the wall was as follows: It began with a fort near the present site of the Tower, was continued along the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a> course, and the back of Houndsditch, across Bishopsgate-street, in a straight line by London wall to Cripplegate; then returned southward by Crowder's Well alley (where several remnants of lofty towers were lately to be seen), to Aldersgate, thence along the back of Bull-and-Mouth-street to Newgate, and again along the back of the houses in the Old Bailey to Ludgate; soon after which, it probably finished with another fort, where the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, late the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> house, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> Friars, now stands: from hence another wall ran near the river side, along Thames-street, quite to the fort on the eastern extremity. The walls were three miles a hundred and sixty-five feet in circumference, guarded at proper distances on the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> side with fifteen lofty towers; some of them were remaining. maining within these few years, and possibly may still. Maitland mentions one twenty-six feet <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, near Gravel-lane, on the west side of Houndsditch; another, about eighty paces south-east towards Aldgate; and the bases of another, supporting a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> house, at the lower end of the street called the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">Vinegar</a>-yard, south of Aldgate. The walls, when perfect, are supposed to have been twenty-two feet high, the towers forty. These, with the remnants of the wall, proved the Roman structure, by the titles and disposition of the masonry. London-wall, near Moorfields, is now the most entire <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> left of that ancient precinct. The gates which received the great <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>, were four. The Praetorian way, the Saxon Watling-street, passed under one, on the site of the late Newgate; vestiges having been discovered of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGGING">digging</a> above Holburn-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>: it turned <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to Dowgate, or more properly Dwr-gate or Water-gate, where there is a trajeuctus or ferry, to join it to the Watling-street, which was continued to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOVER">Dover</a>. The Hermin-street passed under Cripplegate; and a vicinal way went under Aldgate by Bethnal-green, towards Oldford, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> over the river <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEE">Lee</a> to Duroleiton, the modern Leighton in Essex. After the Romans deserted Britain, a new and fierce <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> succeeded. The Saxons, under their leaders Hengist and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSA">Horsa</a>, landed in 448, having been invited over by the provincials as auxiliaries against the Scots and Piets; but quarrelling with their friends, they found means to establish themselves in the island, and in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of time entirely subdued them, as related under the article ENGLAND, No. 31—44. London fell into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of these invaders about the year 457; and became the chief city of the Saxon <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> in Essex. It suffered much in the wars carried on between the Britons and Saxons: but it soon recovered; so that Bede calls it a princely mart town, under the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of a chief <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>, whose title of portgrave or portreeve, (for we find him called by both names), conveys a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> idea of the mercantile state of London in those early ages, that required a governor or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a> of the port. During the civil wars of the Saxons with each other, the Londoners had always the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> to keep themselves <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEUTER">neuter</a>; and about the year 819, when all the seven Saxon kingdoms fell under the power of Egbert, London became the metropolis of England, which it has ever since continued. During the invasions of the Danes, London suffered greatly. In 849, these invaders entered the Thames with 250 ships, plundered and burnt the city, and massacred the inhabitants; and two years after they returned with a fleet of 350 sail, fully determined to destroy every thing that had escaped their barbarity in the former expedition. At this time, however, they were disappointed; most of their troops being cut in pieces by King <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETHELWOLF">Ethelwolf</a> and his son Athelbald; yet such was the destruction made by those barbarians at London, that it suffered more from these two incursions than ever it had done before. In the reign of King Alfred the Great, London began to recover from its former ruinous state. He rebuilt its walls, drove out the Danish inhabitants who had settled there, restored the city to its former liberties and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, and committed the care of it to his son-in-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-ETHELRED">Ethelred</a> duke of Mercia, in hopes that this might always be a place of secure retreat within its strong walls, whatever might happen from a foreign or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> enemy. In 893, however, he had the mortification to see his capital totally reduced to ashes by an accidental fire, which could not be extinguished, as the houses at that time were all built of wood. The walls, however, being constructed of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INCOMBUSTIBLE">incombustible</a> materials, continued to afford the same protection as before; the houses were quickly rebuilt, and the city divided into wards and precincts, for its better order and government. This king also instituted the office of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of which office made it necessary to have it also in London; so that here we have the glimmerings of the order of magistrates afterwards settled in the city of London: in the person of the portreeve, or portgrave, or governor of the city, as supreme magistrate; in the sheriff, and in the officer or subordinate magistrate by what name soever then distinguished, which, being placed at the head of each <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARD">ward</a> or precinct, were analogous to the more modern title of aldermen and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a>-council men. Alfred having settled the affairs of England in the brick and most prudent manner, directed his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the ornamenting, as much as possible, the city of London, houses first erected. For this purpose, he spirited up the English to an emulation in building their houses of stronger and more durable materials than formerly. At that time their houses were mostly of wood; and a house built of any other materials was looked upon as a kind of wonder. But Alfred having begun to raise his palaces of stone and brick, the opulent Londoners, and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> resident in and about London, followed the example, though the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> did not come into general <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> till some ages after. In 1015, a foreign enemy again appeared before London. Canute king of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a> having invaded by Canute, and plundered the counties of Dorset, Somerset, and Wilts, sailed up the Thames with 200 ships, and laid siege to the city. The citizens continued faithful, notwithstanding the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEFECTION">defection</a> of the greatest part of the kingdom; and made such a brave resistance, that Canute thought fit to withdraw his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, leaving only his fleet to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLOCKADE">blockade</a> the city by water, that when he found a fair opportunity he might renew the siege with better success. At last, however, being defeated in several battles by Edmund Ironside, he was obliged to call off his ships to cover his own army in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>. In the compromise, however, which was afterwards made between Edmund and Canute, the city of London was given to the latter, and owned him for its lawful sovereign. We have a strong proof of the opulence of London even at this time, from the tax laid upon it by Canute in order to pay his army; this being no less than 10,500l. while the rest of the nation was at the same time taxed only at 72,000l. In 1046, we have the first instance of the London Senders sending representatives to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. This happened on settling the succession to the throne after Canute's death. The English in general declared for Edward, son of King Ethelred; or, if that could not be carried, for Hardicanute, son of Canute by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> Emma, and then absent on a tour to Denmark. The city of London espoused the claim and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of Harold Harefoot, son also of Canute, by Queen Elviga. of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHAMPTON">Northampton</a>. Edward's party soon declined; and the Londoners agreed, for the peace of the realm, that the two brothers should divide the kingdom between them; but as Hardicanute did not return in proper time to England, a wittena-gemote was held at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, where <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">Earl</a> Leofric, and most of the thanes on the north of the Thames, with the pilots of London, chose Harold for their king. Here, by pilots we are to understand the directors, magistrates, or leading men of the city; and this manifestly shows, that London was then of such <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, that no important national affair was transacted without the consent of the inhabitants; for the Saxon annals assure us, that none were admitted into this <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> but the nobility and the pilots of London. On the invasion of the Normans under William I., London submitted as well as the rest of the kingdom; and received two charters from that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, confirming all the privileges they had under the Saxon kings, and adding several new ones. But while the citizens were promising themselves all manner of security and tranquillity under the new government, it was almost entirely reduced to ashes by an accidental fire in 1077. It had scarce recovered from this calamity, when it was visited by another of the same kind in 1086, which began at Ludgate, and destroyed the best and most opulent part of the city; consuming, among other buildings, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> of St. Paul's; which, however, was soon rebuilt more magnificently than before. Under the reign of William Rufus, London suffered considerably by fires, hurricanes, and inundations, and seems to have been depressed by the tyranny of that prince; but Henry I. granted large immunities to the city, which again revived its trade, and was favourable to the progress of the arts. The king, however, still retained the privilege of appointing the portreve, or chief magistrate; but the immunities granted to the Londoners secured their affections, and tended much to secure him on the throne. At the same time, there was such a plenty of all kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, that as much corn was sold for 1s. as would suffice 100 people for a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>; 4d. would purchase as much hay and corn as would maintain 20 horses for a day; and a sheep could be bought for a groat. Henry thought proper also to check the licentious behaviour of the Normans, which, by the favour showed them under the two Williams, had carried them into the most barbarous practices. Those who followed William Rufus in his excursions, harassed and plundered the country at <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>. Many of them were so extravagant in their barbarity, that what they could not eat or drink in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>, they either obliged the people to carry to market and sell for their use, or else they would throw it into the fire; and, at their going off, they frequently washed their horses' heels with the drink, and staved the casks containing the remainder. King Henry resolved to put a stop to these excesses and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> customs; and therefore published a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a> at London, commanding that thenceforward all persons who should be convicted of such barbarities should have their eyes pulled out, or their hands or feet cut off, as the ministers of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> should think fit. This effectually checked the insolence of the Normans, and the city continued to flourish throughout the reigns of Henry I. and Stephen. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> of the citizens to Stephen, however, was a crime which never could be forgiven by Henry II.; and, of consequence, he made them sensible of his displeasure, by making frequent demands of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> from them. About this time, indeed, the Londoners were arrived at such a pitch of licentiousness, that their prosperity seemed a curse rather than a blessing. The sons of the most eminent and wealthy citizens entered into a confederacy to commit burglaries, and to rob and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> all that came in their way in the nighttime. The king took an opportunity from these irregularities to enrich himself. He demanded several loans and free gifts; till at last the Londoners, to prevent further inquiries into their conduct, paid into the exchequer 500l. in three years. These disorders, however, were at last stopped by the execution of John Senex; who, though a very rich and reputable citizen, had engaged in these enterprises. He offered 500l. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of silver, a prodigious sum in those days, for his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a>, but was refused. The king, however, still continued to drain the citizens of their money by free gifts; and at last fined every separate guild, fraternity, or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, that had presumed to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> as bodies corporate without the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> letters-patent. On the death of Henry II., the title of the first magistrate of London was changed from portreve to that of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAILIFF">bailiff</a>; and in 1189 claimed and acted in the office of the chief <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTLER">butler</a> at the coronation of Richard I. In 1191 this monarch permitted the bailiff, named Henry Fitz-Alwine, to assume the title of mayor. For, in when first 1192, we find certain orders of the mayor and aldermen to prevent fires; whereby it was ordained, that "all houses thereafter to be erected in London and the liberties thereof, should be built of stone, with party-walls of the same; and covered either with slates or tiles, to prevent those dreadful calamities by fire, which were frequently and chiefly occasioned by houses built of wood, and thatched with straw or reeds." And for this purpose, it was also provided by the discreetest men of the city, "that 12 aldermen of the city should be chosen in full hustings, and there sworn to assist the mayor in appeasing contentions that might arise among neighbours in the city upon enclosure betwixt land and land, and to regulate the dimensions of party-walls, which were to be of stone, 16 feet high and three feet thick; and to give directions about girders, windows, gutters, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a>." Such confidence also did Richard put in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> and faithfulness of the city of London, that when it was resolved to fix a standard for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WEIGHTS_AND_MEASURES">weights and <a class</a>="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> for the whole realm, his majesty committed the execution thereof to the sheriffs of London and Middlesex, whom he commanded to provide measures, gallons, iron rods, and weights, for standards, to be sent to the several counties of England. This happened in 1198, at which time corn was advanced to the enormous price of 18s. 4d. per <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>. The city of London was much favoured by King John, who granted them three charters soon after his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> to accession. The first was a recital and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a> of the city by those granted by Henry I. and II., with the farther privilege of being free from toll and every other duty or custom in his majesty's foreign dominions; for which they paid the sum of 3000 merks. The second was a confirmation of one granted by King Richard. By this the citizens of London had the jurisdiction and conservancy of the river Thames; with a clause to extend that jurisdiction, and the powers therewith granted, to the river Medway; and with another clause to enable the said city, as conservators of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Thames and Medway, to inflict a penalty of 10l. upon any person that should presume to erect a weir in either of these rivers. The third <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> contains a fee-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARM">farm</a>-rent of the sherifswicks of London and Middlesex at the ancient rent, of which they had been deprived by Queen Maud; granting them also the additional power of choosing their own sheriffs. This charter was given by way of conveyance from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> to the citizens for a valuable consideration, by which the sherifswick became their freehold; and this is the first covenant or conveyance we find on record with the legal terms of to have and to hold, which are at this time accounted an essential part in all conveyances of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>. During the reign of Henry III. the city of London was oppressed in many different ways. In 1218, he exacted a fine of 40 marks for selling a sort of cloth not two yards within the lists; and a 15th of the citizens personal estates for the enjoyment of their ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> and privileges. In 1227, he commanded by proclamation all the foreign merchants to depart the city, which drew 32 marks from the Hanseatic company of the Steelyard, to have <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEISIN">seisin</a> of their guild or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a> in Thames-street. But it was the wrestling <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MATCH">match</a> at St Giles's in the fields that brought on their greatest burden. In the year 1221, on St James's day, the citizens of London having carried off the victory from the people of Westminster and other neighbouring villages, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> of Westminster, meditating <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> against the Londoners, proposed another wrestling match with them, and gave a ram for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a>. The citizens resorted to the place at the time appointed; but were unexpectedly assaulted by a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of armed men, who killed and wounded many, and dispersed the rest. This raised a great commotion in the city. The populace breathed revenge; and, by the instigation of Constantine Fitz-Arnolph, a great favourite of the French party during the troubles in King John's reign, they proceeded to Westminster, and pulled down the houses both of the steward and abbot. Hearing afterwards that the abbot was come into the city with his complaint to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> d'Aubney the king's counsel, they pursued him, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> his servants cruelly, took away 12 of his horses, and would have murdered himself, had he not escaped by a back-door. Upon this tumult, Hubert de <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURY">Bury</a>, then chief justiciary, summoned the mayor and many of the principal citizens to attend him in the tower of London; and inquiring for the authors of the riot, Constantine, the ringleader, boldly answered, that "he was one; that they had done no more than they ought; and that they were resolved to avow what they had done, let the consequence be what it would." In this he was seconded by his nephew and one Geoffrey: but the justiciary, having dismissed all the rest, detained these three, and ordered them to be hanged next morning, though Constantine offered 15,000 marks for his pardon. Hubert then coming into the city with a strong <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>, caused the hands and feet of most of the principal rioters he could <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> to be cut off: all which was executed without any legal proceedings or form of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>. After these arbitrary cruelties, he degraded the mayor and all the magistrates; placed a custos over the city, and obliged 30 persons of his own choosing to become securities for the good behaviour of the whole city. Several thousand marks were also exacted by the king, before he would consent to a reconciliation. This arbitrary conduct alarmed the whole nation. The parliament of 1224 began to be uneasy for themselves, and addressed his majesty that he would be pleased to confirm the charter of liberties which he had sworn to observe; and the consequence of this application was a confirmation of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MAGNA_CHARTA">magna <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHARTA">charta</a> in the full parliament at Westminster in the year 1225. At this time, also, the rights and privileges of the citizens were confirmed. They were exempted from prosecution for burles, i.e., listed cloth; and were granted the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of having a common <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>. The necessitous circumstances of this monarch, however, made him often exact money arbitrarily as long as he lived. Under the succeeding reigns, as the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of the people in general was augmented, so the liberty, opulence, and power of the citizens of London, increased, until they became a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> to the power of the crown itself, which in some <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> they still continue to be. Riots indeed, for which they generally suffered, were by no means unfrequent; the city often suffered by fires and plagues. Nothing, however, happened which materially affected the welfare of the city, till the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. in 1665.—This year London Dreadful was ravaged by the most violent <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a> ever known in plague in Britain. The whole <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> had been remarkably still and warm, so that the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> was sometimes suffocating even to people in perfect <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>; and by this unusual <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> and sultry <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>, people were undoubtedly prepared for receiving the infection, which appeared with violence in the months of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, August, and September. A violent plague had raged in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> in the year 1663; on which account the importation of merchandise from that country was prohibited by the British legislature in 1664. Notwithstanding this prohibition, however, it seems the plague had actually been imported; for in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the year 1664, two or three persons died suddenly in Westminster, with marks of the plague on their bodies. Some of their neighbours, terrified at the thoughts of their danger, removed into the city; but their removal proved too late for themselves, and fatal to those among whom they came to reside. They soon died of the plague; and communicated the infection to so many others, that it became impossible to extinguish the seeds of it, by separating those that were infected from such as were not. It was confined, however, through a hard frosty winter, till the middle of February, when it again appeared in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of St Giles's, to which it had been originally brought; and, after another long rest till April, showed its malignant force afresh, as soon as the warmth of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> gave it opportunity.—At first, it took off one here and there, without any certain proof of their having infected each other, and houses began to be shut up, with a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> to prevent its spreading. But it was now too late; the infection gained ground every day, and the shutting up of houses only made the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> spread wider. People, afraid... afraid of being shut up, and sequestered from all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with society, concealed their illness, or found means to escape from their places of confinement; while numbers expired in the greatest torments, destitute of every assistance; and many died both of the plague and other diseases, who would in all probability have recovered, had they been allowed their liberty, with proper <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> and air.—A house was shut up on account of a maid-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a>, who had only spots, and not the gangrenous plague-blotches, upon her, so that her distemper was probably a petechial fever. She recovered; but the people of the house obtained no liberty to stir, either for air or exercise, for 40 days. The bad air, fear, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGER">anger</a>, and vexation, attending this injurious treatment, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> the mistress of the family into a fever. The visitors appointed to search the house, said it was the plague, though the physicians were of a different opinion: the family, however, were obliged to begin their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARANTINE">quarantine</a> anew though it had been almost expired before; and this second confinement afflicted them so much, that most of the family fell sick, some of one distemper and some of another. Every illness that appeared in the family produced a fresh prolongation of their confinement; till at last the plague was actually brought in by some of those who came to inquire into the health of the family, and almost every person in the house died.—Many examples of a similar kind happened, and this was one of the worst consequences of shutting up houses. All means of putting a stop to the infection were evidently ineffectual. Multitudes fled into the country; many merchants, owners of ships, &c. shut themselves up, on board their vessels, being supplied with provisions from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOLWICH">Woolwich</a>, and single farm houses on the Kentish side. Here, however, they were safe; for the infection never reached below <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPTFORD">Deptford</a>, though the people went frequently on shore to the country <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, villages, and farm houses, to buy fresh provisions. As the violence of the plague increased, the ships which had families on board removed farther off; some went quite out to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and then put into such harbours and roads as they could best get at. In the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time, the distemper made the most rapid advances within the city. In the last <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEEK">week</a> of July, the number of burials amounted to 2010; but the first week of August it rose to 3817; thence to 3883; then to 4237; the next week, to 6102; and at last to 7000 and 8000 weekly. In the last week of September, however, the fury of the disease began to abate; though vast numbers were sick, yet the number of burials decreased from 7155 to 5538; the next week there was a farther decrease to 4929, then to 4327, next to 2665, then to 1421, and the next week to 1034. All this while, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> people had been reduced to the greatest distresses, by reason of the stagnation of trade, and the sicknesses to which they were peculiarly liable on account of their manner of living. The rich, however, contributed to their subsistence in a most liberal manner. The sums collected on this occasion are indeed almost incredible; being said to amount to 100,000l. per week. The king is reported to have contributed 1000l. weekly; and in the parish of Cripplegate alone, 17,000l. was distributed weekly among the poor inhabitants.—By the vigilance also of the magistrates, provisions continued remarkably cheap throughout the whole time of this dreadful calamity, so that all riots and tumults on that account were prevented; and at last, on the cessation of the disease in the winter of 1665, the inhabitants who had fled returned to their habitations, and London to appearance became as populous as ever, though it was computed that 100,000 persons had been carried off by the plague. The city was scarcely recovered from the desolation occasioned by the plague, when it was almost totally laid in ashes by a most dreadful fire. This broke out in a baker's shop in Pudding-lane, on Saturday night, September 2, 1666. In a few hours Billingsgate ward was entirely burnt down; and before morning the fire had crossed Thames-street, and destroyed the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of St Magnus. From thence it proceeded to the bridge, and consumed a great pile of buildings there; but was stopped by the want of any thing more to destroy. The flames, however, being scattered by a strong east <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, continued their devastations in other quarters. All efforts to stop it proved unsuccessful throughout the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a>. That day it proceeded up as far as Garlick-hithe; and destroying Canon street, invaded Cornhill and the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">Exchange</a>. On Monday, the flames having proceeded eastward against the wind through Thames-street, invaded Tower street, Gracechurch-street, Fenchurch-street, Dowgate, Old Fish-street, Watling-street, Threadneedle-street, and several others, from all which it broke at once into Cheapside. In a few hours Cheapside was all in flames, the fire having reached it from so many places at once. The fire then continuing its course from the river on one side, and from Cheapside on the other, surrounded the cathedral of St Paul's. This building stood by itself at some distance from any houses; yet such was the violence of the flames, and the heat of the atmosphere occasioned by them, that the cathedral took fire at top. The great beams and massy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> broke through into <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">Faith</a>-church underneath, which was quickly set on fire; after which, the flames invaded Pater-noster-row, Newgate-street, the Old Bailey, Ludgate-hill, Fleet-street, Ironmonger-lane, Old Jewry, Laurence-lane, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">Milk</a>-street, Wood-street, Gutter-lane, Foster-lane, Lothbury, Cateaton-street; and, having destroyed Christ-church, burnt furiously through St Martin's le Grand towards Aldersgate. The fire had now attained its greatest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, and was several miles in compass. The vast <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> obscured the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> so, that he either could not be seen at all, or appeared through it as <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> as blood. The flames reached an immense way up into the air, and their reflection from the smoke, which in the night-time seemed also like <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>, made the appearance still more terrible. The atmosphere was illuminated to a great extent, and this illumination is said to have been visible as far as <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JEDBURGH">Jedburgh</a> in Scotland. Some of the light ashes also are said to have been carried to the distance of 16 miles. Guildhall exhibited a singular appearance. The oak with which it was built was so <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a>, that it would not flame, but burnt like <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a>, so that the building appeared for several hours like an enchanted <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of gold or burnished brass. At last, on Wednesday morning, when every one expected expected that the suburbs as well as the city were to have been burnt, the fire began of itself to abate by reason of the wind having ceased, and some other changes no doubt taken place in the atmosphere. It was checked by the great building in Leadenhall-street, and in other streets by the blowing up several houses with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUN">gun</a>-powder; and on Thursday the flames were quite extinguished.—The following is a calculation of the damage done by this extraordinary conflagration. | Item | Value | |----------------------------------------------------------------------|---------| | Thirteen thousand two hundred houses, at 12 years purchase, supposing the rent of each 23l. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a> | L. 3,960,000 | | Eighty-seven parish churches, at 800l. each | 696,000 | | Six consecrated chapels, at 2000l. each | 12,000 | | The royal exchange | 50,000 | | The customhouse | 10,000 | | Fifty-two halls of companies, at 1500l. each | | | Three city gates, at 3000l. each | 9000 | | Jail of Newgate | 15,000 | | Four stone bridges | 6000 | | Sessions house | 7000 | | Guildhall, with the courts and offices belonging to it | 40,000 | | Blackwell hall | 3000 | | <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDEWELL">Bridewell</a> | 5000 | | <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POULTRY">Poultry</a> compter | 5000 | | Woodstreet compter | 3000 | | St Paul's church | 2,000,000 | | Wares, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> stuff, money, and moveable goods lost or spoiled | 2,000,000 | | Hire of porters, carts, waggons, barges, boats, &c. for removing goods | 200,000 | | Printed books and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> in shops and warehouses | 150,000 | | Wine, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, &c. of which the town was at that time very full | 1,500,000 | L. 10,689,000 It was never certainly known whether this fire was accidental or designed. A suspicion fell upon the Papists; and this gained such general credit, that it is asserted for a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> on the monument which is erected in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of the conflagration. Of the truth of this assertion, however, though there was not sufficient proof, it had the effect of making the Papists most violently suspected and abhorred by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, which some time after proved very prejudicial to the city itself. From this calamity, great as it was, London soon recovered itself, and became much more magnificent than before; the streets, which were formerly crooked and narrow, being now built wide and spacious; and the industry of its inhabitants repaired the losses they had sustained. In 1679, the city was again alarmed by the discovery of a design to destroy it by fire a second time. Elizabeth Oxly, servant to one Rind in Fetter-lane, having set her <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>'s house on fire, was apprehended on suspicion, and confessed, that she had been hired to do it by one Stubbs a Papist, for a reward of 5l. Stubbs being taken into custody, acknowledged that he had persuaded her to it; and that he himself had been prevailed upon by one Father Gifford his confessor, who had assured him, that by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> the houses of heretics he would do a great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to the church. He also owned that he had several conferences with Gifford and two Irishmen on the affair. The maid and Stubbs also agreed in declaring, that the Papists intended to rise in London, expecting to be powerfully supported by a French army. In consequence of this discovery, the Papists were banished from the city, and five miles round, and five Jesuits were hanged for the above-mentioned plot. The Papists thought to revenge themselves by forging what was called the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>-tub plot, in which the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESBYTERIANS">Presbyterians</a> were supposed to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HATCH">hatch</a> treacherous designs against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of the king. Sir Edmondbury Which Godfrey also, who had been very <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> in his proceedings against the Papists, was murdered by some unknown persons; and this murder, together with their discovering the falsehood of the meal-tub plot, so exasperated the Londoners, that they resolved to show their detestation of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPERY">Popery</a>, by an extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXHIBITION">exhibition</a> on the 17th of November, Queen Elizabeth's accession to the throne, on which day they had usually burnt the pope in effigy. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a> began with a person on horseback personating Sir Edmondbury Godfrey, attended by a bellman proclaiming his execrable murder. He was followed by a person carrying a large silver cross, with priests in copes, Carmelites, and Gray-friars, followed by six Jesuits: then proceeded <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> waiters, and after them some bishops with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAWN">lawn</a> sleeves, and others with copes and mitres. Six cardinals preceded the pope, enthroned in a stately <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAGEANT">pageant</a>, attended by divers boys with pots of incense, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a> whispering in his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a>. In this order they marched from Bishopsgate to Flect-street; and there, amidst a great multitude of spectators, committed his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLINESS">holiness</a> to the flames. This procession gave great offence to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, at which the duke of York, afterwards James II. had a great influence. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> was farther widened by the choice of sheriffs for that year. The candidates set up by the court were rejected by a majority of almost two to one; but this did not deter their party from demanding a poll in their behalf, upon which a tumult ensued. This was represented by the Popish party in such colours to the king, that he issued out a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> that same evening for trying the rioters; which, however, was so far from intimidating the rest, that they grew more and more determined, not only to oppose the Popish party, but to exclude the duke of York from his succession to the crown. In the mean time, the king prorogued the parliament, to prevent them from proceeding in their inquiry concerning the Popish plot, and the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCLUSION">exclusion</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">bill</a>. Upon this the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a>-mayor, aldermen, and common-council, presented a petition to his majesty, in which they requested, that he would permit the parliament to sit in order to complete their salutary measures and councils. This petition was highly represented by the king; who, instead of granting it, dissolved the parliament, and could never afterwards be reconciled to the city. From this time it was determined to seize their charter; and fresh provocations having having been given about the election of sheriffs, a quo warranto was at last produced by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTORNEY_GENERAL">attorney-general</a>, in order to overthrow their charter, and thereby to deprive the citizens of the power to choose sheriffs. This information set forth, "That the mayor and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONALTY">commonalty</a> and citizens of the city of London, by the space of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> then last past and more, used, and yet do claim to have and use, without any lawful warrant or legal grant, within the city of London aforesaid, and the liberties and privileges of the same city, the liberties and privileges following, viz. 1. To be of themselves a body corporate and politic, by the name of mayor and commonalty and citizens of the city of London. 2. To have sheriffs civilis, et com. London, et com. Middlesex, and to name, make, and elect, and constitute them. 3. That the mayor and aldermen of the said city should be justices of the peace, and hold sessions of the peace. All which liberties, privileges, and franchises, the said mayor and commonalty, and citizens of London, upon the king did by the space aforesaid usurp, and yet do usurp." Though nothing could be more unjust than this prosecution, the ministry were determined at all events to crush the Londoners; rightly judging, that it would be an easy <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> to make all other corporations surrender their charters into the king's hands, and that they had no other body in the nation to fear. Accordingly they displaced such judges as would not approve of their proceedings; and, on the 12th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1683, Justice Jones pronounced the following <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>: "That a city might forfeit its charter; that the malversations of the common-council were acts of the whole city; and that the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> set forth in the pleadings were <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> grounds for the forfeiting of a charter." Notwithstanding this sentence, however, the attorney-general, contrary to the usual custom in such <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, was directed to move that the judgment might not be recorded: being afraid of the consequences. Yet it was judged that the king might seize the liberties of the city. A common-council was immediately summoned to deliberate on this exigency. The country party moved to have the judgment entered; but they were overruled by the court party, who insisted upon an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> submission to the king before judgment was entered; and though this was in effect a voluntary surrender of the city-liberties, and deprived themselves of the means of getting the judgment reversed, the act of submission was carried by a great majority: and in a petition from the lord mayor, aldermen, and common-council, they acknowledged their own misgovernment, and his majesty's lenity; begged his pardon, and promised constant loyalty and obedience; and humbly begged his majesty's commands and directions." To this his majesty answered, that he would not reject their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a>, if they would agree upon the following particulars. 1. That no lord mayor, sheriff, recorder, common serjeant, town clerk, or coroner, of the city of London, or steward of the borough of Southwark, shall be capable of, or admitted to, the exercise of their respective offices before his majesty shall have approved of them under his sign-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MANUAL">manual</a>. 2. That if his majesty shall disapprove the choice of any person to be lord mayor, and signify the same under his sign-manual to the lord mayor, or in default of a lord mayor, to the recorder or senior <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALDERMAN">alderman</a>, the citizens shall, within one week, proceed to a new choice: and if his majesty shall in like manner disapprove the second choice, his majesty may, if he pleases, nominate a person to be lord mayor for the year ensuing. 3. If his majesty shall, in like manner, disapprove the persons chosen to be sheriffs, or either of them, his majesty may appoint sheriffs for the year ensuing. 4. That the lord mayor and court of aldermen may, with the leave of his majesty, displace any alderman, recorder, &c. 5. Upon the election of an alderman, if the court of aldermen shall judge and declare the person presented to be unfit, the ward shall choose again; and upon a disapproval of a second choice, the court may appoint another in his room. 6. That the justices of the peace should be by the king's commission; and the settling of those matters to be left to his majesty's attorney-general and counsel learned in the law." To these the lord-keeper added, in the king's name, "That these regulations being made, his majesty would not only pardon this prosecution, but would confirm their charter in such a manner as should be consistent with them; concluding thus: 'My lord mayor, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> draws towards an end, and Midsummer-day is at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, when some of the officers used to be chosen; whereof his majesty will reserve the approbation. Therefore, it is his majesty's <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, that you return to the city, and consult the common council, that he may speedily know your resolutions thereupon, and accordingly give his directions. That you may see the king is in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a>, and the matter is not capable of delay, I am commanded to let you know he hath given orders to his attorney-general to enter upon judgment on Saturday next; unless you prevent it by your compliance in all these particulars.'" A common-council was summoned, when the friends of liberty treated those slavish conditions as they deserved; and even declared, that they were ready to sacrifice all that was near or dear to them, rather than submit to such arbitrary impositions: but when it was put to the vote, there appeared a majority of 18 for submission. Thus the king got the government of the city into his own hands, though he and his brothers entirely lost the affections of the Londoners. But, not content with their submission, his majesty departed from his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a>; breaks in commanded the judgment upon the quo warranto to be entered; and commissioned Sir William Pritchard, the lord mayor, to hold the same office during his majesty's pleasure. In the same manner he appointed or displaced the other magistrates as he thought proper; after which the ministry, having nothing to fear, proceeded in the most arbitrary manner. In this subjection to the will of the court, the city Privilege of London continued till the Revolution; but, in 1689, of the immediate restoration of the Londoners to their restored franchises was ordered; and in such a manner and form, as to put it out of the powers of an arbitrary ministry and a corrupt judge and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JURY">jury</a> to deprive them of their chartered liberties for the time to come. Accordingly, a bill was brought into parliament, and passed, for reversing the judgment of the quo warranto against the city of London, and for restoring the same to its ancient rights. That part of this immense capital which is distinguished by the name of The City, stands on the north shore of the river, from the Tower to the Temple, occupying only that space formerly encompassed by the wall, which in circumference measures but three miles and 165 feet. In this wall there were seven gates by land, viz. Ludgate, Aldgate, Cripplegate, Aldersgate, Moorgate, Bishopsgate, which were all taken down in September 1670; and Newgate, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> gaol, which was also taken down in 1776, and a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASSIVE">massive</a> building erected a little south of it, which by the rioters in 1780 received damage to the amount of £8,000. On the side of the water there were Dowgate and Billingsgate, long since demolished, as well as the postern-gate near the Tower. In the year 1670, there was a gate erected called Temple-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">Bar</a>, which terminates the bounds of the city westward. The liberties, or those parts of this great city which are subject to its jurisdiction, and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> without the walls of London, are bounded on the east, in Whitechapel, the Minories, and Bishopsgate, by bars, which were formerly posts and chains, that were frequently taken away by arbitrary power, when it was thought proper to seize the franchises of the city of London; on the north, they are bounded in the same manner in Pickaxe-street, at the end of Fan-alley, and in St John's-street; on the west, by bars in Holborn; at the east end of Middle Row, and at the west end of Fleet-street, by the gate called Temple-Bar, already mentioned; on the south, we may include the jurisdiction which the city holds on the river Thames, and over the borough of Southwark. The city, including the borough, is at present divided into 26 wards. 1. Aldersgate ward takes its name from a city-gate which lately stood in the neighbourhood. It is bounded on the east by Cripplegate ward; on the west, by Farringdon ward within and without; and on the south, by Farringdon ward within. It is very large, and is divided into Aldersgate-within and Aldersgate-without. Each of these divisions consists of four precincts, under one alderman, eight common-council men, of whom two are the alderman's deputies, eight constables, fourteen inquest-men, eight scavengers, and a beadle; exclusive of the officers belonging to the liberty of St Martin's le Grand, which contains 168 houses. 2. Aldgate takes its name also from a gate, which was of great antiquity, being mentioned in King Edgar's charter to the knights of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHTON">Knighton</a> Guild about the year 967; and was probably of a much more ancient foundation, for it was the gate through which the Roman vicinal way lay to the ferry at Oldford. In the time of the wars between King John and his barons, the latter entered the city through this gate, and committed great devastations among the houses of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a>. Aldgate was rebuilt by the leaders of the party after the Roman manner. They made use of stone which they brought from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAEN">Caen</a>, and into Wards, a small brick called the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a> tile, which Mr Pennant thinks has been often mistaken for Roman. The new gate was very strong, and had a deep well within it. In 1471, this gate was assaulted by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASTARD">Bastard</a> of Falconbridge, who got possession of it for a few hours; but the portcullis being drawn up, the troops which had entered were all cut off, and the citizens, headed by the alderman of the ward and recorder, having made a sally, defeated the remainder with great slaughter. In 1606, Aldgate was taken down and rebuilt; and many Roman coins were found in digging the foundations.—The ward of Aldgate is bounded on the east by the city wall, which divides it from Portsoken ward; on the north, by Bishopsgate ward; on the west, by Lime-street and Langbourn wards; and on the south, by Tower-street ward. It is governed by an alderman, six common-council men, six constables, twenty inquest-men, seven scavengers, and a beadle; besides the officers belonging to St James's, Duke's Place.—It is divided into seven precincts. 3. Bassishaw or Basinghall ward, is bounded on the east and south by Coleman-street ward, on the north by part of Cripplegate, and on the west by part of the wards of Cheap and Cripplegate. On the south, it begins at Blackwell-hall; and runs northward to London wall, pulled down some time ago to make way for new buildings in Fore-street, and spreads 88 feet east, and 54 feet west against the place where that wall stood. This is a very small ward, and consists only of two precincts: the upper precinct contains no more than 66, and the lower only 76 houses. It is governed by an alderman, four common-council men, of whom one is the alderman's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a>, three constables, seventeen inquest-men, three scavengers, and a beadle. It has its name from Basinghall, the mansion-house of the family of Basing, which was the principal house in it, and stood in the place of Blackwell-hall. 4. Billingsgate ward is bounded on the east by Tower-street ward; on the north, by Langbourn ward; on the west, by the ward of Bridge-within; and on the south, by the river Thames. There have been many conjectures concerning the origin of the name of Billingsgate, none of which seems to be very well authenticated. It is, for instance, supposed to have derived its name from a British king named Belinus, said to have been an assistant of Brennus king of the Gauls at the taking of Rome, and is the same with the Beli-Maur mentioned in the Welsh genealogies. The name of Ludgate is said to be derived from his son Lud.—It is divided into 12 precincts; and is governed by an alderman, 10 common-council men, one of whom is the alderman's deputy, 11 constables, 14 inquest-men, six scavengers, and a beadle. The situation of Billingsgate, on the river, gives it great advantages with respect to trade and merchandise; so that it is well inhabited, and is in a continual hurry of business at the several wharfs or quays. 5. Bishopsgate ward is bounded on the east by Aldgate ward, Portsoken ward, and part of the Tower-liberty, or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTON">Norton</a>-falgate; on the west, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">Broad</a>-street ward and Moorfields; and on the south, by Langbourn ward. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">Division</a> in ward. It is very large, and divided into Bishopsgate-within and Bishopsgate-without. The first contains all that part of the ward within the city-wall and gate, and is divided into five precincts; the second lies without the wall, and is divided into four precincts. Bishopsgate-without extends to Shoreditch, taking its name from one Sir John de Sorditch, an eminent lawyer much in favour with King Edward III., both on account of his knowledge in the law, and of his personal valour. In the time of Henry VIII., one Barlo, a citizen and inhabitant of this place, was named duke of Shoreditch, on account of his skill in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHERY">archery</a>; and, for a number of years after, the title belonged to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> of the London archers. This ward is governed by an alderman, two deputies, one within and the other without, 12 common-council men, seven constables, 13 inquest-men, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> scavengers, and two beadle. It took its name from the gate, which has been pulled down to make that part of the city more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRY">airy</a> and commodious. This gate was built by Erkenwald bishop of London in 675; and it is said to have been repaired by William the Conqueror soon after the Norman conquest.
