Beaufoy's (K) great work (H) In describing this church, Mr Pennant takes occasion to mention the sad example of fallen majesty in the person of Mary d'<a class="xref" href="../1860/vol9.html#article-ESTE">Este</a>, the unhappy queen of James II.; who, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> with her infant prince from the ruin impending over their house, after crossing the Thames from the abdicated Whitehall, took shelter beneath the ancient walls of this church a whole hour, from the rain of the inclement night of December 6, 1688. Here she waited with aggravated misery, till a common <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COACH">coach</a>, procured from the next inn, arrived, and conveyed her to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVESEND">Gravesend</a>, from whence she sailed, and bade an eternal adieu to these kingdoms. (I) Her repository consists of several very large rooms filled with every ornament, which can be used in architecture. The statue, the vase, the urn, the rich chimney pieces, and, in a few words, every thing which could be produced out of natural stone or marble by the most elegant chisel, is here to be obtained at an easy rate. (K) "Where (says Mr Pennant) the foreign wines are most admirably mimicked. Such is the prodigality and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> of the age, that the demand for many sorts exceeds in a great degree the produce of the native vineyards. We have skilful fabricators, who kindly supply our wants. It has been estimated, that half of the port, and five-sixths of the white wines consumed in our capital, have been the produce of our home wine presses. The product of duty to the state from a single house was in one year, from July 5, 1785 to July 5, 1786, not less than 7363l. gs. 8½d. The genial banks of the Thames opposite to our capital, yield almost every species of white wine; and, by a wondrous <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGIC">magic</a>, Mess. Beaufoy pour forth the materials for the rich Frontiniac, This ground, so profitable to the proprietors, and so productive of revenue to the state, was within memory the scene of low dissipation. Here stood Cuper's garden, noted for its fireworks, and the great resort of the profligate of both sexes. This place was ornamented with several of the mutilated statues belonging to Thomas earl of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARUNDEL">Arundel</a>, which had been for that purpose begged from his lordship by one Bayder Cuper, a gardener in the family. The great timber yards beneath which these antiquities were found, are very well worthy of a visit. One would fear that the forests of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a> and the Baltic would be exhausted, to supply the wants of our overgrown capital, were we not assured that the resources will successively be increased equal to the demand of succeeding ages.—In this parish are also vast distilleries, formerly the property of Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Mawby; where are seldom less than 2000 hogs, which are fed entirely on grain. III. City and Liberties of Westminster. The city of Westminster derives its name from a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINSTER">minster</a>, or abbey, and west, on account of its situation with respect to St Paul's cathedral, which was formerly called Eastminster. In ancient times this district stood upwards of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> from the city of London, and contained only two parishes, which were those of St Margaret and St John, with two chapels of ease; but at present it has seven other parochial churches, viz. St Clement's Danes, St Paul's Covent-garden, St Mary's le Strand, St Martin's in the Fields', St Anne's, St James's, and St George's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HANOVER">Hanover</a>-square. Westminster was anciently called Thorny Island, from its having been covered with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THORN">thorn</a> bushes, and encompassed by a branch of the Thames, which is said to have run through the ground now called St James's Park, from west to east, and to have rejoined the river at Whitehall. Till the general dissolution of religious houses, Westminster was subject to the arbitrary rule of its abbot and monks; but in 1541, upon the surrender of William Benson the last abbot, Henry VIII. not only turned it into an honour, but created it the see of a bishop, and appointed for a diocese the whole county of Middlesex, except <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FULHAM">Fulham</a>, which belonged to the bishop of London. This bishopric, however, soon after its institution, was dissolved by Edward VI. The city of Westminster is governed by a high steward, an office of great dignity, who is usually one of the first peers in the realm; and is chosen for life by the dean and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> of the collegiate church of St Peter. There is also a deputy steward and a high bailiff, who also hold their offices for life; being nominated by the dean and chapter, and confirmed by the high steward. The dean and chapter are invested with an ecclesiastical and civil jurisdiction within the liberties of Westminster, St Martin's le Grand, near Cheapside, in the city of London, and some towns in Essex, which are exempted from the jurisdiction of the bishop of London and the archbishop of Canterbury. St Margaret's Church was founded by Edward the Confessor, since which time it has been frequently rebuilt. In the east end of this church is a window curiously painted, with the history of the crucifixion, and with the figures of several apostles and saints finely executed. It formerly belonged to a private chapel at Copt-hall, near Epping in Essex, and was purchased by the officers of this parish, some years ago for 400 guineas. In this church the house of commons attends divine service on state holidays. The church of St John the Evangelist was erected in 1728, and having sunk considerably whilst it was building, occasioned an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> of the plan. On the north and south sides are magnificent porticoes, supported by vast stone pillars, as is also the roof of the church; at each of the four corners is a beautiful stone tower and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PINNACLE">pinnacle</a>, which were added with the view of making the whole structure sink equally. The parts of this building are held together by iron bars, which run across even the aisles. The most remarkable structure in Westminster is the abbey-church of St Peter. On its site stood once and its temple of Apollo, which according to tradition was thrown down by an earthquake in the time of Antonius Pius; and from the ruins of which Sebert king of the West Saxons raised a Christian church, which was ruined by the Danes. It was repaired by Edward the Confessor, and given to a few monks; and this spot he chose for his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a>-place. Henry III. 160 years after, took down this fabric of Edward's, and erected a new church, which was 50 years in building. It suffered much by fire in 1274, but was repaired by Edward I. Edward II. and the abbots. In 1700 this church being much decayed, the parliament granted money for repairing it, and has frequently repeated the bounty since that time. The form of the abbey is that of a long cross: Frontiniae, to the more elegant tables; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MADEIRA">Madeira</a>, the Caleavella, and the Lisbon, into every part of the kingdom." (1.) "There is a magnificence of business (our author remarks) in this ocean of sweets and sours that cannot fail exciting the greatest admiration; whether we consider the number of vessels or their size. The boasted <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TUN">tun</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEIDELBERG">Heidelberg</a> does not surpass them. On first entering the yard, two rise before you, covered at the top with a thatched dome; between them is a circular turret, including a winding staircase, which brings you to their summits, which are above 24 feet in diameter. One of these conservatories is full of sweet wine, and contains 58,109 gallons, or 1815 barrels of Winchester measure. Its superb associate is full of vinegar, to the amount of 56,799 gallons, or 1774 barrels of the same standard as the former. The famous German vessel yields even to the last by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of 40 barrels.—Besides these, is an avenue of lesser vessels, which hold from 32,500 to 16,974 gallons each. After quitting this Brobdignagian scene, we pass to the acres covered with common barrels: we cannot diminish our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> so suddenly, but at first we imagine we could quaff them off as easily as Gulliver did the little hogsheads of the kingdom of Lilliput." cross; its greatest length is 489 feet, and the breadth of the west front 66 feet; the length of the cross aisle is 189 feet, and the height of the roof 92 feet. At the west end are two towers; the nave and cross aisle are supported by 52 slender pillars of Sussex marble exclusive of pilasters. In the upper and lower ranges there are 94 windows, all which, with the arches, roofs, and doors, are in the Gothic taste. The inside of this church is much better executed than the outside; and the perspective is good; particularly that of the grand aisle. The choir, from which there is an ascent by several steps to a fine altar-piece, is paved with black and white marble; having 23 stalls on the north, the same number on the south, and eight at the west end. The altar is made of a beautiful piece of marble, the gift of Queen Anne, enclosed by a curious balustrade, and upon a pavement of porphyry, jasper, Lydian, and serpentine stones, laid in the mosaic style, at the expense of Abbot Ware, A.D. 1272; and is said to be one of the most beautiful of its kind in the world. On each side of this altar a door opens into St Edward's chapel; round which are 10 other chapels, ranging from the north to the south cross aisles, and are dedicated, 1. To St Andrew. 2. To St Michael. 3. To St John Evangelist. 4. Islip's chapel. 5. To St John Baptist. 6. To St Paul. 7. Henry V.'s chapel. 8. To St Nicholas. 9. To St Edmund. 10. To St Benedict. In St Edward's chapel are still to be seen the remains of his shrine; which, though now in obscurity, and robbed of all its <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> and lustre, was once esteemed the glory of England, so far as art and riches could make it. Here are the tombs of King Edward I. and several other kings and queens of England; and here also is shown the famous chair in which the kings of Scotland used to be crowned at Scone. Henry V.'s chapel is divided from St Edward's by an iron screen, on each side of which are statues as big as life.—St Andrew's chapel, which is next the north cross, and the others which surround the choir, are crowded with the monuments of noble personages, worthy the attention of the curious.—At the corner of St Benedict's chapel, an iron gate opens into the south cross aisle; which from the number of monuments erected therein to celebrated English poets, has obtained the name of the Poets' corner; though here we find a most magnificent monument erected at the south end in memory of the late John duke of Argyle and Greenwich; another to William Camden the antiquarian; and others to the celebrated divine Dr Isaac <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARROW">Barrow</a>, to Thomas Parr who died at the age of 152 years, &c.—The south aisle is adorned with 19 curious monuments of the pious, the brave, and the learned; and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> northward from the west door, we view a great number more. On the east of the abbey, and which, though separate from the other chapels in the choir, seems to be one and the same building with the abbey, stands the chapel of King Henry VII., which that king founded in the year 1502, and was at that time styled the wonder of the world, and is now one of the most expensive remains of the ancient English taste and magnificence. There is no looking upon it without admiration: it conveys an idea of the fine taste of Gothic architecture in that age; and the inside is so noble, majestic, and of such curious workmanship, that it would take a volume to describe each part with justice and propriety. Its original intention was to be a dormitory for the royal blood; and so far the will of the founder has been observed, that none have been interred therein but such as have traced their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> from ancient kings. The tomb of King Henry VII. is most magnificent, enclosed with a screen of cast brass, most admirably designed, and as well executed. Within the rails are the figures of that king and his royal consort, in their robes of state, on a tomb of black marble; and at the head of this tomb lie the remains of Edward VI. In different parts of this chapel are the monuments of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> Stewart duke of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHMOND">Richmond</a>, George Villars duke of Buckingham, John <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHEFFIELD">Sheffield</a> duke of Buckingham, Charles Montague marquis of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALIFAX">Halifax</a>, Edward V. and his brother Richard; the vault of James I. and his queen Anne and daughter Mary, on which is a small tomb adorned with the figure of a child; a lofty monument of Queen Elizabeth, and another of Mary queen of Scots; the monuments for Margaret Douglas daughter of Margaret queen of Scots, Margaret countess of Richmond mother to Henry VII., the vault of King Charles II., and William III., Queen Mary his consort, Queen Anne, and Prince George. Over these royal personages are their effigies (except that of Prince George) in wainscot presses, made of wax to resemble life, and dressed in their coronation robes. And at the corner of the great east window, in another wainscot press, stands the effigy of Mary duchess of Richmond, daughter to James duke of Richmond and Lenox, dressed in the very robes she wore at the coronation of Queen Anne. On leaving the aisle, you are shown another press, containing the effigy of General Monk, who, on account of his loyalty, and the part he took in the restoration of King Charles II., had a vault appropriated to him and his family amongst the royal blood. In a fine vault under Henry the VII.'s chapel, is the burying place of the present royal family, erected by his late majesty King George II. Adjoining to the abbey are the cloisters, built in a quadrangular form, with piazzas towards the court, where several of the prebendaries have their houses. Near the abbey church is the King's school, usually called Westminster school. It was originally founded in the year 1570, and a second time by Queen Elizabeth in 1560, whence it is sometimes called the Queen's College; and is at present one of the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> in the kingdom. The learned antiquary Mr Camden was once master of it, and Ben Johnson one of his scholars. Dr Busby, who was master upwards of 50 years, greatly contributed to keep up its reputation, formed its <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a>, and improved both the master's and his prebendal house.—This school, instead of one master and one usher as at first, has now an upper and under master, and five ushers, who have about 400 youths under their tuition. A plan was set on foot when the present archbishop of York was master, for building a college for the use of the students, but this did not succeed. On the north-east side of the abbey is an old building called Westminster-hall, first built by William Rufus as an addition to a royal palace, and afterwards

LONDON

Pages 228-230

In wheat-flour, for pies and puddings, oat-<a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAL">meal</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, &c. at half a farthing a-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, for a million of people for a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEEK">week</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, capers, olives, and other sauces, at half a farthing a-day, for a million of people for a week. In roots and herbs of all sorts, both for food and physic, at half a farthing a-day, for a million of people for a week. In <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-coal, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a>, candles, and fire-wood of all sorts, at 1d. a-day for a million of people for a week. In <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> of all sorts (a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> being used in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a>) quills, pens, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INK">ink</a>, and wax, at a farthing a-day, for a million of people for a week. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a>, and snuff, at half a farthing a-day, for a million of people for a week. In clothing, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> and woollen, for men, women, and children, shoes, stockings, &c. at 3s. 6d. per week, for a million of people for a week. Expenses for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-meat, in hay, oats, beans, 1000 load of hay, a-week, at 40s. a load, comes to 2000l. in oats, and beans the like value, 2000l. which is in all, for one week. Cyder, rum, brandy, strong waters, coffee, chocolate, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEA">tea</a>, &c. at 1d. a-day, for a million of people for one week. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> firing is pit coal, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called sea-firing, por-coal, of which there are consumed upwards of 766,880 ter. &c. chaldrons every year. The annual consumption of oil in London and Westminster for lamps, amounts to 400,000l. In 1787, the quantity of porter brewed in London for home consumption and foreign <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a>, amounted to 1,176,856 barrels. In 1805 it amounted to 1,200,000 barrels of 36 gallons each. The above was the weekly consumption of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> specified a few years ago. The following is the annual consumption of some of them estimated since the year 1800. Bullocks 110,000; sheep and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMBS">lambs</a> 776,000; calves 210,000; hogs 210,000; sucking pigs 60,000; <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a> in gallons 6,980,000; for which the inhabitants pay 481,666l. and this is the produce of 8,500 cows: vegetables and fruit 3,000,000l.: spirituous liquors and compounds 11,146,782 gallons: wine 32,500 tons; <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a> 16,600,000 pounds: cheese 21,100,000 pounds. This great and populous <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> is happily supplied with abundance of fresh <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a> and water. The New River; which is not only of inconceivable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to every family, but by means of fire plugs everywhere dispersed, the keys of which are deposited with the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> officers, the city is in a great <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> secured from the spreading of fire: for these plugs are no sooner opened, than there are vast quantities of water to supply the engines. This plenty of water has been attended with another advantage, it has given rise... rise to several companies, who ensure houses and goods from fire; an advantage that is not to be met with in any other <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; the premium is small; and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of loss is easy and certain. Every one of these offices keeps a set of men in pay, who are ready at all hours to give their assistance in case of fire; and who are on all occasions extremely bold, dexterous, and diligent: but though all their labours should prove unsuccessful, the person who suffers by this devouring element has the comfort that must arise from a certainty of being paid to the value (upon oath) of what he has ensured. The places for diversion are, Vauxhall, Ranelagh-gardens, the two play-houses, the Pantheon, and the little <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> in the Hay-Market, with Sadler's-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a>, Hughes's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CIRCUS">Circus</a>, and Astley's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROVE">Grove</a>, &c. Covent-Garden Theatre was burnt <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in 1808 and rebuilt in 1809; and Drury-Lane Theatre was burnt down in 1809 and rebuilt in 1811. The Royal <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">Institution</a> owed its origin to a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of noblemen and gentlemen, who held meetings for the avowed purpose of ameliorating the condition of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>. They first projected the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of its foundation, which was matured by the exertions and talents of the indefatigable <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> Rumford. The meetings began in 1809, shortly before which his majesty granted the proprietors a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> of incorporation by the name of the Royal Institution of Great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, for the purpose of facilitating the general introduction of useful <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> inventions and improvements, and for teaching, by courses of philosophical lectures and experiments, the application of science to the common purposes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> consists of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>, 15 managers, and the secretary, chosen by and from among the proprietors. Of the 15 managers, one-third is elected annually, on the first of May. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> is situated in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBEMARLE">Albemarle</a>-street, is extremely spacious, and well adapted to the purposes to which it is applied. The London Institution was formed in the autumn of 1805, by the indefatigable exertions of a few spirited individuals. The house in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> is in the Old Jewry, till the managers can procure a more suitable <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of it is to promote the dissemination of science, literature, and the arts: its view at present being confined to three objects, viz. the acquisition of a valuable and extensive library; the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFUSION">diffusion</a> of useful knowledge by the means of lectures and experiments; and the establishment of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> room, where the foreign and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> journals are provided for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the proprietors and subscribers. The government of the Institution is vested in a president, four vice-presidents, twenty managers, and the secretary. The number of proprietors is limited to 1000, each of whom paid 75 guineas for a share, and the life subscribers pay 25 guineas.

LONDON LONDONDERRY

Pages 230-230
or COLERAIN, a county of Ireland, in the province of Ulster. It is bounded on the south and south-west by the county of Tyrone; by Antrim on the east, from which it is parted by the river Bann: by Donegal on the west; and that country and the Deucalcedonian ocean on the north. Its length is about 32½ miles, its breadth 25, containing about 511,688 acres. In 1813 it contained 186,000 inhabitants. The bogs and heaths of this county are manured with sea-shells, as those of Donegal. Like that, too, it is pretty champagne, and not unfruitful. It is particularly noted for a very clear river called the Bann, abounding with salmon, a fish said to delight in limpid streams. This river, to distinguish it from a lesser of the same name, is called the Greater or Lower Bann. In order to cultivate, settle, and civilize this county, King James I. granted it by letters patent, to a society, by the name of the Governor and Assistants at London of the new plantation of Ulster in the realm of Ireland. It contains four baronies; and besides the two knights of the shire, sends to parliament one member for the city of Londonderry, and one for Colerain. See LONDONDERRY, SUPPLEMENT.

LONDONDERRY

Pages 230-231
or Derry, the capital of the county, and the see of a bishop, stands at the bottom of Lough-Foyle. This city has a very good port, to which ships of the greatest burden have access, and a considerable trade. It will be ever famous for the gallantry and perseverance with which it defended itself in three memorable sieges, in defiance of the greatest hardships and discouragements, namely, 1st, In 1641, when the rebels could not reduce it either by fraud or force. 2dly, In 1649, when it was besieged by the Lord Ardes, and reduced almost to extremity by famine, till at last relieved by troops sent from England. 3dly, When it held out against the French and Irish from the 7th of December 1688, to the last day of July 1689, though it was neither well fortified nor provided with a garrison or stores of provision and ammunition, and hardly any attempt made to relieve it during so long a time. Though the city is 20 miles up the river, yet very large ships can come up to the quay, where there are four or five fathoms of water. It is now well fortified with a strong wall, besides outworks; and along the banks of the river are several castles and a fort. This city is of no great antiquity, having been built and planted in the reign of James I. by a colony sent by the society above mentioned. The trade of the town is very considerable, having not only a large share in the herring fishery, but sending ships also to the West Indies, New England, and Newfoundland, for which they are so advantageously situated, that a vessel bound from thence to America often arrives there before a London ship can get clear of the soundings, or arrive in the latitude of Londonderry. Though there are many shallows in Lough-Foyle, which serves it instead of a road; yet they are easily avoided. There is in the town an Infirmary, a Theatre, and a Linen-Hall. There is also a large and commodious Jail, and an elegant Court-house. The inhabitants of this city are almost all Protestants. It gave the title of earl and baron to a branch of the family of Pitt, which became extinct in 1764; but part of the title was revived in Robert Stewart, who was created Baron Londonderry. Derry in 1789. A late traveller says, "Derry is, perhaps, the cleanest, best built, and most beautifully situated town in Ireland; and excepting Cork, as convenient as any for commerce, foreign and domestic." The lake almost surrounds it; and the whole ground-plot both of it and its liberties belongs to the 12 great companies of London. The imports are flax seed, hardware, iron, timber, and West India goods. The exports are yarn, linen, salmon salted and barrelled, &c. It contains 18,500 inhabitants, and has a wooden bridge 166 feet long, which was erected in 1791. Long. 7° 5' W.; Lat. 55° 4' N.

LONG

Pages 231-231

an epithet given to whatever exceeds the usual standard of length. Long-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">Boat</a>, the largest and strongest boat belonging to any ship. It is principally employed to carry <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> burdens, as anchors, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CABLES">cables</a>, ballast, &c. See BOAT. Long, Roger, D.D. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEMBROKE">Pembroke</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, Lowndes's professor of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a> in that university, rector of Cherryhinton in Huntingdonshire, and of Bradwell juxta mare in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>, was author of a well known and much improved treatise of astronomy, and the inventor of a remarkably curious astronomical machine, thus described by himself. "I have, in a room lately built in Pembroke-hall, erected a sphere of 18 feet diameter, wherein above 30 persons may sit conveniently; the entrance into it is over the south pole by six steps; the frame of the sphere consists of a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> meridians, not complete semicircles, the northern ends of which are screwed to a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> round plate of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, with a hole in the centre of it; through this hole, from a beam in the ceiling, comes the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> pole, a round iron rod, about three inches long, and supports the upper parts of the sphere to its proper elevation for the latitude of Cambridge; the lower <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the sphere, so much of it as is invisible in England, is cut off; and the lower <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> southern ends of the meridians, or truncated semicircles, terminate on, and are screwed <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to a strong circle of oak, of about 13 feet diameter; which, when the sphere is put into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, runs upon large rollers of lignum vitae, in the manner that the tops of some windmills are made to turn round. Upon the iron meridians is fixed a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZODIAC">zodiac</a> of tin painted blue, whereon the ecliptic and heliocentric orbits of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a> are drawn, and the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-CONSTELLATIONS">constellations</a> and stars traced: the Great and Little Bear and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRACO">Draco</a> are already painted in their places round the north pole; the rest of the constellations are proposed to follow; the whole is turned round with a small winch, with as little labour as it takes to <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> up a jack, though the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of the iron, tin, and wooden circle, is about 1000 pounds. When it is made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANETARIUM">planetarium</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be placed in the middle thereof. The whole, with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>, is well supported by a frame of large <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>." Thus far Dr Long, before this curious piece of mechanism was perfected. Since the above was written, the sphere has been completely finished; all the constellations and stars of the northern hemisphere, visible at Cambridge, are painted in their proper places upon plates of iron joined together, which form one concave surface. Dr Long published a Commencement Sermon 1728; and an answer to Dr Galley's pamphlet on Greek Accents; and died <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 16th, 1770, at the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 91. As the materials for this article are scanty, we shall subjoin, from the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">Gentleman</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGAZINE">Magazine</a>*, a few traits of him, as delineated in 1769 by Mr Jones. "He is now in the 88th year of his age, and for his years vegete and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>. He was lately (in October) put in nomination for the office of vice-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>. He executed that trust once before, I think in the year 1737; a very ingenious person, and sometimes very facetious. At the public commencement in the year 1613, Dr Greene (master of Bennet <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, and afterwards bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELY">Ely</a>) being then vice-chancellor, Mr Long was pitched upon for the tripso-performance; it was witty and humorous, and has passed through <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> editions. Some that remembered the delivery of it, told me, that in addressing the vice-chancellor (whom the university wags usually styled Miss Greene), the tripso-orator, being a native of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a>, and assuming the Norfolk dialect, instead of saying, Domine Vice-Cancellarie, did very archly pronounce the words thus, Domina Vice-Cancellaria; which occasioned a general smile in that great auditory. His friend the late Mr Bonfoy of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIPON">Ripon</a> told me this little incident, 'That he and Dr Long walking together in Cambridge, in a dusky evening, and coming to a short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> fixed in the pavement, which Mr B. in the midst of chat and inattention, took to be a boy standing in his way, he said in a hurry, 'Get out of my way, boy.' 'That boy, Sir,' said the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> very calmly and slyly, 'is a post-boy, who turns out of his way for nobody.'—I could recollect several other ingenious repartees <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> there were occasion. One thing is remarkable, he never was a hale and hearty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, always of a tender and delicate <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, yet took great care of it. His <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> drink <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. He always dines with the fellows in the hall. Of late years he has left off eating <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>-meats; in the room thereof, puddings, vegetables, &c. sometimes a glass or two of wine."

LONG-ISLAND

Pages 236-237

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, belonging to the state of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEW_YORK">New <a c</a>lass="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, which is separated from the continent by a narrow channel. It extends from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of New York east 140 miles, terminating with Montauk point; and is not more than ten miles in breadth on a medium. It is divided into three counties, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a>'s, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a>'s, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>. The south side of the island is flat <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, bordered on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> tracts of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEADOW">meadow</a>, extending from the west point of the island to Southampton. This soil, however, is well calculated for raising grain, especially <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> corn. The north side of the island is hilly, and of a strong soil, adapted to the culture of grain, hay, and fruit. A ridge of hills extends from Jamaica to South-hold. Large herds of cattle feed upon <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAMPSTEAD">Hampstead</a> plain and on the salt marshes upon the south side of the island. Hampstead plain in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN_S_COUNTY">Queen's <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> is a curiosity. It is 16 miles in length, east and west, and 7 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 8 miles wide. The soil is <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> and to appearance rich, yet it was never known to have any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> growth, but a kind of wild grass and a few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>. It is frequently visited by vast numbers of plover. Rye grows tolerably well on some parts of the plain. The most of it lies <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> for cattle, horses, and sheep. As there is nothing to impede the prospect in the whole length of this plain, it has a curious but tiresome effect upon the eye, not unlike that of the ocean. The island contained 48,752 inhabitants in 1810.

LONGEVITY

Pages 231-236

length of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. From the different longevities of men in the beginning of the world, after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>, and in these ages, Mr <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DERHAM">Derham</a> draws an argument for the interposition of a divine <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a>. Immediately after the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>, when the world was to be peopled by one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> and one woman, the ordinary <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> was 900 and upwards.—Immediately after the flood, when there were three persons to stock the world, their age was cut shorter, and none of those patriarchs, but Shem, arrived at 500. In the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> century we find none that reached 240: in the third, none but Terah that came to 200 years; the world, at least a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of it, by that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> being so well peopled, that they had built cities, and were cantoned out into distant nations.—By degrees, as the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of people increased, their longevity dwindled, till it came <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> at length to 70 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 80 years: and there it stood, and has <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to stand ever since the time of Moses.—This is found a good medium, and by means hereof the world is neither overstocked, nor kept too thin; but life and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> keep a pretty equal pace. That the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> of man's life has been the same in all ages since the above <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, is plain both from sacred and profane <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. To <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> by others, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a> lived to 81, and was accounted an old man: and the instances of longevity produced by Pliny, lib. vii. c. 48. as very extraordinary, may most of them be matched in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> histories. All the public prints at the end of 1790; and Memoirs, &c. | (R) This man, in 1780, at the age of 120, quitted his native hills, and from the summit of Mount Jura undertook a journey to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSAILLES">Versailles</a>, to behold and return thanks to the national <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> for the vote which had freed him and his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> countrymen from the feudal yoke. In the early part of his life, he was a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> in the family of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> de Beauremont. His <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> continued good to the last <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of his life; and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> inconveniences which he felt from his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> age were, that his sight was weakened, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of his body was so diminished, that he shivered with <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> in the middle of the dog-days if he was not sitting by a good fire. This old man was received in the body of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> by the national assembly, indulged with a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, and directed to keep on his hat lest he should catch cold if he was to sit uncovered. A collection was made for him by the members, which exceeded 500l. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>; but he lived not to return to Mount Jura. He was buried on Saturday the 31st of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1790, with great funeral pomp, in the parish-church of St Eustace at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. (S) He served as a private at the taking of Gibraltar in 1704. (T) Memoirs of the Life and gallant Exploits of the Old <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HIGHLANDER">Highlander</a>, Serjeant Donald Maccod, &c. published 1791, in the 103d year of his age.—This old <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, for it appears that he really is a gentleman both by birth and by behaviour, was born in the year of the Revolution, in the parish of Bracadill, in the isle of Sky, and county of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERNESS">Inverness</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. He is a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CADET">cadet</a> of the family of Ulinish in Sky; and descended, through his mother, from Macdonald of Slatc, the ancestor of the present Lord Macdonald. The earlier part of his life coincided with the famine of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years in Scotland; which was so great as to suggest, even A certain author mentions a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a> collected by himself of 107 persons, who all died at the age of 120 and upwards. Two of them attained the age of 150, three of 152, one of 154, one of 169, and another of 175. In 1763 there were found in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a> 88 females above 90 years of age. We have seen a list of 104 persons, none of whom died under 120 years of age, and one of them, it is said, lived to the prodigious age of 180. Forty-one of them belonged to England, 16 to Scotland, and 24 to Ireland. The <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTEDILUVIANS">antediluvians</a> are purposely omitted, as <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> too little reference to the present <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of mortals, to afford any satisfactory conclusions; and as they have been already taken notice of in a separate article (see Antediluvians). As the improbable stories of some persons who have almost rivalled them in modern times, border too much upon the marvellous to find a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in these tables, the present examples are abundantly sufficient to prove, that longevity does not depend, so much as has been supposed, on any particular climate, situation, or occupation in life: for we see, that it often prevails in places where all these are extremely dissimilar; and it would, moreover, be very difficult, in the histories of the several persons above mentioned, to find any circumstance common to them all, except, perhaps, that of being born of healthy parents, and of being inured to daily labour, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a>, and simplicity of diet. Among the inferior ranks of mankind, therefore, rather than among the sons of ease and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a>, shall we find the most numerous instances of longevity; even frequently, when other <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> circumstances seem extremely unfavourable; as in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of the poor sexton at Peterborough, who, notwithstanding his unpromising occupation among dead bodies, lived long enough to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURY">bury</a> two crowned heads, and to survive two complete generations. The livelihood of Henry Jenkins and old Parre is said to have consisted chiefly of the coarsest fare, as they depended on precarious alms. To which may be added the remarkable instance of Agnes Milbourne, who, after bringing forth a numerous offspring, and being obliged, through <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> indigence, to pass the latter part of her life in St Luke's workhouse, yet reached her 106th year in that sordid and unfriendly situation. The plain diet and invigorating employments of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> life are acknowledged on all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> to be highly conducive to health and longevity, while the luxuries and refinements of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> cities are allowed to be equally destructive to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; and this consideration alone, perhaps, more than counterbalances all the boasted privileges of superior elegance and civilization resulting from a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> life. From country villages, and not from crowded cities, have the preceding instances of longevity been chiefly supplied. Accordingly it appears from the London bills of mortality, during a period of 30 years, viz. from the year 1728 to 1758, the sum of the deaths amounted to 750,322, and that in all this prodigious number, only 242 persons survived the 100th year of their age! This overgrown <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> is computed by Dr Price to contain a ninth part of the inhabitants of England, and to consume annually 7000 persons, who remove into it from the country every year, without increasing it. He moreover observes, that the number of inhabitants in England and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a> has diminished about one-fourth part since the Revolution; and so rapidly of late, that in 11 years, near 200,000 of our common people have been lost. If the calculation be <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a>, however alarming it may appear in a national view, there is this consolation, when considered in a philosophical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, that without partial evil, there can be no general good; and to the patriotic Mr Fletcher, the idea of the people selling themselves as slaves for immediate subsistence. He was bred in the midst of want and hardships, cold, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a>, and for the years of his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPRENTICESHIP">apprenticeship</a> with a mason and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTTER">cutter</a> in Inverness, in incessant fatigue. He enlisted, when a boy, in the Scottish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, in the town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERTH">Perth</a> in the last year of the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> William. The regiment into which he enlisted was the Scots Royals, commanded by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Orkney. That old <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> corps, at that time, used bows and arrows as well as swords, and wore <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> caps. He served in Germany and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a> under the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARLBOROUGH">Marlborough</a>; under the duke of Argyll, in the rebellion 1715; in the Highland Watch, or companies raised for enforcing the laws in the Highlands; in the same companies when, under the name of the 42d regiment, they were sent abroad to Flanders, to join the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> under the duke of Cumberland; in the same regiment in Ireland, and on the breaking out of the French <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, 1757, in America. From the 42d he was draughted to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> as a drill <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERGEANT">sergeant</a> in the 78th regiment, in which he served at the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of Louisburg and Quebec: After this he became an out-pensioner of Chelsea <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">Hospital</a>. But such was the spirit of this brave and hardy veteran, that he served in 1761 as a volunteer in Germany under the marquis of Granby; and offered his services in the American war to Sir Henry Clinton; who, though he declined to employ the old man in the fatigues and dangers of war, treated him with great kindness, allowed him a liberal weekly pension out of his own pocket, and sent him home in a ship <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with despatches to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>.—The sergeant, “as his memory, according to the observation of his biographer, is impaired, does not pretend to make an exact enumeration of all his offspring: but he knows of 16 sons now living, 14 of whom are in the army and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>, besides daughters; the eldest of whom by his present wife is a mantuemaker at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a>.—His eldest son is now 83 years old, and the youngest only <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a>. Nor, in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, would this lad <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> the rear of his immediate progeny, if his present wife, the boy’s mother, had not attained to the 49th year of her age?”—In his prime, he did not exceed five feet and seven inches. He is now inclined through age to five feet five inches. He has an interesting physiognomy, expressive of sincerity, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a>, and manly courage. His biographer very properly submits it to the consideration of the Polygraphic Society, whether they might not do a thing worthy of themselves and their ingenious art, if they should multiply likenesses of this living antiquity, and circulate them at an easy rate throughout Britain and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. They would thus gratify a very general curiosity; a curiosity not confined to the present age. Longevity, and that what a nation loses in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> at one period, it gains at another; and thus, probably, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> number of inhabitants on the surface of the globe continues at all times nearly the same. By this medium, the world is neither overstocked with inhabitants nor kept too thin, but life and death keep a tolerably equal pace. The inhabitants of this island, comparatively speaking, are but as the dust in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a>; yet instead of being diminished, we are assured by other writers, that within these 30 years they are greatly increased. The desire of self-preservation, and of protracting the short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAN">span</a> of life, is so intimately interwoven with our <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, that it is justly esteemed one of the first principles of our <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and, in spite even of pain and misery, seldom quits us to the last moments of our existence. It seems, therefore, to be no less our duty than our <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, to examine minutely into the various means that have been considered as conducive to health and long life: and, if possible, to distinguish such circumstances as are essential to that great end from those which are merely accidental. But here it is much to be regretted, that an accurate history of the lives of all the remarkable persons in the above table, so far as relates to the diet, regimen, and the use of the non-naturals, has not been faithfully handed down to us; without which it is impossible to draw the necessary inferences. Is it not then a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of astonishment, that historians and philosophers have hitherto paid so little <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to longevity? If the present imperfect list should excite others, of more leisure and better abilities, to undertake a full <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a> of so interesting a subject, the inquiry might prove not only curious but highly useful to mankind. In order to furnish materials for a future history of longevity, the bills of mortality throughout the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> ought first to be revised, and put on a better footing, agreeable to the scheme of which Manchester and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a> have already given a specimen highly worthy of our <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, however, might be farther improved with very little trouble, by adding a particular account of the diet and regimen of every person who dies at 80 years of age or upwards; and mentioning whether his parents were healthy, long-lived people, &c. An accurate register, thus established throughout the British dominions, would be productive of many important advantages to society, not only in a medical and philosophical, but also in a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> and moral view. All the circumstances which are most essentially necessary to life, may be comprised under the six following heads: 1. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">Air</a> and climate; 2. Meat and drink; 3. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">Motion</a> and rest; 4. The secretions and excretions; 5. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">Sleep</a> and watching; 6. Affections of the mind. These, though all perfectly natural to the constitution, have by writers been styled the non-naturals, by a strange perversion of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>; and have been all copiously handled under that improper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>. However, it may not be amiss to offer a few short observations on each, as they are so immediately connected with the present subject. 1. Air, &c. It has long been known that fresh air is more immediately necessary to life than food; for a man may live two or three days without the latter, but not many minutes without the former. The vivifying principle contained in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>, so essential to longevity, the support of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>, as well as animal life, concerning which authors have proposed so many conjectures, appears now to be nothing else but that pure dephticated fluid lately discovered by that ingenious philosopher Dr Priestley. The common atmosphere may well be supposed to be more or less healthy in proportion as it abounds with this animating principle. As this exhales in copious streams from the green leaves of all kinds of vegetables, even from those of the most poisonous kinds, may we not, in some <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> account why instances of longevity are so much more frequent in the country than in large cities; where the air, instead of partaking so largely of this salutary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPREGNATION">impregnation</a>, is daily contaminated with noxious animal effluvia and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHLOGISTON">phlogiston</a>? With respect to climate, various observations conspire to prove, that those regions which <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> within the temperate zones are best calculated to promote long life. Hence, perhaps, may be explained, why Italy has produced so many long lives, and why <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in general are more salutary than continents; of which <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERMUDAS">Bermudas</a> and some others afford examples. And it is a pleasing circumstance that our own island appears from the above table (notwithstanding the sudden vicissitudes to which it is liable) to contain far more instances of longevity than could well be imagined. The ingenious Mr Whitehurst assures us, from certain facts, that Englishmen are in general longer lived than North Americans; and that a British constitution <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> last longer, even in that climate, than a native one. But it must be allowed in general, that the human constitution is adapted to the peculiar state and temperature of each respective climate, so that no part of the habitable globe can be pronounced too hot or too cold for its inhabitants. Yet, in order to promote a friendly intercourse between the most remote regions, the Author of nature has wisely enabled the inhabitants to endure great and surprising changes of temperature with impunity. 2. Foods and drink. Though foods and drink of the most simple kinds are allowed to be the best calculated for supporting the body in health, yet it can hardly be doubted but variety may be safely indulged occasionally, provided men would restrain their appetites within the bounds of temperance: for bountiful Nature cannot be supposed to have poured forth such a rich profusion of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, merely to tantalize the human species, without attributing to her the part of a cruel stepdame, instead of that of the kind and indulgent <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARENT">parent</a>. Besides, we find, that by the wonderful powers of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGESTIVE">digestive</a> organs, a variety of animal and vegetable substances, of very discordant principles, are happily assimilated into one bland homogeneous chyle; therefore it seems natural to distrust those cynical writers, who would rigidly confine mankind to one simple <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DISH">dish</a>, and their drink to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> of the brook. Nature, it is true, has pointed out that mild insipid fluid as the universal diluent, and therefore most admirably adapted for our daily <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEVERAGE">beverage</a>. But <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> has equally proved, that vinous and spirituous liquors, on certain occasions, are no less salutary and beneficial, whether it be to support strength against sickness or bodily fatigue, or to exhilarate the mind under the pressure of heavy misfortunes. But, alas! Longevity, what Nature meant for innocent and useful cordials, to be used only occasionally, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> and caprice have by degrees rendered habitual to the human frame, and liable to the most enormous and destructive abuses. Hence it may be justly doubted, whether gluttony and intemperance have not depopulated the world more than even the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, pestilence, and famine. True, therefore, is the old maxim, "Modus utendi ex veneno facit medicamentum, ex medicamento venenum." See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIETETICS">Dietetics</a>, Supplement. 3. and 4. Motion and rest, sleep and watching. It is allowed on all hands, that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a> motion and rest, and sleep and watching, are necessary conditions to health and longevity; and that they ought to be adapted to age, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEMPERAMENT">temperament</a>, constitution, temperature of the climate, &c.; but the errors which mankind daily commit in these respects become a fruitful source of diseases. While some are bloated and relaxed with ease and indolence, others are emaciated, and become rigid through hard labour, watching, and fatigue. 5. Secretions and evacuations. Where the animal functions are duly performed, the secretions go on regularly; and the different evacuations so exactly correspond to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of aliment taken in, in a given time, that the body is found to return daily to nearly the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. If any particular evacuation happen to be preternaturally diminished, some other evacuation is proportionally augmented, and the equilibrium is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> preserved; but continued irregularities, in these important functions, cannot but terminate in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>. 6. Affections of the mind. The due regulation of the passions, perhaps, contributes more to health and longevity than that of any other of the non-naturals. The animating passions, such as joy, hope, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>, &c., when kept within proper bounds, gently excite the nervous influence, promote an equable circulation, and are highly conducive to health; while the depressing affections, such as fear, grief, and despair, produce the contrary effect, and lay the foundation of the most formidable diseases. From the light which history affords us, as well as from some instances in the above table, there is great reason to believe, that longevity is in a great measure <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a>; and that healthy long-lived parents would commonly transmit the same to their children, were it not for the frequent errors in the non-naturals, which so evidently tend to the abbreviation of human life. Where is it, but from these causes, and the unnatural modes of living, that, of all the children which are born in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> cities of Europe, nearly one half die in early infancy? To what else can we <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> this extraordinary mortality? Such an amazing proportion of premature deaths is a circumstance unheard of among <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> nations, or among the young of other animals! In the earliest ages, we are informed, that human life was protracted to a very extraordinary length; yet how few persons, in these latter times, arrive at that period which nature seems to have designed! Man is by nature a field animal, and seems destined to rise with the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, and to spend a large portion of his time in the open air, to inure his body to robust exercises and the inclemency of the seasons, and to make a plain homely repast only when hunger dictates. But art has studiously defeated the kind intentions of nature; and by enslaving him to all the Longevity blandishments of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, has left him, alas! an easy victim to folly and caprice. To enumerate the various abuses which take place from the earliest infancy, and which are continued through the succeeding stages of modish life, would carry us far beyond our present intention. Suffice it to observe, that they prevail more particularly among people who are the most highly polished and refined. To compare their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of life with that of nature, or even of the long-livers in the list, would probably afford a very striking <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a>; and at the same time supply an additional reason why, in the very large cities, instances of longevity are so very rare.

LONGFORD

Pages 236-236

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, situated on the river Cromlin, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Longford and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEINSTER">Leinster</a>, 64 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>; which river falls a few miles below this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHANNON">Shannon</a>. It is a borough, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>, market, and fair town; and formerly returned two members to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">Patron</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Longford. It gave <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> to the family of Augier; of viscount, to the family of Micklothwaite; and now gives that of baron to the family of Packenham. Within a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> and a half of the town is a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a>-school for above 40 children. This place has a barrack for a troop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>. It is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and well built; and in a very early <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> was founded here, of which St Idus, one of St Patrick's disciples, was <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a>. In the year 1400, a fine <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> was founded to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the virgin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, for Dominican friars, by O'Ferral <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of Annaly. This monastery being destroyed by fire, Pope Martin V. by a bull in the year 1429, granted an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a> to all who should contribute to the rebuilding of it. In 1433, Pope Eugene IV. granted a bull to the same purpose; and in 1438 he granted another to the like effect. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of this friary, now the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> church, is in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of Ardagh. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> are four in the year.

LONGIMETRY

Pages 237-237

the art of measuring lengths, both accessible and inaccessible. See <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">GEOMETRY</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIGONOMETRY">TRIGONOMETRY</a>.

LONGING

Pages 237-237

a preternatural appetite in pregnant women, and in some sick persons when about to recover. It is called <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICA">pica</a>, from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> of that name, which is said to be subject to the same disorder. The disorder consists of both a desire of unusual things to eat and drink, and in being soon tired of one and wanting another. It is called <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MALACIA">malacia</a>, from μαλαξης, "weakness." In pregnant women it is somewhat relieved by bleeding, and in about the fourth <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of their pregnancy it leaves them. Chlorotic girls, and men who labour under suppressed hemorrhoids, are very subject to this complaint, and are relieved by promoting the respective evacuations. In general, whether this disorder is observed in pregnant women, in persons recovering from an acute fever, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> those who labour under obstructions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> evacuations, this craving of the appetite should be indulged.

LONGINICO

Pages 237-237

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, in the Morea, anciently called <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OLYMPIA">Olympia</a>, famous for being the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the Olympic games were celebrated, and for the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> Olympus, about a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> distant. It is now but a small place, situated on the river Alpheus, 10 miles from its mouth, and 50 south of Leptanto. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 22°. N. Lat. 37°. 32'.

LONGINUS

Pages 237-237

Dionysius, a celebrated Greek critic of the third century, was probably an Athenian. His father's name is unknown, but by his mother he was allied to the celebrated Plutarch. His youth was spent in travelling with his parents, which gave him an opportunity to increase his knowledge, and improve his mind. After his travels, he fixed his residence at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, and with the greatest assiduity applied to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>. Here he published his Treatise on the Sublime; which raised his reputation to such a height, and gave the Athenians such an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of his judgment and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, that they made him sovereign judge of all authors, and every thing was received and rejected by the public according to his decisions. He seems to have staid at Athens a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; here he taught the academic <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, and among others had the famous Porphyry for his pupil. But it was at length his fortune to be drawn from Athens, and to mix in more <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> scenes; to train up young princes to virtue and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>; to guide the busy passions of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> to noble objects; to struggle for, and at last to die in the cause of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>. Zenobia, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of the East, prevailed on him to undertake the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of her sons; and he soon gained an uncommon share in her esteem; she spent the vacant hours of her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in his conversation, and modelled her sentiments and conduct by his instructions. That princess was at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with Aurelian; and being defeated by him near Antioch, was compelled to shut herself up in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALMYRA">Palmyra</a>, her <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> wrote her a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>, in which he ordered her to surrender; to which she returned an answer, drawn up by Longinus, which filled him with resentment. The emperor laid siege to the city; and the Palmyrians were at length obliged to open their gates and receive the conqueror. The queen and Longinus endeavoured to fly into <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>; but were unhappily overtaken and made prisoners when they were on the point of crossing the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a>. The queen, intimidated, weakly laid the blame of vindicating the liberty of her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> on its true author; and the brave Longinus, to the disgrace of the conqueror, was carried away to immediate execution. The writings of Longinus were numerous, some on philosophical, but the greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> on critical subjects. Dr Pearce has collected the titles of 25 treatises, none of which, excepting that on the Sublime, have escaped the depredations of time and barbarians. On this imperfect piece the great fame of Longinus is raised, who, as Pope expresses it—"is himself the great sublime he draws." The best edition of his works is that by Tollius, printed at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a> in 1694, cum notis variiorum. It has been translated into English by Mr Smith. LONGISSIMUS DORSI. See ANATOMY, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">Table</a> of the Muscles.

LONGITUDE

Pages 237-247

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">Navigation</a>, is the distance of any <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> from another eastward <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> westward, counted in degrees upon the equator; but when the distance is reckoned by leagues or miles and not in degrees, or in degrees on the meridian, and not of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> of latitude, in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> it includes both latitude and longitude, it is called departure. To find the longitude at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, is a problem to which the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of navigators and mathematicians has been drawn ever since navigation began to be improved.—The importance of this problem soon became so well known, that, in 1598, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> III. of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> offered a reward of 1000 crowns for the solution; and his example was soon followed by the States General, who offered 10,000 florins. In 1714 an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> was passed in the British <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, empowering certain commissioners to make out a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">bill</a> for a sum not exceeding 2000l. for defraying the necessary expenses of experiments for ascertaining this point; and likewise granting a reward to the person who made any progress in the solution, proportionable to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of accuracy with which the solution was performed: 10,000l. was granted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the longitude should be determined to one degree of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> circle, or 60 geographical miles; 15,000l. if to two-thirds of that distance; and 20,000l. if to half the distance. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of these proffered rewards, innumerable attempts were made to discover this important secret.
