The word is Saxon, but abbreviated from two syllables into one; for it was originally Hlaford, which by dropping the aspiration became Laford, and afterwards by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a> Lord. "The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ETYMOLOGY">etymology</a> of the word (says J. Coates) is well worth observing; for it was composed of hlaf "a loaf of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>," and ford, "to give or afford;" so that Hlaford, now Lord, implies "a giver of bread;" because, in those ages, such <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> men kept extraordinary houses, and fed all the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>; for which reason they were called givers of bread, a thing now much out of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a>, great men being fond of retaining the title, but few regarding the practice for which it was first given. See Lady. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">House</a> of Lords, one of the three estates of parliament, and composed of the Lords Spiritual and Temporal. 1. The Spiritual Lords consist of two archbishops and 24 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>; and, at the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of monasteries by Henry VIII., consisted likewise of 26 mitred abbots and two priors; a very considerable body, and in those times equal in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> to the temporal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>. All these hold, or are supposed to hold, certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> baronies under the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>: for William the Conqueror thought proper to change the spiritual tenor of frankalmogin or free alms, under which the bishops held their lands during the Saxon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, into the feudal or Norman <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a> by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BARONY">barony</a>; which subjected their estates to all civil charges and assessments, from which they were before exempt; and in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of succession to those baronies, which were unalienable from their respective dignities, the bishops and abbots were allowed their seats in the house of lords. But though these lords spiritual are in the eye of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> a distinct estate from the lords temporal, and are so distinguished in most of our acts of parliament; yet in practice they are usually blended together under the name of the lords: they intermix in their votes, and the majority of such intermixture joins both estates. And from this want of a separate <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>, and separate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a> of the prelates, some writers have argued very cogently, that the lords spiritual and temporal are now in reality only one estate: which is unquestionably true in every effectual sense, though the ancient distinction between them still nominally continues. For <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">bill</a> should <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> their house, there is no doubt of its validity, though every lord spiritual should vote against it; of which Selden and Sir Edward <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COKE">Coke</a> give many instances; as, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, doubtless it would be equally good, if the lords temporal present were inferior to the bishops in number, and every one of those temporal lords gave his vote to reject the bill; though this Sir Edward Coke seems to doubt of. 2. The Temporal Lords consist of all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a> of the realm (the bishops not being in strictness held to be such, but merely lords of parliament), by whatever title of nobility distinguished; dukes, marquises, earls, viscounts or barons*. Some of these sit by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>, as do all ancient peers; some by creation, as do all new new made ones; others, since the union with Scotland, by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a>, which is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of the 16 peers who represent the body of the Scots nobility. Their number is indefinite, and may be increased at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> by the power of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>: and once, in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, there was an instance of creating no less than 12 together; in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a> of which, in the reign of King George I., a bill passed the house of lords, and was countenanced by the then ministry, for limiting the number of the peerage. This was thought by some to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> a great acquisition to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, by restraining the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a> from gaining the ascendant in that august assembly, by pouring in at <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> an unlimited number of new-created lords. But the bill was ill relished, and miscarried in the house of commons, whose leading members were then desirous to keep the avenues to the other house as open and easy as possible. The distinction of ranks and honours is necessary in every well governed state: in order to reward such as are eminent for their services to the public, in a manner the most desirable to individuals, and yet without burden to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a>; exciting thereby an ambitious yet laudable ardour and generous emulation in others. And emulation, or virtuous ambition, is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> which, however dangerous or invidious in a more republic or under a despotic sway, will certainly be attended with good effects under a free <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>; where, without destroying its existence, its excesses may be continually restrained by that superior power from which all honour is derived. Such a spirit, when nationally diffused, gives <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and vigour to the community; it sets all the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a> of government in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, which, under a wise regulator, may be directed to any beneficial purpose; and thereby every individual may be made subservient to the public good, while he principally means to promote his own particular views. A body of nobility is also more particularly necessary in our mixed and compounded constitution, in order to support the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of both the crown and the people, by forming a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a> to withstand the encroachments of both. It creates and preserves that gradual <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> which proceeds from the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEASANT">peasant</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>; rising like a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYRAMID">pyramid</a> from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> foundation, and diminishing to a point as it rises. It is this ascending and contracting proportion that adds stability to any government; for when the departure is sudden from one <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> to another, we may pronounce that state to be precarious. The nobility therefore are the pillars, which are reared from among the people, more immediately to support the throne; and, if that falls, they must also be buried under its ruins. Accordingly, when in the last century the commons had determined to extirpate monarchy, they also voted the house of lords to be useless and dangerous. And since titles of nobility are thus expedient in the state, it is also expedient that their owners should form an independent and separate branch of the legislature. If they were confounded with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of the people, and like them had only a vote in electing representatives, their privileges would soon be borne <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> and overwhelmed by the popular <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TORRENT">torrent</a>, which would effectually <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> all distinctions. It is therefore highly necessary that the body of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a> should have a distinct assembly, distinct deliberations, and distinct powers from the commons. See also King, Nobility, Parliament, Commons, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONALTY">Commonalty</a>. As to the peculiar laws and customs relating to the house of lords: One very ancient privilege is that declared by the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> of the forest, confirmed in parliament 9 Hen. III.; viz. that every lord spiritual or temporal summoned to parliament, and passing through the king's forests, may, both in going and returning, kill one or two of the king's deer without warrant; in view of the forester if he be present, or on blowing a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">horn</a> if he be absent; that he may not seem to take the king's venison by stealth. In the next <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, they have a right to be attended, and constantly are, by the judges of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of king's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENCH">bench</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMMON_PLEAS"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> pleas, and such of the barons of the exchequer as are of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of the coif, or have been made sergeants at law; as likewise by the king's learned counsel, being sergeants, and by the masters of the court of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>; for their advice in point of law, and for the greater dignity of their proceedings. The secretaries of state, with the attorney and solicitor general, were also used to attend the house of peers, and have to this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> (together with the judges, &c.) their regular writs of summons issued out at the beginning of every parliament, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> tradandum et consilium impendendum, though not ad consentendum, but, whenever of late years they have been members of the house of commons, their attendance here hath fallen into disuse. Another privilege is, that every peer, by license obtained from the king, may make another lord of parliament his proxy, to vote for him in his absence: A privilege, which a member of the other house can by no means have, as he is himself but a proxy for a multitude of other people. Each peer has also a right, by leave of the house, when a vote passes contrary to his sentiments, to enter his dissent on the journals of the house, with the reasons for such dissent; which is usually styled his protest. All bills likewise, that may in their consequences any way affect the rights of the peerage, are by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of parliament to have their first rise and beginning in the house of peers, and to suffer no changes or amendments in the house of commons. There is also one statute peculiarly relative to the house of lords; 6 Ann. c. 23., which regulates the election of the 16 representative peers of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the 22d and 23d <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of the Union: and for that purpose prescribes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a>, &c. to be taken by the electors; directs the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of balloting; prohibits the peers electing from being attended in an unusual manner; and expressly provides, that no other <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> shall be treated of in that assembly, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> only the election, on pain of incurring a praemunire. See also the articles Nobility and Peers.

LORDOSIS

Pages 249-249

(of λογδος, bent inwards), in the medical writings, a name given to a distempered state of the spine, in which it is bent inwards, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> towards the anterior parts. It is used in opposition to gibbous, or hump-backed. See <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>.

LORETO

Pages 249-252

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the Marca <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Marche of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCONA">Ancona</a>, with a bishop's see. It is small but fortified; and contains the famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASA">casa</a> santa, or holy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LORETTO">Loretto</a> holy chapel, so much visited by pilgrims. This chapel, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEGEND">legend</a>, was originally a small <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAZARETH">Nazareth</a>, inhabited by the virgin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, in which she was saluted by the angel, and where she bred our Saviour. After their deaths, it was held in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> veneration by all <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELIEVERS">believers</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a>, and at length consecrated into a chapel, and dedicated to the Virgin; upon which occasion St Luke made that identical image, which is still preserved here, and dignified with the name of our Lady of Loretto. This sanctified edifice was allowed to sojourn in Galilee as <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> as that district was inhabited by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>; but when infidels got possession of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, a band of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a>, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> it from pollution, took it in their arms, and conveyed it from Nazareth to a castle in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a>. This fact might have been called in question by incredulous people, had it been performed in a secret manner; but, that it might be manifest to the most short-sighted spectator, and evident to all who were not perfectly deaf as well as <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLIND">blind</a>, a blaze of celestial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONCERT">concert</a> of divine music, accompanied it during the whole journey; besides, when the angels, to rest themselves, set it <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in a little wood near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, all the trees of the forest bowed their heads to the ground, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in that respectful posture as long as the sacred chapel remained among them. But not having been entertained with suitable respect at the castle above mentioned, the same indefatigable angels carried it over the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and placed it in a field belonging to a noble lady called Lauretta, from whom the chapel takes its name. This field happened unfortunately to be frequented at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> by highwaymen and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MURDERERS">murderers</a>: a circumstance with which the angels undoubtedly were not acquainted when they placed it there. After they were better informed they removed it to the top of a hill belonging to two brothers, where they imagined it would be perfectly secure from the dangers of robbery or assassination; but the two brothers, the proprietors of the ground, being equally enamoured of their new visitor, became jealous of each other, quarrelled, fought, and fell by mutual wounds. After this fatal catastrophe, the angels in waiting finally moved the holy chapel to the eminence where it now stands, and has stood these 400 years, having lost all relish for travelling. The sacred chapel stands due east and west, at the farther end of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of the most durable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> of Istria, which has been built around it. This may be considered as the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> covering, or as a kind of great coat to the casa santa, which has a smaller coat of more precious materials and workmanship nearer its body. This internal covering, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, is of the choicest marble, after a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of San Savino's, and ornamented with basso relievos, the workmanship of the best sculptors which Italy could furnish in the reign of Leo X. The subjects of these basso relievos are the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the Blessed Virgin, and other parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>. The whole case is about 50 feet long, 30 in breadth, and the same in height: but the real house itself is no more than 32 feet in length, 14 in breadth, and at the sides about 18 feet in height; the centre of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> is four or five feet higher. The walls of this little holy chapel are composed of pieces of a reddish substance, of an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> shape, laid one upon another, in the manner of brick. At first sight, on a superficial view, these <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>-coloured oblong substances appear to be nothing else than <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> Italian bricks; and, which is still more extraordinary, on a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> and third view, with all possible <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, they still have the same appearance. Travellers, however, are assured with great earnestness, that there is not a single particle of brick in their whole <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, being entirely of a stone, which, though it cannot now be found in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>, was formerly very common, particularly in the neighbourhood of Nazareth. The holy house is divided within into two unequal portions, by a kind of grate-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of silver. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> towards the west is about three-fourths of the whole; that to the east is called the Sanctuary. In the larger division, which may be considered as the main body of the house, the walls are left bare, to show the true original fabric of Nazareth stone; for they must not be supposed to be bricks. At the lower or western wall there is a window, the same through which the angel Gabriel entered at the Annunciation. The architraves of this window are covered with silver. There are a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> and silver lamps in this chapel: one of the former, a present from the republic of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, is said to weigh 37 pounds, and some of the silver lamps weigh from 120 to 130 pounds. At the upper end of the largest room is an altar, but so low, that from it you may see the famous image which stands over the chimney in the small room or sanctuary. Golden and silver angels, of considerable size, kneel around her, some offering hearts of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, enriched with diamonds, and one an infant of pure gold. The wall of the sanctuary is plated with silver, and adorned with crucifixes, precious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and votive gifts of various kinds. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of the Virgin herself by no means corresponds with the fine furniture of her house: She is a little woman, about four feet in height, with the features and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a> of a negro. Of all the sculptors that ever existed, assuredly St Luke, by whom this figure is said to have been made, is the least of a flatterer; and nothing can be a stronger <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the Blessed Virgin's contempt for external <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> than her being satisfied with this representation of her. The figure of the infant Jesus, by St Luke, is of a piece with that of the Virgin: he holds a large golden globe in one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and the other is extended in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of blessing. Both figures have crowns on their heads, enriched with diamonds: these were presents from Ann of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of France. Both arms of the Virgin are enclosed within her robes, and no <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> but her <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> is to be seen; her dress is most magnificent, but in a wretched bad <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>: this is not surprising, for she has no <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> attendant. She has particular clothes for the different feasts held in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of her, and, which is not quite so decent, is always dressed and undressed by the priests belonging to the chapel; her robes are ornamented with all kinds of precious stones down to the hem of her garment. There is a small <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> behind the sanctuary, in which are shown the chimney, and some other furniture, which they pretend belonged to the Virgin when she lived at Nazareth; particularly a little earthen porringer, out of which the infant used to eat. The pilgrims bring rosaries, little crucifixes, and agnus dei's which the obliging <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> shakes for half a mi- Loretto. nute in this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DISH">dish</a>; after which it is believed they acquire the virtue of curing various diseases, and prove an excellent preventive of all temptations of Satan. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOWN">gown</a> which the image had on when the chapel arrived from Nazareth is of red camlet, and carefully kept in a glass shrine. Above 100 masses are daily said in this chapel, and in the church in which it stands. The jewels and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> to be seen at any one time in the holy chapel are of a small value in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> of those in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>, which is a large room adjoining to the vestry of the great church. In the presses of this room are kept those presents which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a>, noble, and rich bigots of all ranks, have, by oppressing their subjects and injuring their families, sent to this place. To enumerate every particular would fill volumes. They consist of various utensils and other things in silver and gold; as lamps, candlesticks, goblets, crowns, and crucifixes; lamps, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAGLES">eagles</a>, saints, apostles, angels, virgins, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a>: then there are cameos, pearls, gems, and precious stones, of all kinds and in great numbers. What is valued above all the other jewels is, the miraculous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEARL">pearl</a>, wherein they assert that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a> has given a faithful delineation of the Virgin sitting on a cloud with the infant Jesus in her arms. There was not room in the presses of the treasury to hold all the silver pieces which had been presented to the Virgin. Several other presses in the vestry are completely full. It is said that those pieces are occasionally melted down by his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLINESS">holiness</a> for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the state: and also that the most precious of the jewels are picked out and sold for the same purpose, false stones being substituted in their room. Pilgrimages to Loretto are not so frequent with foreigners, or with Italians of fortune and distinction, as formerly; nineteen out of twenty of those who make this journey now are <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> people, who depend for their maintenance on the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> they receive on the road. To those who are in such a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> as precludes them from availing themselves of the charitable institutions for the maintenance of pilgrims, such journeys are attended with expense and inconvenience; and fathers and husbands, in moderate or confined circumstances, are frequently brought to disagreeable dilemmas, by the rash vows of going to Loretto which their wives or daughters are apt to make on any supposed deliverance from danger. To refuse, is considered by the whole neighbourhood as cruel, and even impious; and to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a>, is often highly distressing, particularly to such husbands as, from affection or any other motives, do not choose that their wives should be long out of their sight. But the poor, who are maintained during their whole journey, and have nothing more than a bare maintenance to expect from their labour at home, to them a journey to Loretto is a party of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> as well as <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>, and by much the most agreeable road they can take to heaven. The greatest concourse of pilgrims is at the seasons of Easter and Whitsuntide. The rich travel in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a>: A great number come on horseback or on mules; or, what is still more common, on asses. Great numbers of females come in this manner, with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> friend walking by them as their guide and protector: but the greatest number of both sexes are on foot. The pilgrims on foot, as soon as they enter the suburbs, begin a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYMN">hymn</a> in honour of the Virgin, which they continue till they reach the church. The poorer sort are received into an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>, where they have <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> and board for three days. The only trade of Loretto consists of rosaries, crucifixes, little madonas, agus dei's, and medals, which are manufactured here, and sold to pilgrims. There are great numbers of shops full of these commodities, some of them of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> price; but infinitely the greater part are adapted to the purses of the buyers, and sold for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> trifle. The evident poverty of those manufacturers and traders, and of the inhabitants of this town in general, is a sufficient proof that the reputation of our Lady of Loretto is greatly on the decline. In the great church which contains the holy chapel are confessionals, where the penitents from every country of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> may be confessed in their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, priests being always in waiting for that purpose: each of them has a long <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> rod in his hand, with which he touches the heads of those to whom he thinks it proper to give <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTION">absolution</a>. They place themselves on their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a> in groups around the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONFESSIONAL">confessional</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>; and when the holy father has touched their heads with the expiatory rod, they retire, freed from the burden of their sins, and with renewed courage to begin a fresh account. In the spacious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> before this church there is an elegant marble fountain, supplied with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> from an adjoining hill by an aqueduct. Few even of the most inconsiderable <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of Italy are without the useful ornament of a public fountain. The embellishments of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> are employed with great propriety on such works, which are continually in the people's view; the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> is refreshed and the eye delighted by the streams of water they pour forth; a sight peculiarly agreeable in a warm <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>. In this area there is also a statue of Sixtus V. in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRONZE">bronze</a>. Over the portal of the church itself is a statue of the Virgin; and above the middle gate is a Latin inscription, importing that within is the house of the mother of God, in which the Word was made <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>. The gates of the church are likewise of bronze, embellished with basso relievos of admirable workmanship: the subjects taken partly from the Old and partly from the New <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, and divided into different compartments. As the gates of this church are shut at noon, the pilgrims who arrive after that time can get no nearer the santa casa than these gates, which are by this means sometimes exposed to the first violence of that holy ardour which was designed for the chapel itself. All the sculpture upon the gates which is within reach of the mouths of those zealots, is in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> effaced by their kisses. There are also several paintings to be seen here, some of which are highly esteemed, particularly two in the treasury. The subject of one of these is the Virgin's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATIVITY">Nativity</a>, by Annibal Caracci; and of the other, a Holy Family by Raphael. There are some others of considerable merit which ornament the altars of the great church. These altars, or little chapels, of which this fabric contains a great number, are lined with marble and embellished by sculpture; but nothing within this church interests a traveller of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a> so much as the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRATES">grates</a> before those chapels, which were were made of the fetters and chains of the Christian slaves, who were freed from <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BONDAGE">bondage</a> by the glorious victory of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEPANTO">Lepanto</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> where the governor resides stands near the church; and the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a> who are employed in it lodge in the same palace, where they receive the pilgrims of high distinction. The environs of this town are very agreeable, and in fine <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> the high <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Croatia may be seen from hence. It is seated on a mountain, in E. Long. 13° 50' N. Lat. 43° 24'.

LORGAN-GREEN

Pages 280-280

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUTH">Louth</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEINSTER">Leinster</a>, 37 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>; a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> beyond which is a handsome seat of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Charlemont. LURIDÆ, the name of the 28th order in Linnaeus's fragments of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, Natural Orders.

LORICA

Pages 252-252

was a cuirass, brigantine, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> coat of mail, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> among the Roman <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>. It was generally made of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, and is supposed to be derived from forum.—The lorice were set with plates of metal in various forms: sometimes in hooks or rings like a chain, sometimes like feathers, and sometimes like the scales of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERPENTS">serpents</a> or fishes, to which plates of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> were often added. There were other <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> cuirasses, consisting only of many folds of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> cloth, or of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a> made strong enough to resist weapons. Such soldiers as were rated under 1000 drachms, instead of the loricæ now described, wore a pectorale.—The Roman lorica was made like a shirt, and defended the wearer both before and behind, but was so contrived that the back <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> could be occasionally separated from the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a>. Some of the lorice were made of cords of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a> or flax, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> set together; whence they are called thoraces bilices, trilices, &c. from the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the cords fixed one upon another; but these were used rather in hunting than in the field of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>.

LORIMERS

Pages 252-252

one of the companies of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, that make bits for bridles, spurs, and such like small <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARE">ware</a>. They are mentioned in statute I Rich. II. c. 12.—The word seems derived from the Latin word lorum, "a thong."

LORME

Pages 252-252

Philibert de, one of the most celebrated architects in the 16th century, was born at Lyons. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> Catherine de Medicis gave him the superintendence of buildings, and he had the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of those of the Louvre, the Thuilleries, the castle of St Anet, St Germain, and other edifices erected by her orders. He also wrote several books on <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>. He died about the year 1577.

LORNE

Pages 252-252

a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of Argyllshire in Scotland, which gives the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of marquis to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Argyll. It extends above 30 miles in length from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> to south, and about <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> at its utmost breadth; bounded on the east by Braidalbin; on the west by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>; on the north by Lochaber; and is divided from Knapdale on the south by Loch Etive, on the banks of which stands the castle of Beregonium, wherein the courts of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> were anciently held. This district, abounding with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, is the most pleasant and fertile <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Argyllshire, producing plenty of oats and barley. It once belonged to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family of Macdougal, still residing on the spot; but devolved to the lords of Argyll in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> with the heiress, at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> a branch of the Stuart family. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a> in this district is the castle of Dunstaffnage, a seat of the Scottish kings previous to the conquest of the Picts in 843 by Kenneth II. In this place was <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> preserved the famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALLADIUM">palladium</a> of North <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>; brought, says <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEGEND">legend</a>, out of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, where it was first used as a seat of justice by Cathelus, coeval with Moses. It <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> here as the coronation <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> till the reign of Kenneth II. who removed it to Scone, in order to secure his reign; for, according to the inscription, Nil fallat fatum, Scoti quoque locatum, Invenient lapidem, regnare teneantur ibidem. Some of the ancient regalia were preserved till the present century, when the keeper's servants, during his infirm years, embezzled them for the silver ornaments; and left only a battleaxe, nine feet long, of beautiful workmanship, and ornamented with silver. The castle is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>; the inside only 87 feet; partly ruinous, partly habitable. At three of the corners are round towers; one of them projects very little. The entrance is towards the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> at present by a staircase, in old times probably by a drawbridge, which fell from a little gateway. The masonry appears very ancient; the tops battlemented. This pile is seated on a rock at the mouth of Loch Etive, whose waters expand within to a beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, where ships may safely ride in all <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>. Of this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, the founder of which is unknown, nothing remains except the outer walls, which though roofless, are still in good order; and within which some buildings have been erected, which serve as the residence of the laird. The duke of Argyll is <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> keeper under the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>.—At a small distance from the castle is a ruined chapel, once an elegant building; and at one end an enclosure, a family cemetery. Opposite to these is a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> precipice, ending abrupt, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> suddenly towards the south-east. A person concealed in the recess of the rock, a little beyond the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a>, surprises friends stationed at some distance beneath the precipice with a very remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECHO">echo</a> of any word, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> even <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>, he pronounces; which reaches the last distinct and unbroken. The repetition is single, but remarkably clear. In 1307, this castle was possessed by Alexander Macdougal <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of Argyll, a friend to the English: but was that year reduced by Robert Bruce, when Macdougal sued for peace with that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, and was received into favour. We find, about the year 1455, this to have been a residence of the lords of the isles; for here James last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Douglas, after his defeat in Annandale, fled to Donald, the Regulus of the time, and prevailed on him to take arms and carry on a plundering <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> against his monarch James II. The situation of this regal seat was calculated for <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> as well as strength. The views of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, valleys, waters, and islands, are delightful. On the north side of Loch Etive stood the town of Beregonium, supposed to have been the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the West Highlands. It seems from certain mounds, excavations, and other appearances, to have been a strong fortress, to prevent invasion, or to secure a retreat, as occasions might require. On the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the same loch is the site of Ardchattan, a priory of monks of Valliscaulium in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>, founded in 1230 by Donald MacCoul, ancestor of the Macdougals of Lorne. Here Robert Bruce, who remained <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> before he got entire possession of Scotland, held a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>.

LORRAIN

Pages 253-253

Robert le, an eminent sculptor, born at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1666. From his infancy, he made so rapid a progress in the art of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGNING">designing</a>, that at the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 18 the celebrated Girardon intrusted him with the care of teaching his children and correcting his disciples. He committed to him also, in conjunction with Nouilsson, the execution of the famous <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Richelieu in the Sorbonne, and his own tomb at St Landres in Paris. On his return from Rome, he finished several pieces at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARSEILLES">Marseilles</a>, which had been left imperfect by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of M. Puget. He was received into the academy of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a> in 1701. His chef d'œuvre is Galatea, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> universally admired. Lorrain afterwards made a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a> for the gardens at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSAILLES">Versailles</a>, a Faun for those of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARLY">Marly</a>; and several bronzes, among which is an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANDROMEDA">Andromeda</a>; all in an excellent <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. This <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> succeeded chiefly in heads; and more particularly in that of young girls, which he performed with incomparable delicacy and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>.

LOTEN

Pages 253-253

John, a good landscape painter of the English school; though a native of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> led him to solemn and dreary scenes, as landstorms accompanied with showers of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, &c. and he seldom omitted to introduce oak trees in his prospects: his landscapes are generally <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>; and he painted with <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, and force. But the effect of his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> had been much greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he had been less <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> in his colouring; for the judicious eye is not pleased with the darkish tint that predominates in it. He died in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> about 1681.

LOTHIAN

Pages 253-261

a name given to three counties of Scotland, viz. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HADDINGTONSHIRE">Haddingtonshire</a>, Edinburghshire, and Linlithgowshire; otherwise called East, Mid, and West, Lothians. 1. East Lothian, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Haddingtonshire, is bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west by the frith of Forth; and on the east by the German <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; on the south-east by <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol4.html#article-BERWICKSHIRE">Berwickshire</a>; and on the west by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>. It extends about 25 miles from east to west, and where broadest, nearly 15 from north to south; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> is about 297 <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles. Of the whole county about 64 parts in the hundred are arable, 16 meadows or low lying ground, and 20 hills and wastes. This is one of the most fruitful counties in Scotland, producing <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> quantities of wheat and all sorts of grain, well watered, and plentifully supplied with fish, fowl, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>, and all the necessaries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. It abounds with <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, villages, and farms, interspersed with a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of agreeable houses belonging to persons of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> and fortune. Beside farming, which is successfully carried on, the people towards the sea-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> employ themselves in the fishery, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>-making, and in foreign trade; and some of the more inland inhabitants engage in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> and woollen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">Limestone</a> and coal are found in most parts of the county, and great numbers of sheep are fed on the hills of Lammermuir. See HADDINGTONSHIRE, Supplement. 2. Edinburghshire, or Mid Lothian, is about 35 miles <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, but varies in its breadth in different places from five to 16 miles; area 358 square miles. It is bounded on the east by Haddingtonshire; on the west by the shire of Linlithgow; on the south, by Peeblesshire; and on the north, by <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of West Lothian and the frith of Forth. The aspect of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is in general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> and pleasant, interspersed with a few hills, that help to exhibit agreeable prospects. It is well watered with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, and shaded with woods. It produces plenty of coal, limestone, a soft <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> marble, and some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> ore. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, of itself fertile, is finely cultivated, and yields as plentiful harvests of excellent wheat as are found in any part of Great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. The whole shire is interspersed with noble houses and plantations belonging to noblemen and gentlemen of fortune. The farmers, in general, are skilful and wealthy. The country is well inhabited, and presents us with a good number of towns and populous villages. Along the sea coast the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people subsist by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a>, and traffic in coals and salt, and some few carry on a smuggling <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>. Those in the inland are employed in farming, and some branches of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEAVING">weaving</a> manufacture. Edinburgh is a county within itself. See EDINBURGHSHIRE, Supplement. 3. The shire of Linlithgow, or West Lothian, is bounded on the north by the frith of Forth. The small river Almond divides it from Edinburghshire on the east. On the south-west it joins the county of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LANARK">Lanark</a>; and on the west, it is parted from <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-STIRLINGSHIRE">Stirlingshire</a> by Avon, a small river. Its form, though <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>, approaches to a parallelogram. It <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> from north-east to south-west, 20 miles. It breadth, except on the shore of the frith, does not exceed 12.—The country is pleasant and fertile, abounding with corn and pasturage. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">LOT</a> Lothian pastorage. Here is found plenty of coal, limestone, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> ore; nay, in the reign of James VI. it produced a rich mine of silver. See Linlithgowshire. Supplement. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOTION">Lotion</a> is, strictly speaking, such washing as concerns beautifying the skin, by cleansing it of those deformities which a distempered blood throws upon it. Medicines of this kind, however, are for the most part insignificant, and sometimes very dangerous; the only proper method of treating these disorders is, by administering such medicines as tend to correct the morbid state of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> from whence they arise. Lotion, in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of medicines, by washing them in some liquid, either made very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, so as to take away only the dregs; or sharp, so as to penetrate them, in order to clear them of some salt or corrosive spirit, as is done to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTIMONY">antimony</a>, precipitates, magisteries, &c., or intended to take away some foulness or ill <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, or to communicate some good one. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOTOPHAGI">Lotophagi</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a people of the Regio Syrtica (so called from their living on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOTUS">lotus</a>); inhabiting between the two Syrtes, from the Cynthus to the Triton. The lotus was said to be a food so luscious, as to make strangers forget their native country. A sweet wine was expressed from it, which did not keep above ten days (Pliny). Lotophagi of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>. See Meninx. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOTTERY">Lottery</a>, a kind of public <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAME">game</a> at hazard, frequent in Britain, France, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, in order to raise <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the state; being appointed with us by the authority of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, and managed by commissioners appointed by the lords of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a> for that purpose. It consists of several numbers of blanks and prizes, which are drawn out of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a>, one of which contains the numbers, and the other the corresponding blanks or prizes. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> invented lotteries to enliven their Saturnalia. This festival began by the distribution of tickets which gained some <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a>. Augustus made lotteries which consisted of things of little value; but Nero established some for the people, in which 1000 tickets were distributed daily, and several of those who were favoured by fortune got rich by them. Heliogabalus invented some very singular: the prizes were either of great value or of none at all: one gained a prize of six slaves, and another of six flies; some got valuable vases, and others vases of common <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. The first English lottery we find mentioned in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> was drawn A.D. 1569. It consisted of 40,000 lots, at 10s. each lot: the prizes were plate; and the profits were to go towards repairing the havens of this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. It was drawn at the west door of St Paul's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> began on the 11th of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1569, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> incessantly, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> and night, till the 6th of May following; as Maitland, from Stowe, informs us in his history, vol. i. p. 257. There were then only three lottery offices in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. The proposals for this lottery were published in the years 1567 and 1568. It was at first intended to have been drawn at the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Mr Dericke, her majesty's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a>, i.e. her jeweller, but was afterwards drawn as above mentioned. Dr Rawlinson showed the Antiquarian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, 1748, "A proposal for a very rich lottery general without any blankes, containing a great number of good prizes, as well of redy money as of plate and certain sorts of merchandizes, having been valued and prised by the commandment of the queene's most excellent majestie's order, to the intent that such commodities as may chance to arise thereof after the charges borne may be converted towards the reparations of the havens and strength of the realme, and towards such other publick good workes. The number of lotts shall be foure hundred thousand, and no more; and every lott shall be the summe of tenne shillings <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>, and no more. To be filled by the feast of St Bartholomew. The shew of prizes are to be seen in Cheapside, at the signe of the Queene's Armes, the house of Mr Dericke, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOLDSMITH">goldsmith</a>, servant to the queene. Some other orders about it in 1567-8. Printed by Hen. Bynneymen." In the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, it was thought necessary to suppress lotteries, as nuisances to the public. Since that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, however, they have been licensed by an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of parliament, under various regulations. The act passed in 1778 restrains any person from keeping an office for the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of tickets, shares, or chances, or for buying, selling, ensuring, or registering, without a license; for which license each office-keeper must pay 50l. to continue in force for one year, and the produce to be applied towards defraying the expense of the lottery. And no person is allowed to sell any share or chance less than a sixteenth, on the penalty of 50l. All tickets divided into shares or chances are to be deposited in an office, to be established in London by the commissioners of the treasury, who are to appoint a person to conduct the business thereof; and all shares are to be stamped by the said officer, who is to give a receipt for every ticket deposited with him. The numbers of all tickets so deposited are to be entered in a book, with the names of the owners, and the number of shares into which they are divided. All tickets deposited in the office are to remain there three days after the drawing. And any person keeping an office, or selling shares, or who shall publish any scheme for receiving moneys in consideration of any <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> to be granted in any ticket in the said lottery, &c., without being in possession of such ticket, shall forfeit 500l. and suffer three months imprisonment. And no business is to be transacted at any of the offices after eight in the evening, except on the evening of the Saturday preceding the drawing. No person is to keep any office for the sale of tickets, &c., in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, on penalty of 20l. Before this regulating statute took <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, there were upwards of 400 lottery offices in and about London only; but the whole number afterwards, for all Britain, as appeared by the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a> published by authority, amounted to no more than 51. They have, however, increased greatly again. Some farther regulations to prevent the frauds committed by insurances were made in 1793. In 1808 the reports of a committee of the house of commons disclosed a dreadful <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of vice and misery brought on by lotteries, and recommended their abolition, or at least that they should be put under other regulations. Their suggestions, however, have had but little effect hitherto. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> sum received by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> from the lottery, is estimated to be 750,000l. per annum, of which 500,000l. is for tickets, and the remainder for postages, stamps, &c. Lotus, or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">Bird</a>'s-foot Trefoil; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> plants belonging to the diadelphia class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 32d order, *Papilio-nacea*. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. **Lotus of Homer.** See *Diospyros*, Egyptian Lotus. See *Nymphæa*. **Libyan Lotus.** See *Rhamnus*, Index. **Lovage.** See *Ligusticum*. **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">Love</a>,** in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of the word, denotes all those affections of the pleasing kind which objects and incidents raise in us; thus we are said to love not only intelligent agents of morally good dispositions, but also sensual pleasures, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>, and honours. But Love, in its usual and more appropriate signification, may be defined, "that affection which, being compounded of animal desire, esteem, and benevolence, becomes the bond of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> and union between individuals of the different sexes; and makes them feel in the society of each other a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> which they <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> nowhere else." We call it an *affection* rather than a *<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>*, because it involves a desire of the happiness of its object: And that its constituent parts are those which have been <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> enumerated, we shall first endeavour to prove, and then proceed to trace its rise and progress from a selfish appetite to a generous sentiment. Animal desire is the actual energy of the sensual appetite: and that it is an essential part of the complex affection, which is properly called love, is apparent from this consideration, that though a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> may have sentiments of esteem and benevolence towards women who are both old and ugly, he never supposes himself to be in love of any woman, to whom he feels not the sensual appetite to have a stronger tendency than to other individuals of her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a>. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, that animal desire alone cannot be called the affection of love is evident; because he who gratifies such a desire without esteeming its object, and wishing to communicate at the same time that he receives enjoyment, loves not the woman, but himself. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">Mere</a> animal desire has nothing in view but the species and the sex of its object; and before it make a selection, it must be combined with sentiments very different from itself. The first sentiment with which it is combined, and by which a man is induced to prefer one woman to another, seems to be that by which we are delighted with gracefulness of person, regularity of features, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a>. It is not indeed to be denied that there is something irresistible in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> beauty. The most severe <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not pretend that they do not feel an immediate prepossession in favour of a handsome woman; but this prepossession, even when combined with animal desire, does not constitute the whole of that affection which is called love. Savages feel the influence of the sensual appetite, and it is extremely probable that they have some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of beauty; but among savages the affection of love is seldom felt. Even among the lower orders of civil society it seems to be a very gross passion, and to have in it more of the selfishness of appetite than of the generosity of esteem. To these observations many exceptions will no doubt be found (A): but we speak of savages in general, and of the great body of the labouring <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, who in the choice of their mates do not <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>—who indeed are incapable of studying, that rectitude of mind, and those delicacies of sentiment, without which neither man nor woman can deserve to be esteemed. In the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> state, and even in the first stages of refinement, the bond of union between the sexes seems to consist of nothing more than mere animal desire and instinctive tenderness for their infant progeny. The former impels them to unite for the propagation of the species; and the latter preserves the union, till the children, who are the fruit of it, be able to provide for their own subsistence. That in such unions, whether casual or permanent, there is no mutual esteem and benevolence, is apparent from the state of subjection in which women are held in rude and uncultivated nations, as well as from the manner in which marriages are in such nations contracted. Sweetness of temper, a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> article with us in the female character, displays itself externally in mild looks and gentle manners, and is the first and perhaps the most powerful inducement to love in a cultivated mind. "But such graces (says an ingenious writer) *Sketches* are scarce discernible in a female savage; and even of the History in the most polished woman would not be perceived by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> savage. Among savages, strength and boldness are the only valuable qualities. In these, females are miserably deficient; for which reason they are contemned by the males as beings of an inferior order. The North American tribes <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> in idleness; the drudgery of labour degrades a man in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, and is proper for women only. To join young persons in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> is accordingly the business of the parents; and it would be unpardonable meanness in the bridegroom to show any fondness for the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDE">bride</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUIANA">Guiana</a> a woman never eats with her husband, but after every <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAL">meal</a> attends him with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> for washing; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARIBBEE_ISLANDS">Caribbee <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> she is not even permitted to eat in the presence of her husband. Dampier observes in general, that among all the wild nations with which he was acquainted, the women carry the burdens, while the men walk before and carry nothing but their arms; and that women even of the highest rank are not better treated. In <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>, and even in Russia, the capital excepted, men till very lately treated their wives in every respect like slaves. It might indeed be thought, that animal desire, were there nothing else, should have raised women to some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of estimation among men; but male savages, utter strangers to decency and refinement, gratify animal desire with as little <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> as they do <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a> or thirst. "Hence it was that in the early ages of society a man purchased a woman to be his wife, as one purchases an ox or a sheep to be food; and valued her only as she contributed to his sensual gratification. Instances innumerable might be collected from every <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> of which we are acquainted with the early history; but --- (A) Such as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a> whose story is so pathetically told by Addison in No 215, of the Spectator; the two lovers who were killed by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a> at Staunton-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARCOURT">Harcourt</a>, August 9, 1718, (see Pope's Letters); and many others which will occur to every reader. we shall content ourselves with mentioning a few. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a> bought Rebekah, and gave her to his son <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> for a wife*. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a> having nothing else to give, served Laban 14 years for two wives†. To <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a>, demanding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAUL">Saul</a>’s <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> in marriage, it was said, ‘The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> desireth not any dowry, but an hundred foreskins of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILISTINES">Philistines</a>.’ In the Iliad Agamemnon offers his daughter to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACHILLES">Achilles</a> for a wife; and says that he would not demand for her any price§. By the laws of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETHELBERT">Ethelbert</a> king of England, a man who committed <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADULTERY">adultery</a> with his neighbour’s wife was obliged to pay the husband a fine, and to buy him another wife||. But it is needless to multiply instances; the practice has prevailed universally among nations emerging from the savage state, or in the rudest stage of society: and wherever it prevailed, men could not possibly have for the fair sex any of that tender regard and esteem which constitute so essential a part of the complex affection of love. Accordingly we find the magnanimous Achilles an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> stranger to that generous affection, though his heart was susceptible of the warmest and purest friendship. His attachment to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATROCLUS">Patroclus</a> was so heroically disinterested, that he willingly sacrificed his own life to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his friend; but when Agamemnon threatened to rob him of his favourite female captive, though he felt the insult offered to his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a>, he never spoke of the woman but as a slave whom he was concerned to preserve in point of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, and as a testimony of his glory. Hence it is that we never hear him mention her but as his spoil, the reward of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, or the gift which the Grecians gave him. "And dar'st thou threat to snatch my prize away, Due to the deeds of many a dreadful day? A prize as small, O <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a>! <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MATCH">match</a>'d with thine, As thy own actions <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> compar'd with mine. Thine in each conquest is the wealthy prey, The' mine the sweat and danger of the day: Some trivial present to my ships I bear, Or barren praises pay the wounds of war." And again, after upbraiding the general with his tyranny and want of regard to merit, he adds, with the greatest indifference as to the charms of the woman, "<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEIZE">Seize</a> on Briseïs, whom the Grecians doom'd My prize of war, yet tameely see resum'd; And seize secure; no more Achilles draws His conquering <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> in any woman's cause." (b) The original <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> are: καὶ ἐν μοι γέρης αὐτὸς ἀφείρονται ἀπελάσις, ὡς τι πολὺ μυργήσῃ, δοκῶ δὲ μεν ὑπὸ θεῶν Ἀχαιῶν, οὐ μεν ἐν τῷ ἐν ἐμῇ γερής, ὅτε Ἀχαιοὶ Τρωῶν εἰκότων ἐναντίον πολεμῆσθε. Αλλὰ τοῦ μεν πλεῖον πολεμίων πολεμῆσθε Χείρες ἐμὲ διατείνω, ἀτελεῖς ἂν πολὺ μεταστρεψιν ἤδη, Σοὶ τὸ γέρης πολὺ μεῖζον, ἐν τῷ ἐλύθη τε φίλου τε Εὔχομαι ἐν τῷ μεῖζον, ἐν τῷ μεῖζον πολεμῆσθε. Iliad, lib. i. And, Ἀλλὰ ἐν τῷ ἐξελθεῖν, σὺ δ' ἐν Φρεσί βαλλεῖν ὄνοι Νεῖσι μὲν ἐν τῷ ἐναντίῳ μεταχειρίσαι, ἐναντία κατενευσεῖν, In this latter passage the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> says expressly, “I will not fight with you or with any other man for the sake of a girl; but you shall not rob me of any other part of my <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>,” which is surely the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of a man to whose heart love must have been an utter stranger. Pope has made the language of this rough <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WARRIOR">warrior</a> less inconsistent with the peculiar resentment natural to an injured lover than it is in the original (b); but from the last quoted passage, even as translated by him, it is apparent that Achilles would have been equally hurt had Agamemnon threatened to deprive him of any other part of his plunder. Accordingly he yields up Briseïs, not in grief for a mistress whom he loses, but in sullenness for an injury that is done him. Nor let it be imagined, that this coldness proceeded from the pride of the hero, which would not permit him to acknowledge his love of a captive. With the generous affection of love captives and princesses were equally incapable of inspiring him. He repeatedly affirmed indeed that he delighted in his fair Lyrnessian slave, but it was only as an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of sensual gratification; for as to every thing else in a woman, he was so totally indifferent, that he declared he would not, when he should be disposed to marry, give himself the trouble to make a choice, but leave the whole <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> to his father. "If heav'n restore me to my realms with life, "The rev'rend <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PELEUS">Peleus</a> shall elect my wife." Even Agamemnon, of whom Pope and Madame Dacier think more favourably as a lover, speaks the very same language when mentioning his favourite captive Chryseïs. In his furious debate with Achilles he calls her indeed— "A maid, unmatch'd in manners as in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a>, "Skill'd in each art, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>'d with ev'ry <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>." And adds, "Not half so dear were <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLYTEMNESTRA">Clytemnestra</a>'s charms, "When first her blooming beauties blest my arms." But this was said merely to enhance the value of the prize, which for the public good he was about to resign; for that she was dear to him only as ministering to his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, is past dispute from the language which he had previously held with her father, as well as from his requiring grateful <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> to pay a just <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a>, and to repair his private loss. A man who really loves would have thought nothing an equivalent for the object of his love; much less would he have insinuated to her father father a possibility of his dismissing from his embrace a woman whom he esteemed, when time should have robbed her of every youthful grace. Since, then, it is so apparent, that in the heroic <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of Greece even princes and kings were strangers to the generous affection of love, it needs not occasion much surprise that the same affection has very little influence upon mankind in the lowest ranks of the most polished <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. That this is actually the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, that among the generality of uneducated men and women there is no other bond of attachment than the sensual appetite, every year furnishes multiplied proofs.
