We daily see youths, rejected by their mistresses, paying their addresses without delay to girls who, in looks, temper, and disposition, are diametrically opposite to those whom so lately they pretended to love: We daily see maidens, slighted by their lovers, receiving the addresses of men, who, in nothing but their sex, resemble those to whom a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEEK">week</a> before they wished to be married: and we believe it is not very uncommon to find a girl entertaining several lovers together, that if one or more of them should prove false, she may still have a chance not to be totally deserted. Did esteem and benevolence, placed on manners and character, constitute any part of vulgar love, these people would act very differently; for they would find it impossible to change their lovers and their mistresses with the same ease that they change their clothes. To this account of love, as it appears in savage nations, some one may perhaps oppose the paintings of the softer passion in the poems of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OSSIAN">Ossian</a>. That bard describes the female character as commanding respect and esteem, and the Caledonian heroes as cherishing for their mistresses a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> so pure and elevated as never was surpassed, and has seldom been equalled, in those ages which we <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> call most enlightened. This is indeed true: and it is one of the many reasons which have induced Johnson and others to pronounce the whole a modern fiction. Into that debate we do not enter. We may admit the authenticity of the poems, without acknowledging that they furnish any exception to our general <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a>. They furnish indeed in the manners which they describe a wonderful anomaly in the general history of man. All other nations of which we read were in the hunter state savage and cruel. The Caledonians, as exhibited by Ossian, are gentle and magnanimous. The heroes of Homer fought for plunder, and felt no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLEMENCY">clemency</a> for a vanquished foe. The heroes of Ossian fought for fame; and when their enemies were subdued, they took them to their bosoms. The first of Greeks committed a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> insult on the dead body of the first of Trojans. Among the Caledonians insults offered to the dead, as well as cruelty to the living, were condemned as infamous. The heroes of Ossian appear in no instance as savages. How they came to be polished and refined before they were acquainted with <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a> and the most useful arts of life, it is not our business to inquire; but since they unquestionably were so, their treatment of the female sex, instead of opposing, confirms our theory; for we never conceived rich clothes, superb houses, highly-dressed food, or even the knowledge of foreign tongues, to be necessary to the acquisition of a generous sentiment. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUXURY">Luxury</a> indeed appears to be as inimical to love as barbarism: and we believe, that in modern nations, the tender and exalted affection which deserves that name is as little known among the highest orders of life as among the lowest. Perhaps the Caledonian ladies of Ossian resembled in their manners the German ladies of Tacitus, who accompanied their husbands to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHASE">chase</a>, fought by their sides in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, and partook with them of every danger. If so, they could not fail to be respected by a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of heroes among whom courage took place of all other virtues: and this single circumstance, from whatever cause it might proceed, will sufficiently account for the estimation of the female character among the ancient Germans and Caledonians, so different from that in which it has been held in almost every other barbarous nation. But if among savages and the vulgar, love be unknown, it cannot possibly be an instinctive affection: and therefore it may be asked, How it gets possession of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> heart; and by what means we can judge whether in any particular instance it be real or imaginary? These questions are of importance, and deserve to be fully answered; though many circumstances conspire to render it no easy task to give to them such answers as shall be perfectly satisfactory. Love can subsist only between individuals of the different sexes. A man can hardly love two women at the same time; and we believe that a woman is still less capable of loving at once more than one man. Love, therefore, has a natural tendency to make men and women <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a>, or, in other words, it is the source of marriage: but in polished society, where alone this affection has any place, so many things besides mutual attachment are necessary to make the married life comfortable, that we rarely see young persons uniting from the impulse of love, and have therefore but few opportunities of tracing the rise, progress, and consequences of the affection. We shall, however, throw together such reflections as have occurred to us on the subject, not without indulging a hope, that they may be useful to the younger part of our readers when forming the most important connexion in life. We have said, that the perception of beauty, combined with animal desire, is the first inducement which a man can have to prefer one woman to another. It may be added, that elegance of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, a placid masculine countenance, with a person which indicates strength and agility, are the qualities which first tend to attach any woman to a particular man. Beauty has been defined *, "That particular form, which is the most common of all particular forms to be met with in the same species of beings." Let us apply this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> to our own species, and try, by means of Truths, and of it, to ascertain what constitutes the beauty of the human face. It is evident, that of countenances we the Idlest find a number almost infinite of different forms, of which forms one only constitutes beauty, whilst the rest, however numerous, constitute what is not beauty, but <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEFORMITY">deformity</a> or ugliness. To an attentive observer, however, it is evident, that of the numerous particular forms of ugliness, there is not one which includes so many faces as are formed after that particular <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> which constitutes beauty. Every particular species of the animal as well as the vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>, may be said to have a fixed or determinate form, to which, as to a centre, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> is continually inclining. Or it may be compared to pendulums vibrating in different directions over one central point; and as they all <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> the centre, though only one passes through any other point; so it will be found that perfect beauty is oftener produced by nature than deformity: we do not mean than deformity in general, but than any one kind and degree of deformity. To instance in a particular part of a human feature; the line which forms the ridge of the nose is deemed beautiful when it is straight; but this is likewise the central form, which is oftener found than any one particular degree of concave, convex, or any other irregular form that shall be proposed. As we are then more accustomed to beauty than deformity, we may conclude that to be the reason why we approve and admire it, just as we approve and admire fashions of dress for no other reason than that we are used to them. The same thing may be said of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> as of form: it is <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> alone which determines our preference of the colour of the Europeans to that of the Ethiopians, and which makes them prefer their own colour to ours; so that though <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> and custom cannot be the cause of beauty (see Beauty), they are certainly the cause of our liking it. That we do like it cannot be denied. Every one is conscious of a pleasing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMOTION">emotion</a> when contemplating beauty either in man or woman; and when that pleasure is combined with the gratification of the sensual appetite, it is obvious that the sum of enjoyment must be greatly increased. The perception of beauty, therefore, necessarily directs the energy of the sensual appetite to a particular object; but still this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> is a mere selfish feeling, which regards its object only as the best of many similar instruments of pleasure. Before it can deserve the name of love, it must be combined with esteem, which is never bestowed but upon moral character and internal worth; for let a woman be ever so beautiful, and of course ever so desirable as an instrument of sensual gratification, if she be not possessed of the virtues and dispositions which are peculiar to her sex, she will inspire no man with a generous affection. With regard to the outlines, indeed, whether of internal disposition or of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> form, men and women are the same; but nature, intending them for mates, has given them dispositions, which though concordant, are, however, different, so as to produce together delicious <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a>. "The man, more robust, is fitted for severe labour, and for field <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>; the woman, more delicate, is fitted for sedentary occupations, and particularly for nursing children. The man, bold and vigorous, is qualified for being a protector*; the woman, delicate and timid, requires protection. Hence it is, that a man never admires a woman for possessing bodily strength or personal courage; and women always despise men who are totally destitute of these qualities. The man, as a protector, is directed by nature to govern; the woman, conscious of inferiority, is disposed to obey. Their intellectual powers correspond to the destination of nature. Men have penetration and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> judgment to fit them for governing; women have sufficient understanding to make a decent figure under a good government: a greater proportion would excite dangerous rivalry between the sexes, which nature has avoided by giving them different talents. Women have more imagination and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a> than men, which make all their enjoyments more exquisite; at the same time that they are better qualified to communicate enjoyment. Add another capital <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of disposition: the gentle and insinuating manners of the female sex tend to soften the roughness of the other sex; and wherever women are indulged with any freedom, they polish sooner than men. "These are not the only particulars that distinguish the sexes. With respect to the ultimate end of love, it is the privilege of the male, as superior and protector, to make a choice: the female, preferred, has no privilege but barely to consent or refuse. Whether this distinction be the immediate result of the originally different dispositions of the sexes, or only the effect of associations inevitably formed, may be questioned; but among all nations it is the practice for men to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, and for women to be courted; and were the most beautiful woman on earth to invert this practice, she would forfeit the esteem, however by her external grace she might excite the desire, of the man whom she addressed. The great moral virtues which may be comprehended under the general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> integrity, are all absolutely necessary to make either men or women estimable; but to procure esteem to the female character, the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> peculiar to their sex is a very essential circumstance. Nature hath provided them with it as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> against the artful solicitations of the other sex before marriage, and also as a support of conjugal fidelity. A woman, therefore, whose dispositions are gentle, delicate, and rather timid than bold, who is possessed of a large share of sensibility and modesty, and whose manners are soft and insinuating, must, upon moral principles (see <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORAL_PHILOSOPHY">Moral <a class="</a>xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>), command the esteem and benevolence of every individual of the other sex who is possessed of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> understanding; but if her person be deformed, or not such as to excite some degree of animal desire, she will attract no man's love. In like manner, a man whose moral character is good, whose understanding is acute, and whose conversation is instructive, must command the esteem of every sensible and virtuous woman; but if his figure be disagreeable, his manner unpolished, his habits slovenly, and, above all, if he be deficient in personal courage, he will hardly excite desire in the female <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>. It is only when the qualities which command esteem are, in the same person, united with those which excite desire, that the individual so accomplished can be an object of love to one of the other sex; but when these qualities are thus united, each of them increases the other in the imagination of the lover. The beauty of his mistress gives her, in his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a>, a greater share of gentleness, modesty, and every thing which adorns the female character, than perhaps she really possesses; whilst his persuasion of her internal worth makes him, on the other hand, apprehend her beauty to be absolutely unrivalled. To this theory an objection readily offers itself, which it is incumbent upon us to obviate. Men and women sometimes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> in love at first sight, and very often before they have opportunities of forming a just estimate of each other's moral character: How is this circumstance to be reconciled with the progressive <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> of love? We answer, By an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASSOCIATION">association</a> of ideas, which is formed upon principles of physiogno- Every passion and habitual disposition of mind gives a particular cast to the countenance, and is apt to discover itself in some feature of the face. This we learn by experience; and in time, without any effort of our own, the idea of each particular cast of countenance comes to be so closely associated in our minds with the internal disposition which it indicates, that the one can never afterwards be presented to our view without instantly suggesting the other to the imagination. (See <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METAPHYSICS">Metaphysics</a> and Physiognomy.) Hence it is that every man, who has been accustomed to make observations, naturally forms to himself, from the features and lineaments of a stranger's face, some opinion of his character and fortune. We are no sooner presented to a person for the first time, than we are immediately impressed with the idea of a proud, a reserved, an affable, or a good-natured man; and upon our going into a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of absolute strangers, our benevolence or aversion, our awe or contempt, rises instantly towards particular persons, before we have heard them speak a word, or know so much as their names or designations. The same thing happens when we are presented to the fair sex. If a woman, seen for the first time, have that particular cast of countenance, and that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of features, to which we have associated notions of gentleness, modesty, and other female virtues, she instantly commands our esteem; and if she have likewise so much beauty as to make her an object of particular desire, esteem and desire become suddenly combined; and that combination constitutes the affection of love. Such, too, is the nature of all mental associations, that each part of which they are composed adds strength and vividness to the other parts; so that, in the present instance, desire makes us imagine virtues in the woman which her countenance perhaps does not indicate; and the virtues which are there actually visible, make us apprehend her beauty as more perfect than it is. The affection thus <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a> is more or less pure, and will be more or less permanent, according as the one or the other part of which it is compounded predominates. "Where desire of possession* prevails over our esteem of the person and merits of the desirable object, love loses its benevolent character: the appetite for gratification becomes ungovernable, and tends violently to its end, regardless of the misery that must follow. In that state love is no longer a sweet agreeable affection: it becomes a selfish, painful passion, which, like hunger and thirst, produceth no happiness but in the instant of fruition; and when fruition is over, disgust and aversion generally succeed to desire. On the other hand, where esteem, founded on a virtuous character and gentle manners, prevails over animal desire, the lover would not for the world gratify his appetite at the expense of his mistress's honour or peace of mind. He wishes, indeed, for enjoyment; and to him enjoyment is more exquisite than to the mere sensual lover, because it unites sentiment with the gratification of sense; at the same time that, so far from being succeeded by disgust or aversion, it increases his benevolence to the woman, whose character and manners he esteems, and who has contributed so much to his pleasure. Benevolence to an individual, having a general end, admits of acts without number, and is seldom fully accomplished. Hence mutual love, which is composed chiefly of esteem and benevolence, can hardly be of a shorter <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> than its objects. Frequent enjoyment endears such lovers to each other, and makes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTANCY">constancy</a> a pleasure; and when the days of sensual enjoyment are over, esteem and benevolence will remain in the mind, making sweet, even in old age, the society of that pair, in whom are collected the affections of husband, wife, lover, friend, the tenderest affections of human nature." From the whole of this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a>, we think it appears, that the affection between the sexes which deserves the name of love, is inseparably connected with virtue and delicacy; that a man of loose morals cannot be a faithful or a generous lover; that in the breast of him who has ranged from woman to woman for the mere gratification of his sensual appetite, desire must have effaced all esteem for the female character; and that, therefore, the maxim too generally received, "that a reformed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RAKE">rake</a> makes the best husband," has very seldom a chance to be true. We think it may likewise be inferred, that thousands fancy themselves in love who know not what love is, or how it is generated in the human breast: and therefore we beg leave to advise such of our readers as may imagine themselves to be in that state, to examine their own minds, with a view to discover, whether, if the objects of their love were old and ugly, they would still esteem them for the virtues of their character, and the propriety of their manners. This is a question which deserves to be well weighed by the young and the amorous, who in forming the matrimonial connexion, are too often blindly impelled by the mere animal desire inflamed by beauty. "It may indeed happen, after† Elements of Criticism, refined by esteem and benevolence, go it must with a swift pace), that a new bond of attachment may be formed upon more dignified and more lasting principles; but this is a dangerous experiment. Even supposing good sense, good temper, and internal worth of every sort, yet a new attachment upon such qualifications is rarely formed; because it commonly or rather always happens, that such qualifications, the only solid foundation of that indissoluble connexion, if they did not originally make esteem predominate over animal desire, are afterwards rendered altogether invisible by satiety of enjoyment creating disgust." Love, in Medicine. The symptoms produced by this passion as a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, according to medical writers, are as follow: The eyelids often twinkle; the eyes are hollow, and yet appear as if full with pleasure: the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a> is not peculiar to the passion, but the same with that which attends solicitude and care. When the object of this affection is thought of, particularly if the idea is sudden, the spirits are confused, the pulse changes, and its force and time are very variable: in some instances, the person is sad and watchful; in others, the person, not being conscious of his state, pines away, is slothful, and regardless of food; though the wiser, when they find themselves in love, seek pleasant company and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> entertainments. As the force of love prevails, sighs grow deeper; a tremor affects the heart and pulse; the countenance is alternately <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> is suppressed in the fauces; the eyes grow dim; <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> sweats <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> out; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> absents itself, at least until the morning; the secretions... become disturbed; and a loss of appetite, a hectic fever, melancholy, or perhaps madness, if not death, constitutes the sad catastrophe. On this subject the curious may consult Ægineta, lib. iii. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 17. Oribat. Synopsis, lib. viii. cap. 9; or a treatise professedly written on love, as it is a distemper, by James Ferrard, Oxford, printed 1640. The manners of the Greeks and Romans were similar to each other in the affairs of love. They generally made a discovery of their passion by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> upon trees, walls, doors, &c. the name of their beloved. They usually decked the door of their dalcinea with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> and garlands, made libations of wine before their houses, sprinkling the posts with the same liquor, as if the object of their affection was a real <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a>. For a man's garland to be untied, and for a woman to compose a garland, were held to be indubitable indications of their love. When their love was without success, they used several arts to excite affection in the object of their desire. They had recourse to enchantresses, of whom the Thessalian were in the highest estimation. The means made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of were most commonly philtres or love potions, the operation of which was violent and dangerous, and frequently deprived such as drank them of their reason. Some of the most remarkable ingredients of which they were composed were, the hippocampe, the jynx, insects bred from <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a>, the fish renora, the lizard, brains of a calf, the hairs on the tip of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WOLF">wolf</a>'s tail, his secret parts, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> of the left side of a toad eaten with ants, the blood of doves, bones of snakes, feathers of screech-owls, twisted cords of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> in which a person had hanged himself, rags, torches, reliques, a nest of swallows hurled and famished in the earth, bones snatched from hungry bitches, the marrow of a boy famished in the midst of plenty, dried human <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVER">liver</a>; to these may be added several herbs growing out of putrid substances. Such were the ingredients that entered into the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of that infernal draught a love potion. But, besides the philtres, various other arts were used to excite love, in which the application of certain substances was to have a magical influence on the person against whom they levelled their skill. A hyena's udder worn under the left arm, they fancied would draw the affections of whatever woman they fixed their eyes upon. That species of olives called πιλοξε, and barley-bran made up into a paste, and thrown into the fire, they thought would excite the flame of love. Flour was used with the same intention. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">Burning</a> laurel, and melted wax, were supposed to have the like effect. When one heart was to be hardened, and another mollified, clay and wax were exposed to the same fire together. Images of wax were frequently used, representing the persons on whom they wished to make an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a>; and whatever was done to the substitute of wax, they imagined was felt by the person represented. Enchanted medicaments were often sprinkled on some part of the house where the person resided. Love-pledges were supposed to be of singular use and efficacy; these they placed under their threshold, to preserve the affections of the owner from wandering. Love-knots were of singular power, and the number three was particularly observed in all they did. But no good effect was expected, if the use of these things was not attended with charms or magical verses and forms of words. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGIC">Magic</a>. Having mentioned their arts of exciting love, it may not be amiss to take notice, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> imagined, that love excited by magic may be allayed by more powerful spells and medicaments, or by applying to demons more powerful than those who had been concerned in raising that passion. But love inspired without magic had no cure; <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> himself could find no remedy, but cried out *Hci mihi quod nullis amor est medicabilis herbis.* The antidotes against love were generally *agnus castus*, which has the power of weakening the generative <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a>; sprinkling the dust in which a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MULE">mule</a> had rolled itself; tying tonds in the hide of a beast newly slain; applying amulets of minerals or herbs, which were supposed of great efficacy in other <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>; and invoking the assistance of the inferior deities. Another cure for love was <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATHING">bathing</a> in the waters of the river Selemus; to which we may add the lover's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAP">leap</a>, or jumping <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from the Leucadian promontory. **Love-Apple.** See Solanum, Botany Index. **LOVENTINUM,** or Luventinum, in Ancient Geography, a town of the Demetæ in Britain, near the mouth of the Turobris or Tivy. Supposed to have been afterwards swallowed up by an earthquake, and to have stood where is now the lake called Llyn Scautan in Brecknockshire. **LOUGHBOROUGH,** a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEICESTERSHIRE">Leicestershire</a> in England, 110 miles from London. It is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> town in the county, and was in the Saxons time a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> village. Its market is on Thursday; the number of inhabitants in 1811 was 5400. It has a large <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and a free school; besides a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> school for 80 boys, and another for 20 girls. It has been very much reduced by fires; but is still a very agreeable town, with rich <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEADOW">meadow</a>-ground, on the fosse, which runs here almost <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> with the river Soar. The new canal has made the coal trade here very extensive. **LOUGHBRICKLAND,** a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, situated in the county of Down, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Ulster, 38 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>. The name signifies the lake of the speckled <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TROUT">trout</a>; and it was so called from a lake near it, which abounds with those fish. It consists of one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> street, at the end of which is the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> church, said to have been built by Dr Taylor when bishop of Dromore, soon after the Restoration. The linen manufacture is carried on here very extensively; and the town is a great thoroughfare, the turnpike <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> from Dublin to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELFAST">Belfast</a> passing near it. **LOUGH-DERG,** anciently Derg-abhan, i.e. "the river of the woody morass," from a river which issues out of this lake. This lough is situated in the county of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DONEGAL">Donegal</a> and province of Ulster in Ireland, and is famous for having in it the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> that contains St Patrick's purgatory, which is a narrow little <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CELL">cell</a>, hewn out of the solid rock, in which a man could scarce stand upright. There is also a lake of this name situated between the counties of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GALWAY">Galway</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIPPERARY">Tipperary</a>. **LOUGH-NEAGH,** a loch or lake of Ireland, situated in the counties of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMAGH">Armagh</a>, Down, Derry, and Antrim, and province of Ulster. This lake is 20 miles in in length, and varies from 8 to 12 miles in breadth. The area of this lake is computed to be 100,000 acres. It is remarkable for a healing virtue; and likewise for petrifying wood, which is not only found in the water but in the adjacent soil at a considerable depth. On its shores several beautiful gems have been discovered. Its ancient name was Loch-Éacha, or Loch-Neach, from loch, "a lake," and Neach, "wonderful, divine, or eminent." Its petrifying powers are not instantaneous, as several of the ancients have supposed, but require a long <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of ages to bring them to perfection, and appear to be occasioned by a fine mud or sand, which insinuates itself into the pores of the wood, and which in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of time becomes hard like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. On the borders of this lake is Shane's castle, the elegant seat of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> O'Neil. Dr Smyth seems to doubt whether the healing quality in this lake is not to be confined to one side of it, called the fishing-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a>; and he informs us, that this virtue was discovered in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II., in the instance of the son of one Mr Cunningham, who had an evil which run on him in eight or ten places; and notwithstanding all applications, seemed incurable: at length he was perfectly healed, after bathing in this lough about eight days. Hence that writer gives us another derivation of the name Loch-Neach, which (he says) seems to him to hint at this quality; Neasg or Neas, in Irish, signifying "a sore or ulcer," which might not improbably be corrupted into Neach: Hence he apprehends, this lake was remarked at a much earlier <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> for its healing property. As to its petrifying power, it is mentioned by Nenius, a writer of the 9th century, who says, "Est aliquid stagnum quod facit ligna duoscere in lapides. Homines autem findunt ligna, et postquam formaverunt, proiciunt in stagnum, et manent in eo usque <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> caput anni, et in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITE">capite</a> anni lapsus inventur; et vocatur stagnum Lacle-Echach." Lough-Neagh gives <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of baron to the family of Skeffington.

LOU

Pages 261-261
or St Louis, Knights of, the name of a military order in France, instituted by Louis XIV. in 1693. Their colours were of a flame colour, and pass from left to right; the king was their grand master. There were in it eight great crosses, and 24 commanders; the number of knights was not limited. At the time of their institution, the king charged his revenue with a fund of 900,000 livres for the pensions of the commanders and knights. Louis, Lewis, Louis d'or, or Louvidore, a French coin, first struck in 1640, under the reign of Louis XIII., and which has now a considerable currency. See Money-Table.

LOUGH-STRANGFORD

Pages 261-261

a lake of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, situated in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">Down</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Ulster. It takes its present name from a small port-town called Strangford, seated on the west side of the narrow entrance into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. It was formerly known by the name of Longh-Cone <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Longh Coupne. It is a deep <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> or inlet of the sea, about 17 miles <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and four or five <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; it goes west as far as <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol8.html#article-DOWNPATRICK">Downpatrick</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> as far as Comber and Newton, and by computation covers 25,775 acres, Irish plantation <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>. It abounds with excellent fish, particularly smelts; and off the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> there is a periodical <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERRING">herring</a> fishery in or about August. The bar or entrance into the lough is about three miles below Strangford. There is a long rock at the entrance in the middle of the passage, dangerous to strangers on account of the current; yet there is a broad passage on either side, and deep <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. The current here is very strong and rapid, running at the rate of six or <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> miles an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>. There are but few vessels that go higher up than Strangford. A good many vessels bound up the channel put in here, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> is unfavourable to their passage. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in this lake are numerous; Dr <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">Boat</a> enumerates them at 260. But from an actual survey, made at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> Dr Smyth wrote his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of that county, it appears, there are 54 islands small and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, known by particular names, and many others nameless; the contents of these 54 islands added together amount to 954 acres and a half. The great and profitable manufacture carried on in these islands, and the flat stony coasts surrounding the lake, is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> of sea-weed into kelp, which employs a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, and has been computed to produce to the several proprietors a neat profit of 1000l. per annum and upwards. Four of the islands here are called Swan islands, from the number of swans that frequent them.

LOUISIANA

Pages 261-262

an extensive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, lying between <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a> and the river <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MISSISSIPPI">Mississippi</a>, and now forming one of the united states of the North American republic. The name was originally given to a region extending from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of Mexico, northward and westward to an unknown distance, but is now confined to the southern <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of this territory. Louisiana was originally discovered and settled by the French; and, after remaining in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> for about a century, it was transferred to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> in 1762. In 1801 Spain gave up the colony again to France, by whom it was sold to the United States in 1803 for sixty millions of francs. In 1812 Louisiana was erected into a state, and admitted as a member of the union. It extends between 29° and 33° of north latitude, and between the river Sabine on the west, and the Perdido on the east, embracing an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> of 45,860 <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles. The greater part of the country is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> plain, and that part which reaches from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-shore, 20 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 30 miles inward, is a morass on a level with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, without trees or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>. The Mississippi flows through the eastern part of it; and as its waters have generally a higher level than the adjoining country, the cultivated parts are protected from inundation by embankments. This <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> river sends off part of its waters by lateral courses to the sea, and forms a kind of delta. A considerable part of the country is overflowed during the annual swell of the river in May and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, which then rises 50 feet in the upper part of its course; but at New <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a>, within 100 miles of the sea, the rise is only 12 feet. The richest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is along the banks of the Mississippi and its branches; the other parts are either swampy, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a>. It abounds with a great variety of wood, and the wild vine is extremely <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a>. The settlements are confined chiefly to the banks of the streams. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> in 1810 was 86,556; but in 1814 was estimated at 101,700. Of this population 30,000 reside in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, New Orleans, which is situated about 100 miles from the mouth of the river, and carries on a very extensive trade. It has now become the centre of trade for the states situated on the western side of the Alleghany <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. Louisiana, mountains, and has increased more rapidly within the last ten years than any other town in the United States. The produce received from the upper country is immense; between 300 and 400 sea vessels arrive and depart annually, and about 900 flat-bottomed boats and barges descend the river from the western territories. The river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> has been much improved by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STEAM">steam</a>-boats, which are now numerous upon the Mississippi and Ohio. These have also been employed as drag-boats to assist loaded vessels in ascending from the sea to New Orleans. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> exports are cotton, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, and flour. The exports of Louisiana in 1817 amounted to $9,024,812 dollars, of which $8,241,254 were <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> produce, and $783,558 foreign produce. The tonnage belonging to New Orleans in 1815 was 17,204. (Warden's Account of the United States.) The agricultural productions of Louisiana are the same with those of the other southern states; but sugar is now cultivated to a greater <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> here than in any other part of the union. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANE">cane</a> is planted in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>, February, or <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, and ripens in October. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> produce is estimated at 800 or 1000 pounds per <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACRE">acre</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> made on the Mississippi alone in 1812 was estimated at ten millions of pounds. It is computed that there are one million of acres in the state adapted to the culture of sugar. Tobacco and cotton are also cultivated to a considerable extent. Of the latter 20,000 bales were exported in 1812. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">Rice</a> is cultivated in swampy places unfit for any other <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of grain, and the produce is estimated at 15 barrels per acre, each weighing 200 pounds. Maize is raised, but this plant, as well as wheat, rye, barley and oats, do not thrive so well as in states farther north, and are not very much cultivated. Figs and olives succeed, and it is believed that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> would be found profitable. The sweet <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CITRON">citron</a>, lemon, and lime, are cultivated below the 30th <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a>. Immense herds of cattle are raised in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> meadows of Opelousas and Atakapas. The mutton is considered to be superior to that of the northern states, the other kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> inferior. In the richest and most populous parts of the country plantations bring from 40 to 50 dollars an acre, exclusive of slaves and buildings. The profits of a slave are estimated at 140 dollars per annum. Negro tradesmen are let or hired at from 20 to 30 dollars a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a>. Some planters have a yearly income of 20,000 dollars, and possess from 10,000 to 20,000 head of cattle. There are no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of much importance in this state. <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">Salt</a> is made at two or three places. Within 60 miles above, and an equal distance below New Orleans, there are 36 <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>, some of which are driven by steam, and others by water let off by small openings in the banks of the Mississippi. Pitch and tar are manufactured, and of the cane or reed are made <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-HATS">hats</a>, sieves, baskets, mats, &c. Candles are made of the vegetable wax derived from the Myrtica cerifera. Louisiana is in many parts rather unhealthy. Bilious fever prevails generally in autumn, and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> fever has several times made its appearance. Sore throat, tetanus, and dysentery are also not uncommon. The most sickly season at New Orleans is August. The births in that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> in the year ending March 1808 were 456, the deaths 769. Snow seldom falls in this state, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FROST">frost</a> is only experienced in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> and January. In <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> the thermometer sometimes rises to 93 in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> temperature of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> water is said to be 65°. About the 1st of February peach and plum trees are in blossom. The most considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are the Mississippi, which has generally a breadth of 880 yards in this state. Its depth near New Orleans exceeds 150 feet. The <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol18.html#article-RED_RIVER"><a class=</a>"xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> river falls into the Mississippi near Fort Adams. The Sabine river falls into the gulf of Mexico. The Lafourche, Atchafalaga, and Iberville, are outlets of the Mississippi. There are also several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, of which those of Ponchartrain and Chetimache are the most considerable. Lake Borgne is an arm of the sea. By its rivers and lakes Louisiana enjoys an inland <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> of 4000 miles. A <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of native <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> weighing 3000 pounds was lately discovered on the banks of Red river. Iron ore, silver, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, coal, and potter's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, are found in the state. There are also salt <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> at different places. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of this state was framed by a convention at New Orleans in 1812. The legislature consists of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> chosen for four years, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of representatives for two. All free <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> citizens of 21 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and paying taxes, are electors. The members of both houses receive four dollars a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> for their services. The governor is elected for four years. The judges of all the courts hold their offices during good behaviour. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a> consists of all the free white citizens. This country was invaded by a British force in December 1814. It advanced to within six miles of New Orleans, but was defeated there on the 8th January 1815, with the loss of its commander General Packenham and 2600 men in killed and wounded. The Americans, who were commanded by General Jackson, and fought behind an entrenchment, lost according to their own account, only 7 killed and 8 wounded. Soon after Louisiana was ceded to the United States, there were two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> established for the promotion of science and literature, one of them at New Orleans, and another at Natchez. The former designs to publish a monthly <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGAZINE">magazine</a> for the purpose of diffusing a knowledge of the country, and to amuse the readers of it with a variety of useful subjects. The latter, which was established in 1803, called the Mississippi <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> for the Acquisition and Dissemination of useful Knowledge, consists of near 40 members, and has correspondents in various parts of the United States. The American <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> has granted it a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> of incorporation. LOUSE. See Pediculus, Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. LOUSY <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">DISEASE</a>. See Medicine Index.

LOUTH

Pages 263-263

a town in the above <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, having a yearly fair.

LOUVAIN

Pages 263-263

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Brabant, pleasantly seated on the river Dyle, in a plentiful and agreeable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The walls are about eight <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> miles in circumference; but they include several fields and vineyards. The castle stands on a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> hill, surrounded with fine gardens, and has a charming prospect all over the country. This town contains nine market places, 14 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>, 126 streets, 16 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> bridges, and several handsome palaces. The town-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> is a venerable old <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, adorned with <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> on the outside; and the churches are very handsome, particularly the collegiate <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of St <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>; but the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a>-ornament is the university, founded only in 1426 by John IV. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Brabant, with the concurrence of Pope Martin V. It contains about 40 colleges, four of which are called Pedagogia. There is in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> also an English <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of friars-preachers, which owes its establishment to the liberalities of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> Howard, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> to the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a>, who, before he was raised to the purple, had been private chaplain to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> Catherine, consort to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. The Irish have likewise a seminary, erected in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> under the care of Eugenius Matheus, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TITULAR">titular</a> archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>, anno 1623, which receives its appointments from the Propaganda at Rome. Besides the above, there are two <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a> for the Irish, one of Recollects and the other of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMINICANS">Dominicans</a>, where <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> and the mathesis are taught. In the last century the number of scholars exceeded 4000; but in the year 1744 the inhabitants amounted to 12,000, including 2000 students only.—At the beginning of the 14th century, under John III. it flourished considerably in the manufacture of woollen cloth: 400 houses were then occupied by substantial clothiers, who gave employment to an incredible number of weavers, so <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, it is said, that a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELL">bell</a> was rung to prevent any injuries which the children in the street might receive from the crowd and hurry on their returning from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. In 1382, these weavers, however, took up arms, and rebelled against their sovereign <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Wenceslaus, throwing from the windows of the town <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a> 17 of the aldermen and counsellors, and afterwards proceeded to lay waste great part of Brabant; but being besieged and reduced to great extremities, they submissively implored his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLEMENCY">clemency</a>; which was granted after the execution of some of the principal ringleaders. The weavers, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> instigators to this revolt, were banished, the greater part of whom took refuge in England; where they first introduced, or at least augmented very much, the woollen manufacture. The town, by this circumstance, being almost depopulated, the university was established to supply in some <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> the loss of the rebellious clothiers. Since that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the manufacture gradually declined, no cloth of any account being made there at present. This impolitic step of the duke Wenceslaus sent treasures to England, through the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of those exiled people: an important lesson to governors, that they should <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> with great precaution respecting such useful members of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a>. Upon the ruins of these looms was formed the cloth manufacture of Limbourg, which is carried on with good advantage to this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. There is yet standing at Louvain part of the old drapers-hall, now converted into four public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, where lectures in divinity, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and physic, are given, and the public acts are made. Adjoining to the schools is the university library which altogether compose a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> pile of building. Over the door of the chief entrance we read these words, Sapientia adificavit sibi domum. The principal church is collegiate, dedicated to St Peter, which had formerly three very large towers with elevated spires, one considerably higher than the two collaterals; these were blown <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in the year recorded by this chronogram, oMnIaCuDVnt. From the name of this church, the burghers have acquired the nickname of Petermen, whose <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> having clothed the back by a noble woollen manufacture, the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Petermen now compose an ignoble mixture for the belly, called after them Peterman bcer, a sort of whitish muddy ale, which they notwithstanding send in large quantities to all parts of the country, as well as to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a>. Louvain was anciently the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the province, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> before <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUSSELS">Brussels</a> had any claim to that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>. It was taken by the French in 1792, afterwards lost, and retaken in 1794. E. Long. 4. 40. N. Lat. 51. 12.

LOUYS

Pages 263-263
or Louis, John, an engraver of considerable eminence, who flourished about the middle of the 16th century. According to Basan he was a native of Flanders. He learned the art of engraving from Peter Soutman, at the time that Snyderhoef studied under the same master; and his usual style of engraving bears some resemblance to that of his master's. One of his best prints is Diana, with her nymphs, reposing after the chase; a middling-sized plate, lengthwise, from Rubens.

LOW

Pages 264-264

East, a town of Cornwall in England, 231 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLYMOUTH">Plymouth</a>. It is an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> borough by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESCRIPTION">prescription</a>, made a corporation by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, consisting of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> burgesses (one of whom is yearly chosen mayor), a recorder, aldermen, &c.; and the mayor, magistrates, and freemen, who are about 68, choose the members of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. This being a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANOR">manor</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Cornwall, was settled by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> William on <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Somers, and is now held by the corporation at the fee-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARM">farm</a> rent of 20s. a-year. It is seated pretty commodiously on a creek of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, over which there is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, supported by 15 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>, which leads to West Low. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> benefit which the inhabitants have is in their fishery. Here is a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a> of four guns, and a small chapel. It contained 608 inhabitants in 1811. Low, West, called also Port Pigham, a town of Cornwall, divided from East Low by a stone bridge of 15 arches over the river Low, from whence both <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> receive their name, as the river does from the lowness of its current between its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> banks. The corporation, by charter of Queen Elizabeth, consists of 12 burgesses, one of whom is annually chosen mayor, and, with the other burgesses, has power to choose a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a>. Its members, whom it has sent to parliament ever since the 6th of Edward VI., are elected by the corporation and freemen, who are about 60. There was a chapel of ease here in the reign of Henry VIII., which was afterwards converted into a town-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a>; and the town lying in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of Talland, the people go thither to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. There is a pretty little harbour here; near the mouth of which is a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> called St George's, which abounds with sea pikes. The river here is navigable for vessels of 100 tons. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">Population</a> in 1811, 433.

LOW-BELL

Pages 263-264

in birding, a name given to a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELL">bell</a>, by means of which they take birds in the night, in open <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a> countries, and among stubble, in October. The method is to go out about <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> o'clock at night in a still evening, when the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> is mild and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a> does not shine. The low-bell should be of a deep and hollow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>, and of such a size that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> may conveniently carry it in one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. The person who carries it is to make it toll all the way he goes, as nearly as may be, in that manner in which the bell on the neck of a sheep tolls as it goes on and feeds. There must also be a box made like a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> lanthorn, about a foot <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, and lined with tin, but with one side open. Two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> three <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> lights are to be set in this; and the box is to be fixed to the person's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, with the open side forwards, so that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> may be <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> forward to a great distance. It <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> spread as it goes goes out of the box; and will distinctly show to the person that carries it whatever there is in the large space of ground over which it extends, and consequently all the birds that roost upon the ground. Two persons must follow him who carries the box and bell, one on each side, so as not to be within the reach of the light to show themselves. Each of these is to have a hand-<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">net</a>, of about three or four feet square, fastened to a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> stick or pole; and on whichever side any <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> is seen at roost, the person who is nearest is to lay his net over it, and take it with as little noise as possible. When the net is over the bird, the person who laid it is not to be in a hurry to take the bird, but must stay till he who carries the light is got beyond it, that the motions may not be discovered. The blaze of the light and the noise of the bell terrify and amaze the birds in such a manner that they remain still to be taken; but the people who are about the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> must keep the greatest quiet and stillness that may be. Some people are fond of going on this scheme alone. The person then fixes the light box to his breast, and carries the bell in one hand and the net in the other; the net in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> may be somewhat smaller, and the handle shorter. When more than one are out at a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, it is always proper to carry a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUN">gun</a>; as it is no uncommon thing to spy a hare when on this expedition.

LOWER

Pages 264-264

Richard, an eminent English physician in the 17th century, was born in Cornwall, and educated at Westminster school and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>; after which he studied medicine, and practised under Dr Thomas Willis, whom he instructed in some parts of anatomy, especially when the latter was <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> his Cerebri Anatomie. He, with Dr Willis, in 1674, discovered the medicinal waters at Ashop in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHAMPTONSHIRE">Northamptonshire</a>; which, upon their recommendation, became very much frequented. In 1666, he followed Dr Willis to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; practised physic under him; and became fellow of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, and of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a> of Physicians. In 1669 he published his Tractatus de Corde; and after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Dr Willis in 1675, he was esteemed the most eminent physician in London. Upon the breaking out of the Popish plot in 1678, says Mr Wood in his Athene Oxoniensis, he closed with the Whigs, supposing that party would carry all before them; but, being mistaken, he lost his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> and practice. He died in 1691.

LOWERING

Pages 264-264

among distillers, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used to express the debasing the strength of any spirituous liquor, by mixing <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> with it. The standard and marketable price of these liquors is fixed in regard to a certain strength in them called <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>; this is that strength which makes them, when shaken in a phial <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> poured from on <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> into a glass, retain a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FROTH">froth</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of bubbles for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. In this state, spirits consist of about half pure or totally inflammable spirit, and half water; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any foreign or home spirits are to be exposed to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>, and are found to have that proof wanting, scarce any body <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> buy it till it has been distilled again and brought to that strength; and if it is above that strength, the proprietor usually adds water to it to bring it <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to that standard. See the article Proof. There is another kind of lowering among the retailers of spirituous liquors to the vulgar, by reducing it under the standard proof. Whoever has the art of doing this without destroying the bubble proof, which is easily done by means of some addition that gives a greater tenacity to the parts of the spirits, will deceive all that judge by this proof alone. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, the best way to judge of liquors is by the eye and tongue, and especially by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> called Hydrometer.

LOWTH

Pages 264-267

William, D.D., a learned divine, born at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in 1661, was the son of an apothecary, and took his degrees at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. His eminent worth and learning recommended him to Dr Mew bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a>, who made him his chaplain, gave him two livings in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAMPSHIRE">Hampshire</a>, and conferred on him a prebend in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> of Winchester. He acquired an unusual share of critical learning. Thus situated in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, the labours of Mr Lowth appear to have been strictly confined within the limits of his own <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, and applied solely to the peculiar duties of his functions; yet, in order that he might acquire himself the better in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, he had pursued his studies with a more general and extensive view. Few were more deeply versed in critical learning; there being scarcely any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> author, Greek <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Latin, profane or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a>, especially the latter, but what he had read with accuracy, constantly accompanying his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> with critical and philological remarks. Of his collections in this way he was upon all occasions very communicative. Hence his notes on Clemens Alexandrinus, which are to be met with in Potter's edition of that father. Hence his remarks on Josephus, communicated Lowth communicated to Hudson for his edition, and acknowledged in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a>; as also those larger and more numerous annotations on the Ecclesiastical Historians, inserted in Reading's edition of them at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>. The author of Bibliotheca Biblica was indebted to him for the same kind of assistance. Chandler, late bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURHAM">Durham</a>, while engaged in his "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">Defence</a> of Christianity, from the Prophecies of the Old <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, against the Discourse of the Grounds and Reasons of the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">Religion</a>," and in his "Vindication of the Defence, in answer to The Scheme of Literal Prophecy considered," held a constant correspondence with him, and consulted him upon many difficulties that occurred in the course of that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. The most valuable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his character was that which least appeared in the eyes of the world, the private and retired part, that of the good Christian and the useful <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>. His piety, his diligence, his hospitality and beneficence, rendered his life highly exemplary, and greatly enforced his public exhortations. He married Margaret, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Robert Pitt, Esq. of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLANDFORD">Blandford</a>, by whom he had two sons and three daughters. (See the next article.) He died in 1732, and was buried by his own orders in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCHYARD">churchyard</a> of Buriton. He published, 1. A Vindication of the Divine Authority and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSPIRATION">Inspiration</a> of the Old and New Testaments; 2. Directions for the profitable reading of the Holy Scriptures; 3. Commentaries on the Prophets; and other works. Lowth, Robert, D.D., <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> son of the preceding Dr William Lowth, and bishop successively of St <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a>'s, Oxford, and London, was born on the 29th of November 1710, probably at Buriton in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Hants. He received the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> at Winchester <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, where his school exercises were distinguished by uncommon elegance; and having resided the requisite <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of years in that seminary, in 1730 he succeeded on the foundation at New College, Oxford. He took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of M.A. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 8, 1737. Though his abilities must have been known to those with whom he was connected, he was not forward to appear before the world as a writer. At Oxford he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> many years improving his talents, with little notice from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, and with preferment so small as to have at present escaped the distinct recollection of some of his contemporaries. He was not, however, suffered to languish for ever in obscurity. His genius and his learning forced themselves upon the notice of the illustrious <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of which he was a member; and he was placed in a station where he was eminently qualified to shine. In 1741 he was elected by the university to the professorship of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, re-elected in 1743, and whilst he held that office he read his admirable lectures De sacra poesi Hebræorum. In 1744 Bishop Hoadley collated him to the rectory of Ovington in the county of Hants; added to it, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> years afterwards, the rectory of East Weedhay in the same county; and in the interim raised him to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of archdeacon of Winchester. These repeated favours he some years afterwards acknowledged in the following manly and respectful terms of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a>: "This <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>, my <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>, is not more necessary on account of the subject, than it is in respect of the author. Your Lordship, unsolicited and unasked, called him from one of those colleges to a station of the first dignity in your <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a>, and took the earliest opportunity of accumulating your favour upon him, and of adding to that dignity a suitable support. These obligations he is now the more ready thus publicly to acknowledge, as he is removed out of the reach of further favours of the like kind. And though he hath relinquished the advantages so generously conferred on him, yet he shall always esteem himself highly honoured in having once enjoyed the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> of the great advocate of civil and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>." On the 8th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1754 the university of Oxford conferred upon him the degree of D.D. by diploma; an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> which, as it is never granted but to distinguished merit, was probably conferred on Mr Lowth in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of his prelections on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> poetry, which had then been lately published. Having in 1749 travelled with Lord George and Lord Frederick Cavendish, he had a claim upon the patronage of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a> family; and in 1755, the late <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> being then lord <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, Dr Lowth went to that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> as his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>'s first chaplain. Soon after this appointment he was offered the bishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIMERICK">Limerick</a>; but preferring a less dignified station in his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, he exchanged it with Dr Leslie, prebendary of Durham and rector of Sedgefield, for these preferments. In November 1765 he was chosen F.R.S. In June 1766 he was, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Dr Squire, preferred to the bishopric of St David's; which, in the October following, he resigned for that of Oxford, vacant by the translation of Bishop Hume to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALISBURY">Salisbury</a>. In April 1777, he was translated to the see of London, vacant by the death of Bishop Terrick; and in 1783 he declined the offer of the primacy of all England.
