Having been <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> afflicted with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, and having long borne the severest sufferings of pain and sickness with the most exemplary fortitude and resignation, this great and good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> died at <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FULHAM">Fulham</a>, Nov. 3, 1787; and on the 12th his remains were privately interred in a vault at Fulham <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, near those of his predecessor. He had married in 1752, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, the daughter of Laurence Jackson of Christ-church, Hants, Esq. by whom he had two sons and five daughters. His lady and two children only survived him. His literary character may be estimated from the value and the importance of his works; in the account of which we may begin with his Prelections on the Hebrew Poetry. The choice of so interesting a subject naturally attracted general <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>; and the work has been read with equal applause abroad and at home. In these Prelections the author has acquitted himself in the most masterly manner, as a poet, a critic, and a divine; and such is the classic purity of his Latin style, that though we have read the work with the closest attention, and with no other view than to discover, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> possible, an Anglicism in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, we never found a single phrase to which, we believe, a critic of the Augustan <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> could possibly have objected. This is an excellence to which neither <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a> nor Johnson has attained; to which indeed no other English writer of Latin with whom we are acquainted has attained, unless perhaps Atterbury must be excepted. To the Prelections was subjoined a short <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFUTATION">confutation</a> of Bishop Hare's system of Hebrew metre; which occasioned a Latin <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> from Dr Edwards of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLARE">Clare</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, Clare-hall, Cambridge, to Dr Lowth, in vindication of the Harian metre. To this the author of the prelections replied in a larger confutation, in which Bishop Hare's system is completely overthrown, and the fallacy upon which it was built accurately investigated. After much attentive consideration, Bishop Lowth has pronounced the metre of the Hebrews to be perfectly irrecoverable. In 1758 he published *The life of William of Wykeham*, bishop of Winchester, with a dedication to Bishop Hoadley; which involved him in a dispute concerning a decision which that bishop had lately made respecting the wardenship of Winchester-college. This controversy was on both sides carried on with such abilities, that, though relating to a private concern, it may yet be read, if not with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, at least with improvement. The life of Wykeham is drawn from the most authentic sources; and affords much information concerning the manners, and some of the public transactions of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> in which Wykeham lived, whilst it displays some private intelligence respecting the two literary <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> of which he was the founder. In these two societies Dr Lowth was educated, and he gratefully expresses his obligations to them. In 1762 was first published his *Short Introduction to English <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>*, which has since gone through many editions. It was originally designed only for private and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>; but its judicious remarks being too valuable to be confined to a few, the book was given to the world; and the excellence of its method, which teaches what is <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> by showing what is wrong, has insured public approbation and very general use. In 1765 Dr Lowth was engaged with Bishop Warburton in a controversy, which made much noise at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, which attracted the notice even of royalty, and of which the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> is still recent. If we do not wish to dwell on the particulars of this controversy, it is because violent literary contention is an evil, which though like other <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> it may sometimes be unavoidable, is yet always to be regretted; and because the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of learned, ingenious, and amiable men, never appear to less advantage than under the form which that state of hostility obliges them to assume. The two combatants indeed engaged with crudition and ingenuity, such as is seldom brought into conflict; but it appears that, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of Dr Johnson, Warburton had the most scholastic learning, and that Lowth was the most correct scholar; that, in their contest with each other, neither of them had much argument, and that both were extremely abusive. We have heard, and we hope it is true, that they were afterwards reconciled, and expressed mutual regret for the violence of their past conduct. In 1778 Bishop Lowth published his last great work, *A Translation of Isaiah*. To his literary and theological abilities, the translator joined the most critical knowledge of the character and spirit of the eastern poetry; and, accordingly, the prophecies of Isaiah (which, though almost always sublime or elegant, are yet sometimes obscure) were translated in a manner adequate to the highest expectations of the public. Several occasional discourses, which the bishop, by his station, was at different times called upon to deliver, were of course published, and are all worthy of their excellent author; but there is one on the kingdom of God, on the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> and progressive improvement of Christ's religion, and on the means of promoting these by the advancement of religious knowledge, by freedom of inquiry, by toleration, and mutual <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>, which may be distinguished above the rest, as exhibiting a most comprehensive view of the successive states of the Christian church, and containing the truest principles of Christianity. Of the bishop's poetical pieces, none display greater merit than Verses on the Genealogy of Christ, and the Choice of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, both written very early in his life. He wrote a spirited <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">Imitation</a> of an Ode of Horace, applied to the alarming situation of this country in 1745; and likewise some verses on the death of Frederic <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, with a few smaller poems. The following inscription on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of his daughter, beautifully displays his paternal affection and classic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. As it is short, and, in our opinion, has all the merit of the ancient epitaph, the reader <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> probably be pleased with such a specimen of his lordship's Latinity. *Cara, vale, ingenio prestans, pietate, pudore, Et plasquam nate nomine cara, vale.* *Cara <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARIA">Maria</a>, vale. At veniet felicius ævum, Quando iterum tecum, sim modo dignus, ero.* *Cara, redi, lesta tum dicam voce, paternos.* *Pju, agc in amplexus, cara Maria, redi.* Learning and taste, however, did not constitute Bishop Lowth's highest excellence. Eulogium itself can scarcely ascend to extravagance when speaking of him either as a private man, or as a pastor of the church of Christ. His amiable manners rendered him an ornament to his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> station, whilst he endeared him to all with whom he conversed; and his zeal for the interests of true religion made him eager to promote to places of trust and dignity such clergymen as he knew were best qualified to fill them. Of his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a>, gentleness, and pleasing conversation, we have the testimony of one whose decision will hardly be disputed.—"It would answer no end (says Bishop Warburton) to tell you what I thought of the author of Hebrew poetry, before I <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> him. But this I may say, I was never more surprised, when I did see him, than to find him of such amiable and gentle manners, of so modest, sensible, and disengaged a deportment." He united, indeed, in an eminent degree, the qualities of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> with those of the scholar: he conversed with elegance, as he wrote with accuracy. As a husband, a father, or the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of a family, he was as nearly faultless as the imperfections of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> will easily permit. His temper, when roused by what he thought improper conduct was indeed susceptible of considerable warmth; but if he could be highly offended, upon a slight concession he could likewise forgive. His heart was tender and sympathetic. He possessed a mind which felt its own strength, and decided on whatever came before it with promptitude and firmness. In those trials where affliction was to be suffered or subdued, he behaved as a man and a Christian. His piety had no tincture of moroseness; his charity no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAVEN">leaven</a> of ostentation. To his whole diocese he was endeared by his laudable <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a> and his useful zeal. To the world he was a benefit by his exemplary life and his splendid abilities. And whilst virtue and learning are reverenced... reverenced among men, the memory of Lowth will be respected and admired.

LOXIA

Pages 267-267

a genus of birds of the order of passeres. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

LOZENGE

Pages 267-267

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, a four-cornered <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, resembling a pane of glass in old casements. See Heraldry. Though all heralds agree that single ladies are to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> their arms on lozenges, yet they differ with respect to the causes that gave rise to it. Plutarch says, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THESEUS">Theseus</a>, that in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEGARA">Megara</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> under which the bodies of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMAZONS">Amazons</a> lay, were shaped after that form; which some conjecture to be the cause why ladies have their arms on lozenges. S. Petra Sancta <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have this shield to represent a cushion, whereupon women used to sit and spin, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> do other housewifery. Sir J. Ferne thinks it is formed from the shield called <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TESSERA">tessera</a>, which the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> finding unfit for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, did allow to women to place their ensigns upon, with one of its <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> always uppermost.

LOZENGES

Pages 267-267

among jewellers, are <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to brilliant and rose diamonds. In <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRILLIANTS">brilliants</a>, they are formed by the meeting of the skill and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAR">star</a> facets on the bezil; in the latter, by the meeting of the facets in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> ribs of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. See Facets. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOZENGE">LOZENGE</a> is also a form of medicine, made into small pieces, to be held <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> chewed in the mouth till they are melted there: the same with what are otherwise called trochisci, "troches."

LUBEC

Pages 267-267

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> and port-town of Germany, in the circle of Lower <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLSTEIN">Holstein</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 10° 50'. N. Lat. 53° 55'. It stands at the confluence of several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, the largest of which is the Trave, 12 miles from the Baltic, where it has a fine harbour, and 40 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of Hamburgh. By the Steckenitz, another of those rivers, it has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELBE">Elbe</a>, and consequently with the German ocean. The city lies on the side of a hill, with the Trave, increased by the Steckenitz on the one side, and the Wakenitz on the other; and is strongly fortified with bastions, moats, walls, and ramparts; the last of which are planted with trees, and form an agreeable walk. Lubec being formerly the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANSE">Hanse</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, was very powerful in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the vast trade carried on; but a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of that trade is now transferred to Hamburgh; however, it is still said to employ 150 of its own ships, and has a great share of the Baltic trade. It is about two miles in length, and more than one in breadth. The houses are all of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, but old fashioned. Several of the streets have on each side rows of lime trees, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> in the middle, like those of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>. The public structures consist of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> of the bishopric of Lubec, and several other Lutheran churches; a nunnery for 22 ladies, with an abbess and prioress; a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, an alms-house, and house of correction; an orphan-house; an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> dedicated to the Holy Ghost; a house in which poor travellers are entertained three days, and then sent forward with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>; the city armoury, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>-school of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> classes, the Calvinist <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and the Popish chapel. The deputies of the Hanse-towns used to meet here formerly in the townhouse. An <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> still subsists between Lubec, Hamburgh, and Bremen; and these cities, under the name of Hanse Towns, negotiate treaties with foreign powers. Here are <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, and the city's territory is about 60 miles in compass. In the diet of the empire Lubec is possessed of the third seat among the Rhenish imperial cities; and among those of the circle, has the first. In the matricula, its assessment is 480 florins, and to the chamber of Wetzlar it pays 557 rix-dollars and 88 kruitzers. The city is a republic within itself, and both makes and executes laws in regard to civil and criminal matters, &c. A father and son, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> two brothers, cannot be in the regency at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. The famous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> of the Hanse-towns was begun here in 1164. This city had its <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> of privileges from the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Frederic II. Formerly it carried on wars, both offensive and defensive, for several years, not only against the dukes of Mecklenburg, but against the kings of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>; particularly in 1428, when it fitted out 250 ships of force against Eric X. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Denmark. There are about 20 churches in Lubec, with lofty steeples or spires. The Trave brings ships of burden into the very heart of the city; but the largest unload at Travemunde, i.e. the mouth of the Trave, eight or ten miles distant. Formerly it is said to have employed no less than 600 ships, but its trade is now greatly reduced. In the famous cellar here, it is said, there is wine 200 years old. The town's garrison consists of about 700 or 800 men. The revenue of its Lutheran bishop, though he is a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of the empire, is said not to exceed 3000l. Lubec fell into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the French in 1806, when Bonaparte overran the Prussian dominions; and many of the inhabitants were cruelly massacred and plundered; but it has since been restored to its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> as a free city. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> is 42,000.

LUBEN

Pages 267-267

a town of Germany, in the marquisate of Lower <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUSATIA">Lusatia</a>. It is situated on the river Spree, and is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a small circle of the same name. It is the seat of the diets, and of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> tribunals and offices; and has several churches, with a noble <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 14° 25'. N. Lat. 52°.

LUBIENIETSKI

Pages 267-267

Stanislaus, a Polish <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, descended from a noble family, and born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CRACOW">Cracow</a> in 1623, was educated by his father with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. He became a celebrated <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-SOCINIAN">Socinian</a> minister; and took great pains to obtain a toleration from the German princes for his Socinian brethren. His labours, however, were ineffectual; being himself persecuted by the Lutheran ministers, and banished from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to place; until at length he was banished out of the world, with his two daughters, by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POISON">poison</a>, his wife narrowly escaping, in 1675. We have of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> A <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the Reformation in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>; A Treatise on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMETS">Comets</a>; with other works, in Latin.

LUBIN

Pages 267-268

Eilhard, was professor of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> in the university of Rostock in 1595; and ten years afterwards was promoted to the professorship of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>. He wrote notes on Anacreon, Juvenal, Persins, &c., and several other works; but that which made the most noise is a treatise on the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and origin of evil, entitled Phosphorus de Causa prima et Natura Mali, printed at Rostock in 1596; in which we have a curious <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a> to account for the origin of moral evil. He supposed two co-eternal principles, not <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VACUUM">vacuum</a>, as Epicurus did; but God, and Nihilum <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Nothing. This being published against by Graver, was defended by Lubin; but after all he is deemed better acquainted with polite literature than with divinity. He died in 1621.

LUBLIN

Pages 268-268

a handsome and considerable town of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the palatinat of the same name, with a citadel, a bishop's see, an university, and a handsome Jewish synagogue. Here the judicial courts for all Poland were held. It has three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a>, frequented by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> from all nations. It is seated on the river Bystrzna. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 22. 31. N. Lat. 51. 26.

LUCANIA

Pages 268-268

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Magna Graecia; bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the river Silarus by which it was separated from the Picentini, and by the river Bradanus by which it was parted from the Apuli Peucetii; on the south by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAIS">Lais</a>, which separated it from the Bruttii; on the east by the Sinus Tarentinus; and on the west by the Tuscan <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. Lucani, the people, descendants of the Sannites. Lucanus the epithet, (Horae.) Lucan boves denoted elephants; first seen in Pyrrhus's wars in Lucania, whence the appellation (Pliny.)

LUCANUS

Pages 268-273

MARCUS ANNÆUS, a Latin poet, born at Corduba in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, about A.C. 39. He was the son of Annæus Mela, the youngest <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of Seneca; and was conveyed to Rome from the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATIVITY">nativity</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of eight months; a circumstance, as his more indulgent critics observe, which sufficiently refutes the censure of those who consider his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> as <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a>. At Rome he was educated under the Stoic Cornutus, so warmly celebrated by his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> Persius the satirist, who was the intimate friend of our poet. In the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, Lucan is said to have passed some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>. On his return to Rome he rose to the office of quaestor, before he had attained the legal age. He was afterwards enrolled among the augurs; and married a lady of noble birth, and of a most amiable character. Lucan had for some time been admitted to familiarity with Nero, when the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> chose to contend for poetical honours by the public recital of a poem he had composed on Niobe; and some verses of his imperial production are supposed to be preserved in the first satire of Persius. Lucan had the hardiness to repeat a poem on <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORPHEUS">Orpheus</a>, in competition with that of Nero; and, what is more remarkable, the judges of the contest were <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> and bold enough to decide against the emperor. From hence Nero became the persecutor of his successful rival, and forbade him to produce any <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> in public. The well known <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> of Piso against the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> soon followed; and Tacitus, with his usual sarcastic severity, concludes that Lucan engaged in the enterprise from the poetical injuries he had received: "a remark (says Mr Hayley*, who has endeavoured to refute the imputation) which does little <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> to the candour of the historian; who might have found a much nobler, and, I <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> add, a more probable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> for his conduct, in the generous ardour of his character, and his passionate <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADORATION">adoration</a> of freedom. In the sequel * In the Notes to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">Second</a> Epistle on Epic Poetry. of his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NARRATION">narration</a>, Tacitus alleges a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> against our Lucan poet, which, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it were true, must <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> us to detest him as the most abject of mankind. The historian asserts, that Lucan, when accused of the conspiracy, for some time denied the charge; but corrupted at last by a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> of impunity, and desirous to atone for the tardiness of his confession, accused his mother Atilla as his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ACCOMPLICE">accomplice</a>. This circumstance is so improbable in itself, and so little consonant to the general character of Lucan, that some writers have treated it with contempt, as a calumny invented by Nero, to vilify the object of his envious abhorrence. But the name of Tacitus has given such an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> of authority to the story, that it may seem to deserve a more serious discussion, particularly as there are two subsequent events related by the same historian, which have a tendency to invalidate the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a> so injurious to our poet. The events I <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> are, the fate of Annæus, and the escape of Atilla, the two parents of Lucan. The former died in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of an accusation brought against him, after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his son, by Fabius Romanus, who had been an intimate with Lucan, and forged some letters in his name, with the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of proving his father concerned in the conspiracy. These letters were produced to Nero, who sent them to Annæus, from an eager desire, says Tacitus, to get possession of his wealth. From this fact two inferences may be drawn, according to the different lights in which it may be considered:—If the accusation against Annæus was just, it is clear that Lucan had not betrayed his father, and he appears the less likely to have endangered by his confession the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARENT">parent</a>, to whom he owed a still tenderer regard:—If Annæus was not involved in the conspiracy, and merely put to death by Nero for the sake of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>, we may the more readily believe, that the tyrant who murdered the father from avarice, might calumniate the son from envy. But the escape of Atilla affords us the strongest reason to conclude that Lucan was perfectly innocent of the abject and unnatural treachery of which Tacitus has supposed him guilty. Had the poet really named his mother as an accomplice, would the vindictive and sanguinary Nero have spared the life of a woman whose family he detested, particularly when other females were put to death for their share in the conspiracy? That Atilla was not in that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, the historian himself informs us in the following remarkable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>, "Atilla mater Annæi Lucani, sine absolitione, sine supplicio, dissimulata;" thus translated by Gordon: "The information against Atilla, the mother of Lucan, was disseminated; and, without being cleared, she escaped unpunished." The preceding remarks will, our author hopes, vindicate to every candid mind the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Lucan, whose firmness and intrepidity of character are indeed very forcibly displayed in that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of his death which Tacitus himself has given us. He was condemned to have his veins cut, as his uncle Seneca had before him. Lucan, "while his blood issued in streams, perceiving his feet and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> to grow <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and stiffen, and life to retire by little and little from the extremities, while his heart was still <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> with vital warmth, and his faculties nowise impaired, recollected some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of his own, which described a wounded soldier expiring in a manner that resembled this. The lines themselves he rehearsed; and they were the last words he he ever uttered." The critics differ concerning the verses of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARSALIA">Pharsalia</a> which the author quoted in so memorable a manner. The two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> he is supposed to have repeated are the following; of which Lupius contends for the latter. Sanguis erant lachrymae: quæcunque foramina nova Humor, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">ab</a> his largus manat crutor: ora redundant, Et patulae nares: sudor rubet: omnia plenis Membræ fluant venis: totum est pro vulnerc corpus. Lib. ix. v. 814. Now the warm blood at once, from every <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> Ran purple <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POISON">poison</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and drain'd the fainting heart. Blood falls for tears; and o'er his mournful <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> The ruddy drops their tainted passage trace. Where'er the liquid juices find a way, There streams of blood, their crimson <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> stray, His mouth and gushing nostrils pour a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>, And e'en the pores ooze out the trickling blood; In the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> deluge all the parts <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> drown'd, And the whole body seems one bleeding wound. Scinditur avulsus; nec sic ut vulnere sanguis Emicuit lentus; ruptis cadit undique venis, Discursusque animæ, diversa in membra meantis, Interceptus aquis. Lib. iii. v. 638. No single wound the gaping rupture seems, Where trickling crimson <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a> in slender streams; But, from an op'ning horrible and wide, A thousand vessels pour the bursting tide: At once the winding channel's course was broke, Where wand'<a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RING">ring</a> life her mazy journey took; At once the currents all forgot their way, And lost their purple in the azure <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. Such was the death of Lucan before he had completed his 27th year.—His wife, Polla Argentaria, is said to have transcribed and corrected the three first books of the Pharsalia after his death. It is much to be regretted (Mr Hayley observes) that we possess not the poem which he wrote on the merits of this amiable and accomplished woman; but her name is immortalized by two surviving poets of that age. The veneration which she paid to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of her husband is recorded by Martial; and more poetically described in that pleasing and elegant little production of Statius, Genethliacum Lucani, a poem said to have been written at the request of Argentaria. The author, after invoking the poetical deities to attend the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>, touches with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> delicacy and spirit on the compositions of Lucan's childhood, which are lost, and the Pharsalia, the production of his early youth: he then pays a short compliment to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and talents of Argentaria; laments the cruel fate which deprived her so immaturely of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>; and concludes with an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> of Lucan, which, with Mr Hayley's translation, we shall subjoin in a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">Note</a>, as it seems to furnish a strong presumption of Lucan's innocence in regard to one of the accusations mentioned above (A). "Had he been really guilty of basely endangering (a) At tu, seu rapidum poli per axem Fama curribus arduis levatus, Qua surgunt animæ potentiores, Terras despicis et sepulchra rides: Seu pacis meritum nemus recluse Felix Elysia tenes in oris, Quo Pharsalica turba congregatur; Et te nobile carmen insontem Pompeii comitantur et Catones: Tu magna sacer et superbus umbra Nescis Tartaron, et procul nocentum Andis verbera, pallidumque visa Matris lampade respiciis Neronom. Adsis lucidus; et vocante Polla Unam, queso, diem deos silentum Exores; solet hoc patere limen <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">Ad</a> nuptas redeuntibus maritis. Hec te non thiasis procax dolosis Palsi numinis induit figuras; Ipsum sed colit, et frequentat ipsum Imis altius insitum medullis; Ac solatia yana subministrat Vultus, qui simili notatus, auro Stratis praemit, excubatque somno Securae. Procui hinc abite mortes; Hec vitae genitalis est origo; Cedat luctus atroce, genisque manent Jam dulces lachrymae dolorque festus Quicquid fleverat ante nunc adoret. But you, O! whether to the skies On Fame's triumphant car you rise, (Where mightier souls new life assume) And mock the confines of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">Or</a> whether in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELYSIUM">Elysium</a> blest You <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> the groves of sacred rest, Where the Pharsalian heroes dwell; And, as you strike your epic shell, The Pompeys and the Catons throng To catch the animating song; Of Tartarus the dread controul Binds not your <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and hallow'd <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>: Distant you hear that wailing <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, And see the guilty Nero's ghost Grow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> with anguish and affright, His mother flashing on his sight. Be present to your Polla's vows, While to your honour'd name she bows! One <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> let your entreaties <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> From those who rule the shadowy train! Their gates have op'd to bless a wife, And given a husband back to life. In you the tender fair invites No fancied god with frantic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a>: You are the object of her prayers, You in her inmost heart she bears: And stamp't on mimic <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, your head Adorns the faithful mourner's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>, And soothes her eyes before they close, The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a> of her chastè repose. Away with all funereal state! From hence his nobler life we <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a>: Let <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOURNING">mourning</a> change the pang severe, To fond <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>'s grateful tear! And festal grief, its anguish o'er, What it lamented, now adore! Lucanus endangering the life of his mother (says Mr Hayley), it is not probable that his wife would have honoured his memory with such enthusiastic veneration; or that Statius, in verses designed to do him honour, would have alluded to the mother of Nero. If his character as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> has been injured by the historian (continues Mr Hayley), his poetical reputation has been treated not less injuriously by the critics. Quintilian, by a frivolous distinction, disputes his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> to be classed among the poets; and Scaliger says, with a brutality of language disgraceful only to himself, that he seems rather to bark than to sing. But these insults may appear amply compensated, when we remember, that in the most polished <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, the most elevated and poetic spirits have been his warmest admirers; that in France he was idolized by Corneille, and in England translated by Rowe.—The severest censures on Lucan have proceeded from those who have unfairly compared his language to that of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>: but how unjust and absurd is such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a>! It is comparing an uneven <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLOCK">block</a> of porphyry, taken rough from the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARRY">quarry</a>, to the most beautiful superficies of polished marble. How differently should we think of Virgil as a poet, if we possessed only the verses which he wrote at that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of life when Lucan composed his Pharsalia! In the disposition of his subject, in the propriety and elegance of diction, he is undoubtedly far inferior to Virgil; but if we attend to the bold originality of his design, and to the vigour of his sentiments; if we consider the Pharsalia as the rapid and uncorrected sketch of a young poet, executed in an age when the spirit of his countrymen was broken, and their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> in literature corrupted; it may justly be esteemed as one of the most noble and most wonderful productions of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> mind.—Lucan wrote several poems; but we have none remaining beside his Pharsalia, of which an excellent English version has been given by Mr Nicholas Rowe. Lucanus, the Stag-Beetle, a genus of insects of the order of coleoptera. See Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Lucar de Barameda (St.), a handsome and considerable town of Spain, with a very good harbour, well defended, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANDALUSIA">Andalusia</a>. It was once the greatest port in Spain, before the galleons unloaded their treasure at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CADIZ">Cadiz</a>. It is seated at the mouth of the river Guadalquivir. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6. 5. N. Lat. 36. 40. Lucar de Guadiana (St.), a strong town of Spain, in Andalusia, on the confines of Algarve; seated on the river Guadiana, with a little harbour. W. Long. 5. 59. N. Lat. 37. 32. Lucar de <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a> (St.), a small town of Spain, in Andalusia, with the title of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a>. It is seated on the river Guadiana, in W. Long. 6. 32. N. Lat. 37. 21. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LUCARIA">Lucaria</a>, a feast celebrated at Rome on the 18th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, in memory of the flight of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> into a great wood, where they found an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a>, and saved themselves from destruction. This wood, in which they found protection, was situated between the Tyber and the Via Salaria. The enemies from whom the Romans fled were the Gauls.—On this festival, Plutarch tells us, it was customary to pay the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTORS">actors</a>, such as contributed to the public amusement, with the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> arising from the felling of wood. This money was called lucar. It is obvious, from what has been observed, that lucar and lucaria are derived from Lucaria, lucus, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROVE">grove</a>. Lucas Jacobs, an eminent <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>, more generally known by the name of Lucas van <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, or Hugense, was born at Leyden in 1494. He received his first instructions in the art of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> from his father Hugues Jacobs; but completed his studies in the school of Cornelius Engelbrecht. He gained much money by his profession; and being of a generous turn of mind, he spent it freely, dressed well, and lived in a superior style. It is said, that, a few years before his death, he made a tour into <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a> and Brabant; and during his journey, a painter of Flushing, envious of his great abilities, gave him poison at an entertainment; which, though very slow, was too fatal in its effect, and put an end to his life, after six years languishing under its cruel influence. Others, denying the story of the poison, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> his death to his incessant industry. The superiority of this artist's genius manifested itself in his infancy: for his works, even from the age of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a>, were so excellent as to excite the admiration of all cotemporary artists; and when he was about 15, he painted a St Hubert, which gained him great applause. His tone of colouring (Mr <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PILKINGTON">Pilkington</a> observes) is good; his attitudes (making a reasonable allowance for the stiff German taste) are well chosen; his figures have a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> in their faces, and his pictures are very highly finished. He endeavoured to proportion the strength of his colouring to the different degrees of distance in which his objects were placed: for in that early time, the true principles of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol8.html#article-PERSPECTIVE">perspective</a> were but little known, and the practice of it was much less observed. In the town <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a> at Leyden, the most <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> picture of Lucas, the subject of which is the Last Judgment, is preserved with great care; the magistrates having refused very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> sums which have been offered for it. This artist painted not only in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, but also in distemper and upon glass. Nor was he less eminent for his engraving than for his painting. He carried on a familiar and friendly correspondence with Albert Durer, who was his cotemporary; and, it is said, that as regularly as Albert Durer published one print, Lucas published another, without the least jealousy on either side, or wish to depreciate each other's merit. And when Albert came into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> upon his travels, he was received by Lucas in a most cordial and affectionate manner. His style of engraving, however, according to Mr Strutt, differed considerably from that of Albert Durer, "and seems evidently to have been founded upon the works of Israel van Mechlen. His <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a> are very neat and clear, but without any powerful effect. The strokes are as fine and delicate upon the objects in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a>, as upon those in the distances; and this want of variety, joined with the feebleness of the masses of shadow, give his engravings, with all their neatness, an unfinished appearance, much unlike the firm substantial effects which we find in the works of Albert Durer. He was attentive to the minutiae of his art. Every thing is carefully made out in his prints, and no part of them is neglected. He gave great character and expression to the heads of his figures; but on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of his works, we find the same heads heads too often repeated. The hands and feet are rather mannered than correct; and when he attempted to draw the naked <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, he succeeded but very indifferently. He affected to make the folds of his draperies long and flowing; but his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> figures are frequently so excessively loaded with girdles, bandages, and other ornamental trappings, that much of the elegance of the design is lost. He engraved on wood, as well as on <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>; but his works on the former are by no means numerous. They are, however, very spirited; though not equal, upon the whole, to those of his friend Albert. The prints of this <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> are pretty numerous, but very seldom met with complete; especially fine impressions of them. For though they are, generally speaking, executed with the graver only, yet, from the delicacy of the execution, they soon suffered in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a>. Of his engravings the few following may be mentioned as among the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a>. 1. Mahomet sleeping, with a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> murdered by his side, and another figure stealing his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, a middling-sized upright plate, dated 1508, said to be one of his most early productions. 2. An ecce homo, a large plate, lengthwise, dated 1510. 3. The crucifixion on Mount Calvary, the same. 4. The wise men's offering, the same, dated 1513. 5. Return of the prodigal son, a middling-sized plate, lengthwise, dated 1518. 6. A large print, lengthwise, called the dance of Magdalen, dated 1519. 7. His own <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a>, a small upright plate, dated 1525. 8. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a> playing before <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAUL">Saul</a>, a middling-sized upright plate, dated ———. This is a very fine print; the expression of Saul's countenance, in particular, is admirable. 9. A print known by the name of Ulespiegle, which is the rarest of all the works of this master. It is in the collection of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of France; and said by Marolles, and other masters, to be unique. But Basan informs us, that M. Mariette had also an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> of this plate; and it has been since found in one or two other collections. It represents a travelling bagpiper with his family; himself playing as he goes along, and carrying two children in a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASKET">basket</a> at his back; his wife trudging by his side, supporting with one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> an infant on her shoulder, and with the other leading an ass loaded with two baskets, having two children in each; and another child going before, with a little dog, completes the singular <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROUP">group</a>. This rare print is dated 1520, and is known to have been sold for 16 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">louis</a> d'ors.—It is nearly 7½ inches high by 4½ <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; and has been twice copied. One of the copies is the reverse way: but the other is the same way with the original; and, though not so well executed, might without a comparison be mistaken for it. Lucas, Richard, D.D., a learned English divine, was born in 1648, and studied at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>; after which he entered into holy orders, and was for some time master of the free school at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABERGAVENNY">Abergavenny</a>. Being esteemed an excellent preacher, he became <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a> of St Stephen's, Coleman street, in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and lecturer of St Olave's in Southwark. He was <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>; and in 1666 was installed prebendary of Westminster. His sight began to fail him in his youth; and he totally lost it in his middle age. He was greatly esteemed for his piety and learning; and published several works, particularly, 1. Practical Christianity. 2. An Inquiry after Happiness. 3. Several sermons. 4. A Latin translation of the Whole Duty of Man. He died in 1715. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-LUCCA">Lucca</a>, a small republic of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, on the coast of the Mediterranean, between the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a> on the west, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODENA">Modena</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a> on the east. According to Keysler, it is only about 30 miles in circumference, but is exceeding fertile and populous. It contains, besides the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Lucca, 150 villages. The number of inhabitants is computed at 120,000. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> is lodged in a gonfalonier, whose power is much the same with that of the doges of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> and Genoa. He is assisted by nine counsellors: but the power of all the ten continues only for two months; during which time they live in the state-<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, and at the public expense. They are chosen out of the great <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, which consists of 240 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a>; but even this council is changed by a new <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> every two years. The revenues of the republic are about 400,000 scudi or crowns; out of which they maintain 500 men by way of regular force, and 70 Swiss as a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> to their acting magistrates. The city of Lucca is situated in a plain, terminating in most delightful eminences, adorned with villas, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>-houses, corn-fields, and plantations of every kind; so that nothing either for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> or for <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> is here wanting. The city, which is about three Italian miles in circumference, has regular well-lined fortifications; and its streets though <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>, are wide, well paved, and full of handsome houses. The number of its inhabitants is computed to be above 40,000; and they carry on large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, especially of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> stuffs. Lucca has a bishop, who enjoys several extraordinary privileges; and its <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> is Gothic. The city stands in E. Long. 11. 27. N. Lat. 43. 52. Lucenti, Lucentia, or Lucentum, a town of the Hither Spain, now Alicant, a sea-port of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VALENCIA">Valencia</a>. W. Long. 32. Lat. 38. 37. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LUCERES">Luceres</a>, in Roman antiquity, the third in order of the three tribes into which <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a> divided the people; including all foreigners: so called from the lucus or grove, where Romulus opened an asylum. Luceria, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of Apulia in Italy; which in Strabo's time still exhibited marks of Diomed's sovereignty in those parts. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> has Nuceria; whether from mistake, or the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of his time, uncertain. Now Nocera de Pagani, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>. E. Long. 15. o. N. Lat. 40. 40. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LUCERIUS">Lucerius</a>, in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">Mythology</a>, a name given to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, as Luceria was given to Juno, as the deities which gave <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> to the world. Lucerne, one of the 13 cantons of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>. It holds the third place among the 13; and is the head of the Catholic cantons. Though less than <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZURICH">Zurich</a>, and consequently much less than <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BERNE">Berne</a>, it is, however, far more extensive than any of the rest, being 15 or 16 leagues long, and eight broad. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> is estimated at 100,000. Even the mountainous part is not barren, but abundant in wood and pasture, furnishing cattle, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIDES">hides</a>, cheese, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>, for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a>. All the north part is fertile in grain, fruit, and hay; supplying sufficient for the consumption of the inhabitants; but as the mountaineers of the little cantons come to their market for corn, the people of Lucerne purchase this commodity from other parts of Switzerland, but especially from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALSACE">Alsace</a> and Swabia. Lucerne. Suabia. Their manufactures are very inconsiderable; consisting only in a little silk and cotton thread.—The government is oligarchical. The councils are chosen from among 500 citizens only. The great council of 64 members is the nominal sovereign; but in fact the power resides in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, or little council of 36, having for their chiefs the two avoyers.—The whole <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTON">canton</a> professes the Roman Catholic <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. The pope's nuncio, with the title of legate à latere, usually resides at Lucerne.—They threw off the Austrian yoke in 1352, and by entering into a perpetual <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with the three ancient cantons, they gave such <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> to the confederacy, as to enable it in 1386 to resist all the efforts of the enemy at the bloody <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Sempach. The town of Lucerne is situated at the extremity of a most beautiful lake of the same name, where the river Reuss issues from it. The buildings are ancient, and the streets narrow; nor is Lucerne populous in proportion to its <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, the inhabitants being only between 3000 and 4000. Since this is the great passage to Italy by Mount St Gothard, and the merchandise which passes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a> on mules, and is to be transported by the rivers Reuss, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AAR">Aar</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, is all deposited here, it might have a flourishing trade if arts and manufactures were attended to. The Reuss separates the town into two unequal parts, which are connected by three bridges: one wide for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a>; and two narrow covered ones for foot passengers: besides these, there is a fourth over an arm of the lake, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> to the cathedral. Three of these bridges have old bad paintings of the Dance of Death, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>, and of Switzerland. They make a commodious dry walk for the inhabitants.—Of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> edifices, the principal are the cathedral, or collegiate <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of St Leger; the convent of Cordeliers; the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of the Jesuits; the convent of Capuchins; and two <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a> of nuns. Of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> buildings, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOTEL">hotel</a> de ville is the principal. The arsenal is well furnished. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> tower is remarkable only for its position and antiquity; it is said to have been a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHAROS">pharos</a> or <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LIGHTHOUSE">lighthouse</a>. What greatly attracts the notice of most strangers is, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> in relief of part of the cantons of Lucerne, Zug, and Berne, and the whole of Schweitz, Uri, and Unterwald, executed by General Pfister on a large <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>. He has completed about 60 <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> leagues; the plan is 12 feet long, and nine and a half broad: every mountain is accurately measured; and every object distinctly placed. The lake of Lucerne exhibits greater variety and more picturesque scenery than any other of the Swiss <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>. It is <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> leagues long in a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> line, and three wide about Kussnacht; but the shape is very irregular. The whole south side is bordered by high <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>; but the north exhibits hills of no great height. The narrow <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> that extends towards the west, is bordered on the west and north-west by Mount Pilat, which is a single mountain rising boldly more than 6000 feet above the lake; and on the south by Mount Burgenberg. Stanz Stadt, belonging to the canton of Unterwald, is on this side; and at this place the lake is deepest. Kussnacht is on the point of the other gulf, which extends towards the east, and is wider than the former. All the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> to the west of these gulfs, and part of it to the north of the latter, belongs to the canton of Lucerne; but that which is to the south and north-east is dependent on the canton of Zug. All the mountains on the left shore of the lake belong to the canton of Unterwald; those on the right, partly to the canton of Uri, partly to that of Schweitz, partly to the little republic of Gersaw, but principally to the canton of Lucerne. Lucerne, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>. See Medicago, Botany Index.—For the culture of this plant, see <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a> Index. Lucia, St, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARIBBEE_ISLANDS">Caribbee <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in the West Indies, about 22 miles long, and 11 broad, the middle of it lying in N. Lat. 39. 14. W. Long. 27. 0. It was first settled by the French in 1650; but was reduced by the English in 1664, who evacuated it in 1666. The French immediately resettled the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, but were again driven away by the Caribs. As soon as the savages were gone, the former inhabitants returned, but only for a short time; for being afraid of falling a prey to the first privateer that should visit their coasts, they removed either to other French settlements that were stronger, or which they might expect to be better defended. There was then no regular culture or colony at St Lucia; it was only frequented by the inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARTINICO">Martinico</a>, who came thither to cut wood, and to build canoes, and who had considerable docks on the island. In 1718 it was again settled by the French; but four years after, it was given by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of London to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Montague, who was sent to take possession of it. This occasioned some disturbance between the two courts; which was settled, however, by an agreement made in 1731, that, till the respective claims should be finally adjusted, the island should be evacuated by both nations, but that both should wood and water there. This precarious agreement furnished an opportunity for private <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> to exert itself. The English no longer molested the French in their habitations; but employed them as their assistants in carrying on with richer colonies a smuggling trade, which the subjects of both governments thought equally advantageous to them. This trade has been more or less considerable till the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of 1763, when the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of St Lucia was secured to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of France. After that time the colony flourished considerably. In the beginning of the year 1772, the number of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> people amounted to 2018 souls, men, women, and children; that of the blacks to 663 free men, and 12,795 slaves. The cattle consisted of 928 mules or horses, 2070 head of horned cattle, and 3184 sheep or goats. There were 38 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> plantations, which occupied 978 pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>; 5,195,889 coffee-trees; 1,321,600 cocoa <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; and 367 plots of cotton. There were 706 dwelling places. The annual revenue at that time was about 175,000l. which, according to the Abbé Raynal, must have increased one-eighth yearly for some time. It was taken by the British in 1778; restored to France in 1783. It fell again into the hands of the British in 1794, was evacuated in 1795, and was again retaken in 1796. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> of St Lucia is tolerably good, even at the sea side; and is much better the farther one advances into the country. The whole of it is capable of cultivation, except some high and eraggy mountains which bear bear evident marks of old volcanoes. In one deep valley there are still eight or ten ponds, the water of which boils up in a dreadful manner, and retains some of its <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> at the distance of 6000 toises from its reservoirs. The air in the inland parts, like that of all other uninhabited countries, is foul and unwholesome; but grows less noxious as the woods are cleared and the ground laid open. On some parts of the sea coast, the air is still more unhealthy, on account of some small rivers which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> from the foot of the mountains, and have not sufficient slope to wash down the sands with which the influx of the ocean stops up their mouths, by which means they spread themselves into unwholesome marshes on the neighbouring grounds. St Lucia was restored to France in 1815.

LUCIA

Pages 273-273

St., a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and mountainous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, and one of those of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Verde, is about <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> leagues <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and lies in the latitude of 16° 18' N. according to the English geographers; but according to all others, it is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> farther to the northward. On the east-south-east side is a harbour, with a bottom and shore of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> sand; but its best <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> is opposite to St Vincent's to the south-west, where there are at least 20 fathoms of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. On the west side there is no water: it abounds with goats, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> fowl, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TORTOISES">tortoises</a>, &c. but whether it hath any inhabitants is not certainly known.

LUCIAN

Pages 273-273

a celebrated Greek author in the first century, was born at Samosata, of obscure parents, in the reign of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Trajan. He studied <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and practised some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> as an advocate; but growing weary of the wrangling oratory of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a>, he commenced rhetorician. He lived to the time of Marcus Aurelius, who made him <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>; and, according to Suidas, he was at last worried by dogs. Lucian was one of the finest wits in all antiquity. His Dialogues, and other works, are written in Greek. In these he has joined the useful to the agreeable, instruction to satire, and erudition to elegance; and we everywhere meet with that fine and delicate raillery which characterizes the Attic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>.—Those who censure him as an impious soffer at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, have reason on their side, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> religion consisted in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a> of the Pagan poets, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in the extravagant opinions of philosophers; for he perpetually throws such <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a> on the gods and philosophers, with their vices, as inspires hatred and contempt for them; but it cannot be said that he writes anywhere against an overruling <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">providence</a>.

LUCIANISTS

Pages 273-273
or Lucanists, a religious sect, so called from Lucianus, or Lucanus, a heretic of the second century, being a disciple of Marcion, whose errors he followed, adding some new ones to them. Epiphanius says he abandoned Marcion; teaching that people ought not to marry, for fear of envieing the Creator: and yet other authors mention that he held this error in common with Marcion and other Gnostics. He denied the immortality of the soul; asserting it to be material. There was another sect of Lucianists, who appeared some time after the Arians. They taught, that the Father had been a father always, and that he had the name even before he begot the Son; as having in him the power or faculty of generation; and in this manner they accounted for the eternity of the Son.

LUCID INTERVALS

Pages 273-273

the fits of lunatics <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> maniacs, during which the phrenzy leaves them in possession of their reason.

LUCIFER

Pages 273-273

according to the poets, was the son of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AURORA">Aurora</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, Lucifer is the bright planet Venus, which either goes before the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> in the morning, for 290 days, and is our morning <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAR">star</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in the evening follows the sun, during the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and then is called Hesperus or the evening star.

LUCIFERA

Pages 273-273

in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">Mythology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> given to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a>, under which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> she was invoked by the Greeks in childhood. She was represented as covered with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> veil, interspersed with stars, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRESCENT">crescent</a> on her head, and holding in her <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> a lighted <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAMBEAU">flambeau</a>.

LUCIFERIANS

Pages 273-273

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a>, who adhered to the schism of Lucifer, bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAGLIARI">Cagliari</a>, in the fourth century, who was banished by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Constantius, for having defended the Nicene doctrine concerning the three Persons in the Godhead.—St Augustine seems to intimate, that they believed the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, which they considered as of a carnal <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, to be transmitted to the children from their fathers. Theodoret says, that Lucifer was the author of a new <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a>. The Luciferians increased mightily in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, &c. The occasion of the schism was, that Lucifer would not allow any acts he had done to be abolished. There were but two Luciferian <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, but a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of priests and deacons. The Luciferians bore a peculiar aversion to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARIANS">Arians</a>.

LUCILIUS

Pages 273-273
CAIUS, a Roman knight, and a Latin poet, was born at Suessa in Italy, about 140 B.C. he served under Scipio Africanus in the war with the Numantines; and was in great favour with that celebrated general, and with Lælius. He wrote 30 books of satires, in which he lashed several persons of quality very sharply. Some learned men ascribe the invention of satire to him; but M. Dacier has maintained, with great probability, that Lucilius only gave a better turn to that kind of poetry, and wrote it with more wit and humour than his predecessors Ennius and Pacuvius had done. His fragments have been carefully collected by Francis Douza at Leyden in 1599, with notes. But they require still to be better illustrated by some learned critic.

LUCINA

Pages 273-273

a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, who presided over women in labour. Some take her to be <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a>, others Juno. She was called Lucina, because she brought children to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>; from the Latin word lux, "light."

LUCIUS

Pages 273-273

the specific name of the pike. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESOX">Esox</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. LUCONIA. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANILLA">Manilla</a>.

LUCRETIA

Pages 273-273

the famous Roman matron, wife of Collatinus, and the cause of the revolution in Rome from a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a> to a republic: this lady being ravished by Sextus, the eldest son of Tarquin <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Rome, stabbed herself, 509 B.C. See the article Chastity. The bloody poniard, with her dead body exposed to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, was the signal of Roman <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>; the expulsion of the Tarquins, and abolition of the regal <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, was instantly resolved on, and carried into execution. See Rome.

LUCRETIUS

Pages 273-274
or Titus Lucretius, Caius, one Lucius of the most celebrated of the Latin poets, was born of an ancient and noble Roman family, and studied at Athens, where he became one of Epicurus's sect. He acquired great reputation by his learning and eloquence; but in the flower of his age fell into a frenzy, occasioned by a philtre given him by his wife, who was distractedly fond of him. Lucretius, during the intervals of his madness, put Epicurus's doctrines into verse, and composed his six books *De Rerum Natura*, which are still extant. It is said that he killed himself in a fit of madness, in the 54th year before the Christian era, when 51 years old. The most correct edition of Lucretius is that of Simon de Coline. The cardinal de Polignac has refuted Lucretius's arguments, in his excellent Latin poem entitled *Anti-Lucretius*. His poem *De Rerum Natura* has been translated into English by Mr Creech.

LUCRINUS LACUS

Pages 274-274

in *<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>*, a lake of Campania, between Baiae and Puteoli, famous for its oysters (Horace, Martial, Juvenal); *Lucrinenses* (Cicero), the people dwelling on it. Now a perfect <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> since the earthquake in 1538.

LUCULLUS

Pages 274-274

Lucius Lucinius, a Roman general celebrated for his eloquence, his victories, and his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>. In his youth he made a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a>; and being afterwards made quaestor in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, and praetor in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, governed those provinces with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> moderation and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>.
