Scarce was he known as a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, when he twice <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> the fleet of Hamilcar, and gained two great victories over him. His happy genius was greatly improved by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>; for he employed his leisure in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> the best authors on military affairs. Being made <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> with Aurelius Cotta, during the third <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MITHRIDATES">Mithridates</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Pontus, he was sent against this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>: and this expedition was attended with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of victories, which did him less <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> than an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of generosity towards his colleague; who, willing to take advantage of his absence to signalize himself by some great exploit, hastened to fight Mithridates; but was defeated and shut up in Chalcedonia; where he must have perished, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> Lucullus, sacrificing his resentment to the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> of saving a Roman citizen, had not flown to his assistance, and disengaged him. All Pontus then submitted to Lucullus; who being <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of Asia, entered the territories of Tigranes, the most powerful king in Asia. That prince marched with a formidable <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> against Lucullus: who defeated him with a handful of men, and killed great numbers of his forces; took Tigranocertes, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>; and was ready to put an end to the war, when the intrigues of a tribune got him deposed, and Pompey nominated in his room. Lucullus having brought home prodigious riches, now gave himself up to excessive <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a>; and his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> was served with a profusion till that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> unknown. He brought from the East a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of books, which he formed into a library, and gave admittance to all men of learning, who frequented it in great numbers. Toward the end of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, he fell into a kind of madness: and Lucullus, his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, was appointed his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a>. He is said to have been the first who brought cherries into <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, having brought the grafts from the kingdom of Pontus.

LUCUS

Pages 274-274

in general, denotes a wood <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROVE">grove</a> sacred to a deity; so called *à lucendo*, because a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of lights were usually <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the god (Isidorus); a practice <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> with idolaters, as we learn from Scripture: hence <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>'s *αὐλήνας*.

LUDAMAR

Pages 274-274

a Moorish <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> in the interior <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of which is situated in N. Lat. 15°. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 60°. which Mr <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARK">Park</a> considers as little superior to a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>. The Moors of Ludamar subsist chiefly on the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> of their cattle. The barrenness of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is such, that it furnishes few materials for manufacture: but the inhabitants contrive to weave a strong cloth, with which their tents are covered; the thread is spun by the women from goats <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, and with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIDES">hides</a> of their cattle they furnish saddles, bridles, pouches, and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>. They can also convert the native <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> procured from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a> into spears, knives, and pots for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> their food; but they purchase their fire-arms and other weapons of a similar <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> from the Europeans, in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> for slaves. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> perfection are truly singular, since a woman, to have the smallest pretensions to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, must be one who requires a slave under each arm to support her as she walks; and a perfect beauty, according to Mr Park, is a load for a camel. The wealth of the Moors chiefly consists in their numerous herds of cattle, yet the majority of the people spend their days in a state of idleness. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENT">tent</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of rendezvous for the indolent, where they appear to enjoy an unlimited <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of speech; yet in the praise of their sovereign they are wholly unanimous, singing songs to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, which never fail to be filled with the grossest adulation. The king sometimes eats out of the same basin with the driver of his camels, and during the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> reposes himself upon the same <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>. Cavalry constitute the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> strength of Ludamar, which are well mounted, and are very expert in attacking by surprise. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> of every soldier is furnished by himself, as also his military implements, consisting of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> sabre, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a>-barrelled <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUN">gun</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> leather bag for holding his balls, and a powder-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">horn</a> slung over his shoulder. He has no pay, and his only compensation arises from plunder. They have no intercourse with civilized nations, yet they boast an advantage over the negroes, as they possess, though in a very limited <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, the knowledge of letters. They are esteemed the vainest, proudest, and most bigotted, ferocious, and intolerant of all the nations of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, blending in their character the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> of the negro with the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> cruelty and treachery of the Arab. It was with the utmost difficulty that Mr Park made his escape from this cruel and inhospitable people.

LUDLOW

Pages 274-275

Edmund, son of Sir Henry Ludlow, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAIDENHEAD">Maidenhead</a>, and educated in Trinity <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. His father opposing the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, Mr Ludlow joined with the same party, and was present at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Edgehill as a volunteer under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>. Upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his father, he was chosen <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> of the shire for Wilts, and obtained the command of a regiment of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. He was one of King <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I.'s judges; after whose death he was sent by the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>-general of the horse; which employment he discharged with diligence and success till the death of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a> Ireton, when he acted for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> as general, though without that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>; Cromwell, who knew him to be sincerely in the interest of the commonwealth, always finding out some <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRETEXT">pretext</a> to hinder the conferring of that character upon him. The last stroke had been given by Ludlow to the Irish rebellion, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the usurpation of Cromwell had not prevented it. Under his power he never acted; and though Cromwell used his utmost efforts, he remained inflexible. After Cromwell's death, he endeavoured to restore the commonwealth; but Charles II. being recalled, he thought proper to conceal himself, and escaped into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, where he settled. After the Revolution, he came over into England, in order to be employed in Ireland against King James: but appearing publicly in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, it gave <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> offence; and an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> was presented by Sir Edward Seymour to King William III. for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a> in order to apprehend <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLONEL">Colonel</a> Ludlow, attainted for the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> of King Charles I. Upon this he returned to Switzerland, where he died. During his retirement in Switzerland he wrote his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a>. Ludlow, a town of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHROPSHIRE">Shropshire</a> in England, situated at the conflux of the Teme and Corve, 18 miles from Shrewsbury, and 139 from London. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of the marches, established by Henry VIII., generally kept his courts in it, by which the town was much benefitted, these courts not having been abolished till the 1st of William and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>. Its neighbourhood to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a> makes it a great thoroughfare, and engages many of the Welsh to send their children of both sexes to it for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>. It was incorporated by Edward IV. and among other privileges has that of trying and executing criminals within itself. It is one of the neatest <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> in England, with walls and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> gates. It is divided into four wards; and is governed by 2 bailiffs, 12 aldermen, 25 <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a>-council men, a recorder, a town-clerk, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a>, chamberlain, coroner, &c. From the castle on the top of the hill on which the town stands is a most delightful prospect. In an apartment of the outer gatehouse Samuel <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTLER">Butler</a> is said to have written the first <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Hudibras. Of this castle, which was besieged and taken by King Stephen, some of the offices are fallen <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and great part of it turned into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOWLING">bowling</a>-green; but part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> apartments and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> of state are still left. The walls were at first a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> in compass, and there was a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAWN">lawn</a> before it for near two miles, of which much is now enclosed. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BATTLEMENTS">battlements</a> are very <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and thick, and adorned with towers. It has a neat chapel, where are the coats of arms of abundance of Welsh gentry, and over the stable-doors are the arms of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, the earls of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEMBROKE">Pembroke</a>, &c. This castle was a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of Wales, in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of his principality. The river Teme has a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> over it, several weirs across it, and turns a great many <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>. Here is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> parochial <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, which was formerly collegiate; in the choir whereof is an inscription relating to Prince <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTHUR">Arthur</a>, elder <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> to King Henry VIII. who died here, and whose bowels were here deposited, though it is said his heart was taken up some time ago in a leaden box. In this choir is a closet, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called God's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">House</a>, where the priests used to keep their consecrated utensils; and in the market-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is a conduit, with a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> on it, and a niche wherein is the image of St Laurence, to whom the church was dedicated. On the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side of the town there was a rich priory, whereof there are few ruins to be seen except those of its church. Here are an alms-house for 30 <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> people, and two <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> where 50 boys and 30 girls are both taught and clothed. It has a market on Monday, and three lesser ones on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> are on the Tuesday Easter, Whit-Wednesday, August 21. Sept. 28. and Dec. 8. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">Provisions</a> are very cheap here; and at the annual horse races there is the best of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>. The country round is exceedingly pleasant, fruitful, and populous, especially that part called the Corvedale. Ludlow sends two members to parliament, and contained 4150 inhabitants in 1811.

LUDOLPH

Pages 275-276
Job, a very learned writer of the 17th century, was born at Erfurt in Thuringia. He travelled much, and was master of 26 languages, visited libraries, searched after natural curiosities and antiquities everywhere, and conversed with learned men of all nations. He published a History of Ethiopia, and other curious books. Ludolph, Henry William, nephew of Job above mentioned, was born at Erfurt in 1655. He came over to England as secretary to M. Lenthe, envoy from the court of Copenhagen to that of London; and being recommended to Prince George of Denmark, was received as his secretary. He enjoyed this office for some years, until he was incapacitated by a violent disorder; when he was discharged with a handsome pension: after he recovered, he travelled into Muscovy, where he was well received by the czar, and where his knowledge made the Muscovite priests suppose him to be a conjurer. On his return to London in 1694, he was cut for the stone; and as soon as his health would permit, in acknowledgment of the civilities he had received in Muscovy, he wrote a grammar of their language, that the natives might learn their own tongue in a regular method. He then travelled into the East, to inform himself of the state of the Christian church. LUG Ludolph in the Levant; the deplorable condition of which induced him, after his return, with the aid of the bishop of Worcester, to print an edition of the New Testament in the vulgar Greek, to present to the Greek church. In 1709, when such numbers of Palatines came over to England, Mr Ludolph was appointed by Queen Anne one of the commissioners to manage the charities raised for them; and he died early the following year. His collected works were published in 1712.

LUDWIGIA

Pages 276-276

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the tetrandria class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 17th order, Calycanthaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

LUFF

Pages 276-276

the order from the pilot to the steersman to put the helm towards the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEE">lee</a>-side of the ship, in order to make the ship sail nearer the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>. Hence, luff round, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> luff a-lee, is the excess of this movement, by which it is intended to throw the ship's head up in the wind, in order to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TACK">tack</a> her, &c. A ship is accordingly said to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> her luff when she yields to the effort of the helm, by sailing nearer to the line of the wind than she had done before. See also Hauling the Wind. LUFF-Tackle, a name given by sailors to any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> tackle that is not destined for a particular <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, but may be variously employed as occasion requires. It is generally somewhat larger than the jigger tackle, although smaller than those which serve to hoist the heavier materials into and out of the vessel, which latter are the main and fore tackles, the stay and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> tackles, &c.

LUG-SAIL

Pages 276-276

a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SQUARE_SAIL"><a class="x</a>ref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> sail, hoisted occasionally on the mast of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> small vessel upon a yard which hangs nearly at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> with the mast. These are more particularly used in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARCA">barca</a> longas, navigated by the Spaniards in the Mediterranean.

LUGDUNUM

Pages 276-276

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the Segusiani in Gallia Celtica, situated at the confluence of the Arar and Rhodanus, on an eminence, as the Celtic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> dune signifies; built by Manutius Plancus under Augustus, while commanding in that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>; and whither he led a colony. Now Lyons, capital of the Lyonnais.

LUGDUNUM CONVERARUM

Pages 276-276

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a> in Aquitain, at the foot of the Pyrenees. Now S. Bertrand, in Gascony.

LUGDUNUSI BAVATORORUM

Pages 276-276

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of the Batavi in Gallia <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELGICA">Belgica</a>. Now <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>.

LUGEUS LACUS

Pages 276-276

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a lake of Japydia, the westmost district of Illyricum, to the south of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">Save</a>, and near the head of the Arsia. Now <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called the Zirichnitz Lake, from a small adjoining town. It is locked on every side with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>; from which scanty currents run <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>; the less in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> their waters, because drank up by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; till at length they are swallowed up in rocky furrows, so formed as to resemble <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a>. In these the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> being so redundant as to refuse receiving any more, they regurgitate, and return the water with extraordinary celerity, which thus spreading itself, forms a lake, in most places 18 cubits deep. These waters afterwards retire with no less celerity than they came on, not only through the furrows, but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through the whole of the bottom, as through a sieve; which when perceived by the inhabitants, they directly stop up the larger apertures, and thus take <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantities of fish: when the lake is dry, they cut down their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a> on the spot where they sowed, and sow again before the inundation comes on: and grass shoots so quick on it, that it may be cut down in three weeks <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, (Lazius, Werulcrus.)

LUGGERSHALL

Pages 276-276

a borough of Wiltshire, 12 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALISBURY">Salisbury</a>, and 75 north by west of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It is an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> borough by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESCRIPTION">prescription</a>, though but a small <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAMLET">hamlet</a>, near the forest of Chute, in a delightful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and was the residence of several kings. It had formerly a castle. It is governed by a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAILIFF">bailiff</a> chosen yearly at the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANOR">manor</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>-leet. On the neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWNS">downs</a> there used to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-races. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">Population</a> in 1811, 487.

LUKE

Pages 276-276

St, the evangelist, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of the apostles, was originally of Antioch in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, and by profession a physician. He particularly attached himself to St Paul, and was his faithful <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> in his travels and labours. He went with him to Troas in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a> about the year 51. He wrote his gospel in Achaea about the year 53; and, ten years after, the acts of the Apostles, which contains a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of 30 years. Of all the inspired writers of the New <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, his works are written in the most elegant Greek. It is believed that St Luke died at Rome, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in Achaea. Gospel of St Luke, a canonical book of the New Testament. Some think that it was properly St Paul's Gospel; and that, when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a> speaks of his Gospel, he means what is called St Luke's. Irenæus says, that St Luke digested into <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> what St Paul preached to the Gentiles; and Gregory Nazianzen tells us, that St Luke wrote with the assistance of St Paul. St Luke the Evangelist's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">Day</a>, a festival in the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, observed on the 18th of October.

LULLY

Pages 276-277

RAYMOND, a writer on <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALCHEMY">alchemy</a>, surnamed the Enlightened <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a>, was born in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MAJORCA">Majorca</a> in 1225. He applied himself with indefatigable labour to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the Arabian <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>, physic, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>; and acquired <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation by his works. He at length went to preach the gospel in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>; and was stoned to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MAURITANIA">Mauritania</a>, at the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 80. He is honoured as a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARTYR">martyr</a> at Majorca, whither his body was carried. He wrote many treatises on all the sciences, in which he shows much study and subtlety, but little judgment <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> solidity. A complete edition of his works has been printed at <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENTZ">Mentz</a>.—He ought not to be confounded with Raymond Lully of Terraca, surnamed Neophyte, who from being a Jew turned Dominican friar. This last Lully maintained several opinions that were condemned by Pope Gregory XI.

LUMBAGO

Pages 277-277

a fixed pain in the small of the back. See MEDICINE <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

LUMBARIS

Pages 277-277

a name given to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTERIES">arteries</a> and veins which spread over the loins.

LUMBRICAL

Pages 277-277

a name given to four muscles of the fingers and to as many of the toes.

LUMBRICUS

Pages 277-277

the Worm, a genus of animals belonging to the order of vermes intestina. See <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELMINTHOLOGY">HELMINTHOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

LUMELLO

Pages 277-277

a village in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, which gives name to the Lumellin, a small district in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, lying along the river Po, and of which Mortaria and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VALENCIA">Valencia</a> are the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> places. It was ceded to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Savoy in 1707, and confirmed by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a> in 1713. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8. 42. N. Lat. 45. 5.

LUMINOUS

Pages 277-277

an epithet applied to any thing that shines <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> emits <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. LUMINOUS Emanations have been observed from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> bodies, as also from those of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUTES">brutes</a>. The light arising from currying a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, or from rubbing a cat's back, are known to most. Instances of a like kind have been known on combing a woman's head. Bartholin gives us an account, which he entitles nudus splendens, of a lady in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> whose body would shine whenever slightly touched with a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>. These effluvia of animal bodies have many properties in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> with those produced from glass; such as their being lucid, their snapping, and their not being excited without some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of friction; and are undoubtedly electrical, as a cat's back has been found strongly electrical when stroked. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTRICITY">ELECTRICITY</a> and LIGHT. LUMINOUSNESS OF THE <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">SEA</a>. See LIGHT and Sea. LUMINOUSNESS of Putrescent Substances. See LIGHT. LUMP-FISH. See CYCLOPTERUS, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

LUNA

Pages 277-277

a town and port of Liguria, at the mouth of the Macra. The town was but small, but the port <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and beautiful, according to Strabo. Now extinct, and its ruins called Luna Distruuta. It was famous for its quarries of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> marble, thence called Lunense; and for its cheese, remarkable rather for its size than goodness, each being a thousand <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>.

LUNA CORNEA

Pages 277-277

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> of muriatic acid with silver. See SILVER, MURIATE OF, Chemistry <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

LUNACY

Pages 277-277

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>. See IDIOCY and LUNATIC. LUNÆ MONS, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a promontory of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUSITANIA">Lusitania</a>. Now Rock of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 10. N. Lat. 38. 50.—Another <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUNA">Luna</a> Mons of Ethiopia, from which the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a> was supposed to take its rise. LUNÆ Portus, a very extensive port, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> more truly a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, of Liguria, between Portus Veneris and Portus Ericis, 20 miles in compass. Now il Golfo della Spezia, on the east <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>.

LUNAR

Pages 277-277

something relating to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">Moon</a>. LUNAR <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">Month</a>. See MONTH. LUNAR Year, consists of 354 days, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 12 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNODICAL">synodical</a> months. See YEAR. LUNAR <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIAL">Dial</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIALLING">DIALLING</a>.

LUNARE OS

Pages 277-277

in Anatomy, is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> bone in the first row of the carpus. It has its name from the Latin, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUNA">luna</a>, "the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>," because one of its sides is in form of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRESCENT">crescent</a>.

LUNARIA

Pages 277-277

Satin-flower, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Moonwort; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the tetradyamia class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 39th order, Siligoseae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

LUNARIUM

Pages 277-277

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a promontory of the Hither <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, between Blanda and Bactulo. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">Commonly</a> called el Cabo de Palafigel, in Catalonia, on the Mediterranean; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Cabo de Tosa, on the same <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, and in Catalonia, 15 miles from the former, to the west.

LUNATIC

Pages 277-278

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>. Under the general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of non compos mentis (which Sir Edward <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COKE">Coke</a> says is the most legal name), are comprised not only lunatics, but persons under frenzies, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> who lose their intellects by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>; those that grow deaf, dumb, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLIND">blind</a>, not being born so; or such, in short, as are judged by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a> incapable of conducting their own affairs. To these also, as well as idiots, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a>, but to a very different purpose. For the law always imagines, that these accidental misfortunes may be removed; and therefore only constitutes the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> a trustee for the unfortunate persons, to protect their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, and to account to them for all profits received, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they recover, or after their decease to their representatives. LUNATIC representatives. And therefore it is declared by the statute 17 Edw. II. c. 10. that the king shall provide for the custody and sustentation of lunatics, and preserve their lands, and the profits of them, for their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> when they come to their <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> mind; and the king shall take nothing to his own use: and if the parties die in such estate, the residue shall be distributed for their souls by the advice of the ordinary, and of course (by the subsequent amendments of the laws of administrations) shall now go to their executors or administrators. On the first attack of lunacy, or other occasional insanity, when there may be hopes of a speedy restitution of reason, it is usual to confine the unhappy objects in private custody under the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of their nearest friends and relations; and the legislature, to prevent all abuses incident to such private custody, hath thought proper to interpose its authority, by 14 Geo. III. c. 49. for regulating private mad-houses. But when the disorder is grown permanent, and the circumstances of the party <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> bear such additional expence, it is thought proper to apply to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> authority to warrant a lasting confinement. The method of proving a person non compos is very similar to that of proving him an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IDIOT">idiot</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>, to whom, by special authority from the king, the custody of idiots and lunatics is intrusted, upon petition or information, grants a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the writ de idiota inquirendo, to inquire into the party's state of mind; and if he be found non compos, he usually commits the care of his person, with a suitable allowance for his maintenance, to some friend, who is then called his committee. However, to prevent sinister practices, the next heir is seldom permitted to be of this committee of the person; because it is his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> that the party should die. But it hath been said, there lies not the same objection against his next of kin, provided he be not his heir; for it is his interest to preserve the lunatic's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, in order to increase the personal estate by savings, which he or his family may hereafter be entitled to enjoy. The heir is generally made the manager or committee of the estate, it being clearly his interest by good management to keep it in condition: accountable, however, to the court of chancery, and to the non compos himself, if he recovers; or otherwise, to his administrators. See IDIOCY.

LUNATION

Pages 278-278

the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> space of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> between one new <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a> and another; also called <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNODICAL">synodical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a>. See CYCLE and EPACT.

LUNDEN

Pages 278-278
or LUND, a considerable town of Sweden, in Gothland; and capital of the territory of Schonen, with an archbishop's see and an university. It was added to the Swedes by the Danes in 1658. E. Long. 13. 25. N. Lat. 55. 40.

LUNDY ISLAND

Pages 278-278

situated 50 miles in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, off the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, is five miles <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, but so encompassed with inaccessible rocks, that it has but one entrance to it, so narrow that two men can scarcely go abreast. It is reckoned in the hundred of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRANDON">Brandon</a>. It had once both a fort and a chapel. The south <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of it is indifferent good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, but the north part of it is barren, and has a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> pyramidal rock called the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTABLE">Constable</a>. Here are horses, kine, hogs, and goats, with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> store of sheep and rabbits; but the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> commodity is fowl, with which it abounds much, their eggs being very thick on the ground at their season of breeding. No venomous creature <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> live in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. In the reign of Henry VIII. one William Morisco, who had conspired to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> him at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOODSTOCK">Woodstock</a>, fled to this island, which he fortified, turned <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIRATE">pirate</a>, and did much damage to this coast; but was taken by surprise at length, with 16 of his accomplices, and put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>.

LUNEBURG

Pages 278-278

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the principality of the same name, is a pretty <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> town of Germany, on the river Elmen, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the Ilmenau, which is navigable from the town to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELBE">Elbe</a>, at the distance of 13 miles. It is 27 miles from Hamburgh, 43 from Zell, 65 from Brunswic.

LUNENBURG

Pages 278-279

Brunswic, 76 from Bremen, 68 from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HANOVER">Hanover</a>; and stands in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 10° 40' N. Lat. 53° 28'. Its inhabitants are reckoned at between 8000 and 9000. Formerly this was one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANSE">Hanse</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, and an imperial <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. Some derive its name from Lina, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> name of the Ilmenau; others from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUNA">Luna</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, an image of which is said to have been worshipped by the inhabitants in the times of Paganism. Here were anciently several <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>, viz. one of Minims, another of Premontretratians, another of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENEDICTINES">Benedictines</a>, and a fourth of Minorites. Out of the revenues of the Benedictine <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> was founded an academy for the martial exercises, where young gentlemen of the principality of Lunenburg are maintained gratis, and taught French, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FENCING">fencing</a>, riding, and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a>; but foreigners are educated at a certain fixed price. A Latin school was also founded, consisting of four classes, and well endowed out of these revenues. The superintendency and management of these, and the estates appropriated to their maintenance, belongs to the landschaft <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a>, and the ausreiter, who are both chosen from among the Lunenburg <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>. The first came in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the Popish <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a>, and as such is head of the states of the principality, and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>. He has the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of excellency; and in public instruments styles himself, by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> of God landschaft director and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of the mansion of St Michael in Lunenburg. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> public edifices are three <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>-churches, the ducal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, three <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>, the town-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGAZINE">magazine</a>, the anatomical <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, the academy; the conventual <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of St Michael, in which <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> interred the ancient dukes, and in which is the famous <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> eight feet long, and four wide, plated over with chased <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, with a rim embellished with precious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, of an immense value, which was taken from the Saracens by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Otho, and presented to this church: but in 1698, a gang of thieves stripped it of 200 rubies and emeralds, together with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIAMOND">diamond</a>, and most of the gold, so that at present but a small <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of it remains. Here are some very rich salt <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>. Formerly, when there was a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> demand for the salt, upwards of 120,000 tons have been annually boiled here, and sold off; but since the commencement of the present century, the salt trade hath declined greatly. A fifth of the salt made here belongs to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, but is farmed out. It is said to excel all the other salt made in Germany. This town is well fortified; and has a garrison, which is lodged in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARRACKS">barracks</a>. In the neighbourhood is a good <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">limestone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARRY">quarry</a>; and along the Ilmenau are warehouses, in which are lodged goods brought from all parts of Germany, to be forwarded by the Ilmenau to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAMBURG">Hamburg</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> by the Asche to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUBECK">Lubeck</a>, from whence other goods are brought back the same way. The town itself carries on a considerable traffic in wax, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, salt, lime, and beer.

LUNENSE MARMOR

Pages 279-279

in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, the name of that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> marble now known among us by the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRARA">Carrara</a> marble, and distinguished from the statuary kind by its greater <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a> and less splendour. It was ever greatly esteemed in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> and ornamental works, and is so still. It is of a very <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> and fine texture, of a very pure white, and much more transparent than any other of the white marbles. It has always been found in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> quantities in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and is so to this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. See Marmor.

LUNETTE

Pages 279-279

in the manege, is a half <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHOE">shoe</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> such a shoe as wants the sponge, i.e. that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the branch which runs towards the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of the foot. LUNETTE is also the name of two small pieces of felt, made round and hollow, to clap upon the eyes of a vicious horse that is apt to bite, and strike with his fore feet, or that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not suffer his rider to mount him.

LUNGS

Pages 279-280

in Anatomy, a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body, serving for respiration. See Anatomy, No. 117. In the Journal de Médecine for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1789, is a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">Instrument</a> for Inflating the Lungs, invented by Mr. Gorcy, physician to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> at Neufbrisack, which appears to be extremely well adapted to the purpose, whilst it may be used with the greatest ease and facility. This instrument, which the inventor styles apodopic, that is, "restorer of respiration," consists of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of bellows, BCLM, fig. 1, the two different parts of which have no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with each other. In the lower side BM, is an aperture A for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VALVE">valve</a> constructed on the principles of those of Mr. Nairne's <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUMP">pump</a>. It consists of a rim of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, closed at one end by a plate of the same metal, in which plate are <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> small holes placed at equal distances. This plate is covered with pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> coated with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUM">gum</a>, in which are six transverse incisions of two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> in length. Each incision is so made as to be situated between two of the holes, and at an equal distance from each: see D, fig. 2. The silk must be made very secure by a thread passing several times round the rim. It is obvious, that a stream of air applied to that side of the plate which is opposite the silk, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through the holes, and lifting up the silk, escape through the incisions. On the contrary, a stream of air applied to the other side will press the silk upon the plate, and thus <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> the holes, so that it will be impossible for it to pass through them. This valve opens internally, so as to admit the air from without. At B is another valve, on the same <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>, but opening in a contrary <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, thus permitting the air to escape out of the lower part into the tube EF; but preventing its entrance. At C is another valve, opening internally to admit the air from the tube EF; and at D there is a fourth, opening externally to discharge the air from the upper part. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a> tube EF, screwed on at the end CB, being introduced into one of the nostrils, whilst the mouth and the other nostril are closed by an assistant, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we separate the two handles LM, which were close together at the introduction of the tube, it is evident, that the air in the lungs will rush into the upper part through the valve C, whilst the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> air will fill the lower part through the valve A: the two handles being... being again brought into contact, the atmospheric air will be forced into the lungs through the valve B, and at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the air in the upper part will be discharged at the valve D. Thus by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a> play of the double bellows, the lungs will be alternately filled and emptied as in respiration. In using the instrument care should be taken not to be too violent; as the more perfectly the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of respiration is imitated, the better. To prevent any substances from without injuring the valves <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">AD</a>, fig. 1, the rim is made with a screw, B, fig. 3, in order to receive a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AA">AA</a>, fig. 3, full of small holes. This screw has also another <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. If air or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXYGEN">oxygen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAS">gas</a> be preferred, a bladder filled with it, fig. 4, may, by means of the screw A, be fastened to the valve A, fig. 1; and, to prevent waste, as this air may serve several times, a flexible tube may be screwed on the valve D, fig. 1, communicating with the bladder by means of the opening d, fig. 4; thus it may be employed as often as the operator thinks proper. There is a handle K to the partition in the middle, in order that, if it be at any time necessary to use either of the divisions alone, the other may be confined from acting. c, b, fig. 5, represent the two valves to be applied at the end of the instrument C, B, fig. 1; and fig. 6, is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECTION">section</a> of the end CB, showing the valves in their proper places. It is proper to add, that the capacity of the instrument should be proportioned to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of air received into the lungs in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a>, which Dr Goodwyn has ascertained to be twelve cubical inches or somewhat more. Each <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the instrument, therefore, should be capable of containing that quantity. LUNGE-WORT. See Pulmonaria, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

LUNISOLAR YEAR

Pages 280-280

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">Chronology</a>, the space of 532 <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> years; found by multiplying the cycle of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> by that of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>. LUNULA. See LUNE.

LUPERCALIA

Pages 280-280

feasts instituted in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Rome, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the god <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAN">Pan</a>. The word comes from Lupercal, the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> under the Palatine mountain, where the sacrifices were performed. The Lupercalia were celebrated on the 15th of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KALENDS">Kalends</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, that is, on the 15th of February, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, as Ovid observes, on the 3rd <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> after the ides. They are supposed to have been established by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVANDER">Evander</a>. On the morning of this feast, the Luperci, or priests of Pan, ran naked through the streets of Rome, striking the married women they met on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> and belly with a thong or strap of goats <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, which was held an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OMEN">omen</a> promising them fecundity and happy deliveries. See Luperci. This feast was abolished in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Augustus; but afterwards restored, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to the time of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Anastasius.—Baronius says it was abolished by the pope in 496.

LUPERCI

Pages 280-280

a name given to the priests of the god <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAN">Pan</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUPERCALIA">Lupercalia</a>. The luperci were the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> order of priests in Rome; they were divided into two colleges <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> companies, the one called Fabri and the other Quintilii. To these Caesar added a third, which he called Juli.

LUPINUS

Pages 280-280

Lupine; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the diadelphia class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>- ing under the 32d order, Papilionaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Lupinus <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

LUPUS

Pages 280-280

the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WOLF">Wolf</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANIS">Canis</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">Mammalia</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Lupus Marinus, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>-wolf, a fish. See Anarhichas, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> Ind.x.

LURCHER

Pages 280-280

a kind of hunting-dog, much like a mongrel greyhound, with pricked ears, a shagged coat, and generally of a yellowish <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>: they are very swift runners, so that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they get between the burrows and the conies they seldom miss; and this is their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> practice in hunting; yet they <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> other subtleties, as the tumbler does, some of them bringing in their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAME">game</a>, and those are the best. It is also observable, that a lurcher <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> run <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> a hare at stretch.

LURGAN

Pages 280-280

a town in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMAGH">Armagh</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Ulster in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, 66 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>. It is a flourishing town, agreeably situated in the midst of a much improved <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and the inhabitants are extensively engaged in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> manufacture. It stands on a gentle eminence, about two miles from Lough Neagh, of which it commands a most beautiful and extensive prospect. N. Lat. 54° 35'. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6° 31'.

LUSATIA

Pages 280-283

a marquisate of Germany, in Upper <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, subject to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>; bounded to the east by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SILESIA">Silesia</a>, to the west by Misnia, to the south by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, and to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the marquisate of Brandenburgh. Till towards the middle of the 15th century, the Upper Lusatia was called the Mark, i.e. the marquisate <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> of Budissin and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GORLITZ">Gorlitz</a>; and the Lower only Lusatia, which it is said, in the Selavonie, signifies "a woody or marshy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>." The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> of the Upper Lusatia, which is hilly or mountainous, is better than that of the lower, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of which is moorish and boggy. Both abound in wood, especially the Lower, and turf for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>. The heathy and mountainous tracts are generally barren; but the lower champaign and marsh lands are tolerably fertile, producing pasture, wheat, rye, oats, barley, buck-wheat, pease, lentils, beans, and millet; together with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, hops, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> wine, and what is called <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANNA">manna</a>. Of several of these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>, however, considerable quantities are imported. In this country are found also quarries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, medicinal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASTARD">bastard</a> diamonds, agates, and jaspers, earths and clays for tobacco-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a> and all sorts of earthen <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARE">ware</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, good <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> stone, vitriolic and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; nor is it destitute of cattle, fish, and venison. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Spree, the Schwarze or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> Elster, and the Pulznitz, have their sources in the Lusatias, which are also watered by the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEISSE">Neisse</a> and Queis. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> inhabitants of this country were the Saxons, who were succeeded by the Vandals, and these by the Sober-Wends, a Slavonian people. The present inhabitants, the descendants of the Wends, have an odd dress; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> is so inarticulate and guttural, that it hath been said, it might be pronounced without lips, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, or tongue; but the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> are almost wholly peopled by Germans. In the Upper Lusatia are six towns which appear at the land-diets, 16 smaller country towns, and four market towns. In the Lower are four diet towns, 13 country towns, and two market ones. Both marquises were formerly subject either to the kings of Bohemia, the archdukes of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, or electors of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a>; but, in 1636, both were absolutely ceded to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of Saxony, in lieu of the 72 tons of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> which he expended in assisting the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Ferdinand II. against the Bohemians. Christianity was first planted in Lusatia in the seventh century; but it was several centuries after that before <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPERY">Popery</a> was fully established. In the 11th century many cloisters were erected in the country; but at the Reformation such numbers embraced Lutheranism, that it became the predominant <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, and still continues, though there are still several Roman Catholic foundations, churches, market-towns, and villages. The enthusiastic <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of Hennhutters possesses a great influence and esteem here. There are considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of woollen and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> stuffs in the Lusatias, especially the Upper. At Budissen, and in the adjacent country, prodigious quantities of stockings, spatteredashes, caps, and gloves are made. The linen manufactures also flourish here, chiefly in the Upper Lusatia, where all sorts of linen are made, printed, and dyed. Exclusive of these, there are considerable manufactures of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-HATS">hats</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a>, iron, glass, bleached wax, &c. Though the demand and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a> of these commodities, particularly linen and woollens, is not so great as formerly, yet it is still considerable, and more than overbalances their importations in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, yarn, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, wines, spices, corn, fresh and baked <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, garden stuff, and hops. Disputes of many years standing have subsisted between the country artificers and linen manufacturers on the one side, and the diet-towns on the other; the latter unjustly seeking to exclude the former from any share in the linen trade. The natives of this country are said to have quick <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> parts, but to be sordidly penurious. We are told they observe the Saxon laws much better than they did the Bohemian. Learning hath been much esteemed and encouraged in both marquises since the Reformation. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> in the six diet towns of Upper Lusatia, particularly at Gorlitz, Budissen, and Zittau, greatly distinguish themselves, having handsome stipends. In Lower Lusatia also are some good schools, with stipends for the maintenance of students. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTING">Printing</a> is said to be much followed, and brought to great perfection in this country. In Upper Lusatia, the states consist, 1st, of those called state-lords; 2dly, of the prelates; 3dly, of the gentry and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONALTY">commonalty</a>, under which are comprehended the counts, barons, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a>, and burgesses, possessors of fees and fief-estates; and, 4thly, of the representatives of the six <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> towns. Without the consent of these states no taxes can be imposed, nor anything of importance, that regards the public, transacted. The diets are ordinary or extraordinary. The ordinary meet once in three years, and the extraordinary when summoned by the sovereign upon particular emergencies. As to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> matters, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> of Budissen and his consistory <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> all manner of episcopal jurisdiction; and among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, the jurisdiction belongs either to the superior, the upper-office, or the patrons. The revenues arising to the superior or sovereign, from Upper Lusatia, consist partly of the subsidies granted by the states, among which, at present, are reckoned <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITULATION">capitulation</a> and estate-<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>; and partly of the beer-tax, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXCISE">excise</a>, tolls, &c. —Upper Lusatia is divided into two great circles, viz. those of Budissen and Gorlitz, which are again divided into lesser circles. The land states of Lower Lusatia consist, like those of the Upper, of prelates, lords, and knights, and the representatives of the state towns, which are Luckan, Gubben-Lubben, and Kalau. Two land diets are yearly held at Lubben, called voluntary-diets; but when the superior causes the states to be summoned together at his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a> to be laid before them, by commissaries deputed for that purpose, such convention is called a great land diet. The marquise is divided into five circles, each of which holds a circle assembled in its circle town. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> officers appointed either by the superior or the states are, the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the upper office, the land <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>, and the land judge. The principal tribunals are, the land <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, and the upper office, to which <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> appeals from the inferior judicatories. There are also officers for the several circles. Spiritual matters belong here to a consistory, erected in 1668. The ordinary taxes are paid into the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEST">chest</a> of the circle; and from thence consigned to the general chest, of which the upper tax-receiver is superintendant. By him an annual account of the receipts is made out, which is examined and passed by the deputies of the states.

LUSITANIA

Pages 283-283

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, one of the divisions of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, extending to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TAGUS">Tagus</a>, quite to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> of Cantabria, at least to the Promontorium Celticum. But Augustus, by a new regulation, made the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANAS">Anas</a> its boundary to the south, the Durius to the north; and thus constituting only a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>. Lusitani the people, (Diodorus, Stephanus.)

LUSTRAL

Pages 283-284

an epithet given by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> used in their ceremonies to sprinkle and purify the people. From them the Romanists have borrowed the holy water used in their churches. Lustral <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">Day</a> (Dies Lustricus), that whereon the lustrations were performed for a child, and its name given; which was usually the ninth day from the birth of a boy, and the eighth from that of a girl. Though others performed the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> on the last day of that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEEK">week</a> wherein the child was born, and others on the fifth day from its birth. Over this feast-day the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> Nundina was supposed to preside; the midwives, nurses, and domestics handed the child backwards and forwards, around a fire <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> on the altars of the gods, after which they sprinkled it with water; hence this feast had the name <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUSTRATION">Lustration</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIATION">expiation</a>, of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Lustration Jews, see Expiation.

LUSTRE

Pages 284-284

an appellation given to a branched <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANDLESTICK">candlestick</a>, when made of glass. See Branch and Jesse. LUSTRINGS. A <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> was incorporated for making, dressing, and lustering alamodes and lustrings in England, who were to have the sole benefit thereof, by stat. 4 and 5 William and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>. And no foreign silks known by the name of lustrings <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> alamodes are to be imported but at the port of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, &c. Stat. 9 and 10 William III. c. 43. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">Silk</a>.

LUSTRUM

Pages 284-284

in Roman antiquity, a general muster and review of all the citizens and their goods, which was performed by the censors every fifth year, who afterwards made a solemn <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUSTRATION">lustration</a>. See the article Lustration. This <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> was first instituted by Servius Tullius, about 180 years after the foundation of Rome. In course of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the lustra were not celebrated so often; for we find the fifth lustrum celebrated at Rome only in the 574th year of that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>.

LUTE

Pages 284-284
or Loting, among chemists, a mixed, tenacious, ductile substance, which grows solid by drying, and, being applied to the juncture of vessels, stops them up so as to prevent the air from getting in or out. Lute is also a musical instrument with strings.—The lute consists of four parts, viz. the table, the body or belly, which has nine or ten sides: the neck, which has nine or ten stops or divisions, marked with strings; and the head or cross, where the screws for raising and lowering the strings to a proper pitch of tone are fixed. In the middle of the table there is a rose or passage for the sound; there is also a bridge that the strings are fastened to, and a piece of ivory between the head and the neck to which the other extremities of the strings are fitted. In playing, the strings are struck with the right hand, and with the left the stops are pressed. The lutes of Bologna are esteemed the best on account of the wood, which is said to have an uncommon disposition for producing a sweet sound.

LUTETIA

Pages 284-285
