LUTETIA PARISIORUM, in Ancient Geography, a town of the Parisii, in Gallia Celtica, situated in an island in the Sequana or Seine. It received its name, as some suppose, from the quantity of clay, lutum, which is in its neighbourhood. J. Caesar fortified and embellished it, from which circumstance some authors call it Juli Civitas. Julian the apostate resided there for some time. It is now PARIS, the capital of France; so called from its name Parys in the lower age.

LUTHER

Pages 285-290

MARTIN, the celebrated author of the Reformation, was a native of Eisleben in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, and born in 1483. Though his parents were <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, he received a learned <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>; during the progress of which, he gave many indications of uncommon vigour and acuteness of genius. As his mind was naturally susceptible of serious impressions, and tinctured with somewhat of that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> melancholy which delights in the solitude and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> of a monastic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, he retired into a convent of Augustinian friars; where he acquired <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation, not only for piety, but for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of knowledge and unwearied application to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>. The cause of this retirement is said to have been, that he was once struck by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>, and his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> killed by his side by the same flash. He had been taught the scholastic <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> which was in vogue in those days, and made considerable progress in it: but happening to find a copy of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a> which lay neglected in the library of his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>, he applied himself to the study of it with such eagerness and assiduity, as quite astonished the monks; and increased his reputation for sanctity so much, that he was chosen professor first of philosophy, and afterwards of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WITTENBERG">Wittenberg</a> on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELBE">Elbe</a>, where Frederic <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of Saxony had founded an university. While Luther <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to enjoy the highest reputation for sanctity and learning, Tetzel, a Dominican friar, came to Wittenberg in order to publish indulgences. Luther beheld his success with great concern; and having first inveighed against indulgences from the pulpit, he afterwards published 95 theses, containing his sentiments on that subject. These he proposed, not as <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> fully established, but as subjects of inquiry and disputation. He appointed a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> on which the learned were invited to impugn them either in person <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>; and to the whole he subjoined solemn protestations of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> respect for the apostolic see, and of his implicit submission to its authority. No opponent appeared at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> prefixed; the theses spread over Germany with astonishing rapidity, and were read with the greatest eagerness. Though Luther met with no opposition for some little time after he begun to publish his new doctrines, it was not <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> before many zealous champions arose to defend those opinions with which the wealth and power of the clergy were so strictly connected. Their cause, however, was by no means promoted by these endeavours; the people began to call in question even the authority of the canon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> and of the pope himself.—The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Rome at first despised these new doctrines and disputes; but at last the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of the pope being raised by the great success of the reformer, and the complaints of his adversaries, Luther was summoned in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1518, to appear at Rome, within 60 days, before the auditor of the chamber. One of Luther's adversaries, named Prierias, who had written against him, was appointed to examine his doctrines, and to decide concerning them. The pope wrote at the same time to the elector of Saxony, beseeching him not to protect a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> whose heretical and profane tenets were so shocking to pious ears; and enjoined the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> of the Augustinians to check by his authority the rashness of an arrogant monk, which brought disgrace upon their order, and gave offence and disturbance to the whole <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. From these letters, and the appointment of his open enemy Prierias to be his judge, Luther easily <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> what <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> he might expect at Rome; and therefore discovered the utmost solicitude to have his cause tried in Germany, and before a less suspected tribunal. He wrote a submissive <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to the pope, in which he promised an unreserved obedience to his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, for as yet he entertained no doubt of the divine original of the pope's authority; and by the intercession of the other professors, Cajetan, the pope's legate in Germany was appointed to hear and determine the cause. Luther appeared before him without hesitation: but Cajetan thought it below his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> to dispute the point with a person so much his inferior in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>; and therefore required him by virtue of the apostolic powers with which he was clothed, to retract the errors which he had uttered with regard to indulgences and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, and to abstain for the future from the publication of new and dangerous opinions; and at the last forbade him to appear in his presence, unless he proposed to comply with what had been required of him. This haughty and violent manner of proceeding, together with some other circumstances, gave Luther's friends such strong reason to suspect that even the imperial safe-conduct would not be able to protect him from the legate's power and resentment, that they prevailed on him secretly to withdraw from Augsburg, where he had attended the legate, and to return to his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. But before his departure, according to a form of which there had been some examples, he prepared a solemn <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> from the pope, ill-informed at that time concerning his cause, to the pope, when he should receive more full intimation with respect to it.—Cajetan, enraged at Luther's abrupt retreat, and at the publication of his appeal, wrote to the elector of Saxony, complaining of both; and requiring him, as he regarded the peace of the church, or the authority of its head, either to send that seditions monk a prisoner to Rome, or to banish him out of his territories. Frederick had hitherto, from <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> motives, protected Luther, as thinking he might be of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in checking the enormous power of the see of Rome, and though all Germany resounded with his fame; the elector had never yet admitted him into his presence. But upon this demand made by the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a>, it became necessary to throw off somewhat of his former reserve. He had been at great expense and bestowed much attention on founding a new university, an object of considerable importance to every German <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>; and foreseeing how fatal a blow the removal of Luther would be to its reputation, reputation, he not only declined complying with either of the pope's requests, but openly discovered great concern for Luther's safety. The situation of our reformer, in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time, came daily more and more alarming. He knew very well what were the motives which induced the elector to afford him protection, and that he could by no means depend on a continuance of his friendship. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> he should be obliged to quit Saxony, he had no other <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a>, and must stand exposed to whatever <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> the rage or bigotry of his enemies could inflict; and so ready were his adversaries to condemn him, that he had been declared a heretic at Rome before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of the 60 days allowed him in the citation for making his appearance. Notwithstanding all this, however, he discovered no symptoms of timidity or remissness; but continued to vindicate his own conduct and opinions, and to inveigh against those of his adversaries with more vehemence than ever. Being convinced, therefore, that the pope would soon proceed to the most violent <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> against him, he appealed to a general <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, which he affirmed to be the representative of the Catholic church, and superior in power to the pope, who being a fallible man, might err, as St <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>, the most perfect of his predecessors, had done. The court of Rome were equally assiduous in the mean time to crush the author of these new doctrines which gave them so much uneasiness. A bull was issued by the pope, of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> to Luther's appeal, in which he magnified the virtues of indulgences, and subjected to the heaviest <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> censures all who presumed to teach a contrary doctrine. Such a clear decision of the sovereign pontiff against him might have been very fatal to Luther's cause, had not the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Maximilian, which happened on <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 17, 1519, contributed to give matters a different turn. Both the principles and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of Maximilian had prompted him to support the authority of the see of Rome; but, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of his death, the vicariate of that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Germany which is governed by the Saxon laws devolved to the elector of Saxony; and, under the shelter of his friendly administration, Luther himself enjoyed tranquillity; and his opinions took such root in different places, that they could never afterwards be eradicated. At the same time, as the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> of an emperor was a point more interesting to the pope (Leo X.) than a theological controversy which he did not understand, and of which he could not foresee the consequences, he was so extremely solicitous not to irritate a prince of such considerable influence in the electoral <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> as Frederick, that he discovered a great unwillingness to pronounce the sentence of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCOMMUNICATION">excommunication</a> against Luther, which his adversaries continually demanded with the most clamorous importunity. From the reason <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> now given, and Leo's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> aversion to severe measures, a suspension of proceeding against Luther took <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> for 18 months, though perpetual negociations were carried on during this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> in order to bring the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> to an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMICABLE">amicable</a> issue. The manner in which these were conducted having given our reformer many opportunities of observing the corruption of the court of Rome, its obstinacy in adhering to established errors, and its indecision about <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, however clearly proposed or Luther strongly proved, he began, in 1520, to utter some doubts with regard to the divine original of the papal authority, which he publicly disputed with Eccius, one of his most learned and formidable antagonists. The dispute was indecisive, both parties claiming the victory; but it must have been very mortifying to the partizans of the Romish church to hear such an essential point of their doctrine publicly attacked. The papal authority being once suspected, Luther proceeded to push on his inquiries and attacks from one doctrine to another, till at last he began to shake the firmest foundations on which the wealth and power of the church were established. Leo then began to perceive that there were no hopes of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECLAIMING">reclaiming</a> such an incorrigible heretic; and therefore prepared to denounce the sentence of excommunication against him. The college of cardinals was often assembled, in order to prepare the sentence with due deliberation; and the ablest canonists were consulted how it might be expressed with unexceptionable formality. At last it was issued on the 15th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1520. Forty-one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a>, extracted out of Luther's works, were therein condemned as heretical, scandalous, and offensive to pious ears; all persons were forbidden to read his writings, upon pain of excommunication; such as had any of them in their custody were commanded to commit them to the flames; he himself, if he did not, within 60 days, publicly recant his errors, and burn his books, was pronounced an obstinate heretic, excommunicated, and delivered to Satan for the destruction of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>: and all <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> princes were required, under pain of incurring the same censure, to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> his person, that he might be punished as his crimes deserved. Luther was not in the least disconcerted by this sentence, which he had for some time expected. He renewed his appeal to a general council; declared the pope to be that antichrist, or man of sin, whose appearance is foretold in the New <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>; declaimed against his tyranny with greater vehemence than ever; and at last, by way of retaliation, having assembled all the professors and students in the university of Wittemberg, with great pomp, and in the presence of a vast multitude of spectators, he <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> the volumes of the canon law, together with the bull of excommunication, into the flames. The manner in which this <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> was justified gave still more offence than the action itself. Having collected from the canon laws some of the most extravagant propositions with regard to the plenitude and omnipotence of the pope's power, as well as the subordination of all secular jurisdiction to his authority, he published these with a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMENTARY">commentary</a>, pointing out the impiety of such tenets, and their evident tendency to subvert all civil <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. On the accession of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. to the empire, Luther found himself in a very dangerous situation. Charles, in order to secure the pope's friendship, had determined to treat him with great severity. His eagerness to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> this point, rendered him not averse to gratify the papal legates in Germany, who insisted, that without any delay or formal deliberation, the diet then sitting at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORMS">Worms</a> ought to condemn a man whom the pope had already excommunicated as an incorrigible heretic. Such an abrupt manner of proceeding, however, being deemed unprecedented and unjust by the members members of the diet, they made a point of Luther's appearing in person, and declaring whether he adhered or not to those opinions which had drawn upon him the censures of the church. Not only the emperor, but all the princes through whose territories he had to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>, granted him a safe-conduct; and Charles wrote to him at the same time, requiring his immediate attendance on the diet, and renewing his promises of protection from any injury or violence. Luther did not hesitate one moment about yielding obedience; and set out for Worms, attended by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALD">herald</a> who had brought the emperor's letter and safe-conduct. While on his journey, many of his friends, whom the fate of Huss, under similar circumstances, and notwithstanding the same security of an imperial safe-conduct, filled with solicitude, advised and entreated him not to rush wantonly into the midst of danger. But Luther, superior to such terrors, silenced them with this reply, "I am lawfully called (said he) to appear in that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>; and thither will I go in the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>, though as many devils as there are tiles on the houses were there combined against me." The reception which he met with at Worms, was such as might have been reckoned a full reward of all his labours, if vanity and the love of applause had been the principles by which he was influenced. Greater crowds assembled to behold him than had appeared at the emperor's public entry; his apartments were daily filled with princes and personages of the highest rank; and he was treated with an homage more sincere, as well as more flattering, than any which pre-eminence in birth or condition can command. At his appearance before the diet, he behaved with great decency, and with equal firmness. He readily acknowledged an excess of acrimony and vehemence in his controversial writings; but refused to retract his opinions unless he were convinced of their falshood, or to consent to their being tried by any other rule than the word of God. When neither threats nor intreates could prevail on him, to depart from this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>, some of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a> proposed to imitate the example of the council of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTANCE">Constance</a>, and by punishing the author of this pestilent <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a>, who was now in their power, to deliver the church at once from such an evil. But the members of the diet refusing to expose the German integrity to fresh reproach by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> violation of public faith, and Charles being no less unwilling to bring a stain upon the beginning of his administration by such an ignominious action, Luther was permitted to depart in safety. A few days after he left the city, a severe edict was published in the emperor's name, and by authority of the diet, depriving him, as an obstinate and excommunicated criminal, of all the privileges which he enjoyed as a subject of the empire, forbidding any prince to harbour or protect him, and requiring all to seize his person as soon as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> specified in his protection should be expired. But this vigorous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> had no considerable effect; the execution of it being prevented partly by the multiplicity of occupations which the commotions in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, together with the wars in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> and the Low Countries, created to the emperor; and partly by a prudent precaution employed by the elector of Saxony, Luther's faithful <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a>. As Luther, on his return from Worms, was passing near Altenstrain in Thuringia, a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of horsemen in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MASKS">masks</a> rushed suddenly out of a wood, where the elector had appointed them to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in wait for him, and surrounding his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, carried him, after dismissing all his attendants, to Worburg, a strong castle not far distant. There the elector ordered him to be supplied with every thing necessary or agreeable; but the place of his retreat was carefully concealed, until the fury of the present storm against him began to abate, upon a change in the political system of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. In this solitude, where he remained <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> months, and which he frequently called his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATMOS">Patmos</a>, after the name of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> to which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a> John was banished, he exerted his usual vigour and industry in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of his doctrines, or in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFUTATION">confutation</a> of his adversaries, publishing several treatises, which revived the spirit of his followers, astonished to a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> and disheartened at the sudden disappearance of their leader. Luther, weary at length of his retirement, appeared publicly again at Wittenberg, upon the 6th of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1522. He appeared indeed without the elector's leave; but immediately wrote him a letter to prevent his taking it ill. The edict of Charles V., as severe as it was, had given little or no check to Luther's doctrine; for the emperor was no sooner gone to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, than his edict was neglected and despised, and the doctrine seemed to spread even faster than before. Carolostadius, in Luther's absence, had pushed things on faster than his leader; and had attempted to abolish the use of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a>, to remove images out of the churches, to set aside auricular confession, invocation of saints, the abstaining from meats; had allowed the monks to leave their monasteries, to neglect their vows, and to marry; in short, had quite changed the doctrine and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> of the church at Wittenberg: all which, though not against Luther's sentiments, was yet blamed by him, as being rashly and unseasonably done. Lutheranism was still confined to Germany; it was not got to France; and Henry VIII. of England made the most rigorous acts to hinder it from invading his realm. Nay, he did something more: to show his zeal for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> and the holy see, and perhaps his skill in theological learning, he wrote a treatise Of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> sacraments, against Luther's book Of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a>; which he presented to Leo X. in October 1521. The pope received it very favourably; and was so well pleased with the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of England, that he complimented him with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Defender of the Faith. Luther, however, paid no regard to his kingship; but answered him with great sharpness, treating both his person and performance in the most contemptuous manner. Henry complained of Luther's rude usage of him to the princes of Saxony; and Fisher, bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROCHESTER">Rochester</a>, replied to his answer, in behalf of Henry's treatise: but neither the king's complaint, nor the bishop's reply, was attended with any visible effects. Luther, though he had put a stop to the violent proceedings of Carolostadius, now made open <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with the pope and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>: and, that he might make the people despise their authority as much as possible, he wrote one book against the pope's bull, and another against the order falsely called the order of bishops. The same year, 1522, he wrote a letter, dated July the 29th to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of the states of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>; Luther, to which he assured them that he was labouring to establish their doctrine in Germany, and exhorted them not to return to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> of the church of Rome; and he published also this year, a translation of the New Testament in the German tongue, which was afterwards corrected by himself and Melancthon. This translation having been printed several times, and being in every body's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, Ferdinand archduke of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, the emperor's <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, made a very severe edict, to hinder the farther publication of it; and forbade all the subjects of his imperial majesty to have any copies of it, or of Luther's other books. Some other princes followed his example; and Luther was so angry at it, that he wrote a treatise Of the secular power, in which he accuses them of tyranny and impiety. The diet of the empire was held at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUREMBERG">Nuremberg</a>, at the end of the year; to which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HADRIAN">Hadrian</a> VI. sent his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a>, dated November the 25th: for Leo X. died upon the 2d of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1521, and Hadrian had been elected pope upon the 9th of January following. In this brief, among other things, he observes to the diet, how he had heard with grief, that Martin Luther, after the sentence of Leo X., which was ordered to be executed by the edict of Worms, continued to teach the same errors, and daily to publish books full of heresies: that it appeared strange to him, that so <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and so religious a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> could be seduced by a wretched apostate friar: that nothing, however, could be more pernicious to Christendom; and that therefore he exhorts them to use their utmost endeavours to make Luther, and the authors of these tumults, return to their duty: or, if they refuse and continue obstinate, to proceed against them according to the laws of the empire, and the severity of the last edict. The resolution of this diet was published in the form of an edict, upon the 6th of March 1523; but it had no effect in checking the Lutherans, who still went on in the same triumphant manner. This year Luther wrote a great many pieces: among the rest, one upon the dignity and office of the supreme <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>; which Frederic elector of Saxony is said to have been highly pleased with. He sent, about the same time, a writing in the German <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> to the Waldenses, or Pickards, in Bohemia and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORAVIA">Moravia</a>, who had applied to him "about worshipping the body of Christ in the eucharist." He wrote also another book, which he dedicated to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> and people of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAGUE">Prague</a>, "about the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> of ministers of the church." He drew up a form of saying mass. He wrote a piece, entitled, An example of Popish doctrine and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>; which Dupin calls a satire against nuns and those who profess a monastic life. He wrote also against the vows of virginity, in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> to his commentary on 1 Cor. viii. And his exhortations here were, it seems, followed with effects; for soon after, nine nuns, among whom was Catharine de Bore, eloped from the nunnery at Nimptschen, and were brought, by the assistance of Leonard Coppen, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGESS">burgess</a> of Torgau, to Wittenberg. Whatever offence this proceeding might give to the Papists, it was highly extolled by Luther; who, in a book written in the German language, compares the deliverance of these nuns from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a> of a monastic life to that of the souls which <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ has delivered by his death. This year Luther had occasion to canonize two of his followers, who, as Melchior <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a> relates, were burnt at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUSSELS">Brussels</a> in the beginning of July, and were the first who suffered martyrdom for his doctrine. He wrote also a consolatory epistle to three noble ladies at Misnia, who were banished from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Saxony's court at Friburg, for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> his books. In the beginning of the year 1524, Clement VII. sent a legate into Germany to the diet, which was to be held at Nuremburg. Hadrian VI. died in October 1523, and was succeeded by Clement upon the 19th of November. A little before his death he canonized Benno, who was bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEISSEN">Meissen</a> in the time of Gregory VII., and one of the most zealous defenders of the holy see. Luther, imagining that this was done directly to oppose him, drew up a piece with this title, Against the New Idol and Old <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVIL">Devil</a> set up at Meissen; in which he treats the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of Gregory with great freedom, and does not spare even Hadrian. Clement VII.'s legate represented to the diet of Nuremburg the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of enforcing the execution of the edict of Worms, which had been strangely neglected by the princes of the empire; but, notwithstanding the legate's solicitations, which were very pressing, the decrees of that diet were thought so ineffectual, that they were condemned at Rome, and rejected by the emperor. It was in this year that the dispute between Luther and Erasmus, about free-will, began. Erasmus had been much courted by the Papists to write against Luther; but he was all along of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that writing would not be found an effectual way to end the differences and establish the peace of the church. However, tired out at length with the importunities of the pope and the Catholic princes, and desirous at the same time to clear himself from the suspicion of favouring a cause which he would not seem to favour, he resolved to write against Luther, though, as he tells Melancthon, it was with some reluctance, and chose free-will for the subject. His book was entitled, A Diatribe, or Conference about Free-will; and was written with much moderation, and without personal reflections. He tells Luther in the preface, "That he ought not to take his dissenting from him in opinion ill, because he had allowed himself the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of differing from the judgment of popes, councils, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, and doctors of the church." Luther was some time before he answered Erasmus's book; but at last published a treatise De Servo Arbitrio, or Of the Servitude of Man's Will; and though Melancthon had promised Erasmus, that Luther should answer him with civility and moderation, yet Luther had so little regard to Melancthon's <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a>, that he never wrote anything sharper. He accused Erasmus of being careless about religion, and little solicitous what became of it, provided the world continued in peace; and that his notions were rather philosophical than Christian. Erasmus immediately replied to Luther in a piece called Hyperaspistes; in the first part of which he answers his arguments, and in the second his personal reflections. In October 1524, Luther threw off the monastic <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>; which, though not premeditated and designed, was yet a very proper preparative to a step he took the year after; we mean, his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> with Catharine de Bore. Catharine de Bore was a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, who had been a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUN">nun</a>, and was taken, as we have observed, out of the nunnery of Nimptschen, in the year year 1525. Luther had a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, as Melchior Adam related, to marry her to Glacius, a minister of Orta- <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol15.html#article-MUNDEN">munden</a>; but she did not like Glacius; and so Luther married her himself upon the 13th of June 1525. This conduct of his was blamed not only by the Ca- tholics, but, as Melanchthon says, by those of his own party. He was even for some time ashamed of it him- self; and owns, that his marriage had made him so despicable, that he hoped his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HUMILIATION">humiliation</a> would rejoice the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a>, and vex the devils. Melanchthon found him so afflicted with what he had done, that he wrote some letters of consolation to him. It was not so much the marriage, as the circumstances of the time, and the pre- cipitation with which it was done, that occasioned the censures passed upon Luther. He married all of a sud- den, and at a time when Germany was groaning under the miseries of a war which was said at least to be owing to Lutheranism. Then, again, it was thought an indecent thing in a man of 42 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, who was then, as he pretended, restoring the Gospel, and reforming mankind, to involve himself in marriage with a woman of 26, either through incontinence, or any account whatever. But Luther, as soon as he had re- covered himself a little from this abashment, assumed his former <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> of intrepidity, and boldly supported what he had done with reasons. "I took a wife (says he), in obedience to my father's commands; and hastened the consummation, in order to prevent <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-IMPEDIMENTS">impediments</a>, and stop the tongues of slanderers." It appears from his own confession, that this reformer was very fond of Mrs de Bore, and used to call her his Catharine, which made profane people think and say wicked things of him: "And therefore (says he) I mar- ried of a sudden, not only that I might not be obliged to hear the clamours which I knew would be raised against me, but to stop the mouths of those who re- proached me with Catharine de Bore." Luther also gives us to understand, that he did it partly as con- curring with his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> scheme of opposing the Catho- lics. Luther, notwithstanding, was not himself altogether satisfied with these reasons. He did not think the step he had taken could be sufficiently justified upon the principles of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>; and therefore we find him, in other places, endeavouring to account for it from a supernatural impulse. But whether there was any thing divine in it or not, Luther found himself extremely happy in his new state, and especially after his wife had brought him a son. "My rib Kate (says he in the joy of his heart) desires her compliments to you, and thanks you for the favour of your kind let- ter. She is very well, through God's mercy. She is obedient and complying with me in all things; and more agreeable, I thank God, than I could have ex- pected; so that I would not change my poverty for the wealth of Cæsars." He was heard to say (Seck- endorf tells us), that he would not <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> his wife for the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of France, nor for the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> of the Venetians; and that for three reasons: Because she had been given him by God, at the time when he implored the assistance of the Holy Ghost, in finding a good wife; secondly, Because, though she was not without faults, yet she had fewer than other women; and, thirdly, Because she religiously observed the conjugal fidelity she owed him. There went at first a report, that Catharine de Bore was brought to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> soon after her marriage with Luther; but Erasmus, who had wrote that news to his friends, acknowledged the falsity of it a little after. His marriage, however, did not retard his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> and diligence in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of reformation. He revised the Augsburg confession of faith, and apology for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, when the Protestant religion was first es- tablished on a firm basis. See Protestants and Re- formation. After this, Luther had little else to do than to sit <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> and contemplate the mighty work he had finish- ed: for that a single monk should be able to give the church so rude a shock, that there needed but such another entirely to overthrow it, may very well seem a mighty work. He did indeed little else: for the re- mainder of his life was spent in exhorting princes, states, and universities, to confirm the reformation which had been brought about through him; and pub- lishing from time to time such writings as might en- courage, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a>, and aid them in doing it. The em- peror threatened temporal punishment with armies, and the pope eternal with bulls and anathemas; but Luther cared for none of their threats. His friend and co- adjutor Melanchthon was not so indifferent; for Me- lancthon had a great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of softness, moderation, and diffidence in his make, which made him very uneasy, and even sorrowful, in the present disorders. Hence we find many of Luther's letters written on purpose to support and comfort him under these several distresses and anxieties. In the year 1533, Luther wrote a consolatory epistle to the citizens of Oschatz, who had suffered some hardships for adhering to the Augsburg confes- <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SION">sion</a> of faith: in which, among other things, he says, "The devil is the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOST">host</a>, and the world is his inn; so that wherever you come, you shall be sure to find this ugly host." He had also about this time a terrible controversy with George duke of Saxony, who had such an aversion to Luther's doctrine, that he obliged his subjects to take an oath that they would never em- brace it. However, 60 or 70 citizens of Leipsic were found to have deviated a little from the Catholic way in some point or other, and they were known previ- ously to have consulted Luther about it; upon which George complained to the elector John, that Luther had not only abused his person, but also preached up rebellion among his subjects. The elector ordered Lu- ther to be acquainted with this; and to be told at the same time, that if he did not clear himself of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>, he could not possibly escape punishment. But Luther easily refuted the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a>, by proving, that he had been so far from stirring up his subjects against him, on the score of religion, that, on the contrary, he had exhorted them rather to undergo the greatest hard- ships, and even suffer themselves to be banished. In the year 1534, the Bible translated by him into German was first printed, as the old privilege, dated at Bibliopolis, under the elector's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, shows: and it was published the year after. He also published this year a book against masses and the consecration of priests, in which he relates a conference he had with the devil upon those points; for it is remarkable in Luther's whole <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, that he never had any conflicts of any kind within, but the devil was always his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANTA">anta</a>- gonist. Luther. In February 1537, an assembly was held at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SMALKALD">Smalkald</a> about matters of religion, to which Luther and Melancthon were called. At this meeting Luther was seized with so grievous an illness, that there were no hopes of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a>. He was afflicted with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, and had a stoppage of urine for 11 days. In this terrible condition he would needs undertake to travel, notwithstanding all that his friends could say or do to prevent him: his resolution, however, was attended with a good effect; for the night after his departure he began to be better. As he was carried along, he made his will, in which he bequeathed his detestation of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPERY">Popery</a> to his friends and brethren; agreeably to what he often used to say: *Pestis cram virus, moriens ero <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORS">mors</a> tua, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPA">papa</a>*; that is, "I was the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a> of Popery in my life, and shall continue to be so in my death." This year the pope and the court of Rome, finding it impossible to deal with the Protestants by force, began to have recourse to stratagem. They affected therefore to think, that though Luther had indeed carried things on with a high hand and to a violent <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a>, yet what he had pleaded in defense of these measures was not entirely without foundation. They talked with a seeming show of moderation: and Pius III., who succeeded Clement VII., proposed a reformation first among themselves, and even went so far as to fix a place for a council to meet at for that purpose. But Luther treated this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARCE">farce</a> as it deserved to be treated; unmasked and detected it immediately; and, to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a> it the more strongly, caused a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> to be drawn, in which was represented the pope seated on high upon a throne, some cardinals about him with foxes tails on, and seeming to evacuate upwards and downwards (*sursum deorsum repurgare*, as Melchior Adam expresses it). This was fixed over against the title-page, to let the readers see at once the scope and design of the book; which was, to expose that cunning and artifice with which those subtle politicians affected to cleanse and purify themselves from their errors and superstitions. Luther published about the same time A Confutation of the Pretended <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">Grant</a> of Constantine to Sylvester Bishop of Rome; and also some letters of John Huss, written from his prison at Constance to the Bohemians. In this manner was Luther employed till his death, which happened in the year 1546. That year, accompanied by Melancthon, he paid a visit to his own country, which he had not seen for many years, and returned again in safety. But soon after he was called thither again by the earls of Mansfeldt, to compose some differences which had arisen about their boundaries. Luther had not been used to such matters; but because he was born at Eisleben, a town in the territory of Mansfeldt, he was willing to do his country what <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> he could, even in this way. Preaching his last sermon therefore at Wittemberg, upon the 17th of January, he set off on the 23rd; and at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">Hall</a> in Saxony lodged with Justus Jonas, with whom he staid three days, because the waters were out. Upon the 28th, he passed over the river with his three sons and Dr Jonas; and being in some danger, he said to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a>, "Do not you think it would rejoice the devil exceedingly, if I and you, and my three sons, should be drowned?" When he entered the territories of the earls of Mansfeldt, he was received by 100 horsemen or more, and conducted in a very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> manner; but was at the same time so very ill, that it was feared he would die. He said, that these fits of sickness often came upon him when he had any great business to undertake: of this, however, he did not recover; but died upon the 18th of February, in the 63rd year of his age. A little before he expired, he admonished those that were about him to pray to God for the propagation of the Gospel: "because (said he) the council of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a>, which had sat once or twice, and the pope, would <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVISE">devise</a> strange things against it." Soon after, his body was put into a leaden <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COFFIN">coffin</a>, and carried with funeral pomp to the church at Eisleben, when Dr Jonas preached a sermon upon the occasion. The earls of Mansfeldt desired that his body should be interred in their territories; but the elector of Saxony insisted upon his being brought back to Wittemberg; which was accordingly done; and there he was buried with the greatest pomp that perhaps ever happened to any private man. Princes, earls, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a>, and students without number, attended the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a>; and Melancthon made his funeral <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORATION">oration</a>. A thousand lies were invented by the Papists about Luther's death. Some said that he died suddenly; others, that he killed himself; others, that the devil strangled him: others, that his corpse stunk so abominably, that they were forced to leave it in the way, as it was carried to be interred. Nay, lies were invented about his death, even while he was yet alive. Luther, however, to give the most effectual refutation of this account of his death, put forth an advertisement of his being alive; and, to be even with the Papists for the malice they had shown in this lie, wrote a book at the same time to prove, that "the papacy was founded by the devil." Luther's works were collected after his death, and printed at Wittemberg in 7 vols. folio. Catharine de Bore survived her husband a few years; and continued the first year of her widowhood at Wittemberg, though Luther had advised her to seek another place of residence. She went from thence in the year 1547, when the town was surrendered to the emperor Charles V. Before her departure, she had received a present of 50 crowns from Christian III., king of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>; and the elector of Saxony, and the counts of Mansfeldt, gave her good tokens of their liberality. With these additions to what Luther had left her, she had where-withal to maintain herself and her family handsomely. She returned to Wittemberg, when the town was restored to the elector; where she lived in a very devout and pious manner, till the plague obliged her to leave it again in the year 1552. She sold what she had at Wittemberg, and retired to Torgau, with a resolution to end her life there. An unfortunate mischance befell her in her journey thither, which proved fatal to her. The horses growing unruly, and attempting to run away, she leaped out of the vehicle she was conveyed in; and, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAPING">leaping</a>, got a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>, of which she died about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a year after, at Torgau, upon the 20th of December 1552. She was buried there in the great church, where her <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> and epitaph are still to be seen; and the university of Wittemberg, which was then at Torgau because the plague raged at Wittem-

LUTHERANISM

Pages 290-291

the sentiments of Martin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a> with regard to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. See LUTHER. Lutheranism has undergone some alterations since the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of its founder.—Luther rejected the epistle of St James as inconsistent with the doctrine of St Paul, in relation to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTIFICATION">justification</a>; he also set aside the Apocalypse: both which are now received as canonical in the Lutheran <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. Luther reduced the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of sacraments to two, viz. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>, and the eucharist: but he believed the impanation, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> consubstantiation, that is, that the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> and wine remain with the body and blood of Christ; and it is in this article that the main <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the Lutherans and English churches consists. Luther maintained the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> to be no sacrifice; exploded the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADORATION">adoration</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOST">host</a>, auricular confession, meritorious works, indulgences, purgatory, the worship of images, &c. which had been introduced in the corrupt times of the Romish church. He also opposed the doctrine of free <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, maintained <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREDESTINATION">predestination</a>, and asserted our justification to be solely by the imputation of the merits and satisfaction of Christ. He also opposed the fastings in the Roman church, monastical vows, the celibate of the clergy, &c.

LUTHERANS

Pages 291-291

the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> who follow the opinions of Martin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a>, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> reformers of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> in the 16th century. See LUTHER. The Lutherans, of all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, are those who differ least from the Romish church; as they affirm, that the body and blood of Christ are materially present in the sacrament of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a>, though in an incomprehensible manner; and likewise represent some <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> and institutions, as the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of images in churches, the distinguishing vestments of the clergy, the private confession of sins, the use of wafers in the administration of the Lord's supper, the form of exorcism in the celebration of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>, and other ceremonies of the like <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, as tolerable, and some of them as useful. The Lutherans maintain, with regard to the divine decrees, that they respect the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALVATION">salvation</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> misery of men, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of a previous knowledge of their sentiments and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, and not as free and unconditional, and as founded on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> of God. Towards the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the last century, the Lutherans began to entertain a greater liberality of sentiment than they had before adopted; though in many places they persevered longer in severe and despotic principles than other Protestant churches. Their public teachers now enjoy an unbounded <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of dissenting from the decisions of those symbols or creeds which were once deemed almost infallible rules of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> and practice, and of declaring their dissent in the manner they judge the most expedient. Mosheim attributes this change in their sentiments to the maxim which they generally adopted, that Christians were accountable to God alone for their religious opinions; and that no individual could be justly punished by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> for his erroneous opinions, while he conducted himself like a virtuous and obedient subject, and made no attempts to disturb the peace and order of civil <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>.

LUTHERN

Pages 291-291

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, a kind of window over the cornice, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>; standing perpendicularly over the naked of a wall, and serving to illuminate the upper story. Lutherns are of various forms; as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, semicircular, round, called bull's eyes, flat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>, &c.

LUTTI

Pages 291-291

BENEDITTO, an eminent painter, born at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a> in 1666. He was the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Antonio Dominico Gabiani, and his merit was judged equal to that of his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>: he painted few beside easel pieces; and his works were much valued and sought for in England, France, and Germany. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> knighted him; and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENTZ">Mentz</a>, together with his patent of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a>, sent him a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> set with diamonds. Lutti was never satisfied in finishing his pictures; yet though he often retouched them, they never appeared laboured. He died in 1724.

LUTZEN

Pages 291-291

a town of Upper <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a> in Germany; famous for a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> fought here in 1632, when Gustavus Adolphus <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a> was killed. It is situated on the river Elster, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 12. 37. N. Lat. 51. 20.

LUXATION

Pages 291-291

is when any bone is moved out of its <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of articulation, so as to impede <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> destroy its proper office or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">SURGERY</a>.

LUXEMBURG

Pages 291-292

Francois Henry de Montmorenci, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of, and marshal of France, a renowned general in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. was born in 1628. He was with the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of Condé at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Rocroy, in 1643; and in 1668 distinguished himself at the conquest of Franche Comté. In 1672, he commanded in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> the French <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>; when he defeated the enemy near Woerden and Bodegrave, and was universally admired for the fine retreat he made in 1673. He became marshal of France in 1675; gained the battle of Fleurs in 1690, that of Steenkirk in 1692, and that of Nerwind in 1693. He died in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSAILLES">Versailles</a> in 1695.

LUXURIANS FLOS

Pages 292-292

"a luxuriant <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> flower;" a flower, some of whose parts are increased in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, to the diminution or entire <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCLUSION">exclusion</a> of others. The parts that are augmented or multiplied in luxuriant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, are the flower-cup and petals, which Linnæus considers as the teguments or covers of the flower; the parts that are diminished, or entirely excluded, are the stamens or chives, which the same author denominates the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> organs of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>. Luxuriance in flowers is capable of the three following varieties. 1. A flower is said to be **MULTIPLIED (flos multiplicatus)**, when the increase of the petals is not such as to exclude all the stamens: in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, flowers are properly said to be double, triple, or quadruple, according to the number of multiplications of the petals. 2. A flower is said to be **FULL (flos plenus)**, when, by the multiplication of the petals, all the stamens are excluded. Such are most of the double flowers that engage the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of florists. 3. A flower is said to be **PROLIFIC (flos prolifer)**, which produces flowers, and sometimes leaves, from its centre. For a particular <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of each of these kinds of luxuriance in flowers, see the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> **MULTIPLICATUS Flos**, **PLENUS Flos**, and **PROLIFER Flos**. Many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> orders of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> do not in any circumstances produce luxuriant flowers. Of this kind are the masqued flowers of Tournefort, excepting calve's-snot; the rough-leaved, umbelliferous, starry plants, and such as flower at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a>, of Ray: some umbelliferous flowers, however, are prolific. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEA">pea</a>-bloom, or butterfly-shaped flowers, are rarely rendered double; some instances, however, of luxuriance, are observed in a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of lady's finger, coromilla, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROOM">broom</a>. All luxuriant flowers are vegetable monsters. Such as are perfectly full, by which we <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of luxuriance, cannot be propagated by seeds; because these, for want of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPREGNATION">impregnation</a>, can never <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIPEN">ripen</a>. Full flowers therefore are very properly denominated by Linnæus *cunuchs*. This highest degree of luxuriance is very <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in carnation, lychnis, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ANEMONE">anemone</a>, stock, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> cress, rose, marsh marigold, ranunculus, violet, peony, and narcissus. Flowers which do not exclude all the stamens, perfect their seeds. Of this kind are poppy, fennel-flower, campanula, and some others. Some flowers, as those of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>-lily, fig-marigold, and cactus, have many rows or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of petals, without the number of stamens being in the least diminished. Such flowers are by no means to be reckoned luxuriant, in the slightest degree. Luxuriance in flowers is generally owing to excess of nourishment.

LUXURY

Pages 292-294

voluptuousness, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> an extravagant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a> in diet, dress, and equipage. Luxury, among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, prevailed to such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, that several laws were made to suppress, or at least limit it. The extravagance of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> began about the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIUM">Actium</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> excess till the reign of Galba. Peacocks, cranes of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a>, nightingales, venison, wild Luxury, and tame fowl, were considered as delicacies. A profusion of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> was the reigning <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. Whole wild boars were often served up, and sometimes they were filled with various small animals, and birds of different kinds: this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DISH">dish</a> they called the Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, in allusion to the wooden horse filled with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>. Fowls and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAME">game</a> of all sorts were served up in whole pyramids, piled up in dishes as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> as moderate tables. Lucullus had a particular name for each apartment; and in whatever room he ordered his servants to prepare the entertainment, they knew by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> the expense to which they were to go. When he supped in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>, the expence was fixed at 50,000 drachmae, that is 1250l. M. Antony provided eight boars for 12 guests. Vitellius had a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> silver platter, said to have cost a million of sesterces, called <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>'s buckler. In this he blended together the livers of gilt-heads, the brains of pheasants and peacocks, the tongues of phoenicopters, and the milt of lampreys. Caligula served up to his guests pearls of great value dissolved in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>; the same was done also by Clodius the son of Æsop the tragician. Apicius laid aside 90,000,000 of sesterces, besides a mighty revenue, for no other purpose but to be sacrificed to luxury; finding himself involved in debt, he looked over his accounts, and though he had the sum of 10,000,000 of sesterces still left, he poisoned himself for fear of being starved to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. The Roman laws to restrain luxury were Lex Orchia, Fannia, Didia, Licinia, Cornelia, and many others: But all these were too little; for as <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> increased amongst them, so did sensuality. What were the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of luxury entertained in England about two centuries ago, may be gathered from the following passage of Holinshed; who, in a discourse prefixed to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, speaking of the increase of luxury, says, "Neither do I speak this in reproach of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, God is my judge; but to show, that I do rejoice rather to see how God has blessed us with his good gifts, and to behold how that in a time wherein all things are grown to the most excessive prices, we yet do find means to obtain and achieve such furniture as heretofore was impossible. There are old men yet dwelling in the village where I remain, which have noted three things to be marvellously altered in England within their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a>. One is the multitude of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIMNEYS">chimneys</a> lately erected; whereas in their young days there were not above two or three, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> so many, in most uplandish <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of the realm (the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> houses, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANOR">manor</a> places of their lords, always excepted, and peradventure some great personages), but each made his fire against a reredoss [skreen] in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, where he dressed his meat and dined.—The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> is the great amendment of lodging; for, say they, our fathers and we ourselves have lain full oft upon straw pallets covered only with a sheet, under coverlets made of a dogswaine or horharris (to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> their own terms), and a good log under their head instead of a bolster.—If it were so that the father or goodman of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> had a matrass, or flock <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> and sheets, a sack of chaff to rest his head upon, he thought himself to be as well lodged as the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of the town. So well were they contented, that pillows (said they) were thought meet only Luxury only for women in childbirth; as for servants, if they had any sheet above them it was well; for seldom had they any under their bodies to keep them from pricking straws, that ran off through the canvas and their hardened <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIDES">hides</a>.—The third thing they tell of, is the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> of treene [wooden] platters into <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEWTER">pewter</a>, and wooden spoons into silver or tin; for so <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> were all sorts of treene vessels in old times, that a man should hardly find four pieces pewter (of which one was peradventure a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>) in a good <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a>'s house. Again, In times past, men were contented to dwell in houses builded of sallow, willow, &c., so that the use of oak was in a manner dedicated wholly unto churches, religious houses, princes palaces, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, &c. But now willow, &c., are rejected, and nothing but oak anywhere regarded; and yet see the change, for when our houses were builded of willow, then had we oaken men; but now that our houses are come to be made of oak, our men are not only become willow, but a great many altogether of straw, which is a sore <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a>. In these the courage of the owner was a sufficient defense to keep the house in safety; but now the assurance of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> must defend the men from robbing. Now have we many chimneys, and yet our tenderlins complain of rheums, catarrhs, and poses; then had we none but reredoses, and our heads did never ache. For as the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> in those days were supposed to be sufficient hardening for the timber of the house; so it was reputed a far better medicine to keep the goodman and his family from the quacks or posc; wherewith, as then, very few were acquainted. Again, Our pewterers in time past employed the use of pewter only upon dishes and pots, and a few other trifles for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>; whereas now they are grown into such exquisite cunning, that they can in a manner imitate by infusion any form or fashion of cup, dish, salt, bowl, or goblet, which is made by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOLDSMITH">goldsmith</a>'s craft, though they be ever so curious and very artificially forged. In some places beyond the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, a garnish of good flat English pewter (I say flat, because dishes and platters in my time began to be made deep, and like basons, and are indeed more convenient both for sauce and keeping the meat warm) is esteemed so precious as the like <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of vessels that are made of fine silver." Particular instances of luxury, in eating, however, might be adduced from an earlier <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, surpassing even the extravagance of the Romans. Thus, in the roth year of the reign of Edward IV. (1470), George Nevill, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARWICK">Warwick</a>, at his installment into the archiepiscopal see of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, entertained most of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> clergy; when his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">bill</a> of fare was 350 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of wheat, 350 tuns of ale, 104 tuns of wine, a pipe of spiced wine, 80 fat oxen, six wild bulls, 1004 weathers, 300 hogs, 300 calves, 3000 geese, 3000 capons, 300 pigs, 100 peacocks, 200 cranes, 200 kids, 2000 chickens, 4000 pigeons, 4000 rabbits, 204 bitterns, 4000 ducks, 200 pheasants, 500 partridges, 200 woodcocks, 400 plowers, 30 curlews, 100 quails, 1000 egrets, 200 rocs, 400 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUCKS">bucks</a>, does, and roebucks, 1506 hot venison pasties, 4000 <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DITTO">ditto</a>, 1000 dishes of jelly parted, 4000 dishes of jelly plain, 4000 cold custards, 2000 hot custards, 300 pikes, 300 breams, eight seals, four porpoises, 400 tarts. At this feast the earl of Warwick was <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a>, the earl of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEDFORD">Bedford</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>, and Lord Has- tings comptroller, with many more noble officers; 1000 servitors, 62 <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COOKS">cooks</a>, 515 menial apparitors in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a>.—But such was the fortune of the man, that after his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> prodigality he died in the most abject but unpitied poverty, vinctus jecuit in summa inopia. And as to dress, luxury in that article seems to have attained a great height <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> before Holinshed's time: For in the reign of Edward III. we find no fewer than <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> sumptuary laws passed in one session of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> to restrain it. It was enacted, that men servants of lords, as also of tradesmen and artisans, shall be content with one <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAL">meal</a> of fish or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>; and the other meals, daily, shall be of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, cheese, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a> and the like. Neither shall they use any ornaments of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMBROIDERY">embroidery</a>; nor their wives and daughters any veils above the price of twelvepence. Artisans and yeomen shall not wear cloth above 40s. the whole piece (the finest then being about 6l. per piece), nor the ornaments before named. Nor the women any veils of silk, but only those of thread made in England. Gentlemen under the degree of knights, not having 100l. yearly in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, shall not wear any cloth above 4½ marks the whole piece. Neither shall they or their females use cloth of gold, silver, or embroidery, &c. But esquires having 200l. per annum or upwards of rent, may wear cloths of five marks the whole piece of cloth; and they and their females may also wear stuff of silk, silver, ribbons, girdles, or furs. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">Merchants</a>, citizens, burglers, and artificers or tradesmen, as well of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> as elsewhere, who have goods and chattels of the clear value of 500l. and their females, may wear as is allowed to gentlemen and esquires of 100l. per annum. And merchants, citizens, and burgesses, worth above 1000l. in goods and chattels, may (and their females) wear the same as gentlemen of 200l. per annum. Knights of 200 marks yearly may wear cloth of six marks the cloth, but no higher; but no cloth of gold, nor furred with ermine: but all knights and ladies having above 400 marks yearly, up to 1000l. per annum, may wear as they please, ermine excepted; and they may wear ornaments of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEARL">pearl</a> and precious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> for their heads only. Clerks having degrees in cathedrals, colleges, &c., may wear as knights and esquires of the same income. Plowmen, carters, shepherds, and such like, not having 40s. value in goods or chattels, shall wear no sort of cloth but <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLANKET">blanket</a> and russet <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAWN">lawn</a> of 12d. and shall wear girdles and belts; and they shall only eat and drink suitable to their stations. And whosoever uses other apparel than is prescribed by the above laws shall forfeit the same.
