Concerning the general utility of luxury to a state, there is much <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> among <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> writers. Baron Montesquieu asserts, that luxury is necessary in monarchies, as in France; but ruinous to democracies, as in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>. With regard therefore to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, whose <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> is compounded of both <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, it is held to be a dubious question, how far private luxury is a public evil; and, as such, cognizable by public laws. And indeed our legislators have several times changed their sentiments as to this point; for formerly there were a number of penal laws existing to restrain excess in apparel, chiefly made in the reigns of Edward III., IV. and Henry VIII., a specimen of which we have inserted above. But all of them it appeared expedient to repeal at an after period. In fact, although luxury <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> increase according to the influx of wealth, it may not be for the general benefit of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> to impose, as in the above cited laws, an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> prohibition of every degree of it; yet, for the good of the public, it may be necessary that such as go beyond proper bounds in eating, drinking, and wearing what by no means is suitable to their station, should be taxed accordingly, could it be done without including those who have a better <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> to such indulgence. This is certainly, however, a point which should be maturely weighed before executed; and, in mercantile countries at least, such restraints may be found prejudicial, most likely impracticable, especially where true <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> is established. Sir William Temple observes, speaking of the trade and riches, and at the same time of the frugality of the Hollanders, "That some of our maxims are not so certain as current in politics: that encouragement of excess and luxury if employed in the consumption of native commodities, is of advantage to trade. It may be so to that which impoverishes, but not to that which enriches a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. It is indeed less prejudicial, if it lies in native than in foreign wares: but the humour of luxury and expense cannot stop at certain bounds; what begins in native will proceed to foreign commodities; and though the example arise among idle persons, yet the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> will run into all degrees, even of those men by whose industry the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> subsists. And besides, the more of our own we spend, the less shall we have to send abroad; and so it will come to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>, that while we drive a vast trade, yet, by buying much more than we sell, we shall come to be <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> at last."

LYBIA

Pages 294-294
or LIBYA, a name anciently given to all that part of Africa lying between the border of Egypt and the river Triton; and comprehending Cyrenaica, Marmarica, and the Regio Syrtica. See these articles. LYCÆUM, Auxtov, in antiquity, the name of a celebrated school or academy at Athens, where Aristotle explained his philosophy. The place was composed of porticoes and trees planted in the quincunx form, where the philosophers disputed walking. Hence philosophy of the Lyceum is used to signify the philosophy of Aristotle, or the Peripatetic philosophy. Suidas observes, that the Lyceum took its name from having been originally a temple of Apollo Lyceus; or rather a portico or gallery built by Lyceus son of Apollo; but others mention it to have been built by Pisistratus or Pericles. LYCÆUS, in Ancient Geography, a mountain of Arcadia, sacred to Jupiter; whence Jupiter Lycaeus (Pliny). Sacred also to Pan (Virgil); and hence Lycea, the rites performed to Pan on this mountain; which Evander carrying with him to Latium, were called Lupercale (Virgil).

LYCAON

Pages 294-294

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the first <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a>, son of Pelasgus and Meliboea. He built a town called Lycosura, on the top of Mount Lycaeus, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>. He had many wives, by whom he had a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> called Callisto, and 50 sons. He was succeeded on the throne by Nyctimus, the eldest of his sons. He lived about 1820 years before the Christian era.—Another king of Arcadia, celebrated for his cruelties. He was changed into a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WOLF">wolf</a> by Jupiter, because he offered <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> victims on the altar of the god <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAN">Pan</a>. Some <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> this metamorphosis to another cause. The sins of mankind, as they relate, were become so enormous, that Jupiter visited the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> to punish wickedness and impiety. He came to Arcadia, where he was announced as a god, and the people began to pay proper <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADORATION">adoration</a> to his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>. Lycaon, however, who used to sacrifice all strangers to his wanton cruelty, laughed at the pious prayers of his subjects; and to try the divinity of the god, he served up human <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> on his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>. This impiety so irritated Jupiter, that he immediately destroyed the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Lycaon, and changed him into a wolf.

LYCAONIA

Pages 294-294

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of the Hither <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, contained between Pamphylia to the south, Cappadocia to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, Pisidia and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a> to the west, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMENIA">Armenia</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a> to the east. Lycaones, the people. This country, though situated very near Mount Taurus, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of it on it, yet the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> reckoned it in Asia intra Taurum. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a>, anciently called Lycaonia (Stephanus).—Also an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Tiber, joined to Rome by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, and to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> by another, namely, the Cestius and Fabricius.

LYCHNIS

Pages 294-294
CAMPION, including also Catch-fly, &c.; a genus of plants belonging to the decandra class, and order pentagynia; and in the natural method ranking under the 22d order, Caryophyllæ. See Botany Index.

LYCIA

Pages 294-294

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASIA_MINOR"><a class="</a>xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>, bounded by the Mediterranean on the south, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARIA">Caria</a> on the west, Pamphylia on the east, and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>. It was anciently called Milyas and Tremile, from the Milyæ, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Solymi, a people of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, who came to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> there. The country received the name of Lycia from Lycus the son of Pandon, who established himself there. The inhabitants have been greatly commended by all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> for their sobriety and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>. They were conquered by Croesus <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Lydia, and afterwards by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYRUS">Cyrus</a>. Though they were subject to the power of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, yet they were governed by their own kings, and only paid a yearly tribute to the Persian monarch. They became <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Macedonian empire when Alexander came into the east, and afterwards were ceded to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of the Seleucidae. The country was reduced into a Roman <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Claudius.

LYCIUM

Pages 294-294

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 28th order, Lurideæ. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

LYCODONTES

Pages 294-294

the petrified <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> of the lupuspiscis, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WOLF">wolf</a>-fish, frequently found fossil. They are of different shapes; but the most <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> kind rise into a semibicicular form, and are hollow within, somewhat resembling an acorn-cup; this hollow is found sometimes empty, and sometimes filled with the stratum in which it is immersed. Many of them have an outer circle of a different <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> from the rest.

LYCOMEDES

Pages 294-295

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Scyros, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Ægean <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. He was son of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> and Parthenope. He was secretly intrusted with the care of young <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACHILLES">Achilles</a>, whom his mother Thetis had disguised in woman's clothes, to remove him from the Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, where she knew he must unavoidably perish. Lycomedes has rendered himself famous for his treachery to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THESEUS">Theseus</a>, who had implored his protection when. Lycomedes when driven from his throne of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> by the usurper Mnestheus. Lycomedes, as it is reported, either envious of the fame of his illustrious guest, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> bribed by the emissaries of Mnestheus, led Theseus to an elevated <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, on pretence to show him the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of his dominions, and perfidiously threw him <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> a precipice, where he was killed.

LYCOPERDON

Pages 295-295

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the cryptogamia class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. LYCOPERSICON. See Solanum, Botany Index.

LYCOPHRON

Pages 295-295

a famous Greek poet and grammarian, born at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLCHIS">Colchis</a> in Euboea, flourished about 304 B.C. and, according to Ovid, was killed by an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARROW">arrow</a>. He wrote 20 tragedies; but all his works are lost, except a poem entitled <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASSANDRA">Cassandra</a>, which contains a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> train of predictions, which he supposes to have been made by Cassandra, Priam's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>. This poem is extremely obscure. The best edition of it is that of Dr Potter, printed at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> in 1697, folio.

LYCOPODIUM

Pages 295-295
or Club-moss; a genus of plants belonging to the cryptogamia class. See Botany Index.

LYCOPOLIS

Pages 295-295
or Lycon, in Ancient Geography, so called from the worship of wolves. Lycopolita, the people; Lycopolitis, the district. There were two towns of this name, one in the Delta, or Lower Egypt, near the Mediterranean; the other in the Thebais, or Higher Egypt, in the northern part, to the west of the Nile.

LYCOPSIS

Pages 295-295

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 41st order, Asperifolioe. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

LYCOPUS

Pages 295-295

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the diandra class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 42d order, Verticillate. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

LYCURGIA

Pages 295-295

a festival observed by the Spartans, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of their lawgiver <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LYCURGUS">Lycurgus</a>, whom they honoured with a temple and anniversary sacrifice.

LYCURGUS

Pages 295-295

the celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a> of the Spartans, was the son of Eunomes <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPARTA">Sparta</a>.—He travelled to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, and even to the Indies, to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a> with the sages and learned men of those countries, and to learn their manners, their customs, and their laws. After the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Polydectes, who was king of Sparta, his widow offered the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> to Lycurgus, promising that she would make herself miscarry of the child of which she was pregnant, provided he would marry her; but Lycurgus nobly refused these advantageous offers, and afterwards contented himself with being <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> to his nephew Charillus, and restored to him the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> when he came of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>; but notwithstanding this regular and generous conduct, he was accused of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> to usurp the crown. This calumny obliged him to retire to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Crete, where he applied himself to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the laws and customs of nations. At his return to Lacedemon, he reformed the government: and, to prevent the disorders occasioned by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>, he prohibited the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver; placed all the citizens in a state of equality; and introduced the strictest <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a>, the most exact <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>, and those admirable laws which (a few excepted) have been celebrated by all historians. It is said, that, to engage the Lacedemonians to observe them inviolably, he made them <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> with an oath not to change any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of them till his return; and that he afterwards went to the island of Crete, where he killed himself, after having ordered that his ashes should be thrown into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, for fear lest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> his body should be carried to Sparta the Lacedemonians would think themselves absolved from their oath. He flourished about 870 B.C.

LYDGATE

Pages 295-295

John, called the Monk of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURY">Bury</a>; not, as Cibber conjectures, because he was a native of that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, for he was born about the year 1382, in the village of Lydgate: but because he was a monk of the Benedictine convent at St Edmund's-Bury. After studying some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in our English <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, he travelled to France and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>: and, having acquired a competent knowledge of the languages of those countries, he returned to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, where he opened a school, in which he instructed the sons of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> in polite literature. At what time he retired to the convent of St Edmund's-Bury, does not appear; but he was certainly there in 1415. He was living in 1446, aged about 66; but in what year he died is not known. Lydgate, according to Pits, was an elegant poet, a persuasive rhetorician, an expert mathematician, an acute <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, and a tolerable divine. He was a voluminous writer; and, considering the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> in which he lived, an excellent poet. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> is less obsolete, and his versification much more harmonious, than the language and versification of Chaucer, who wrote about half a century before him. He wrote, 1. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the Theban <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, printed at the end of Chaucer's works, 1561, 1602, 1687. 2. Poemation of good counsel; at the end of Chaucer's works. 3. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of Hector; London 1594, folio, printed by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROSS">Gross</a>, dedicated to Henry V. 4. Life of the blessed Virgin; printed by Caxton. 5. The proverbs of Lydgate upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of princes; printed by Wink. Word, London, 4to. 6. Dispute of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, the sheep, and the goose; printed in Caxton's Collect. 4to. 7. The temple of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>; among the works of Chaucer. 8. London lippenny; vide Stow's history, &c. &c. Besides an incredible <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of other poems and translations preserved in various <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a>, and of which the reader <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> find a catalogue in Bishop Tanner.

LYDIA

Pages 295-299

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASIA_MINOR"><a class="</a>xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>.—All the ancient writers tell us, that Lydia was first called Maeonia <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Meonia, from Meon <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a> and Lydia; and that it was known under no other denomination till the reign of Atys, when it began to be called Lydia from his son Lydus. Bochart finding in his learned collection of Phoenician words the verb luze, signifying "to <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>," and observing that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> we are speaking of is watered by the Maeander so famous for its windings, concludes that it was thence named Lydia, or Ludia. As to the ancient name of Mæonia, he takes it to be a Greek translation of the Phœnician word lud; wherein he agrees in some <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> with Stephanus, who derives the name of Mæonia from Maeon the ancient name of the Maeander. Some take the word mæonia to be a translation of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> word signifying "metal," because that country, say they, was in former times enriched above any other with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>. Though Lydia and Mæonia are by most authors indifferently used for one and the same country, yet they are sometimes distinguished; that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> where Mount Tmolus stood, watered by the Pactolus, being properly called Mæonia; and the other, lying on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, Lydia. This distinction is used by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, Callimachus, Dionysius, and other ancient writers. In after ages, when the Ionians, who had planted a colony on the coast of the Egean <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, began to make some <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, that part was called <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IONIA">Ionia</a>, and the name of Lydia given to the ancient Mæonia.—Lydia, according to Pliny, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, and other ancient geographers, was bounded by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSIA">Mysia</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARIA">Caria</a> on the south, by Phrygia Major on the east, and Ionia on the west, lying between the 37th and 39th degrees of north latitude. What the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> style the kingdom of Lydia was not confined within these narrow boundaries, but extended from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALYS">Halys</a> to the Egean sea. Pliny's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> includes Æolia, lying between the Hermus and the Caicus. As to the origin of the Lydians, Josephus, and after him all the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> writers, derive them from Lud, Shem's fourth son; but this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> has no other foundation than the similitude of names. Some of the ancients <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have the Lydians to be a mixed colony of Phrygians, Mysians, and Carians. Others finding some conformity in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> ceremonies between the Egyptians and Tuscanos who were a Lydian colony, conclude them, without any farther <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a>, to be originally Egyptians. All we know for certain is, that the Lydians were a very ancient <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, as is manifest from their very fables; for Atys, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TANTALUS">Tantalus</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PELOPS">Pelops</a>, Niobe, and Arachne, are all said to have been the children of Lydus. And Zanthus in his Lydiaca, quoted by Stephanus, informs us, that the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASCALON">Ascalon</a>, one of the five satrapies of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILISTINES">Philistines</a>, mentioned in the books of Joshua and the Judges, was built by one Ascalus a Lydian, whom Achiamus king of Lydia had appointed to command a body of troops which he sent, we know not on what occasion, into <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>. The Heraclidae, or kings of Lydia descended from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, began to reign before the Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>; and had been preceded by a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of sovereigns sprung from Atys, and hence styled Atyadæ; a strong <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the antiquity of that kingdom. The Lydians began very early to be ruled by kings, whose <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> seems to have been truly despotic, and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a>. We read of three distinct races of kings reigning over Lydia, viz. the Atyadæ, the Heraclidae, and the Mermnadæ. The Atyadæ were so called from Atys the son of Cotys, and grandson of Manes the first Lydian king. But the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of this family is obscure and fabulous. The Atyadæ were succeeded by the Heraclidae, or the descendants of Hercules. For Hercules being, by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the oracle, sold as a slave to Omphale a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of Lydia, to expiate the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> of Iphitus, had, during his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a>, by one of her slaves, a son named Cleostratus, whose grandson Argon was the first of the Heraclidae that ascended the throne of Lydia. This <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> is said to have reigned 505 years; the son succeeding the father for 22 generations. They began to reign about the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the Trojan war. The last of the family was the unhappy Candaules, who lost both his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and kingdom by his imprudence; an event of which we have the following account by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>. Candaules had a wife whom he passionately loved, and believed the most beautiful of her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a>. He extolled her charms to Gyges his favourite, whom he used to intrust with his most important affairs; and the more to convince him of her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, resolved to show her to him quite naked; he accordingly placed him in the porch of her chamber where the queen used to undress when she went to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>, ordering him to retire after he should have seen her, and take all possible care not to be observed. But notwithstanding all the caution he could <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, she plainly discovered him going out; and though she did not doubt but it was her husband's contrivance, yet she passed that night in a seeming tranquillity, suppressing her resentment till next morning, when she sent for Gyges, and resolutely told him that he must either by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> atone for the criminal <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> he had been guilty of, or put to death Candaules the contriver of it, and receive both her and the kingdom of Lydia for his reward. Gyges at first earnestly begged of her that she would not drive him to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of such a choice. But finding that he could not prevail with her, and that he must either kill his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> or die himself, he chose the former part of the alternative. Being led by the queen to the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where her husband had posted him the night before, he stabbed the king while he was asleep, married the queen, and took possession of the kingdom, in which he was confirmed by the answer of the Delphic oracle. The Lydians having taken up arms to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> the death of their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, an agreement was made between them and the followers of Gyges, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the oracle should declare him to be lawful king of Lydia, he should be permitted to reign; if not, he should resign the crown to the Heraclide. The answer of the oracle proving favourable to Gyges, he was universally acknowledged for lawful king of Lydia. Candaules is said to have purchased a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> painted by Bularchas, representing a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of the Magnetes, for its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>; a circumstance which shows how early the art of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> began to be in request, for Candaules was <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a>. Gyges having thus possessed himself of the kingdom of Lydia, sent many rich and valuable presents to the oracle of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DELPHOS">Delphos</a>; among others, six cups of gold weighing 30 talents, and greatly esteemed for the workmanship. He made war on <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILETUS">Miletus</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SMYRNA">Smyrna</a>, took the city of Colophon, and subdued the whole country of Troas. In his reign, and by his permission, the city of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABYDOS">Abydos</a> was built by the Milesians. Plutarch and other writers relate his accession to the crown of Lydia in a quite different manner, and tell us, without making any mention of the queen, that Gyges rebelled against Candaules and slew him in an engagement. In Gyges began the third race, race, called Mermnadæ; who were also, properly speaking, Heraclidæ, being descended from a son of Hercules by Omphale. Gyges reigned 38 years, and was succeeded by his son Ardyes. This prince carried on the war against the Milesians which his father had begun, and possessed himself of Priene, in those days a strong city. In his reign the Cimmerians invaded and overran all Asia Minor; but what battles were fought against the Lydians and these invaders, and with what success, we find no where mentioned. Herodotus only informs us, that in the time of Ardyes they possessed themselves of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDIS">Sardis</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> of Lydia, but could never reduce the castle. Ardyes reigned 49 years, and was succeeded by his son Sadyattes, who reigned 12 years, and warred most part of his reign with the Milesians. After him came his son Alyattes, who for the space of five years <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> the war which his father had begun against the Milesians, ravaging their country, and about <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a> time carrying away all their corn yearly, in order to oblige them, for want of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, to surrender their city, which he knew he could not reduce any other way, the Milesians being at that time masters of the sea. In the 12th year of this war the Lydians having set fire to the corn in the fields, the flames were carried, by a violent wind, which happened to blow at that time, to the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a> at Assesus, and burnt it <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the ground. Not long after, Alyattes falling sick, sent to consult the oracle at Delphos; which refused to return any answer till such time as the king should rebuild the temple of Minerva at Assesus. Alyattes, thus warned, despatched ambassadors to Miletus, enjoining them to conclude a truce with the Milesians till the temple should be rebuilt. On the arrival of the ambassadors, Thrasybulus, then king of Miletus, commanded all the corn that was at that time in the city to be brought into the market-place, ordering the citizens to banquet in public, and revel as if the city were plentifully stored with all manner of provisions. This stratagem Thrasybulus practised, to the end that the ambassadors seeing such quantities of corn, and the people everywhere diverting themselves, might acquaint their master with their affluence, and divert him from pursuing the war. As Thrasybulus had designed, so it happened; for Alyattes, who believed the Milesians greatly distressed for provisions, receiving a different account from his ambassadors, changed the truce into a lasting peace, and ever afterwards lived in amity and friendship with Thrasybulus and the Milesians. He was succeeded, after a reign of 57 years, by his son Croesus, whose uninterrupted prosperity, in the first years of his reign, far eclipsed the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of his predecessors. He was the first that made war on the Ephesians, whose city he besieged and took, notwithstanding their consecrating it to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a>, and fastening the walls by a rope to her temple, which was <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> stadia distant from the city. After the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of Ephesus, he attacked, under various pretences, the Ionians and Æolians, obliging them, and all the other Greek states of Asia, to pay him a yearly tribute. Having met with such extraordinary success by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, the Lydian prince determined to render his power equally conspicuous by sea. For this purpose he thought seriously of equipping a fleet; with which he purposed to invade and conquer the Grecian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> directly fronting his dominions. But this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, which, considering the slow progress in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> power among the nations most diligent to attain it, would probably have failed of success, was prevented by the advice of a philosophical traveller, conveyed in such a lively turn of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> as easily changed the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> of the king. Bias of Priene in Ionia, some say Pittacus of Mitylene in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LESBOS">Lesbos</a>, while he travelled after the Grecian <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, from curiosity and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of knowledge, was presented to Croesus at the Lydian <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>; and being asked by that prince what news from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>; he answered with a republican freedom, that the islanders had collected powerful squadrons of cavalry with an intention of invading Lydia. "May the gods <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> (said Croesus), that the Greeks, who are unacquainted with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORSEMANSHIP">horsemanship</a>, should attack the disciplined valour of the Lydian cavalry; there would soon be an end to the contest." "In the same manner (replied Bias), as if the Lydians, who are totally unexperienced in naval affairs, should invade the Grecians by sea." Struck by the acuteness of this unexpected observation, Croesus desisted from his intended expedition against the islands, and instead of employing new means for extending his conquests, determined peaceably to enjoy the laurels which he had won, and to display the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> which he had attained. But his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> was soon after allayed by the death of his favourite son Atys, who was unfortunately killed at the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHASE">chase</a> of a wild boar. For this loss he continued disconsolate for two years and in a state of inaction, till the conquests of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYRUS">Cyrus</a>, and growing power of the Persians, roused up his martial spirit, and diverted his mind to other thoughts. He apprehended that the success which attended Cyrus in all his undertakings, might at last prove dangerous to himself, and therefore resolved to put a stop, if possible, to his progress. In taking this resolution, which might probably be attended with the most important consequences, he was desirous to learn the will of heaven concerning the issue of the war. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-ORACLES">oracles</a> which he consulted were those of Branchis in Ionia, of Hammon in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBYA">Libya</a>, and of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DELPHI">Delphi</a> in Greece. Among these respected shrines, the oracle of Delphi maintained its ascendant, as the most faithful interpreter of fate. Croesus was fully persuaded of its veracity; and desirous generously to compensate for the trouble which he had already given, and still meant to give, the priests of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>, he sacrificed 3000 oxen to the god, and adorned his shrine with dedications equally valuable for the workmanship and for the materials; precious vessels of silver, ewers of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> beautifully inlaid and enamelled; various ornaments of pure gold, particularly a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> lion weighing ten talents, and a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> figure three cubits or near five feet <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. In return for these magnificent presents, the oracle, in ambiguous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, flattered Croesus with obtaining an easy victory over his enemies, and with enjoying a long life and a prosperous reign. The god at the same time enjoined him to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with the most powerful of the Grecian states. Elevated with these favourable predictions of Apollo, Croesus prepared to yield a ready obedience to the only condition required on his part for the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCOMPLISHMENT">accomplishment</a> of his aspiring purpose. Not deeming himself sufficiently acquainted with the affairs of Greece, to know what particular particular republic was meant by the oracle, he made particular inquiry of those best informed concerning the state of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; and discovered, that among all the members of the Grecian confederacy, the Athenians and Lacedemonians were justly entitled to the pre-eminence. In order to learn which of these communities deserved the epithet of most powerful, it was necessary to send ambassadors into Greece. The Lydians despatched with this important <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>, soon discovered that the Athenians after having been long harassed by internal dissensions, were actually governed by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PISISTRATUS">Pisistratus</a>. The Spartans, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, though anciently the worst regulated of all the Grecian communities, had enjoyed <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> peace and foreign prosperity ever since they had adopted the wise institutions of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LYCURGUS">Lycurgus</a>. After that memorable <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, they had repeatedly conquered the warlike Argives, triumphed over the hardy Arcadians; and notwithstanding the heroic exploits of Aristomenes, subdued and enslaved their unfortunate rivals of Messene. To the Lydian ambassadors, therefore, the Spartan republic appeared to be pointed out by the oracle, as the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a> whose alliance they were enjoined to solicit. Having repaired accordingly to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPARTA">Sparta</a>, they were introduced not only to the kings and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, but, as the importance of the negociation required, to the general <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of the Lacedemonians, to whom they, in few words, declared the object of their commission; "We are sent, O Lacedemonians! by Croesus, king of the Lydians and of many other nations, who being commanded by the oracle of Apollo to seek the friendship of the most powerful people of Greece, now summons you, who justly merit that epithet, to become his faithful allies, in obedience to the will of the god whose authority you acknowledge." The Lacedemonians, pleased with the alliance of a warlike king, and still more with the fame of their valour, readily accepted the proposal. To the strict connexion of an offensive and defensive <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a>, they joined the more respected ties of sacred hospitality. A few years before this transaction, they had sent to purchase gold at Sardis for making a statue of Apollo. Croesus had on that occasion gratuitously supplied their want. Remembering this generosity, they gave the Lydian ambassadors at their departure, as a present for their master, a vessel of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> containing 300 amphoras (above 12 hogsheads), and beautifully carved on the outside with various forms of animals. Croesus, having thus happily accomplished the design recommended by the oracle, was eager to set out upon his intended expedition. He had formerly entered into alliance with Amasis king of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, and Labynetus king of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a>. He had now obtained the friendship of the most warlike nation of Europe. The newly raised power of Cyrus and the Persians seemed incapable of resisting such a formidable confederacy. Elevated with these flattering <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of his own invincible greatness, Croesus waited not to attack the Persian dominions until he had collected the strength of his allies. The sanguine impetuosity of his temper, unexperienced in adversity, unfortunately precipitated him into <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> no less ruinous than daring. Attended only by the arms of Lydia, and a numerous band of mercenaries, whom his immense wealth enabled him at any time to call into his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, he marched towards the river Halys; and having crossed with much difficulty that deep and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> stream, entered the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Cappadocia, which formed the western frontier of the Median dominions. That unfortunate country soon experienced all the calamities of invasion. The Pterian plain, the most beautiful and the most fertile district of Cappadocia, was laid waste; the ports of the Euxinoe, as well as several inland cities, were plundered; and the inoffensive inhabitants were either put to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> or dragged into captivity. Encouraged by the unresisting softness of the natives of those parts, Croesus was eager to push forwards; and if Cyrus did not previously meet him in the field, he had determined to proceed in triumph to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>. Against this dangerous resolution he was in vain exhorted by a Lydian named Sandanis; who, when asked his opinion of the war, declared it with that freedom which the princes of the east have in every <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> permitted, amidst all the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> and caprices of despotic power, to men distinguished by the gifts of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>. "You are preparing, O king, to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> against a people who <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> a laborious and a miserable life; whose daily subsistence is often denied them, and is always scanty and precarious; who drink only <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and who are clothed with the skins of wild beasts. What can the Lydians <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> by the conquest of Persia; they who enjoy all the advantages of which the Persians are destitute? For my part, I deem it a blessing of the gods, that they have not excited the warlike poverty of these miserable barbarians to invade and plunder the luxurious wealth of Lydia." The moderation of this advice was rejected by the fatal presumption of Croesus; who confounding the dictates of experienced <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> suggestions of pusillanimity, dismissed the counsellor with contempt. Meanwhile, the approach of Cyrus, who was not of a temper to permit his dominions to be ravaged with impunity, afforded the Lydian king an opportunity of bringing the war to a more speedy issue than by his intended expedition into Persia. The <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of Cyrus gradually augmented on his march: the tributary princes cheerfully contributing with their united strength towards the assistance of a master whose valour and generosity they admired, and who now took arms to protect the safety of his subjects, as well as to support the grandeur of his throne. Such was the rapidity of his movement, especially after being informed of the destructive ravages of the enemy in Cappadocia, that he arrived from the shores of the Caspian to those of the Euxine sea before the army of Croesus had provided the necessaries for their journey. That prince, when apprised of the neighbourhood of the Persians, encamped on the Pterian plain; Cyrus likewise encamped at no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> distance; frequent skirmishes happened between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> troops; and at length a general engagement was fought with equal fury and perseverance, and only terminated by the darkness of night. The loss on both sides hindered a renewal of the battle. The numbers, as well as the courage of the Persians, much exceeded the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> of Croesus. As they discovered not any intention to harass his retreat, he determined to move back towards Sardis, to spend the winter in the amusements of his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LACE">lace</a>; and after summoning his numerous allies to his standard, to take the field early in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> with such increase of force as seemed sufficient to overpower the Persians. But this design was defeated by the careful vigilance of Cyrus. That experienced leader allowed the enemy to retire without molestation; carefully informing himself of every step which they took, and of every measure which they seemed determined to pursue. Patiently watching the opportunity of a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> revenge, he waited until Croesus had re-entered his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, and had disbanded the foreign mercenaries, who composed the most numerous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of his army. It then seemed the proper time for Cyrus to put his Persians in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>; and such was his celerity, that he brought the first news of his own arrival in the plain of Sardis. Croesus, whose firmness might well have been shaken by the imminence of this unforeseen danger, was not wanting on the present occasion to the duties which he owed to his fame and the lustre of the Lydian throne. Though his mercenaries were disbanded, his own subjects, who served him from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a>, who had been long accustomed to victory, and who were animated with a high <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of national <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, burned with a desire of enjoying an opportunity to check the daring insolence of the invaders. Croesus indulged and encouraged this generous ardour. The Lydians in that age fought on horseback, armed with long spears; the strength of the Persians consisted in infantry. They were so little accustomed to the use of horses, that camels were almost the only animals which they employed as beasts of burden. This circumstance suggested to a Mede, by name Harpagus, a stratagem, which being communicated to Cyrus, was immediately adopted with approbation by that prince. Harpagus, having observed that horses had a strong aversion to the shape and smell of camels, advised the Persian army to be drawn up in the following order: All the camels which had been employed to carry baggage and provisions were collected into one body, arranged in a long line fronting the Lydian cavalry. The foot <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> of the Persians were posted immediately behind the line, and placed at a due distance. The Median <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> (for a few squadrons of these followed the standard of Cyrus) formed the rear of the army. As the troops on both sides approached to join battle, the Lydian cavalry, terrified at the unusual appearance of the camels, mounted with men in arms, were thrown into disorder, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> their heads, endeavoured to escape from the field. Croesus, who perceived the confusion, was ready to despair of his fortune; but the Lydians, abandoning their horses, prepared with uncommon bravery to attack the enemy on foot. Their courage deserved a better fate; but unaccustomed as they were to this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of fighting, they were received and repelled by the experienced valour of the Persian infantry, and obliged to take refuge within the fortified strength of Sardis, where they imagined themselves secure. The walls of that city bid defiance to the rude art of attack, as then practised by the most warlike nations. If the Persian army should invest it, the Lydians were provided with provisions for several years; and there was reason to expect, that in a few months, and even weeks, they would receive such assistance from Egypt, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLONIA">Babylonia</a>, and Greece (to which countries they had already sent ambassadors), as would oblige the Persians to raise the siege. The Lydian ministers despatched into Greece met with great sympathy from the Spartans. That people were particularly observant of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> of treaties; and while they punished their enemies with unexampled severity, they behaved with generous compassion towards those whom they had once accepted for allies. They immediately resolved therefore to send him a speedy and effectual relief; and for this purpose assembled their troops, made ready their vessels, and prepared every thing necessary for the expedition. The valour of the Spartans might perhaps have upheld the sinking empire of Lydia; but before their armament could set sail, Croesus was no longer a sovereign. Notwithstanding the strength of Sardis, that city had been taken by storm on the 20th <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the siege; the walls having been scaled in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>, which appearing altogether inaccessible, was too carelessly guarded. This was effected by the enterprise of Hyreades a Mede, who accidentally observed a centinel descend part of the rock in order to recover his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HELMET">helmet</a>. Hyreades was a native of the mountainous province of Mardia, and being accustomed to clamber over the dangerous precipices of his native country, resolved to try his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> in passing the rock upon which he had discovered the Lydian. The design was more easily accomplished than he had reason to expect; emulation and success encouraged the bravest of the Persians to follow his example; these were supported by greater numbers of their countrymen; the garrison of Sardis was surprised; the citadel stormed; the rich capital of Lower Asia subjected to the vengeful rapacity of an indignant victor. Thus ended the ancient kingdom of Lydia, which continued subject to the Persians till they also were conquered by the Macedonians. For the fate of the Lydian monarch, see the article CROESUS.

LYDIAT

Pages 299-299

THOMAS, a learned English divine, born in 1572, and educated at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. About the year 1609, he became acquainted with Dr James Usher, afterwards archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMAGH">Armagh</a>, who carried him to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>. He was at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> for about two years, after which he returned to England; and the rectory of Alkrington becoming vacant, he was presented to it; but at length, being engaged for the debts of a near relation, which for the present he was unable to pay, having before spent his patrimony in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> several books, he was sent to prison; and was confined at Oxford, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENCH">Bench</a>, and elsewhere, till Sir William Boswell, a generous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of learned men, Dr Robert Pink, warden of New college, Bishop Usher, and Dr Laud, discharged the debt. In the civil wars, he suffered much in his rectory of Alkrington from the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> party; was four times pillaged to the value of at least 70l.; and was forced for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a year together to borrow a shirt to shift himself. He died in 1646. He wrote some pieces in English, and many works in Latin, on <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">chronology</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>.

LYDIUS LAPIS

Pages 299-300

in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>; the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> used by way of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOUCHSTONE">touchstone</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver, and called by some Heraclius <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPIS">lapis</a>; both of which names were also applied by the ancients to the loadstone; and hence has arisen Lydius no small misunderstanding of their works. Pliny has observed, that both the loadstone and touchstone were at times called Lydium and Heracleus lapis. The true lapis Lydium, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the touchstone, was anciently found only in the river Tmolus; but was afterwards found in many other places, and is now very <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in many of the German <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>. The ancients give us very remarkable and circumstantial accounts of the uses they made of it; and it is plain they were able to discern the alloys of gold by means of it with very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> exactness. We at present <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> several different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> under this name, and for the same purpose. In <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, a green marble called verdello, is most frequently used; and with us, very frequently small pieces of basalt.

LYGEUM

Pages 300-300

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the triandria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the fourth order, Graminae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

LYGII

Pages 300-300

LIGII, Lugii, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Logiones, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a people of Germany, to the west of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VISTULA">Vistula</a>, where it forms a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> like a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRESCENT">crescent</a>; Ligii, (Dio); Lugii, (Strabo); Logiones, (Zo-imus). Their name Lugii is conjectured to be derived from their mutually <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> confederacy or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a>. The Vistula was their boundary to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, east, and south, with Mount Ascburgius to the west. Now the whole of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> lies in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, on this side the Vistula. LYING-IN WOMEN. See <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MIDWIFERY">Midwifery</a>. LYING-to, or Lying-by, the situation of a ship, when she is retarded in her course, by arranging the sails in such a manner as to counteract each other with nearly an equal effort, and render the ship almost immoveable, with respect to her progressive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, or headway. A ship is usually brought to by the main and fore top sails, one of which is laid <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABACK">aback</a>, whilst the other is full; so that the latter pushes the ship forward, whilst the former resists this impulse, by forcing her astern. This is particularly practised in a general engagement, when hostile fleets are drawn up in two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> opposite each other. It is also used to wait for some other ship, either approaching or expected; or to avoid pursuing a dangerous course, especially in dark or foggy <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>.

LYME-REGIS

Pages 300-300

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> port town of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DORSETSHIRE">Dorsetshire</a> in England, 148 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It lies near the sea, on the very borders of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, in a cavity between two rocky hills, which makes it difficult of access. As it lies on the declivity of a hill, the houses make a good show, rising one above another; and some of them are built of free-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, and covered with blue slate. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of inhabitants in 1811 was estimated at 1925. The corporation consists of a mayor (who is <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of peace during his mayoralty and the year after, and in the third year both justice and coroner), a recorder, 15 <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> burgesses, and a town clerk. This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> had formerly a very flourishing trade to France, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, the Straits, Newfoundland, and the West Indies; during which, the customs amounted some years to 16,000l. But it stands on such a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> steep rock, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> are obliged to load and unload their goods at a place a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> off, called the Cobb, originally built in the reign of Edward III. which costs a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> sum to maintain, but forms such a harbour as perhaps is not to be equalled in the world, the ships being sheltered by a high thick stone wall, raised in the main sea Lime regis, a good way from the shore, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> enough for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a> and warehouses, and the customhouse officers have one Lyncurium upon it. The cellars of the low <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the town, near the sea, are however often overflowed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">tides</a> 10 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 12 feet. There are guns planted for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> both of the Cobb and of the town, the shore here being very proper for batteries. The customhouse stands on pillars, with the corn market under it. There is an alms-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a>-street, also Presbyterian and Anabaptist meeting-houses. The town <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a> is near Broad-street. The church stands at the east end of the town on a rising ground. The market here is on Friday, and there are two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> in the year. We read, that in 774, the Saxon <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> Kinwulf gave <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> hereabouts to the church of Sherborn, for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> there to supply its necessities. At this place the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Monmouth landed in 1685. A few years ago above 2000l. worth of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a> of Char. I. and II., were discovered by some labourers.

LYMINGTON

Pages 300-300

a borough town of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAMPSHIRE">Hampshire</a> in England, 97 miles south-west of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It stands about a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> from the channel running between the main <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Wight; and has a harbour for vessels of considerable burden. The tide flows near a mile above the town. It has a market on Saturdays; and sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> in 1811 was estimated at 2641.

LYMPH

Pages 300-300

a fine colourless fluid, separated in the body from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of blood, and contained in peculiar vessels called lymphatics. See Anatomy. LYMPHÆA, were <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> caves <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> grottos amongst the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, furnished with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many tubes, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a>, and various hydraulic <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> through which the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> gushed out upon the spectators unexpectedly whilst they were admiring the beautiful arrangement of the shell-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> in the grotto.

LYMPHATI

Pages 300-300

was a name given by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> to such as were seized with madness. It is supposed to be used for Nymphati, because the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> imagined that every person who had the misfortune to see a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NYMPH">Nymph</a> was instantly struck with phrenzy. Lymphati may indeed signify "madmen," as derived from lympha, "<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>," over which element the Nymphs were thought to preside: But it appears most likely, that distracted people were called lymphati, from the circumstance of madmen's being affected with the hydrophobia <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> dread of water after the bite of a mad dog; for this peculiarity, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of canine madness, was unknown to the Romans.

LYNCEUS

Pages 300-300

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, one of the Argonauts, who went with Jason in the expedition to obtain the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEECE">fleece</a>. He was of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> to the Argonauts, by enabling them to avoid the sand banks and rocks they found in their way. The poets say, that Lynceus had so piercing a sight, that it could not only penetrate to the bottom of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, but even to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELL">hell</a>. Some mythologists suppose, that this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> is taken from Lynceus's skill in observing the stars, and discovering the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver concealed in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>.

LYNCURIUM

Pages 300-301

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> thought to be the same with with the tourmalin. The name is derived from λύκος, "lynx," and γένος, "urine."

LYNCURIUS LAPIS

Pages 301-301

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> capable of producing <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MUSHROOMS">mushrooms</a>. In the Ephemerides of the Curious, we find mention made of a stone, so called by Dr John George Wolckamerus, who <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> one in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, which never ceases to produce in a few days mushrooms of an excellent flavour by the most simple and easy <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> imaginable. "It is (says he) of the bigness of an ox's head, rough and uneven on its surface, and on which also are perceived some clefts and crevices. It is <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> in some parts, and in others of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> and grayish <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. Internally it is porous, and nearly of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the pumice-stone, but much heavier; and it contains a small piece of flint, which is so incorporated with it as to appear to have been formed at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the stone itself received its form. This gives room to judge, that those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> have been produced by a fat and viscid juice, which has the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of indurating whatever <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> it filtrates into. The stone here spoken of, when it has been lightly covered with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and sprinkled with warm <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, produces mushrooms of an exquisite flavour, which are usually round, sometimes oval, and whose borders, by their inflexions and different curvities, represent in some <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> ears. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> colour of these mushrooms is sometimes yellowish, and sometimes of a bright purple; but they are always disseminated with different spots, of a deep <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> colour, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>; and when these spots are recent, and still in full bloom, they produce a very agreeable effect to the sight. But what appears admirable is, that the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the stalk which remains adhering to the stone, when the mushroom has been separated from it, grows gradually hard, and petrifies in time, so that it seems that this fungites restores to the stone the nutritive juice it received from it, and that it thus contributes to its increase." John Baptist Porta pretends, that this stone is found in several parts of Italy; and that it is not only to be met with at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, taken out of Mount <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VESUVIUS">Vesuvius</a>, but also on Mount Pantherico, in the principality of Arellino; on Mount Garganus, in Apulia; and on the summits of some other very <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. He adds, that the mushrooms which grow on those sorts of stones, and are usually called *fungi lynceuri*, have the property of dissolving and breaking the stone of the kidneys and bladder; and that, for this purpose, nothing more is required than to dry them in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>, and being reduced to powder, to make the patient fasting, take a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of this powder in a glass of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> wine, which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> so cleanse the excretory ducts of the urine, that no stones will ever after be collected in them. As to the form of those mushrooms, their root is stony, uneven, divided according to its longitudinal <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, and composed of fibres as fine as hairs, interwoven one with another. Their form, on first <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHOOTING">shooting</a> out, resembles a small bladder, scarce then larger than the bud of a vine; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> in this state they are squeezed between the fingers, an aqueous subacid liquor issues out. When they are at their full growth, their pedicle is of a finger's length, larger at top than at bottom, and becomes insensibly slenderer in proportion as it is nearer the earth. These mushrooms are also formed in an umbrella, and variegated with an infinity of little specks situated very near one another. They are smooth and even on the upper part, but underneath leafy like the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> mushrooms. Their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> is likewise very agreeable, and the sick are not debarred eating of them when they have been dressed in a proper manner. Curiosity having prompted some naturalists and physicians to submit these stones to a chemical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a>, in order to be more competent judges of the uses they might be put to in medicine, there first came forth, by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a>, an insipid water, and afterwards a spirituous liquor. The retort having been heated to a certain point, there arose an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, which had nearly the smell and taste of that of guaiacum; and a very acrid <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> was extracted from the ashes.

LYNN-REGIS

Pages 301-302

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a>, in England, distant 98 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It is a handsome, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, well-built <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. It was a borough by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESCRIPTION">prescription</a> in 1298. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> John, on account of its adherence to him against the barons, made it a free borough, with large privileges. He appointed it a provost, and gave it a large silver cup of 73 ounces doubly gilt and enamelled, and a large silver <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> that is carried before the mayor; though this last, according to some, is Henry VIII's sword, which he gave to the town when it came into his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> with the bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWICH">Norwich</a>; after which it was called King's Lynn, whereas before it was Bishop's Lynn. Henry III, made it a mayor town, for its serving him against the barons. It has had 15 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> charters; and is governed by a mayor, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a>, under-steward, recorder, 12 aldermen, and 18 <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> men. It has two churches, besides St Nicholas, a chapel of ease to St Margaret's, a Presbyterian and a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUAKERS">Quakers</a> meeting-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, with a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDEWELL">bridewell</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> workhouse, and several almshouses, and a free school.
