In September 1741 the spires of its two churches were both blown <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by a storm of <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>; and that of St Margaret's, which was 193 feet in height, having <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> in the body of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, it has been since rebuilt, towards which King George II gave 1000l. and the late <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Orford, then Sir Robert Walpole, 500l. This church was formerly an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>, and afterwards one of the largest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>-churches in England. The town house, called Trinity-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, is a noble old fabric; and so is the Exchange, which is of free-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, with two orders of columns. St Nicholas's chapel is very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, and reckoned one of the fairest and largest of the kind in England. It has a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELL">bell</a> tower of free stone, and an octagonal spire over it, both which together are 170 feet from the ground. There is a library in it that was erected by subscription; and there is another at St Margaret's. Here have been formerly several monasteries; but the only fabric remaining that belongs to any <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> order is the Gray-friars steeple, a noted landmark. The situation of this town, near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of the Ouse into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, after having received several other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, of which some are navigable, gives it an opportunity of extending its trade into eight different countries; by which many considerable cities and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, viz. Peterborough, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELY">Ely</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAMFORD">Stamford</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEDFORD">Bedford</a>, St Ives, Huntingdon, St Neot's, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHAMPTON">Northampton</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, St Edmundsbury, and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUCKS">Bucks</a>, as well as the inland parts of Norfolk and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>, are supplied with heavy goods, not only from our own produce, Lynn regis produce, as coals and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a>, but also of merchandise imported from abroad, especially wine; of which two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>, viz. coals and wine, this is the greatest port for importation of any place on all the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of England; and those wherein the Lynn <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> more largely than any town in England, except London, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a>, and Newcastle. In return for this, Lynn receives back all the corn which the counties <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> mentioned produce, for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a>; and therefore sends more of it abroad than any port except <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HULL">Hull</a>. The foreign trade of the merchants here, is very considerable, especially to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>, and the Baltic, and also to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>; and formerly they drove a good trade to France, till it was turned off, by treaties on one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and by prohibitions, high duties, &c. on the other, to Spain and Portugal. The harbour is safe when ships are in it, but difficult to enter by reason of the many flats and shoals in the passage; which, however, are well buoyed, and good pilots are always ready. The town consists of about 2400 houses; and appears to have been very strong, by the ruins of the works demolished in the civil wars. St Ann's <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATFORM">platform</a> at the north end mounts 12 <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> guns, and commands all the ships passing near the harbour: and towards the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, besides the wall, there is a ditch. Four rivulets run through the town; and the tide of the Ouse, which is about as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> here as the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a> at London <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, rises 20 feet perpendicular. In the great market-place a statue was erected in 1686 to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of King James II. There is another spacious market-place, adorned with a statue of King William III. and a fine <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOME">dome</a> and gallery round it, supported by 16 pillars. The market-house is of free-stone, supported by 16 columns, and is 70 feet high, erected on four steps, neatly adorned with <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, &c. Every first Monday in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a>, the mayor, aldermen, preachers, &c. meet to hear and determine all controversies amicably, for preventing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>-suits. This was first established in 1588, and is called The Feast of Reconciliation. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> are on Tuesdays and Saturdays; and it has two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a>; one of which, beginning Feb. 14, lasts for a fortnight, and is called Lynn mart; the other is a cheese fair on Oct. 6. The adherence of this town to King John and to Henry VIII., as above mentioned, are not the only instances of its loyalty to its sovereigns; for, in the late civil wars, it held out for King <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I., and sustained a formal siege of above 18,000 men of the parliament <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> for above three weeks; but, for want of relief, was obliged to surrender, and submit to the terms of paying 10s. a-head for every inhabitant, and a month's pay to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> the town from plunder. There are more gentry, and consequently more gaiety, in this town than in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YARMOUTH">Yarmouth</a> or even Norwich; there being such plenty of eatables and drinkables, that Spelman says, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CERES">Ceres</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a> seem to have established their magazines at this place; the east side abounding with corn, sheep, rabbits, hares, &c. the west side with cheese, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle, swans, and the wild-fowl common to marshes, besides the abundance of sea and river fish; so that he thinks there is no place in Great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, has such a variety in so small a compass of ground. At a small distance from the town, stands a mount, called the Lady's or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> Mount, which was once a chapel dedicated to the Virgin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, which was a resting-place for pilgrims on their way towards her convent at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WALSINGHAM">Walsingham</a>. The king's staith-yard, or quay, where the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the imported wines is landed and put into large vaults, is a handsome <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>. People <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> hence into the fen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and over the famous washes into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a> in boats, which are often lost, by venturing out at an improper season and without guides. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> in 1811 was 10,259. LYNX. See Felis, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">Mammalia</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. LYON King of Arms. See King; and Law, No civii. 16. This office is of great antiquity and respect in Scotland; and although the precise <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of its <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> is unknown, yet it must have been as early as the introduction of armorial figures as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> marks of gentility and distinction into this country, which was in the 12th century. His regalia are, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, with a crimson velvet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>, a gold tassel, and an ermine lining; a velvet robe reaching to his feet, with the arms of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> embroidered thereon before and behind in the proper tinctures; a triple row of gold chain round his neck, with an oval gold medal pendant thereto, on one side of which is the royal <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a>, and on the other St Andrew with his cross enamelled in proper colours, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATON">baton</a> of gold enamelled green, powdered with the badges of the kingdom. The <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> lyon's <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> is superior to that of any other king of arms, as he holds his office immediately from the sovereign by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> under the great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>; whereas the kings of arms in England are deputies to the earl marshal, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> under his authority. Formerly Scotland was divided into two provinces, the one on the north and the other on the south side of Forth; and these provinces were under the management of two deputies appointed by the lord lyon, to superintend the execution of all the business of his office. Before the Revolution, the lord lyon, at his admission into office, was most solemnly crowned by the sovereign or his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMISSIONER">commissioner</a>, in presence of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, the officers of state, and other great men, after a suitable sermon preached in the royal chapel; and his crown was of the same form with the imperial crown of the kingdom. On solemn occasions he wears the regalia above described; at all other times he wears the oval gold medal or badge on his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, suspended by a broad green ribbon. He has the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> disposal of all the offices in his own <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, and of the heralds and pursuivants places. The messengers at arms throughout Scotland are also created by him, and are amenable to his jurisdiction. And the powers vested in him by his commission are the same with those of the sovereign in all matters relative to the marks of gentility.

LYONET

Pages 302-303
Peter, an ingenious naturalist, and member of several learned societies, was born at Maestricht, and was descended from a very ancient and respectable family of Lorrain. He had scarcely attained his seventh year before he displayed an uncommon strength and agility in all bodily exercises; but he was not less diligent in the improvement of his mind. Being placed at the Latin school, he learned chronology, and exercised himself in Latin, Greek, and French poetry, as also in Hebrew, logic, and the Cartesian physics. He was particularly fond of the study of languages, Lyons, languages, whereof he understood no less than nine, living and dead. Having entered the university of Leyden, he studied the Newtonian philosophy, geometry, algebra, &c.; but his father (who was a clergyman), desiring he should attach himself to divinity, he reluctantly abandoned the former studies, as his passion for them was not easily to be overcome. He at the same time applied himself to anatomy, and also to music and drawing. He began afterwards to practise sculpture; and performed several pieces in wood, some of which are preserved, and have been greatly admired by the artists. After this, he betook himself to drawing portraits of his friends from life; wherein, after three or four months practice, he became a great proficient. Having attained the degree of candidate in divinity, he resolved to study law, to which he applied himself with so much zeal, that he was promoted at the end of the first year. Arrived at the Hague, he undertook the study of deciphering; and became secretary of the cyphers, translator of the Latin and French languages, and patent-master to their High Mightinesses. Meanwhile, having taken a strong liking to the study of insects, he undertook an historical description of such as are found about the Hague, and to that end collected materials for several volumes; and having invented a method of drawing adapted thereto, he enriched this work with a great number of plates, universally admired by all the connoisseurs who had seen them. In the year 1724 was printed at the Hague a French translation of a German work, the 'Theology of Insects,' by Mr Lesser. Love of truth engaged by Mr Lyonet to defer the publication of this above-mentioned description, and to make some observations on that work, to which he has added two most beautiful plates, engraved from his designs. This performance caused his merit to be universally known and admired. The celebrated M. de Reaumur had the above translation reprinted at Paris, not so much on account of the work itself, as of Mr Lyonet's observations; and bestowed on it, as did also many other authors, the highest encomiums. He afterwards executed drawings of the fresh water polypus for Mr Trembley's beautiful work, 1744. The ingenious Wandelaar had engraved the first five plates; when Mr Lyonet, who had never witnessed this operation, concerned at the difficulties he experienced in getting the remaining eight finished in the superior style he required, resolved to perform the task himself. He accordingly took a lesson of one hour of Mr Wandelaar, engraved three or four small plates, and immediately began upon the work himself, which he performed in such a manner as drew on him the highest degree of praise, both from Mr Trembley and from many other artists, particularly the celebrated Van Gool; who declared that the performance astonished not only the amateurs, but also the most experienced artists. In 1748 he was chosen member of the Royal Society of London. In 1749 he began (by mere chance) his amazing collection of horns and shells, which, according to the universal testimony of all travellers and amateurs who have visited it, is at present the most beautiful, and certainly one of the most valuable in Europe. In 1753 he became member of the newly-established Dutch Society of Sciences at Haarlem; and in 1757, after the celebrated M. le Cat, professor in anatomy and surgery, and member of almost all the principal societies in Europe, had seen Mr Lyonet's incomparable Traité Anatomique de la Chenille qui roule le Bois de Saule, with the drawings belonging to it (which work was afterwards published), he was elected member of the Royal Academy of Sciences of Rome, whereof M. le Cat was perpetual secretary. After the publication of this treatise he became, in 1762, member of the Royal Academy of Sciences of Berlin; in 1761, of the Imperial Academy of Naturalists; and, in 1762, of the Imperial Academy of Sciences at St Petersburgh. In order to enable such as might be desirous of following him in his intricate and most astonishing discoveries respecting the structure of this animal, Mr Lyonet published, in the Transactions of the Dutch Society of Sciences at Haarlem, a description and a plate (as he also afterwards did in French at the beginning of his Traité Anatomique) of the instrument and tools he had invented for the purpose of dissection, and likewise of the method he used to ascertain the degree of strength of his magnifying glasses. Notwithstanding all this labour, which was considerably increased by the extensive correspondence which he for many years carried on with several learned and respectable personages, he still found means to set apart a large proportion of his time (as he himself mentions it in his preface) for the immediate service of his country; but was not fortunate enough (as appears by his writings) to get any other recompense for his exertions than sorrow and disappointment. During the last fifteen or twenty years of his life, Mr Lyonet added to the valuable treasure he had already collected of natural curiosities, a most superb cabinet of paintings, consisting of more than 560 performances; among which are many of the most eminent works of the first Dutch masters. He did this with a view to procure himself some amusement during the latter part of his life, when old age and infirmities must weaken his powers, and set bounds to his activity. He had always indeed accustomed himself to employment, inso much that he has written some pieces of Dutch poetry; and this disposition remained with him till within a fortnight of his death, when he was attacked with an inflammation in his breast, which, though apparently cured, was, in the end, the cause of his dissolution. He died at the Hague in January 1789, aged 83 years, leaving behind him a most estimable character.

LYONOIS

Pages 303-303

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of France; bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>; on the east, by Dauphiny, Bresse, and the principality of Dombes; on the south, by Vivarais and Velay; and on the west by Auvergne and a small <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Bourbonnais. It comprehends Lower Lyonois, Beaujolais, and Forez; and it produces corn, wine, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, and more especially excellent chestnuts. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RHONE">Rhone</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOIRE">Loire</a>. Lyons is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> town.

LYONS

Pages 303-304

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, rich, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, and famous town of France, being the most considerable in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, next to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>; with an archbishop's see, an academy of sciences and belles lettres, and an academy of arts and sciences settled here in 1736. It is seated at the confluence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RHONE">Rhone</a> and Saone; on the side of of it are two <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>; and the mountain of St Sebastian serves as a bulwark against the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> winds, which often blow here with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> violence. It contains nearly 100,000 inhabitants; and the houses, in general, are high and well built. It has six gates, and as many suburbs. The town-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, the arsenal, the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a> built by the ancient <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>, and the numerous palaces, are worthy of a traveller's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> is a superb structure, and the canons that compose the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> are all persons of distinction. It was a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of great trade, and was especially distinguished by its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, which however have been greatly reduced by the Revolution. It derives vast advantages from the rivers near it; and is situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4° 59'. N. Lat. 45° 46'. Lyons was the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of some of the horrid transactions of the French revolution. See France.

LYRE

Pages 304-306

a musical <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of the stringed kind, much used by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. Concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of strings with which this instrument was furnished, there is <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> controversy. Some assert it to be only three; and that the sounds of the two remote were acute, and that of the intermediate one a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> between those two extremes; that <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>, the inventor, resembled those three chords to as many seasons of the year, which were all that the Greeks reckoned, namely, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, winter, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>; assigning the acute to the first, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, and the mean to the third. Others assert that the lyre had four strings; that the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> between the first and the fourth was an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OCTAVE">octave</a>; that the second was a fourth from the first, and the fourth the same distance from the third, and that from the second to the third was a tone. Another class of writers contend that the lyre of Mercury had <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> strings. Nicomachus, a follower of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of them, gives the following account of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>: "The lyre made of the shell was invented by Mercury; and the knowledge of it, as it was constructed by him of seven strings, was transmitted to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORPHEUS">Orpheus</a>: Orpheus taught the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of it to Thamyris and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LINUS">Linus</a>; the latter of whom taught it to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, who communicated it to Amphion the Theban, who built the seven gates of Thebes to the seven strings of the lyre." The same author proceeds to relate, "That Orpheus was afterwards killed by the Thracian women; and that they are reported to have <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> his lyre into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, which was afterwards thrown up at Antissa, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LESBOS">Lesbos</a>: that certain fishers finding it, they brought it to Terpander, who carried it into <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, exquisitely improved, and showing it to the Egyptian priests, assumed to himself the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of its <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>." This <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> among authors seems to have arisen from their confounding together the Egyptian and the Grecian Mercuries.—The invention of the primitive lyre with three strings was due to the first Egyptian Hermes, as mentioned under that article.—The lyre attributed to the Grecian Mercury is described by almost all the poets to be an instrument of seven strings.* See Mr Vincenzo Galilei has collected the various opinions of the several Greek writers who have mentioned the invention of the chelys <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> testudo; and the late Mr Spence has done the same in a very circumstantial but ludicrous manner. "Horace talks of Mercury as a wonderful musician, and represents him with a lyre. There is a ridiculous old <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEGEND">legend</a> relating to this invention, which informs us, that Mercury, after stealing some bulls from <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>, retired to a secret grotto, which he used to frequent, at the foot of a mountain in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">Just</a> as he was going in, he found a tortoise feeding at the entrance of his cave: he killed the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> creature, and perhaps ate the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> of it. As he was diverting himself with the shell, he was mightily pleased with the noise it gave from its concave <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. He had possibly been cunning enough to find out, that a thong pulled strait and fastened at each end, when struck with the finger, made a sort of musical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>. However that was, he went immediately to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, and cut several thongs out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIDES">hides</a> he had lately stolen, and fastened them as tight as he could to the shell of this tortoise; and, in playing with them, made a new kind of music with them to divert himself in his retreat." This, considered only as an account of the first invention of the lyre, is not altogether so unnatural. The most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> representations of this instrument agree very well with the account of its invention: the lyre, in particular on the old celestial globes, was represented as made of one entire shell of a tortoise; and that of Amphion in the celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROUP">group</a> of the Dirce or Toro, in the Farnese <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> at Rome, which is of Greek <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>, and very <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> antiquity, is figured in the same manner. There have, however, been many other claimants to the seven-stringed lyre. For though Mercury invented this instrument in the manner already related, it is said he afterwards gave it to Apollo, who was the first that played upon it with method, and made it the constant <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. According to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>'s account of this transaction, in his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYMN">hymn</a> to Mercury, it was given by that god to Apollo, as a peace-offering and indemnification for the oxen which he had stolen from him: To Phoebus <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MAIA">Maia</a>'s son presents the lyre, A gift intended to appease his ire, The god receives it gladly, and essays The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVEL">novel</a> instrument a thousand ways; With dextrous skill the plectrum wields; and sings With <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> accordant to the trembling strings, Such strains as gods and men approv'd, from whence The sweet <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> sprung of sound and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>. Diodorus informs us, that Apollo soon repenting of the cruelty with which he had treated Marsyas in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of their musical contest, broke the strings of the lyre, and by that means put a stop for a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to any further progress in the practice of that new instrument. "The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">Muses</a> (adds he) afterwards added to this instrument the string called mese; Linus, that of tichanos;" and Orpheus and Thamyris, those strings which are named hypate and parhypate (A). Again, Many ancient and respectable authors tell us, that, before the time of Terpander, the Grecian lyre had only four strings; and, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we may believe Suidas, it remained in this state 856 years, from the time of Amphion, till Terpander added to it three new strings, which extended the musical <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> to a heptachord, or seventh, and supplied the player with two conjoint tetrachords. It was about 150 years after this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, that Pythagoras is said to have added an eighth string to the lyre, in order to complete the octave, which consisted of two disjoint tetrachords. Boetius gives a different <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the scale, and tells us, that the system did not <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> remain in such narrow limits as a tetrachord. Choribus, the son of Athis, or Atys, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Lydia, added a fifth string; Hyagnis, a sixth; Terpander, a seventh; and at length Lychon of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAMOS">Samos</a>, an eighth. But all these accounts are irreconcilable with Homer's hymn to Mercury, where the chelys, or testudo, the invention of which he ascribes to that god, is said to have had seven strings. There are many claimants among the musicians of ancient <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> to the strings that were afterwards added to these, by which the scale, in the time of Aristoxenus, was extended to two octaves. Athenaeus, more than once, speaks of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a>-stringed instrument; and Ion of Chios, a tragic and lyric poet and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, who first recited his pieces in the 82d Olympiad, 452 B.C., mentions, in some verses quoted by Euclid, the ten-stringed lyre; a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> that the third conjoint tetrachord was added to the scale in his time, which was about 50 years after Pythagoras is supposed to have constructed the octachord. The different claimants among the Greeks to the same musical discoveries, only prove that music was cultivated in different countries, and that the inhabitants of each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> invented and improved their own instruments, some of which happening to resemble those of other parts of Greece, rendered it difficult for historians to avoid attributing the same invention to different persons. Thus the single <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUTE">flute</a> was given to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a> and to Marsyas; the syrinx or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISTULA">fistula</a>, to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAN">Pan</a> and to Cybele; and the lyre or cithara, to Mercury, Apollo, Amphion, Linus, and Orpheus. Indeed, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> addition of a string or two to an instrument without a neck, was so obvious and easy, that it is scarce possible not to conceive many people to have done it at the same time. With respect to the form of the ancient lyre, as little agreement is to be found among authors as about the number of strings. The best evidences concerning it, are the representations of that instrument in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of ancient <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, bas reliefs, &c. See Plate CCXCVIII., CCXCVIII. Fig. 1. is a representation of the testudo, or lyre of Fig. 1. Amphion, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a>, as it appears on the base of the celebrated Toro Farnese at Rome. This admirable work, consisting of four figures bigger than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, besides the toro or bull, was found in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARACALLA">Caracalla</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>, where the Farnese Hercules was likewise discovered: and, except the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAOCOON">Laocoon</a>, is the only piece of Greek sculpture mentioned by Pliny that is now remaining. The two projections near the bottom, seem to have been fastenings for the strings, and to have answered the purpose of tail-pieces in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> instruments. Fig. 2. The lyre held by Terpsichore, in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> Fig. 2. of that muse dug out of Herculaneum. Fig. 3. The Abyssinian testudo, or lyre in use at present in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Tigre, from a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> of Mr Bruce, communicated to Dr Burney. "This instrument (says he) has sometimes five, sometimes six, but most frequently seven strings, made of the thongs of raw sheep or goat skins, cut extremely fine, and twisted; they rot soon, are very subject to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> in dry <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, and have scarce any sound in wet. From the idea, however, of this instrument being to accompany and sustain a voice, one would think that it was better mounted formerly. "The Abyssinians have a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>, that the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SISTRUM">sistrum</a>, lyre, and tambourine, were brought from Egypt into Ethiopia, by Thot, in the very first ages of the world. The flute, kettle-drum, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRUMPET">trumpet</a>, they say, were brought from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>, with Menelek, the son of their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of Saba by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>, who was their first Jewish king. "The lyre in Amharic is called beg, 'the sheep;' in Ethiopia it is called mesinko; the verb sinko signifies to strike strings with the fingers: no plectrum is ever used in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABYSSINIA">Abyssinia</a>; so that mesinko, being literally interpreted, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> signify the 'stringed instrument played upon with the fingers.' "The sides which constitute the frame of the lyre, were anciently composed of the horns of an animal of the goat kind, called agazen, about the size of a small cow, and (A) It has been already related, that the lyre invented by the Egyptian Mercury had but three strings; and, by putting these two circumstances together, Dr Burney observes, we may perhaps acquire some knowledge of the progress of music, or at least, of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> of its scale, in the highest antiquity. Mese, in the Greek music, is the fourth sound of the second tetrachord of the great system, and first tetrachord invented by the ancients, answering to our A, on the fifth line in the base. If this sound then was added to the former three, it proves two important <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a>; first, that the most ancient tetrachord was that from E in the base to A; and that the three original strings in the Mercurian and Apollonian lyre were tuned E, F, G, which the Greeks called Hypate Meson, Parhypate Meson, Meson Diatonos. The addition therefore of Mese to these, completed the first and most ancient tetrachord, E, F, G, A. The string lichanos, then, being added to these, and answering to our D on the third line in the base, extended the compass downwards, and gave the ancient lyre a regular <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of five sounds in the Dorian <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a>, the most ancient of all the Greek modes; and the two strings called Hypate and Parhypate, corresponding with our B and C in the base, completed the heptachord, or seven sounds, B, C, D, E, F, G, A, a compass that received no addition till after the time of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PINDAR">Pindar</a>, who calls the instrument then in use the seven-tongued lyre. and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in the province of Tigre. I have seen several of these instruments very elegantly made of such horns, which <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> seems to have shaped on purpose. Some of the horns of an African <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of this animal may be seen in M. Buffon's history of the king of France's cabinet. They are bent, and less regular than the Abyssinian; but after fire-arms became common in the province of Tigre, and the woods were cut <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, this animal being more scarce, the lyre has been made of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> wood; however, it is always cut into a spiral twisted form, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the ancient materials of which the lyre was composed. The drawing I send you was one of these instruments made of wood. "The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Tigre, which is the largest and most populous province of Abyssinia, and was during many ages the seat of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, was the first which received letters, and civil <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>; it extended once to the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RED_SEA">Red sea</a>: various reasons and revolutions have obliged the inhabitants to resign their sea <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> to different barbarous nations, Pagan and Mahometan: while they were possessed of it, they say that the Red sea furnished them with tortoise-shells, of which they made the bellies of their lyres, as the Egyptians did formerly, according to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLODORUS">Apollodorus</a> and Lucian; but having now lost that resource, they have adopted in its <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> a particular species of gourd, or pumpkin, very hard and thin in the bark, still imitating with the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a> the squares, compartments, and figure of the shell of the tortoise. "The lyre is generally from three feet to three feet six inches high; that is, from a line drawn through the point of the horns, to the lower <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the base of the sounding board. It is exceedingly light, and easy of carriage, as an instrument should naturally be in so rugged and mountainous a country. "When we consider the parts which compose this lyre, we cannot deny it the earliest antiquity. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">Man</a> in his first state was a hunter and a fisher, and the oldest instrument was that which partakes most of that state. The lyre, composed of two <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> pieces, owes the one to horns of an animal, the other to the shell of a fish. "It is probable, that the lyre <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> with the Ethiopians in this rude state as long as they confined themselves to their rainy, steep, and rugged <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>; and afterwards, when many of them descended along the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a> into Egypt, its portability would recommend it in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> heats and weariness of their way. Upon their arrival in Egypt, they took up their habitation in caves, in the sides of mountains, which are inhabited to this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. Even in these circumstances, an instrument larger than the lyre must have been inconvenient and liable to accidents in those caverns; but when these people increased in numbers and courage, they ventured down into the plain, and built Thebes. Being now at their ease, and in a fine <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, all nature smiling around them, music and other arts were cultivated and refined, and the imperfect lyre was extended into an instrument of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> its compass and volume. The size of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HARP">harp</a> could be now no longer an objection; the Nile carried the inhabitants everywhere easily, and without effort; and we may naturally suppose in the fine evenings of that country, that the Nile was the favourite <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> upon which this instrument was practised; at least the sphinx and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOTUS">lotus</a> upon its head, seem to hint that it was someway connected with the overflowings of that river." See Harp. Fig. 4. An Etruscan lyre, with seven strings, in the collection of Etruscan, Greek and Roman antiquities, published from the cabinet of the Hon. Sir William <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAMILTON">Hamilton</a>, Vol. I. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a> 1766. Plate CIX. With respect to this instrument, it is worthy of observation, that though the vase upon which it is represented is of such indisputable and remote antiquity, the tail-piece, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, belly and sound-holes, have a very modern appearance, and manifest a knowledge in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of musical instruments among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-ETRUSCANS">Etruscans</a> superior to that of the Greeks and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> in much latter times. The lower part of the instrument has much the appearance of an old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASS">bass</a>-viol, and it is not difficult to discover in it more than the embryo of the whole violin family. The strings <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> round, as if intended to be played on with a bow; and even the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> on the tail-piece are such as we frequently see on the tail-pieces of old viols. Fig. 5. The Tripodian lyre of Pythagoras the Zacynthian, from a bass relief in the Maecii palace at Rome representing the whole choir of the muses. Athenæus gives the following account of this extraordinary instrument, Lib. XIV. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. xv. p. 637. Many ancient instruments are recorded (says Artemon), of which we have so little knowledge, that we can hardly be certain of their existence; such as the tripod of Pythagoras the Zacynthian, which, on account of its difficulty, continued in use but a short time. It resembled in form the Delphic tripod, whence it had its name. The legs were equidistant, and fixed upon a moveable base that was turned by the foot of the player: the strings were placed between the legs of the stool; the vase at the top served for the purpose of a sound-board, and the strings of the three sides of the instrument were tuned to three different modes, the Doric, Lydian, and Phrygian. The performer sat on a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> made on purpose: striking the strings with the fingers of the left <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and using the plectrum with the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, at the same time <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> the instrument with his foot to whichever of the three modes he pleased: so that by great practice he was enabled to change the modes with such velocity, that those who did not see him would imagine they heard three different performers playing in three different modes. After the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of this admirable musician, no other instrument of the same kind was ever constructed." Fig. 6. A lyre in the famous ancient picture dug out of Herculaneum, upon which <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIRON">Chiron</a> is teaching young <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACHILLES">Achilles</a> to play. See Chiron.

LYRIC POETRY

Pages 306-306

was such as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> sung to the lyre <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HARP">harp</a>.—It was originally employed in celebrating the praises of gods and heroes, and its characteristic was sweetness. Who was the author of it is not known. It was much cultivated by the Greeks: and Horace was the first who attempted it in the Latin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. Anacreon, Alceus, Stesichorus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAPPHO">Sappho</a>, and Horace, were the most celebrated lyric poets of antiquity.

LYRODI

Pages 306-307

among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, a kind of musicians who played on the lyre, and sung at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. This appellation was also given to such as made it their employment to sing lyric poems composed by others.

LYSANDRIA

Pages 307-307

a Samian festival, celebrated with games and sacrifices in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the Lacedaemonian general Lysander. It was anciently called herea: but this name the Samians abolished by a public <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DECREE">decree</a>.

LYSIARCH

Pages 307-307

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>, who superintended the sacred games, and presided in matters of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Lycia. He was created in a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> consisting of deputies from all the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> cities, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> 23. The lysiarchs were both heads of the council and pontiffs of the province.

LYSIAS

Pages 307-307

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Grecian orator, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRACUSE">Syracuse</a> in the 8th Olympiad. At 15, he went to Thurion, a colony of the Athenians; and when grown up, assisted in the administration of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> there many years. When about 47 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, he returned to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>; whence, being afterwards banished by the 30 tyrants, he went to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEGARA">Megara</a>. Upon his return, Thrasybulus would have had him employed again in state matters; but this not taking <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, he spent the remainder of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> as a private <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. He was very familiar with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>, and other illustrious philosophers. He professed to teach the art of speaking; not that he pleaded at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> himself, but he supplied others with speeches. "Puit Lysias in causis forensibus non versatus (says Cicero), sed egregie subtilis scriptor atque elegans, &c. Quinilian calls him, "subtilis atque elegans, et quo nihil si oratorio satis sit docere, quaerat perfectius. Nihil enim est inane, nihil arcessitum; puro tamen fonti, quam magno flumini, propriior." Plutarch and Phoebadius relate, that 425 orations were formerly exhibited under the name of Lysias; of which 34 only are now extant. The best edition of them is by Dr John Taylor at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, 1739, 4to; <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, 1740, 8vo.

LYSIMACHIA

Pages 307-307

Loosestrife, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 20th order, Rotaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

LYSIPPUS

Pages 307-307

a celebrated Greek statuary, was born at Sicyone, and first followed the business of a locksmith, which he quitted in order to practice <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>: But he afterwards applied himself entirely to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>; in which he acquired an immortal reputation, and made a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> that were the admiration of the people of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> and Rome. His <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> statue of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">Sun</a> represented in a car drawn by four horses, was worshipped at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RHODES">Rhodes</a>. He made several statues of Alexander and his favourites, which were brought to Rome by Metellus after he had reduced the Macedonian empire; and the statue of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> wiping and anointing himself after <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATHING">bathing</a>, being particularly excellent, was placed by Agrippa before his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a> in that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. He lived in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Alexander the Great, about 334 B.C.; and left three sons, Lysippos who were all famous statuaries.

LYTHIRUM

Pages 307-307

Purple Loosestrife, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the decandria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 17th order, Calycanthaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

LYTTELTON

Pages 307-309

Edward, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Lyttelton, keeper of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. was eminent for his probity and his moderation at the commencement of that monarch's disputes with his subjects. Without forfeiting his fidelity to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, he preserved the esteem of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> till 1644, when he was made <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLONEL">colonel</a> of a regiment in the king's <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>. He died in 1645. Besides several of his speeches which have been printed, he wrote reports in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMMON_PLEAS"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> pleas and exchequer, printed at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in 1683, in folio; several arguments and discourses, &c. **Lyttelton**, George Lord, eldest son of Sir Thomas Lyttelton, Bart. descended from the great judge Lyttelton, was born in 1700, at <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> months; and the midwife, supposing him to be dead, threw him carelessly into the cradle; where, had not some signs of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> been taken notice of by one of the attendants, he might never have recovered. He received the elements of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> at Eaton school, where he showed an early inclination to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. His pastorals and some other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> pieces were originally written in that seminary of learning; from whence he was removed to the university of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, where he pursued his classical studies with uncommon avidity, and sketched the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of his Persian Letters; a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> which afterwards procured him great reputation, not only from the elegance of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> in which they were composed, but from the excellent observations they contained on the manners of mankind. In the year 1728, he set out on the tour of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; and, on his arrival at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, accidentally became acquainted with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> Mr Poyntz, then our minister at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSAILLES">Versailles</a>; who was so struck with the extraordinary capacity of our young traveller, that he invited him to his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and employed him in many <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> negotiations, which he executed with great judgment and fidelity. Mr Lyttelton's conduct, while on his travels, was a lesson of instruction to the rest of his countrymen. Instead of lounging away his hours at the coffee-houses frequented by the English, and adopting the fashionable follies and vices of France and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> was passed alternately in his library and in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of men of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> and literature. In this early <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his life, he wrote a poetical epistle to Dr Ayscough, and another to Mr Pope, which show singular <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and correctness. After continuing a considerable time at Paris with Mr Poyntz, who, to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> his own words, behaved like a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> father to him, he proceeded to Lyons and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>; and from thence to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURIN">Turin</a>, where he was honoured with great marks of friendship by his Sardinian majesty. He then visited <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>, and Rome, where he applied himself closely to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the fine arts; and was, even in that celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>, allowed a perfect judge of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>. During his continuance abroad, he constantly corresponded Lyttelton responded with Sir Thomas, his father. Several of his letters are yet remaining, and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FILIAL">filial</a> affection in a very distinguished light. He soon after returned to his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and was elected representative for the borough of Okchampton in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>; and behaved so much to the satisfaction of his constituents, that they several times re-elected him for the same place without putting him to the least expense. About this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, he received great marks of friendship from Frederic <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, father of his present majesty; and was, in the year 1737, appointed <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> secretary to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> highness, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in the strictest intimacy with him till the time of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to public business did not, however, prevent him from exercising his poetical <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALENT">talent</a>. A most amiable young lady, Miss Fortescue, inspired him with a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>, which produced a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of little pieces, remarkable for their tenderness and elegance; and he had a happy facility of striking out an extemporaneous compliment, which obtained him no small share of reputation. One evening being in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> with Lord Cobham and several of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> at Stowe, his lordship mentioned his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of putting up a bust of Lady <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a> in his beautiful gardens; and, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> to Mr Lyttelton, said, "George, you must furnish me with a motto for it." "I <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, my lord," answered Mr Lyttelton; and directly produced the following couplet: Her <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> for a court were made, But <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> and goodness fit her for a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>. When Mr Pitt, afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHATHAM">Chatham</a>, lost his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> in the guards, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of his spirited conduct in parliament, Mr Lyttelton was in waiting at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEICESTER">Leicester</a>-house, and, on hearing the circumstance, immediately wrote these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>: <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a> had thy virtue mark'd thee out for fame, Far, far superior to a corner's name; This generous Walpole <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a>, and griev'd to find So <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> disgrace that noble mind; The servile standard from thy free-born <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> He took, and bade thee <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> the patriot band. In the year 1742, he married Lucy, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Hugh Fortescue, Esq. of Filleigh in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Devon, the lady above mentioned, whose exemplary conduct, and uniform practice of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> and virtue, established his conjugal <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> upon the most <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> basis. In 1744, he was appointed one of the lords commissioners of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>; and, during his continuance in that station, constantly exerted his influence in rewarding merit and ability. He was the friend and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of the late Henry Fielding, James Thomson author of the Seasons, Mr <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALLET">Mallet</a>, Dr Young, Mr Hammond, Mr West, Mr Pope, and Voltaire. On the death of Thomson, who left his affairs in a very embarrassed condition, Mr Lyttelton took that poet's sister under his protection. He revised the tragedy of Coriolanus, which that writer had not put the last hand to; and brought it out at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>-royal, Covent-garden, with a prologue of his own <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, in which he so affectingly lamented the loss of that delightful bard, that not only Mr Quin, who spoke the lines, but almost the whole audience, spontaneously burst into tears. In the beginning of the year 1746, his felicity was interrupted by the loss of his wife, who died in the 29th year of her <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>; leaving him one son, Thomas, the late Lord Lyttelton; and a daughter, Lucy, who afterwards married Lord Viscount Valentia. The remains of his amiable lady were deposited at Over-Arley in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORCESTERSHIRE">Worcestershire</a>; and an elegant monument was erected to her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Hagley, which contains the following inscription written by her husband: Made to engage all hearts, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARM">charm</a> all eyes: Tho' meek, magnanimous; tho' witty, wise; Polite, as all her life in courts had been; Yet good, as she the world had never seen: The noble fire of an exalted mind, With gentlest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> tenderness combin'd. Her speech was the melodious <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>, Her song the warbling of the vernal <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROVE">grove</a>. Her eloquence was sweeter than her song, Soft as her heart, and as her reason strong. Her form each beauty of her mind express'd, Her mind was virtue by the Graces dress'd. Besides these beautiful lines, Mr Lyttelton wrote a monody on the death of his lady, which will be remembered while conjugal affection and a taste for poetry exist in this country. His masterly observations on the conversion and apostleship of St Paul, were written at the desire of Gilbert West, Esq. in consequence of Mr Lyttelton's asserting, that, beside all the proofs of the Christian religion, which might be drawn from the prophecies of the Old <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, from the necessary connection it has with the whole system of the Jewish religion, from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a> of Christ, and from the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> given of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a> by all the other apostles, he thought the conversion of St Paul alone, duly considered, was of itself a demonstration sufficient to prove Christianity to be a divine <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a>. Mr West was struck with the thought; and assured his friend, that so compendious a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> would be of great use to convince those unbelievers that will not attend to a longer <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of arguments; and time has shown he was not out in his conjecture, as the tract is esteemed one of the best defences of Christianity which has hitherto been published. In 1754, he resigned his office of lord of the treasury, and was made cofferer to his majesty's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>, and sworn of the privy-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>: previous to which, he married a second time, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> daughter of Field-marshal Sir Robert Rich; whose indiscreet conduct gave him great uneasiness, and from whom he was separated, by mutual consent, a few years after his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>. After being appointed <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>, and under <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> of the court of exchequer, he was, by letters-patent dated the 16th of November 1757, 31 Geo. II. created a peer of Great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, by the style and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Lord Lyttelton, baron of Frankley, in the county of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORCESTER">Worcester</a>. His speeches on the Scotch and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUTINY">mutiny</a> bills in the year 1747, on the Jew <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">bill</a> in 1753, and on the privilege of parliament in 1763, showed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> judgment, powerful eloquence, and inflexible integrity. During the last ten years he lived chiefly in retirement, in the continual <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of all the virtues which can ennoble private life. His last work was Dialogues of the Dead, in which the morality of Cambrey and the spirit of Fontenelle are happily united. He was suddenly seized with an inflammation of the bowels, in the middle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1773, at his seat at Hagley; which terminated in his death, on the 22d of that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a>. His last moments were attended with Lyttelton unimpaired understanding, unaffected greatness of mind, calm resignation, and humble but confident hopes in the mercy of God. As he had lived universally esteemed, he died lamented by all parties. A complete collection of his works has been published since his decease, by his nephew George Ayscough, Esq. M. M, a liquid consonant, and the twelfth <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a>. It has one unvaried sound, and is pronounced by striking the upper lip against the lower; in which the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRONUNCIATION">pronunciation</a> of this letter agrees with that of b; the only <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the two consisting in a little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> made in the nose in pronouncing m, and not in b: whence it happens that those who have taken <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, for m ordinarily pronounce b; the nose in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> being disabled from making the necessary motion. All <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSONANTS">consonants</a> are formed with the aid of <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-VOWELS">vowels</a>; in cm the vowel precedes, in be it follows; and m is never <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MUTE">mute</a>. Quintilian observes, that the m sometimes ends Latin words but never Greek ones; the Greeks always changing it in that case into n, for the sake of the better sound. M is also a numeral letter, and among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> was used for a thousand; according to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, \[ M \text{ coput est numeri, quem scimus mille teneri.} \] When a dash is added to the top of it, as \( \overline{M} \); it signifies a thousand times a thousand. M, as an abbreviature, stands for Manlius, Marcus, Martius, and Mucius: M.A. signifies magister artium, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts; MS. manuscript, and MSS. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a>. M, in astronomical tables, and other things of that kind, is used for meridional or southern; and sometimes for meridian or mid-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. M, in medicinal <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESCRIPTION">prescription</a>, is frequently used to signify a manipule or handful; and it is sometimes also put at the end of a recipe, for miscere, "mingle;" or for mixtura, "a mixture." Thus m.f. julapum, signifies "mix and make a julep." M, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, the brand or stigma of a person convicted of manslaughter, and admitted to the benefit of his clergy. It is to be burnt on the brawn of his left thumb.

MABILLON

Pages 309-309

JOHN, a very learned writer of France in the 17th century, was born at Perremonte, on the frontiers of Champagne, in 1632. He was educated in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHEIMS">Rheims</a>, and afterwards entered into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENEDICTINES">Benedictines</a> of St Remy. In the year 1663, he was appointed keeper of the treasures and monuments of France at St Dennis: but Mabillon having unfortunately broke a looking glass there, which was pretended to have belonged to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, he desired leave of his superiors to quit an employment which frequently obliged him to tell things he did not believe. Next year he went to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>; and was very serviceable to Father d'Acheri, who was desirous of having some young monk who could assist him in compiling his Spicilegium. This made him known. Soon after, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> of St Maur having formed a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of publishing new editions of the fathers, revised from the MSS. in the <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a> of the Benedictines, Mabillon was <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with the edition of St Bernard, which he prepared with extraordinary diligence. After that, he published many other works, which are evidences of his vast capacity and industry. In 1682, he was employed by Mr Colbert in examining some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> titles relating to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> family. The year following he sent him into Germany, to search the archives and libraries of the ancient abbeys, for what was most curious and proper to illustrate the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> in general, and that of France in particular. He has published an account of this journey. In 1685, he undertook another journey into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, by order of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of France; and returned the year following with a very noble collection. He placed in the king's library above 3000 volumes of rare books, printed and in MSS. and composed two volumes of the pieces which he had discovered in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. He was highly esteemed for his virtues as well as his learning.

MACAO

Pages 309-309

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTON">Canton</a>, seated in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> at the mouth of the river Tac. The Portuguese have been in possession of the harbour for 150 years. Formerly they had a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> trade here; but now they have only a fort with a small garrison. The houses are built after the European manner; and there is a Chinese mandarin, as well as a Portuguese governor, to take care of the town and the neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 109. N. Lat. 22. 12. MACAO. See <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PSITTACUS">PSITTACUS</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ORNITHOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MACARIANS

Pages 309-310

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the followers of Macarius, an Egyptian monk, who was distinguished Macarians distinguished towards the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the fourth century for his sanctity and virtue. In his writings there are some <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MACASSAR">Macassar</a> superstitious tenets, and also certain opinions that seem tainted with Origenism. The name has been also applied to those who adopted the sentiments of Macarius a native of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, who about the close of the ninth century, propagated in France the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a> afterwards maintained by Averroes, that one individual intelligence <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> performed the spiritual and rational functions in all the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MACARONI">MACARONI</a>. See FOLENGIO, and the next article.

MACARONIC

Pages 310-310
or MACARONIAN, a kind of burlesque poetry, consisting of a jumble of words of different languages, with words of the vulgar tongue Latinized, and Latin words modernized. Macaroni among the Italians, as has been observed by Cælius Rhodiginus, signifies a coarse clownish man; and because this kind of poetry is patched out of several languages, and full of extravagant words, &c. the Italians, among whom it had its rise, gave it the name of macaronian or macaronic poetry. Others choose to derive it from macaronibus, from macaroons, a kind of confection made of meal not bolted, sweet almonds, sugar, and the white of eggs, accounted a great dainty among the country people in Italy; which, from their being composed of various ingredients, occasioned this kind of poetry, which consists of Latin, Italian, Spanish, French, English, &c. to be called by their name. Example.—A bold fellow in the macaronic style, says, Enflavi omnes scadrones et regimandos, &c.
