The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> kind was of a circular form, made of metal, and either hung round with little bells, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> furnished with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> rings suspended on a rod or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> that passed across the circle. Kircher supposes that it was moved to and fro by a handle fixed to it, and thus emitted a melancholy kind of murmur.

MACHYNLETH

Pages 344-344

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTGOMERYSHIRE">Montgomeryshire</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, 198 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and 32 from <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTGOMERY">Montgomery</a>. It is an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town, and has a market on Mondays, and several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a>. In 1811 it contained 1252 inhabitants. It is seated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOUAY">Douay</a>, over which there is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, which leads into <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERIONETHSHIRE">Merionethshire</a>. It was here that Owen Glyndwr exercised the first acts of his royalty in 1402. Here he accepted the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of Wales, and assembled a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> wherein they met is now standing, divided into tenements.

MACKENZIE

Pages 344-344

Sir George, an able lawyer, a polite scholar, and a celebrated <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUNDEE">Dundee</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGUS">Angus</a> in Scotland in 1636, and studied at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> of Aberdeen and St Andrew's; after which he applied himself to the civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, travelled into France, and prosecuted his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> in that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> for about three years. At his return to his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> he became an advocate in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>; and soon gained the character of an eminent pleader. He did not, however, suffer his abilities to be confined entirely to that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>. He had a good <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for polite literature; and he gave the public, from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to time, incontestable proofs of an uncommon proficiency therein. He had practised but a few years, when he was promoted to the office of a judge in the criminal <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>; and, in 1674, was made <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s advocate, and one of the lords of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRIVY_COUNCIL">privy <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> in Scotland. He was also knighted by his majesty. In these stations he met with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of trouble, on account of the rebellions which happened in his time; and his office of advocate requiring him to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> with severity, he did not escape being censured, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> in the deaths of some particular persons who were executed he had stretched the laws too far. But there does not seem to have been any <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> foundation for this clamour against him; and it is generally agreed, that he acquitted himself like an able and upright <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>. Upon the abrogation of the penal laws by King James II. our advocate, though he had always been remarkable for his loyalty, and even censured for his zeal against traitors and fanatics, thought himself obliged to resign his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>; being convinced, that he could not discharge the duties of it in that point with a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a>. But he was soon after restored, and held his offices till the Revolution; an event which, it seems, he could not bring himself to approve. He had hoped that the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a> would have returned to his own country when matters were adjusted between the king and his subjects; and upon its proving otherwise, he quitted all his employments in Scotland, and retired into England, resolving to spend the remainder of his days in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. He arrived there in September 1689, and prosecuted his studies in the Bodleian library, being admitted a student there by a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> passed in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 2, 1690. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> following, he went to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, where he fell into a disorder, of which he died in May 1691. His corpse was conveyed by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> to Scotland, and interred there with great pomp and solemnity. "The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a> of his learning, and the sprightliness of his wit, were (says the reverend Mr Granger) conspicuous in all his pleadings, and shone in his ordinary conversation." Mr Dryden acknowledges, that he was unacquainted with what he calls the beautiful turn of words and thoughts in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, till they were explained and exemplified to him in a conversation with that noble wit of Scotland Sir George Mackenzie.—He wrote several pieces of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and antiquities; Institutions of the laws of Scotland; Essays upon various subjects, &c. His works were printed together at Edinburgh in 1716, in 2 vols. folio. MACEREL. See SCOMBER, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MACLAURIN

Pages 344-346

Colin, a most eminent mathematician and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, was the son of a clergyman, and born at Kilmoddan in Scotland in 1698. He was sent to the university of Glasgow in 1709; where he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> five years, and applied himself to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> in a most intense manner. His <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> genius for mathematical learning discovered itself so early as at twelve years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>; when, having accidentally met with an Euclid in a friend's chamber, he became in a few days <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the first six books without any assistance; and it is certain, that in his 16th year he had invented many of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a> which were afterwards published under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Geometria Organica. In his 17th year he took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of master of arts; on which occasion he composed and publicly defended a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THESIS">thesis</a>, On the power of Gravity, with great applause. After this he quitted the university, and retired to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>-seat of his uncle, who had the care of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>; for his parents had been dead some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. Here he spent two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> three years in pursuing his favourite studies; but, in 1717, he offered himself a candidate for the professorship of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> in the Marischal <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of Aberdeen, and obtained it after a ten days <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> with a very able competitor. In 1719, he went to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, where he became acquainted with Dr Hoadley then bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANGOR">Bangor</a>, Dr Clarke, Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton, and other eminent men; at which time also he was admitted a member of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>; and in another journey in 1721, he contracted an intimacy with Martin Folkes, Esq. the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of it, which lasted to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. In 1722, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Polwarth, plenipotentiary of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONGRESS">congress</a> of Cambrey, engaged him him to go as a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> to his eldest son, who was then to set out on his travels. After a short stay at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, and visiting other <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> in France, they fixed in Lorraine; where Maclaurin wrote his piece On the Percussion of Bodies, which gained the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> of the Royal Academy of Sciences for the year 1724. But his pupil dying soon after at Montpelier, he returned immediately to his profession at Aberdeen. He was hardly settled here, when he received an invitation to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>; the curators of that university being desirous that he should supply the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of Mr James Gregory, whose great age and infirmities had rendered him incapable of teaching. He had some difficulties to encounter, arising from competitors, who had good <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> with the patrons of the university, and also from the want of an additional <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FUND">fund</a> for the new professor, which however at length were all surmounted, principally by the means of Sir Isaac Newton. In November 1725, he was introduced into the university. After this, the mathematical classes soon became very numerous, there being generally upwards of 100 young gentlemen attending his lectures every year; who being of different standings and proficiency, he was obliged to divide them into four or five classes, in each of which he employed a full <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, from the first of November to the first of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>. He lived a bachelor to the year 1733: but being not less formed for society than for <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a>, he then married <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Mr Walter Stewart solicitor-general for Scotland. By this lady he had <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> children, of whom two sons and three daughters, together with his wife, survived him. In 1734, Berkeley, bishop of Cloyne, published a piece called "The Analyst;" in which he took occasion, from some disputes that had arisen concerning the grounds of the fluxionary method, to explode the method itself, and also to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> mathematicians in general with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INFIDELITY">infidelity</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. Maclaurin thought himself included in this charge, and began an answer to Berkeley's book: but, as he proceeded, so many discoveries, so many new theories and problems occurred to him, that instead of a vindictory pamphlet, his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> came out, A complete system of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUXIONS">fluxions</a>, with their application to the most considerable problems in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. This work was published at Edinburgh in 1742, 2 vols. 4to; and as it cost him infinite pains, so it is the most considerable of all his works, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> do him immortal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>. In the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time, he was continually obliging the public with some performance or observation of his own; many of which were published in the fifth and sixth volumes of the "Medical Essays" at Edinburgh. Some of them were likewise published in the Philosophical Transactions; as the following: 1. Of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of curves, No 356. 2. A new method of describing all kinds of curves, No 359. 3. A <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to Martin Folkes, Esq, on equations with impossible roots, May 1726, No 394. 4. Continuation of the same, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1729, No 458. 5. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> the 21st, 1732, on the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of curves; with an account of farther improvements, and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> dated at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NANCY">Nancy</a>, November 27, 1722, No 439. 6. An account of the treatise of fluxions, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 27, 1742, No 467. 7. The same continued, March 10, 1742, No 469. 8. A rule for finding the meridional parts of a spheroid with the same exactness as of a Maclaurin sphere, August 1741, No 461. 9. Of the basis of the cells wherein the bees deposite their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>; Nov. 3, 1734, No 471. In the midst of these studies, he was always ready to lend his assistance in contriving and promoting any scheme which might contribute to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of his country. When the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Morton set out in 1739 for Orkney and Shetland, to visit his estates there, he desired Mr Maclaurin to assist him in settling the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a> of those countries, which is very erroneous in all our maps; to examine their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY">natural <a clas</a>s="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, to survey the coasts, and to take the measure of a degree of the meridian. Maclaurin's family affairs, and other connexions, would not permit him to do this; he drew, however, a memorial of what he thought necessary to be observed, furnished the proper instruments, and recommended Mr Short, the famous optician, as a fit operator for the management of them. He had still another scheme for the improvement of geography and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, of a more extensive <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>; which was the opening of a passage from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GREENLAND">Greenland</a> to the South <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> pole. That such a passage might be found, he was so fully persuaded, that he has been heard to say, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> his situation could admit of such adventures, he would undertake the voyage, even at his own charge. But when schemes for finding it were laid before the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> in 1744, and himself consulted by several persons of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> concerning them, before he could finish the memorials he proposed to send, the premium was limited to the discovery of a north-west passage: and he used to regret, that the word west was inserted, because he thought that passage, if at all to be found, must <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> not far from the pole. In 1745, having been very <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> in fortifying the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Edinburgh against the rebel <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, he was obliged to fly from thence to the north of England; where he was invited by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERRING">Herring</a>, then archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, to reside with him during his stay in this country. In this expedition, however, being exposed to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and hardships, and naturally of a weak and tender <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, he laid the foundation of an illness which put an end to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, in June 1746, at the age of 48. Mr Maclaurin was a very good as well as a very great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, and worthy of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> as well as admiration. His peculiar merit as a philosopher was, that all his studies were accommodated to general utility; and we find, in many places of his works, an application even of the most abstruse theories, to the perfecting of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> arts. He had resolved, for the same purpose, to compose a course of practical mathematics, and to rescue several useful branches of the science from the bad treatment they often met with in less skilful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. But all this his death prevented; unless we should reckon, as a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his intended work, the translation of Dr <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a> Gregory's "Practical Geometry," which he revised, and published with additions, 1745. In his lifetime, however, he had frequent opportunities of serving his friends and his country by his great skill. Whatever difficulty occurred concerning the constructing or perfecting of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a>, the working of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, the improving of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, the conveying of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, or the execution of any other public work, he MacLaurin, he was at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> to resolve it. He was likewise employed to terminate some disputes of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> that had arisen at Glasgow concerning the gauging of vessels; and for that purpose presented to the commissioners of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXCISE">excise</a> two elaborate memorials, with their demonstrations, containing rules by which the officers now <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a>. He made also calculations relating to the provision, now established by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, for the children and widows of the Scots clergy, and of the professors in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, entitling them to certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNUITIES">annuities</a> and sums, upon the voluntary annual payment of a certain sum by the incumbent. In contriving and adjusting this wise and useful scheme, he bestowed a great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of labour, and contributed not a little towards bringing it to perfection. It may be said of such a man, that "he lived to some purpose;" which can hardly be said of those, how uncommonsoever their abilities and attainments, who spend their whole time in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> speculations, and produce nothing to the real <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> and service of their fellow creatures. Of his works, we have mentioned his Geometria Organica, in which he treats of the description of curve <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> by continued <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. We need not repeat what has been said concerning his piece which gained the prize of the Royal Academy of Sciences in 1724. In 1749, the academy adjudged him a prize, which did him still more honour, for solving the motion of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">tides</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of gravity; a question which had been given out the former year, without receiving any solution. He had only ten days to draw this paper up in, and could not find leisure to transcribe a fair copy; so that the Paris edition of it is incorrect. He afterwards revised the whole, and inserted it in his Treatise of Fluxions; as he did also the substance of the former piece. These, with the Treatise of Fluxions, and the pieces printed in the Philosophical Transactions, of which we have given a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a>, are all the writings which our author lived to publish. Since his death, two volumes more have appeared; his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALGEBRA">Algebra</a>, and his Account of Sir Isaac Newton's Philosophical Discoveries. His Algebra, though not finished by himself, is yet allowed to be excellent in its kind: containing, in no <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> volume, a complete elementary treatise of that science, as far as it hath hitherto been carried. His Account of Sir Isaac Newton's Philosophy was occasioned in the following manner: Sir Isaac dying in the beginning of 1728, his nephew, Mr Conduitt, proposed to publish an account of his life, and desired Mr MacLaurin's assistance. The latter, out of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> to his great benefactor, cheerfully undertook, and soon finished, the history of the progress which philosophy had made before Sir Isaac's time, and this was the first draught of the work in hand; which not going forward, on account of Mr Conduitt's death, was returned to Mr MacLaurin.—To this he afterwards made great additions, and left it in the state in which it now appears. His main <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> seems to have been, to explain only those parts of Sir Isaac's philosophy which have been, and still are, controverted; and this is supposed to be the reason why his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> discoveries concerning <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and colours are but transiently and generally touched upon. For it is known, that ever since the experiments, on which his doctrine of light and colours is founded, have been repeated with due care, this doctrine has not been contested; whereas his accounting for the Macquer celestial motions, and the other great appearances of nature, from gravity, is misunderstood, and even ridiculed by some to this day.

MACQUER

Pages 346-347

Pierre <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> to the former, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> the 9th of October, 1718, and died there February 16, 1784. He was a member of the Academy of Sciences, and professor of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARMACY">pharmacy</a>; and was engaged in the Journal de Scavans, for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of medicine and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>. With the latter science he was intimately acquainted. He had a share in the Pharmacopoeia Parisiensis, published in 1738, in 4to. His other works are, 1. Elemens de Chimie theorique; Paris, 1749, 1753, 12mo; which have been translated into English and German.—2. Elemens de Chimie pratique, 1751, 2 vols. 12mo. These two works were republished together, in 1756, in 3 vols. 12mo. 3. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">Plan</a> d'un cours de Chimie experimentale et raisonnée, 1757, 12mo; in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of which he was associated with M. Beaumé. 4. Formule Medicamentorum Magistralium, 1763. 5. L'Art de la Teinture en Soie, 1763. 6. Dictionnaire de Chimie, contenant la Théorie et la Pratique de cet art, 1766, 2 vols. 8vo; which has been translated into German, with notes; and into English, with notes, by Mr Kier. Macquer has, by his labours and writings, greatly contributed to render useful an art which formerly tended only to ruin the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> of the patient by foreign remedies, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to reduce MACQUER reduce the professors of it to beggary, while they prosecuted the idle <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DREAMS">dreams</a> of converting every thing into <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>.

MACRIN

Pages 347-347

SALMON, one of the best Latin poets of the 16th century, was born at Loudun. His true name was John Salmon; but he took that of Macrin, from his being frequently so called in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a> by Francis I. on account of his extraordinary leanness. He was preceptor to Claudius of Savoy, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> of Tende; and to Honorius the count's <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>; and wrote several pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> in lyric <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, which were so admired, that he was called the Horace of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. He died of old <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, at Loudun, in 1555.—<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Macrin, his son, was not inferior to him as a poet, and surpassed him in his knowledge of the Greek tongue. He was preceptor to Catharine of Navarre, the sister of Henry the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>; and perished in the massacre on St Bartholomew's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> in 1572.

MACROBII

Pages 347-347

a people of Ethiopia, celebrated for their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, and the innocence of their manners; also a people in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Meröe. The Hyperboreans were also called Macrobii: they generally lived to their 120th year; and from their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGEVITY">longevity</a> they obtained their name (μακρός ζωής, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>.)

MACROBIUS

Pages 347-347

AMBROSIIUS AURELIUS THEODOSIUS, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Latin writer, who flourished towards the latter <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the fourth century.—Of what <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> he was, is not clear: Erasmus, in his Ciceronianus, seems to think he was a Greek; and he himself tells us, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> to his Saturnalia, that he was not a Roman, but laboured under the inconveniences of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> which was not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> to him. Of what <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> he was, Christian <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Pagan, is uncertain. Barthins ranks him among the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>; but Spanheim and Fabricius suppose him to have been a heathen. This, however, is certain, that, he was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of consular <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, and one of the chamberlains or masters of the wardrobe to Theodosius; as appears from a rescript directed to Florentius, concerning those who were to obtain that office. He wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMENTARY">commentary</a> upon Cicero's Somnium Scipionis, and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> books of Saturnalia, which treat of various subjects, and are an agreeable mixture of criticism and antiquity. He was not an original writer, but made <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of other people's works, borrowing not only their materials, but even their language, and for this he has been satirically rallied by some <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> authors, though rather unfairly, considering the express <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> and apology which he makes on this head, at the very entrance of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. "<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DON">Don</a>'t blame me," says he, "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> what I have collected from multifarious <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a>, I shall frequently express in the very words of the authors from whom I have taken it: for my view in this present work is, not to give proofs of my eloquence, but to collect and digest into some regularity and order such things as I thought might be useful to be known. I shall therefore here imitate the bees, who suck the best juices from all sorts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, and afterwards work them up into various forms and orders with some mixture of their own proper spirit." The Somnium Scipionis and Saturnalia have been often printed; to which has been added, in the later editions, a piece entitled De Differentiis et Societatibus Graeci Latineque Verbi. MACROCEPHALUS (compounded of μάκρος, "great," and κεφαλή, "head," denotes a person with a head larger or longer than the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> size. Macrocephali, or <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>-heads, is a name given to a certain people, who, according to the accounts of authors, were famous for the unseemly length of their heads; yet <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> so far habituated them to it, that instead of looking on it as a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEFORMITY">deformity</a>, they esteemed it a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, and, as soon as the child was born, moulded and fashioned its head in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> to as great a length as possible, and afterwards used all such rollers and bandages as might seem most likely to determine its growing long. The greater part of the islanders in the Archipelago, some of the people of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, and even some of those of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, still press their children's heads out lengthwise. We may observe also, that the Fpirots, many people of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, &c. are all born with some singularity in the conformation of their heads; either a flatness on the top, two extraordinary protuberances behind, or one on each side; singularities which we can only regard as an effect of an ancient and strange <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a>, which at length is become <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. According to the report of many travellers, the operation of compressing the head of a child lengthwise, while it is yet soft, is with a view insensibly to enlarge the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> between the two eyes, so that the visual rays <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> more to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> and left, the sight would embrace a much larger portion of the horizon; the advantage of which they are well acquainted with, either in the constant <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of hunting, or on a thousand other occasions. Ever since the 16th century, the missionaries established in the countries inhabited by the savages of America, have endeavoured to destroy this custom; and we find in the sessions of the third <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIMA">Lima</a>, held in 1585, a canon which expressly prohibits it. But if it has been repressed one way, the free <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a> and Maroons, although Africans, have adopted it, since they have been established among the Caribs, solely with the view of distinguishing their children, which are born free, from those who are born in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>. The Omaguas, a people of South America, according to P. Veigh, press the heads of their children so violently between two planks that they become quite sharp at the top, and flat before and behind. They say they do this to give their heads a greater resemblance to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>.

MACROCERCI

Pages 347-347

a name given to that class of animals, which have tails longer than their bodies.

MACROCOLUM

Pages 347-347
or MACROCOLLUM (formed of μάκρος, "large, and κεφαλή, "I join,") among the Romans, the largest kind of paper then in use. It measured sixteen inches, and frequently two feet.

MACROCOSM

Pages 347-347

a word denoting the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> world <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> universe. It is compounded of the Greek words μάκρος, "great," and κόσμος, "world."

MACROOMP

Pages 347-348
or MACROOM, a town of Ireland in the barony of Muskerry, county of Cork, and province of Munster, 142 miles from Dublin; it is situated amongst hills, in a dry gravelly limestone soil.—This place is said to take its name from an old crooked oak, so called in Irish, which formerly grew here. The castle was first built in King John's time, soon after the English conquest (according to Sir Richard Cox), by the Carews; but others attribute it to the Daltons. It was repaired and beautified by Teague Macarty, who died in the year 1565, and was father to Macroom the celebrated Sir Cormac Mac Teague mentioned by Camden and other writers as an active person in Queen Elizabeth's time. The late earls of Glanearty altered this castle into a more modern structure, it being burnt down in the wars of 1641. Opposite to the bridge is the parish-church, dedicated to St Colman of Cloyne. Here is a barrack for a foot company, a market-house, and a handsome Roman Catholic chapel. A considerable number of persons have been employed in this town in combing wool and spinning yarn, and some salt-works have been erected here. At half a mile's distance is a spaw, that rises on the very brink of a bog; its waters are a mild chalybeate, and are accounted serviceable in hypochondriacal cases, and in cutaneous eruptions. The fairs are four in the year.

MACROURUS

Pages 348-348

MACTATIO

Pages 348-348

in the Roman sacrifices, signifies the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of killing the victim. This was performed either by the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> himself, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> some of his inferior officers, whom we meet with under the names of popea, agones, culturarii, and victimarii; but, before the beast was killed, the priest, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> himself to the east, drew a crooked line with his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>, from the forehead to the tail. Among the Greeks, this <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> was performed most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> by the priest, or, in his absence, by the most <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> person present. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the sacrifice was offered to the celestial gods, the victim's throat was bent up towards heaven; if to the infernal, or to heroes, it was killed with its throat towards the ground. The manner of killing the animal was by a stroke on the head, and, after it was fallen, thrusting a knife into its throat. Much notice was taken, and good or ill success predicted, from the struggles of the beast, or its quiet submission to the blow, from the flowing of the blood, and the length of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> it happened to live after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>, &c. MACULÆ, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, dark spots appearing on the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUMINOUS">luminous</a> surfaces of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, and even some of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>. See Astronomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. MAD-APPLE. See Solanum, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index.

MADAGASCAR

Pages 348-356

the largest of the African <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, is situated between 43° and 51° of E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>., and between 12° and 26° of S. Lat.; extending in length near 1000 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west-east to south-west, and about 300 in breadth where broadest. It was discovered in 1506 by Laurence Almeyda; but the Persians and the Arabians were acquainted with it from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> immemorial under the name of Scandib. Alphonzo <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBUQUERQUE">Albuquerque</a> ordered Ruy Pereira dy Conthito to visit the interior parts, and that general intrusted Tristan d'Acunha with the survey. The Portuguese called it the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of St Lawrence; the French who visited it in the reign of Henry IV. named it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> Dauphine; its proper name is Madagasca. It is now, however, by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> consent, called Madagascar. This <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> island, according to many learned geographers, is the Cerné of Pliny, and the Menuthiasde of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>. It is everywhere watered by large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, streams and rivulets, which have their sources at the foot of that long chain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> which runs through the whole <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of the island from east to west. * Voyage à Madagascar. The two highest promontories are called Vivagora and Botistmenc. These mountains (according to the abbé Rochon*) enclose within their bosoms a variety of precious minerals and useful fossils. The traveller (who for the first time rambles over <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> and mountainous countries, intersected with valleys and with hills, where <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> left to herself brings forth the most singular and the most varied productions) is involuntarily surprised and terrified at the sight of precipices, the summits of which are crowned with monstrous trees, that seem coeval with the world. His astonishment is redoubled at the noise of those <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> cascades, the approach to which is generally inaccessible. But to those views so sublimely picturesque, rural scenes soon succeed; little hills, gently rising grounds, and plains, the vegetation of which is never repressed by the intemperance <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the vicissitude of the seasons. The eye contemplates with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> those vast savannas which nourish numberless herds of bullocks and of sheep. You behold a flourishing <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, produced almost solely by the fertilizing womb of nature. The fortunate inhabitants of Madagascar do not bedew the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> with their sweat; they scarcely stir the ground with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RAKE">rake</a>, and even that slight <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> is sufficient. They scrape little holes at a small distance from each other, into which they scatter a few grains of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, and cover them with their feet; and so <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> is the fertility of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, that the lands sown in this careless manner produce a hundred fold. The forests present a prodigious variety of the most useful and the most beautiful trees; ebony, wood for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DYEING">dyeing</a>, bamboos of an enormous thickness, and palm trees of every kind. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> employed in shipbuilding is no less common than those kinds so much prized by the cabinetmaker. We are told by the French governor Flacourt, in his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of this island†, that in the year 1650 he sent to France 52,000 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of aloes of an excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>. All of these various trees and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a> are surrounded by an infinite <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of parasitical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MUSHROOMS">mushrooms</a> of an infinite diversity of kinds and colours are to be met with everywhere in the woods; and the inhabitants know well how to distinguish those which are prejudicial to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>. They collect large quantities of useful <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUMS">gums</a> and resins; and out of the milky sap of a tree, denominated by them finguiorc, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of jatropha, the inhabitants, by means of coagulation, make that singular substance known to naturalists by the name of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUM">gum</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a>, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> rubber. Besides the aromatic and medicinal herbs which abound in the forests, the island produces <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a> of a length and strength which surpass any in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">Sugar</a>-canæs, wax, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a> of different kinds, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIGO">indigo</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>, gum-lac, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBERGRIS">ambergris</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, and cotton, would long since have been objects of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> which Madagascar would have yielded in profusion, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the Europeans, in visiting the island, had furnished the inhabitants with the necessary information for preparing and improving these several productions. The sugar-canæs (as we are informed by another traveller‡) are much larger and finer than any in the West Indies; being as thick as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WRIST">wrist</a>, and so full of juice, that a foot of them <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> weigh two pounds. When the natives travel, they carry a sugar-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANE">cane</a> along with them, which will support them for two or three days. Here are also plenty of tamarinds; and such quantities of limes and oranges, that very large casks may Madagascar may be filled with their juices at a trifling expense, as they may be purchased for <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> pots, muskets, powder, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, &c. During the short time that <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">Admiral</a> Watson's squadron stood here in 1754, Mr Ives preserved about half a hogshead full of those juices, which proved afterwards of the greatest <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to the ships crews. It must be observed, however, that no good <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> is to be had at St Augustine in the south-west <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the island, where ships usually touch, unless boats are sent for it four or five miles up the river; and instead of filling their casks at low water (as is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> in most other rivers), they must begin to fill at about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>: The reason assigned for this is, that the river has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> at other places besides this of St Augustine's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>; and it has been found by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, that the sea water brought into the river by the flood tide is not discharged till a quarter's flood of the next tide in St Augustine's bay; and for three miles up the river, the water is always very brackish, if not quite <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>. The abundance and variety of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> of every kind, which a fine <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> and fertile soil can produce, are on no part of the globe, according to M. Roehon, superior to those of Madagascar: <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAME">game</a>, wild-fowl, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a>, fish, cattle, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, are alike plentiful. The oxen, Mr Ives also informs us, are large and fat, and have each a protuberance of fat between the shoulders, weighing about 20 pounds. Their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> is greatly esteemed by all the European nations trading to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, and ships are sent to Madagascar on purpose to kill and salt them on the island. The protuberance of fat above mentioned is particularly esteemed after it has lain some time in salt; but our author says, that he could not join in the encomiums either on this piece or the beef in general; as the herbage on which the creatures feed gives their flesh a particular <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, which to him was disagreeable. The sheep differ little from the goats; being equally hairy, only that their heads are somewhat larger: their necks resemble that of a calf, and their tails weigh at least ten pounds. Vast quantities of locusts rise here from the low lands in thick <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>, extending sometimes to an incredible length and breadth. The natives eat these insects, and even prefer them to their finest fish. Their method of dressing them is to strip off their legs and wings, and fry them in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>. The inhabitants (termed Melagaches or Madecasses), M. Roehon informs us, are in person above the middle size of Europeans. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of the skin is different in different tribes: among some it is of a deep <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, among others tawney; some of the natives are of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> colour, but the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a> of by far the greatest number is olive. All those who are black have woolly <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> like the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>: those, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, who resemble Indians and Mulattoes, have hair equally straight with that of the Europeans; the nose is not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and flat; the forehead is large and open; in short, all the features are regular and agreeable. Their physiognomy displays the appearance of frankness and of satisfaction; they are desirous only of learning such things as may administer to their necessities; that species of knowledge which demands reflection is indifferent to them; sober, agile, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>, they spend the greatest part of their time either in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> or in amusement. In fine, according to the Abbé, the native of Madagascar, like savages in general, possesses a character equally devoid of vice and of virtue; the gratifications of the present moment solely occupy his reflections; he possesses no kind of foresight whatever; and he cannot conceive the idea that there are men in the world who trouble themselves about the evils of futurity. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of the island has been estimated at four millions; but this calculation is thought exaggerated by our author, and indeed it appears incredible to us. Every tribe or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> inhabits its own <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTON">canton</a>, and is governed by its own customs. Each of these acknowledges a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>; this chief is sometimes <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTIVE">elective</a>, but more usually <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a>. The lands are not divided and portioned out, but belong to those who are at the trouble of cultivating them. These islanders make <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of neither locks nor keys; the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> part of their food consists in rice, fish, and flesh; their rice is moistened with a soup which is seasoned with pimento, ginger, saffron, and aromatic herbs. They display wonderful cunning in catching a variety of birds, many of which are unknown in Europe; they have the pheasant, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PARTRIDGE">partridge</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUAIL">quail</a>, the pintado, the wild duck, teal of five or six different kinds, the blue hen, the black paroquet, and the turtle-dove, in great plenty; and also a bat of a monstrous size, which is much prized on account of its exquisite flavour. These last are so hideous in their appearance, that they at first terrify the Europeans sailors: but after they have vanquished their repugnance to them, they <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> their flesh infinitely before that of the pullets of their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The Melagaches also catch an immense <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of sea-fish: such as the dorado, the sole, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERRING">herring</a>, the mackerel, the turtle, &c. with oysters, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CRABS">crabs</a>, &c. The rivers afford excellent eels, and mullets of an exquisite flavour. The inhabitants near St Augustine's bay, Mr Ives informs us, speak as much broken English as enables them to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> their provisions for European <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>. These, on the part of the Melagaches are cattle, poultry, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, fruit, rice, salt, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORCELAIN">porcelain</a>, potatoes, yams, fish, lances, and shells. From the Europeans they receive muskets, powder, bullets, flints, clouties, (including handkerchiefs, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> of all kinds), beads, iron pots, &c.—Silver, which they call manila, is in great esteem with them, and is made by them into bracelets for their wives. That part of the island at which the English squadron touched, is in the dominions of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Babo, who, by the account of Mr Ives, seemed greatly to affect to be an Englishman. They had no sooner touched at the island, than they were waited on by one called Robin Hood, and another person, both of whom bore the office of pursers. Along with these were Phillibey the general; John Anderson and Frederic Martin, captains. Nor did the king himself and his family disdain to pay them a visit; who, in like manner, were distinguished by English names; the king's eldest son being called the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> not being without a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a>, a Prince Augustus, princesses, &c. as in England. All these grandees came on board naked, excepting only a slight covering about their loins and on their shoulders, made of a kind of grass growing on the island; which they had adorned with small glass beads by way of border or fringe. Their hair resembled that of the Indians. Madagas-Indians in being long and black, rather than the woolly heads of the African negroes. "The wives of the Melagaches (according to our author) take great pains with their husbands hair; sometimes putting it in large and regular curls; at other times braiding it in great order, and making it shine with a particular oil which the island produces. The men always carry in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> a wooden <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANCE">lance</a> headed with iron, which is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> made very neat; and they are such excellent marksmen, that they will strike with it a very small object at 30 or 40 yards distance. They have also commonly a musket, which they get from Europeans in exchange for cattle, and are always sure to keep in excellent order. I am sorry to say (continues Mr Ives) that the English are frequently guilty of great impositions in this kind of traffic, by disposing of cheap and ill-tempered barrels among the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> inhabitants, who sometimes lose their lives by the bursting of these pieces. Such iniquitous practises as these must in the end prove injurious to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>; and has indeed already made the name of more than one-half of these traders truly infamous among the deluded but hitherto friendly Madagascarians. "They are a civil and good-natured people, but easily provoked, and apt to show their resentment on the least provocation, especially when they think themselves injured or slighted. Another characteristic of them is, the very <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> notions of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> they entertain of their king; which is carried to such a height, that they are never more sensibly hurt than when they imagine he is treated with incivility or disrespect. This mighty monarch resides in a town built with mud, about 12 miles up the country from St Augustine's bay. On the east side of the bay, as you enter, there resided one Prince William, a relation and tributary to the king; but who in most <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> acted as an independent prince, and always used his utmost endeavours with the officers to cause them buy their provisions from him, and not from the king or his subjects. In this prince's territories, not far from the sea, are the remains of a fort built by Avery the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIRATE">pirate</a>. "All the women of Madagascar, excepting the very poorest sort, wear a covering over their breasts and shoulders, ornamented with glass beads, and none go without a cloth about their loins. They commonly walk with a long slender rod or stick. The men are allowed to marry as many women as they can support. "During our stay at this island (says Mr Ives), I observed with great concern, several miserable objects in the last stage of the venereal <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>. They had not been able to find any cure; and as far as I could learn, their doctors are totally ignorant of medicine. The only method they use for curing all distempers, as well <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> as internal, is the wearing on the arm or neck a particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARM">charm</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMULET">amulet</a>; or besmearing the part affected with earth moistened with the juice of some plant or tree, and made up into soft paste. "I took some pains to learn their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> tenets; and find that they worship one Universal Father; whom, when they speak in English, they call God; and in whom they conceive all kinds of perfection to reside. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> they look upon as a glorious body; and, I believe, as a spiritual being, but created and dependent. They frequently look up to it with wonder, if not with praise and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADORATION">adoration</a>. They make can their supplications to the One Almighty, and offer sacrifices to him in their distresses. I had the curiosity to attend a sacrifice, at the hut of John Anderson, whose father had for a long time been afflicted with sickness. About sunset an ox was brought into the yard; and the son, who officiated as a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, slew it. An altar was reared nigh, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> of it was sprinkled with the blood of the victim. The head, after its being severed from the body, was placed, with the horns on, at the foot of the altar: the caul was burned on the fire, and most of the pluck and entrails boiled in a pot. The sick man, who was brought to the door, and placed on the ground so as to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> the sacrifice, prayed often, and seemingly with great fervency. His eyes were fixed attentively towards the heavens, and his hands held up in a supplicating posture. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> ended with the son's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> up the ox into small pieces; the greatest part of which he distributed amongst the poor slaves belonging to his father and himself; reserving, however, some of the best pieces for his own use. Upon the whole, I <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> so many circumstances in this Madagascarian sacrifice, so exactly resembling those described in the Old <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a> as offered up by the Jews, that I could not turn my thoughts back to the original, without being sensibly struck by the exactness of the copy." When the squadron first arrived at Madagascar, the king of Baba, a man of about 60 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, was ill of the gout. Having demanded of Admiral Watson some presents, the latter complimented him, among other things, with some brandy. The monarch then asked him if he had any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> with him, and if he was a great doctor, and a king's doctor? To all which being answered in the affirmative, he desired him to bring some mahomets (medicines) for his sick knee. With this requisition Mr Ives designed to comply; but having waited until some officers should be ready to accompany him, his majesty in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time, took such a dose of brandy as quickly sent the gout into his head, and occasioned his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. Mr Ives observes, that it happened very luckily for him that the monarch's decease happened without his having taken any of the medicines intended for him, as it would have been impossible to avoid the imputation of having poisoned him, which would certainly have been resented by his loyal subjects. The king's death occasioned great confusion; the grandees being desirous that it should be concealed for some time. This, however, was found impossible; on which they set off for the Mud Town about 11 o'clock the same evening. All the inhabitants of the village followed their example; leaving only the dogs, who set up the most hideous howling. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Frederic Martin coming to take leave of the English, begged with great earnestness for a fresh supply of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a>; whispering that the king was dead, and that they should in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> go to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> about making another. They had been formerly told, that one who had the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of duke of Baba would certainly succeed to the throne; but they afterwards learned, that Philibey the general having espoused the cause of Raphani the late king's son, and taken him under his tutelage and protection, this youth, who was only about years of age, succeeded his father as king of Baba. The following is a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the southern <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the island, from the Abbé Rochon. "That part of Madagascar in which Fort-Dauphin is situated is very populous. Almost all the villages are placed on eminences, and surrounded with two rows of strong palisadoes, somewhat in the manner of such of our fences as are composed of hurdles and turf. Within, is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARAPET">parapet</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> earth about four feet in height; large pointed bamboos placed at the distance of five feet from each other, and sunk in a pit, form a kind of loop-holes, which contribute towards the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of these villages, some of which are besides fortified with a ditch ten feet in breadth and six in depth. The dwelling of the chief is called a donac. When the chiefs go abroad, they are always provided with a musket and a stick armed with iron, and adorned at the extremity with a little tuft of cow's hair. They wear a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BONNET">bonnet</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>. It is chiefly by the colour of their bonnet that they are distinguished from their subjects. Their authority is extremely limited: however, in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Carcanossi, the lands by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> belong to their chiefs, who distribute them among their subjects for the purposes of cultivation; they exact a trifling quit-rent in return, which in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> is called luensa. The people of Carcanossi are not altogether ignorant of the art of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>; they even possess some historical works in the Madagascar tongue: but their learned men, whom they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> Ombiasses, make use of the Arabic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> alone. They have treatises on medicine, geomancy, and judicial astrology; the most renowned live in the province of Matatane; it is in that district that <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGIC">magic</a> still remains in all its <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>; the Matanes are actually dreaded by the other Madagascan on account of their excellence in this delusive art. The Ombiasses have public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> in which they teach geomancy and astrology. The natives have undoubtedly learned the art of writing from the Arabians, who made a conquest of this island about 300 years since. "The people of the province of Anossi, near Fort Dauphin, are lively, gay, sensible, and grateful; they are passionately fond of women; are never melancholy in their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>; and their principal occupation is to please the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a>; indeed, whenever they meet their wives, they begin to sing and dance. The women, from being happy, are always in good humour. Their lively and cheerful character is extremely pleasing to the Europeans. I have often been present at their assemblies, where affairs of importance have been agitated; I have observed their dances, their sports, and their amusements, and I have found them free from those excesses which are but too common among polished nations. Indeed I was too young at this time for my observations to be of much weight; but if my experience be insufficient to inspire confidence, I beg the reader will rather consider the nature of things, than the relations given by men without principles or intelligence, who fancy that they have a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to tyrannize over the inhabitants of every country which they can subdue. If the people of Madagascar have sometimes availed themselves of treachery, they have been forced to it by the tyranny of the Europeans. The weak have no other arms against the strong. Could they defend themselves by any other means from our <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a> and bayonets? They are uninformed and helpless; and we avail ourselves of their weakness, in order to make them submit to our covetousness and caprice. They receive the most cruel and oppressive treatment, in return for the hospitality which they generously bestow on us; and we call them traitors and cowards, when we force them to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> the yoke with which we have been pleased to load them." In the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> volume of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> Benyowsky's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> and Travels we have the following account of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, &c. of the people of this island. "The Madagascar nation believe in a Supreme Being, whom they call Zanhare, which denotes creator of all things. They <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> and revere this Being; but have dedicated no temple to him, and much less have they substituted idols. They make sacrifices, by killing oxen and sheep, and they <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> all these libations to God. It has been asserted, that this nation likewise makes offerings to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a>: but in this there is a deception; for the piece of the sacrificed beast which is usually thrown into the fire is not intended in honour of the devil, as is usually pretended. This custom is very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, and no one can tell the true reason of it. With regard to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMMORTALITY">immortality</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, the Madagascar people are persuaded, that, after their death, their spirit will return again to the region in which the Zanhare dwells; but they by no means admit that the spirit of man, after his death, can suffer any evil. As to the distinction of evil or good, they are persuaded that the good and upright man shall be recompensed, in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, by a good state of health, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTANCY">constancy</a> of his friends, the increase of his fortunes, the obedience of his children, and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of beholding the prosperity of his family: and they believe that the wicked man's fate shall be the contrary to this. The Madagascar people, upon this conviction, when they make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a>, add benedictions in favour of those who keep them, and curses against those who break them. In this manner it is that they <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> to the judgment of Zanhare, in making agreements; and it has never been known, or heard of, that a native of Madagascar has broken his oath, provided it was made in the usual manner, which they say was prescribed by their forefathers. "As to their kings and form of government, &c. the Madagascar people have always acknowledged the line of Ramin, as that to which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of Ampansacabe or sovereign belongs. They have considered this line as extinct since the death of Dian Rami ni Larizon, which happened 66 years ago, and whose body was buried upon a mountain, out of which the river Manangourou <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>; but having acknowledged the heir of this line on the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> side, they re-established this title in the year 1776. The right of the Ampansacabe consists in nominating the Rohandrians to assist in the cabars, at which all those who are cited are bound to appear, and the judgment of the Ampansacabe in his cabar is decisive. Another <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a> of the Ampansacabe is, that each Rohandrian is obliged to leave him by will a certain proportion of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, which the successors usually purchase by a slight tribute or fine. Thirdly, The Ampansacabe has a right to exact from each Rohandrian one-tenth Madagas. tenth of the produce of his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, and a number of horned cattle and slaves, in proportion to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> of the country possessed by each Rohandrian. The second order is composed of the Rohandrians, or princes. Since the loss of the Ampansacabe, three of these Rohandrians have assumed the title of kings, namely the Rohandrian of the province of Mahavelou, named Hiavi; of the province of Voemar, named Lambouni; and a third at Bombetoki, named Cinamounpou. The third order consists of the Voadziri, or lords of a district, composed of several villages. The fourth order consists of the Lohavohits, or chiefs of villages. The fifth order, Ondatzzi, who are freemen, compose the attendants or followers of the Rohandrians, Voadziri, or Lohavohits. The sixth order consists of Ombiasses, or learned men; and this order forms the warriors, workmen, physicians, and diviners; these last possess no <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>. The seventh order consists of Ampurias or slaves. "Having made inquiries from Bombetoki passing to the northward, and as far as Itapere, the result proved that there are 38 Rohandrians actually reigning, and 287 Voadziri. With respect to the Lohavohits, Ondatzzi, and Ombiasses, it was not possible to obtain any accurate determination of their number. These orders preserve a regular gradation, respecting which it would be very difficult to give a detailed account. They live in the manner we read of concerning the ancient patriarchs. Every father of a family is priest and judge in his own <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, though he depends upon the Lohavohits, who superintend his conduct. This last is answerable to his Voadziri, and the Voadziri to the Rohandrian. "The Madagascan people having no communication with the main land of Æthiopia, have not altered their primitive laws; and the language throughout the whole extent of the island is the same. It would be a rash attempt to determine the origin of this nation; it is certain that it consists of three distinct races, who have for ages past formed intermixtures which vary to infinity. The first <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> is that of Zafe Ibrahim, or descendants of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a>; but they have no vestige of Judaism, except circumcision, and some names, such as <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a>, Reuben, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a>, &c. This race is of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> colour.—The second race is that of Zafaramini: with respect to this, some books which are still extant among the Ombiasses, affirm that it is not more than six centuries since their arrival at Madagascar.—With respect to the third race of Zafe Canambou, it is of Arabian <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a>, and arrived much more lately than the others from the coasts of Æthiopia: hence it possesses neither power nor <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>, and fills only the charges of writers, historians, poets, &c. "In regard to arts and trades, the Madagascar nation are contented with such as are necessary to make their moveables, tools, utensils, and arms for defense; to construct their dwellings, and the boats which are necessary for their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>; and lastly, to fabricate cloths and stuffs for their clothing. They are desirous only of possessing the necessary supplies of immediate utility and convenience. The principal and most respected business, is the manufacture of iron and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>. The artists in this way call themselves ampanafa vilo.
