They are very expert in fusing the ore, and forging utensils, such as hatchets, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HAMMERS">hammers</a>, anvils, knives, spades, sagayes, razors, pincers, or tweezers for pulling out the hair, &c. The second class consists of the goldsmiths (ompanca vola mena): they <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> in ingots, and make up bracelets, buckles, earrings, drops, rings, &c. The third are called ompanvilanga, and are potters. The fourth are the ompaneva <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TA">ta</a>, or turners in wood, who make boxes called ratta, plates, wooden and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">horn</a> spoons, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEE">bee</a>-hives, coffins, &c. The fifth ompan cacassou, or carpenters. They are very expert in this business, and make use of the rule, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPASSES">compasses</a>, &c. The sixth are the ompania vi, or ropemakers. They make their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> of different kinds of bark of trees, and likewise of hemp. The seventh, ampan lamba, or weavers. This business is performed by women only, and it would be reekoned disgraceful in a man to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> it. The ombiasses are the literary men and physicians, who give advice only. The herauvits are comedians and dancers. "The Madagascan people always live in society; that is to say, in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and villages. The towns are surrounded by a ditch and pallisades (as already mentioned), at the extremities of which a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> of from 12 to 20 armed men is kept. The houses of private people consist of a convenient cottage, surrounded by several small ones: the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the house dwells in the largest, and his women or slaves lodge in the smaller. These houses are built of wood, covered with leaves of the palm tree or straw. "The houses of the great men of the country are very spacious; each house is composed of two walls and four apartments: round about the principal house other smaller habitations are built for the accommodation of the women, and the whole family of the chief; but the slaves cannot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> the night within them.—Most of the houses inhabited by the Rohandrians are built with taste and admirable symmetry." The French attempted to conquer and take possession of the whole island, by order, and for the use of, their Most Christian Majesties <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIII. and XIV., and they maintained a footing on it from the year 1642 to 1657. During this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, by the most cruel treachery, they taught the native princes the barbarous traffic in slaves, by villainously selling to the Dutch governor of Mauritius a number of innocent people, who had been assisting them in forming a settlement at Fort Dauphin. The Abbé Roehon tells us, that the insalubrity of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> in Madagascar determined his countrymen in 1664 to quit that immense island, in order to establish themselves at so inconsiderable a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> as the isle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOURBON">Bourbon</a>, which is scarcely perceptible in a map of the globe: but it is apparent, from the account of the state of the French affairs on the island of Madagascar, in 1661, when Flacourt's narrative was published, that their ill treatment of the natives had raised such a general and formidable opposition to their residence in the country, that the French were obliged to abandon their possessions for other reasons than the unhealthy qualities of the climate. We have not room here for a detail of all the oppressive <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> of the French, which the abbé himself candidly censures in the strongest terms; but shall extract the following narrative, both because it is interesting in itself, and exhibits the causes and the means of their expulsion. La Case, one of the French officers employed by the governor of Fort Dauphin against the natives, was so successful in all his enterprises, that they called him Deacn Pous, the name of a chief who had formerly conquered the whole island. The French governor, jealous of his renown, treated him harshly, and refused to allow him the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> or honours due to his valour. The sovereign of the province of Amboulle, called Deacn Rascitat, taking advantage of his discontent, prevailed on him to become his general. Five Frenchmen followed him. Deacn Nong, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Rascitat, captivated by the person and heroism of La Case, offered him her hand with the consent of her father. The chief, grown old, infirm, and arrived at the last stage of existence, had the satisfaction of securing the happiness of his subjects, by appointing his son-in-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> master of the rich province of Amboulle. La Case, in marrying Deacn Nong, refused to take the titles and honours attached to the sovereign power; he would accept of no other character, than that of the first subject of his wife, who was declared sovereign at the death of her father. Secure in the affection of this princess, who was not only possessed of personal charms, but of courage and great qualities, he was beloved and respected by her family, and by all the people of Amboulle, who reverenced him as a father; and yet, how much soever he wished it, he was unable to contribute to the prosperity of his countrymen at Fort Dauphin, whom he knew to be in the utmost distress. The governor, regarding him as a traitor, had set a price on his head, and on the heads of the five Frenchmen who had followed him. The neighbouring chiefs, irritated at this treatment of a man whom they so much venerated, unanimously refused to supply the fort with provisions. This occasioned a famine in the place, which, with a contagious fever and other maladies, reduced the French garrison to 80 men. The establishment at Fort Dauphin, on the point of being totally destroyed, was preserved for a short time from ruin by the arrival of a vessel from France, commanded by Keradie an officer of Brittany, who, with the assistance of a young advocate who had been kidnapped on board the vessel, prevailed on the envious and implacable governor Charnagou to make peace with La Case and his sovereign spouse Deacn Nong. This peace, however, lasted but for a short time; the French, restless and insolent to the neighbouring nations, again drew on them the vengeance of the natives. Even the few friends whom they had been able to acquire by means of La Case, were rendered hostile to them by the tyrannic zeal of the missionaries; who, not contented with being tolerated and allowed to make converts, insisted on Deacn Manang, sovereign of Mandrary, a powerful, courageous, and intelligent chief, well disposed to the French, to divorce all his wives but one. This prince, not convinced of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of such a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, assured them that he was unable to change his habits and way of living, which were those of his forefathers. "You would allow me (says he) to have one wife; but if the possession of one woman is a blessing, why should a numerous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERAGLIO">seraglio</a> be an evil, while peace and concord reign among those of whom it is composed? Do you see among us any indications of jealousy or hatred? No, all our women are good; all try to make me happy; and I am more their slave than their master." This speech had no effect on Father Stephen, superior of the Madagascar mission. He peremptorily ordered him instantly to repudiate all his wives except one; and threatened, in presence of the women, to have them taken from him by the French <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, if he hesitated in complying with his commands. It is easy to imagine, says M. Rochin, with what indignation this language must have been heard in the donac or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of this prince. The females assailed the missionary on all sides; loaded him with execrations and blows; and in their fury, would doubtless have afforded him no more quarter than the Thracian women did <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORPHEUS">Orpheus</a>, if Deacn Manang, notwithstanding his own agitation, had not made use of all his authority to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> him. In order to free himself from the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a> of this priest, he removed with his family 70 or 80 miles up into the country; but he was soon followed by Father Stephen and another missionary, with their attendants. The chief, Manang, still received them civilly; but he intreated them no longer to insist on the conversion of him and his people, as it was impossible to oblige them to quit the customs and manners of their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>. The only reply which Father Stephen made to this intreaty, was by tearing off the oth, and the amulets and charms which the chief wore as sacred badges of his own religion; and, throwing them into the fire, he declared war against him and his nation. This violence instantly cost him and his followers their lives: they were all massacred by order of Manang, who vowed the destruction of all the French in the island; in which intention he proceeded in a manner that has been related by an eye witness, who was afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMISSARY">commissary</a> of artillery, in a narrative published at Lyons in 1722, entitled Voyage de Madagascar. "Our yoke (says the Abbé Rochin) was become odious and insupportable. Historians, for the honour of civilized nations, should <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURY">bury</a> in oblivion the afflicting narratives of the atrocities exercised on these people, whom we are pleased to call barbarous, treacherous, and deceitful, because they have revolted against European adventurers, whose least crime is that of violating the sacred <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> of hospitality." It was about the year 1672 that the French were totally driven from the island of Madagascar; and no considerable attempts were made to form fresh establishments there till within these few years, by M. de Modave, and by Count Benyowski; neither of which was attended with success, for reasons given by the Abbé, but which we have not room to detail. Madder, a plant used in dyeing. See Rubia, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>; and for its dyeing properties, see Dyeing. Madeiras, a cluster of islands, belonging to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, situated in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a>, in W. Long. 16°, and between 32° and 33° N. Lat.—The largest of them, called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MADEIRA">Madeira</a>, from which the rest take their name, is about 55 English miles long, and 10 miles broad; and was first discovered on the 2d of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, in the year 1419, by Joao Gonzales Zarco, there being no historical foundation for the fabulous report of its discovery by one Machin an Englishman. It is divided into two capitains, named <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FUNCHAL">Funchal</a> and Maxico, from the towns of Madeiras of those names. The former contains two judicatures, viz. Funchal and Galhetta; the latter being a town with the title of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, belonging to the family of Castello Melhor. The second <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITANIA">capitania</a> likewise comprehends two judicatures, viz. Maxico (read Mashico) and San Vicente. Funchal is the only citadel or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> in the island, which has also <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> villas or towns; of which there are four, Calheta, Camara de Lobos, Ribeira Braba, and Ponta de Sol in the capitania of Funchal, which is divided into 26 parishes. The other three are in the capitania of Maxico, which consists of 17 parishes; these towns are called Maxico, San Vicente, and Santa Cruz. There is one curiosity in the town of Funchal, which deserves to be taken notice of, and that is a chamber in one of the corners of the Franciscan convent, the walls and ceiling of which are completely covered with rows of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> skulls and human thigh <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>, so arranged that in the obtuse <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> made by each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of the latter, crossing each other obliquely, is placed a skull. The only vacant space that appears is in the centre of the side opposite to the door, on which there is an extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> above a kind of altar, but what the subject it is intended to represent, it is difficult to determine. A <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> probably intended for St Francis, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> saint, seems to be intent on trying in a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> the comparative weight of a sinner and a saint. A dirty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMP">lamp</a> suspended from the ceiling, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> glimmering in the socket, serves dimly to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> up this dismal den of skulls. The monk who attends as shewman, is careful to impress on the minds of those who visit it, the idea that they are all relics of holy men who died on the island, although Mr <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARROW">Barrow</a> is of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-yard must have been frequently robbed, in order to accumulate such a prodigious number of skulls, which from a rough computation made by that <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, could not be under 3000. The governor is at the head of all the civil and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> departments of this island, of Porto-Santo, the Salvages, and the Ilhas Desertas; which last only contain the temporary huts of some fishermen, who <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> thither in pursuit of their business; his salary is computed to be worth 2000l. per annum, 200l. of which is in the form of a present from the English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>. The law department is under the corregidor, who is appointed by the king of Portugal, commonly sent from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a>, and holds his place during the king's pleasure. All causes come to him from inferior courts by appeal. Each judicature has a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>; and a Juiz or judge, whom they choose, presides over them. At Funchal he is called Juiz da Fora; and in the absence, or after the death of the corregidor, acts as his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a>. The foreign merchants elect their own judge, called the Provider, who is at the same time collector of the king's customs and revenues, which amount in all to about 12,000l. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>. Far the greatest part of this sum is applied towards the salaries of civil and military officers, the pay of troops, and the maintenance of public buildings. This revenue arises, first from the tenth of all the produce of this island belonging to the king, by virtue of his office as grand master of the order of Christ; secondly, From ten per cent duties laid on all imports, provisions excepted; and lastly, From the eleven per cent <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> Madeiras on all exports. The island has but one company of regular soldiers of 100 men; the rest of the military force is a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a> consisting of 3000 men, divided into companies, each commanded by a captain, who has one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> under him and one ensign. There is no pay given to either the private men or the officers of this militia; and yet their places are much sought after, on account of the rank which they communicate. These troops are embodied once a-year, and exercised once a-<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a>. All the military are commanded by the Serjeante Mor. The governor has two Capitanos de Sal about him, who do duty as aides-de-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> priests on the island are about 1200, many of whom are employed as private tutors. Since the expulsion of the Jesuits, no regular public school is to be found here; unless we except a seminary, where a priest, appointed for that purpose, instructs and educates ten students at the king's expense. These wear a red cloak over the usual black gowns worn by ordinary students. All those who intend to go into orders, are obliged to qualify themselves by studying in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COIMBRA">Coimbra</a>, lately re-established in Portugal. There is also a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> at Madeira, with a bishop at their head, whose income is considerably greater than the governor's; it consists of 110 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a> of wine, and of 40 mugs of wheat, each containing 24 bushels; which amounts in common years to 3000l. sterling. Here are likewise 60 or 70 Franciscan friars, in four monasteries, one of which is at Funchal. About 300 nuns live on the island, in four <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>, of the order of Merci, Sta Clara, Incarnacao, and Dom <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a>. Those of the last-mentioned <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> may marry whenever they choose, and leave their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>. In the year 1768, the inhabitants living in the 43 parishes of Madeira, amounted to 63,913, of whom there were 31,341 males and 32,572 females. But in that year 5243 persons died, and no more than 2198 children were born; so that the number of the dead exceeded that of the born by 3045. It is highly probable that some epidemical distemper carried off so disproportionate a number in that year, as the island would shortly be entirely depopulated if the mortality were always equal to this. Another circumstance concurs to strengthen this supposition, namely, the excellence of the climate. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> is in general mild and temperate: in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> is very moderate on the higher parts of the island, whither the better sort of people retire for that season; and in the winter the snow remains there for several days, whilst it is never known to continue above a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> or two in the lower parts. The common people of this island are of a tawney colour, and well shaped; though they have large feet, owing perhaps to the efforts they are obliged to make in climbing the craggy paths of this mountainous country. Their faces are <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a>; their eyes dark; their black hair naturally falls in ringlets, and begins to crisp in some individuals, which may perhaps be owing to intermarriages with negroes; in general, they are hard featured, but not disagreeable. Their women are too frequently ill-favoured, and want the florid complexion, which, when united to a pleasing assen- Madeira's blage of regular features, gives our northern fair ones the superiority over all their sex. They are small, have prominent cheek bones, large feet, an ungraceful gait, and the colour of the darkest brunette. The just proportion of the body, the fine form of their hands, and their large lively eyes, seem in some measure to compensate for those defects. The labouring men, in summer, wear linen trousers, a coarse shirt, a large hat, and boots; some have a short jacket made of cloth, and a long cloak, which they sometimes carry over their arm. The women wear a petticoat, and a short corselet or jacket, closely fitting their shapes, which is a simple, and often not an elegant dress. They have also a short but wide cloak; and those that are unmarried tie their hair on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of their head, on which they wear no covering. The country people are exceeding sober and frugal; their diet in general consisting of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> and onions, or other roots, and little animal food. However, they avoid eating tripe, or any offals, because it is proverbially said of a very poor man, "He is reduced to eat tripe." Their common drink is water, or an infusion of the remaining rind or skin of the grape (after it has passed through the wine press), which when fermented acquires some tartness and acidity, but cannot be kept very long. The wine for which the island is so famous, and which their own hands prepare, seldom if ever regales them. Their principal occupation is the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a> and raising of vines; but as that branch of agriculture requires little attendance during the greatest part of the year, they naturally incline to idleness. The warmth of the climate, which renders great provision against the inclemencies of weather unnecessary, and the ease with which the cravings of appetite are satisfied, must tend to indolence, wherever the regulations of the legislature do not counteract it, by endeavouring, with the prospect of increasing happiness, to infuse the spirit of industry. It seems the Portuguese government does not pursue the proper methods against this dangerous <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETHARGY">lethargy</a> of the state. They have lately ordered the plantation of olive trees here, on such spots as are too dry and barren to bear vines; but they have not thought of giving temporary assistance to the labourers, and have offered no premium by which these might be induced to conquer their reluctance to innovations and aversion to labour. The vineyards are held only on an annual <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a> reaps but four-tenths of the produce, since other four-tenths are paid in kind to the owner of the land, one-tenth to the king, and one to the clergy. Such small profits, joined to the thought of toiling merely for the advantage of others, if improvements were attempted, entirely preclude the hopes of a future increase. Oppressed as they are, they have however preserved a high <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of cheerfulness and contentment; their labours are commonly alleviated with songs, and in the evening they assemble from different cottages to dance to the drowsy music of a guitar. The inhabitants of the towns are more ill-favoured than the country people, and often <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> and lean. The men wear French clothes, commonly black, which do not seem to fit them, and have been in fashion in the polite world about half a century ago. Their ladies are delicate and have agreeable features; but the characteristic jealousy of the men still locks them up, and deprives them of a happiness which the country women, amidst all their distresses, enjoy. Many of the better people are a sort of petite noblesse, which we would call gentry, whose genealogical <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> makes them unsociable and ignorant, and causes a ridiculous affectation of gravity. The landed property is in the hands of a few ancient families, who live at Funchal, and in the various towns on the island. Madeira consists of one large mountain, whose branches rise everywhere from the sea towards the centre of the island, converging to the summit, in the midst of which is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEPRESSION">depression</a> or excavation, called the Val by the inhabitants, always covered with a fresh and delicate herbage. This and another cavity of the same description are supposed on good grounds to have been craters of volcanoes. The rocks consist of three or four different species of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAVA">lava</a>, some of which have assumed a regular prismatic form, some of the prisms being extremely perfect, and of 30 or 40 feet in length. They also contain olivine, and occasionally carbonate of lime and zeolite; and intermixed with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STRATA">strata</a> of lava are beds of clay, with layers of pumice and ashes. The soil of the island is clay on the surface, and large masses of it as hard as brick are found underneath. Many brooks and small rivulets descend from the summits in deep chasms or glens, which separate the various parts of the island. The beds of the brooks are in some places covered with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> of all sizes, carried <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from the higher parts by the violence of winter rains or floods of melted snow. The water is conducted by weirs and channels in the vineyards, where each proprietor has the use of it for a certain time; some being allowed to keep a constant supply of it, some to use it thrice, others twice, and others only once a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEEK">week</a>. As the heat of the climate renders this supply of water to the vineyards absolutely necessary, it is not without great expense that a new vineyard can be planted; for the maintenance of which, the owners must purchase water at a high price, from those who are constantly supplied, and are thus enabled to spare some of it. Wherever a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> piece of ground can be contrived in the higher hills, the natives make plantations of eddoes, enclosed by a kind of dyke to cause a stagnation, as that plant succeeds best in swampy ground. Its leaves serve as food for hogs, and the country people use the roots for their own nourishment. The sweet <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-POTATO">potato</a> is planted for the same purpose, and makes a principal article of diet; together with chestnuts, which grow in extensive woods, on the higher parts of the island, where the vine will not thrive. Wheat and barley are likewise sown, especially in spots where the vines are decaying through age, or where they are newly planted. But the crops do not produce above three months provisions; and the inhabitants are therefore obliged to have recourse to other food, besides importing considerable quantities of corn from North <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> in exchange for wine. The want of manure, and the inactivity of the people, are in some measure the causes of this disadvantage; but supposing husbandry to be carried to its perfection here, Madeiras here, they could not raise corn sufficient for their consumption. They make their <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-THRESHING">threshing</a>-floors of a circular form, in a corner of a field, which is cleared and beaten solid for the purpose. The sheaves are laid round about it; and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> board, stuck full of sharp flints below, is dragged over them by a pair of oxen, the driver getting on it to increase its weight. This machine cuts the straw as if it had been chopped, and frees the grain from the husk, from which it is afterwards separated. The great produce of Madeira is the wine, from which it has acquired fame and support. Where the soil, exposure, and supply of water, will admit of it, the vine is cultivated. One or more walks, about a yard or two wide, intersect each vineyard, and are included by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> walls two feet high. Along these walks which are arched over with laths about seven feet high, they erect wooden pillars at regular distances, to support a lattice-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of bamboos, which slopes down from both sides of the walk, till it is only a foot and a half or two feet high, in which elevation it extends over the whole vineyard. The vines are in this manner supported from the ground, and the people have room to root out the weeds which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> up between them. In the season of the vintage, they creep under this lattice-work, cut off the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>, and lay them into baskets: some bunches of these grapes weigh six pounds and upwards. This method of keeping the ground clean and moist, and ripening the grapes in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>, contributes to give the Madeira wines that excellent flavour and body for which they are remarkable. The owners of vineyards are however obliged to allot a certain spot of ground for the growth of bamboos; for the lattice-work cannot be made without them: and it is said some vineyards <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> quite neglected for want of this useful reced. The wines are not all of equal goodness, and consequently of different prices. The best, made of a vine imported from Candia by order of the Infante of Portugal, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DON">Don</a> Henry, is called Madeira Malmsey, a pipe of which cannot be bought on the spot for less than 40l. or 42l. sterling. It is an exceeding rich sweet wine, and is only made in a small quantity. The next sort is a dry wine, such as is exported for the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> market, at 30l. or 31l. sterling the pipe. Inferior sorts for the East India, West India, and North American <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a>, sell at 28l. 25l. and 20l. sterling. About 49,000 pipes are annually exported, one half of which goes to the British settlements in the East and West Indies. The best vines grow on the south side of the island, and on the side of the hill which <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> to the east. The inhabitants import Indian corn and wheat from North America, great quantities of salt fish from Newfoundland, and fresh meat and live sheep and oxen from Barbary. The total amount of imports from England in the 17 years ending in 1809, was 3,278,043l. and of exports to England only 216,167l. The enclosures of the vineyards consist of walls, and hedges of prickly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEAR">pear</a>, pomegranates, myrtles, brambles, and wild roses. The gardens produce peaches, apricots, quinces, apples, pears, walnuts, chestnuts, and many other European fruits; together with now and then some tropical plants, such as bananas, goavas, and pine-apples. All the common <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> animals of Europe are likewise found at Madeira; and their mutton and beef, though small, is very well tasted. Their horses are small, but sure-footed; and with great agility climb the difficult paths, which are the only means of communication in the country. They have no wheel-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a> of any kind: but in the town they use a sort of drays or sledges, formed of two pieces of plank joined by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> pieces, which make an acute angle before; these are drawn by oxen, and are used to transport casks of wine, and other heavy goods, to and from the warehouses. The animals of the feathered tribe, which live wild here, are more numerous than the wild <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a>; there being only the common gray rabbit here, as a representative of the last-mentioned class. Tame birds, such as turkeys, geese, ducks, and hens, are very rare, which is perhaps owing to the scarcity of corn. There are no snakes whatsoever in Madeira; but all the houses, vineyards, and gardens, swarm with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIZARDS">lizards</a>. The friars of one of the convents complained to Mr Forster, that these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VERMIN">vermin</a> destroyed the fruit in their garden; they had therefore placed a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>-kettle in the ground to catch them, as they are constantly running about in quest of food. In this manner they daily caught <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a>, which could not get out on account of the smooth sides of the kettle, but were forced to perish. The shores of Madeira, and of the neighbouring Salvages and Desertas, are not without fish; but as they are not in plenty enough for the rigid observance of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LENT">Lent</a>, pickled herrings are brought from <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GOTTENBURG">Gottenburg</a> in English bottoms, and salted cod from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEW_YORK">New <a c</a>lass="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a> and other American ports, to supply the deficiency.

MADIAN

Pages 356-356

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> Petraea, near the Arnon; so called from one of the sons of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a> by Ketura; in ruins in Jerome's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. Jerome mentions another Madian, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Midian, beyond Arabia, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>, to the south of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; and hence Madianæi, and Madianitari, the people; and Madianæa Regio, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>.

MADNESS

Pages 356-356

a most dreadful kind of delirium, without fever. See Medicine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MADRAS">MADRAS</a>. See St GEORGE.

MADRE DE POPA

Pages 356-356

a town and convent of South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, in Terra Firma, seated on the river Grande. It is almost as much resorted to by pilgrims of America as <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LORETTO">Loretto</a> is in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; and the image of the Virgin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> is said to have done many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a> in favour of the seafaring people. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 76° N. Lat. 11° O.

MADREPORA

Pages 356-356

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, the name of a genus of submarine substances; belonging to the order lithophyta. See <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELMINTHOLOGY">Helminthology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MADRID

Pages 356-357

a town of New Castile in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the whole <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, though it never had the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, is situated in W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3° 5' N. Lat. 40° 26'. It stands in the centre of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> plain, surrounded with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, and in the very heart of Spain, on the banks of the little river Manzanares, which is always very low and shallow, except when it is swelled by the melting of the snow on the mountains. The city is in general well laid out; the streets are very handsome; and the houses are fair and lofty, but built of brick, with lattice-windows, excepting those of the rich, Madrid, rich, who have glass in their windows; only, during the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> heats, they <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAUZE">gauze</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> some such thin stuff, instead of it, to let in the fresh <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>. There are two stately bridges here over the Manzanares, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many magnificent churches, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>, and palaces. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, which stands on the west side of the town, on an eminence, is spacious and magnificent consisting of three courts, and commanding a fine prospect. At the east end of the town is the prado, or pardo; which is a delightful plain, planted with regular rows of poplar trees, and watered with a great many fountains; where the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> and gentry take the air on horseback, or in their coaches, and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people on foot, or divert themselves with a variety of sports and exercises. Almost all the streets of Madrid are straight, wide, clean, and well paved. The largest and most frequented are the street of Alcalá, that of Atocha, that of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOLEDO">Toledo</a>, and the Calle Grande or great street. Madrid has also several squares, which in general are not very regular. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> are those of San Joachim, Sol, Lasganitas, San Domingo, La Cevada, and the Plaza Mayor. The latter especially deserves notice for its spaciousness and regularity, and the elegant and lofty houses it contains. It is 136 feet in circuit. The houses, of which there are 136, are of five stories, ornamented with balconies; the first of which, supported by pillars, forms a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIAZZA">piazza</a> round the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, where the inhabitants many walk under cover. In the middle of the square a market is kept.—The streets and squares of Madrid, except the Plaza Mayor which has been <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> described, are ornamented with fountains in a very ill <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. Those most to be distinguished in this particular are the fountain of the small <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> square called Plaza de Antonio Martín, and that of the square named Puerto del Sol. The others are not more magnificent, though less ridiculous. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> of all these fountains is excellent; and the air of Madrid, though the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> be variable and uncertain, is extremely pure. This purity of the air and excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the water which induced <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> II. and his successors to fix their residence in this city, arises from its great height, the plain on which the city stands being more than 2000 feet above the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. It is also well supplied with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> of all kinds at reasonable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RATES">rates</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, with the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> and residence of the quality, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> colleges and offices that are kept here, occasion a brisk trade and circulation of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>. The sacred edifices in this city have nothing remarkable in their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>; those of St. Pasqual, St. Isabella, and the Carmelites, contain highly valuable collections of pictures, which may be seen with admiration even after the paintings of the Escorial and the new palace. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of St. Isidro, which heretofore belonged to the Jesuits, has a portal which has escaped the contagion of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> in which it was built. There is another church, much more <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>, which on account of its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> has a venerable appearance, but which true taste may justly disavow: it is that of St. Salesas, or the Visitation, founded by Ferdinand VI. and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARBARA">Barbara</a> his wife.—Besides a variety of charitable foundations, there are here three confraternities, the revenues of which are appropriated to the succour of the wretched; and an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> similar to the Mont de Pieté in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, the principal object of which is to advance money to the necessitous. The city of Madrid contains 15 gates, 18 parishes, 35 convents of monks, and 31 of nuns; 39 colleges, hospitals, or houses of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>; 7398 dwelling-houses, and about 168,000 inhabitants. The Lombard traveller Father Caimo, tells us, that 50,000 sheep and 12,000 oxen are annually consumed there; to which his editor has added a ludicrous estimate of the onions and leeks devoured there, which he says amounts to $970,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000$ 4. But this writer (M. Bourgoanne observes) would not at present have any reason to complain of the disagreeable smells of the streets, nor would he find all the perfumes of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> necessary to defend himself from them. By the vigilance of the modern <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol18.html#article-POLICE">police</a>, for which (M. Bourgoanne informs us) it is indebted to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> d'Aranza, it is rendered one of the cleanest cities in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. There are four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">academies</a> in Madrid: The first is the Spanish academy, founded in 1714, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the French academy, and consisting of 24 members, including the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>. Its device is a crucible on <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> coals, with the motto tympia, fixa, y da esplender; “it purifies, fixes, and gives luster.” Its first object was the compilation of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTIONARY">dictionary</a> of the Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, which was published in six volumes folio, and of which a new edition, with great additions, has been lately put to the press. The same academy is also employed on a superb edition of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DON">Don</a> Quixote, adorned with elegant engravings far superior to the last, and collated with all the former editions. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> is the academy of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>; which owes its origin to a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of individuals, the object of whose meetings was to preserve and illustrate the historical monuments of the kingdom of Spain. Their labours met the approbation of Philip V. who in 1738 confirmed the statutes by a royal cédula. This academy consists of 24 members, including the president, secretary, and censor. Its device is a river at its source; and the motto, In patriam populismque fluit. The other two academies are, the academy of the fine arts, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>, and architecture; and the academy of medicine. The latter is held in no great esteem. The environs of Madrid contain several royal seats; among which are El Buen Retiro, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASA">Casa</a> del Campo, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORIDA">Florida</a>, Le Pardo Sarsuela, and San <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ILDEFONSO">Ildefonso</a>; but the most magnificent, not only in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> but perhaps in the whole world, is the Escorial, which takes its name from a small village near which it stands, about 22 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west from Madrid; and of which a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> is given under the article ESURIAL. Another royal palace, greatly admired, particularly for its delicious gardens and surprising <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER_WORKS">water-works</a>, is <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARANJUEZ">Aranjuez</a>, which is situated on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TAGUS">Tagus</a>, about 30 miles south of Madrid. See ARANJUEZ.

MADRIGAL

Pages 357-358

a short amorous poem, composed of a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of free and unequal verses, neither confined to the regularity of a sonnet, nor to the point of an epigram; but only consisting of some tender and delicate thought, expressed with a beautiful, noble, and elegant simplicity. Menage derives the word from mandra, which in Latin and Greek, signifies “a sheep-fold;” imagining Madrigal it to have been originally a kind of pastoral <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> shepherd's song; whence the Italians formed their madrigale, and we madrigal. Others rather choose to derive it from the word madrugar, which in the Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> signifies "to rise in the morning;" the madrigales being formerly sung early in the morning by those who had a mind to serenade their mistresses.

MADURA

Pages 358-358

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> on this side the Ganges; bounded on the east by Tanjour and Marava, on the south-east by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, on the west by the Balagate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, which separate it from Malabar, and on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Visiapour and Carnate. The inhabitants are Gentoos, and of a thievish disposition. The commodities are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, elephants <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, and cotton cloth; of which last a good <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> is made here, and very fine. At this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEARL">pearl</a> fishery, which brings in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> sum annually.

MAECENAS

Pages 358-359
CAIUS CILNIUS, the great friend and counsellor of Augustus Caesar, was himself a very polite scholar, but is chiefly memorable for having been the patron and protector of men of letters. He was descended from a most ancient and illustrious origin, even from the kings of Heturia, as Horace often tells us; but his immediate forefathers were only of the equestrian order. He is supposed to have been born at Rome, because his family lived there; but in what year antiquity does not tell us. It says as little about his education: but we know it must have been of the most liberal kind, and perfectly agreeable to the dignity and splendour of his birth, since he excelled in every thing that related to arms, politics, and letters. How Maecenas spent his younger years is also unknown to us, any farther than by effects; there being no mention made of him by any writer before the death of Julius Caesar, which happened in the year of Rome 709. Then Octavius Caesar, who was afterwards called Augustus, went to Rome, to take possession of his uncle's inheritance; and then Maecenas became first publicly known, though he appears to have been Augustus's intimate friend, and as it should seem guardian, from his childhood. From that time he accompanied him through all his fortunes, and was his counsellor and adviser upon all occasions; so that Paedo Albinovanus justly called him Caesaris dextrum, "Caesar's right-hand." In A.R. 710, the year that Cicero was killed and Ovid born, Maecenas distinguished himself by his courage and military skill at the battle of Modena, where the consuls Hirtius and Pansa were slain in fighting against Antony; as he did afterwards at Philippi. After this last battle began the memorable friendship Maecenas between Maecenas and Horace. Horace, as Suetonius relates, was a tribune in the army of Brutus and Cassius, and upon the defeat of those generals made a prisoner of war. Maecenas, finding him an accomplished man, became immediately his friend and protector; and afterwards recommended him to Augustus, who restored him his estate with no small additions. In the mean time, though Maecenas behaved himself well as a soldier in these and other battles, yet his principal province was that of a minister and counsellor. He was the adviser, the manager, the negociator, in everything that related to civil affairs. When the league was made at Brundusium between Antony and Augustus, Maecenas was sent to act on the part of Augustus. This we learn from Horace in his journey to Brundusium: Huc venturus crat Maecenas optimus, atque Cocceius, missi magnis de rebus uterque Legati, aversos soliti componere amicos. Sat. v. lib. i. And afterwards, when this league was near breaking, through the suspicions of each party, Maecenas was sent to Antony to ratify it anew. In the year 717, when Augustus and Agrippa went to Sicily to fight Sextus Pompeius by sea, Maecenas went with them; but soon after returned to appease some commotions which were rising at Rome: for though he usually attended Augustus in all his military expeditions, yet whenever there was any thing to be done at Rome either with the senate or people, he was always despatched thither for that purpose. Upon the total defeat of Antony at Actium, Maecenas returned to Rome, to take the government into his hands, till Augustus could settle some necessary affairs in Greece and Asia. Agrippa soon followed Maecenas; and when Augustus arrived, he placed these two great men and faithful adherents, the one over his civil, the other over his military concerns. While Augustus was extinguishing the remains of the civil wars in Asia and Egypt, young Lepidus, the son of the triumvir, was forming a scheme to assassinate him at his return to Rome. This conspiracy was discovered at once, by the extraordinary vigilance of Maecenas; who, as Velleius Paterculus says, "observing the rash councils of the headstrong youth with the same tranquillity and calmness as if nothing at all had been doing, instantly put him to death, without the least noise and tumult; and by that means extinguished another civil war in its very beginning." The civil wars being now at an end, Augustus returned to Rome; and from this time Maecenas indulged himself at vacant hours in literary amusements, and the conversation of men of letters. In the year 734 Virgil died, and left Augustus and Maecenas heirs to what he had. Maecenas was excessively fond of this poet, who, of all the wits of the Augustan age, stood highest in his esteem; and if the Georgics and the Æneid be owing to the good taste and encouragement of this patron, as there is some reason to think, posterity cannot commemorate him with too much gratitude. Horace may be ranked next to Virgil in Maecenas's good graces: we have already mentioned how and at what time their friendship commenced. Propertius also acknowledges Maecenas for his favourer and protector, lib. ii. eleg. 7. Nor must Varius be forgot, though we have nothing of his remaining; since we find him highly praised by both Virgil and Horace. He was a writer of tragedies; and Quintilian thinks he may be compared with any of the ancients. In a word, Maecenas's house was a place of refuge and welcome to all the learned of his time; not only to Virgil, Horace, Propertius, and Varinus, but to Fundarius, whom Horace extols as an admirable writer of comedies; to Fuscus Aristius, a noble grammarian, and Horace's intimate friend; to Plotius Tucea, who assisted Varius in correcting the Aeneid after the death of Virgil; to Valgus, a poet and very learned man, who, as Pliny tells us, dedicated a book to Augustus, De usu Herbarum; to Asinius Pollio, an excellent tragic writer; and to several others, whom it would be tedious to mention. All these dedicated their works, or some part of them at least, to Maecenas, and celebrated his praises in them over and over: and we may observe farther, what Plutarch tells us, that even Augustus himself inscribed his Commentaries to him and to Agrippa. Maecenas continued in Augustus's favour to the end of his life, but not uninterruptedly. Augustus had an intrigue with Maecenas's wife: and though the minister bore this liberty of his master very patiently, yet there was a coldness on the part of Augustus, which, however, soon went off. Maecenas died in the year 745; but at what age we cannot precisely determine, though we know he must have been old. He must have been older than Augustus, because he was a kind of tutor to him in his youth: and we find him often called an old man by Pædo Albinovanus, a contemporary poet, whose elegy upon his dead patron is still extant. He made Augustus his heir; and recommended his friend Horace to him in those memorable last words, "Horatii Flacci, ut mei, memor esto," &c. Horace, however, did not probably survive him long, as there is no elegy of his upon Maecenas extant, nor any account of one having ever been written, which there certainly would have been had Horace survived him any time. Nay, Father Sanadon, the French editor of Horace, will have it, that the poet died before his patron; and that these last words were found only in Maecenas's will, which had not been altered. Maecenas is said never to have enjoyed a good state of health in any part of his life: and many singularities are related of his bodily constitution. Thus Pliny tells us, that he was always in a fever; and that, for three years before his death, he had not a moment's sleep. Though he was certainly an extraordinary man, and possessed many admirable virtues and qualities, yet it is agreed on all hands, that he was very luxurious and effeminate. "Maecenas (says Velleius Paterculus) was of the equestrian order, but sprung from a most illustrious origin. He was a man, who, when business required, was able to undergo any fatigue and watching; who consulted properly upon all occasions, and knew as well how to execute what he had consulted; yet a man who in seasons of leisure was luxurious, soft, and effeminate, almost beyond a woman. He was no less dear to Caesar than Agrippa, but distinguished by him with fewer honours; for he always continued of the equestrian rank, in which he was born: not that he could not have been advanced upon the least intimation, but he never solicited it." But let moralists and politicians determine of Maecenas as they please, the men of letters are under high obligations to celebrate his praises and revere his memory: for he countenanced, protected, and supported, as far as they wanted his support, all the wits and learned men of his time; and that too, out of a pure and disinterested love of letters, when he had no little views of policy to serve by their means: whence it is no wonder, that all the protectors and patrons of learning, ever since, have usually been called Maecenas's.

MAELSTROM

Pages 359-361

a very dangerous whirlpool on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>, in the 68th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of latitude, in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Nordland, and the district of Lofoten and near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Moskoe, from whence it also takes the name of Moskoe-strom. Its violence and roarings exceed that of a cataract, being heard to a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> distance, and without any intermission, except a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> every sixth <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, that is, at the turn of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and low <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, when its impetuosity seems at a stand, which short <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> is the only <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the fishermen can venture in; but this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> soon returns, and, however calm the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> may be, gradually increases with such a draught and vortex, as absorb whatever comes within their sphere of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, and keep it under water for some hours, when the fragments, shivered by the rocks, appear again. This circumstance, among others, makes strongly against Kircher and others, who imagine that there is here an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABYSS">abyss</a> penetrating the globe, and issuing in some very remote parts, which Kircher is so particular as to assign, for he names the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of Bothnia. But after the most exact researches which the circumstances <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> admit, this is but a conjecture without foundation; for this and three other vortices among the Ferroe <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, but smaller, have no other cause than the collision of waves rising and falling, at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUX">flux</a> and reflux, against a ridge of rocks and shelves, which confine the water so that it precipitates itself like a cataract; and thus the higher the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a> rises, the deeper must the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> be; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> result of this is a whirlpool <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> vortex, the prodigious suction whereof is sufficiently known by lesser experiments. But what has been thus absorbed, remains no longer at the bottom than the ebb lasts; for the suction then ceases, and the flood removes all <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTRACTION">attraction</a>, and permits whatever had been sunk to make its appearance again. Of the situation of this amazing Moskoe-strom we have the following account from Mr Jonas Ranus: "The mountain of Helseggen, in Lofoten, lies a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> from the island Ver, and betwixt these two runs that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and dreadful stream called Moskoe-strom, from the island Moskoe, which is in the middle of it, together with several circumjacent isles, as Ambaaren, half a quarter of a league northward, Hfesen, Hochholm, Kieldholm, Svarven, and Buckholm. Moskoe lies about half a quarter of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> south of the island of Ver, and betwixt them these small islands, Otterholm, Flimen, Sanflesen, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STOCKHOLM">Stockholm</a>. Betwixt Lofoden and Moskoe, the depth of the water is between 36 and 40 fathoms; but on the other side, towards Ver, the depth decreases, so as not to afford a convenient passage for a vessel, without the risk of splitting on the rocks, which happens even in the calmest <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>: when it is flood, the stream runs up the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> between Lofoden and Moskoe with a boisterous rapidity: but the roar of its impetuous ebb... Mæotis Palus or Lacus, Mæotica Palus, or Mæoticus Lacus, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a large lake or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the sea between <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, at the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of the Euxine, to which it communicates by the Cimmerian Bosphorus. It was worshipped as a deity by the Massagetae. It extends about 350 miles from southwest to northeast, and is about 600 miles in circumference. Still called Palus Mæotis, reaching from Crim <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a> to the mouth of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DON">Don</a>. Mæstlin, Michael, in Latin Mæstlinus, a celebrated astronomer of Germany, was born in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WITTENBERG">Wittenberg</a>; but spent his youth in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, where he made a speech in favour of Copernicus's system, which brought Galileo over from <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, to whom he had been hitherto entirely devoted. He afterwards returned to Germany, and became professor of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> at Tubingen; where, among his other scholars, he taught the great Kepler, who has praised several of his ingenious inventions, in his Astronomia Optica. Though Tycho Brahe did not assent to Mæstlin's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, yet he allowed him to be an extraordinary person, deeply skilled in the science of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>. Mæstlin published many mathematical and astronomical works; and died in 1590. Mæstricht, an ancient town of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>; is about four miles in circumference, and strongly fortified. The inhabitants, the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of whom is estimated at 18,000, are noted for making excellent firearms. It contains an arsenal, a handsome townhouse, and a good library. Both Papists and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> are allowed the free <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, and the magistrates are composed of both. It is situated on the river Maese, which separates it from Wyck, and with which it communicates by a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>. Mæstricht revolted from the Spaniards in 1570, but was reduced in 1579. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. became <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of it in 1673; but it was restored to the states by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of Nimeguen in 1678. It was again taken by the French in 1794, and remained in their possession till 1814. It now belongs to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of the Netherlands. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5° 50'. N. Lat. 50° 52'. Maffæus, Vegio, a Latin poet, born in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LOMBARDY">Lombardy</a> in 1497, was greatly admired in his time. He wrote epigrams, and a humorous supplement to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, which he called The thirteenth book of the Æneid: this was as humorously translated into English a few years since by Mr Ellis. Maffæus wrote also some prose works. He was <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of Rome towards the end of the pontificate of Martin V.; and died in 1548. Maffei, Scipio, a celebrated Italian poet, born of an illustrious and ancient family at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERONA">Verona</a>, in 1675. After having finished his studies, he took arms, and distinguished himself by his valour at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Denawert; but he more particularly distinguished himself by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of learning, which made him undertake several voyages into France, England, and Germany. He conversed with the learned in all those countries, and obtained their friendship and esteem. He was a member of the academy of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a> at Rome, an honorary foreign member of that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">Inscriptions</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>; and died in 1755. He wrote many works in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> and prose, which are esteemed; the most known of which are, 1. The tragedy of Merope, of which there there are two French translations in prose. 2. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">Ceremony</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a>. 3. A translation, into Italian verse, of the first book of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>'s Iliad. 4. Many other pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, in a collection entitled <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RHYME">Rhyme</a> and Prose; quarto. His <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> works in prose are, 1. Verona illustrata. 2. Istoria diplomatica. 3. Scienza cavalleresca; an excellent <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, in which he attacks duelling. 4. An edition of Theatro Italiano. 5. An edition of Cassiodorus on the Epistles, Acts of the Apostles, and Apocalypse. 6. Galliae Antiquitates quaedam selectae, atque in plures epistolae distributae; and several other works.

MAGADA

Pages 361-361

in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">Mythology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> under which Venus was known and worshipped in Lower <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>; where this <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> had a famous temple, which was treated with respect even by the Huns and Vandals when they ravaged the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. It is said to have been destroyed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a>.

MAGADOXO

Pages 361-361

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> town of a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of the same name, in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, and on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Ajan. It is seated near the mouth of a river of the same name, defended by a citadel, and has a good harbour. The inhabitants are Mahometans. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 45. 15. N. Lat. 3. o.

MAGAS

Pages 361-361

MAGADIS, (from μαγάδης, "to sing, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> play in unison or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OCTAVE">octave</a>,") the name of a musical <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. There were two kinds of magades, the one a string instrument, formed of 20 chords arranged in pairs, and tuned to unison or octave, so that they yielded ten sounds: the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> whereof is ascribed by some to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAPPHO">Sappho</a>; by others to the Lydians; and by some, to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMOTHEUS">Timotheus</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILETUS">Miletus</a>. The other was a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUTE">flute</a>, which at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> yielded very <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and very low notes. The former kind was at least much improved by Timotheus of Miletus, who is said to have been impeached of a crime, because by increasing the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of chords he spoiled and discredited the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> music.

MAGAZINE

Pages 361-362

a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in which stores are kept, of arms, ammunition, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, &c. Every fortified town ought to be furnished with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> magazine, which should contain stores of all kinds, sufficient to enable the garrison and inhabitants to hold out a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> siege; and in which smiths, carpenters, wheelwrights, &c. may be employed in making everything belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a>, wagons, &c. Powder Magazine, is that place where the powder is kept in very large quantities. Authors differ greatly both with regard to their situation and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>; but all agree that they ought to be arched and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOMB">bomb</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>. In fortifications, they are frequently placed in the rampart; but of late they have been built in different parts of the town. The first powder magazines were made with Gothic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>: but M. Vauban finding them too weak, constructed them in a semicircular form; whose dimensions are 60 feet long within, and 25 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; the foundations are eight <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> feet thick, and eight feet <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> from the foundation to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> is two feet from the ground, which keeps it from dampness. One of our engineers of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> since had observed, that after the centres of semicircular arches are struck, they <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> and rise up at the hanches, even with a straight <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> extrados, and still much more so in powder magazines, whose outside at top is formed like the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, by two inclined planes joining in an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> over the top of the arch, to give a proper <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>; which effects are exactly what might be expected agreeable to the true <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of arches. Now, as this shrinking of the arches must be attended with very ill consequences, by breaking the texture of the cement after it has been in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> dried, and also by opening the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> of the voussoirs at one end, so a remedy is provided for this inconvenience with regard to bridges, by the arch of equilibration in Mr Hutton's book on bridges; but as the ill effect is much greater in powder magazines, the same ingenious <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> proposed to find an arch of equilibration for them also, and to construct it when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAN">span</a> is 20 feet, the pitch or height 10 (which are the same dimensions as the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEMICIRCLE">semicircle</a>), the inclined exterior walls at top forming an angle of 113 degrees, and the height of their angular point above the top of the arch equal to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> feet. This very curious question was answered in 1775 by the reverend Mr Wildbore, to be found in Mr Hutton's Miscellanea Mathematica. Artillery Magazine. In a siege, the magazine is made about 25 or 30 yards behind the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a>, towards the parallels, and at least three feet under ground, to hold the powder, loaded shells, portfires, &c. Its sides and roof must be well secured with boards to prevent the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> from falling in: a door is made to it, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> trench or passage is sunk from the magazine to the battery, one to go in and the other to come out at, to prevent confusion. Sometimes traverses are made in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> to prevent ricochet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> from plunging into them. Magazine, on shipboard, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> room or storehouse, built in the fore or after-<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the hold to contain the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a> used in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. This apartment is strongly secured against fire, and no person is allowed to enter it with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMP">lamp</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a>: it is therefore lighted, as occasion requires, by means of the candles or lamps in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>-room contiguous to it. Magazine <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">Air</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUN">Gun</a>. See Air-Gun. Magazine, Literary; a well-known <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of periodical publications, of which the first that appeared was The Gentleman's, set on foot by the projector Mr Edward Cave in the year 1731: (see the article Cave.) This, as Dr Kippis observes, "may be considered as something of an epocha in the literary <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The periodical performances before that time were almost wholly confined to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> transactions, and to foreign and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> occurrences; but the monthly magazines have opened a way for every kind of inquiry and information.
