Majorca, an island of the Mediterranean, lying between Yvica on the west and Minorca on the east. These three islands were anciently called Baleares, supposed to be from the skill of their inhabitants in slinging, for which they were very remarkable. Originally they belonged to the Carthaginians; but during the wars of that people with the Romans they seem to have regained their liberty. In 122 B.C. they were subdued by Metellus the Roman consul, who treated the inhabitants with such cruelty, that out of 30,000 he scarce left 1000 alive. He then built two cities on Majorca; one called Palma, now Majorca, to the east; the other to the west, named Pollentia, now no longer in being. The island continued subject to the Romans, and to the nations who overran the western part of the empire, for many ages. At last it was subdued by the Moors about the year 800. By them the island was put in a much better condition than it ever was before or since. The Moors being very industrious, and also populous, surrounded the whole coast with fortifications, that is, with a kind of towers and lines between them; cultivated every spot in the island that was not either rock or sand; and had no fewer than 15 great towns, whereas now there are not above three. Neither was it at all difficult for the Moorish monarch to bring into the field an army much superior in number to the inhabitants that are now upon it, taking in all ranks, sexes, and ages. In 1229, the island was subdued by the king of Arragon, who established in it a new kingdom, feudatory to that of Arragon, which was again destroyed in 1341 by the same monarch; and ever since, the island hath been subject to Spain, and hath entirely lost its importance. It is about 60 miles long, and 45 broad. The air is clear and temperate; and, by its situation, the heat in summer is so qualified by the breezes, that it is by far the most pleasant of all the islands in the Mediterranean. There are some mountains; but the country is generally flat, and of such an excellent soil, that it produces great quantities of corn as good in its kind as any in Europe. Oil, wine, and salt, are very plentiful, as also black cattle and sheep; but deer, rabbits, and wild-fowl, abound so much, that they alone are sufficient for the subsistence of the inhabitants. There are no rivers, but a great many springs and wells, as well as several good harbours. The inhabitants are robust, active, and good seamen. Majorca, a handsome, large, rich, and strong town in the island of the same name, with a bishop's see. It contains about 6000 houses, and 22 churches, besides the cathedral. The squares, the cathedral, and the royal palace, are magnificent structures. A captain-general resides there, who commands the whole island; and there is a garrison against the incursion of the Moors. It was taken by the English in 1706; but was retaken in 1715, since which time it has been in the hands of the Spaniards. It is seated on the southwest part of the island, where there is a good harbour, 70 miles north-east of Yvica, 120 south-east of Barcelona, 140 east of Valencia, and 300 from Madrid. E. Long. 2. 55'. N. Lat. 39. 36. Mairan, Jean Jacques d'Ortous de, descended from a noble family at Besiers, was born in that city in 1678, and died at Paris of a fluxion on the lungs on the 20th of February 1771, at the age of 93. He was one of the most illustrious members of the Academy of Sciences and of the French Academy. Being early connected with the former society, he, in the year 1741, succeeded Fontenelle in the office of secretary. This station he filled with the most distinguished success till the year 1744; and, like his predecessor, possessed the faculty of placing the most abstract subjects in the clearest light; a talent which is very rare, but which appears conspicuous in all his works. The chief of them are, 1. Dissertation sur la Glace, the last edition of which was printed in 1749, 12mo. This excellent little tract has been translated into German and Italian. 2. Dissertation sur la cause de la lumiere des Phosphores, 1717, 12mo. 3. Traité historique et physique de l'Aurore Boreale, first published in 12mo, 1733, and afterwards much enlarged and printed in 4to in 1754. The system embraced by the author is liable to be controverted; but the book displays great taste and erudition. 4. Lettre au Pere Parennin, contenant diverses questions sur la Chine, 12mo. This is a very curious work, and is full of that philosophical spirit which characterizes the author's other publications. 5. A great number of papers in the memoirs of the Academy of Sciences (since 1719), of which he published some volumes. 6. Several dissertations on particular subjects, which form only small pamphlets. 7. The Eloges of the Academicians of the Academy of Sciences, who died in 1741, 1742, 1743, in 12mo, 1747. Without imitating Fontenelle, the author attained almost equal excellence by his talent of discriminating characters, appreciating their worth, and giving them their due share of praise, without at the same time concealing their defects. Mairan's reputation extended itself into foreign countries. He was a member of the Imperial Academy at Petersburgh, of the Royal Academy of London, of the Institution at Bologna, of the Royal Societies of Edinburgh and Upsal, &c. The gentleness and sweetness of his manners made him be considered as a perfect model of the social virtues. He possessed that amiable politeness, that agreeable gaiety, and that steady firmness, which never fail to procure love and esteem. But we must add, says M. Saverien, that every thing had a reference to himself; self-love and a regard to his own reputation were the motives of all his actions. He was deeply affected with censure or applause, and yet he had many friends. Uniting much gentleness of disposition to an ingenious and agreeable expression of countenance, he possessed the art of insinuating himself into the good graces of others, so as to pave the way to elevation and success. He was honoured with protection and particular marks of regard by the duke of Orleans the regent, who bequeathed to him his watch in his will. The prince of Conti loaded him with favours; and the chancellor Daguessaux, observing in him great originality and ingenuity of thought, appointed him president of the Journal des Savans: a station which he filled very much to the satisfaction of the public and of the learned. The private and selfish views imputed to him by M. Saverien never made him deficient in what was due to the strictest probity. An expression of his is remembered, which could have proceeded only from sentiment; "An honest man (said he) is one whose blood is refreshed with the recital of a good action."

MALABAR

Pages 447-447

the name given to a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the west <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> of Hindostan on this side of the Ganges, extending from the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Baglala to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Comorin, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> extremity of the kingdom of Canara as far as Cape Comorin, and lying between 9° and 14° N. Lat. It is bounded by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Balagate on the east; by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DECCAN">Deccan</a> on the north; and on the west and south is washed by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>.

MALACA

Pages 447-447

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, surnamed *Ficederatum* by Pliny; a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> town of Batica; a Carthaginian colony according to Strabo; so called from *Malach,* signifying "<a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>;" a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> noted for pickled <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> salted meat. Now <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALAGA">Malaga</a>, a port town of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANADA">Granada</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4. 45. N. Lat. 36. 40.

MALACCA

Pages 447-449

the most southerly <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> beyond the Ganges, is about 600 miles in length, and contains a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of the same name. It is bounded by the kingdom of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIAM">Siam</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>; by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of Siam and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> ocean on the east; and by the straits of Malacca, which separate it from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMATRA">Sumatra</a>, on the south-west. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is more to the south than any other in the East Indies; and comprehends the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and kingdoms of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATAN">Patan</a>, Palan, Ighor, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERA">Pera</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEDA">Queda</a>, Borkelon, Ligor; and to the north the town and kingdom of Tanassery, where the Portuguese formerly carried on a great trade. This last either does <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> did belong to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Siam. The people of Malacca are in general subject to the Dutch, who possess all the strong places on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, and compel them to trade on their own terms, excluding all other nations of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> from having any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> with the natives. The Malays are governed by feudal laws. A <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, who has the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of king or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a>, issues his commands to his great vassals, who have other vassals in subjection to them in a similar manner. A small part of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> live independent, under the title of orangat or noblc. (A) The awkwardness of this title has induced many collectors to dispose of their first volume, as thinking it superseded by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> edition: but this is by no means the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>; the volume of 1719 being equally necessary to complete the set as that of 1733, which is a revision of all the former volumes. The whole <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, when properly bound, consists, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> libitum, either of five volumes or of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a>. Malacca, and sell their services to those who pay them best; while the body of the nation is composed of slaves, and live in perpetual servitude. The generality of these people are restless, fond of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, plunder, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMIGRATION">emigration</a>, colonies, desperate enterprises, adventures, and gallantry. They talk incessantly of their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> and their bravery; whilst they are universally considered by those with whom they have intercourse, as the most treacherous, ferocious people on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. This ferocity, which the Malays qualify under the name of courage, is so well known to the European companies who have settlements in the Indies, that they have universally agreed in prohibiting the captains of their ships who may put into the Malay <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, from taking on board any seamen from that nation, except in the greatest distress, and then on no account to exceed two or three. It is not in the least uncommon for a handful of these horrid savages suddenly to embark, attack a vessel by surprise, massacre the people, and make themselves masters of her. Malay batteaux, with 24 or 30 men, have been known to board European ships of 30 or 40 guns, in order to take possession of them, and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> with their poniards great part of the crew. Those who are not slaves go always armed: they would think themselves disgraced <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they went abroad without their poniards, which they call criu. As their lives are a perpetual round of agitation and tumult, they cannot endure the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> flowing garments in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> among the other Asiatics. Their habits are exactly adapted to their shapes, and loaded with a multitude of buttons, which fasten them <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to their bodies. The country possessed by the Malays is in general very fertile. It abounds with odoriferous woods, such as the aloes, the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SANDAL">sandal</a>, and cassia. The ground is covered with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> of the greatest fragrance, of which there is a perpetual succession throughout the year. There are abundance of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of the most precious <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, said to be richer even than those of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRAZIL">Brazil</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>, and in some places are mines of diamonds. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> also abounds with excellent fish, together with ambergrise, pearls, and those delicate <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>-nests so much in request in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, formed in the rocks with the spawn of fishes and the foam of the sea, by a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of small-sized swallow peculiar to those seas. These are of such an exquisite flavour, that the Chinese for a long <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> purchased them for their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, and still buy them at an excessive price. See Birds-Nest. Notwithstanding all this plenty, however, the Malays are miserable. The culture of the lands, abandoned to slaves, is fallen into contempt. These wretched labourers, dragged incessantly from their rustic employments by their restless masters, who delight in war and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> enterprises, have never time or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> to give the necessary <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the labouring of their grounds; of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> the lands for the most part are uncultivated, and produce no kind of grain for the subsistence of the inhabitants. The sago tree indeed supplies in part the defect of grain. It is a species of the palm tree, which grows naturally in the woods to the height of about 20 or 30 feet; its circumference being sometimes from five to six. Its ligneous bark is about an inch in thickness, and covers a multitude of long fibres, which being interwoven one with another Malacca envelope a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of a gummy kind of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>. As soon as this tree is ripe, a whitish dust, which transpires through the pores of the leaves, and adheres to their extremities, indicates that the trees are in a state of maturity. The Malays then cut them <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> near the root, and divide them into several sections, which they split into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>; they then scoop out the mass of mealy substance, which is enveloped by and adheres to the fibres; they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DILUTE">dilute</a> it in pure <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> it through a straining bag of fine cloth, in order to separate it from the fibres. When this paste has lost part of its moisture by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVAPORATION">evaporation</a>, the Malays throw it into a kind of earthen vessel of different shapes, where they allow it to dry and harden. This paste is wholesome nourishing food, and preserves for many years. Malacca, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the country of the same name, is situated in a flat country close to the sea. The walls and fortifications are founded on a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> rock, and are carried up to a great height; the lower part of them is washed by the sea at every tide, and on the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> side is a wide canal or ditch, cut from the sea to the river, which makes it an inland. In 1641 it was taken from the Portuguese by the Dutch, from which time it <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in their possession till 1795, when it was taken by the British. It was restored at the peace of Amiens, retaken in 1807 by the British, but appears to have been included in the cessions made to the Dutch by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of 13th August 1814. The houses are tolerably well built, and some of them have gardens behind or on one side. The inhabitants consist of a few Dutch, many Malaysans, Moors, Chinese, and other Indians. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> is well situated for navigation; but the trade of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is trifling. E. Long. 102. N. Lat. 2. 12. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MALACHI">Malachi</a>, or the prophecy of Malachi, a canonical book of the Old <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, and the last of the 12 lesser prophets. Malachi prophesied about 300 years before Christ, reproving the Jews for their wickedness after their return from <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a>, charging them with rebellion, sacrilege, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADULTERY">adultery</a>, profaneness, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INFIDELITY">infidelity</a>; and condemning the priests for being scandalously careless in their ministry; at the same time not forgetting to encourage the pious few, who, in that corrupt <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, maintained their integrity. This prophet distinctly <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> at the Messiah, who was suddenly to come to his temple, and to be introduced by Elijah the prophet, that is, John the Baptist, who came in the spirit and power of Elias or Elijah. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MALACIA">Malacia</a>, in Medicine, is a languishing disorder incident to pregnant women, in which they long sometimes for one kind of food and sometimes for another, and eat it with extraordinary greediness. Malacoptyterygeous, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a>, an appellation given to fishes having the rays of their fins <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BONY">bony</a> at the extremities, but not pointed, like those of acanthopterygeous fishes. Malacostomous fishes, those destitute of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> in the jaws, called in English <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>-mouthed, as the tench, carp, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BREAM">bream</a>, &c. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALAGA">Malaga</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, rich, and strong town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in the kingdom of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANADA">Granada</a>, with two castles, a bishop's see, and a good harbour, which renders it a place of considerable commerce. The advantage Malaga, of this commerce, according to M. Bourgoanne, is entirely in favour of Spain, but almost without any to its navigation; of 842 vessels which arrived at this port in 1782, from almost every commercial nation, scarcely 100 were Spanish, even reckoning the ships of war which anchored there. The English, who are in possession of the greatest part of the trade, carry thither woollens and great quantities of small <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARE">ware</a>; the Dutch carry spice, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTLERY">cutlery</a> ware, laces, ribbons, thread, &c. These nations, those of the north, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, export to the amount of two millions and a half of piastres in wines, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUMACH">sumach</a>, pickled anchovies, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, &c., and all they carry thither amounts only to about a million and a half. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> would be still more advantageous for Malaga if the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> of Granada were exported from this port; but these are employed in the country where they are produced. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">Sugar</a> has been cultivated in the vicinity of this town for 700 years. The streets of Malaga are narrow, but there are some good squares; and the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> is a superb <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, said to be as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> as St Paul's. The bishop's <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> is a large edifice, but looks insignificant from its being situated near the other. Its prelate enjoys a revenue of 16,000l. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>. Malaga is seated on the Mediterranean sea, at the foot of a craggy mountain. W. Long. 4° 10' N. Lat. 36° 51'.

MALAGRIDA

Pages 449-449

Gabriel, an Italian Jesuit, was chosen by the general of the order to conduct missions into <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>. To <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> ease and fluency of speech, for which he was indebted to enthusiasm, he added the most ardent zeal for the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> to which he belonged. He soon became the fashionable <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a>; and everyone, small <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> great, placed himself under his conduct. He was respected as a saint, and consulted as an oracle. When a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> was formed by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> d'<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVEIRO">Aveiro</a> against the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Portugal, it is asserted by the enemies of the society, that three Jesuits, among whom was Malagrida, were consulted concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>. They add (what is very improbable), that it was decided by these casuists, that it was only a venial crime to kill a king who persecuted the saints. At that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the king of Portugal, spurred on by a minister who had no favour for the Jesuits, openly declared himself against them, and soon after banished them from his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. Only three of them were apprehended, Malagrida, Alexander, and Mathos, who were accused of having approved this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>. But either the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> could not be proceeded in without the consent of the pope, which was not granted, or no <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> could be got sufficient to condemn Malagrida; and therefore the king was obliged to deliver him to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">Inquisition</a>, as being suspected of having formerly advanced some rash <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a> which bordered on <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a>. Two publications which he acknowledged, and which give the fullest indications of complete insanity, were the foundation of these suspicions. The one was written in Latin, and entitled Tractatus de vita et imperio Antichristi; the other in Portuguese, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of the "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a> of St <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, composed with the assistance of the blessed Virgin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> and her most holy Son." They are full of extravagance and absurdity.—This enthusiast pretended to have the gift of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a>. He confessed before the judges of the Inquisition, that God himself had declared him his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a>, and prophet; that he was united to God by a perpetual union; and that the Virgin Mary, with the consent of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ and of the whole Trinity, had declared him to be her son. In short, he confessed, as is pretended, that he felt in the prison, at the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 72, some emotions very uncommon at that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of life, which at first gave him great uneasiness, but that it had been revealed to him by God that these emotions were only the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> effect of an involuntary agitation, wherein there was the same merit as in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>. It was for such extravagancies, that this unfortunate wretch was condemned by the Inquisition; but his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> was hastened by a vision which he eagerly revealed. Upon occasion of the death of the marquis de Tancourt, commander in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESTREMADURA">Estremadura</a>, mournful and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> discharges were made in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of him by the castle of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a>, and by all the forts on the banks of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TAGUS">Tagus</a>. These being heard by Malagrida in his dungeon, he instantly supposed, from their extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and from their happening during the night, that the king was dead. The next <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> he demanded an audience from the members of the Inquisition: which being granted, he told them that he had been ordered by God to show the minister of the holy office that he was not a hypocrite, as was pretended; for the king's death had been revealed to him, and he had seen in a vision the torments to which his majesty was condemned for having persecuted the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> of his order. This was sufficient to accelerate his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>: he was burnt on the 21st of September 1761; not as the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ACCOMPLICE">accomplice</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARRICIDE">parricide</a>, but as a false prophet, for which he deserved to be confined in bedlam rather than tied to the stake. The acts of impiety whereof he was accused were nothing more than extravagancies proceeding from a mistaken <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> and an overheated brain.

MALALEUCA

Pages 449-449

the CAYPUTI TREE, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the polyadelphia class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. This plant, which is a native of the Moluccas, yields the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> called Cayputi.

MALDEN

Pages 449-449

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>, 37 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, situated on an eminence at the conflux of the Chalmer and Pant <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Blackwater, where they enter the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. It was the first Roman colony in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, and the seat of some of the old British kings. It was besieged, plundered, and burnt by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOADICEA">Boadicea</a>; but the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> repaired it. It was again ruined by the Danes, but rebuilt by the Saxons. It has a convenient haven on an arm of the sea for vessels of 400 tons; and a considerable trade in coals, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, corn, and deals. A little beyond it begins Blackwater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, famous for the Wallfleet oysters. The channel called Malden <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> is navigable to the town. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Edward the elder (of the Saxon <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>) resided here whilst he built Witham and <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol10.html#article-HERTFORD">Hertford</a> castles. On the west side of the town are the remains of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> in 1811 was 2679.

MALDIVIA ISLANDS

Pages 449-450

a cluster of small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> ocean, 500 miles south-west of the continent of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Ceylon. They are about 1000 in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, and are very small; extending from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of south latitude to the seventh degree of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude. They are generally <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> low lands, surrounded by rocks and sands. The natives are of the same <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a> with the Arabians, profess the Mahometan Mahometan <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, and are subject to one sovereign. The channels between the islands are very narrow, and some of them are fordable. They produce neither <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, corn, nor herbage; but the natives live upon cocoanuts, and other <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, roots, and fish. They carry on a little trade with the British Indian settlements, exchanging their <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>-fish, turtle-shells, and cocoa, for rice, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, hardware, cloth, &c. They have also a considerable trade among themselves. Their manners are mild and inoffensive. **<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">MALE</a>,** among zoologists, that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a> of animals which has the parts of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> situated externally. See SEX and GENERATION. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> male has also from some similitude to that sex in animals, been applied to several inanimate things; thus we say, a male flower, a male screw, &c. See MAS Plant, MASCULUS Flos, and SCREW; also <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">FEMALE</a> and FLOS.

MALEBRANCHE

Pages 450-450

NICHOLAS,** an eminent French metaphysician, the son of Nicholas Malebranche, secretary to the French <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, was born in 1638, and admitted into the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> of the oratory in 1660. He at first applied himself to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of languages and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>: but afterwards meeting with Des Cartes’s Treatise of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">Man</a>, he gave himself up entirely to the study of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. In 1699, he was admitted an honorary member of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Academy of Sciences at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. Notwithstanding he was of a delicate <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, he enjoyed a pretty good state of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which happened in 1715, at the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 77. Father Malebranche read little, but thought a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a>. He despised that kind of philosophy which consists only in knowing the opinions of other men, since a person may know the history of other men’s thoughts without thinking himself. He could never read ten verses together without disgust. He meditated with his windows shut, in order to keep out the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, which he found to be a disturbance to him. His conversation turned upon the same subjects as his books; but was mixed with so much <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> and deference to the judgment of others, that it was extremely and universally desired. His books are famous; particularly his Recherche de la Verité, i.e. “Search after <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>;” his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> in which is, to point to us the errors into which we are daily led by our senses, imagination, and passions; and to prescribe a method for discovering the truth, which he does, by starting the notion of seeing all things in God. And hence he is led to think and speak meanly of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> knowledge, either as it lies in written books, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in the book of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, compared with that light which displays itself from the ideal world; and, by attending to which, with pure and defecate minds, he supposes knowledge to be most easily had. The fineness of this author’s sentiments, together with his fine manner of expressing them, made every body admire his genius and abilities; but he has generally passed for a visionary <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>. Mr Locke, in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of Malebranche’s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of seeing all things in God, styles him, “an acute and ingenious author;” and tells us, that there are “a great many very fine thoughts, judicious reasonings, and uncommon reflections in his Recherches.” But Mr Locke, in that piece, endeavours to refute the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> principles of his system. He wrote many other pieces besides that we have mentioned, all tending to confirm his main system, established in the Recherche, and to clear it from the objections which were brought against it, or from the consequences which were deduced from it; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he has not attained what he aimed at in these several productions, he has certainly shown great abilities and a vast force of genius. See Supplement, FIRST DISSERTATION, p. 113.

MALESHERBES

Pages 450-451

CHRISTIAN-WILLIAM DE LAMOIGNON DE,** was born at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1721. He was son of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of France, William de Lamoignon, who was descended of an illustrious family. His early <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> he received at the Jesuits <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, applying himself afterwards to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> assiduity, as well as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> economy. He was chosen a counsellor of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> of Paris at the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 24, and succeeded his father as <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of aids in the year 1750. With the presidentship of the court of aids he received the superintendence of the press, in whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> it became the means of promoting <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> beyond all former example in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. As he firmly believed that despotism alone had any reason to dread the liberty of the press, he was anxious to give it every <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> consistent with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> policy and the state of public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>. Through his favour the French Encyclopedia, the works of Rousseau, and many other free speculations, issued from the press, in defiance of the terrific anathemas of the Sorbonne. This had its own <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAVING">paving</a> the way to the horrors of the revolution, which Malesherbes did not probably foresee; yet it had also the happy effect of freeing the minds of men from the fetters of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>, and of enlightening them respecting their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> and duties in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>. The superintendence of the press having been taken from him, to confer it on that tool of despotism Maupeou, he was only the more intent on fulfilling the duties of his presidentship, and opposing arbitrary power with all his vigour, being thus freed from a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of other cares. When the proceedings of the court of aids were to be prohibited, on account of the spirited conduct of Malesherbes in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of one Monnerat, who had been most unjustly treated by the farmers of the revenue, he presented a remonstrance to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, containing a free protest against the enormous abuses of lettres de cachet, by which every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>’s liberty was rendered precarious, concluding with these memorable words; “no one is great enough to be secure from the hatred of a minister, nor little enough not to merit that of a clerk.” Soon after this he was banished to his country-seat by a lettre de cachet, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> de Richelieu at the head of an armed force abolished the tribunal. In this state of retirement he committed to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> a number of observations on the political and judicial state of France, on <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> history, which all perished in the wreck of the revolution. On the accession of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XVI. to the throne in 1774, he received an order to appear at the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the court of aids had sat, and resume the presidentship of the tribunal thus restored. He laid before the new sovereign an ample memoir on the calamitous state of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, with a free exposure of the faults by which it had been produced, from a firm conviction that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> at all times should have access to the throne. His sentiments so fully accorded with those of the young king, whose mind was not yet corrupted, that he was chosen minister of state in the year 1775, in which elevated <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> he was only ambitious to extend the sphere of his usefulness. His first care was to visit the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRISONS">prisons</a>, and restore to liberty the innocent victims of the former reign. His administration was also distinguished by the powerful encouragement of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> and agriculture, being supported in his laudable endeavours by the able and virtuous Turgot, at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> comptroller-general of the revenue, who having lost his place through the intrigues of financiers, Malesherbes did not <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> retain his office after him. As he failed in his benevolent endeavours to ameliorate the condition of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> respecting the solemnization of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> and the legitimating of their children, he resigned his office in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of May 1776. Being fond of travelling, and resolved to mix freely with people of every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>, in order to acquire an accurate knowledge of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, he assumed the humble <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of M. Guillaume, and commenced his journey in a simple, frugal manner. He travelled through France, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, frequently on foot, and lodged in villages, to have a nearer survey of the state of the country. He made memorandum, with the greatest care, of whatever he conceived to be worthy of observation respecting the productions of nature and the operations of industry; and after an absence of some years he returned to his favourite mansion, fully fraught with such a stock of valuable knowledge as his age and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> qualified him to appreciate. Finding on his return that his native country was far advanced in philosophical principles, he drew up two elaborate <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a> to the king, one of them on the condition of the Protestants, and the other on civil liberty and toleration in general; and the difficulties with which ministers now found themselves surrounded, induced the king to call him to his councils, being a man who stood <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> in the esteem of the whole <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, but he received no appointment to any particular office. In the critical state in which he clearly <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the king stood, he made one effort for opening his eyes, by means of two spirited and energetic memoirs, "On the calamities of France, and the means of repairing them;" but, as the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>'s party carried everything before it, he was not even permitted to read them, and also denied a private interview with the ill-fated monarch, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which he took his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FINAL">final</a> leave of the court. When by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> of the national convention the unfortunate Louis was to be tried for his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, Malesherbes generously offered to plead his cause, nobly forgetting the manner in which he had been banished from his councils. He was the person who announced to him his cruel doom, and one of the last who took leave of him, when taken out to suffer. After this eventful <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, he withdrew to his retreat with a deeply wounded heart, and refused to hear anything more of what was acting on the bloody <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> of Paris. Walking one morning in his garden, he perceived four men coming towards his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, sent by the convention to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARREST">arrest</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> Mad. Lepelletier Rossambo and her husband, once president of the parliament of Paris; and the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a> of Malesherbes was followed, as a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of course, by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. The truth is, the convention never forgave his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the king; an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, however, in which he himself always gloried. On the fatal <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, this great man left the prison with a serene countenance; and, happening to stumble against a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, he said (with the pleasantry of Sir Thomas More), "a Roman would have thought this an unlucky <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OMEN">omen</a>, and walked back again." He conversed with his children in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CART">cart</a>, took an affectionate farewell, and received the stroke in April 1794, in the 73rd year of his age. Thus fell, by the insatiable cruelty of a monster, whose hatred to men of virtue and abilities was implacable, one of the most spotless and exemplary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of the period at which he lived. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> afterwards made some reparation for the injustice done him, by ordering his bust to be placed among those of the great men who have reflected <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> upon their country.

MALHERBE

Pages 451-451

FRANCIS DE, the best French poet of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAEN">Caen</a> about the year 1556, of a noble and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family. He quitted Normandy at 17 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>; and went into Provence, where he attached himself to the family of Henry <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGOULEME">Angouleme</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> son of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Henry II. and was in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> till he was killed by Altoviti in 1586. At length <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> de Perron, being informed of his merit and abilities, introduced him to Henry IV., who took him into his service. After that monarch's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> de Medicis settled a pension of 500 crowns upon our poet, who died at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1628. The best and most complete edition of his poetical works is that of 1666, with Menage's remarks. Malherbe so far excelled all the French poets who preceded him, that Boileau considers him as the father of French <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>; but he composed with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> difficulty, and put his mind on the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACK">rack</a> in correcting what he wrote. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of singular humour, and blunt in his behaviour. When the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> used to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> him, that they would pray to God for him, he answered them, that "he did not believe they could have any great <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> in heaven, since they were left in such a bad condition upon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; and that he should be better pleased <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> de Layne, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> some other favourite, had made him the same promise." He would often say that "the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of gentlemen was that of their prince." During his last sickness he had much ado to resolve to confess to a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>: for which he gave this facetious reason, that "he never used to confess but at Easter." And some few moments before his death, when he had been in a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETHARGY">lethargy</a> two hours, he awakened on a sudden to reprove his landlady, who waited on him, for using a word that was not good French; saying to his confessor, who reprimanded him for it, that "he could not help it, and he would defend the purity of the French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> to the last moment of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>."

MALICE

Pages 451-452

in Ethics and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is a formed <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of doing mischief to another; it differs from hatred. In <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, it is malice makes the crime; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, having a malicious intent to kill another, in the execution of his malice kills a person not intended, the malice shall be connected to his person, and he shall be adjudged a murderer. The words ex malitia praecogitata are necessary to an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDICTMENT">indictment</a> of murder, &c. And this malitia praecogitata, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> malice prepense, may Malice may be either express or implied in law. Express malice is, when one, with a sedate, deliberate mind, and formed design, kills another; which formed design is evidenced by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> circumstances discovering that intention; as lying in wait, antecedent menaces, formed grudges, and concerted schemes to do him some bodily harm. Besides, where no malice is expressed, the law <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> imply it; as where a man wilfully poisons another, in such a deliberate <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> the law presumes malice, though no particular enmity can be proved. And if a man kills another suddenly, without any, or without a considerable provocation, the law implies malice; for no person, unless of an abandoned heart, would be guilty of such an act upon a slight or no apparent cause.

among physicians, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied to diseases of a very dangerous <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and generally infectious; such are the dysentery, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> fever, &c., in their worst stages.

y among physicians signifies much the same with contagion. See Contagion.

MALLEABLE

Pages 452-452

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, whereby they are capable of being extended under the hammer. MALLENDERS. See Farriery <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MALLEOLI

Pages 452-452

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> art of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, were bundles of combustible materials, set on fire to give <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> in the night, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to annoy the enemy: when they were employed for the latter purpose they were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> out of a bow, or fixed to a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAVELIN">javelin</a>, and thus thrown into the enemies engines, ships, &c., in order to burn them. Pitch was always a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> ingredient in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>. The malleoli had also the name of pyroboli.

MALLET

Pages 452-454
or Malloch, David, an English poet, but a Scotsman by birth, was born in that country about 1700. By the penury of his parents, he was compelled to be janitor of the high school at Edinburgh; but he surmounted the disadvantages of his birth and fortune; for when the duke of Montrose applied to the college of Edinburgh for a tutor to educate his sons, Malloch was recommended. When his pupils went abroad, they were intrusted to his care; and having conducted them through their travels, he returned with them to London. Here, residing in their family, he naturally gained admission to persons of high rank and character. His first production was the popular and pathetic ballad of "William and Margaret," which was printed in the Plain Dealer, No. 36, 1724. In the last edition of his works it appears considerably altered. In 1733, he published a poem on verbal Criticism, on purpose to make his court to Pope. In 1740, he wrote a Life of Lord Bacon, which was then prefixed to an edition of his works; but with so much more knowledge of history than of science, that, when he afterwards undertook the Life of Marlborough, some were apprehensive lest he should forget that Marlborough was a general, as he had forgotten that Bacon was a philosopher. The old duchess of Marlborough assigned in her will this task to Glover and Mallet, with a reward of 100l. and a prohibition to insert any verses. Glover is supposed to have rejected the legacy with disdain, so that the work devolved upon Mallet; who had also a pension from the duke of Marlborough to promote his industry, and who was continually talking of the discoveries he made, but left not when he died any historical labours behind. When the prince of Wales was driven from the palace, and kept a separate court by way of opposition, to increase his popularity by patronizing literature, he made Mallet his under secretary, with a salary of 200l. a-year.—Thomson likewise had a pension; and they were associated in the composition of the Masque of Alfred, which, in its original state, was played at Cliefden in 1740. It was afterwards almost wholly changed by Mallet, and brought upon the stage of Drury Lane in 1751, but with no great success. He had before published two tragedies; Eurydice, acted at Drury Lane in 1731; and Mustapha, acted at the same theatre in 1739. It was dedicated to the prince his master, and was well received, but never was revived. His next work was Amyntor and Theodora (1747), a long story in blank verse; in which there is a copiousness and elegance of language, vigour of sentiment, and imagery well adapted to take possession of the fancy. In 1753, his masque of Britannia was acted at Drury Lane, and his tragedy of Elvira in 1763; in which year he was appointed keeper of the book of entries for ships in the port of London. In the beginning of the war, which ended in 1763, when the nation was exasperated by ill success, he was employed to turn the public vengeance upon Byng, and wrote a letter of accusation under the character of a Plain Man. The paper was with great industry circulated and dispersed; and for his seasonable intervention he had a considerable pension bestowed upon him, which he retained to his death. Towards the end of his life he went with his wife to France; but after a while, finding his health declining, he returned alone to England, and died in April 1765. He was twice married, and by his first wife had several children. One daughter, who married an Italian of rank named Cilesia, wrote a tragedy called Almida, which was acted at Drury Lane. His stature was diminutive, but he was regularly formed; his appearance, till he grew corpulent, was agreeable, and he suffered it to want no recommendation that dress could give it. His conversation was elegant and easy. Mallet, Edme, was born at Melun in 1713, and enjoyed a curacy in the neighbourhood of his native place till 1751, when he went to Paris to be professor of theology in the college of Navarre, of which he was admitted a doctor. Boyer, bishop of Mirepoix, was at first much prejudiced against him; but being afterwards undeceived, he conferred upon him the see of Verdun as a reward for his doctrine and morals. Jansenism had been imputed to him by his enemies with his prelate; and the gazette which went by the name of Ecclesiastical, accused him of impiety. Either of these imputations was equally undeserved by the abbé Mallet: as a Christian, he was grieved at the disputes of the French church; and as a philosopher, he was astonished that the government had not, from the very beginning of those dissensions imposed silence on both parties. He died at Paris in 1755, at the age of 42. The principal of his works are, 1. Principes pour la lecture des Poètes, 1745, 12mo, 2 vols. 2. Essai sur l'Etude des Belles Lettres, 1747, 12mo. Mallet, 12mo. 3. *Essai sur les bienveillance oratoires*, 1753, 12mo. 4. *Principes pour la lectures des Orateurs*, 1753, 12mo. 3 vols. 5. *Histoire des Guerres civiles de France sous les regnes de Francois II. Charles IX. Henri III. et Henri IV.* translated from the Italian of d'Avila.—In Mallet's work on the Poets, Orators, and the Belles Lettres, his object is no more than to explain with accuracy and precision the rules of the great masters, and to support them by examples from authors ancient and modern. The style of his different writings, to which his mind bore a great resemblance, was neat, easy, and unaffected. But what must render his memory estimable, was his attachment to his friends, his candour, moderation, gentleness, and modesty. He was employed to write the theological and belles lettres articles in the *Encyclopédie*; and whatever he wrote in that dictionary was in general well composed. Abbé Mallet was preparing two important works when the world was deprived of him by death. The first was *Une Histoire generale de nos Guerres depuis le commencement de la Monarchie*; the second, *Une Histoire de Concile de Trente*, which he intended to set in opposition to that of Father Paul translated by Father le Courayer. **Mallet**, a large kind of hammer made of wood; much used by artificers who work with a chissel, as sculptors, masons, and stone-cutters, whose mallet is ordinarily round; and by carpenters, joiners, &c. who use it square. There are several sorts of mallets used for different purposes on ship-board. The calking mallet is chiefly employed to drive the oakum into the seams of a ship, where the edges of the planks are joined to each other in the sides, deck, or bottom. The head of this mallet is long and cylindrical, being hooped with iron to prevent it from splitting in the exercise of calking. There is also the serving mallet, used in serving the rigging, by binding the spun yarn more firmly about it than it could possibly be done by hand, which is performed in the following manner; the spun-yarn being previously rolled up in a large ball or clue, two or three turns of it are passed about the rope, and about the body of the mallet, which for this purpose is furnished with a round channel in its surface, that conforms to the convexity of the rope intended to be served. The turns of the spun-yarn being strained round the mallet, so as to confine it firmly to the rope, which is extended above the deck, one man passes the ball continually about the rope, whilst the other, at the same time, winds on the spun-yarn by means of the mallet, whose handle acting as a lever strains every turn about the rope as firm as possible. **Mallicollo**, one of the largest of the New Hebrides, in the Pacific ocean. It extends twenty leagues from north to south. Its inland mountains are very high, and clad with forests. Its vegetable productions are luxuriant, and in great variety; cocoa-nuts, breadfruit, bananas, sugar-canes, yams, eddoes, turmeric, and oranges. Hogs and common poultry are the domestic animals. The inhabitants appear to be of a race totally distinct from those of the Friendly and Society islands. Their form, language, and manners, are widely different. They seem to correspond in many particulars with the natives of New Guinea, particularly in their black colour and woolly hair. They go almost naked, are of a slender make, have lively but very irregular ugly features, and tie a rope fast round their belly. They use bows and arrows as their principal weapons, and the arrows are said to be sometimes poisoned. They keep their bodies entirely free from punctures, which is one particular that remarkably distinguishes them from the other tribes of the Pacific ocean. The population, according to Mr Forster, may amount to 50,000, who occupy 600 square miles of ground. The same author informs us that very few women were seen, but that those few were no less ugly than the men, were of small stature, and their heads, faces, and shoulders were painted red. They had bundles on their backs containing their children, and the men seemed to have no kind of regard for them. They appeared in fact to be oppressed, despised, and in a state of servility. The men use bows and arrows, and a club about 30 inches long, which they hang on their right shoulder, from a thick rope made of a kind of grass. They live chiefly on vegetables, and apply themselves to husbandry. Their music had nothing remarkable in it, either for harmony or variety, but seemed to Mr Forster to be of a more lively turn than that at the Friendly islands. In some of their countenances he thought he could trace a mischievous, ill-natured disposition, but he confesses that he might mistake jealousy for hatred. It is in 16° 28' S. Lat. and 167° 36' E. Long. **Mallow**, a manor, and also a borough town in the county of Cork, province of Munster, in Ireland, above 118 miles from Dublin, pleasantly situated on the north bank of the Blackwater, over which there is an excellent stone bridge. Not far distant is a fine spring of a moderately tepid water, which bursts out of the bottom of a fine limestone rock, and approaches the nearest in all its qualities to the hot-well waters of Bristol of any that has been yet discovered in this kingdom, which brings a resort of good company there frequently in the summer months, and has caused it to be called the Irish Bath. **Mallow.** See Malva, Botany Index. **Marsh-Mallow.** See Althaea, Botany Index. **Indian-Mallow.** See Sida, Botany Index. **Malmsbury,** a town of Wiltshire in England, 95 miles from London. It stands on a hill, with six bridges over the river Avon at the bottom; with which and a brook that runs into it, it is in a manner encompassed. It formerly had walls and a castle, which was pulled down to enlarge the abbey, which was the largest in Wiltshire, and its abbots sat in parliament. The Saxon king Athelstan granted the town large immunities, and was buried under the high altar of the church, and his monument still remains in the nave of it. The memory of Aldhelm, its first abbot, who was the king's great favourite, and whom he got to be canonized after his death, is still kept up by a meadow near this town, called Aldhelm's Mead. By charter of King William III. the corporation consists of an alderman, who is chosen yearly, 12 capital burgesses, and 4 assistants. Here is an alms-house for 4 men and 4 women, and near the bridge an hospital for lepers, where it is supposed there was formerly a nunnery. This town contained, in 1811, 1152 inhabitants, and has a considerable trade in the woollen manufactory; Malmesbury, has a market on Saturday, and three fairs. It has sent members to parliament ever since the 26th of Edward I. William of Malmsbury. Sec William.

MALO

Pages 454-454

Maclou, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Mahout, Saint, the son of an Englishman, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUSIN">cousin</a> to St Magloire, was educated in a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, and afterwards chosen bishop of Gui-Castel, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> which his humility prevented him from accepting. The people wishing to compel him, he went to Brittany, and put himself under the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of a holy anchoret called <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AARON">Aaron</a>, in the neighbourhood of Aleth. Some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> after, about the year 541, he was chosen bishop of that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and there cultivated piety and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> success. He afterwards retired to a solitude near Xaintes, where he died November 15, 565. From him the city of St Malo derives its name; his body having been carried thither, after the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of Aleth to a small village railed Guidalet or Guichalet, and the transference of the episcopal see to St Malo.

MALOUIN

Pages 454-455

PAUL-JAQUES, born at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAEN">Caen</a> in 1701, was professor of medicine in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, physician in ordinary to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>, and a member of the Royal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and of the Academy of Sciences of Paris. These stations were a proper reward for his very extensive information in medicine and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>; and his amiable and steady character procured him many friends and protectors. He was very unlike some <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> physicians, who put little trust in medicine; and was greatly displeased to hear any ill spoken of his profession. He observed one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> to a young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who took this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, that all <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> men had respected medicine: Ah! said the young fellow, you must at least except from the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a> one Moliere. But then, instantly replied the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a>, you see he is dead. He is said to have believed the certainty of his art as firmly as a mathematician does that of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>. Having prescribed a great many medicines for a celebrated man of letters, who followed his directions exactly, and was cured, Malouin eagerly embraced him, saying, You deserve to be sick. As he valued the rules of medicine still more on his own account than on that of others, he observed, especially in the latter <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, a very austere regimen. He strictly practised the preservative part of medicine, which is much more certain in its effects than the restorative. To this regimen Malouin was indebted, for what many philosophers have desired in vain, a healthy old <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> and an easy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. He was a stranger to the infirmities of age; and died at Paris of an apoplexy, the 3d of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1778, in the 77th year of his age. By his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> he left a legacy to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of medicine, upon condition of their holding a public meeting every year for the purpose of giving the public an account of his labours and discoveries. Malouin was economical, but at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> very disinterested. After two years of very lucrative practice, he left Paris and went to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSAILLES">Versailles</a>, where he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> very few patients, observing that that he had retired to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> works are, 1. Traité de Chimie, 1734, 12mo. 2. Chimie Medicinale, 2 vols. 12mo, 1755; a book full of curious observations, and written in a chaste and well adapted style. He had the character of a laborious chemist; and he was a well-informed and even a distinguished one for the age in which he lived; but his knowledge of chemistry, it must be confessed, was very imperfect, compared with the state of the science in the present age, in which it has assumed a new <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a>, that probably will not be the last. 3. Some of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> in the Collection published by the Academy of Sciences on the arts and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROFESSIONS">professions</a>. A circumstance which happened at a meeting of the academy does as much <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to his heart, as any of his works do to his understanding. A new treatise on the art of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAKING">baking</a>, wherein some of Malouin's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> were combated, was read by M. Parmentier before his fellows, among whom was the old doctor. The young academician, who knew how easily self-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> is hurt, was afraid to meet his looks: but no sooner was the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> finished, than Malouin went up to him, and embracing him, "Receive my respects (said he), you have seen farther into the subject than I did." 4. He was likewise the author of the chemical articles in the Encyclopédie. Of the same family was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Malouin, who graduated as a doctor of medicine in the university of Caen, and died in 1718 in the flower of his age. He published a Treatise on Solids and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">Fluids</a>, Paris 1718, 12mo.

MALPAS

Pages 455-455

a town of Cheshire, 166 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It stands on a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> hill, nor far from the river <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEE">Dee</a>, on the borders of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHROPSHIRE">Shropshire</a>; has a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> school, and an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>, and had formerly a castle. It is called in Latin Mala Platea, i.e. "Ill Street," and was, for the same reason, by the Normans, called Mal Pas; but its three streets, of which it chiefly consists, are now well paved; and here is a benefice rich enough to support two rectors, who officiate alternately in its stately <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in 1811 was 938.

MALPIGHI

Pages 455-455

Marcellus, an eminent Italian physician and anatomist in the 17th century. He studied under Massari and Mariano. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a> invited him to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PISA">Pisa</a>, to be professor of physic there. In this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> he contracted an intimate acquaintance with Borelli, to whom he ascribed all the discoveries he had made. He went back to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> of Pisa not agreeing with him. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Antonio Pignatelli, who had known him while he was legate at Bologna, being chosen pope in 1691, under the name of Innocent XII, immediately sent for him to Rome, and appointed him his physician. But this did not hinder him from pursuing his studies, and perfecting his works, which have immortalized his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>. He died in 1694; and his works, with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> written by himself, prefixed, were first collected and printed at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, in folio, in 1667.

MALPIGHIA

Pages 455-455

Barbadoes Cherry; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the decandria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 23d order, Trihilate. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALPLAQUET">MALPLAQUET</a>; a village of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, in Hainault, famous for a most bloody <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> fought here on the 11th of September 1709, between the French under old Marshal Villars, and the allies commanded by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Eugene and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARLBOROUGH">Marlborough</a>. The French <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> amounted to 120,000 men; and were posted behind the woods of La Marte and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENIERS">Teniers</a>, in the neighbourhood of Malplaquet. They had fortified their situation in such a manner with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, hedges, and trees laid across, that they seemed to be quite inaccessible.
