Rest your firelock: i.e. Bring your right hand as far as the swell; raise the firelock <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> up in a perpendicular line from the ground with your right hand, and seize it with your left above the spring, the cock being at the height of the waist-belt; step back with your right foot, placing it behind your left heel, and come to the rest. 19. Shoulder your firelock: i.e. Lift up your right foot, and place it by your left; bring the firelock at the same time to your left shoulder, and seize the butt-end with the left hand, keeping it in the same position as above described; throw your right hand briskly back. 20. Secure your firelock: i.e. Bring the right hand briskly up, and place it under the cock, keeping the firelock steady in the same position; quit the butt with the left hand, and seize the firelock with it at the swell, bringing the elbow close down upon the lock; the right hand being kept fast in this motion, and the piece still upright; quit the right hand, and bring it down your right side, bringing the firelock nimbly down to the secure; the left hand in a line with the waist-belt. 21. Shoulder your firelock: i.e. Bring the firelock up to a perpendicular line, seizing it with the right hand under the cock; quit the left hand, and place it strong upon the butt, quit the right hand, and bring it smartly down the right side. 22. Fix your bayonet: i.e. First and second motions, as in the two first of the secure; quit the right hand, and bring the firelock smartly down to the left side with the left hand, as far as it will admit without constraint, seizing the bayonet at the same time with the right hand, and fixing it, placing that hand just below the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, with the piece kept close to the hollow of the shoulder. 23. Shoulder your firelock: i.e. Quit the right hand, and bring up the firelock with the left; seize it again under the cock with your right, as in the second motion of the secure; quit the left hand, and place it strong upon the butt; quit the right hand, and bring it down the right side. 24. Present your arms: i.e. as explained in the three motions of the 14th word of command. 25. To the right face: i.e. Bring up the firelock with a quick motion high before you, till your left hand comes even with your eyes, both the fingers of that hand extended along the stock, just above the feather-spring, the right foot to be brought close up to the left heel in this motion; face to the right, taking care in facing to hold the firelock right up and down, and steady in your hands; step back with your right foot, and come down to your present, as in the foregoing explanation. 26. To the right face: i.e. as in the foregoing explanation, facing to the right. 27. To the right about face: i.e. as in the 25th explanation, only coming to the right about instead of to the right. 28. To the left face: i.e. Bring the right foot briskly to the hollow of your left, with the firelock in the same position as in the first motion of facing to the right; face to the left; come down to the present, as before. 29. To the left face: i.e. as in the foregoing explanation. 30. To the left about face: i.e. as before, coming to the left-about instead of to the left. 31. Shoulder your firelock: i.e. as in the two motions of the 19th explanation. 32. Charge your bayonets: i.e. as in the first explanation: bring the swell of the firelock down strong upon the palm of the hand, grasping the piece at the small, behind the lock, and as high as the waist-belt; the firelock upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> with the barrel upwards. 33. Shoulder your firelock: i.e. Bring up the firelock to the shoulder, place the left hand upon the butt, bringing the feet square to the front; quit the right hand, and throw it down the right side. 34. Advance your arms: i.e. first and second motions, as in the first explanation; bring the firelock down the right side, with the right hand as low as it will admit without constraint, slipping up the left hand at the same time to the swell, the guard between the thumb and forefinger of the right hand, the three last fingers under the cock, with the barrel to the rear; quit the left hand, 35. Shoulder your firelock: i.e. Bring up the left hand, and seize it Manual. it at the swell; come smartly up to the poise; shoulder. 36. Prime and load: i.e. Come smartly to the receiver: by springing the firelock straight up with the left hand, turning the barrel inwards to the proper height of the receiver: at the same time that the left hand <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> the firelock, the right hand is raised briskly from the right side, and seizes the firelock across the breast: as it rises below the cock, the left hand comes with a quick motion from the butt, and seizes the firelock strong above the lock, the little finger of the left hand at the spring of the lock, the left hand at an equal height with the face, the butt close to the body, but not pressed, the firelock perpendicular opposite the left side of the face: bring the firelock down with a brisk motion to the priming position, the left hand holding the firelock, as in priming; the thumb of the right hand placed against the face of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>, the fingers clenched, and the elbow a little turned out, that the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WRIST">wrist</a> may be clear of the cock: open the pan, by throwing up the steel with a strong motion of the right arm, turning the elbow in, and keeping the firelock steady in the left hand; handle your cartridge, prime, shut your pan, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> about, load, draw rammers, ram down the cartridge, return the rammers, shoulder. N.B. The motion of recover, and coming down to the priming position and opening pans, are to be done in the usual time. The motions of handling cartridge to shutting the pans, are to be done as quick as possible: when the pans are shut, a small pause is to be made, and then cast about together; then the loading motions are to be done as quick as possible; but before the rammer is returned, another small pause is to be made, counting 1, 2, between each motion, till the firelock is shouldered.—Front <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> make ready: i.e. Spring the firelock briskly to the receiver, keeping the left foot fast in this motion: as soon as the firelock is at the receiver, without any stop, sink the body briskly without stooping forward, with a quick motion down upon the right knee; the butt-end of the firelock at the same time falls upon the ground, the front part of the butt being in a line with the heel of the left foot. As soon as the butt comes to the ground, the firelock is to be cocked, immediately seizing the cock and steel in the right hand; the firelock to be held firm in the left hand, about the middle of that part of the firelock between the lock and the swell of the stock; the point of the left thumb to be close to the swell, pointing upwards. As the body is sinking, the right knee is to be thrown as far back as the left leg may be right up and down; the right foot to be thrown a little to the right; the body to be kept straight; the head up, looking to the right along the rank, the same as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> shouldered; the firelock to be upright, and the butt about four inches to the right of the inside of the left foot. Present: i.e. Bring the firelock briskly down to the present, by extending the left arm to the full length with a strong motion; at the same time spring up the butt by the cock with the right hand, and raise the butt so high upon the right shoulder, that you may not be obliged to stoop too much with the head; the right cheek to be close to the butt, and the left eye shut, and look along the barrel with the right eye from the breech-pin to the muzzle; keep the left elbow down in an easy position, and stand as steady as possible; the thumb of the right hand to remain in the position as described in the third explanation of the manual. Fire: i.e. Pull the trigger as directed in the manual; and as soon as the piece is fired, give yourself a strong spring upon your left leg, raising your body briskly, and straight up, keeping your left foot fast, and bringing the right heel to the inside of the left; at the same time the firelock is to be brought up to the priming position, and half-cocked immediately: a short pause is to be made; then handle cartridge, and go on with the loading motions described in the explanation of prime and load.—Centre rank make ready: i.e. Spring the firelock briskly to the receiver; so soon as the left hand seizes the firelock above the lock, the right elbow is to be nimbly raised a little, placing the thumb of that hand upon the cock; the fingers open by the plate of the lock, and as quick as possible force the piece to the cock, by dropping the elbow, and forcing down the cock with the thumb, stepping at the same time a moderate pace to the right, keeping the left foot fast; as the firelock is cocked, the thumb is to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> below the cock, the right hand seizing the firelock close under the cock firmly, the fore finger not to be before the trigger; the piece to be held in this position perpendicular, opposite the left side of the face, the butt close to the left breast, but not pressed; the body to be straight, and as full to the front as possible: the head kept up, looking to the right of the rank, that the body and the firelock may not stoop forward, nor lean much out of the rank. Present: i.e. Spring the firelock from the body to the arm’s length with a quick motion, pressing down the muzzle with the left hand, and springing up the butt with the right hand, as in the foregoing explanation of the front rank. Fire: As in explanation 4, in the manual, with this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, that the left foot is to be brought up to the right, at the same time that the firelock is brought down to the priming position. The loading motions as in the explanations of priming and loading; and at the last motion of shouldering, to spring to the left again, and cover the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FILE">file</a>-leaders.—Rear rank, make ready: i.e. Recover the firelock, and cock as before directed for the centre rank; as the firelock is recovered and cocked, step briskly straight to the right, with the right foot, a full pace; bring the left heel about six inches before the right foot; the body straight, and as square to the front as possible, as in the explanation of the centre rank. Present: As in explanation present, before. Fire: As in explanation of the centre rank; and as the firelock is coming down to the priming position, the left is to be brought back to the right; and at the last motion of shouldering, to spring to the left again, and cover the file-leader (A). (a) The manual exercise now described is not precisely the same that it is at present (1807). The difference indeed is not <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>; but depending partly on the peculiar views of commanding officers, it is so subject to change that it would be useless to detail it in its present form. There are some peculiar words of command at the manual exercise of the grenadiers, when apart from the battalion; and also for the cavalry and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>. **MANUDUCTOR,** a name given to an ancient officer in the church; who, from the middle of the choir, where he was placed, gave the signal for the choristers to sing, and marked the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> time, and regulated the music. The Greeks called him *me-suchoros*, because seated in the middle of the choir; but in the Latin church he was called *manuductor*; from *manus* and *duco*, "I <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>;" because he led and guided the choir by the motions and gesture of the hand. **MANUFACTURE,** a commodity produced from raw or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> materials, either by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of the hand or by machinery. **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURER">MANUFACTURER</a>,** one who works up a natural product into an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> commodity. **MANUMISSION,** an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> whereby a slave or villain is set at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, or let out of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BONDAGE">bondage</a>. The word comes from the Latin *manus*, "hand;" and *mittere*, "to send;" *quia servus mittatur extra manum seu potentatem domini sui*. Some authors define manumission an act by which a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> enfranchises his tenants, who till that time had been his vassals, and in a state of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a> inconsistent with the sanctity of the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>. Among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, the manumission of slaves was performed three several ways. 1. When, with his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>'s consent, a slave had his name entered in the census or public <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a> of the citizens. 2. When the slave was led before the praetor, and that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> laid his wand called *vindicta* on his head. 3. When the master gave the slave his freedom by his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">testament</a>. Servius Tullius is said to have set on foot the first manner; and P. Valerius Publicola the second. A particular account is given of the third in the Institutes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTINIAN">Justinian</a>. It was not necessary that the praetor should be on his tribunal to perform the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of manumission: he did it anywhere indifferently, in his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, in the street, in going to bathe, &c. He laid the rod on the slave's head, pronouncing these words, *Dieo eum liberum esse more Quiritium*, "I declare him a freeman, after the manner of the Romans." This done, he gave the rod to the lictor, who struck the slave with it on the head, and afterwards with his hand on his face and back; and the notary or scribe entered the name of the new freedman in the register, with the reasons of his manumission. The slave had likewise his head shaved, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a> given him by his master as a token of freedom. Tertullian adds, that he had then also a third name given him: if this were so, three names were not a token of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, but of freedom. The emperor Constantine ordered the manumissions at Rome to be performed in the churches. Of manumission there have also been various forms in England. In the time of the Conqueror, villains were manumitted, by the master's delivering them by the right hand to the viscount, in full <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, showing them the door, giving them a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANCE">lance</a> and a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, and proclaiming them free. Others were manumitted by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a>. There was also an implicit manumission: as when the lord made an obligation for payment of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol3.html#article-BONDMAN">bondman</a> at a certain <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, or sued him where he might enter without <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a>, and the like. **MANURE,** any thing used for fattening and improving <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>. See **<a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">AGRICULTURE</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>**. **MANUSCRIPT,** a book or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> written with the hand; by which it stands opposed to a printed book or paper. A manuscript is usually denoted by the two letters MS. and in the plural by MSS. What makes public <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a> valuable, is the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of ancient <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> reposed in them; see **<a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIAN">ALEXANDRIAN</a>**, **<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">CAMBRIDGE</a>**, **CLERMONT**, **COTTONIAN**, **HARLEIAN**, **VATICAN**, &c.

MANUTIUS

Pages 627-628

Aldus,** the first of those celebrated Venetian printers who were as illustrious for their learning as for uncommon skill in their profession. He was born at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BASSANO">Bassano</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> about the middle of the 15th century; and hence is sometimes called *Basianus*, though generally better known by the name of *Aldus*. He was the first who printed Greek neatly and correctly; and acquired so much reputation by it, that whatever was finely printed was proverbially said to have come from the press of Aldus. We have a kind of Greek <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> of his; with notes upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, Horace, &c. He died at <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, where he exercised his profession, in 1516. **Manutius, Paulus,** son of the former, was brought up to his father's profession. He was more learned than he; and he acquired, by continual <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> of Tully, such a purity in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> Latin, as even Scaliger allows a Roman could not exceed. Pope Pius IV. placed him at the head of the apostolical press, and gave him the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of the Vatican library. His Epistles are infinitely laboured, and very correct; but, as may be said of most of the Ciceronians, they contain scarcely anything but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> words. This constant reading of Tully, however, together with his profound knowledge of antiquity, qualified him extremely well for an editor of Tully; whose works he accordingly published, with Commentaries on them, in 4 vols. folio, at Venice in 1523. He died in 1574. **Manutius, Aldus, the Younger,** the son of Paulus, and the grandson of Aldus, was esteemed one of the greatest geniuses and most learned men of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. Clement VIII. gave him the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the Vatican <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>: but probably the profits of that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> were very small, since Manutius was obliged, for his subsistence, to accept of a professor of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, and to sell the excellent library that was in his family, which his father, his uncle, and his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> uncle, had collected with extraordinary care, and which it is said contained 80,000 volumes. He died at Rome in 1597, without any other recompense than the praises due to his merit. He wrote, 1. Commentaries on Cicero. 2. A Treatise on Orthography. 3. Three books of Epistles; and other works in Latin and Italian, which are esteemed. **MAON,** in *<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>*, a town of the tribe of Judah, to the south east, towards the Dead <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>. It gave name to the wilderness of Moan, 1 Sam. xxii. **<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MAOUNA">MAOUNA</a>,** one of the Navigator's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in the south <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PACIFIC_OCEAN">Pacific ocean</a>. Here M. de la Perouse, commander of the French ships the Boussole and Astrolabe, met with his first fatal accident in 1787; M. de Langle, Langle, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> of the Astrolabe, with 11 officers and sailors, were massacred by the natives. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 169. S. Lat. 14. 19.

MAPPARIUS

in Roman antiquity, the officer who gave the signal to the gladiators to begin fighting.

MARACANDA

Pages 628-628

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the Sogdiana. Now thought to be Samarqand, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Usbec <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> residence of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TAMERLANE">Tamerlane</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAMARCAND">SAMARCAND</a>.

MARACAYBO

Pages 628-628

a lake in South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, 150 miles <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and 90 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, which communicates with the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. It is well defended by strong forts; which, however, did not hinder Sir Henry Morgan, a bucanier, from plundering several <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARACCAS">CARACCAS</a>, Supplement.

MARAGNAN

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRAZIL">Brazil</a> in South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, which comprehends a fertile populous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, 112 miles in circumference. The French settled here in 1612, and built a small town; but they were driven from it by the Portuguese, who have possessed it ever since. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> is pleasant, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> fertile. MARALDI

Pages 628-628

James-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a>, a learned mathematician and astronomer, of the Academy of Sciences at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, was born in 1665. He was the son of Francis Maraldi and Angela Catharine Cassini, the sister of the famous astronomer of that name. His uncle sent him to France in 1687, where he acquired <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation on account of his learning and observations. He made a catalogue of the fixed stars, which is more particular and exact than Bayer's; and has given a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of curious and interesting observations in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a> of the academy. He died in 1729.

MARANA

Pages 628-628

John Paul, an ingenious writer of the 17th century, was of a distinguished family, and born at <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>; where he received an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> suitable to his birth, and made <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> progress in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of polite literature and the sciences. Having been engaged in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> of Raphael della Terra, to deliver up Genoa to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Savoy, he was in 1670, when 28 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, imprisoned in the tower of that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and remained there four years. Being at length set at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, he was ordered to write the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of that conspiracy; but, when finished, it was seized and prevented from being published. When the republic of Genoa was at variance with the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of France, Marana, who had always an inclination for that court, was afraid of being imprisoned a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; and retired to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONACO">Monaco</a>, where he again wrote the history of the conspiracy in Italian; and, in 1682, went to Lyons to get it printed. From Lyons he went to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, where his merit soon acquired him powerful protectors. He spent the rest of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in a happy and tranquil mediocrity, devoted to study and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of men of learning; and died in 1693. His history of the conspiracy contains many curious and interesting anecdotes. He also wrote several other works; the most known of which is the Turkish Spy, in six volumes 12mo, which was in 1742 augmented to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a>. Of this ingenious <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> we have an excellent English translation.

MARANO

It contains about 1000 inhabitants.

It carries on a very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> trade in corn; and is seated in W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0. 54. N. Lat. 46. 18.

MARATHON

Pages 628-630

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, one of the demi <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> hamlets of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a>; about 10 miles to the northeast of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, towards <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOEOTIA">Boeotia</a>, near the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. It still retains its ancient name (Dr Chandler informs us); but is very inconsiderable, consisting only of a few houses and gardens. The plain of Marathon, famous for Miltiades's victory over the Persians, by which the liberties of Athens and other cities of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> were saved, is <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and narrow, but consisting chiefly of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> ground, and therefore admitting the operations of cavalry, which formed the main strength of the barbarian <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, and with which the Greeks were very poorly provided. Here the Persians, under the command of Datis, pitched their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>, by the advice of Hippias, the banished <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Athens, whose solicitations and intrigues had promoted the expedition, and whose perfect knowledge of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and intimate acquaintance with the affairs of Greece, rendered his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> on all occasions respectable. The Persian army is said to have consisted of 100,000 infantry, and 10,000 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>.—Athens was in the utmost consternation and dismay. She had, upon the first Marathon. first appearance of the Persian fleet, sent to implore assistance from the other nations of Greece; but some had submitted to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DARIUS">Darius</a>, and others trembled at the very name of the Medes and Persians. The Lacedemonians alone promised troops; but various obstacles did not allow them immediately to form a junction with those of Athens. This <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> therefore could only rely on its own strength; and happily at this moment there appeared three men destined to give new energy to the state. These were Miltiades, Aristides, and Themistocles; whose example and harangues kindled the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> of the noblest heroism in the minds of the Athenians. Levies were immediately made. Each of the ten tribes furnished 1000 foot <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> with a commander at their head. To complete this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> it was necessary to enrol the slaves (A). No sooner were the troops assembled than they marched out of the city into the plain of Marathon, where the inhabitants of Platæa in Boeotia sent them a reinforcement of 1000 infantry. Scarcely were the two armies in sight of each other, before Miltiades proposed to attack the enemy. Aristides and several of the commanders warmly supported this <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>; but the rest, terrified at the excessive disproportion of the armies, were desirous of waiting for the succours from Lacedaemon. Opinions being divided, they had recourse to that of the polemarch, or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a>, who was consulted on such occasions, to put an end to the equality of suffrages. Miltiades addressed himself to him, with the ardour of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> deeply impressed with the importance of present circumstances: "Athens (said he to him) is on the point of experiencing the greatest of vicissitudes. Ready to become the first power of Greece, or the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> of the tyranny and fury of Hippias, from you alone, Callimachus, she now awaits her <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DESTINY">destiny</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> we suffer the ardour of the troops to cool, they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> shamefully bow beneath the Persian yoke; but if we <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> them on to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, the gods and victory will favour us. A word from your mouth must now precipitate your country into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a> or preserve her <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>." Callimachus gave his suffrage, and the battle was resolved. To ensure success, Aristides, and the other generals after his example, yielded to Miltiades the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the command which belonged to them in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROTATION">rotation</a>; but, to secure them from every hazard, he preferred waiting for the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> which of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> placed him at the head of the army. When that day arrived, Miltiades drew up his troops at the foot of a mountain, on a spot of ground scattered over with trees to impede the Persian cavalry. The Platæans were placed on the left wing; Callimachus commanded the right; Aristides and Themistocles were in the centre of the battle, and Miltiades everywhere. An <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> of nearly a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> separated the Grecian army from that of the Persians. At the first signal the Greeks advanced over this space running. The Persians, astonished at a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of attack so <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVEL">novel</a> to both nations, for a moment remained motionless; but to the impetuous fury of the enemy they soon opposed a more sedate and not less formidable fury. After an obstinate conflict of some hours, victory began to declare herself in the two wings of the Grecian army. The right dispersed the enemy in the plain, while the left drove them back on a morass that had the appearance of a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEADOW">meadow</a>, in which they stuck fast and were lost. Both these bodies of troops now flew to the succour of Aristides and Themistocles, ready to give way before the flower of the Persian troops placed by Datis in the centre of his battle. From this moment the rout became general. The Persians, repulsed on all sides, found their only <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a> in the fleet which had approached the shore. The conquerors pursued them with fire and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, and took, burnt, or sunk the greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of their vessels; the rest escaped by dint of rowing. The Persian army lost about 6400 men; that of the Athenians 192. Miltiades was wounded; Hippas was left dead on the field, as were Stesileus and Callimachus, two of the Athenian generals. Scarcely was the battle over, when a soldier, worn out with fatigue, forms the project of carrying the first news of so signal a success to the magistrates of Athens, and without quitting his arms, he runs, flies, arrives, announces the victory, and falls dead at their feet. This battle was fought on the 6th of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOEDROMION">Boedromion</a>, in the third year of the 72nd Olympiad (or 29th September anno 490 B.C.). The next day 2000 Spartans arrived. In three days and nights they had marched 1200 stadia. Though informed of the defeat of the Persians, they <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> to Marathon, nor did they enviously shun to behold those fields where a rival <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> had signalized itself by so heroic an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>: they there beheld the tents of the Persians still standing, the plain strewn over with dead, and covered with costly spoils: they there found Aristides, who with his tribe was guarding the prisoners and booty; and did not retire until they had bestowed <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> applauses on the victors. The Athenians neglected nothing to eternalize the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of those who fell in the battle. It had been usual to inter the citizens who perished in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> at the public expense, in the Ceramieus without the city; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of these was deemed uncommonly meritorious. They were buried, and a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARROW">barrow</a> was made for them, where their bravery had been manifested. Their names were engraven on half columns erected on the plain of Marathon. These monuments, not excepting those of the generals Callimachus and Stesileus, were in a style of the greatest simplicity. In the intervals between them were erected trophies <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> the arms of the Persians. An <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> of eminence had painted all the circumstances of the battle in one of the most frequented porticoes of the city: Miltiades was there represented at the head of the generals, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of exhorting the troops to fight for their country. Pausanias examined the field of battle about 600 years (A) Travels of Anacharsis; authority, Pausan. i. 79. But Dr Gillies seems to think that the armed slaves were not included in the 10,000; but amounted of themselves to a greater number, and which formed the centre of the battle. Marathon years after this event. His account of it is as follows: "The barrow of the Athenians is in the plain, and on it are pillars containing the names of the dead under those of the tribes to which they belonged; and there is another for the Platæans and slaves; and a distinct monument of Miltiades the commander, who survived this exploit. There may be perceived nightly the neighing of horses and the clashing of arms. No person has derived any good from waiting on purpose to behold the spectres; but their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGER">anger</a> does not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> on any one who happens to see them without <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>. The Marathonians worship those who were slain in the battle, styling them heroes.—A trophy also of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> marble has been erected. The Athenians say the Medes were buried, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> requiring that the corpse of a man be covered with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; though I was not able to find any <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of sepulture, for there is no barrow or other sign visible; but they threw them promiscuously into a pit.—Above the lake are the marble mangers of the horses of Artaphernes, with marks of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENT">tent</a> on the rocks." Many centuries have elapsed since the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of Pausanias; but the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> barrow, it is likely that of the gallant Athenians, still towers above the level of the plain. It is of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> fine earth, and has a bush or two growing on it. Dr Chandler informs us, that he enjoyed a pleasant and satisfactory view from the summit; and looked, but in vain, for the pillars on which the names were recorded, lamenting that such memorials should ever be removed. Marathon has since been visited by Dr Clarke, who has given an interesting account of the topography of the field of battle in the 4to vol. of his Travels. MARATTA. See MARHATTAS.

MARATTI

Pages 630-630

CARLO, a celebrated painter, was born at Camorano, near <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCONA">Ancona</a>, in 1625. He came a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> boy to Rome, when only 11 years old; and at 12 recommended himself so effectually to Andrea Sacchi, by his drawings after Raphael in the Vatican, that he took him into his school, where he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> 25 years till his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. His graceful and beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> occasioned his being generally employed in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> madonas and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> saints. No <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> ever performed in a better style, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> with a greater elegance. From the finest <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> and pictures, he made himself master of the most perfect forms, and the most charming <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRS">airs</a> of heads, which he sketched with equal ease and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>. He has produced a noble variety of draperies, more artfully managed, more richly ornamented, and with greater propriety, than even the best of the moderns. He was inimitable in adorning the heads, in the disposal of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, and the elegance of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> and feet, which are equal to those of Raphael; and he particularly excelled in gracefulness. In his younger days he etched a few <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a>, as well of his own <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> as after others, with equal spirit and correctness. It would be endless to recount the celebrated paintings done by this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> man. Yet he executed nothing slightly, often changed his designs, and almost always for the better, whence his pictures were <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. By the example of his master, he made several admirable portraits of popes, cardinals, and other people of distinction, from whom he received the highest testimonies of esteem, as he likewise did from almost all the monarchs and princes of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. Inno- cent XI. appointed him keeper of the paintings in his chapel and the Vatican. Maratti erected two noble monuments for Raphael and A. Caracci, at his own expense, in the Pantheon. How well he maintained the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of his profession, appears by his answer to a Roman <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, who complaining of the excessive price of his pictures, he told him there was a vast debt due from the world to the famous artists his predecessors, and that he, as their rightful successor, was come to claim those arrears. His abilities in painting were accompanied with many virtues, and particularly with an extensive <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>. This great painter died at Rome in 1713, in the 88th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>.

MARAUDING

Pages 630-630

in a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, means a party of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, who, without any order, go into the neighbouring houses and villages, when the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> is either in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> garrison, to plunder and destroy, &c. Marauders are a disgrace to the camp, to the military profession, and deserve no better <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> from their officers than they give to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> peasants, &c.

MARAVEDI

Pages 630-630

a little Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, worth somewhat more than a French <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENIER">denier</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> half a farthing English. The Spaniards always <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> by maravedis, both in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> and in their finances, though the coin itself is no longer current among them. Sixty-three maravedis are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to a rial of silver; so that the piaster, or piece of eight rials, contains 504; and the pistole of four pieces of eight, 2016 maravedis. This smallness of the coin produces vast numbers in the Spanish accounts and calculations; insomuch that a stranger correspondent would think himself indebted several millions for a commodity that cost but a few pounds. In the laws of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, we meet with several kinds of maravedis; Alphonsine maravedis, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> maravedis, maravedis of good <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, maravedis Combrenos, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> maravedis, and old maravedis. When we find maravedis alone, and without any addition, it is to be understood of those mentioned above. The rest are different in value, fineness of metal, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, &c. Mariana asserts, that this coin is older than the Moors; that it came from the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a>; that it was ancientsly equal to a third <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the rial, and consequently of 12 times the value of the present maravedi. Under Alphonsus XI. the maravedi was 17 times, under Henry II. ten times, under Henry III. five times, and under John II. two times and a half, the value of the present maravedi.

MARBELLA

Pages 630-630

a town of Grenada in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, situated at the mouth of the Rio Verde, 30 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of Gibraltar, and 28 south-west of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALAGA">Malaga</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4° 59'. N. Lat. 36° 31'.

MARBLE

Pages 630-632

a calcareous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, of which there are many beautiful varieties. The word comes from the French marbre, and from the Latin marmor, of the Greek μαρμάριον, to "shine <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> glitter." See <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERALOGY">MINERALOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">Elastic</a> Marble, an extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of fossil which has surprised all the naturalists who have seen it. There are several tables of it preserved in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Borghese at Rome, and shown to the curious. F. Jacquier, a celebrated mathematician, has given a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> in the Literary Gazette of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, but the naturalists cannot be contented with it. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> permission was given to make the requisite experiments, ments, this curious phenomenon might be better illustrated. There are five or six tables of that marble; their length is about two feet and a half, the breadth about ten inches, and the thickness a little less than three. They were dug up, as the Abbé Fortis was told, in the field of Mondragone; the grain is of Carrarese marble, or perhaps of the finest Greek. They seem to have suffered some attack of fire; though the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of pulverization observable in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>, can, perhaps, scarcely be called that of imperfect calcination. They are very dry, do not yield to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a>, resound to the hammer, like other conglomerate marble, and are perhaps susceptible of a polish. Being set on end, they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> oscillating backwards and forwards; when laid horizontally, and raised at one end, they form a curve, beginning towards the middle; if placed on a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, and a piece of wood or any thing else is laid under them, they make a salient curve, and touch the table with both ends. Notwithstanding this flexibility, they are liable to be broken if indiscreetly handled; and therefore one table only, and that not the best, is shown to the curious. Formerly they were altogether in the prince's apartment on the ground <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>. **Colouring of Marble.** This is a nice art; and in order to succeed in it, the pieces of marble on which the experiments are tried, must be well polished, and free from the least spot or vein. The harder the marble is, the better <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> it bear the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> necessary in the operation; therefore alabaster and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> soft <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> marble are very improper for performing these operations upon. Heat is always necessary for opening the pores of marble, so as to render it fit to receive the colours; but the marble must never be made <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> hot; for then the texture of it is injured, and the colours are burnt, and lose their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. Too small a degree of heat is as bad as one too <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>; for, in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, though the marble receives the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, it will not be fixed in it, nor strike deep enough. Some colours will strike even <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>; but they are never so well sunk in as when a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> degree of heat is used. The proper degree is that which, without making the marble red, will make the liquor boil upon its surface. The menstruums used to strike in the colours must be varied according to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the colour to be used. A lixivium made with horses or dogs urine, with four parts of quicklime and one of potashes, is excellent for some colours; common ley of wood-ashes is very good for others; for some, spirit of wine is best; and lastly, for others, oily liquors, or common white wine. The colours which have been found to succeed best with the peculiar menstruums, are these: Stone-blue dissolved in six times the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of spirit of wine, or of the urinary lixivium, and that colour which the painters call *<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LITMUS">litmus</a>*, dissolved in common ley of wood-ashes. An extract of saffron, and that colour made of buckthorn berries, and called by painters *sap-green*, both succeed well when dissolved in urine and quicklime; and tolerably well when dissolved in spirit of wine. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERMILION">Vermilion</a>, and a very fine powder of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COCHINEAL">cochineal</a>, also succeed very well in the same liquors. Dragon's blood succeeds in spirit of wine, as does also a tincture of logwood in the same spirit. Alkanet-root gives a fine colour; but the only menstruum to be used for it is <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of turpentine; for neither spirit of wine, nor any lixivium, will do with it. There is another kind of *sanguis draconis*, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called dragon's blood in tears, which, mixed with urine, gives a very elegant colour. Besides these mixtures of colours and menstruums, there are other colours which must be laid on dry and unmixed. These are, dragon's blood of the purest kind, for a red; gamboge, for a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>; green wax, for a green; common brimstone, pitch, and turpentine, for a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> colour. The marble for these experiments must be made considerably hot, and then the colours are to be rubbed on dry in the lump. Some of these colours, when once given, remain immutable, others are easily changed or destroyed. Thus, the red colour given by dragon's blood, or by a decoction of logwood, will be wholly taken away by oil of tartar, and the polish of the marble not hurt by it. A fine gold colour is given in the following manner: Take crude sal ammoniac, vitriol, and verdigris, of each equal quantities. White vitriol succeeds best; and all must be thoroughly mixed in fine powder. The staining of marble to all the degrees of red or yellow, by solutions of dragon's blood or gamboge, may be done by reducing these <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUMS">gums</a> to powder, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> them with the spirit of wine in a glass <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>. But, for smaller attempts, no method is so good as the mixing a little of either of those powders with spirit of wine in a silver spoon, and holding it over <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a>. By this means a fine tincture will be extracted; and with a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a> dipt in this, the finest traces may be made on the marble while <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a>; which, on the heating of it afterwards, either on sand, or in a baker's oven, will all sink very deep, and remain perfectly distinct on the stone. It is very easy to make the ground colour of the marble red or yellow by this means, and leave white veins in it. This is to be done by covering the places where the whiteness is to remain with some white paint, or even with two or three doubles only of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>; either of which will prevent the colour from penetrating. All the degrees of red are to be given to marble by this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUM">gum</a> alone; a slight tincture of it, without the assistance of heat to the marble, gives only a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> colour; but the stronger tinctures give it yet deeper; to this the assistance of heat adds greatly; and finally, the addition of a little pitch to the tincture, gives it a tendency to blackness, or any degree of deep red that may be desired. A blue colour may be given also to marble by dissolving turnsole in lixivium, in lime and urine, or in the volatile spirit of urine; but this has always a tendency to purple, whether made by the one or the other of these ways. A better blue, and used in an easier manner, is furnished by the Canary turnsole, a substance well known among the dyers. This needs only to be dissolved in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and drawn on the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> with a pencil: it penetrates very deeply into the marble, and the colour may be increased, by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> the pencil wetted afresh several times over the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>. This colour is subject to spread and diffuse itself irregularly; but it may be kept in regular bounds, by circumscribing its lines with beds of wax, or any such substance. It is also to be observed, that this colour should always be laid on cold, and no heat given even afterwards to the marble; and one great advantage of this colour is, that it is therefore easily added to marbles already stained with other colours, is a very beautiful tinge, and lasts a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>.

MARBLED

Pages 632-632

something veined <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> clouded, resembling marble. See MARBLING. MARBLED <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARE">ware</a>, a name given by many to a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORCELAIN">porcelain</a> or china-ware, which seems to be full of cemented flaws. It is called by the Chinese, who are very fond of it, tsou tehi. It is generally plain <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, sometimes blue, and has exactly the appearance of a piece of china which had been first broken, and then had all the pieces cemented in their places again, and covered with the original <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VARNISH">varnish</a>. The manner of preparing it is easy, and might be imitated with us. Instead of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> varnish of the china-ware, which is made of what they call <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> and oil of fern mixed together, they cover this with a simple thing made only of a sort of coarse agates, calcined to a white powder, and separated from the grosser parts by means of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, after <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> in mortars. When the powder has been thus prepared, it is left moist, or in form of a sort of cream, with the last water that is suffered to remain in it, and this is used as the varnish. Our crystal would serve as well as those coarse agates, and the method of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> is perfectly easy. The occasion of the singular appearance of this sort of porcelain is, that the varnish never spreads evenly, but runs into ridges and veins. These often run naturally into a sort of mosaic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, which can scarce be taken for the effect of chance. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the marbled china be desired blue, they first give it a general coat of this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIPPING">dipping</a> the vessel into a blue varnish; and when this is thoroughly dry, they add another coat of this <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGATE">agate</a> oil. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">Artificial</a> Marbles. The stucco, of which <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, busts, basso-relievos, and other ornaments of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> are made, ought to be marble pulverized, mixed in a certain proportion with <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a>; the whole well sifted, worked up with water, and used like common plaster. See STUCCO. There is also a kind of artificial marble made of the flaky selenites, or a transparent stone resembling plaster; which becomes very hard, receives a tolerable polish, and may deceive a good eye. This kind of selenite resembles Muscovy talc. There is also another sort of artificial marble formed by corrosive tinctures, which, penetrating into white marble to the depth of a line or more, imitate the various colours of other dearer marbles. There is also a preparation of brimstone in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of marble. To do this, you must provide yourself with a flat and smooth piece of marble; on this make a border or wall, to encompass either a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> or oval <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, which may be done either with wax or clay. Then having several sorts of colours, as white <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERMILION">vermilion</a>, lake, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORPIMENT">orpiment</a>, masticot, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SMALT">smalt</a>, Prussian blue, &c.; melt on a slow fire some brimstone in several glazed pipkins; put one particular sort of colour into each, and stir it well together; then having before oiled the marble all over within the wall, with one colour quickly drop spots upon it of larger and less size; after this, take another colour and do as before, and so on till the stone is covered with spots of all the colours you <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. When this is done, you are Marbling, next to consider what colour the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> or ground of your table is to be; if of a gray colour, then take fine sifted ashes, and mix it up with melted brimstone; or if <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, with English red ochre; if white, with white lead; if <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMP">lamp</a> or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a> black. Your brimstone for the ground must be pretty hot, that the colour dropped on the stone may unite and incorporate with it. When the ground is poured even all over, you are next, if judged necessary, to put a thin wainscoat board upon it; this must be done while the brimstone is hot, making also the board hot, which ought to be thoroughly dry, in order to cause the brimstone to stick the better to it. When the whole is <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, take it up, and polish it with a cloth and oil, and it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> look very beautiful. Arundelian Marbles, marbles, with a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRONICLE">chronicle</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> on them (as was supposed) many years before our Saviour's birth; presented to the university of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> by Thomas <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARUNDEL">Arundel</a>, whence the name. See ARUNDELIAN Marbles. Playing Marbles, are mostly imported from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>; where it is said they are made by breaking the stone alabaster, or other substance, into pieces or chips, of a suitable size; these are put into an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> mill which turns by water: there are several partitions with rasps within, cut float-wise, not with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, which turn constantly round with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> swiftness; the friction against the rasps makes them round, and as they are formed, they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> out of different holes, into which size or chance throws them. They are brought from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUREMBERG">Nuremberg</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROTTERDAM">Rotterdam</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, and from thence dispersed over <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>.

MARBLING

Pages 632-633

the method of preparing and colouring the marbled <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>. There are several kinds of marbled paper; but the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of them lies in the forms in which the colours are laid on the ground: some being disposed in whirls <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> circumvolutions; some in jagged lengths; and others only in spots of a roundish or oval <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. The general manner of managing each kind is, nevertheless, the same; being the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIPPING">dipping</a> the paper, in a solution of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUM">gum</a>-tragacanth, or, as it is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called, gum-dragon; over which the colours, previously prepared with ox-<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GALL">gall</a> and spirit of wine, are first spread. The peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> necessary for this purpose, is a trough for containing the gum-tragacanth and the colours; a comb for disposing them in the figure usually chosen; and a burnishing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> for polishing the paper. The trough may be of any kind of wood; and must be somewhat larger than the sheets of paper, for marbling which it is to be employed; but the sides of it need only rise about two inches above the bottom; for by making it thus shallow, the less <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of the solution of the gum <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> serve to fill it. The comb may be also of wood, and five inches in length; but should have <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, which may be about two inches <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and placed at about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of an inch distance from each other. The burnishing stone may be of jasper or <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGATE">agate</a>; but as those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> are very dear when of sufficient largeness, marble or glass may be used, provided their surface be polished to a greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of smoothness. These implements being prepared, the solution of gum-tragacanth must be made, by putting a sufficient proportion of the gum, which should be <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> and clear from all foulness, into clean <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and letting it remain there a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> or two, frequently breaking the lumps, and stirring it till the whole shall appear dissolved and equally mixed with the water. The consistence of the solution should be nearly that of strong gum-water used in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINIATURE">miniature</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it appear thicker, water must be added; or if thinner, more of the gum. When the solution is thus brought to a due state, it must be passed through a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> cloth; and being then put into the trough, it will be ready to receive the colours. The colours employed for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> are carmine, lake, rose-pink, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERMILION">vermilion</a>; but the two last are too hard and glaring, unless they be mixed with rose-pink or lake, to bring them to a softer <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a>; and with respect to the carmine and lake, they are too dear for <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> purposes. For <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, Dutch pink and yellow ochre may be employed:—for blue, Prussian blue and verditer may be used:—for green, verdigris, a mixture of Dutch pink and Prussian blue or verditer, in different proportions:—for <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a>, the orange lake, or a mixture of vermilion, or red <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, with Dutch pink:—for purple, rose pink and Prussian blue. These several colours should be ground with spirit of wine till they be of a proper fineness; and then, at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of using them, a little fish-gall, or in default of it the gall of a beast, should be added, by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> them over again with it. The proper proportion of the gall must be found by trying them: for there must be <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> so much as will suffer the spots of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, when sprinkled on the solution of the gum-tragacanth, to join together, without intermixing or running into each other. When every thing is thus prepared, the solution of the gum-tragacanth must be poured into the trough; and the colours, being in a separate pot, with a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a> appropriated to each, must be sprinkled on the surface of the solution, by shaking the pencil, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with its proper colour, over it; and this must be done with the several kinds of colour desired, till the surface be wholly covered. When the marbling is proposed to be in spots of a simple form, nothing more is necessary; but where the whirls or snail-shell figures are wanted, they must be made by means of a quill; which must be put among the spots to turn them about, till the effect be produced. The jagged lengths must be made by means of the comb above described, which must be passed through the colours from one end of the trough to the other; and will give them that appearance: but if they be desired to be pointed both ways, the comb must be again passed through the trough in a contrary <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>; or if some of the whirls or snail-shell figures be required to be added, they may be yet made by the means before directed. The paper should be previously prepared for receiving the colours, by dipping it over-night in water; and laying the sheets on each other with a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> over them. The whole being thus ready, the paper must be held by two corners, and laid in the most gentle and even manner on the solution covered with the colours; and there softly pressed with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, Marbling that it may bear everywhere on the solution. After which it must be raised and taken off with the same care, and then hung to dry across a proper <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a>, suspended near at hand for that purpose; and in that state it must continue till it be perfectly dry. It then remains only to give the paper a proper polish: in order to which, it is first rubbed with a little <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>; and then must be thoroughly smoothed by the glass polishers, such as are used for linen, and called the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALENDAR">calendar</a>-glasses. After which it should be again rubbed by a burnisher of jasper or agate; or, in default of them, of glass ground to the highest polish; for on the perfect polish of the paper depends in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and value. <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">Gold</a> or silver powders may be used, where desired, along with the colour; and require only the same treatment as them, except that they must be first tempered with gum-water. Marbling of books or paper is performed thus: Dissolve four ounces of gum arabic into two quarts of fair water; then provide several colours mixed with water in pots or shells; and, with pencils peculiar to each colour, sprinkle them by way of intermixture upon the gum-water, which must be put into a trough or some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> vessel; then with a stick curl them, or draw them out in streaks, to as much variety as may be done. Having done this, hold your book or books <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> together, and only dip the edges in, on the top of the water and colours, very lightly; which done, take them off, and the plain <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> of the colours in mixture will be upon the leaves; doing as well the ends as the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of the book in the like manner. Marbling a book on the covers is performed by forming <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> with aquafortis or spirit of vitriol mixed with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INK">ink</a>, and afterwards glazing the covers. See Book Binding. MARCAntonio. See Raimondi.

MARCASITE

Pages 633-633

an old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERALOGY">mineralogy</a>, given indifferently to ores, pyrites, and to semimetals. But more lately confined to pyrites, and to such pyrites as are regularly formed. See Pyrites, Mineralogy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MARCELLIANISM

Pages 633-633

the doctrines and opinions of the Marcellians, a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> heresies, towards the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> century, so called from Marcellus of Ancyra, their leader, who was accused of reviving the errors of Sabellius. Some, however, are of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that Marcellus was orthodox, and that they were his enemies the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARIANS">Arians</a>, who fathered their errors upon him. St Epiphanius observes, that there was a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of dispute with regard to the real tenets of Marcellus; but that, as to his followers, it is evident they did not own the three hypostases: for Marcellus considered the Son and Holy Ghost as two emanations from the divine <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, which, after performing their respective offices, were to return again into the substance of the Father; and this opinion is altogether incompatible with the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> of three distinct persons in the Godhead.

MARCELLUS

Pages 633-634

Marcus Claudius, a famous Roman general, who, after the first Punic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, had the management of an expedition against the Gauls. Here he Marcellus he obtained the *spolia opima*, by killing with his own <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> Viridomarus the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of the enemy. Such success rendered him popular, and soon after he was intrusted to oppose <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HANNIBAL">Hannibal</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. He was the first Roman who obtained some advantage over this celebrated Carthaginian, and showed his countrymen that Hannibal was not invincible. The troubles which were raised in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a> by the Carthaginians at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Hieronnius, alarmed the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; and Marcellus, in his third consulship, was sent with a powerful force against <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRACUSE">Syracuse</a>. He attacked it by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>; but his operations proved <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> ineffectual, and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> and industry of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHIMEDES">Archimedes</a> were able to baffle all the efforts, and to destroy all the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> and stupendous <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> engines of the Romans, during three successive years. The perseverance of Marcellus at last obtained the victory. After this conquest, Marcellus was called upon by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to oppose Hannibal. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a> he behaved with greater vigour than before; the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of the Samnites, which had revolted, were recovered by force of arms, and 3000 of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> of Hannibal made prisoners. Some time after, in an engagement with the Carthaginian general, Marcellus had the disadvantage: but on the morrow a more successful skirmish vindicated his military character and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the Roman soldiers. Marcellus, however, was not sufficiently vigilant against the snares of his adversary. He imprudently separated himself from his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>, and was killed in an ambuscade in the 65th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, in his 5th consulship, A.U.C. 544. His body was honoured by the conqueror with a magnificent funeral, and his ashes were conveyed in a silver urn to his son.
