Marcellus claims our commendation for his private as well as public virtues; and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> of a general <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> ever be remembered, who, at the surrender of Syracusene, wept on the thought that many were going to be exposed to the avarice and rapaciousness of an incessed soldiery, which the policy of Rome and the laws of war rendered inevitable.

MARCGRAVE

Pages 634-634
or **MARGRAVE**, a kind of dignity in Germany, answering to our marquis; (see Marquis). The word is derived from the German Marche, or Marcke, which signifies "a frontier;" and Graff, "count, governor;" Margraves being originally governors of cities lying on the frontiers of a country or state.

MARCH

Pages 634-635

(*Martius*), the third <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of the year, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> way of computing. See Month and Year. Among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, March was the first month; and in some <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> computations, that order is still preserved; as particularly reckoning the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of years from the incarnation of our Saviour; that is, from the 25th of March. It was <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a> who divided the year into months; to the first of which he gave the name of his supposed father <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>. Ovid, however, observes, that the people of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> had the month of March before Romulus's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; but that they placed it very differently, some making it the third, some the fourth, some the fifth, and others the tenth month of the year. In this month it was that the Romans sacrificed to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNA">Anna</a> Perenna; that they began their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMITIA">comitia</a>; that they adjudged the public farms and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEASES">leases</a>; that the March mistresses served the slaves and servants at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, as the masters did in the Saturnalia; and that the vestals renewed the sacred fire. The month of March was always under the protection of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>, and always consisted of 31 days.—The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> held it an unhappy month for <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, as well as the month of May. March, in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> art, is the moving of a body of men from one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to another. Nothing is laid <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> particularly concerning the marches of the Jewish armies; only this much we may collect, that they made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of trumpets, to the different sounds of which they prepared themselves by packing up their baggage, putting themselves in readiness, and attending at the standards, to wait the signal for marching. We are told that the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of the Israelites marched in general no more than one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> and a half; but this appears to hold good only of their progress through difficult <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>: For Folkard says they might, in an open <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, march four leagues in a day <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> more. The Rabbins suppose that the Israelites marched in the same order they were placed in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>. The Greeks, let the posture of their affairs be what it would, never marched against their enemies till favourable omens encouraged the enterprise. An eclipse of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, or any untoward accident, or the intervening of what they esteemed an unlucky day, entirely prevented their march. But of all the Greeks the Lacedæmonians were the most nice and scrupulous. The heavenly bodies directed all their motions; and it was an invariable maxim with them never to march before the full moon. The Greeks are particularly remarked by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> for marching in good order and profound silence; whereas the Barbarian forces were all noise, clamour, and confusion. It is needless to say any thing concerning the marches of the Roman armies, more than that they were performed with the greatest order and despatch, insomuch that their unexpected presence frequently damped the spirits of their enemies. The Roman <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> were inured to the military pace, that is, to walk 20 miles in five hours, though at the same time they carried burdens of 60 pounds <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. Of all the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> parts of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times, none is more essential than that of marching. It may be justly called the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEY">key</a> which leads to all sublime motions and manoeuvres of an army; for they depend entirely on this point. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> can be attacked in four different ways; in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a>, on both flanks, and in the rear: but he can defend himself, and annoy the enemy, only when placed with his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> towards him. Hence it follows, that the general object of marching is reduced to three <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> only; to march forwards, and on both sides, because it is impossible to do it for any time backwards, and by that means face the enemy wherever he presents himself.—The different steps to be made use of are three: slow, fast, and oblique. The first is proper in advancing, when at a considerable distance from the enemy, and when the ground is unequal, that the line may not be broke, and a regular fire kept up without intermission. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> is chiefly necessary when you want to anticipate the enemy in occupying some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>, in passing a defile, and, above all, in attacking an intrenchment, to avoid being a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> while exposed to the fire of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a> and small arms, &c. The third step is of infinite <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, both in the infantry and cavalry; columns may be opened and formed into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, and vice versa, lines into columns, by this kind of step, in a lesser space, and consequently in less time, than by any other method whatsoever. In coming out of a defile, you may instantly form the line without presenting the flank to the enemy. The line may be formed, though ever so near to the enemy, with safety; because you face him, and can with ease and safety protect and cover the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the troops, while they are coming out of the defiles, and forming. The same thing may be equally executed, when a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> is to be formed in order to advance or retreat; which is a point of infinite consequence, and should be established as an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AXIOM">axiom</a>. The order of march of the troops must be so disposed, that each should arrive at their rendezvous, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> possible, on the same day. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>-general or his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a>, with an able engineer, should sufficiently reconnoitre the country, to obtain a perfect knowledge of it and the enemy, before he forms his routes. Before a march, the army generally receives several days <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>. The quarter-masters, camp-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>-men, and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIONEERS">pioneers</a>, parade according to orders, and march immediately after, commanded by the quarter-master-general or his deputy. They are to clear the roads, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> the ways, make <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> for the march of the army, &c. The general, for instance, beats at two, the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> at three, and the army to march in 20 minutes after. Upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> the general, the village, and general officer's guards, quarter and rear guards, join their respective corps; and the army pack up their baggage. Upon beating the assembly, the tents are to be struck, and sent with the baggage to the place appointed, &c. The companies draw up in their several streets, and the rolls are called. At the time appointed, the drummers are to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> a march, and fifers play at the head of the line, upon which the companies march out from their several streets, form battalions, as they advance to the head of the line, and then halt. The several battalions <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be formed into columns by the adjutant-general, and the order of march, &c., be given to the general officers who <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> the columns. The cavalry generally march by regiments or squadrons. The heavy artillery always keeps the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> roads in the centre of the columns, escorted by a strong party of infantry and cavalry. The field pieces march with the columns. Each soldier generally marches with 36 <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROUNDS">rounds</a> of powder and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a>, and two good flints; one of which is to be fixed in the cock of his firelock. The routes must be formed so that no columns <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> one another on the march.

MARCHAND

Pages 635-635

Professor, was from his youth brought up at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in the profession of a bookseller, and in the knowledge of books. He kept a regular correspondence with several learned men, among whom was Bernard the continuator of the Nouvelles de la République des Lettres, and furnished this writer with the literary anecdotes of France. Marchand, having embraced the Protestant <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, went to join Bernard in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, where he might be at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to profess Marchand his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> opinions. He <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> the trade of bookseller for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; but afterwards quitted it, Marches. He might dedicate himself wholly to the pursuits of literature. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of France, together with a knowledge of books and authors, was always his favourite <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>. In the latter he was so eminently distinguished, that he was consulted from all parts of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. He was also one of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> authors of the Journal Litteraire, one of the best periodical works which have appeared in Holland; and he furnished excellent extracts for the other journals. This valuable and learned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> died at an advanced <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, the 14th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1756; and left the little fortune which he had to a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> instituted at the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAGUE">Hague</a>, for the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> and instruction of a certain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> people. His library, which was excellently chosen for literary history, together with his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a>, was left by his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> to the university of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>. From him we have, 1. The History of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTING">Printing</a>, a new edition of which has been promised by one of his friends. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, which is full of notes and critical discussions, appeared in 1740 at the Hague, in 4to. There is such a prodigious display of erudition, and remarks and quotations are heaped together in such confusion, that when you get to the end of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAOS">chaos</a>, you know not what conclusion to form concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> which have been discussed. Abbé Mercier, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> of Saint Leger de <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOISSONS">Soissons</a>, gave in 1775, 4to, a supplement to this history, which is equally curious and accurate. 2. An Historical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> Critical and Literary, printed at the Hague in 1758, in two small volumes, folio. In this work we meet with historical singularities, literary anecdotes, and a discussion of points of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BIBLIOGRAPHY">bibliography</a>; but too <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> minuteness prevails in it, the style is deficient in point of purity, and the author is too much carried away by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> and eagerness of his character. More erudition could not well be collected; especially upon subjects which, at least to the generality of readers, are so uninteresting. 3. A new edition of Bayle's Dictionary, and Letters of the Cynbalum mundi, &c.

MARCHANTIA

Pages 635-635

a genus of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> order of algae, belonging to the cryptogamia class of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MARCHE

Pages 635-635

before the revolution, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of France, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Berry, on the east by Auvergne, on the west by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGOUMOIS">Angoumois</a>, and on the south by Limosin; about 55 miles in length, and 25 in breadth, and fertile in corn and wine.

MARCHENA

Pages 635-635

a handsome, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, and considerable town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANDALUSIA">Andalusia</a>, with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a>, and a suburb as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> as the town, seated in the middle of a plain, particularly fertile in olives, though very destitute of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5. 20. N. Lat. 37. 20.

MARCHERS

Pages 635-635
or Lords-Marchers, were those noblemen that lived on the marches of Wales or Scotland; who, in times past, according to Camden, had their laws, and potestatem vitae, &c. like petty kings, which are abolished by the stat. 27 Hen. VIII. c. 26. and 1 Edw. VI. c. 10. In old records the lords marchers of Wales were styled Marchianae de Marchia Walliae. See 1 et 2 P. et M. c. 15.

MARCHES

Pages 635-636

from the German <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a>, i.e. Marches i.e. limes, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> from the French marque, viz. signum (being the notorious distinction between two countries or territories), are the limits between England and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, or between England and Scotland, which last are divided into west and middle marches, 4 Hen. V. c. 7. 22 Ed. IV. c. 8. 24 Hen. VIII. c. 9. And there was formerly a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> called the court of the marches of Wales, where pleas of debt or damages, not above the value of 50 pounds, were tried and determined; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of the marches held <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLEA">plea</a> for debts above that sum, &c. a prohibition might be awarded. Hill. 14 Car. I. Cro. Car. 38.

MARCHET

Pages 636-636
or MARCHETTA, a pecuniary fine anciently paid by the tenant to his lord, for the marriage of one of the tenant's daughters. This custom obtained, with some difference, throughout all England and Wales, as also in Scotland; and it still continues to obtain in some places. According to the custom of the manor of Drovver in Caermarthenshire, every tenant at the marriage of his daughter pays ten shillings to the lord; which, in the British language, is called gwabr-merched, i.e. maid's fee. In Scotland, and the north parts of England, the custom was, for the lord to lie the first night with the bride of his tenant; but this usage was abrogated by King Malcolm III. at the instance of his queen; and, instead thereof, a mark was paid by the bridegroom to the lord: whence it was called merchetta mulieris. See BOROUGH English.

MARCIANA SILVA

Pages 636-636

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a forest situated between the Rauraci and the Danube, before it comes to be navigable; a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Hercynia. Now Schwartzwald, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-BLACK_FOREST"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> Forest, in the south-west of Swabia, near the rise of the Danube and Neckar.

MARCIANITES

Pages 636-636
or MARCIONISTS, Marcionista, a very ancient and popular sect of heretics, who, in the time of St Epiphanius, were spread over Italy, Egypt, Palestine, Syria, Arabia, Persia, and other countries; they were thus denominated from their author Marcion. Marcion was of Pontus, the son of a bishop, and at first made profession of the monastical life; but he was excommunicated by his own father, who would never admit him again into the communion of the church, not even on his repentance. On this he abandoned his own country, and retired to Rome, where he began to broach his doctrines. He laid down two principles, the one good, the other evil: between these he imagined an intermediate kind of deity of a mixed nature, who was the creator of this inferior world, and the god and legislator of the Jewish nation: the other nations, who worshipped a variety of gods, were supposed to be under the empire of the evil principle. These two conflicting powers exercise oppressions upon rational and immortal souls; and therefore the supreme God, to deliver them from bondage, sent to the Jews a being more like unto himself, even his son Jesus Christ, clothed with a certain shadowy resemblance of a body; this celestial messenger was attacked by the prince of darkness, and by the god of the Jews, but without effect. Those who follow the directions of this celestial conductor, mortify the body by fastings and austerities, and renounce the precepts of the god of the Jews and of the prince of darkness, shall after death ascend to the mansions of felicity and perfection. The rule of manners which Marcion prescribed to his followers was excessively austere, containing an express prohibition of wedlock, wine, flesh, and all the external comforts of life. Marcion denied the real birth, incarnation, and passion of Jesus Christ, and held them to be all apparent only. He denied the resurrection of the body; and allowed none to be baptized but those who preserved their continence; but these, he granted, might be baptized three times. In many things he followed the sentiments of the heretic Cerdon, and rejected the law and the prophets. He pretended the gospel had been corrupted by false prophets, and allowed none of the evangelists but St Luke, whom also he altered in many places, as well as the epistles of St Paul, a great many things in which he threw out. In his own copy of St Luke he threw out the two first chapters entire.

MARCIANUS

Pages 636-636

a native of Thrace, born of an obscure family. After he had for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> served in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> as a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> soldier, he was made private secretary to one of the officers of Theodosius. His winning <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> and uncommon talents raised him to higher stations; and on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Theodosius II. A.D. 450, he was invested with the imperial purple in the east. The subjects of the Roman empire had reason to be satisfied with their choice. Marcianus showed himself <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> and resolute; and when <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTILA">Attila</a>, the barbarous <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of the Huns, asked of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> the annual tribute, which the indolence and cowardice of his predecessors had regularly paid, the successor of Theodosius firmly said, that he kept his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> for his friends, but that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> was the metal which he had prepared for his enemies. In the midst of universal popularity, Marcianus died, after a reign of six years, in the 69th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, as he was making warlike preparations against the barbarians that had invaded <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. His death was <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> lamented; and indeed his merit was <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, since his reign has been distinguished by the appellation of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">Golden</a> Age. Marcianus married Pulcheria the sister of his predecessor. It is said, that in the years of his obscurity he found a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who had been murdered, and that he had the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> to give him a private <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a>; for which circumstance he was accused of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMICIDE">homicide</a>, and imprisoned. He was condemned to lose his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> would have been executed, had not the real murderer been discovered, and convinced the world of the innocence of Marcianus.—Another emperor of the Marcian east, A.D. 479, &c.

MARCITES

Pages 636-636

MARCITAE, a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of heretics in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> century, who also called themselves the perfecti, and made profession of doing every thing with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> and without any fear. This doctrine they borrowed from Simon Magus, who however was not their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>; for they were called Marcites from one Marcus, who conferred the priesthood, and the administration of the sacraments, on women.

MARCOMANNI

Pages 636-637

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> people of Germany, who seem to have taken their name from their situation on the limits <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> marches, to the east of the Higher <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of the Danube. Cluverius allots to them the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Wurtemburg, a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALATINATE">palatinate</a> between the Rhine and the Necker, the Brisgau, and a part of Swabia, lying between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> of the Danube and the river Bregenz; they afterwards removed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of the Boii, whom they expelled and forced to withdraw more to the east, occupying what is now called <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>. (Strabo, Vel- leius).

MARCOSONS

Pages 637-637
or COLOBARSIANS, an ancient sect in the church, making a branch of the VALENTINIANs. St Irenaeus speaks at large of the leader of this sect, Marcus, who it seems was reputed a great magician. The Marcosians had many apocryphal books which they held for canonical, and out of which they picked several idle fables touching the infancy of Jesus Christ. Many of these fables are still in use and credit among the Greek monks.

MARCUS

Pages 637-637

among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, a knocker <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> to knock at doors with. MARCUS AURELIUS ANTONINUS. See Antoninus.

MARDIKERS

Pages 637-637
or TOFASSES, a mixed breed of Dutch, Portuguese, Indians, and other nations, incorporated with the Dutch at Batavia, in the East Indies.

MARENGO

Pages 637-637

a village of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> which has risen to distinction in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of a bloody <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> between the Austrians and French, which was fought on the 14th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1800, in which the French say, 15,000 of the former were killed, wounded, and made prisoners.—Marengo lies 3 miles S.E. of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALESSANDRIA">Alessandria</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a>.

MAREOTIS

Pages 637-637

a lake in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> near <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>. Its neighbourhood was famous for wine; though according to some the Mareoticum vinum is the produce of Epirus, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of a certain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBYA">Libya</a>, called also Mareotis, near Egypt.

MARETS

Pages 637-637

Samuel de, one of the most celebrated divines of the reformed <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, was born in Picardy, in 1599. In 1620, he was settled in the church of Marets, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAON">Laon</a>; but, in 1624, accepted a call to that of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEDAN">Sedan</a>, Margaret, to succeed James Cappel in the office of pastor and professor of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>. Having soon after obtained leave of absence from his flock, he visited <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, where he was admitted to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of divinity at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, in 1625. From Holland he took a voyage to England, and after a short stay in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> he returned to Sedan, where he commenced his labours in the divinity <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>. These he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> for about <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years with reputation to himself, but not without being sometimes involved in troubles, which he bore with a commendable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>. In 1631 he was made chaplain to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> de Bouillon in Holland; but that nobleman having married a Roman Catholic lady, M. de Marets, advised him to adhere steadily to the Protestant <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, on which account he incurred the displeasure of the duchess. Thus circumstanced, he received in 1636, an invitation to become pastor to the church of Boisleu, with which he complied, and in the following year he was appointed professor of the schola illustris of the same <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. The duties of this office he discharged with such diligence and success, that in 1640, the curators of the university of Franeker sent him the offer of a professorship, which he declined; but two years after he accepted a similar offer from the university of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRONINGEN">Groningen</a>, to which his services were devoted for upwards of thirty years. In 1652 he was made sole minister of the Walloon church at Groningen, where till that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he had gratuitously preached once every <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a> to assist the pastor. Influenced by the fame of his extraordinary merits, the magistrates of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BERNE">Berne</a> in 1661 offered him the chair of professor of divinity at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAUSANNE">Lausanne</a>, with considerable emoluments, but he declined this offer; and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> happened before he took possession of a similar <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> at Leyden, of which he had accepted. His System of Divinity was found to be so methodical, that it was made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of at other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">academies</a>; and at the end of it may be found a chronological <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> of all his works. Their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> is prodigious; and their variety shows the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of his genius. He was moreover engaged in many disputes and controversies, and died in 1673.

MARFURG

Pages 650-650

a town of Germany, in Lower Styria, seated on the river Drave, 25 miles south-west of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRATZ">Gratz</a>, and 60 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of Laubach. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 16° 10'. N. Lat. 46° 42'.

MARGARET

Pages 637-639

St., a celebrated virgin, who, as is supposed, received the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of martyrdom at Antioch in the year 275: the manner of her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> is not known. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> martyrologists make no mention of her name, and she did not become famous till the 11th century. There is no more foundation for what is said concerning her relics and girdles than for the stories which are told of her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. A festival, however, is still held in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> on the 20th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>: See Baillet's Lives of the Saints, for that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. "Her actions (says this authority) have been so falsified and altered, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> even of Metaphrastus, that the Romish <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> have not thought proper to insert any of them into their breviary." The Orientals pay reverence to her by the name of Saint Pelagia <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Saint Marina, and the western church by that of Saint Geruma or Saint Margaret. Margaret, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> and heiress of Florent <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, who is famous on account of a story repeated by a hundred compilers even of the 18th century. Having refused <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> to a woman whom she at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> accused of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADULTERY">adultery</a>, she was, as Margaret, Countess of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHMOND">Richmond</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DERBY">Derby</a>, the learned and pious mother of Henry VII., was born at Betshe in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEDFORDSHIRE">Bedfordshire</a>, in 1441; and was the sole heiress of John <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAUFORT">Beaufort</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Somerset, grandson to John of Gaunt. Her mother was the heiress of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Beauchamp of Powick. Whilst yet very young, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> duke of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>, minister to Henry VI., or rather to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> Margaret, sought her in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> to his son; and she was at the same time solicited by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> for his half <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Edmund <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Richmond. To the latter she gave her <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. Henry VII. was the sole fruit of this marriage, his father dying when he was but 15 weeks old. Her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> husband was Sir Henry <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STAFFORD">Stafford</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a>, second son to the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUCKINGHAM">Buckingham</a>; by whom she had no issue. Soon after his death, which happened in the year 1482, she sought consolation in a third husband, Thomas Lord Stanley, who, in the first year of her son's reign, was created earl of Derby. He died in the year 1504, without issue, being then <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTABLE">constable</a> of England. She survived her lord not quite five years, dying at Westminster in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1509, in the 60th year of her <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. She was buried in Henry VII.'s chapel; on the south side of which was erected to her memory an altar-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> marble, with her statue of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>. From her funeral sermon preached by her confessor Margaret Bishop Fisher, who says Ballard, knew the very secrets Margaret of her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, we learn, "that she possessed almost all things that were commendable in a woman, either in mind or body." She understood the French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> perfectly, and had some knowledge of the Latin. She was devout even to austerity, in humility romantic, profuse in the encouragement of learning, and singularly chaste; but this last virtue became conspicuous only towards the latter end of a third marriage. "In her last husband's days (says Baker), she obtained a licence of him to live chaste, whereupon she took upon her the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOW">vow</a> of celibacy." "A boon (says Mr Walpole), as seldom requested, I believe of a third husband, as it probably would be easily granted." Her life, from the turbulence of the times, and vicissitudes of her son's fortune, must necessarily have been subject to infinite disquiet, which however she is said to have supported with singular fortitude. She wrote, 1. The Mirroure of Golde for the sinful soul, translated from a French translation of a book called Speculum aureum peccatorum. Emprynated at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, in Flete-strete, at the signe of St George, by Richard Pynson, quarto, with cuts on <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VELLUM">vellum</a>. 2. Translation of the fourth book of Dr Gersen's Treatise of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">Imitation</a> and following the blessed Life of our most merciful Saviour Christ. Printed at the end of Dr William Atkinson's English translation of the three first books, 1504. 3. A <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to the king: in Howard's collection. 4. By her son's order and authority, she also made the orders for great estates of ladies and noble women, for their precedence, and wearing of barbes at funerals, over the chin and under the same. Margaret, the daughter of Woldemar III., king of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, styled the Semiramis of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a>; she succeeded her father in the throne of Denmark, her husband in that of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>; and the crown of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a> was given her as a recompense for delivering the Swedes from the tyranny of Albert their king. Thus possessed of the three kingdoms, she formed the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of a perpetual union, which she accomplished, pro tempore only, by the famous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> styled the union of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALMAR">Calmar</a>. She died in 1412, aged 59. Margaret of Anjou, daughter of René d'Anjou, king of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, and wife of Henry VI., king of England: an ambitious, enterprising, courageous woman. Intrepid in the field, she signalized herself by heading her troops in several battles against the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> she had not been the authoress of her husband's misfortunes, by putting to death the duke of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLOUCESTER">Gloucester</a> his uncle, her name would have been immortalized for the fortitude, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>, and policy, with which she supported the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of her husband and son, till the fatal defeat at Tewksbury; which put an end to all her enterprises, the king being taken prisoner, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Edward their only son basely murdered by Richard duke of York. Margaret was ransomed by her father, and died in Anjou in 1482. See ENGLAND, No 201—226. Margaret, Duchess of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a>. See CAVENDISH. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARGARITA">Margarita</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEARL">Pearl</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, an island of South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, the middle of which is situated in W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. Margarita Long. 64. 2. N. Lat. 11. 30. It was discovered by Columbus, and is about 35 leagues in compass. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is very fertile in maize and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, and abounds in pasture and verdant groves; yet is totally destitute of fresh <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, which the inhabitants are obliged to bring from the continent. When the Spaniards first landed here, they found the natives busy in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> for oysters. Columbus ordered some of the savages aboard his ship, who were so far from being terrified, that they very soon became familiar with the Spaniards. The latter at first imagined that the oysters served them for food; but on opening the shells, they found they contained valuable pearls. Upon this discovery they immediately landed, and found the natives ready to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> with their pearls for the merest trifles. In <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of time the Spaniards built a castle, called Monpadre, and employed prodigious numbers of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGOLA">Angola</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a> in the pearl fishery; cruelly forcing them to tear up the oysters from the rocks to which they stuck, during which time many of them were destroyed by the sharks and other voracious fishes. The present <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> is about 14,000; of whom 5,500 are whites, 2,000 Indians, and 6,500 slaves and free persons of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. It has for some time been in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the party who are endeavouring to overturn the Spanish authority in Caracas. Margarita, the Pearl, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>. See Pearl and Mya.

MARGARITINI

Pages 639-639

are glass ornaments, made at <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, of small glass tubes of different colours, which are blown at Murano, and which the women of the lower class wear about their arms and necks. The largest sort are used for making rosaries. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> is performed with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> dispatch, the artisan taking a whole handful of these tubes at once, and breaking them off one after another with an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> tool. These short cylinders are mixed with a kind of ashes, and put over the fire in an iron <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAN">pan</a>; and when the two ends begin to melt, by stirring them about with an iron wire, they are brought to a round <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>; but care is taken not to leave them too <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> over the fire, lest the hole through which they are to be strung should be entirely closed by the melting of the glass. There are several streets at Francesco de Vigna entirely inhabited by people whose sole occupation is to make and string these margaritini.

MARGATE

Pages 639-639

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Thanet, near the North Foreland. It is noted for shipping vast quantities of corn (most, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not all, the product of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>) for <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; and has a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> bath at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, which has performed <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> cures in nervous and paralytic <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, and numbness of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a>. It lies in St John's <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>, which is a member of the port of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOVER">Dover</a>, at the distance of 14 miles, 12 from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, and 72 from London. It has become one of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> watering places for the idle, the opulent, and the invalid, where they meet with every requisite accommodation; and the adjacent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> abounds with most extensive prospects and pleasant rides. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> in 1811 was 6,126. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 30. N. Lat. 51. 24.

MARHATTAS

Pages 639-641

Merhattahs, Marattas, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Marhattas; a people of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, and by far the most considerable of all the Hindoo powers. The Marhattas boast a very <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> antiquity; they profess the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of Brama; speak a dialect of the Sanscrit <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, in which they have introduced all the technical terms of Mogul administration; <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> a character of their own in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, though not very different from some of the other tribes around them; and are divided into four casts or classes of people, with the various subdivisions of professional distinction found over the rest of Hindostan; but with this remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, that among the Marhattas every individual may, as in fact he occasionally does, follow the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of a soldier. As a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> inhabiting immemorially the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> properly denominated Marhat or Merhat, and comprehending the greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Paishwa's present dominions in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DECCAN">Deccan</a>, they were completely subjugated, and afterwards for many centuries depressed, first by the Patans, then by the Mogul conquerors of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DELHI">Delhi</a>. At length, towards the end of Alemgeer's reign, they united, rebelled, and under the famous Seewajee or Seeva-jee, a leader of their own tribe, laid the foundations of their present vast empire, which has risen gradually on the ruins of the Mohamedan power, as related under the article HINDOSTAN. Seeva-jee was succeeded by his son Rajah Sahou, who considerably extended the Marhatta dominions. When Rajah Sahou grew old and infirm, and the fatigues of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> began to press heavy upon him, he appointed Bisoonat Balajee, a Brahman born at Gokum, and leader of about 25,000 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, to the office of Paishwa or vicegerent. Rajah Sahou died without issue, but left nephews by his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>. The courage and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> of Balajee had gained him, during the latter years of the old rajah, the affection and esteem of all the nation. But, under an appearance of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> and self-denial, his prevailing <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> was ambition; and the sentiments of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> and loyalty were absorbed in the desire to command. He made use of the influence he had acquired under his benefactor so firmly to establish his own power, that he not only retained the high office of Paishwa during his life, but transmitted it to his posterity. The Marhattas, gradually forgetting a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> they knew nothing of, became accustomed to obey his vicegerent only: yet a certain respect for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>, or the dread of the consequences of violating the strong <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> which the nation still retains in favour of the family of its founder, have served perhaps to preserve it; and the descendants of Rajah Sahou's nephews yet exist, but are kept in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> at Sattarah. The eldest is styled Ram Rajah, or sovereign; his name is on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a> of the Marhatta state; but his person is unknown, except to those who immediately surround him. He resides in his splendid prison, encompassed with the appendages of eastern <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>, but debarred of all power, and kept totally ignorant of business. The seat of government was transferred from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> royal residence of Sattarah to Poonah; and the usurper, as well as his successors, seem still to have acted under the supposed authority of the deposed prince, by their assuming no other <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> or character than that of Paishwa or prime minister. From this change, the empire of the Ram Rajah has been distinguished only Marhattas by the appellation of the Paishwaship, or otherwise the Government of Poonah, from the name of its present <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>. Bissonat Balajee was succeeded as Paishwa by his eldest son Balajee Row (called also Nana Sahcb, or Na- nah Row), who left three sons, the eldest of whom, Ba- lajee Pundit, sometimes called Nanah Pundit, succeed- ed him. The two others were Rogobah or Ragonat Row, and Shamsheer Row. Balajee Pundit left two sons; Mahadava Row, who was Paishwa twelve years; and Narrain Row, who suc- ceeded him. During the latter part of the life of Mahadava Row, his uncle Rogobah was confined to the palace at Poo- nah, for reasons with which we are not acquainted. Mahadava Row died without issue; and upon the ac- cession of Narrain his brother, a youth of about 19 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, Rogobah in vain applied to be released from his confinement. He is therefore suspected of having entered into a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> with two officers in his nephew's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, Somair Jing and Yusuph Gardie, in order to procure that by force which he could not obtain by entreaty. The correspondence between the conspirators was carried on with so much secrecy, that the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> had not the least intimation or suspicion of their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, till every avenue leading to the palace had been secured, and the whole <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> surrounded by the troops under the command of those two offi- cers. It is said, that on the first alarm, Narrain Row, suspecting his uncle, ran to his apartment, threw him- self at his feet, and implored his protection: "You are my uncle (said he), spare the blood of your own family, and take possession of a government which I am willing to resign to you." Somair and Yusuph entered the room whilst the young Paishwa was in this suppliant posture. Rogo- bah, with apparent surprise and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGER">anger</a>, ordered them to withdraw; but as they either knew him not to be sincere, or thought they had proceeded too far to re- treat, they stabbed Narrain with their poniards whilst he clung to his uncle's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a>. The office of Paishwa being now vacant, the chiefs of the nation then at Poonah were assembled, and Ro- gobah being the only survivor of the family of Bisso- nat Balajee, to whose <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> the Marhattas in those parts are enthusiastically attached, he was named to fill it. Being naturally of a warlike temper, he re- solved to undertake some foreign expedition; for be- sides gratifying his passion for the field, he probably hoped, by the splendour of his exploits, to draw off the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of the public from inquiring into the late ca- tastrophe. A pretence for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> was not difficult to be found. He renewed the claim of his nation to the chout, and marched his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> towards Hydrabad, the capital of the Nizam. The vigour of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> procured him an accommodation of his demand; and he was proceed- ing to enforce a similar one upon the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARNATIC">Carnatic</a>, when he received intelligence which obliged him to return hastily to Poonah. Although the Marhatta chiefs had acknowledged Rogobah as Paishwa, yet they and the people in ge- neral were much dissatisfied with his conduct. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MURDERERS">murderers</a> of Narrain Row had not only escaped pu- nishment, but, as was reported, had been rewarded. The crime was unexampled, and the perpetrators were beheld with uncommon horror and detestation. The Paishwa had hitherto so fully possessed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of the people, that, till then, guards were considered as un- necessary about the person of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> whose character rendered him inviolable. Every one therefore had free access to his palace, and he relied with confidence for his safety upon the affections of those who approach- ed him. These reflections operated powerfully upon the minds of the Marhattas; but perhaps no violent consequences would have ensued, had it not been discovered, soon after the departure of Rogobah from Poonah, that the widow of Narrain Row, Ganga Bae, was pregnant. This determined their wavering resolutions. Frequent consultations were held among the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> men then in the capital; and it was finally resolved to abjure the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a> they had sworn to Rogobah, and declare the child, yet unborn, to be the legal successor of the late- paishwa. A <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of regency was immediately appointed to govern the country until the child should become of age; and it was agreed to reserve their deliberations, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> it should prove a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> or die, till the event should render them necessary. They who principally conducted these measures, and whose names <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> on that account be remembered, were Sackharam Babou and Balajee Pundit, called also Nanah Phcr Nevees from his having been <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> the principal secretary of the Marhatta state. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">Nine</a> other Marhatta leaders ap- proved of these measures, and swore to maintain them. As the first step towards the execution of their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, the widow of Narrain Row was conveyed to Poorend- her, a fort of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> strength, situated on a high moun- <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TAIN">tain</a>, about 25 miles from Poonah. As soon as Rogo- bah received intimation of this revolution, he <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a>- ed back towards the capital. But discontent had al- ready infected his troops; some of the chiefs retired to their estates, and others joined the standard of the regents. He however risked a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> with an army of the revolters commanded by Trimbee Row, in which the latter was slain; but though he obtained a vic- tory, the strength of the confederates daily increased, while his own troops were diminished by continual de- sertions. He therefore found it necessary to retire to Ugein, and to solicit the assistance of the Marhatta chiefs Scindia and Holkar; but meeting with a refu- sal, he went to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURAT">Surat</a>, and applied for succour to the English. Rogobah's success in this application was the cause of two wars with the Marhatta state; which, after much waste of blood and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>, we were obliged to conclude by relinquishing his claim, and acknowledg- ing as legal paishwa the son of Narrain Row, who was born about <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> months after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his father. See INDIA and HINDOSTAN. The Marhatta dominions, as already observed, are governed by a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of separate chiefs, all of whom acknowledge the Ram Rajah as their sovereign; and all except Moodajee Boonsalah, own the paishwa as his vicegerent. The country immediately subject to the paishwa, including all the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> territories that were left by the Rajah Sahou to the Ram Rajah, Marhattas, and those that have been acquired and added to them since in his name, extends along the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> nearly from Goa to Cambay; on the south it borders on the possessions of Tippoo Saib, eastward on those of the Nizam and of the Marhatta rajah of Berar, and towards the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> on those of the Marhatta chiefs Scindia and Holkar. Moodajee Boonsalah, rajah of Berar, possessed, besides Berar, the greatest part of Orixia. This prince being descended from the line of the Ram Rajah, eyes the power of the paishwa, by whom a branch of his family is kept in ignominious confinement, with ill will; has often refused to support his measures; and, on some occasions, has even seemed inclined to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> against him. Next to Moodajee, in point of importance, must be ranked Madajee Scindia, a bold and aspiring <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, who possesses the greatest part of the extensive soubadary or government of Malva, together with part of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Candeish. The remainder is under the dominion of Holkar. Both he and Scindia pretend to be descended from the ancient kings of Malva. Scindia resides chiefly at Ugein, near the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Mundu, once the capital of these kings; and Holkar at Indoor, a town little more than 30 miles west of it. The dominions of these, and of some chiefs of less <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, extend as far as the river Jamna. The measures pursued by the Marhattas for some years left little room to doubt that they aspired at the sovereignty of all Hindostan, or at least at the expulsion of the Mohamedan princes: And in this last design they appear to have succeeded*, and to have gained a great accession of territory, through the arms of Scindia, both by the capture of the cities of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRA">Agra</a> and Delhi, with their territorial dependencies, and the consequent captivity of the unfortunate monarch who ruled there as the last imperial representative of the great Mogul race of Timur. "The whole of the dominion thus newly established is of vast <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, stretching near 1200 miles along the frontiers of Tippoo and the Nizam in a north-east <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, from Goa on the Malabar coast to Balasore in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORISSA">Orissa</a> adjoining to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>; and from thence north-westerly 1000 miles more, touching the confines of the British and allied states, on the borders of the Ganges and Jamna, to the territory of the Seiks at Paniput, rendered famous in 1761 for the last memorable defeat sustained by the Marhattas in their ambitious contest for empire with the united declining power of the Mohamedans. From this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in a southerly course, with great encroachment on the old eastern boundary of the Rajepoot country of Ajmere, it runs about 260 miles to the little Hindoo principality of Kotta, and thence south-westery, 540 miles further to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> point of the soubah of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUJERAT">Gujerat</a> at Duarka, including the whole of that fertile province; from whence, along the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-coasts of Cambay and Malabar to Goa, the distance may be reckoned 800 miles. Thus the overgrown empire of the Marhattas may be said to extend east 19 degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>, near the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> of 22 degrees north latitude, from the mouths of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDUS">Indus</a> to those of the Ganges; and about 13 degrees of latitude north, from the Kistnah to Paniput; comprehending at least an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> of 400,000 <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> geographical miles, being considerably more than a third part of Hindostan, including the Decan, and equal perhaps Marhattas in dimensions to all the British and allied states in India, with those of Golconda and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSORE">Mysore</a>, taken together. Such was the state of affairs in India so far as the Marhattas were concerned a few years ago. By consulting the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of India, the reader will observe, that the power and dominion of these enterprising chiefs have been since greatly abridged by the successful progress of the British arms. See India.

MARIA

Pages 641-641

St, a handsome and considerable town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANDALUSIA">Andalusia</a>, with a small castle. It was taken by the English and Dutch in 1702, for the archduke of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>. It is seated on the Guadaleta, at the mouth of which is a tower and a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5. 33. N. Lat. 36. 35. MARIAN <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">ISLANDS</a>. See Ladrones Islands.

MARIANA

Pages 641-641

John, a learned Spanish historian, born at Talavera in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOLEDO">Toledo</a>. He entered among the Jesuits in 1554, at 17 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>; and became one of the most learned men of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> divine, a good humanist, and profoundly versed in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> as well as profane <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. He taught at Rome, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; and died at Toledo in 1624. His <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> works are, 1. An excellent history of Spain in 30 books: which he himself translated from the Latin into Spanish, without servilely following his own Latin edition. 2. <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCHOLIUM">Scholium</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> short notes on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>. 3. A treatise on the changes the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> has undergone in Spain; for which he was thrown into prison by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Lerma, the Spanish minister. 4. A famous treatise De regio et regiae institutione, which made much noise, and was condemned by the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> of Paris to be burnt by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> hangman, for his asserting in that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, that it is lawful to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> tyrants. 5. A work on the faults of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of Jesuits, which has been translated into Spanish, Latin, Italian, French, &c.

MARIANUS SCOTUS

Pages 641-641

an Irish monk, was related to the venerable Bede, and wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRONICLE">chronicle</a> which is esteemed. He died in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> of Fuld in 1086, aged 58.

MARIBONE

Pages 641-642
or St Mary le Bone, or rather Bone, from the neighbouring brook, a parish of Middlesex, on the north-west side of London. The manor appears to have belonged anciently to the bishop of London. Maribone London. The houses in this parish are very numerous, comprising several extensive streets and squares, which are every year increasing. The Paddington road from Islington passes through this parish, which gives it communication with the eastern part of London without passing through the streets. Here were three conduits erected about the year 1238, for supplying the city of London with water; but anno 1703, when it was plentifully served by the New River, the citizens let them out at 700l. a-year for 43 years. There were two for receiving its water at the north-east corner of the bridge on the river Tyburn, and over them stood the lord's mayor's banqueting house, to which (the use of coaches being not then known) his lordship and the aldermen used to ride on horseback, as their ladies did in waggons. This banqueting house, after being many years neglected, was taken down in 1737, and the cisterns arched over.

MARIDUNUM

Pages 642-642

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of the Demetæ in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. Now Caer Mardin, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAERMARTHENSHIRE">Caermarthenshire</a>.

MARIETTA

Pages 642-642

a town in the United States of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, situated in the state of Ohio, at the junction of the Ohio river with the Muskingum. The town and township contained 1463 inhabitants in 1810. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>-rigged vessels are built here, though it is 2000 miles inland.

MARIGALANTE

Pages 642-642

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, and one of the least of the Caribbees, lies in N. Lat. 16° 32' and W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 61° 5', from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, at the distance of four leagues from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUADALOUPE">Guadaloupe</a>, to the south. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, produce, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, are pretty much the same as the other Caribbees. Columbus discovered it in his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> American voyage in 1483, and called it by the name of his ship <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARIA">Maria</a> Galanta, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Gallant <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>. It is about six leagues long, and between three and four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. Viewed at a distance from on board a ship, it appears like a floating island, because, as it is for the most <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> flat, the trees seem to swim; but a nearer prospect shows it to be intersected by some rising grounds, which give a fine variety to the landscape. The French settled here in 1648. It was taken by the British in 1759, but afterwards restored at the peace in 1763. It was taken again in 1808, and restored to France by the peace of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1814.—This island was thought, on its first discovery, to want <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; but a charming running stream has in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> been discovered, no less convenient than refreshing and wholesome, on the banks of which are some wealthy planters, and excellent plantations of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>. A little village in a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the island, and here the commandant resides. The whole island is very capable of improvement; the soil being almost equally good, and the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> rising nowhere too <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> affords many little bays, and safe anchorage and shelter to ships.

MARINE

Pages 642-642

a general name for the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> state; as also the whole economy of naval affairs; or whatever respects the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, rigging, arming, equipping, navigating, and fighting ships. It comprehends also the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of naval armaments, and the state of all the persons employed therein, whether civil or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the marine affairs of any one state is a very comprehensive subject, much more that of all nations. Those who would be informed of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> affairs of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> it has made at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> in all ages, may find abundance of curious <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> in Selden's Mare Clausum; and from his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to ours, we may trace a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of facts in Lediard's and Burchet's Naval History; but above all in the Lives of the Admirals, by the accurate and judicious Dr Campbell.

MARINE ACID

Pages 643-643

an old name given to muriatic acid, which see in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MARINE SURVEYOR

Pages 643-643

is the name of a machine contrived by Mr H. de Sanmarez for measuring the way of a ship in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. This machine is in the form of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> Y, and is made of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> any other metal. At each end of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> which constitute the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> or upper <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of that letter, are two pallets, not much unlike the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of the log; one of which falls in the same proportion as the other rises. The falling or pendent pallet meeting a resistance from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, as the ship moves, has by that means a circular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> under water, which is faster or slower according as the vessel moves. This motion is communicated to a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIAL">dial</a> within the ship, by means of a rope fastened to the tail of the Y, and carried to the dial. The motion being thus communicated to the dial, which has a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELL">bell</a> in it, it strikes exactly the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of geometrical paces, milcs, or leagues, which the ship has run. Thus the ship's distance is ascertained; and the forces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">tides</a> and currents may also be discovered by this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>: which, however, has been very little used.

MARINER

Pages 643-643

the same with a sailor <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> seaman. See these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>. Method of preserving the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> of MARINERS. See SEAMEN. MARINER'S COMPASS. See Compass.

MARINES

Pages 642-643
or MARINE Forces, a body of soldiers raised for the sea service, and trained to fight either in a naval engagement or in an action ashore. The great service of this useful corps was manifested frequently in the course of the war before last, particularly at the siege of Belleisle, where they acquired a great character, although lately raised and hardly exercised in military discipline. At sea they are incorporated with the ship's crew, of which they make a part; and many of them learn in a short time to be excellent seamen, to which their officers are ordered by the admiralty to encourage them, although no sea officer is to order them to go aloft against their inclination.
