In a sea fight their small arms are of very great advantage in scouring the decks of the enemy; and when they have been long enough at sea to stand firm when the ship rocks, they must be infinitely preferable to seamen if the enemy attempts to board, by raising a battalion with their fixed bayonets to oppose him. The sole direction of the corps of marines is vested in the lords commissioners of the admiralty; and in the admiralty is a distinct apartment for this purpose. The secretary to the admiralty is likewise secretary to the marines, for which he has a salary of 300l. a-year; and he has under him several clerks for the management of this department. The marine forces of Great Britain in the time of peace are stationed in three divisions; one of which is quartered at Chatham, one at Portsmouth, and another at Plymouth. By a late regulation, they are ordered to do duty at the several dock-yards of those ports, to prevent embezzlement of the king's stores, for which a captain's guard mounts every day; which certainly requires great vigilance, as so many abuses of this kind have been committed, that many of the inhabitants, who have been long used to an infamous traffic of this kind, expect these conveyances at certain periods as their due, and of course resent this regulation in the highest degree as an infringement of their liberties as British subjects. The marine corps are under the command of their own field officers, who discipline them, and regulate their different duties. His late majesty in 1760 formed a new establishment of marine officers, entitled, the general, lieutenant-general, and three colonels of marines (one for each division), to be taken from officers in the royal navy. The two first are always enjoyed by flag officers, the last by post captains only. This establishment was formed to reward such officers who distinguished themselves in the service of their country. MARINE Discipline, is the training up soldiers for sea service, in such exercise as the various positions of the firelock and body, and teaching them every manoeuvre that can be performed on board ships of war at sea. See Exercise. MARINE Chair, a machine invented by Mr Irwin for viewing the satellites of Jupiter at sea, and of course course determining the longitude by their eclipses. An account of it is given in the Journal Estranger for March 1760. An account of its accuracy was published in the year following by M. de l'Isle astronomer in the Imperial academy of Petersburgh; but notwithstanding the encomiums bestowed upon it by this gentleman, it hath never come into general use; and therefore we may conclude, that it is much inferior to the inventions of Mr Harrison for the same purpose. See HARRISON and LONGITUDE.

MARINO

Pages 643-643

John Baptist, a celebrated Italian poet, born at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a> in 1569. His father, who was an able civilian, obliged him to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>; at which being disgusted, he left his parents, and retired to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of the Sieur Manzi, who was a friend to all persons of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>. He at length became secretary to Matthew of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPUA">Capua</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Naples, and contracted a friendship with Tasso. A short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> after, he went to Rome, and entered into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Aldobrandini, nephew to Pope Clement VIII., who took him with him to Savoy. Marino was in great favour with the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURIN">Turin</a>; but afterwards created himself many enemies there, the most furious of whom was the poet Gaspard Murtola, who, attempting to shoot him with a pistol, wounded one of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Savoy's favourites. Marino being obliged to leave Turin, went to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> at the desire of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> de Medicis, and published there his poem on <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADONIS">Adonis</a>. He afterwards went to Rome, where he was made <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of the academy of the humoristi; from thence to Naples, where he died while he was preparing to return home. He had a very lively imagination, but little judgment; and, giving way to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> and conceits then in vogue, his authority, far from correcting the false <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of the Italians, served rather to keep it farther from reformation. His works, which are numerous, have been often printed. [Merged from ST MARINO, p.643] a small town and republic of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 13. 44. N. Lat. 44. 21. This small republic consists only of a mountain, and a few hillocks, that <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> scattered about the bottom of it. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the inhabitants is about 5000. The mountain yields good wine, but they have no other than <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> snow <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. The founder of the republic was a Dalmatian, and a mason, who upwards of 1300 years ago turned hermit, and retired to this mountain. Here his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> and austerity, and, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of that, his reputation for sanctity, were such, that the princes of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> made him a present of the mountain; on which many, out of veneration for the saint, soon after took up their abode. Thus was the foundation laid of the town and republic, which still bears the name of the saint. The town stands on the top of the mountain, and there is only one way by which it can be come at. In the whole territory are only three castles, three <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>, and five churches. The largest of the churches is dedicated to the saint, and contains his ashes and his statue. He is looked upon as the greatest saint, next to the blessed Virgin; and to speak disrespectfully of him is accounted blasphemy, and punished as such. The republic is under the protection of the pope. All that are capable of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> arms are exercised, and ready at a minute's call. In the ordinary course of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, the administration is in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of 60, which, notwithstanding its name, consists only of 40; one-half of the members of which are of the noble families, and the other of the plebeian; on extraordinary occasions, however, the arengo, in which every house has its representative, is called together. The two <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> officers are the capitaneos, who are chosen every half year; and next to them is the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMISSARY">commissary</a>, who judges in civil and criminal matters, and is joined in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> with the capitaneos; both he and the physician must be foreigners, and both have their salaries out of the public stock. When any person, after due summons, neglects to assist at the council according to their statute book, he is to be fined in about a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENNY">penny</a> English; and when an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> is to be sent to any foreign state, he is to be allowed about 1s. a-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>.

MARINUS

Pages 643-643

an engraver, who flourished about the year 1630, and resided principally at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a>. His plates, Mr Strutt observes, are executed in a very singular style, with the graver only: The strokes are very fine and delicate, and crossed over each other in a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOZENGE">lozenge</a>-like form, which he filled up with thin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> dots. His <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a>, though generally very neat, want the style of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> in the determination of the folds of the draperies and the outline of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>; the extremities of which are heavy, and not marked with precision. Fine impressions from his best plates are, however, much sought after by collectors; those especially after Rubens and Jordaens are held in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> estimation.

MARIONIS

Pages 643-643

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of Germany: now <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAMBURG">Hamburg</a>, a famous trading <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELBE">Elbe</a>, in Lower <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLSTEIN">Holstein</a>. Another Marionis (<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>), thought to be Wismar, a town of Lower Saxony, in the duchy of Mecklenburgh.

MARITIME

Pages 644-646

something relating to, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> bounded by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. Thus a maritime <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is one bounded by the sea; and a maritime <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> is one that makes a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, or that is very powerful at sea. Hence, by maritime powers among the European states, are understood <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> and formerly <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>. MARITIME State, in British policy, one of the three general divisions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAITY">laity</a>: (See Laity). This state is nearly connected with the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a>; though much more agreeable to the principles of our free <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a> of England hath ever been its greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> and ornament; it is its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> strength; the floating bulwark of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>; an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> from which, however strong and powerful, no danger can ever be apprehended to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>; and accordingly it has been assiduously cultivated from earliest ages. To so much perfection was our naval reputation arrived in the 12th century, that the code of maritime laws, which are called the laws of Oleron, and are received by all nations in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> as the ground and substruction of all their marine constitutions, was confessedly compiled by our <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> Richard I. at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Oleron on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of France, then <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the possessions of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of England. And yet so vastly inferior were our <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> in this point to the present <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, that even in the maritime reign of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, Sir Edward <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COKE">Coke</a> thinks it <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of boast, that the royal navy of England then consisted of three and thirty ships. The present condition of our marine is in great <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> owing to the salutary <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> of the statutes called the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> acts; whereby the constant increase of English shipping and seamen was not only encouraged, but rendered unavoidably necessary. By the statute 5 Richard II. c. 3, in order to augment the navy of England, then greatly diminished, it was ordained, that none of the king's <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIEGE">liege</a> people should ship any merchandise out of or into the realm, but only in ships of the king's liegeance, on pain of forfeiture. In the next year, by statute 6 Rich. II. c. 8, this wise provision was enervated, by only obliging the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> to give English ships (<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> able and sufficient) the preference. But the most beneficial statute for the trade and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> of these kingdoms is that navigation <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of which were first framed in 1659, with a narrow partial view; being intended to mortify our own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, which were disaffected to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, and still held out for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. by stopping the gainful trade which they then carried on with the Dutch, and at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to clip the wings of those our opulent and aspiring neighbours. This prohibited all ships of foreign nations from trading with any English plantations, without license from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of state. In 1651, the prohibition was extended also to the mother country: and no goods were suffered to be imported into England, or any of its dependencies, in any other than English bottoms; or in the ships of that European <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> of which the merchandise imported was the genuine growth or manufacture. At the Restoration, the former provisions were <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>, by stat. 12 Car. II. c. 18, with this very material improvement, that the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> and three-fourths of the mariners shall also be English subjects. Many laws have been made for the supply of the royal navy with seamen; for their regulation when on board; and to confer privileges and rewards on them during and after their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. 1. For their supply. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a>, but the most odious, though often necessary method for this purpose, is by impressing; see IMPRESSING. But there are other ways that tend to the increase of seamen, and manning the royal navy. Parishes may bind out <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> boys apprentices to the masters of merchantmen, who shall be protected from impressing for the first three years; and if they are impressed afterwards, the masters shall be allowed their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WAGES">wages</a>: great advantages in point of wages are given to volunteer seamen, in order to induce them to enter into his majesty's service; and every foreign seaman, who, during a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, shall serve two years in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of war, merchantmen, or privateer, is naturalized ipso facto. About the middle of King William's reign, a scheme was set on foot for a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a> of seamen to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of 30,000, for a constant and regular supply of the king's fleet; with great privileges to the registered men; and, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, heavy penalties in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of their non-appearance when called for; but this registry, being judged to be rather a badge of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>, was abolished by stat. 9 Ann. c. 21. 2. The method of ordering seamen in the royal fleet, and keeping up a regular <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> there, is directed by certain express rules, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>, and orders, first enacted by the authority of parliament soon after the Restoration; but since new modelled and altered, after the peace of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIX">Aix</a>-la-Chapelle, to remedy some defects which were of fatal consequences in conducting the preceding war. In these articles of the navy almost every possible offence is set <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> thereof annexed; in which respect the seamen have much the advantage over their brethren in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> service; whose articles of war are not enacted by parliament, but framed from time to time at the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> of the crown. Yet from whence this distinction arose, and why the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXECUTIVE_POWER">executive power</a>, which is limited so properly with regard to the navy, should be so extensive with regard to the army, it is hard to assign a reason: unless it proceeded from the perpetual establishment of the navy, which rendered a permanent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> for their regulation expedient, and the temporary <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> of the army, which subsisted only from year to year, and might therefore with less danger be subjected to discretionary <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. But, whatever was apprehended at the first formation of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUTINY">mutiny</a> act, the regular renewal of our standing force at the entrance of every year has made this distinction idle. For, if from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> past, we may judge of future events, the army is now lastingly ingrafted into the British constitution; with this singularly fortunate circumstance, that any branch of the legislature may annually put an end to its legal existence, by refusing to concure in its continuance. 3. The privileges conferred on sailors, are pretty much the same with those conferred on <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, with regard to relief, when maimed, or wounded, or superannuated, either by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RATES">rates</a>, or the royal <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a>; with regard also to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of trades, and the power of making noncursive testaments; and farther, no seaman on board his majesty's ships can be arrested for any debt, unless the same be sworn to amount at least to twenty pounds; though, by the annual mutiny acts, a soldier may be arrested for a debt which extends to half that value, but not to a less amount. Marius, the famous Roman general, and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> times <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a>, who sullied his great military reputation by <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> barbarities. He was born at Arpinum, of obscure and illiterate parents. He forsook the meaner occupations of the country for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>; and signalized himself under Scipio, at the siege of Numantia. The Roman general <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the courage and intrepidity of young Marius, and foretold the era of his future greatness. By his seditions and intrigues at Rome, while he exercised the inferior offices of the state, he rendered himself known; and his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> with Julia, who was of the family of the Caesars, contributed in some manner to raise him to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>. He passed into <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> to the consul Metellus against Jugurtha; and after he had there ingratiated himself with the soldiers, and raised enemies to his friend and benefactor, he returned to Rome and canvassed for the consulship. The extravagant promises he made to the people, and his malevolent insinuations about the conduct of Metellus, proved successful. He was elected and appointed to finish the war against Jugurtha. He showed himself capable in every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> to succeed to Metellus. Jugurtha was defeated, and afterwards betrayed into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> by the perfidy of Bocchus. No sooner was Jugurtha conquered, than new honours and fresh trophies awaited Marius. The provinces of Rome were suddenly invaded by an army of 300,000 barbarians, and Marius was the only man whose <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> and boldness could resist so powerful an enemy. He was elected consul, and sent against the Teutones. The war was prolonged, and Marius was a third and fourth time invested with the consulship. At last two engagements were fought, and not less than 200,000 of the barbarian forces of the Ambiones and Teutones were slain in the field of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, and 90,000 made prisoners. The following year, A. U. C. 651, was also marked by a total overthrow of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CIMBRI">Cimbri</a>, another horde of barbarians; in which 140,000 were slaughtered by the Romans, and 60,000 taken prisoners. After such <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> victories, Marius with his colleague Catullus entered Rome in triumph; and for his eminent services he received the appellation of the third founder of Rome. He was elected consul a sixth time; and as his intrepidity had delivered his country from its foreign enemies, he sought employment at home, and his restless ambition began to raise seditions, and to oppose the power of Sylla. This was the foundation of a civil war. Sylla refused to deliver up the command of his forces, with which he was empowered to prosecute the Mithridatic war; and he resolved to oppose in person the authors of a demand which he considered as arbitrary and improper. He advanced to Rome, and Marius was obliged to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> by flight. The unfavourable winds prevented him from seeking a safer retreat in Africa, and he was left on the coast of Campania, where the emissaries of his enemy soon discovered him in a marsh, where he had plunged himself in the mud, and left only his mouth above the surface for respiration. He was violently dragged to the neighbouring town of Minturnae; and the magistrates, all devoted to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of Sylla, passed <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> of immediate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> on their magnificent prisoner. A <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a> was commanded to cut off his head in the dungeon; but the stern countenance of Marius disarmed the courage of the executioner: and when he heard the exclamation of Tunc, homo, audes occidere Caenum Marium? the dagger dropped from his hand. Such an uncommon adventure moved the compassion of the inhabitants of Minturnae. They released Marius from prison; and favoured his escape to Africa, where he joined his son Marius, who had been arming the princes of that country in his cause. Marius landed near the walls of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a>, and he received no small consolation at the sight of the venerable ruins of a once powerful <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, which like himself had been exposed to calamity, and felt the cruel vicissitude of fortune. This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his retreat was soon known; and the governor of Africa, to conciliate the favour of Sylla, compelled Marius to fly to a neighbouring island. He soon after learned that Cinna had embraced his cause at Rome, when the Roman <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> had stripped him of his consular <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, and bestowed it upon one of his enemies. This intelligence animated Marius; he set sail to assist his friend only at the head of 1000 men. His army, however, was soon increased, and he entered Rome like a conqueror. His enemies were inhumanly sacrificed to his fury; Rome was filled with blood; and he, who once had been called the father of his country, marched through the streets of the city, attended by a number of assassins, who immediately slaughtered all those whose salutations were not answered by their leader. Such were the signals for bloodshed. When Marius and Cinna had sufficiently gratified their resentment, they made themselves consuls; but Marius, already worn out with old age and infirmities, died sixteen days after he had been honoured with the consular dignity for the seventh time, A. U. C. 666. Such was the end of Marius, who rendered himself conspicuous by his victories and by his cruelty. As he was brought up in poverty and among peasants, it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not appear wonderful that he always betrayed rusticity in his behaviour, and despised in others those polished manners and that studied <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>, which <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> had denied him. He hated the conversation of the learned only because he was illiterate; and if he appeared an example of sobriety and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a>, he owed these advantages to the years of obscurity which he passed at Arpinum. His countenance was stern, his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> firm and imperious, and his disposition intractable. He was in the 70th year of his age when he died; and Rome seemed to rejoice at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of a man whose ambition had proved so fatal to many of her citizens. His only qualifications were those of a great general; and with these he rendered himself the most illustrious and powerful of the Romans, because he was the only one whose ferocity seemed capable to oppose the barbarians of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>. Marius, C., the son of the great Marius, was as cruel as his father, and shared his good and his adverse fortune. He made himself consul in the 25th year of his age, and murdered all the senators who opposed his ambitious views. He was defeated by Sylla, and fled to Præneste, where he killed himself. Marius, M. Aurelius, a native of Gaul; who, from the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> employment of a blacksmith, became one of the generals of Gallienus, and at last caused himself to be saluted <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>. Three days after this elevation, a man who had shared his poverty without partaking of his more prosperous fortune, publicly assassinated him, and he was killed by a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> which he himself had made in the time of his obscurity. Marius has been often celebrated for his great strength; and it is confidently reported, that he could stop, with one of his fingers only, the wheel of a chariot in its most rapid course. Marius, Maximus, a Latin writer, who published an account of the Roman emperors from Trajan to Alexander, now lost. His compositions were entertaining, and executed with great exactness and fidelity. Some have accused him of inattention, and complain that his writings abounded with many fabulous and insignificant stories.

MARIVAX

Pages 646-646
Peter Carlet de, a French writer in the dramatic way and in romance, was born of a good family at Paris in 1688. A fine understanding, well improved by education, distinguished him early. His first object was the theatre, where he met with the highest success in comic productions; and these, with the merit of his other works, procured him a place in the French academy. The great characteristic of both his comedies and romances was, to convey an useful moral under the veil of wit and sentiment: "My only object (says he) is to make men more just and more humane;" and he was as amiable in his life and conversation as he was in his writings. He died at Paris in 1763, aged 75. His works consist of, 1. Pièces de Theatre, 4 vols. 12mo. 2. Homore travesti, 12mo; which is not supposed to have done much honour to his taste. 3. Le Spectateur François, 2 vols. 12mo. 4. Le Philosophe Indégent, 12mo. 5. Vie de Marianne, 2 vols. 12mo; one of the best romances in the French language. 6. L.: Paysan Parvenu, 12mo. 7. Pharsamon; inferior to the former.

MARJORAM

Pages 643-644

See ORIGANUM, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. MARITAGIUM. In the feudal customs, maritagium Maritatum (as contradistinguished from matrimonium) signifies the power which the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a> in chivalry had of disposing of his infant <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARD">ward</a> in matrimony. For while the infant was in ward, the guardian had the power of tendering him or her a suitable <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MATCH">match</a> without disparagement or inequality; which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a> refused, they forfeited the value of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, valorem maritagii, to their guardian; that is, so much as a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JURY">jury</a> would assess, or any one would <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BONA">bona</a> fide give to the guardian for such an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a>: and if the infants married themselves without the guardian's consent, they forfeited <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> the value, duplicem valorem maritagii.

MARK

Pages 646-647

St., was by birth a Jew, and descended of the tribe of Levi. He was converted by some of the apostles, probably by St <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>; to whom he was a constant <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> in all his travels, supplying the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of an amanuensis and interpreter. He was by St Peter sent into <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, fixing his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> residence at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, and the places thereabout; where he was so successful in his ministry, that he converted multitudes both of men and women. He afterwards removed westwards, towards the parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBYA">Libya</a>, going through the countries of Marmorica, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENTAPOLIS">Pentapolis</a>, and others thereabouts; where, notwithstanding the barbarity and idolatry of the inhabitants, he planted the Mark gospel. Upon his return to Alexandria, he ordered the affairs of that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and there suffered martyrdom in the following manner. About Easter, at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the solemnities of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERAPIS">Serapis</a> were celebrated, the idolatrous people, being excited to vindicate the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of their deity, broke in upon St Mark, while he was performing divine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, and binding him with cords, dragged him through the streets, and thrust him into prison, where in the night he had the comfort of a divine vision. Next <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> the enraged multitude used him in the same manner, till his spirits failing, he expired under their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. Some add, that they burnt his body, and that the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> decently interred his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> and ashes near the place where he used to preach. This happened in the year of Christ 68. Some writers assert, that the remains of St Mark were afterwards, with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> pomp, translated from Alexandria to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>. However, he is the tutelar saint and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of that republic, and has a very rich and stately church erected to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a> is author of one of the four gospels <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> with his name. See the following article. St Mark's Gospel, a canonical book of the New <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, being one of the four gospels. St Mark wrote his gospel at Rome, where he accompanied St Peter in the year of Christ 44. Tertullian and others pretend, that St Mark was no more than an amanuensis to St Peter, who dictated this gospel to him; others affirm, that he wrote it after St Peter's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. Nor are the learned less divided as to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> it was written in; some affirming that it was composed in Greek, others in Latin. Several of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> heretics received only the gospel of St Mark; others, among the Catholics, rejected the 12 last verses of this gospel. The gospel of St Mark is properly an abridgement of that of St Matthew. St Mark the Evangelist's Day, a festival of the Christian church, observed April 25. Canons of St Mark, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> of regular canons founded at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a>, by Albert Spinola, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, towards the end of the 12th century. Spinola made a rule for them, which was approved, corrected, and confirmed by several succeeding popes. About the year 1450 they were reformed, and followed only the rule of St Augustine. This congregation having flourished for the space of 400 years, declined by little and little, and is now become extinct. Knights of St Mark, an order of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a> in the republic of Venice, under the protection of St Mark the evangelist. The arms of the order are, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULES">gules</a>, a lion winged <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>; with this device, Pax tibi MARCE EVANGELISTA. This order is never conferred but on those who have done signal service to the commonwealth. Mark, or Marc, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> used in several states of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and for several commodities, especially <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver. In France, the mark is divided into eight ounces, 64 drachms, 192 deniers or <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENNY">penny</a>-weights, 160 esterliens, 300 mails, 640 felins, or 4608 grains. In <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, the mark weight is also called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>-weight, and is equal to that of France. When gold and silver are sold by the mark, it is divided into 25 carats. MARK is also used among us for a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> of account, and in some other countries for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>. See Money-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">Table</a>. The English mark is two-thirds of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>, or 13s. 4d.; and the Scotch mark is of equal value in Scots money of account, viz. 13½d.

MARKET

Pages 647-647

a public <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> town, in which live cattle, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, or other goods, are set to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>; and also a privilege, either by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESCRIPTION">prescription</a>, by which a town is enabled to keep a market. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">Court</a> of the Clerk of the MARKET, is incident to every fair and market in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, to punish misdemeanors therein; and a court of pie poindre is to determine all disputes relating to private or civil <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>. The object of this jurisdiction (see stat. 17 Car. II. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 10. 22 Car. II. cap. 8. 23 Car. II. cap. 12.) is principally the cognizance of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WEIGHTS_AND_MEASURES">weights and <a class</a>="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> to try whether they be according to the true standard thereof or not; which standard was anciently committed to the custody of the bishop, who appointed some clerk under him to inspect the abuse of them more narrowly; and hence this officer, though now usually a layman, is called the clerk of the market.—<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> they be not according to the standard, then, beside the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of the party by fine, the weights and measures themselves ought to be burnt. This is the lowest court of criminal jurisdiction in the kingdom.

MARKLAND

Pages 647-647

JEREMIAH, one of the most learned scholars and acute critics of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, was born in 1692, and received his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> in Christ's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>. He became first publicly known by his Epistola Critica, addressed to Bishop Hare. In this he gave many proofs of extensive erudition and critical sagacity. He afterwards published an edition of Statius, and some plays of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EURIPIDES">Euripides</a>; and assisted Dr Taylor in his editions of Lysias and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEMOSTHENES">Demosthenes</a>, by the notes which he communicated to him. He has also very happily elucidated some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> in the New <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, which may be found in Mr Boyer's edition of it; and was author of a very valuable volume of remarks on the epistles of Cicero to Brutus, and of an excellent little treatise under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Questio Grammatica. He died in 1775, at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a> near <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DORKING">Dorking</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SURREY">Surrey</a>; and was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> not more valued for his universal <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a>, than beloved for the excellency of his heart and primitive simplicity of his manners.

MARLBOROUGH

Pages 647-647

a town of Wiltshire in England, situated near the source of the Kennet, at the foot of a chalky hill, 75 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It has its name from the chalky <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, which was formerly called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARL">marl</a>. It was a Roman station. In the year 1627 a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> was held in the castle here, which made those laws called Marlborough statutes. There are still some small remains of its walls and ditch. The town, which is an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> borough by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESCRIPTION">prescription</a>, sends two members to parliament. It contained, in 1811, 2,579 inhabitants; and is governed by a mayor, two justices, twelve aldermen, &c. It consists chiefly of one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> street, with piazzas all along one side of it, two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> churches, and several commodious inns, it being the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> thoroughfare from London to Bath and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a>. To the south are some relics of a priory, particularly the Gatehouse; and the site of a Roman castrum, the foundations of which have been discovered there, with Roman coins. The ditches still in some parts 20 feet wide; and towards the river, without the garden walls, one <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of the castrum is very visible with the rampart and ditch entire. The mount at the west end of the town, which was the keep <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> main <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> of the castle, is converted into a pretty spiral walk; at the top of which is an octagon <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. This town has often suffered by fire, particularly in 1692, whereupon the parliament passed an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> to prevent its houses from being thatched.

MARLBOROUGH-PORT

Pages 647-647

an English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTORY">factory</a> on the west <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMATRA">Sumatra</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>; seated three miles west of the town of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENCOOLEN">Bencoolen</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 101. 12. S. Lat. 4. 21.

MARLE

Pages 647-647

a mixture of calcareous with silicous and argillaceous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, very much used in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a> as a manure. See Agriculture and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MARLINE

Pages 647-647

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> affairs, are tarred <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> skains, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> wreaths or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of untwisted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, dipped in pitch or tar, with which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CABLES">cables</a> or other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> are wrapped round, to prevent their fretting or rubbing in the blocks or pulleys through which they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>. The same serves in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a> upon ropes used for rigging guns, usually put up in small parcels called skains.

MARLOE

Pages 647-647

CHRISTOPHER, an English dramatic author, was a student in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>; but afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> player, he trode the same stage with the inimitable Shakespeare. He was accounted an excellent poet even by Ben Johnson himself. He wrote six tragedies, one of which called Lust's Dominion, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the Lascivious <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a>, has been altered by Mrs Behn, and acted under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Abdelazar, or the Moor's <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">Revenge</a>. Some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> before his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, he had made a considerable progress in an excellent poem entitled <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">Hero</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEANDER">Leander</a>: which was afterwards finished by George Chapman, who is said to have fallen short of the spirit and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> discovered by Marloe. Mr Anthony Wood represents him as a freethinker, in the worst <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of the word; and gives the following account of his death. Falling deeply in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> with a low girl, and having for his rival a fellow in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIVERY">livery</a>, Marloe, imagining that his mistress granted him favours, was fired with jealousy, and rushed upon him in order to stab him with his dagger: but the footman avoided the stroke, and, seizing his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WRIST">wrist</a>, stabbed him with his own weapon; of which wound he died, in the year 1593.

MARLOW

Pages 647-649

a town of Buckinghamshire, in England, 31 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, lies under the Chiltern hills, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARLY">marly</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>. It is a pretty <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> borough, though not incorporated, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> over the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, not far from its conflux with Wycomb, and has a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> and town-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a>. It first sent members to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> in the reign of Edward II. Bone <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LACE">lace</a> is its <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> manufacture. The Thames brings goods hither from the neighbouring <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, especially <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> quantities of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAL">meal</a> and malt from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">High</a> Wycomb, and beech from several parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, which abounds with this wood more than any in England. In the neighbourhood are frequent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> races; and here are several corn and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>, particularly Marlow, on the river Loddon, between this town and High Wycomb. There are, besides, the Temple-mills for making thimbles, and another for pressing <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAPE">rape</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a> seeds. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> in 1811 was 2799. At Great Marlow there is an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> supported by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of young men destined for the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. The pupils are entirely under <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>, and are instructed by able professors in the various branches of education connected with military <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TACTICS">tactics</a>. Marly, a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of France, between <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSAILLES">Versailles</a> and St German; seated in a valley, near a village and forest of the same name. It is noted for its fine gardens and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER_WORKS"><a class="x</a>ref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>-works, there being a curious machine on the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a>, which not only supplies them with water, but also those of Versailles. It is 10 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 11. N. Lat. 48. 52. Marly, Machine at. When <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> the Great had fixed upon a favourite situation in the forest of Marly, where he intended to erect a splendid castle, he found that it wanted nothing either in point of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> convenience but a fountain of water; and he immediately determined to supply by the assistance of art what <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> had denied it. An ingenious and self-taught carpenter from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIEGE">Liege</a>, named Ramequin, undertook to conduct from the Seine a copious supply of water, and for this purpose contrived and erected the celebrated and complicated machine which we are now to describe. The machinery is driven by 14 undershot water <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a> of 36 feet diameter, reckoning from the ends of the floatboards, disposed in three rows. In the first row there are <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> wheels, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> six, and in the third only one. By these wheels the water is raised through pumps into the first reservoir about 160 feet above the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the river, then to a second reservoir 346 feet high, and from this to the summit of a tower about 533 feet above the Seine. The two extremities of the axle of each wheel extend beyond the gudgeons on which they rest, and are bent into a crank so as to form a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEVER">lever</a> two feet long. The crank which is towards the mountain drives the water of the river into the first reservoir, and the other crank gives <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> to the balances. An engine of eight pumps is wrought by one of the cranks of each of the six wheels in the first row. These engines consist of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a>, at each end of which hangs a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> piece of wood that supports and directs four pistons. This balance is moved by a beam in the form of a T, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of which is connected at one end with the balance by the intervention of a vertical regulator or beam, and at the other with the crank of the wheel by means of a horizontal <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> rod. One of the cranks of each of the six wheels of the first row, (excepting that which is next the mountain), and two of the cranks of the 14th wheel, or that in the last row, give motion to the pumps in the river, and carry the water into the first reservoir. This motion is communicated from the cranks by means of an iron rod which is fixed to the lower end of a vertical balance. A horizontal regulator or beam is fixed to each end of this balance, and to these regulators are fastened chains which follow the declivity of the mountain till they reach the superior reservoirs. When the wheel is revolving, therefore, one of these chains <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be dragged towards the river, and the other towards the mountain. In order to produce this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a> motion, the chains are supported and kept at equal distances by a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of vertical balances, placed along the mountain at every three toises, and moving upon a centre supported by a frame lying between the two chains and equidistant from them. When these chains reach the first reservoir they are fixed to vertical regulators, which carry frames, to which are adapted the pistons of the sucking pumps. These regulators therefore will be drawn one after another by their corresponding chains; and when one regulator is drawn by its chain, the piston of the pumps which it carries will be raised, and the water will follow them: At the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the pistons of the other regulator are descending to form a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VACUUM">vacuum</a>; and these in their turn ascend with their load of water when the others are in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of descending. In the pumps formerly mentioned which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> in the river, an effect is produced upon the pistons both when they ascend and descend, because they are moved by stiff iron rods; but in the present <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the pistons descend merely by their own <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, as the motion is transmitted only by a chain. By these pumps the water is conveyed to the upper reservoir by two conduit <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a> of eight inches, and three others of six inches diameter. The sixth wheel of the first row, which is the first towards the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DAM">dam</a>, moves a long chain which works the pumps of one of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a> of the upper reservoir. The seventh wheel gives motion to a chain which goes to the first cistern. By means similar to these already described, the six wheels of the second row move by each of their cranks a chain that goes to the second reservoir, and eight of these chains work 16 pumps behind it, to bring back into the reservoir the water which is lost out of the six pipes that go to the tower. These chains go over one of the first cisterns, and five of them at the same time give motion to the pistons of thirty pumps, whilst the other chains go on straight to the great reservoir. These 30 pumps convey their water through two pipes of 8 inches diameter into the upper reservoir. The five chains, after working these 30 pumps, give motion to the pistons of 82 pumps in the second reservoir which raise the water from it to the tower. The basis of the tower which receives the water raised from the river is 610 fathoms distant from it; and the water runs from this basin along an aqueduct of 36 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> by its own weight. From this aqueduct the water is distributed into great reservoirs, from which it is conveyed to the gardens and shruberies around the castle. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of water raised by this machine amounts at a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> rate to 30,000 or 40,000 gallons per <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>; though in favourable circumstances it raises more than 60,000 gallons per hour. But while the Seine either overflows its banks, or is frozen, or when the water is very low, the machine is scarcely capable of performing any work. The yearly expense of the machine at Marly including the salaries of the superintendents and the expenses of repairs, amounts to about 330l. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>, or 9l. per <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, which makes the expense of 90 gallons of water one farthing. But <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we take into the account the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> interest of 333,000l. the original expense of the machine, 90 gallons will cost three halfpence, or 15 gallons one farthing. Notwithstanding the magnificence of this great machine, and the ingenuity which is displayed in its <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>, every person who examines it with care, will perceive innumerable defects, whether he examines it as a whole, or attends to the parts of which it is composed. In several positions the moving forces act with great obliquity, and therefore occasion an immense waste of power; and in order to give an alternate motion to a number of chains of balances extending to a distance of 384 feet, more than <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a>-tenths of the impelling power are destroyed. By a few changes upon the construction of the machine, the water might have been raised from the river to the tower without any intermediate reservoirs. This appears from two experiments made upon the machine in 1738 and 1775. In 1738 M. Camus attempted to raise the water to the tower at once. He was able, however, only to bring it to the bottom of the tower which was considerably higher than the second reservoir. By this experiment the machine was so much strained that several parts required chains to secure it. In 1775 the water was elevated to the second reservoir at one jet at different times, but from the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> and infirmity of the pipes several of them burst during the experiment. Hence it is obvious that if the pipes had been made stronger, the first reservoir and the machinery connected with it might have been dispensed with; and it is very probable that if the machine had been constructed with more judgment, the water might have been conducted at once from the river to the tower.

MARMADE

Pages 649-649

a town of France, in the department of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT_AND_GARONNE"><a class="xref"</a> href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">Lot</a> and Garonne, containing about 4000 inhabitants. It carries on a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> trade in corn and wine, and is seated on the river Garonne, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0. 15. N. Lat. 44. 30.

MARMALADE

Pages 649-649

a confection of plums, apricots, quinces, &c. boiled up to a consistence with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>. In Scotland, it is made of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEVILLE">Seville</a> oranges and sugar only.

MARMORA

Pages 649-649

the name of four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> of the same name. The largest is about 30 miles in circumference; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> of them all produces corn, wine, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>. The sea of Marmora is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a>, which communicates both with the Archipelago and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BLACK_SEA"><a class=</a>"xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> sea by that of Constantinople, being 120 miles in length and 50 in breadth; and all ships must <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through it that sail to Constantinople from the Mediterranean. It was anciently the Propontis.

MARMORICA

Pages 649-649

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> anciently inhabited by the Libyans. It was bounded on the east by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, on the west by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYRENAICA">Cyrenaica</a>, on the south by Sahara, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBYA">Libya</a> Interior, and on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the Mediterranean; and was reckoned a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Egypt.

MARNE

Pages 649-649

the name of two departments in France, and also of a river which has its origin in one of them.

MAROBUDUN

Pages 649-649

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> residence of Marobodus, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of the Marcomanni. Now thought to be <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAGUE">Prague</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>.

MAROLLES

Pages 649-649

MICHEL DE, born in 1600, was Marolles the son of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLAUDE">Claude</a> de Marolles, whom French <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a> make a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a>. Michel, however, was of a different <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>. He entered early into the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> state, and by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of his father obtained two abbeys. He was formed with an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> ardour for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, which never abated all his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>: for, from 1619 when he published a translation of Lucan, to 1681, the year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, he was constantly employed in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a>. He attached himself unfortunately to the translating of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Latin writers: but, being devoid of all classical <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and spirit, they sunk miserably under his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, the poets especially. He was certainly, however, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> learning, and discovered all his life a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> for the arts. He was one of the first who paid any <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a>; and collected about 100,000, which make at this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> one of the ornaments of the French <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s cabinet. He composed memoirs of his own life, which were published by the abbe Goujet, 1755, in 3 vols.

MARONITES

Pages 649-650

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of eastern <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, who follow the Syrian rite, and are subject to the pope; their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> habitation being on Mount Lebanon. Moshheim informs us, that the doctrine of the Monothelites, condemned and exploded by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Constantinople, found a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of refuge among the Mardaites, a people who inhabited the mounts Libanus and Antilibanus, and who, about the conclusion of the seventh century, were called Maronites, after Maro their first bishop; a name which they still retain. None (he says) of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers give any certain account of the first person who instructed these mountaineers in the doctrine of the Monothelites: it is probable, however, from several circumstances, that it was John Maro, whose name they had adopted; and that this ecclesiastic received the name of Maro from his having lived in the character of a monk in the famous convent of St Maro, upon the borders of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORONTES">Orontes</a>, before his settlement among the Mardaites of Mount Lebanon. One thing is certain, from the testimony of Tyrius and other unexceptionable witnesses, as also from the most authentic records, viz. that the Maronites retained the opinions of the Monothelites until the 12th century, when, abandoning and renouncing the doctrine of one <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> in Christ, they were readmitted in the year 1182 to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> of the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. The most learned of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Maronites have left no method unemployed to defend their church against this <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a>; they have laboured to prove, by a variety of testimonies, that their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> always persevered in the Catholic <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, in their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the Roman pontiff, without ever adopting the doctrine of the Monophysites, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Monothelites. But all their efforts are insufficient to prove the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of these assertions to such as have any acquaintance with the history of the church and the records of ancient times; for to all such the testimonies they allege will appear absolutely fictitious and desolate of authority. Faustus Nairon, a Maronite settled at Rome, has published an apology for Maro and the rest of his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. His tenet is, that they really took their name from the Maro who lived about the year 400, and of whom mention is made in Chrysostom, Theodoret, and Maronites, and the Menologium of the Greeks. He adds, that the disciples of this Maro spread themselves throughout all <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>; that they built several monasteries, and among others, one that bore the name of their leader; that all the Syrians who were not tainted with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a> took refuge among them; and that for this reason the heretics of those times called them Maronites. Mosheim observes, that the subjection of the Maronites to the spiritual jurisdiction of the Roman pontiff was agreed to with this express condition, that neither the popes nor their emissaries should pretend to change or abolish anything that related to the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a>, moral precepts, or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> opinions, of this people, so that in reality there is nothing to be found among the Maronites that savours of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPERY">popery</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we except their attachment to the Roman pontiff, who is obliged to pay very dear for their friendship. For, as the Maronites live in the utmost distress of poverty, under the tyrannical yoke of the Mahometans, the bishop of Rome is under the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of furnishing them with such subsidies as may appease their oppressors, procure a subsistence for their bishop and clergy, provide all things requisite for the support of their churches, and the uninterrupted <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of public worship, and contribute in general to lessen their misery. It is certain that there are Maronites in Syria who still behold the church of Rome with the greatest aversion and abhorrence; nay, what is still more remarkable, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> numbers of that nation residing in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, even under the eye of the pontiff, opposed his authority during the last century, and threw the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Rome into great perplexity. One body of these nonconforming Maronites retired into the valleys of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a>, where they joined the Waldenses; another, above 600 in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, with a bishop and several <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a> at their head, fled into Corsica, and implored the protection of the republic of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a> against the violence of the inquisitors. The Maronites have a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a>, who resides in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> of Cannubin, on Mount Libanus, and assumes the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of patriarch of Antioch, and the name of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>, as if he seemed desirous of being considered as the successor of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a>. He is elected by the clergy and the people, according to the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>; but, since their reunion with the church of Rome, he is obliged to have a bull of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a> from the pope. He keeps a perpetual celibacy, as well as the rest of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> his suffragans; as to the rest of the ecclesiastics, they are allowed to marry before ordination; and yet the monastic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> is in great esteem among them. Their monks are of the order of St Anthony, and live in the most obscure places in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, far from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> of the world. As to their faith, they agree in the main with the rest of the eastern church. Their priests do not say <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> singly; but all say it together, standing round the altar. They communicate in unleavened <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAITY">laity</a> have hitherto partaken in both kinds, though the practice of communicating in one has of late been getting footing, having been introduced by little and little. In <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LENT">Lent</a> they eat nothing, unless it be two or three hours before sunrise; their other fastings are very numerous. To MAROON, to put one or more sailors ashore upon a desolate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, under pretence of their having committed some great crime. This detestable expedient has been too often practised by some inhuman commanders of ships.

MAROT

Pages 650-650

Clement, the best French poet of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAHORS">Cahors</a> in 1495; and was the son of John Marot, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VALET">valet</a> de chambre to Francis I. and poet to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> of Brittany. He enjoyed his father's <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> as valet de chambre to Francis I. and was page to Margaret of France wife to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Alençon. In 1521 he followed that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and was wounded and taken prisoner at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PAVIA">Pavia</a>; but at his return to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> was accused of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a>, and thrown into prison, from whence he was delivered by the protection of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Francis I. He at length retired to the queen of Navarre, then to the duchess of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERRARA">Ferrara</a>, and in 1536 returned to Paris: but declaring openly for the Calvinists, he was obliged to fly to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>; which he at length left, and retiring to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a>, died at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURIN">Turin</a> in 1544, aged 50. His verses are agreeably filled with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> beauties. La Fontaine acknowledged himself his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a>, and contributed greatly to restore to vogue the works of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> poet. Marot, besides his other works, has translated <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Psalms into <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, which was <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> by Beza, and are still sung in the Protestant churches abroad.—Michael Marot, his son, was also the author of some verses; but they are not comparable to those of John, and much less to those of Clement Marot.—The works of the three Marots were collected and printed together at the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAGUE">Hague</a> in 1731, in 3 vols. 4to, and in 6 vols. 12mo.
