MARPURG

Pages 650-650

a strong and considerable town of Germany, in the Upper <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, and in the landgraviate of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HESSE">Hesse</a> Cassel, with an university, a castle, a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, a handsome <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, and a magnificent townhouse. It is seated on the river Lohn, in a pleasant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, 15 miles south of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALDECK">Waldeck</a>, and 47 south-east of Cassel. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8° 53'. N. Lat. 50° 42'.

MARQUARD

Pages 650-650

Freher, an eminent German civilian, born at Augsburg in 1565. He studied at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOURGES">Bourges</a>, under the learned Cujas; and acquired <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> skill in polite literature, and in the laws. At his return to Germany, he became counsellor to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> Palatine, and professor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEIDELBERG">Heidelberg</a>; and was afterwards sent by the elector Frederic IV. as his minister, into <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENTZ">Mentz</a>, and several other courts. He died at Heidelberg in 1614. He wrote many works which are esteemed; the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of which are, 1. De re monetaria veterum Romanorum, et hodierni apud Germanos imperii. 2. Rerum Bohemicarum scriptores. 3. Rerum Germanicarum scriptores. 4. Corpus historiae Franciae, &c.

MARQUE

Pages 650-651
or Letters of MARQUE, in military affairs, are letters of reprisal, granting the subjects of one prince or state liberty to make reprisals on those of another.—They are so called from the German marche "limit, frontier;" as being jus concessum in alterius principis marckas seu limites transcendi, sibique jus faciendi; as being a right of passing the limits or frontiers of another prince, and doing one's self justice. Letters of marque among us are extraordinary commissions Marquesas missions granted by authority for reparation to merchants taken and despoiled by strangers at sea; and reprisals is only the retaking, or taking of one thing for another*. The form in these cases is, the sufferer must first apply to the lord privy seal, and he shall make out letters of request under the privy-seal; and if, after such request of satisfaction made, the party required do not, within convenient time, make due satisfaction or restitution to the party grieved, the lord chancellor shall make him out letters of marque under the great seal; and by virtue of these he may attack and seize the property of the aggressor nation, without hazard of being condemned as a robber or pirate.

MARQUESAS ISLANDS

Pages 651-652

the name of certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in the South <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, lying between 8 and 10 degrees of south latitude, and between 139 and 140 degrees of west <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>. They are five in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, viz. La <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MAGDALENA">Magdalena</a>, St Pedro, La <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMINICA">Dominica</a>, Santa <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTINA">Christina</a>, and Hood <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. All the natives of these islands may be supposed to be of the same tribe. Those spots that are fit for culture are very populous; but every island is very mountainous, and has many inaccessible and barren rocks; and the whole <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> is believed not to exceed 6000. The Spaniards, who first visited here, found the manners of this people gentle and inoffensive; but these qualities did not prevent those who landed from wantonly butcherering several of the natives at Magdalena. The inhabitants of these islands, collectively, says <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Cook, are without exception, the finest <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of people in the South sea. For symmetry of shape, and regular features, they perhaps surpass all other nations. Not a single deformed <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ill-proportioned person was seen on the island; all were strong, tall, well-limbed, and remarkably <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>. The men are about five feet ten or six feet <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> are not so good, nor are their eyes so full and lively, as those of many other nations: their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> is of many colours, but none <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>; some have it <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, but the most general <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> is to wear it short, except a bunch on each side of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, which they tie in a knot: their countenances are pleasing, open, and full of vivacity; they are of a tawney <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a>, which is rendered almost <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> by punctures over the whole body. They were entirely naked, except a small piece of cloth round their waist and loins. The punctures were disposed with the utmost regularity, so that the marks on each leg, arm, and cheek, were exactly similar. The women, in two days <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, began to appear in considerable numbers, and the sailors found them not less kind than those of the other islands which they had visited: they were inferior to the men in stature, but well proportioned: their general <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> was <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>; no punctures were observed upon them; they wore a single piece of cloth made of the mulberry bark, which covered them from the shoulders to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> head dress used in the islands, and what appears to be their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> ornament, is a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FILLET">fillet</a>, curiously made of the fibres of cocoa nuts; in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> is fixed a mother-of-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEARL">pearl</a> shell, wrought round to the size of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEA">tea</a> saucer; before that another smaller, of very fine tortoiseshell, perforated into curious figures; also before, and in the centre of that, is another round piece of mother-of-pearl, about the size of half a crown; and before this another piece of perforated tortoiseshell, the size of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHILLING">shilling</a>. Besides this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECORATION">decoration</a> in front, some have it also on each side, but in small pieces; and all have fixed to them the tail feathers of cocks, or tropic birds, which, when the fillet is tied on, stand upright, so that the whole together makes a very sprightly ornament. They wear round the neck a kind of ruff or necklace made of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> wood, the outward and upper sides covered with small pease, which are fixed on with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUM">gum</a>; they also wear some bunches of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> hair fastened to a string, and tied round the legs and arms. But all the above ornaments are seldom seen on the same person. All these ornaments, except the last, they freely parted with for a trifling consideration; but the human hair they valued very highly, though these bunches were the usual residence of many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VERMIN">vermin</a>. It is probable, that these were worn in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a> of their deceased relations, and therefore were looked upon with some veneration; or they may be the spoils of their enemies, worn as the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> testimonies of victory. However, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> nail, or something which struck their eyes, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> got the better of their scruples. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, or chief of the island, came to visit Captain Cook: he was the only one seen completely dressed in this manner. Their ordinary ornaments are necklaces, and amulets made of shells, &c. All of them had their ears pierced, though none were seen with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a>-rings. The king had not much respect paid him by his attendants; he presented Captain Cook with some fruit and hogs; and acquainted him that his name was Honoo, and that he was ho-ka-at, which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> seems to correspond with the arce of Otaheite, and arekee of the Friendly isles. Their dwellings are in the valleys, and on the sides of the hills near their plantations. They are built in the same manner as those at Otaheite, which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be particularly described when we speak of that island; but they are much meaner, and are only covered with the leaves of the breadfruit tree; in general, they are built on a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> pavement of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, raised some height above the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the ground; they likewise have such pavement near their houses, on which they sit to eat and amuse themselves. Along the uppermost edge of the mountain a row of stakes or palisadoes, closely connected together, were seen like a fortification, in which, by the help of glasses, appeared something like huts, which seemed to bear a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> resemblance to the hippas of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-NEW_ZEALAND">New <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a>, which will be described in speaking of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Their canoes resemble those of Otaheite, but not so large; their heads had commonly some flat upright piece, on which the human <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> was coarsely carved; and their sails were made of mats, triangular in shape, and very broad at the top: the paddles which they used were of heavy hard wood; short, but sharp-pointed, and with a knob at the upper end; they were from 10 to 22 feet long, and about 15 inches broad. Their weapons were all made of the club wood, or casuarina; and were either plain spears about 8 or 10 feet long, or clubs which commonly had a knob at one end. They have also slings with which they throw <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> with great velocity, and to a great distance, but not with a good aim. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of these people is much nearer to that of Otaheite than any other dialect in the South sea, except that they could not pronounce the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> r. The only <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a> seen here were hogs, except rats; here were fowls, and several small birds in the woods, whose notes were very melodious. The chief <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the inhabitants of the Marquesas and those of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> islands seems to consist in their different degrees of cleanliness: the former do not bathe two or three times a-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, nor wash their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> and face before and after every <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>, as the latter do; and they are besides very slovenly in the manner of preparing their meals. Their diet is chiefly vegetable; though they have hogs and fowls, and catch abundance of fish at certain times. Their drink is pure <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, cocoa nuts being scarce here. It was not long before the propensity of the natives was discovered to be rather to receive than give; for when they had taken a nail as the price of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>-fruit, the article so purchased could not be obtained from them. To remove this dishonest disposition, Captain Cook ordered a musket to be fired over their heads, which terrified them into fair dealing. Soon after the natives had gathered courage enough to venture on board the ship, one of them unfortunately stole an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> stanchion from the gangway, with which he sprang into the sea, and, notwithstanding its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, swam with it to his canoe, and was making to the shore with all speed. A musket was fired over his head to frighten him back, but to no effect, he still <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to make off with his booty; the whistling of another <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> over his head was as ineffectual; an officer, less patient of such an injury than reason and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> should have taught him to be, levelled a musket at the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> fellow, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> him through the head. Captain Cook had given orders to fire over the canoe, but not to kill any one; he was in a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a>, and came up with the canoe soon after. There were two men in her: one sat bailing out the blood and water in a kind of hysterick laugh; the other, a youth of about 14 or 15 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, who afterwards proved to be the son of the deceased, fixed his eyes on the dead body with a serious and dejected countenance. This <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of severity, however, did not estrange the islanders to the ship, and a traffic was carried on to the satisfaction of both parties; bread-fruit, bananas, plantains, and some hogs, were given in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> for small nails, knives, and pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> cloth; red feathers of the Amsterdam island were greatly esteemed here. Captain Cook, accompanied by the gentlemen of the ship, in their walks about the country, lighted on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> which had been the habitation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who had been shot; there they found his son, who fled at their approach; they inquired for his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> relations, and were told that they remained at the top of the mountain to weep and mourn for the dead. Notwithstanding they were then among the relations of a man who had been killed by them, not the least tokens of animosity or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> were discernible among the natives. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> being extremely hot, the inhabitants made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of large fans to cool themselves, of which great numbers were purchased: the fans were formed of a kind of tough bark, or grass, very firmly and curiously plaited, and frequently whitened with shell-lime. Some had large feathered leaves of a Marquesan kind of palm, which answered the purpose of an umbrella. The natives at length became so familiar as to mount the sides of the ship in great numbers. They frequently danced upon the decks for the diversion of the sailors: their dances very much resembled those of Otaheite; their music too was very much the same. A sailor having been inattentive to his duty, received several blows from Captain Cook; on seeing which, the natives exclaimed tape-a-het-te-tina, "he beats his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>." From other instances that had occurred, it was clear that they knew the difference between the commander and his people, but at the same time they conceived them all brethren; and, says Mr Forster, "to me the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> inference is, that they only applied an idea to us in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, which really existed with regard to themselves; they probably look on themselves as one family, of which the eldest born is the chief or king."

MARQUETRY

Pages 652-653

INLAID <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">WORK</a>; a curious kind of work, composed of pieces of hard fine wood of different colours, fastened, in thin slices, on a ground, and sometimes enriched with other matters, as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TORTOISE_SHELL">tortoise-shell</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>, tin, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>. There is another kind of marquetry made, instead of wood, of glasses of various colours; and a third, where nothing but precious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> and the richest marbles are used: but these are more properly called mosaic work. See MOSAIC. The art of inlaying is very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>; and is supposed to have passed from the east to the west, as one of the spoils brought to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. Indeed it was then but a simple thing; nor did it arrive at any tolerable perfection till the 15th century among the Italians: it seems, however, to have arrived at its height in the 17th century among the French. Till John of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERONA">Verona</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with Raphael, the finest works of this kind were only <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, which are what we now call Morescos; but that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a>, who had a genius for <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, stained his woods with dyes <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> boiled oils, which penetrated them. But he went no farther than the representing buildings and perspectives, which requires no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> variety of colours. Those who succeeded him, not only improved on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DYEING">dyeing</a> the woods, by a secret which they found of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> them without consuming, which served exceedingly well for the shadows; but had also the advantage of a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of fine new woods of naturally bright colours, by the discovery of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. With these assistances the art is now capable of imitating any thing; whence some call it the art of painting in wood. The ground whereon the pieces are to be ranged and glued, is ordinarily of oak or fir well dried; and to prevent warping, is composed of several pieces glued together. The wood to be used, being reduced into leaves, of the thickness of a line, is either stained with some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> or made black for shadow; which some effect by putting it in sand, extremely heated over the fire, others by steeping it in lime-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> and sublimate, and others in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of sulphur.—Thus coloured, the contours of the piece are formed according to the parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> they are to represent. This last is the most difficult <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of marquetry, and that wherein most <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> are required. The two <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> instruments used herein are the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> and the vice; the one to hold the matters to be formed; the other, to take off from the extremes, according to occasion. The vice is of wood, having one of its chaps fixed; the other moveable, and is opened and shut by the foot, by means of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a> fastened to a treadle. Its structure is very ingenious, yet simple enough. The leaves to be formed (for there are frequently three or four of the same kind formed together) are put within the chaps of the vice, after being glued on the outermost part of the design whose profile they are to follow; then the workman pressing the treadle, and thus holding fast the piece, with his saw runs over all the outlines of the design.—By thus joining and forming three or four pieces together, they not only <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, but the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> is likewise the better enabled to sustain the efforts of the saw; which, how delicate soever it may be, and how lightly soever the workman may conduct it, without such a precaution would be apt to raise splinters, to the ruin of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of the work. When the work is to consist of one single kind of wood, or of tortoise-shell, on a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> or tin ground, or vice versa, they only form two leaves on one another, i.e., a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> of metal, and a leaf of wood or shell: this they call sawing in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTER">counter</a> parts; for by filling the vacuities of one of the leaves by the pieces coming out of the other, the metal may serve as a ground to the wood, and the wood to the metal. All the pieces thus formed by the saw, and marked to know them again, and the shadow given in the manner already mentioned; they veneer or fasten each in its <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> ground; using for that purpose the best English <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLUE">glue</a>. The whole is put in a press to dry, planed over, and polished with the skin of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-dog, wax, and shave-grass, as in simple <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENEERING">veneering</a>; with this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, however, that in marquetry the fine branches, and several of the more delicate parts of the figures, are touched up and finished with the graver. It is the cabinetmakers, joiners, and toymen, among us, who work in marquetry; it is the enamellers and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>-cutters who <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> in mosaic works: the instruments used in the former are mostly the same with those used by the ebenists.

MARQUIS

Pages 653-653

a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, next in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> to that of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a>. His office is to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> the frontiers and limits of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, which were called the marches, from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEUTONIC">Teutonic</a> word marche, a "limit:" as, in particular, were the marches of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a> and Scotland while they <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> hostile to England. The persons who had command there, were called lords marchers, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> marquesses; whose authority was abolished by statute 27 Hen. VIII. c. 27, though the title had <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> before been made a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of honour. Robert Vere, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, being created marquis of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a> by Richard II. in the eighth year of his reign. A marquis is created by patent; his mantle is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> ermine, three doublings and a half; his title is most <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a>; and his coronet has pearls and strawberry leaves intermixed round, of equal height.

MARRACCI

Pages 653-653
LEWIS, a learned Italian, was born at Lucca in Tuscany in 1612. After having finished his juvenile studies, he entered into the congregation of regular clerks of the mother of God, and distinguished himself early by his learning and merit. He taught rhetoric seven years, and passed through several offices of his order. He applied himself principally to the study of languages, and attained of himself the knowledge of the Greek, the Hebrew, the Syriac, the Chaldee, and Arabic; which last he taught some time at Rome, by the order of Pope Alexander VII. Pope Innocent XI. chose him for his confessor, and placed great confidence in him. He would have advanced him to ecclesiastical dignities, if Marracci had not opposed him.—Marracci died at Rome in 1700, aged 87.—He was the author of several pieces in Italian; but the grand work, which has made him deservedly famous all over Europe, is his edition of the Alkoran, in the original Arabic, with a Latin version, notes, and confutation of his own. It was beautifully printed in two vols. folio at Padua in 1698. The Latin version of the Alkoran, by Marracci, with notes and observations from him and others, and a synopsis of the Mahometan religion, by way of introduction, was published by Heineccius at Leipsic, 1721, in 8vo. Marracci had also a hand in the "Biblia sacra Arabica, sacre congregationis de propaganda fide jussu edita, ad usum ecclesiarum orientalium," Rome, 1671, in 3 vols. folio.

MARRIAGE

Pages 653-659

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a>, both civil and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a>, between a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> and a woman, by which they engage to live together in mutual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> and friendship for the ends of procreation, &c. See <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORAL_PHILOSOPHY">Moral <a class="</a>xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>. Marriage is <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW_OF_NATIONS"><a class="xref</a>" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> of nations, and is in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> among all people. The Romanists account it a sacrament.—The woman, with all her moveable goods, immediately upon marriage, passes wholly in potestatem viri, into the power and disposal of the husband." The first inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> lived together without marriage. Cecrops, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, is said to have been the first author of this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> among that people. After the commonwealths of Greece were settled, marriage was very much encouraged by their laws, and the abstaining from it was discomfited and in many places punished. The Lacedemonians were very remarkable for their severity towards those who deferred marriage beyond a limited <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, as well as to those who wholly abstained from it. The Athenians had an express law, that all commanders, orators, and persons intrusted with any public affair, should be married men. Polygamy was not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> tolerated in Greece. The time of marriage was not the same in all places. The Spartans were not permitted to marry till they arrived at their full strength; the reason assigned for which <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LYCURGUS">Lycurgus</a> was, that the Spartan children might be strong and vigorous: and the Athenian laws are said to have once ordered, that men should not marry till 35 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. The season of the year which they preferred for this purpose was the winter, and particularly the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>, called <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GAMELION">Gamelion</a>. The Greeks thought thought it scandalous to contract marriage within certain degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSANGUINITY">consanguinity</a>; whilst most of the barbarous nations allowed incestuous mixtures. Most of the Grecian states, especially such as made any <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, required their citizens should <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MATCH">match</a> with none but citizens, and the children were not allowed to marry without the consent of their parents. The usual <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> in promising fidelity was kissing each other, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> giving their <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, which was a general form of ratifying all agreements. Before the marriage could be solemnized, the gods were to be consulted, and their assistance implored by prayers and sacrifices, which were offered to some of the deities that superintended these affairs, by the parents or nearest relations of the persons to be married. When the victim was opened, the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GALL">gall</a> was taken out and thrown behind the altar, as being the seat of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGER">anger</a> and malice, and therefore the aversion of all the deities who had the care of love, as well as those who became their votaries. For the particularities relating to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDE">bride</a> and bridegroom, see BRIDE and BRIDEGROOM. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> as well as the Greeks, disallowed of polygamy. A Roman might not marry any woman who was not a Roman. Among the Romans, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KALENDS">kalends</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NONES">nones</a>, and ides of every month were deemed unlucky for the celebration of marriage, as was also the feast of the parentalia, and the whole month of May. The most happy season in every respect was that which followed the ides of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>. The Roman laws speak of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> marriages in very hard and odious terms: Matre jam secundis nuptiis fustata, L. iii. C. de sec. nuptiis. By these laws it was enacted, that the effects of the husband or wife deceased should <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> over to the children, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the survivor should marry a second time. By the law Hac edictali (Cod. de sec. nupt.), the survivor, upon marrying a second time, could not give the person he married a portion more than equal to that of each of the children. In the primitive <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> the respect to chastity was carried so <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, that a second marriage was accounted no other than a lawful whoredom, or a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of bigamy; and there are some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> canons which forbid the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a> from being present at second marriages. Marriage, by the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOSAIC_LAW">Mosaic law</a>, was subject to several restrictions: thus by Levit. chap. xviii. ver. 16, a man was forbid to marry his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>'s widow unless he died without issue; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> it became enjoined as a duty. So it was forbid to marry his wife's sister, while she was living, ver. 18; which was not forbidden before the law, as appears from the instance of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a>. The ancient Roman law is silent on this head; and Papinian is the first who mentions it, on occasion of the marriage of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARACALLA">Caracalla</a>. The lawyers who came after him stretched the bonds of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a> so far, that they placed <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADOPTION">adoption</a> on the same foot with <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. Affinity, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> canonists, renders marriage unlawful to the fourth <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>, inclusive; but this is to be understood of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> affinity, and not of that which is secondary or collateral. Affinis mei affinis, non est affinis meus. It is farther to be observed, that this impediment of marriage does not only follow an affinity contracted by lawful matrimony, but also that contracted by a criminal <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>; with the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, that this last does not extend beyond the second generation; whereas the other, as has been observed, reaches to the fourth. In Germany they have a kind of marriage called morganatic, wherein a man of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> contracting with a woman of inferior <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, he gives her the left <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> in lieu of the right; and stipulates in the contract that the wife shall continue in her former rank or condition; and that the children born of them shall be of the same, so that they become bastards as to matters of inheritance, though they are legitimate in effect. They cannot bear the name or arms of the family. None but princes and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> lords of Germany are allowed this kind of marriage. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> of Leipsic and Jena have declared against the validity of such contracts; maintaining that they cannot <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> the children, especially when the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>'s consent intervenes in the marriage. The Turks have three kinds of marriages, and three sorts of wives; legitimate, wives in kebin, and slaves. They marry the first, hire the second, and buy the third. Among all the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> nations, whether in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, the wife is commonly bought by the husband from her father or those other relations who have an authority over her; and the conclusion of a bargain for this purpose, together with the payment of the price, has therefore become the usual form or solemnity in the celebration of their marriages. The Hebrews also purchased their wives by paying <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> a competent dowry for them; and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> makes it one argument to prove that the ancient Grecians were an uncivilized people, because they used to buy their wives; and in proportion as they laid aside their barbarous manners they left off this practice. The English law considers marriage in no other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> than as a civil contract; the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLINESS">holiness</a> of the matrimonial state being left entirely to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> law, to which it pertains, to punish or annul incestuous or other unscriptural marriages. The law allows marriage to be good and valid, where the parties at the time of making it were willing and able to contract, and actually did contract, in the proper forms and solemnities required by law. The disabilities for contracting are of two sorts: first, such as are canonical, and therefore sufficient by the ecclesiastical laws to void the marriage in the spiritual <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>; such as pre-contract, consanguinity or relation by blood; and affinity, or relation by marriage, and some particular corporal infirmities. But these disabilities in our law do not make the marriage ipso facto void, but voidable only by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> of separation; and marriages are esteemed valid to all civil purposes, unless such separation is actually made during the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of the parties. Thus when a man had married his first wife's sister, and after her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> the bishop's court was proceeding to annul the marriage and bastardise the issue, the court of king's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENCH">bench</a> granted a prohibition quoad hoc; but permitted them to proceed to punish the husband for <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-INCEST">incest</a>. By 32 Hen. VIII. c. 38, it is declared, that all persons may lawfully marry but such as are prohibited by God's law, &c. And that nothing (God's law excepted) shall impeach any marriage but within the Levitical degrees: these are enumerated in the 18th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a>. Marriage chapter of Leviticus, and are illustrated by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COKE">Coke</a> in this manner: a man may not marry his mother, father's sister, mother's sister, sister, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, daughter of his son or daughter, father's wife, uncle's wife, father's wife's daughter, brother's wife, wife's sister, son's wife, or wife's daughter, and daughter of his wife's son or daughter. And a woman may not marry her father, father's brother, mother's brother, brother, son, son of her husband's son or daughter, mother's husband, aunt's husband, sister's husband, husband's brother, and son of her husband's son or daughter. By the civil law first cousins are allowed to marry; but by the canon law both first and second cousins are prohibited. Therefore when it is vulgarly said that first cousins may marry but second cousins cannot, this probably arose by confounding these two laws; for first cousins may marry by the civil law, and second cousins cannot by the canon law. But by the foresaid stat. 32 Hen. VIII. c. 38. it is clear, that both first and second cousins may marry. By the same statute all <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-IMPEDIMENTS">impediments</a> arising from precontracts to other persons were abolished, and declared of none effect unless they had been consummated with bodily knowledge; in which case the canon law holds such contract to be a marriage de facto. But this branch of the statute was repealed by 2 and 3 Ed. VI. c. 23. How far the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of 26 Geo. II. c. 33. (which prohibits all suits in ecclesiastical courts to compel a marriage in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of any contract) may collaterally extend to revive this clause of Henry VIII.'s statute, and abolish the impediment of precontract, Judge Blackstone leaves to be considered by the canonists. We shall here observe, that on a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> of marriage, if it be mutual on both sides, damages may be recovered in case either party refuses to marry; and though no time for the marriage is agreed on, if the plaintiff avers that he offered to marry the defendant who refused it, an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> is maintainable for the damages; but no action shall be brought upon any agreement except it is in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, and signed by the party to be <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a>. The canonical hours for celebrating marriage are from 8 to 12 in the forenoon. The other sort of disabilities are those which are created, or at least enforced, by the municipal laws. These civil disabilities make the contract void <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">ab</a> initio, by rendering the parties incapable of forming any contract at all. The first legal <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISABILITY">disability</a> is a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> marriage, or having another husband or wife living; in which case, besides the penalties consequent upon it as a felony, the second marriage is to all intents and purposes void. See Bigamy and Polygamy. The next legal disability is want of age: therefore if a boy under 14, or a girl under 12 years of age, marries, when either of them comes to the age of consent, they may disagree and declare the marriage void, without any divorce or sentence in the spiritual court. However, in our law it is so far a marriage, that if at the age of consent they agree to continue together, they need not be married again. Another incapacity arises from want of consent of parents or guardians. By several statutes, viz. 6 and 7 W. III. c. 6, 7, 8, W. III. c. 35, 10 Ann. c. 19. penalties of 100l. are laid on every clergyman who marries a couple either without publication of banns, which may give notice to parents or guardians, or without a license, to obtain which the consent of parents or guardians must be sworn to. And by 4 and 5 Ph. and M. c. 8. whoever marries any woman-child under the age of 16 years, without consent of parents or guardians, shall be subject to fine or five years imprisonment; and her estate during her husband's life shall be enjoyed by the next heir. Thus also in France the sons cannot marry without consent of parents till 30 years of age, nor the daughters till 25; and in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> the sons are at their own disposal at 25, and the daughters at 20. And by the marriage act, viz. 26 Geo. II. c. 33. it is enacted, that all marriages celebrated by license (for banns suppose notice), where either of the parties is under 21, not being a widow or widower, without the consent of the father, or if he be not living, of the mother or guardians, shall be absolutely void. However, provision is made where the mother or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a> is non compos, beyond <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, or unreasonably forward, to dispense with such consent at the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a> of the lord <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>; but no provision is made in case the father should labour under any mental or other incapacity. A fourth incapacity is want of reason. It is provided by 15 Geo. II. c. 30. that the marriage of lunatics and sons under pluriesies (if found lunatics under a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> or committed to the care of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TRUSTEES">trustees</a> by any act of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>) before they are declared of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> mind by the lord chancellor or the majority of such trustees, shall be totally void. Lastly, The parties must not only be willing and able to contract, but must actually contract themselves in due form of law, to make it a good civil marriage. Any contract made per verba de praesenti, or in words of the present tense, and in case of cohabitation per verba de futuro also between persons able to contract, was before the late act deemed a valid marriage to many purposes, and the parties might be compelled in the spiritual courts to celebrate it in facie ecclesiae. But these verbal contracts are now of no force to compel a future marriage. Nor is any marriage at present valid that is not celebrated in some <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> church or public chapel, unless by dispensation from the archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>. It must also be preceded by publication of banns or by license from the spiritual judge. A marriage in pursuance of banns must be solemnized in one of the churches or chapels where the banns were published. No parson, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a>, &c. shall be obliged to publish banns of matrimony, unless the persons to be married shall, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> days before the time required for the first publication, deliver to him a notice in writing of their true names, and of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> or houses of their respective abode within such parish, &c. and of the time that they have dwelt in such house or houses. And the said banns shall be published upon three Sundays preceding the solemnization of marriage during the time of public <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>: in case the parents or guardians, or either of the parties who shall be under the age of 21 years, shall openly and publicly declare, or cause to be declared, in the church or chapel where the banns shall be so published, at the time of such publication, their dissent to such marriage, such publication of banns shall be void. And when the parties dwell in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> parishes, the curate of the one parish shall not solemnize matrimony betwixt them without a certificate of the banns being thrice asked from the curate. Marriage of the other parish. A marriage in pursuance of a license (except a special license), must be solemnized in such church or chapel where the license is granted; and no license of marriage shall be granted by any archbishop, bishop, &c., to solemnize any marriage in any other church, &c., than in the parish church, &c., within which the usual <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of abode of one of the parties shall have been for four weeks immediately before the granting such license. By the same statute all marriages shall be solemnized in the presence of two credible witnesses at the least, besides the minister, who shall sign their attestation thereof; and immediately after the celebration of every marriage, an entry thereof shall be made in the parish <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a>, expressing that the said marriage was celebrated by banns or license; and if both or either of the parties be under age, with consent of the parents or guardians, as the case shall be, signed by the minister, and also by the parties married, and attested by the two witnesses present. It is held to be also essential to a marriage, that it be performed by a person in orders; though the intervention of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> to solemnize this contract is merely juris positivi and not juris naturalis aut divini; it being said that Pope Innocent III. was the first who ordained the celebration of marriage in the church, before which it was totally a civil contract. And in the times of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> rebellion, all marriages were performed by the justices of the peace; and these marriages were declared valid without any fresh solemnization, by 12 Car. II. c. 33. But as the law now stands, we may upon the whole collect, that no marriage by the temporal law is ipso facto void, that is celebrated by a person in orders; in a parish church, a public chapel, or elsewhere, by a special dispensation; in pursuing of banns or a license; between single persons; consenting; of sound mind; and of the age of 21 years; or of the age of 14 in males and 12 in females, with consent of parents or guardians, or without it, in case of widowhood. And no marriage is voidable by the Marriage ecclesiastical law after the death of either of the parties; nor during their lives, unless for the canonical impediments of precontract, if that indeed still exists; of consanguinity; and of affinity or corporal imbecility subsisting previous to the marriage. By 26 Geo. II. c. 33, the substance of which has been already recited, if any person shall solemnize matrimony in any other place than a church, &c., where banns have been usually published, unless by special license, or without publication of banns, unless license of marriage be first obtained from some person having authority to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> the same, every such person knowingly so offending shall be guilty of felony, and transported for 14 years; the prosecution to be within three years. By the same statute, to make a false entry into a marriage register; to alter it when made; to forge or counterfeit such entry, or a marriage license, or aid and abet such forgery; to utter the same as true, knowing it to be counterfeit; or to destroy or procure the destruction of any register in order to vacate any marriage, or subject any person to the penalties of this act; all these offences, knowingly and wilfully committed, subject the party to the guilt of felony without benefit of clergy. But this act doth not extend to the marriages of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> family; nor to Scotland; nor to any marriages among the people called <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUAKERS">Quakers</a>, or among persons professing the Jewish <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, where both the parties are Quakers or Jews respectively; nor to any marriages beyond the seas. In Scotland, the parties living together as husband and wife, or declaring themselves so before witnesses, makes a valid though informal marriage. See Law, Part III. No. 165. For the proportions which marriages bear to births, and births to burials, in several parts of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, Mr <a class="xref" The reader may find many curious calculations and remarks relating to this subject in Dr Price's excellent <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, entitled Observations on Reversionary Payments. From the preceding table it appears, that marriages, one with another, do each produce about four births, both in England and other parts of Europe. Dr Price observes, that the births at Paris, as may be seen in the table, are above four times the weddings; and therefore it may seem, that in the most healthy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> situations, every wedding produces above four children; and though this be the case in Paris, for reasons which he has given, he has observed nothing like it in any other great town. He adds, that from comparing the births and weddings in countries and towns where registers of them have been kept, it appears, that in the former, marriages one with another seldom produce less than four children each; generally between four and five, and sometimes above five; but in towns seldom above four, generally between three and four, and sometimes under three. It is necessary to be observed here, that though the proportion of annual births to weddings has been considered as giving the true <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of children derived from each marriage, taking all marriages one with another: yet this is only true, when, for many years, the births and burials have kept nearly equal. Where there is an excess of the births occasioning an increase, the proportion of annual births to weddings must be less than the proportion of children derived from each marriage; and the contrary must take place where there is a decrease: and by Mr King's computation, about one in a hundred and four persons marry; the number of people in England being estimated at five millions and a half, whereof about forty-one thousand annually marry. In the district of Vaud in Switzerland, the married are very nearly a third part of the inhabitants. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a> Graunt and Mr King disagree in the proportions between males and females, the latter making 10 males to 13 females in London; in other cities and towns, and in the villages and hamlets, 100 males to 99 females: but Major Graunt, both from the London and country bills, computes, that there are in England 14 males to 13 females; whence he justly infers, that the Christian religion, prohibiting polygamy, is more agreeable to the law of nature than Mahometanism and others that allow it. This proportion of males to females Mr Derham thinks pretty <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a>, being agreeable to what he had observed himself. In the hundred years, for instance, of his own parish register of Upminster, though the burials of males and females were nearly equal, being 633 males and 623 females in all that time; yet there were baptized 709 males and but 675 females, which is 13 females to 13.7 males. From a register kept at Northampton for 28 years, from 1741 to 1770, it appears, that the proportion of males to females that were born in that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> is 2361 to 2288, or nearly 13.4 to 13. However, though more males are born than females, Dr Price has sufficiently shown, that there is a considerable difference between the probabilities of life among males and females in favour of the latter; so that males are more shortlived. Marriage is shortlived than females; and as the greater mortality of males takes place among children, as well as among males at all ages, the fact cannot be accounted for merely by their being more subject to untimely deaths by various accidents, and by their being addicted to the excesses and irregularities which shorten life. Mr Kersseboom informs us, that during the course of 125 years in Holland, females have in all accidents of age lived about three or four years longer than the same number of males. In several towns of Germany, &c., it appears that of 7270 married persons who had died, the proportion of married men who died to the married women was 3 to 2; and in Breslaw for eight years, as 5 to 3. In all Pomerania, during <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> years from 1748 to 1756, this proportion was nearly 15 to 11. Among the ministers and professors in Scotland, 20 married men die to 12 married women at a medium of 27 years, or in the proportion of 5 to 3; so that there is the chance of 3 to 2, and in some circumstances even a greater chance, that the woman shall be the survivor of a marriage, and not the man; and this difference cannot be accounted for merely by the difference of age between husbands and their wives, without admitting the greater mortality of males. In the district of Vaud in Switzerland, it appears, that half the females do not die till the age of 46 and upwards, though half the males die under 36. It is likewise an indisputable fact, that in the beginning of life, the rate of mortality among males is much greater than among females. From a table formed by Dr Price, from a register kept for 20 years at Gainsborough, it appears, that of those who lived to 80, the major part, in the proportion of 49 to 32, are females. Mr Deparcieux at Paris, and Mr Wargentin in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, have farther observed, that not only women live longer than men, but that married women live longer than single women. From some registers examined by Mr <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol15.html#article-MURET">Muret</a> in Switzerland, it appears, that of equal numbers of single and married women between 15 and 25, more of the former died than of the latter, in the proportion of 2 to 1. With respect to the difference between the mortality of males and females, it is found to be much less in country parishes and villages than in towns; and hence it is inferred, that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> life in males is more brittle than in females, only in consequence of adventitious causes, or of some particular debility, that takes place in polished and luxurious <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a>, and especially in great towns. From the inequality above stated between the males and females that are born, it is reasonable to infer, that one man ought to have but one wife; and yet that every woman without polygamy may have a husband: this surplusage of males above females being spent in the supplies of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, the seas, &c., from which the women are exempt. Perhaps, says Dr Price, it might have been observed with more reason, that this provision had in view that particular weakness or delicacy in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of males, which makes them more subject to mortality; and which consequently renders it necessary that more of them should be produced, in order to preserve in the world a due proportion between the two sexes. That this is a work of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a>, and not of chance, is well made out by the very laws of chance by Dr Arbuthnot; who supposes Thomas to lay against John, that for 82 years running more males shall be born than females; and giving all allowances in the computation to Thomas's side, he makes the odds against Thomas, that it does not so happen, to be near five millions of millions of millions of millions to one; but for ages of ages, according to the world's age, to be near an infinite number to one. According to Mr Kersseboom's observations, there are about 325 children born from 100 marriages. Mr Kersseboom, from his observations, estimates the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> of marriages one with another, as in the following table: | Ages | Surviving Couples | |------|------------------| | 40 | 24 | | 50 | 22 | | 60 | 23 | | 70 | 19 | | 80 | 17 | | 90 | 14 | | 100 | 12 | Phil. Trans. No 468. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a>. iii. p. 319. Dr Price has shown, that on De Moivre's <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a>, or that the probabilities of life decrease uniformly (see Complement of Life,) the duration of survivorship is equal to the duration of marriage, when the ages are equal; or, in other words, that the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> of two <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> lives, the ages being equal, is the same with the expectation of survivorship; and, consequently, the number of survivors, or (which is the same, supposing no second marriages) of widows and widowers, alive together, which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> arise from any given set of such marriages constantly kept up, will be equal to the whole number of marriages, or half of them (the number of widows in particular) equal to half the number of marriages. Thus, the expectation of two joint lives, both 40, is the third of 46 years, or their complement, i.e. 15 years and 4 months; and this is also the expectation of the survivor. That is, supposing a set of marriages between persons all 40, they will one with another last just this time, and the survivors will last the same time. In adding together the years which any great number of such marriages, and their survivorships, have lasted, the sums would be found to be equal. It is observed farther, that if the number expressing the expectation of single or joint lives, multiplied by the number of single or joint lives whose expectation it is, be added annually to a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> or town, the sum gives the whole number living together, to which such an annual addition would in time grow: thus, since 19, or the third of 57, is the expectation of two joint lives whose <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> age is 29, or common complement 57, 20 marriages every year between persons of this age would in 57 years grow to 20 times 19, or 380 marriages always existing together. The number of survivors also arising from these marriages, and always living together, would in twice 57 years increase to the same number. Moreover, the particular proportion that becomes extinct every year, out of the whole number constantly existing together of single or joint lives, must, wherever this number undergoes no <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a>, be exactly the same with the expectation of those lives at the time when their existence commenced. Thus, if it were found found that a 19th part of all the marriages among any body of men whose numbers do not vary, are dissolved every year by the death of either the husband or wife, it would appear, that 19 was at the time they were contracted, the expectation of these marriages. Dr Price observes, that the annual <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> of weddings among the ministers and professors in Scotland for the last 27 years has been 31; and the average of married persons for 17 years ending in 1767, had been 667. This number, divided by 31, gives 214, the expectation of marriage among them; which, he says, is above 21 years more than the expectation of marriage would be, by Dr Halley's table, on the supposition, that all first, second, and third marriages, may be justly considered as commencing one with another so early as the age of 32; and he has proved, that the expectation of two equal joint lives is to the expectation of a single life of the same age as 2 to 3; consequently, the expectation of a single life at 32, among the ministers in Scotland, cannot be less than 32.25. If we suppose the mean ages of all who marry annually to be 33 and 25, the expectation of every marriage would be 19 years; or one with another they would be all extinct in 19 years: the marriages which continue beyond this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, though fewer in number, enjoying among them just as much more duration as those that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> short of it enjoy less. But it appears from the observations and tables of Mr Muret, that, in the district of Vaud (dividing half the number of married persons, viz. 38,328, by the annual medium of weddings, viz. 808), the expectation of marriage is only 23½ years: so much higher are the probabilities of life in the country than in towns, or than they ought to be, according to De Moivre's hypothesis. Marriage (Maritagium), in Law, signifies not only the lawful joining of man and wife, but also the right of bestowing a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARD">ward</a> or a widow in marriage, as well as the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> given in marriage. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLUTION">Dissolution</a> of Marriage. See Divorce. Forcible Marriage. See Forcible Marriage. Frank Marriage. See Frank. Jactitation of Marriage, in Law, is one of the first and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> matrimonial causes, when one of the parties boasts or gives out, that he or she is married to the other, whereby a common reputation of their matrimony may ensue. On this ground the party injured may <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBEL">libel</a> the other in the spiritual court; and unless the defendant undertakes and makes out a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the actual marriage, he or she is enjoined perpetual silence on that head; which is the only remedy the ecclesiastical courts can give for this injury. Marriage Settlement is a legal act, previous to marriage, whereby a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINTURE">jointure</a> is secured to the wife after the death of the husband. These settlements seem to have been in use among the ancient Germans, and their kindred <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> the Gauls. Of the former Tacitus give us this account: Dotcm non uxor marito, sed uxor maritus affert: intersunt parentes et propinqui, et munera probant (De Mor. Germ. c. 18.) And Caesar (De <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELL">Bell</a>. Gallic. lib. vi. c. 18.) has given us the terms of a marriage settlement among the Gauls, as nicely calculated as any modern jointure: Viri, quantas pecunias ab uxoris dotis nomine accepereunt, tantas ex suis bonis, aestimatione facta, cum dotibus communicant. Hujus omnis pecunia conjunctim ratio habetur, fructusque servatur. Uter corum vita superavit, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> eum pars utriusque cum fructibus superiorum temporum pervenit. The dauphin's commentator supposes that this Gaulish custom was the ground of the new regulations made by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTINIAN">Justinian</a>, Nov. 97, with regard to the provision for widows among the Romans; but surely there is as much reason to suppose, says Judge Blackstone, that it gave the hint for our statutable jointures. Comment. vol. ii. p. 138. See an excellent marriage settlement by Blackstone in the appendix to the second volume of his Commentaries. Duty of Marriage, is a term used in some ancient customs, signifying an obligation on women to marry. To understand this, it must be observed, that old maids and widows about sixty, who held fees in body, or were charged with any personal or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> services, were anciently obliged to marry, to render those services to the lord by their husbands, or to indemnify the lord for what they could not do in person. And this was called duty or service of marriage. Policy of encouraging Marriage.—Till the principles of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> were explained by Malthus, it was generally held to be the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of governments to encourage marriage, and to discourage celibacy. Dr Halley has enlarged on this subject, and has shown by computation, that were it not for the backwardness of people to marry, from the prospect of the necessary trouble and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> in providing for a family, there might be four times as many births as there are. It has been a favourite object, too, with most of the governments of Europe at one time or another, to encourage marriage with the view of increasing the population. But we know now that all such attempts are not merely idle, but mischievous. The motives that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> men to marry are at all times sufficiently powerful, and the most common <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a> of individuals has been, not in resisting, but in yielding to these motives, without a due regard to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>. Population, so far from requiring any <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> stimulus, has a constant tendency to exceed the means of subsistence; and it is only kept down to the proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>, partly by the prudence of those who live in celibacy, and partly by the pressure of misery from the want or the insufficiency of food. To increase the number of marriages, therefore, without regard to the ability of the parents to bring up their offspring, would have the effect of bringing human beings into the world to be destroyed by want or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>.

MARROW

Pages 659-659

in Anatomy, a soft oleaginous substance contained in the cavity of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>. See Anatomy, No. 5.

MARRUBIUM

Pages 659-659
White Horehound; a genus of plants belonging to the didymia class; and in the natural method ranking under the 42d order, Verticillate. See Botany Index.

MARS

Pages 659-661

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, one of the eleven <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>, situated without the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-EARTH_S"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>'s orbit, and remarkable for the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of its <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> and the redness of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. See Astronomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of this planet, according to Dr * Supple-Brewster *, is owing to the same cause as the redness of the morning and evening <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>. When a beam of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> light passes through any medium, its colour in- Astronomy, clines vol. ii. elimes to red, in proportion to the space through which it has travelled, and the density of the medium. The momentum of the red <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> least refrangible rays being greater than that of the violet or most refrangible rays, the former <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> make their way through the resisting medium, while the latter are either reflected or absorbed. The colour of the beam, therefore, when it reaches the eye, must partake of the colour of the least refrangible ray; and the redness of this colour must increase with the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the violet rays that have been obstructed. Hence we see, that the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, and stars appear red, when in the horizon; and that every <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUMINOUS">luminous</a> object seen through a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIST">mist</a> is of a ruddy hue. Now, the planet Mars is allowed to have an atmosphere of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> density and extent, as is manifest from the dim appearance of the fixed stars that are placed at a considerable distance from his disk. The sun's light, therefore, by which this planet is illuminated, having to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> twice through the atmosphere of Mars before it reaches the earth, must be deprived of a great proportion of the violet rays; and consequently the colour of the resulting light by which Mars is visible, must be red. As there is a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of colour among the other planets, and likewise among the fixed stars, are we not entitled to conclude, that those in which the red colour predominates, have the greatest or the densest atmospheres? According to this principle, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a> must have the next greatest atmosphere to that of Mars. Mars, in Pagan worship, the god of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. He was, according to some, the son of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> and Juno; while others say that he was the son of Juno alone, who being displeased at Jupiter's having produced <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a> from his brain, without <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> aid, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> conceived without the assistance of the other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a>, by touching a flower shown to her by Flora in the plains of Oléus, and became the mother of this formidable deity. The amours of Mars and Venus, and the manner in which Vulcan caught and exposed them to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAUGHTER">laughter</a> of the other gods, have been described by several of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> poets. He is represented as having several wives and mistresses, and a considerable number of children. He was held in the highest veneration by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, both from his being the father of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a> their founder, and from their inclination to conquest; and had magnificent <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> erected to him at Rome. Mars is usually represented in a chariot, drawn by furious horses. He is completely armed; and extends his spear with the one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and grasps a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, imbrued in blood, with the other. He has a fierce and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> aspect. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCORD">Discord</a> is represented preceding his car; and Clamour, Fear, and Terror, appear in his train. The victims sacrificed to him were the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WOLF">wolf</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, the woodpecker, the vulture, and the cock. Mars, among the older chemists, denotes <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>; that metal being supposed to be under the influence of the planet Mars. Marsais, Cesar Chesneau Du, an eminent literary character, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARSEILLES">Marseilles</a> 1676. He attached himself at an early <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> to the order of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> of the oratory; but the situation was too narrow for his genius, and he soon left it. At <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> he married, became advocate, and entered on this new profession with great success and approbation. Disappointed, however, in his expectations of making a speedy fortune, he abandoned the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> also. About this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the peevish humour of his wife occasioned a separation. We next find him as governor to the son of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> de Maisons; and when the premature <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the father deprived him of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of his industry, he engaged with the famous Law in the same capacity. After the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of this extraordinary projector, he completed the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of the marquis de Beaufremont's children, and reared pupils worthy of his genius and industry. Although he was accused of a tendency to Deism, and though there was good reason for the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a>, yet he never infused into the minds of his scholars any principle inconsistent with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> morality, or with the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. When he left M. de Beaufremont's family, he took a boarding <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, in which, after a method of his own, he educated a certain number of young men. Unexpected circumstances obliged him to abandon this useful undertaking.
