In the year 1572, in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> IX, many of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> were invited to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, under a solemn oath of safety, upon occasion of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Navarre with the French king's sister; viz. the king of Navarre's mother, Coligni <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a> of France, with other <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>-dowager of Navarre, a zealous Protestant, was poisoned by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of gloves before the marriage was solemnized; and on the 24th of August 1572, being Bartholomew's day, about daybreak, upon the toll of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELL">bell</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of St Germain, the butchery began. The admiral was basely murdered in his own <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>; and then thrown out of the window, to gratify the malice of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Guise; his head was afterwards Massacre, terwards cut off, and sent to the king and queen-mother; and his body, after a thousand indignities offered to it, hung up by the feet on a gibbet. After this, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MURDERERS">murderers</a> ravaged the whole <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Paris, and butchered in three days above ten thousand lords, gentlemen, presidents, and people of all ranks. An horrible <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of things, says Thuanus, when the very streets and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> resounded with the noise of those that met together for <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> and plunder; the groans of those who were dying, and the shrieks of such as were <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> going to be butchered, were everywhere heard; the bodies of the slain thrown out of the windows; the courts and chambers of the houses filled with them; the dead bodies of others dragged through the streets, their blood running <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the channels in such plenty, that torrents seemed to empty themselves in the neighbouring river; and in a word, an innumerable multitude of men, women with child, maidens, and children, were all involved in one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> destruction; and the gates and entrances of the king's <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> all besmeared with their blood. From the city of Paris the massacre spread almost throughout the whole <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. In the city of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEAUX">Meaux</a> they threw above two hundred into jail; and after they had ravished and killed a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of women, and plundered the houses of the Protestants, they executed their fury on those they had imprisoned, and calling them out one by one, they were killed, as Thuanus expresses, like sheep in a market; the bodies of some were flung into ditches, and of others into the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAINE">Maine</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a> they murdered above five hundred men, women, and children, and enriched themselves with their spoil. The same cruelties were practised at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGERS">Angers</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol21.html#article-TROYES">Troyes</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOURGES">Bourges</a>, La Charité, and especially at Lyons, where they inhumanly destroyed above eight hundred Protestants; children hanging on their parents necks; parents embracing their children; putting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> about the necks of some, dragging them through the streets, and throwing them, mangled, torn, and half dead, into the river. It would be endless to mention the butcheries committed at Valence, Romaine, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROUEN">Rouen</a>, &c. We shall, therefore, only add, that, according to Thuanus, above thirty thousand Protestants were destroyed in this massacre, or as others with greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> affirm, above one hundred thousand. Yet medals were struck at Paris in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of it. But how were the news of this butchery received at Rome, that faithful city, that holy mother of churches! How did the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a> of Christ, the successor of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>, and the father of the Christian world, relish it? Let Thuanus tell the horrid <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. When the news, says he, came to Rome, it was wonderful to see how they exulted for joy. On the 6th of September, when the letters of the pope's legate were read in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of the cardinals, by which he assured the pope that all was transacted by the express <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> and command of the king, it was immediately decreed that the pope should <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> with his cardinals to the church of St Mark, and in the most solemn manner give thanks to God for so great a blessing conferred on the see of Rome and the Christian world; and that on the Monday after, solemn <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> should be celebrated in the church of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>; at which the pope, Greg. XII., and cardinals were present; and that a jubilee should be published throughout the whole Christian world, Massacre and the cause of it declared to be, to return thanks to God for the extirpation of the enemies of the truth and church in France. In the evening the cannon of St Angelo were fired, to testify the public joy; the whole city illuminated with bonfires; and no one sign of rejoicing omitted that was usually made for the greatest victories obtained in favour of the Roman church. MASSAGETÆ, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> people about whose seat there is as much doubt as about that of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMAZONS">Amazons</a>; Tibullus and Ammian <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> them near <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBANIA">Albania</a>, beyond the Araxes, which sometimes denotes the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OXUS">Oxus</a>; it is probable they dwelt to the east of Sogdiana, (Dionysius Periegetes, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>, Arrian).

MASSALIANS

Pages 728-728

a set of enthusiasts who sprang up about the year 361, in the reign of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Constantius, who maintained that men have two souls, a celestial and a diabolical, and that the latter is driven out by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>. MASSANIELLO. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>.

MASSETER

Pages 728-728

in Anatomy. See there (<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">Table</a> of the Muscles). MASSICOT. See Masticot.

MASSIEU

Pages 728-728

WILLIAM, a learned French writer, member of the Academy of Belles Lettres, and of the French Academy, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAEN">Caen</a> in Normandy in 1665, and completed his studies at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, when he entered amongst the Jesuits; but afterwards left them, that he might follow his inclination to polite literature with the greater freedom. In 1710 he was made Greek professor in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>; and enjoyed that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which happened at Paris in 1722. He wrote, 1. Several curious dissertations in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of the Academy of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">Inscriptions</a>. 2. A <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the French <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, in 12mo, &c.

MASSILIA

Pages 728-728

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of Gallicia Narbonensis, peopled by a colony of Phoceans, from Phocæa, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IONIA">Ionia</a>, universally celebrated, not only for its port, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, and strength, but especially for its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a> of manners and for its learning. Now <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARSEILLES">Marseilles</a>, a city of Provence.

MASSILLON

Pages 728-730

JEAN BAPTISTE, son of a notary at <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HIERES">Hieres</a> in Provence, was born in 1663, and entered into the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> of the oratory in 1681. He gained the affections of every person in the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> to which he was sent, by the charms of his genius, the liveliness of his character, and by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FUND">fund</a> of the most delicate and unaffected <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a>. His first attempts in the art of eloquence were made at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIENNE">Vienne</a>, while he was professor of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>. His funeral <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORATION">oration</a> on Henry de Villars, archbishop of that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, received universal approbation. This success induced Father de la Tour, who was at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> general of the congregation, to call him to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. After he had been there for some time, he was asked what he thought of the preachers who made a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> on that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>?—“I find them possessed of great genius and abilities (answered he); but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> I preach, I <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not preach like them.” He in fact kept his word, and struck out a new path in this great field of eloquence. P. Bourdaloue was excepted from the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of those whom he proposed not to imitate. If he did not take him for a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> in every thing, the reason was, that his genius led him to a different <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of eloquence.—His His manner of composing, therefore, was peculiar to himself, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of men of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and judgement, was superior to that of Bourdaloue. The affecting and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> simplicity of the father of the oratory, (said a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>), appears fitter to bring home the truths of Christianity to the heart than all the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIALECTICS">dialectics</a> of the Jesuit. We must seek for the logic of the gospel in our own breasts; and the most powerful reasonings on the indispensable duty of relieving the distressed, will make no <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> on that man who has beheld without concern the sufferings of his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>. If logic is necessary, it is only in matters of opinion; and these are fitter for the press than for the pulpit, which ought not to be the theatre of learned discussions. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of these reflections was clearly perceived when he appeared at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. Upon preaching his first Advent sermon at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSAILLES">Versailles</a>, he received this eulogium from the mouth of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. "Father, when I hear others preach, I am very well pleased with them; but whenever I hear you, I am dissatisfied with myself." The first time he preached his famous sermon on the small number of the elect, the whole audience were, at a certain <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of it, seized with a sudden and violent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMOTION">emotion</a>, and almost every person half rose from his seat by a kind of involuntary movement. The murmur of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCLAMATION">acclamation</a> and surprise was so great that it threw the orator into confusion; but this only heightened the impression of that pathetic discourse. What was most surprising in Massillon, were his descriptions of the world, which were so sublime, so delicate, and so striking in the resemblance. When he was asked, whence a man, like him, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> was dedicated to retirement, could borrow them; he answered "From the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> heart; however little we examine it, we will find in it the seeds of every <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>. When I compose a sermon (added he), I imagine myself consulted upon some doubtful piece of business. I give my whole application to determine the person who has recourse to me, to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> the good and proper <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>. I exhort him, and urge him, and I leave him not till he has yielded to my persuasions." His <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECLAMATION">declamation</a> did not fail to be accompanied with success. "We think we see him in our pulpits (say those who had the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> of hearing him), with the simple <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, the modest carriage, the downcast and humble looks, the easy gesture, the affecting tone, and the countenance of a man deeply penetrated with his subject, conveying the clearest information to the understanding, and raising the most tender emotions in the heart." Baron, the famous comedian, having met him one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> which was open for the reception of men of letters, paid him this compliment: "Continue to deliver as you do. Your manner is peculiar to yourself; leave the observance of rules to others." When this famous <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTOR">actor</a> came from hearing one of his sermons, truth drew from him the following confession, which is so humiliating to his profession: "Friend (said he to one of his companions who accompanied him), here is an orator; we are only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTORS">actors</a>." In 1704, Massillon made his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> appearance at court, and displayed still more eloquence than before. Louis XIV. after expressing his satisfaction to him, added, in the most gracious tone of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, Et je veux, mon père, vous entendre tous les deux ans. These flattering encomiums did not lessen his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a>. When Massillon, one of his fellows was congratulating him upon his preaching admirably, according to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>; Oh! give over, Father (replied he), the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a> has told me so already, much more eloquently than you." The duties of his office did not prevent him from enjoying <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> he forgot that he was a preacher, but always without trespassing against decency. One day when he was at the house of M. de Crozat, the latter said to him, "Father, your doctrine terrifies me, but I am encouraged by your life." He was chosen on account of his philosophical and conciliatory disposition of mind, to reconcile the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> de Noailles with the Jesuits. All he gained by his attempts was the displeasure of both parties; and he found that it was easier to convert sinners than to reconcile theologians. In 1717, the regent, personally acquainted with his merit, appointed him to the bishopric of Clermont. The next year, being destined to preach before Louis XV. who was only <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, he composed in six weeks those discourses which are so well known by the name of Petit Carême. These are the chef d'œuvre of this orator, and indeed of the oratorical art. They ought continually to be read by preachers as models for the formation of their taste, and by princes as <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LESSONS">lessons</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>. Massillon was admitted into the French academy a year afterwards, in 1719. The abbacy of Savigny becoming vacant, the cardinal du Bois, to whom he had been weak enough to give an attestation for being a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, procured it for him. The funeral oration of the duchess of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a>, in 1723, was the last discourse he pronounced in Paris. He never afterwards left his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a>, where his gentleness, politeness, and kindness, had gained him the affection of all who knew him. He reduced the exorbitant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of the episcopal roll to moderate sums. In two years, he caused 20,000 livres to be privately conveyed to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOTEL">Hotel</a> Dieu of Clermont. His peaceable disposition was never more displayed than while he was a bishop. He took great pleasure in collecting the fathers of the oratory and the Jesuits at his country house, and in making them join in some diversion. He died on the 28th of September 1742, at the age of 79. His name has become that of eloquence itself. Nobody ever knew better how to touch the passions. Preferring sentiment to everything else, he communicated to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> that lively and salutary emotion which excites in us the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of virtue. What pathetic eloquence did his discourses display! what knowledge of the human heart! what constant disclosing of a mind deeply affected with his subject! what strain of truth, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and humanity! what imagination, at once the most lively, and guided by the soundest judgment! <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">Just</a> and delicate thoughts; splendid and lofty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>; elegant, well chosen, sublime, and harmonious expressions; brilliant and natural images; true and lively colouring; a clear, neat, swelling and copious style, equally suited to the capacity of the multitude, and fitted to please the man of genius, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, and the courtier, form the character of Massillon's eloquence, especially in his Petit Carême. He could at once think, describe, and feel. It has been justly observed concerning him, that he was to Bourdaloue what Racine was to Corneille. To give the finishing stroke An excellent edition of Massillon's works was published by his nephew at Paris in 1745 and 1746, in 14 vols; <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> 12mo, and 12 vols. of a small size.—Among them we find, 1. Complete sets of Sermons for Advent and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LENT">Lent</a>. It is particularly in his moral discourses, such as are almost all these of his sermons for Advent and Lent, that Massillon's genius appears. He excels, says M. d'Alembert, in that species of eloquence, which alone may be preferred to all others, which goes directly to the heart, and which agitates without wounding the soul. He searches the inmost recesses of the heart, and lays open the secret workings of the passions, with so delicate and tender a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, that we are hurried along rather than overcome. His diction, which is always easy, elegant, and pure, everywhere partakes of that noble simplicity, without which there can be neither good taste nor true eloquence; and this simplicity is, in Massillon, joined to the most attractive and the sweetest <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a>, from which it likewise borrows new graces. In short, to complete the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARM">charm</a> produced by this enchanting style, we perceive that these beauties are perfectly natural; that they flow easily from this source, and that they have occasioned no labour to the composer. There even occur sometimes in the expressions, in the turns, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in the affecting <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MELODY">melody</a> of his style, instances of negligence which may be called happy, because they completely remove every appearance of labour. By thus abandoning himself to the natural current of thought and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, Massillon gained as many friends as hearers. He knew, that the more anxious an orator appears to raise admiration, he will find those who hear him the less disposed to bestow it. 2. Several Funeral Orations, Discourses, and Panegyrics, which had never been published. 3. Ten discourses, known by the name of Petit Carême. 4. The Conferences Ecclesiastiques, which he delivered in the seminary of St Magloire upon his arrival at Paris; those which he delivered to the curates of his diocese; and the discourses which he pronounced at the head of the synods which he assembled every year. 5. Paraphrases on several of the Psalms. The illustrious author of these excellent tracts wished that they had introduced into France a practice which prevails in England, of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> sermons instead of preaching them from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>; a custom which is very convenient, but by which all the warmth and fervour of eloquence are lost. He, as well as two others of his brethren, had stopt short in the pulpit exactly on the same day.—They were all to preach at different hours on Good Friday, and they went to hear one another in succession. The memory of the first failed; which so terrified the other two, that they experienced the same fate. When our illustrious orator was asked, what was his best sermon? he answered, "That which I am most <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of." The same reply is ascribed to Bourdaloue. The celebrated P. la Rue was of the opinion of Massillon, that getting by heart was a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a> which deprived the pulpit of a great many orators, and which was attended with many inconveniences to those who dedicated themselves to it. The abbé de la Porte has collected into one vol. 12mo, the most striking ideas, and the most sublime strokes, which occur in the works of the celebrated bishop of Clermont. This collection, Massillon which is made with great judgment, appeared at Paris in 1748, 12mo, and forms the 15th volume of the large edition in 12mo, and the 13th of the small in 12mo. It is entitled, Pensées sur differens sujets de morale et de piété, tirées, &c.

MASSINGER

Pages 730-730
PHILIP, an English dramatic poet, was born at Salisbury about the year 1581, and was educated at Oxford. He left the university without taking any degree; and went to London to improve his poetical genius by polite conversation. There he wrote many tragedies and comedies, which were received with vast applause, and were greatly admired for the economy of the plots and the purity of the style. He was at the same time a person of the most consummate modesty; which rendered him extremely beloved by the poets of his time, particularly by Fletcher, Middleton, Rowley, Field, and Decker, who thought it an honour to write in conjunction with him. He died suddenly at his house on the Bank-side in Southwark, near the playhouse; and was interred in St Saviour's churchyard, in the same grave with Mr Fletcher the poet.

MASSIVE

Pages 730-730

among builders, an epithet given to whatever is too heavy and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a>; thus a massive <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> is one too short and thick for the order whose <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> it bears; and a massive wall is one whose openings <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> lights are too small in proportion.

MASSON

Pages 730-732

JOHN, a reformed minister in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> some years ago. He was originally of France, but fled into England, to enjoy that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> which his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> refused him. He wrote, 1. Histoire critique de la republique des lettres, from 1712 to 1717, in 15 vols 12mo. 2. Vitae Iloratii, Ovidii, et Plini junioris, 3 vols small 8vo, and printed abroad, though dedicated to Englishmen of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>: the first at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, 1708, to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Harvey; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>, 1708, to Sir <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTINIAN">Justinian</a> Isham; the third at Amsterdam, 1709, to the bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORCESTER">Worcester</a>. These lives are drawn up in a chronological order, very learnedly and very critically; and serve to illustrate the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, not only of those particular persons, but of the times also in which they lived. 3. Histoire de Pierre Bayle et des ses ouvrages; Amsterdam, 1716, in 12mo. This at least is supposed to be his, though at first it was given to M. la Monnoye. Masson, Antony, an eminent French engraver, who flourished towards the conclusion of the last century, and resided chiefly at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. It appears that he sometimes amused himself with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> portraits from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, some of which he also engraved. We have no account of the life of this extraordinary <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>; nor are we even informed from what <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> he learned the principles of engraving. He worked entirely with the graver, and handled that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> with astonishing facility. He seems to have had no kind of rule to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> him with respect to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> of the strokes; but twisted and twirled them about, without the least regard to the different forms he intended to express, making them entirely subservient to his own caprice. Yet the effect he has produced in this singular manner (Mr Strutt observes), is not only far superior to what one could have supposed, but is often very picturesque and beautiful. It was not in historical engraving that his greatest strength consisted. He could not draw the naked parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> so correctly as was necessary; but where the subject required the figures to be clothed, he succeeded in a wonderful manner. Among the most esteemed works by this admirable artist, may be reckoned the following: The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASSUMPTION">assumption</a> of the Virgin, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> upright plate from Rubens; a holy family, a middling-sized plate, lengthwise, from N. Mignard; Christ with the pilgrims at Emmaus, a large plate, lengthwise, from Titian, the original <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of which is in the cabinet of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of France. This admirable print is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> known by the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> cloth: for the cloth, with which the table is covered, is executed in a very singular style. Also the following portraits, among others: The Comte de <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARCOURT">Harcourt</a>, a large upright plate, reckoned a masterpiece in this class of subjects; Guillaume de Brissacier, secretary to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of France; a middling-sized upright plate: usually known in England by the name of the Gray-headed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">Man</a>, because the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> in this print is so finely executed. Massuah, a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, near the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABYSSINIA">Abyssinia</a>, about three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and half as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, one-third of which is occupied by houses, another by cisterns for receiving <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and one reserved for a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. It has an excellent harbour, with water sufficiently deep for ships of any size to the very edge of the island; and so well secured, that they may ride in safety, let the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> blow from what <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> with what <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of strength it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>. By the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> it was called Sebasticum Os, and was formerly a place of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> on account of its harbour, from whence a very extensive <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> was carried on, and possessed a share of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> trade in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> with other ports of the Red sea near the Indian ocean. A very considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of valuable goods was also brought thither from the tract of mountainous country behind it, which in all ages has been accounted very inhospitable, and almost inaccessible to strangers. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a> were <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>, elephants and buffaloes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIDES">hides</a>; but above all, slaves, who, on account of their personal qualifications, were more esteemed than those from any other quarter. Pearls of a considerable size, and of a fine water, are likewise found along the coast; from the abundance of all which valuable commodities, the great defect, a want of water, was forgot, and the inhabitants cheerfully submitted to such a great inconvenience. The island of Massuah fell under the power of the Turks in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Selim, soon after the conquest of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> Felix by Sinan Basha, and was for some time governed by an officer from Constantinople. From thence the conquest of Abyssinia was for some time attempted, but always without success. Hence it began to lose its value as a garrison for troops, as it had done in the commercial way after the discovery of the passage to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> of Good Hope. Being thus deprived of its importance in every respect, the Turks no longer thought it worth while to send a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASHAW">bashaw</a> thither as formerly, but conferred the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> upon the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of a tribe of Mahometans named Belowie, who inhabit the coasts of the Red sea under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Habab, in the latitude of about 14° <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>. On this officer they conferred the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Naybe; and on the removal of the bashaw, he remained in fact-master of the place, though, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> appearances, he pretended to hold it from the Ottoman Porte, by a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIRMAN">firman</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a> Signior for that purpose, and the payment of an annual tribute. The Turks had originally put into the town of Massuah a garrison of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JANIZARIES">Janizaries</a>; who, being left there on the withdrawing of the bashaw, and intermarrying with the natives, soon became entirely subjected to the naybe's influence. The latter finding himself at a great distance from his protectors the Turks, whose garrisons were everywhere falling into decay, and that in consequence of this he was entirely in the power of the emperor of Abyssinia, began to think of taking some method of securing himself on that side. Accordingly it was agreed that one half of the customs should be paid to the Abyssinian monarch; who in return was to allow him to enjoy his government un molested. Having thus secured the friendship of the emperor of Abyssinia, the naybe began gradually to withdraw the tribute he had been accustomed to pay to the bashaw of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JIDDA">Jidda</a>, to whose government Massuah had been assigned; and at last to pay as little regard to the government of Abyssinia; and in this state of independence he was when Mr Bruce arrived there in 1769 on his way to Abyssinia. This <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> found both the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> and his people extremely unhospitable and treacherous; so that he underwent a variety of dangers during his residence there, nor was it without great difficulty that he could get away from thence at last. The island of Massuah, as we have said, is entirely destitute of water; nor can it be supplied with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> of any kind but from the mountainous country of Abyssinia on the continent. It is consequently in the power of the emperor of that country, or of his officer the baharnagash, to starve Massuah and Arkeeko, by prohibiting the passage of any provisions from the Abyssinian side of the mountains. The houses of Massuah are generally constructed of long <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a> and bent grass, as is usual with other <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of Arabia: only about 20 are of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, and six or eight of these two stories <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> with which they are built have been drawn out of the sea; and in them the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> of that curious muscle found embodied in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> rock at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MAHON">Mahon</a> is frequently to be seen. These are called *dattoli da mare*, or sea dates; but our author never <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> any of the fish themselves, though he has no doubt that they may be met with in the rocky <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of Massuah, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they would take the trouble of breaking the rocks for them. All the necessaries of life are very dear in this place; and their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> is also very indifferent, owing to the distance from whence they must be brought, and the danger of carrying them through the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> of Samhar, as well as to the extortions of the naybe himself, who, under the name of *customs*, takes whatever <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the goods he thinks proper; so the profit left to the merchant is sometimes little or nothing. Though Massuah has now lost very much of its commercial importance, a considerable trade is still carried on from the place. From the Arabian side are imported blue cotton and other cloths; some of them from India being very fine. Other articles are Venetian beads, crystal, looking and drinking glasses, with coloh or crude <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTIMONY">antimony</a>. These three last articles come in great quantity from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a>, first in the coffee ships to Jidda, and then in small barks to the port of Massuah. Old <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> is also a valuable article of commerce. The Galla and all the various tribes to the westward of Gondar wear bracelets of this metal, which in some parts of that barbarous country is said to sell for its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of gold. Here is also a shell, an univalve of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of volutes, which sells at a high price, and passes for <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> among the various tribes of Galla. The Banians were once the principal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> of Massuah; but their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> is now reduced to six, who are silversmiths, and subsist by making ornaments for the women on the continent. They likewise <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSAY">essay</a> gold, but make a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> livelihood.

MASSUET

Pages 732-732

RENE, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> RENATUS,** a very learned Benedictine of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> of St Maur, was born at S. Owen de Macelles, in 1665. He is chiefly known for the new edition of St Irenaeus, which he published in 1710. He consulted several <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a>, which had never been examined for that purpose, and made new notes and learned prefaces. He died in 1716, after having written and published several other works. **MAST,** a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> round piece of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, elevated perpendicularly upon the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEEL">keel</a> of a ship, to which are attached the yards, the sails, and the rigging. A mast, with regard to its length, is either formed of one single piece, which is called a *pole-mast*, or composed of several pieces joined together, each of which retains the name of mast separately. The lowest of these is accordingly named the *lower mast*, fig. 1; the next in height is the *top-mast*, fig. 2, which is erected at the head of the former; and the highest is the *top-gallant-mast*, fig. 3, which is prolonged from the upper end of the top-mast. Thus the two last are no other than a continuation of the first upwards. The lower-mast is fixed in the ship by an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> described in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> **<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HULK">HULK</a>** and **SHEERS**: the foot, or heel of it rests in a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLOCK">block</a> of timber called the *step*, which is fixed upon the *elson*: and the top-mast is attached to the head of it by the *<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>* and the *trestle-trees*. The latter of these are two strong bars of timber, supported by two prominences, which are as shoulders on the opposite sides of the mast, a little under its upper end: athwart these bars are fixed the *<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>-trees*, upon which the frame of the top is supported. Between the lower mast head and the foremost of the cross-trees, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> space remains vacant, the sides of which are bounded by the two trestle-trees. Perpendicularly above this is the foremost hole in the cap, whose after hole is solidly fixed on the head of the lower-mast. The top-mast is erected by a tackle, whose effort is communicated from the head of the lower-mast to the foot of the top-mast; and the upper end of the latter is accordingly guided into and conveyed up through the holes between the trestle-trees and the cap, as above mentioned. The machinery by which it is elevated, or according to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> phrase, *swayed up*, is fixed in the following manner: the top rope, fig. 4, passing through a block, which is hooked on one side of the cap, and afterwards through a hole, furnished with a sheave or pulley, on the lower end of the top-mast, is again brought upwards on the other side of the mast, where it is at length fastened to an eye-bolt in the cap, which is always on the side opposite to the top-block. To the lower end of the top-rope is fixed the top-tackle, the effort of which being transmitted to the top-rope, and thence to the heel of the top-mast, necessarily lifts the latter upwards, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the lower-mast. When the top-mast is raised to its proper height, the lower end of it becomes firmly wedged in the square hole above described, between the trestle-trees. A <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> of wood or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> called the *fid*, is then thrust through a hole in the heel of it, across the trestle-trees, by which the whole <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of the top-mast is supported. In the same manner as the top-mast is retained at the head of the lower-mast, the top-gallant-mast is erected, and fixed at the head of the top-mast. Besides the parts already mentioned in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>, with respect to their length, the lower masts of the largest ships are composed of several pieces united into one body. As these are generally the most substantial parts of various trees, a mast, formed by this assemblage, is justly esteemed much stronger than one consisting of only a single <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a>, whose internal solidity may be very uncertain. The several pieces are formed and joined together, as represented in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECTION">section</a> of a lower-mast of this sort, fig. 5, where a is the shaft, or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> piece into which the rest are fixed, with their sides or faces <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to each other. The whole is secured by several strong hoops of iron, driven on the outside of the mast, where they remain at proper distances. The principal articles to be considered in equipping a ship with masts are, 1st, the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>; 2d, their situation in the vessel; and, 3d, their height above the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>.

MASTER

Pages 735-739

a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> given to several officers and persons of authority and command; particularly to the chiefs of the orders of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a>, &c.—Thus we say the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> master of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a>; of St Lazarus; of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">Golden</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEECE">Fleece</a>; of the Free Masons, &c. Master (Magister), was a title frequent among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>: they had their master of the people, magister populi, who was the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTATOR">dictator</a>. Master of the cavalry, magister equitum, who held the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> in an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> after the dictator. Under the later emperors there were also masters of the infantry, magistri pedi- tum. A master of the census, magister censae, who had nothing of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of a censor, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> subcensor, as the name seems to intimate; but was the same with the praepositus frumentariorum. Master of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITIA">Militia</a> (magister militiae), was an officer in the lower empire, created, as it is said, by Dioclesian, who had the inspection and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of all the forces, with power to punish, &c. somewhat like a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTABLE">constable</a> of France. At first there were two of these officers instituted, the one for the infantry, and the other for the cavalry; but the two were united into one under Constantine. Afterwards, as their power was increased, so was their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> also; and there was one appointed for the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, another for Thrace, another for the East, and another for Illyria. They were afterwards called comites, counts, and clarissimi. Their power was only a branch of that of the praefectus praetorii, who by that means became a civil officer. Master of Arms (magister armorum), was an officer or comptroller under the master of the militia. Master of the Offices (magister officiorum), had the superintendence of all the officers of the court; he was also called magister officii palatini, simply magister; and Master. His post magisteria.—This officer was the same in the western empire with the europalates in the eastern. **Master at Arms**, among us, is an officer appointed to teach the officers and crew of a ship of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of small arms; to confine and plant sentinels over the prisoners, and superintend whatever relates to them during their confinement. He is also to observe that the fire and lights are all extinguished as soon as the evening <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUN">gun</a> is fired, except those which are permitted by proper authority, or under the inspection of sentinels. It is likewise his duty to attend the gangway when any boats arrive aboard, and search them carefully, together with their rowers, that no spirituous liquors may be conveyed into the ship unless by permission of the commanding officers. In these several duties he is assisted by proper attendants, called his corporals, who also relieve the sentinels and one another at certain periods. **Master of Arts**, the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> taken up in foreign <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, but the second in ours; candidates not being admitted to it till they have studied in the university <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years. **Master-Attendant**, is an officer in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> dockyards, appointed to hasten and assist at the fitting out or dismantling, removing, or securing vessels of war, &c., at the port where he resides. He is particularly to observe, that his majesty’s ships are securely moored, and for this purpose he is expected frequently to review the moorings which are sunk in the harbour, and observe that they are kept in proper repair. It is also his duty to visit all the ships in ordinary, and see that they are frequently cleaned and kept in order; and to attend at the general musters in the dockyards, taking care that all the officers, artificers, and labourers, registered in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>-books, are present at their duty. **Master of the Ceremonies**, is an officer instituted by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> James I. for the more solemn and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> reception of ambassadors, and strangers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, whom he introduces into the presence.—The badge of this office is a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> chain and medal, having on one side an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMBLEM">emblem</a> of peace, with King James’s motto; and on the reverse the emblem of war, with *Dieu et mon droit*. He is always supposed to be a person of good <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>, and a master of languages, and has an appointment of 300l. a-year; he is constantly attending at court, and hath under him an assistant master, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a>, at 6s. 8d. a-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, who holds his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> during the king’s <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. There is also a third officer, called **marshal of the ceremonies**, with 100l. a-year, whose business is to receive and distribute the master’s orders, or the deputy’s, for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>; but without their order he can do nothing. This is the king’s gift. **Masters of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHANCERY">Chancery</a>** are usually chosen out of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BARRISTERS">barristers</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>; and sit in chancery, or at the rolls, as assistants to the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> and the master of the rolls. All these, so late as the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> doctors of the civil law.—To them are also committed interlocutory reports, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of bills in chancery, stating of accounts, taxing costs, &c., and sometimes, by way of reference, they are empowered to make a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FINAL">final</a> determination of causes. They have, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> out of mind, had the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to sit in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of lords, though they have neither writs nor patent to empower them; but they are received as assistants to the lord chancellor and master of the rolls. They had anciently the care of inspecting all writs of summons, which is now performed by the clerk of the petty bag. When any message is sent from the lords to the commons, it is carried by the masters of chancery. Before them also affidavits are made, and deeds and recognizances acknowledged. Besides these, who may be called **masters of chancery ordinary**, (being 12 in number, whereof the master of the rolls is reputed the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>), there are also masters of chancery extraordinary, appointed to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> in the several counties of England beyond 10 miles distance from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, by taking affidavits, recognizances, &c., for the ease of the suitors of the court. **Master of the Faculties**, an officer under the archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, who grants licenses and dispensations: he is mentioned in the statute 22 and 23 Car. II. See COURT OF FACULTIES. **Master Gunner**. See GUNNER. **Master of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">Horse</a>** is reckoned the third <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> officer of the court, and is an office of great honour and antiquity, and always (when not put in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>), filled by noblemen of the highest <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> and abilities. He has the management and disposal of all the king’s stables and bred horses. He has authority over the equerries and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAGES">pages</a>, coachmen, footmen, grooms, riders of the great horse, farriers, and smiths. He appoints all the other tradesmen who <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> for the king’s stables; and by his warrant to the avener, makes them give an oath to be true and faithful. In short, he is intrusted with all the lands and revenues appropriated for the king’s breed of horses, the expenses of the stable, and of the coaches, litters, &c. He alone has the privilege of making <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of any of the king’s horses, pages, footmen, &c.; and at any solemn cavalcade he rides next the king, and leads a horse of state. His salary is 1276l. 13s. 4d. per annum. There is also a master of the horse in the establishment of her majesty’s <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>, with a salary of 800l. a-year. **Master of the Household**, is an officer under the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> of the household, in the king’s gift; his business is to survey the accounts of the household.—He has 66l. 13s. 4d. a-year <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WAGES">wages</a>, and 433l. 6s. 6d. board wages. **Master of the Mint**, was anciently the title of him who is now called warden of the mint; whose office is to receive the silver and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BULLION">bullion</a> which comes to the mint to be coined, and to take care thereof. The office of master and worker is now distinct; and this officer is allowed for himself and three clerks 560l. a-year. **Master of the Ordnance**. See ORDNANCE. **Master of the Revels**, an officer with an appointment of 100l. a-year, whose business is to order all things relating to the performance of plays, masques, balls, &c., at court. Formerly he had also a jurisdiction of granting licenses to all who travel to act plays, puppet shows, or the like diversions; neither could any new play be acted at either of the two houses till it had passed his perusal and license; but these powers were afterwards much abridged, not to say annihilated, by a statute for regulating playhouses, till the licensing plays by the lord chamberlain was established. established. This officer has a yeoman with 46l. 11s. 8d. a-year. **Master of the Rolls**, a patent officer for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; who has the custody of the rolls and patents which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> the great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>, and of the records of the chancery. In the absence of the lord chancellor or keeper, he also sits as judge in the court of chancery; and is by Sir Edward <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COKE">Coke</a> called his assistant. At other times he hears causes in the rolls chapel, and makes orders and decrees. He is also the first of the masters of chancery, and has their assistance at the rolls; but all hearings before him are appealable to the lord chancellor. He has also his writ of summons to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, and sits next to the lord chief <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of England on the second woolpack. He has the keeping of the parliament rolls, and has the rolls-house for his habitation; as also the custody of all charters, patents, commissions, deeds and recognizances, which being made of rolls of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARCHMENT">parchment</a> gave rise to the name. Anciently he was called clerk of the rolls. The authority of the master of the rolls to hear and determine causes, and his general power in the court of chancery, were the subject of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> questions and disputes which were very warmly agitated; to quiet which it was declared by stat. 3 Geo. II. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 30. that all orders and decrees by him made, except such as by the course of the court were appropriated to the great seal alone, should be deemed to be valid; subject nevertheless to be discharged or altered by the lord chancellor, and so as they shall not be enrolled till the same are signed by his lordship. In his gift are the six clerks in chancery, the examiners, three clerks of the petty-bag, and the six clerks of the rolls chapel where the rolls are kept. See Rolls, Clerk, &c. The master of the rolls is always of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRIVY_COUNCIL">privy <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>; and his office is of great profit, though much short of what it has been. **Master of a Ship**, an officer to whom is committed the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of a merchant vessel, who commands it in chief, and is <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with the merchandises on abroad. In the Mediterranean the master is frequently called <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a>, and in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> voyages <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>. It is the proprietor of the vessel that appoints the master; and it is the master who provides the equipage, hires the pilots, sailors, &c. The master is obliged to keep a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a> of the seamen and officers, the terms of their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a>, the receipts and payments, and, in general, every thing relating to his commission. **Master of a Ship of War**, is an officer appointed by the commissioners of the navy, to take charge of navigating a ship from port to port under the direction of the captain. The management and disposition of the sails, the working of a ship into her station in the order of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, and the direction of her movements in the time of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, and in other circumstances of danger, are also more particularly under his inspection. It is likewise his duty to examine the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, and accordingly to admit none into the ship but such as are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>, sweet, and wholesome. He is moreover charged with the stowage; and for the performance of these services he is allowed several assistants who are properly termed mates and quartermasters. **Master of the Temple.** The founder of the order of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEMPLARS">templars</a>, and all his successors, were called magni templi magistri; and ever since the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of the order, the spiritual guide and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a> of the house is called by that name. See Temple and Templar. There were also several other officers under this denomination, as master of the wardrobe, with a salary of 200l. a-year; master of the harriers, with 200l. a-year; master of the staghounds, with 800l. a-year; master of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JEWEL">jewel</a>-office, &c. all now abolished. **Master and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SERVANT">Servant</a>,** a relation founded in convenience, whereby a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> is directed to call in the assistance of others, where his own skill and labour <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not be sufficient to answer the cares incumbent upon him. For the several sorts of servants, and how that character is created or destroyed, see the article Servant. In the present article, we shall consider, first, the effect of this relation with regard to the parties themselves; and, secondly, its effects with regard to others. 1. The manner in which this relation affects either the master or servant. And, first, by hiring and service for a year, or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPRENTICESHIP">apprenticeship</a> under indentures, a person gains a settlement in that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> wherein he last served 40 days. In the next place, persons serving seven years as apprentices to any trade have an exclusive <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to exercise that trade in any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of England. This law, with regard to the exclusive part of it, has by turns been looked upon as a hard law, or as a beneficial one, according to the prevailing humour of the times: which has occasioned a great variety of resolutions in the courts of law concerning it; and attempts have been frequently made for its repeal, though hitherto without success. At common law every man might use what trade he pleased; but this statute restrains that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to such as have served as apprentices: the adversaries to which provision say, that all restrictions (which tend to introduce monopolies) are pernicious to trade; the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a> for it allege, that unskillfulness in trades is equally detrimental to the public as monopolies. This reason indeed only extends to such trades, in the exercise whereof skill is required: but another of their arguments goes much farther; viz. that apprenticeships are useful to the commonwealth, by employing of youth, and learning them to be early industrious; but that no one would be induced to undergo a seven years servitude, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> others, though equally skilful, were allowed the same advantages without having undergone the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>: and in this there seems to be much reason. However, the resolutions of the courts have in general rather confined than extended the restriction. No trades are held to be within the statute, but such as were in being at the making of it: for trading in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> village, apprenticeships are not requisite, and following the trade seven years is sufficient without any hindring; for the statute only says, the person must serve as an apprentice, and does not require an actual apprenticeship to have existed. A master may by law correct his apprentice for negligence Master's diligence or other misbehaviour, so it be done with moderation: though, if the master or master's wife beats any other servant of full <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, it is good cause of departure. But if any servant, workman, or labourer, assaults his master or dame, he shall suffer one year's imprisonment, and other open corporal <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>, not extending to life or limb. By service all servants and labourers, except apprentices, become entitled to their wages; according to agreement, if menial servants; or according to the appointment of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a> or sessions, if labourers or servants in husbandry; for the statutes for regulation of wages extend to such servants only; it being impossible for any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> to be a judge of the employment of menial servants, or of course to assess their wages. 2. Let us now see how strangers may be affected by this relation of master and servant; or how a master may behave towards others on behalf of his servant, and what a servant may do on behalf of his master. And, first, the master may maintain, that is, abet and assist, his servant in any action at law against a stranger: whereas, in general, it is an offence against public justice to encourage suits and animosities, by helping to bear the expense of them, and is called in law maintenance. A master also may bring an action against any man for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> or maiming his servant: but in such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> he must assign, as a special reason for so doing, his own damage by the loss of his service; and this loss must be proved upon the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>. A master likewise may justify an assault in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of his servant, and a servant in defence of his master: the master, because he has an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> in his servant, not to be deprived of his service; the servant, because it is part of his duty, for which he receives his wages, to stand by and defend his master. Also if any person do hire or retain my servant, being in my service, for which the servant departeth from me and goeth to serve the other, I may have an action for damages against both the new master and the servant, or either of them; but if the new master did not know that he is my servant, no action lies; unless he afterwards refuse to restore him upon information and demand. The reason and foundation upon which all this doctrine is built, seem to be the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> that every man has in the service of his domestics; acquired by the contract of hiring, and purchased by giving them wages. As for those things which a servant may do on behalf of his master, they seem all to proceed upon this principle, that the master is answerable for the act of his servant, if done by his command, either expressly given or implied: nam qui facit per alium, facit per se. Therefore, if the servant commit a trespass by the command or encouragement of his master, the master shall be guilty of it: not that the servant is excused, for he is only to obey his master in matters that are honest and lawful. If an innkeeper's servants rob his guests, the master is bound to restitution; for as there is a confidence reposed in him, that he will take care to provide honest servants, his negligence is a kind of implied consent to the robbery; nam qui non prohibet, cum prohibere possit, jubet. So likewise if the drawer at a tavern sells a man bad wine, whereby his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> is injured, he may bring an action against the master; for although the master did not expressly order the servant to sell it to that person in particular, yet his permitting him to draw and sell it at all is implied a general command. In the same manner, whatever a servant is permitted to do in the usual course of his business, is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to a general command. If I pay <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> to a banker's servant, the banker is answerable for it: If I pay it to a clergyman's or a physician's servant, whose usual business it is not to receive money for his master, and he embezzles it, I must pay it over again. If a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a> lets a lease of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARM">farm</a>, without the owner's knowledge, the owner must stand to the bargain: for this is the steward's business. A wife, a friend, a relation, that use to transact business for a man, are quoad hoc his servants; and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> must answer for their conduct: for the law implies, that they act under a general command; and without such a doctrine as this no mutual intercourse between man and man could subsist with any tolerable convenience. If I usually <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> with a tradesman by myself, or constantly pay him ready money, I am not answerable for what my servant takes up upon trust; for here is no implied order to the tradesman to trust my servant: but if I usually send him upon trust, or sometimes on trust and sometimes with ready money, I am answerable for all he takes up; for the tradesman cannot possibly distinguish when he comes by my order and when upon his own authority. If a servant, lastly, by his negligence does any damage to a stranger, the master shall answer for his neglect: if a smith's servant lames a horse while he is shoeing him, an action lies against the master, and not against the servant. But in these <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> the damage must be done while he is actually employed in the master's service; otherwise the servant shall answer for his own misbehaviour. Upon this principle, by the common law, if a servant kept his master's fire negligently, so that his neighbour's house was burned <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> thereby, an action lay against the master; because this negligence happened in his service; otherwise, if the servant, going along the street with a torch, by negligence sets fire to a house; for there he is not in his master's immediate service, and must himself answer the damage personally. But now the common law is, in the former case, altered by statute 6 Ann. c. 3, which ordains, that no action shall be maintained against any in whose house or chamber any fire shall accidentally begin; for their own loss is sufficient punishment for their own or their servant's carelessness. But if such fire happens through negligence of any servant (whose loss is commonly very little), such servant shall forfeit 100l. to be distributed among the sufferers; and, in default of payment, shall be committed to some workhouse, and there kept to hard labour for 18 months. A master is, lastly, chargeable if any of his family layeth or casteth any thing out of his house into the street or common highway, to the damage of any individual, or the common nuisance of his majesty's <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIEGE">liege</a> people; for the master hath the superintendence of all his household. And this also agrees with the civil law; which holds, that the pater familias, in this and similar cases, ob alterius culpam tenetur, sive servi, sive liberi. We may observe, that in all the cases here put, the master may be frequently a loser by the trust reposed in in his servant, but never can be a gainer: he may frequently be answerable for his servant's misbehaviour, but never can shelter himself from punishment by laying the blame on his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGENT">agent</a>. The reason of this is still uniform and the same; that the wrong done by the servant is looked upon in law as the wrong of the master himself; and it is a standing maxim, that no man shall be allowed to make any advantage of his own wrong. **Master Load**, in mining, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used to express the larger vein of a metal, in places where there are several veins in the same mountain. Thus it happens, that there are seven, sometimes five, but more usually three veins or loads, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to each other, in the same mountain. Of these the middle vein is the largest, and is called the **master load**. **Master Wort**. See **Imperatoria, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>**. **Matification**, the action of chewing, or of agitating the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> parts of our food between the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the jaws, the tongue, and the lips, whereby it is broken into small pieces, impregnated with saliva, and so fitted for deglutition and a more easy digestion. See **Anatomy**, No. 104. **Mastic**, a kind of resin exuding from the lenticus tree; and brought from <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHIO">Chio</a>, in small yellowish transparent grains or tears of an agreeable smell, especially when heated or set on fire. See **<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PISTACIA">Pistacia</a>**. This resin is recommended in old coughs, dysenteries, hemoptoës, weakness of the stomach, and in general in all debilities and laxity of the fibres. Geoffroy directs an aqueous decoction of it to be used for these purposes: but <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> extracts little or nothing from this resin. Rectified spirit almost entirely dissolves it, and the solution is very warm and pungent. Mastic is to be chosen in drops, clear, well-scented, and brittle. We meet with a kind of cement sometimes kept in the shops under the name of mastic. It is composed of this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUM">gum</a>, and several other ingredients, and is formed into cakes for use. This is intended for the service of lapidaries, to fill up cracks in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, &c., but is by no means to be used for any medicinal purposes. **Masticot**, Massicot, or **<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">Yellow</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">Lead</a>**, is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CALX">calx</a> or ashes of lead, gently calcined, by which it is changed to yellow of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> or deeper tint, according to the degree of calcination. Masticot is sometimes used by painters, and it serves medicinally as a drier in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of ointments or plasters.
